How one Australian state's corruption inquiry shook a major political party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:59:00 UTC
07:59:00 KST

In brief
- NSW ICAC’s Operation Rosny examined alleged links between Liberal Party figures and developer Jean Nassif over donations and influence.
- The high-profile inquiry exposed damaging allegations ahead of the state election and renewed scrutiny of party fundraising.
Phone calls packed with colourful language, meetings at Nobu, Fijian hideouts, all-day drinks at London pubs, promises of millions of dollars.
It was enough to fill out 38 sitting days as the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) sliced and diced a Liberal Party corruption scandal.
At the heart of the probe, the ICAC examined alleged collusion between fugitive property developer Jean Nassif and party powerbrokers including two brothers of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet.
Jean-Claude Perrottet, Charles Perrottet and his wife Anita Perrottet endured days of grilling in the witness box.
In an inquiry dubbed Operation Rosny, the watchdog investigated alleged kickbacks involving Nassif and his company, Toplace, between 2020 and 2023.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Political donations from developers have been banned in NSW since 2009, yet the ICAC's widening net led to mentions of other powerful Liberals, including federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor.
Former ICAC assistant commissioner and retired Supreme Court judge Anthony Whealy rates Rosny one of the most impactful investigations in the body's almost 40-year history.
"You can already rank it as a very consequential inquiry," he told the Australian Associated Press (AAP) news agency.
"That is because it's taking quite a broad swipe into the machinations of party politics, the relationships between developers and politicians and where those intersections can go seriously wrong."
The inquiry began with a bang in July when counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer launched her opening statement with the adage, "Money in politics, as in other spheres of life, has the potential to corrupt."
It ushered in weeks of forensic accounting and questions over embarrassing text exchanges about surveillance of mayors, sham contracts and fake arrangements spanning Beirut, London and Cessnock.
Twenty witnesses were called, including the bombastic Nassif, who dialled in virtually from his bedroom in Beirut, wrapping up on Tuesday.
Their memories — from a demure Jean-Claude Perrottet and emotional senior Liberal MP Damien Tudehope to brash lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood and a befuddled Anita Perrottet — were put to the test on the stand.
In their responses, revelations were unearthed, and admissions recorded that have damaged the Liberal Party as it heads to a state election in March.
"In terms of the Academy Awards, some would be given out for splendid attempts to shy away from the truth without very much success," Whealy says.
"Overall, the spectacle we saw was rather amusing, but then it wasn't amusing at all; it was really quite serious."
He says a number of witnesses have tarnished their reputations by not being open and honest with the commission.
Central to the probe was how the Reformers, a conservative Christian sub-faction within the Liberal Party, allegedly circumvented donation caps by setting up schemes to hide the money trail.
Taylor, who is not under investigation by the corruption watchdog, has denied making pledges to the ultra-conservative faction.
"I want to shake down Angus for 10K," the now sacked head of Catholic Schools NSW, Dallas McInerney, wrote in a message aired at the inquiry on Tuesday.
The opposition leader said "no payment was made" when questioned about a $15,000 "injection" and monthly $3000 donations to the Reformers.
Former NSW premier Nick Greiner doesn't want to wade into how Operation Rosny will affect the party whose federal executive he served until March this year.
But he credits the creation of ICAC in 1989, during his tenure as premier, as one of his most important contributions to keeping politics accountable.
"ICAC is now close to 40 years old, so in a broad sense it's been successful — and the fact that it's been copied everywhere is a fair indication of that," he says.
Its public airing of dirty laundry, which played a role in Greiner's own political demise, later brought down popular Liberal premier Gladys Berejiklian and Labor heavyweight Eddie Obeid.
Yet it has not been immune from criticism.
Greiner says the commission's sometimes spectacular binge-watching sessions were not all necessary.
"There's room for more common sense and discretion," he insists.
But he reserves sterner ire for how long it often takes the ICAC to establish a probe and make corruption findings, and then whether it recommends prosecutions.
The watchdog aims to have a report tabled in parliament within 180 days of receiving final submissions but in practice it takes much longer.
"Clearly the time frames are absolutely absurd," Greiner says.
"It cannot take years and years when you've got all the powers that ICAC has ... My general impression is it's way too slow."
Rosny was sparked when state Liberal MP Ray Williams used parliamentary privilege in 2022 to claim powerbrokers in his party were engaged in branch-stacking and improper local council dealings.
Whealy says the watchdog's invaluable oversight role should reassure the public that no matter how corrupt political parties might appear, there is always a comeuppance.
"There are some rotten apples around and (the ICAC) reinforces that notion but it doesn't destroy trust altogether in the political system," he says.
"It's a comfort to the community ... that there's a vigilant oversight body doing its job properly."

Christa Pike unconscious after failed execution — attorneys
October 3, 2026
Christa Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator in a Nashville hospital in the hours after her bungled execution attempt in Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing on Friday.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, was audibly snoring after she was injected with two doses of lethal injection on Wednesday.
The court filing is the first account of what Pike went through in the hours after the botched execution attempt.
Pike's attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the lethal drug, called pentobarbital, to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
"Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike's body," they wrote in the court filing.
Instead of "remedying this failure," they prepared and administered a second dose of pentobarbital, her lawyers said.
Pike believed to be first person to survive administration of lethal drugs
There are now questions about what happens next and whether the state can attempt to execute Pike again given her medical state.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, a Republican, temporarily paused the state execution on Thursday, saying there would be a "comprehensive, third-party review" of the case.
Pike, who is 50 years old, was set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years.
She is believed to be the first person to survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs in the modern era of the death penalty, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Alamein Africa Forum opens in Egypt with 1,500 participants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:50:52 UTC
07:50:52 KST

Hussien Elkabany, Mohammad Sio
03 October 2026•Update: 03 October 2026
The Alamein Africa Forum opened on Friday in the northern Egyptian city of New Alamein, bringing together 1,500 officials, business leaders, investors and representatives of financial institutions from Africa.
The three-day forum includes three high-level conferences focused on economic development and continental integration, according to a statement.
Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said at the welcoming session of the inaugural forum that Africa is at an “important moment” that offers significant opportunities for economic transformation and overcoming development challenges.  
He said the continent has vast natural resources, a large market, one of the world’s youngest populations and major opportunities in manufacturing, energy, agriculture, technology, services and the digital economy.
Africa, however, faces challenges related to securing financing, developing infrastructure, high cost of capital, strengthening links between markets and removing barriers that continue to restrict intra-African trade and investment, he said.
Madbouly said the forum is taking place at a time of rapidly accelerating economic and technological changes globally, with supply chains and centers of production, trade and investment being reshaped.
“These transformations require everyone to look at Africa not only as a continent facing development challenges, but also as one that offers real opportunities and has the ability to become an active part of the new global economy,” he said.
The forum's agenda includes trade, food security, energy, infrastructure, financing, digital transformation, artificial intelligence and critical minerals.
Discussions are also aimed at turning development priorities into implementable projects and investments, while boosting intra-African trade.
Egyptian Planning Minister Ahmed Rostom said Africa’s economy is estimated at around $3.6 trillion.
Despite accounting for about one-fifth of the world’s population, he said, Africa’s share of global trade stands at only around 1.5%, while foreign direct investment flows remain limited compared with the continent’s potential.
New Alamein will host a summit on Saturday of the founding states of the African Union Development Agency, or AUDA-NEPAD, the official technical development body of the AU.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi will chair the meet, with broad participation by African leaders and officials, his office said.
The 8th Mid-Year Coordination Meeting of the African Union, meanwhile, is scheduled for Sunday.
The events are part of Egypt’s efforts to strengthen African economic integration, attract investment and mobilize financing for development projects across the continent.
The African Union approved holding the Alamein-Africa Forum every two years in New Alamein at its February 2026 summit.
The forum is co-organized by Egypt, the African Export-Import Bank, or Afreximbank and AUDA-NEPAD.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:49:09 UTC
07:49:09 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s latest rhetoric shows the Kremlin’s ambitions extend far beyond Donbas, as Moscow seeks control over all of Ukraine and the restoration of Soviet-era influence across Russia’s neighborhood.
Speaking remotely at the fifth annual Helsinki Security Forum on Friday, Zelensky cited Putin’s own rhetoric to challenge European skeptics and the idea of neutral mediation.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“So his goal is not the east of Ukraine. It is not Donbas. His aim is to occupy our entire state,” Zelensky said.
Pointing to remarks Putin made at Russia’s Valdai Forum a day earlier, the president argued that the Kremlin’s objectives extend far beyond eastern Ukraine.
“An independent Ukraine, a strong Ukraine, is a big problem for Putin,” Zelensky said.
He highlighted Putin’s assertion that Ukraine cannot exist independently and that other states are supposedly using Ukrainians to wage war against Russia.
“There were important signals yesterday,” he said. “I don’t think he said it accidentally: ‘Ukraine is not a state, and it is not an independent state.’”
Zelensky linked Putin’s latest rhetoric directly to the Russian leader’s long-running fixation on the collapse of the Soviet Union.
He recalled Putin’s infamous 2005 declaration that the fall of the Soviet Union was the greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the 20th century, contrasting that political grievance with the actual human tragedies of the era.
Poland Drafts ‘Pre-War’ Readiness Law to Speed Up Allied Troop Deployment
“He did not speak about the First World War as a tragedy. He did not recognize the Second World War as [the greatest tragedy]. He did not mention other wars,” Zelensky said.
“He could have mentioned Afghanistan and other things, or the Chornobyl disaster – a horrible disaster. He mentioned none of the things that were connected to human lives.”
Instead, Zelensky argued, Putin focused entirely on the loss of Soviet power.
“Therefore, his goal is obvious: to bring it all back, to bring the USSR back.”
“The fact that he was saying this again yesterday serves as yet another indication of what he wants – of his attitude toward peace, whether he wants the war to end and, even if he does, at what price.”
Zelensky argued that Moscow seeks to recreate not necessarily the Soviet Union in its former institutional form, but the sphere of influence the Kremlin once exercised across neighboring states.
“Undoubtedly, this is about bringing back the influence of the USSR – or Russia’s influence – but making it comparable with the influence the former USSR once had,” he said.
“He has total influence over Belarus. But I am sure that he wants all of that back.”
Warning for the Baltic states and Russia’s neighbors
Zelensky warned that the implications extend beyond Ukraine.
If Putin’s ambition is to restore Moscow’s former regional dominance, he argued, the Baltic states and other countries sharing borders with Russia would also face pressure.
“Therefore, these challenges would also concern the Baltic states and countries with which Russia shares borders,” Zelensky said.
He urged those in Europe who remain skeptical about the scale of Russia’s ambitions to look directly at Putin’s own words.
“And nobody stops him in these messages,” Zelensky said. “And that is weakness of the world.”
Asked about Ukraine’s biggest EU obstacle, Zelensky answers: ‘Putin’
Zelensky was also asked what he considers the greatest obstacle facing Ukraine as it pursues European Union membership while simultaneously fighting Russia’s full-scale war.
His answer was one word:
“Putin.”
“He really doesn’t want that to happen,” Zelensky said.
“And it’s not about his opinion, but what he’s doing for this not to happen – against the development of our state, against the geopolitical choice of the people.”
“When we are talking about what the EU means for Ukraine, it is a victory over Russia – even a victory over Putin,” he said.
“Because the EU is the choice of our people.”
Security guarantees, he added, are critical because they protect Ukraine’s ability to follow the geopolitical course chosen by its citizens.
“And therefore it is important to have security guarantees, because these guarantees protect the path that the people of Ukraine have chosen.”
The Helsinki Security Forum is being held in the Finnish capital from Oct. 2–4 under the theme “Layers of Security.” The fifth annual gathering brings together policymakers and experts to discuss European defense, technological sovereignty, transatlantic relations, energy security, nuclear deterrence and Russia’s role in European security.
‘You cannot build total defense’ by buying weapons
Zelensky also used the forum to lay out lessons Ukraine has learned after years of defending itself against Russia.
A country seeking genuine security must first develop strength from within, he said, beginning with its military.
“The main guarantee for Ukraine is the army of our state.”
But an experienced army alone is not sufficient, Zelensky argued.
He emphasized the importance of a technologically advanced force, a domestic military-technology sector and defense production capable of rapidly adapting to battlefield requirements.
Energy resilience is another critical component, he said, particularly decentralization of infrastructure vulnerable to attack.
Ukraine shifts from weapons recipient to security partner
The second layer of security, Zelensky said, is international cooperation.
He thanked the EU, European countries and the US for financial, technological and military assistance since the outbreak of the war.
Ukraine received weapons it previously lacked, including NATO-standard systems, he noted, but its relationship with partners is increasingly becoming a two-way exchange.
Ukraine is now sharing knowledge gained through years of high-intensity warfare.
Zelensky highlighted a recent drone cooperation agreement with Finland as an example.
“It’s not about just selling or buying drones or missiles,” he said.
“It’s about sharing your security experience throughout the duration of this agreement.”
Ukraine is willing to share that knowledge with countries that supported it, Zelensky said, pointing to the trust built between Kyiv and Helsinki.
The third layer is collective security, particularly NATO.
Zelensky congratulated Finland on securing guarantees through membership in both the European Union and NATO.
“These are allies in economy, allies in technology, and allies in security,” he said.
“This is of utmost importance, and this is what Ukraine is counting on.”

'Every fallen hero will be found' — Kyiv to speed up identification of fallen Ukrainians, Budanov says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:37:44 UTC
07:37:44 KST

'Every fallen hero will be found' — Kyiv to speed up identification of fallen Ukrainians, Budanov says
Ukraine is developing a plan to accelerate the process of identifying the bodies and remains of deceased Ukrainians repatriated from Russia, Presidential Office Head Kyrylo Budanov said on Oct. 2.
Repatriation operations are one of the few areas of continued humanitarian cooperation between Kyiv and Moscow. Ukraine regularly repatriates fallen soldiers and civilians from Russian territory, with return efforts increasing after peace talks resumed in early 2025.
Over 26,000 bodies and remains of Ukrainians have now been returned, according to Budanov. But of those tens of thousands, "a significant portion" remain unidentified.
"Why is the identification process so slow, and why are families forced to live in a state of uncertainty for months and years?" Budanov said.
The problem was discussed at an Oct. 2 meeting, chaired by Budanov, between the Families of Fallen Defenders of Ukraine and the Coordinating Council on the Protection of the Rights of War Veterans and Family Members. Participants developed an action plan to accelerate the process of identifying repatriated bodies.
An interagency organization will be established to review the work of forensic departments in various regions of Ukraine and facilitate additional international resources for DNA analysis, Budanov said. The government, in turn, will "adopt all necessary legal and regulatory decisions" in order to speed up identification procedures.
"I am convinced that bureaucratic delays and violations of regulations in the forensic examination system are unacceptable," Budanov said.
Budanov did not specify how many bodies remain unidentified.
read also
Bodies repatriated from Russia can present serious challenges to the forensic examiners and medical personnel tasked with identifying the deceased. These remains are often returned months or years after death, complicating autopsies. Sometimes, only a bone or a finger is returned.
The vast number of Ukrainian war dead has also put a strain on staff and facilities. Following a repatriation event, which occurs roughly once a month, already overwhelmed morgues may be flooded with hundreds of bodies.
The most recent repatriation operation was recorded on Sept. 17, with Ukraine returning the bodies of 252 Ukrainians from Russia.
While Ukraine regularly reports the number of repatriated bodies it receives from Russia, it does not publish data on the remains of Russian soldiers returned to Moscow.
Budanov said that accelerating the identification process was "a matter of state responsibility" for Ukraine.
"Families must receive information about the fate of their loved ones as soon as possible," he said. "Every fallen hero will be found and properly honored."

Google launches satellite carrying AI chips to test performance in space
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
06:34:16 CST
07:34:16 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Google launched a prototype satellite into orbit on Thursday to evaluate how its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) operate in space.
The prototype satellite, carrying four Google TPUs, was launched aboard SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission.
Google said its team has confirmed contact with the satellite and it is operating as expected.
Google said the launch is the first step of its Project Suncatcher, a long-term research project conducted in partnership with Planet Labs PBC to explore whether scalable machine learning infrastructure could eventually be hosted in space.
Over the coming weeks, Google will collect in-orbit data on how its TPUs handle the physical stress, radiation and thermal extremes of space. The company will use it to refine its future designs.
In low Earth orbit, satellites can access near-constant sunlight, generating up to eight times more solar power than on Earth, according to Google.
In the future, multiple satellite constellations could potentially be linked together, enabling them to handle larger AI workloads in orbit, the company said. ■

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Oct 3, 2026
G-7 countries agree on release of diesel and oil stocks
Group of Seven (G-7) countries agreed on Oct 2 to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves and pledged to refrain from energy export restrictions after pressure from US President Donald Trump.
The US led a pressure campaign on the European Union to draw down emergency diesel inventories, with the Trump administration warning that failure to act could lead to a US ban on diesel exports.
Such a ban could sharply reduce supplies to Europe, which has become increasingly reliant on US diesel, and potentially inflict high economic costs on the bloc.
Trump is seeking to cool surging fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections.
Governor vows to close legal loophole after Cornell gang rape
New York Governor Kathy Hochul vowed on Oct 2 to close a legal loophole allowing offenders to avoid rape charges if their victims were willingly intoxicated, as in the case of an alleged gang rape at Cornell University.
There has been an outcry in the United States over a decision by prosecutors not to file charges in the case at the Ivy League college two years ago, prompting the governor to appoint state Attorney-General Letitia James as a special prosecutor.
The investigation was reopened on Sept 28 after the alleged victim filed a civil lawsuit, fuelling allegations that the elite college failed to properly hold the men accountable.
UK murder suspect charged with preparing Farage attack
A 28-year-old man already charged with the murder of one politician, has been charged with preparing acts of terrorism, including against hard-right leader Nigel Farage, British police announced Oct 2.
Police said Joshua Kerry had been charged with one count of preparing acts of terrorism for actions allegedly carried out between May 31, 2024 and July 8, 2026.
In July, Kerry was charged with the murder of former MP and Reform UK spokesperson Ann Widdecombe, who was found dead in her home at the age of 78.
Death row execution survivor Christa Pike on ventilator
Convicted murderer Christa Pike is unconscious, intubated and receiving breathing assistance from a ventilator after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her, her attorneys said on Oct 2, providing the first detailed account of the extent of injuries she suffered during the lethal injection.
Hospital staff are working to save Pike’s life and clear the lethal drug pentobarbital from her system, her attorneys said, in an emergency court filing seeking an order requiring Tennessee’s Department of Correction to preserve evidence from the Sept 30 botched execution.
Pike remains in critical condition, her lawyers said, two days after the state administered two doses of pentobarbital but failed to kill her.
Djokovic survives China Open scare against wildcard Bu
Novak Djokovic survived a scare to beat world No. 104 Bu Yunchaokete 4-6, 7-6 (7/2), 6-2 in the second round of the China Open on Oct 2 in Beijing.
It was not an easy fight for the 39-year-old Serbian, a firm favourite in China who has never lost in Beijing in 31 matches.
Pumped-up home hope Bu, 24, threatened to spoil the party in the marathon two-hour 52-minute match, frustrating Djokovic by pushing him back and forth across the baseline.

Glaciers are disappearing before our very eyes – scientists warn of “catastrophic decades” ahead for the Alps
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Glaciers are disappearing before our very eyes – scientists warn of “catastrophic decades” ahead for the Alps
Kyiv • UNN
In the first 8 months of 2026, Swiss glaciers lost 6.5% of their mass. By the end of the century, they could almost disappear without emissions reductions.
Swiss glaciers have lost almost a fifth of their mass over the past five years and could practically disappear by the end of the century. LRT reports on the rapid changes in the Alps, citing a new report, writes UNN.
Details
In just the first eight months of 2026, Swiss glaciers lost 6.5% of their mass. Scientists estimate that more than 2 trillion liters of water melted away—more than four times the amount of fresh water consumed by Swiss households in a year.
Ice thickness decreased by 2.5–4 meters in some areas in this year alone. Researchers emphasize that the scale of the changes, which just a few years ago seemed like a future climate scenario, has become a reality.
"We are living in a new world"
This year, I would say, was catastrophic. There are no other words for it. But 2022 was already catastrophic, and I am convinced that even more catastrophic years await us in the coming decades
Scientists are recording not only the melting of glaciers but also their destruction from within. Cavities are forming in the ice mass, causing glaciers to break down faster and potentially collapse, posing a danger to surrounding areas.
At the current rate of developments, Switzerland's glaciers could almost completely disappear by the end of the 21st century. At the same time, according to researchers' estimates, stringent measures to reduce emissions and combat climate change could still preserve around 30–40% of the glaciers.

Pope calls on artists to unite against AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:21:41 UTC
07:21:41 KST

Pope calls on artists to unite against AI
Pope Leo XIV has called on artists to join forces to protect human creativity in the age of artificial intelligence.
Speaking to cultural figures at the Vatican on Friday, the pontiff said the Catholic Church hoped to renew its alliance with them to safeguard “what is human.”
“We live in the age of search engines that offer us thousands of instantaneous answers,” he said, contrasting them with art, which he described as a different kind of “search engine” that “does not proceed by indexing but by inquiry.”
The pontiff warned that one of the dangers facing modern culture was “homogenization,” arguing that art could provide a counterweight by challenging people rather than simply giving them what they expect.
”Your art … when it draws our gaze, when it compels us to pause before that which cannot be consumed, is a form of cultural and spiritual regeneration,” he said.
Turning directly to AI, the pope said it was becoming increasingly important to distinguish human art from machine-generated works.
“The Church needs you,” he said. “Algorithms lack the spark of the human, whereas authentic culture and art preserve this spark.”
The American-born pontiff has repeatedly raised concerns about AI since his election in May 2025, warning of its implications for human dignity, justice and labor, and calling for clear ethical limits on its use. His first encyclical, published earlier this year, focused on safeguarding humanity in the age of AI and argued that human judgment and responsibility must remain paramount.
He told reporters this week that he was not in “panic mode” over AI and could still “sleep at night,” but said warnings from experts about its potential dangers should be taken seriously.
Artists and other creative professionals have increasingly pushed back against generative AI, arguing that developers have trained models on copyrighted works without permission or compensation. They have also raised concerns that AI-generated images, music and writing could displace human creators, drive down the value of their work and make it increasingly difficult to distinguish original art from machine-generated imitations.
Concerns over AI have intensified following a series of incidents in which self-improving models circumvented safeguards and accessed external networks without authorization. In July, OpenAI models bypassed controls designed to isolate them from the internet and compromised parts of the company’s internal infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems. OpenAI later described the incident as a “warning shot” over the risks posed by increasingly capable systems.
Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger said last month that he believed there was a greater than 10% chance that AI “could kill all humans” within the next decade.
Others, however, have expressed more optimism, with US President Donald Trump dismissing concerns about an AI takeover as a “hoax.” On Tuesday, he signed a pact with executives from Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI and Nvidia aimed at introducing safeguards to ensure that “their technology behaves as intended.”

Abdel Ra'ouf Arnaout, Lina Altawell
03 October 2026•Update: 03 October 2026
Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir claimed that all three administrative areas of the occupied West Bank “belong to Israel,” contradicting arrangements established under the Oslo Accords between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization.
Under the 1995 Oslo II Accord, the West Bank was divided into Areas A, B and C. Area A is under full Palestinian control, Area B is under Palestinian civilian and Israeli security control. Area C, which accounts for around 60% of the territory, is under full Israeli control.
“There is no difference between Areas A, B and C. The entire land is ours. This is our country,” Ben-Gvir told Israel’s right-wing Channel 14 on Thursday.
Ben-Gvir also threatened to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, and push for the displacement of Palestinians from West Bank and the Gaza Strip if he becomes the defense minister.
He claimed that 60% of Palestinians want to “emigrate,” despite reports to the contrary. “I will dedicate time to this, and I will manage the process continuously. Every week, I will hold a discussion involving all relevant parties,” he said.
Asked how Israel could provide additional forces for West Bank and Gaza, Ben-Gvir said: “It is very simple: The more you allow soldiers to shoot and use force, the less manpower you need.”
“I will remove the restrictions on our soldiers. Today, the police rules of engagement are much more lenient than those of the army,” he added, pointing to police use of gunfire against Palestinians.
Although Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has spoken about Palestinian displacement on several occasions, Ben-Gvir claimed the premier “did not want it enough” and blamed him for failing to advance such a policy.
The remarks come amid campaigning for Israel’s Oct. 27 Knesset election, as opinion polls indicate declining support for the governing coalition and gains for the opposition.
Ben-Gvir recently intensified threats against Palestinians amid heightened competition among Israeli parties, while also making repeated visits to Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem and performing Talmudic rituals at the Western Wall.

Oman grounded Flydubai co-pilot over radical views before Israel-bound attack, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:19:08 UTC
07:19:08 KST

The Omani co-pilot accused of trying to crash a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv had previously been barred from flying in Oman over concerns about his radical ideological views, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday, raising new questions over how he was later hired by the Emirati airline and assigned to one of its most sensitive routes.
Citing people familiar with the matter, the Journal reported that Omani authorities had grounded the co-pilot because of concerns that he had become radicalized. Despite the ban, Flydubai later hired him and allowed him to operate flights between the United Arab Emirates and Israel.
It remains unclear whether Oman shared those concerns with other governments or airlines, according to the report, and the precise nature of the co-pilot’s alleged radicalization has not been disclosed.
The investigation is now being conducted in the United Arab Emirates after the suspect was transferred there from Saudi Arabia. A source familiar with the matter said he is expected to be questioned by the UAE’s State Security Department, which reports directly to President Mohammed bin Zayed.
Israel hopes the transfer will allow closer cooperation with Emirati investigators. Jerusalem’s precise role remains unclear, but Israeli officials expect to receive regular updates from Abu Dhabi whether Israel participates directly in the investigation or observes it from the sidelines. Emirati authorities, however, are expected to keep any Israeli role relatively low-profile.
A UAE spokesperson declined to discuss the suspect’s history in Oman, saying authorities did not want to prejudge the investigation or interfere with it. Separately, US media reported that the co-pilot was cooperating with investigators and had said he intended to crash the aircraft in Israel.
The incident occurred Wednesday aboard Flydubai Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, carrying more than 170 people. The co-pilot attacked Indian captain Smit Machchhar inside the cockpit and attempted to bring the aircraft down.
Despite being wounded, Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew members to intervene and overpower the co-pilot. Reserve pilots traveling aboard the aircraft then took control and landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
The flight plunged more than 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds during the incident, according to Flightradar24.
Israeli security officials currently believe the Omani co-pilot most likely acted alone, despite suggestions by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that investigators were examining whether another party had directed or assisted him.
Two Israeli security officials told Reuters that no evidence of Iranian involvement had been identified so far and that the initial assessment was that the attacker had acted independently, though the investigation remains ongoing.
Netanyahu said in a video Friday that investigators were still examining the possibility of outside involvement.
“As time passes, the picture is becoming clearer,” he said. “The heroes prevented a disaster on the scale of September 11. The attacker underwent Islamist radicalization. He came to crash the plane with its passengers. We are now investigating whether he was sent, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price.”
The new disclosure about the co-pilot’s previous grounding in Oman is also sharpening scrutiny over how he was cleared to serve aboard a flight to Israel.
Airlines are required to provide Israeli authorities with advance information about passengers and crew through Israel’s national passenger-data system. Crew records include identifying details, nationality and travel-document information and can be accessed, under legally defined authorities, by agencies including the Transportation Ministry, Shin Bet, Mossad and police.
Israeli officials initially examined whether the co-pilot may have held a second nationality that could explain how an Omani citizen was assigned to an Israel-bound flight. That possibility has since been ruled out, according to Israeli reports.
His identity and Omani nationality therefore appear to have been included in the crew information transmitted before the flight, leaving authorities to determine how he cleared the relevant screening mechanisms and which body, if any, should have flagged him before departure.
Several Israeli lawmakers, including Efrat Rayten, Ram Ben Barak, Chili Tropper and Oded Forer, have asked the chairman of the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, Boaz Bismuth, to convene an urgent hearing with the head of the Shin Bet over reports of earlier aviation-security warnings involving flights from the UAE.
They said the actions of passengers and crew had prevented a potentially catastrophic disaster and called for a review of aviation-security procedures and the decisions made before the flight.
Meanwhile, the first repatriation flight carrying Israelis stranded in Dubai landed in Israel on Friday after logistical disputes with Emirati authorities were resolved. Another Israir flight was expected to follow.
Flydubai has suspended all flights to Israel until further notice, extending its current suspension through October 15. Etihad Airways said it would operate two additional Abu Dhabi-Tel Aviv flights on Saturday to help return stranded passengers.

Details

The EU explained the purpose of Russia’s threats

Columbia University halts journalism admissions amid visa pressures

Trump administration's changing visa policies have caused a sharp drop in international applications to Columbia University and contributed to the university pausing admissions to one of its top journalism programmes, four people familiar with the matter said.
The journalism school announced on Thursday it was pausing admissions to its Master of Arts offering to conduct a "critical evaluation," without giving further details about the reasons.
Jelani Cobb, the journalism school's dean, said admissions to its Master of Arts programme would pause for one year while the school reworked a degree created in 2005, when the "journalism marketplace looked different."
"The dynamics of visas and all those other kinds of things were part of the consideration," Cobb told Reuters.
Additionally, the department needs time to think through changes to the programme, he added.
The connection between the admissions pause and US visa policies has not been previously reported, nor has the length of the admissions pause.
The drop in international applications shows how uncertainty over the Trump administration's visa policies is affecting one of the preeminent US journalism institutions, which also administers the profession's highest US honour, the Pulitzer Prize. The people did not disclose the exact size of the drop.
Last year, the Trump administration temporarily halted new student-visa appointments, then resumed them with expanded screening of applicants' online activity, saying the checks were needed to identify potential threats to US national security.
Reliance on international students
Columbia was among the universities targeted by his administration over pro-Palestinian campus protests in 2024.
Last year, it agreed to pay over $200 million to settle federal investigations and regain most of its suspended federal funding.
A new rule this year also sought to limit how long foreign students and journalists could stay in the US without seeking extensions, but a federal judge blocked it before it took effect last month, calling its rationale "exceptionally weak."
Visa difficulties and immigration policy uncertainty have deterred prospective Columbia journalism students from abroad, the four people said, who asked to remain anonymous while discussing the admissions process.
International students make up roughly half of the MA programme's enrollment, the people said.
Lower enrollment has prompted changes to the MA programme, including combining science and politics seminars in the 2024-25 academic year, two people familiar with the matter said.

Why Carney’s economic overhaul is clashing with Canada’s unions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:14:34 UTC
07:14:34 KST

Why Carney’s economic overhaul is clashing with Canada’s unions
Unions say proposed changes to Canada’s labour laws could weaken workers’ right to strike.
Toronto, Canada: As Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney races to make the country less dependent on the United States, attract billions in new investment and get major projects built faster, his economic overhaul is running into resistance from a group that says it wants many of the same things: organised labour.
The latest clash, over the right to strike, comes after months of mounting pressure on Ottawa from Washington, DC.
US President Donald Trump, since taking up a second term in office last year, has imposed steep tariffs on Canadian goods and weakened trade agreements – perilous moves as Canada has historically sent close to 80 percent of its exports to its southern neighbour. He has repeatedly piled on with the tariff threats to make Canada the 51st US state.
Canada has responded with retaliatory tariffs, while a broader movement to “Buy Canadian” has taken hold. The hockey-inspired “elbows up” — meaning a readiness to defend against an opponent — has become a national rallying cry.
With trade talks stalled since August, Carney has moved with urgency to shore up the economy and invite new investments. Last month, he announced Bill C-39, known as the Building Canada Strong Act, promising to bring “speed, certainty and predictability” to investors.
Along with measures to speed up approvals for major projects, the bill would also give Ottawa clearer powers to intervene in legal strikes and lockouts in federally regulated workplaces — a provision that has put Carney on a collision course with unions.
Canada’s largest unions have come together against the changes. The largest, the Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE), had its national executive go as far as voting to defy the bill’s proposed limits on the right to strike if it passes Parliament without amendments.
CUPE National President Mark Hancock credited Carney’s handling of Trump and said the union’s 800,000 members, who work everywhere from hospitals to schools to municipal services, want to be part of “Team Canada”.
“But at what cost?” he said in an interview with Al Jazeera.
A fight over the right to strike
The controversy centres on Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code, which already gives the Labour Minister broad powers to step into disputes if needed to maintain “industrial peace”, end work stoppages and force the two sides into a binding arbitration.
Beginning in 2024, Ottawa used the provision eight times to intervene in disputes involving airlines, Canada’s two largest railways, three major ports and Canada Post and again during the Air Canada dispute in 2025 when flight attendants went on strike.
Unions have challenged the use of that law in court and had hoped the proposed C-39 would restrict, if not repeal, that clause while businesses wanted it strengthened.
The bill does neither. Instead, it introduces two conditions that the government would have to fulfil first before turning to Section 107.
Before stepping in, the government would have to appoint a special mediator, wait for a public report and consider whether a work stoppage is hurting the “national interest”.
Once a strike or lockout is underway, the minister could direct the Canada Industrial Relations Board to get operations running again and impose a binding process, such as arbitration.
The government says those steps put clearer guardrails around a power that already exists, and Carney has said the bill “absolutely reinforces the right to strike”, according to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Unions have rejected this defence, pointing out that the meaning of “national interest” would ultimately be decided by the minister. They also argue that the prospect of government intervention is bound to change what happens at the bargaining table.
“The political lesson that employers will draw from it is simple,” Larry Savage, a professor of labour studies at Brock University, told Al Jazeera. “Hold out long enough, emphasise the economic damage, and then Ottawa will remove the union’s leverage for you.”
Disruption, Savage said, is precisely what gives a strike its power. “Every effective strike is disruptive,” he said.
Unions say they have already seen employers expect Ottawa to intervene.
Teamsters Canada alleges the Canadian National Railway (CN) and the Canadian Pacific Kansas City (CPKC) railroad companies were counting on Ottawa to step in when they locked out thousands of workers in 2024. Section 107 was invoked within hours.
“Companies have gotten used to the idea that if there is a labour dispute, they can just wait for the government to intervene,” Christopher Monette, Teamsters Canada’s director of public affairs, told Al Jazeera.
CUPE said it saw a similar dynamic at Air Canada in August 2025. Hancock said bargaining stalled after more than 10,000 Air Canada flight attendants voted overwhelmingly to strike because the airline was “expecting the government of Canada to step in and end the strike” — an account Air Canada disputed.
Less than 12 hours after workers walked out, Ottawa invoked Section 107. Air Canada CEO Michael Rousseau later told BNN Bloomberg the airline had expected the provision to be enforced and did not expect a strike.
“That was why they didn’t have a strategy on how to deal with the strike,” Hancock said.
Building Canada faster
The fight over the right to strike is also part of a much bigger argument taking shape around Carney’s economic agenda: Who gets a say in how Canada should change, and how quickly, in the name of making itself less vulnerable to the US?
Critics accuse Carney of using the economic threat from the US to push through changes that go well beyond responding to Trump’s trade war.
New Democratic Party leader Avi Lewis has accused him of using the “fear and disorientation around the trade war to push through a series of unpopular measures that he did not run on, has no mandate for and would never get away with under normal circumstances”.
That tension was on display in Toronto just a week before C-39 was introduced. Inside Canada’s first national investment summit, hundreds of global investors met with government officials and executives as Carney pitched a country ready to build.
Outside, hundreds of protesters marched through downtown towards the summit’s opening gala under the banner “The Many vs The Money”. The rally brought together labour, Indigenous, environmental and migrant-rights groups, with signs and speeches taking aim at everything from fossil fuel and military projects to AI and the use of public money to attract private investment.
For unions, C-39 has sharpened that debate, pitting the government’s promise of greater certainty for investors against workers’ ability to exert pressure through strikes.
But Jim Stanford, an economist and director of the Vancouver-based Centre for Future Work, questions how much of an economic threat strikes actually pose.
While work stoppages can be costly for individual companies, Stanford said, “It is very, very rare that you would see a noticeable and sustained impact on GDP, employment or incomes.”
Production and transportation are often delayed rather than permanently lost, he added, with businesses catching up once work resumes.
Stanford also questioned the idea that strikes are driving away investment, noting that more than 95 percent of collective bargaining ends without a work stoppage and saying there is “no empirical evidence whatsoever” that strikes have reduced investment.
“This is more of the government giving some icing on the cake for business. It’s not that this has to happen or else our investment won’t work,” he said.
There is also an economic cost to weakening the right to strike, Stanford argued. Workers need bargaining power to win higher wages, which can support consumer spending, productivity and worker retention.
“It may seem like labour peace is a good thing, but if it means that a worker’s share of the pie shrinks, then this actually hurts the economy.”
For labour leaders, that’s where Carney’s economic push goes too far.
“Canada’s unions are part of Team Canada. We have our elbows up,” Canadian Labour Congress President Bea Bruske said in a statement. “But we can’t have our elbows up against Trump with our hands tied at the bargaining table.”
Savage said the government’s “Team Canada” rhetoric risks treating workers’ bargaining power as a national liability.
“I don’t think Canada becomes stronger by telling workers in ports or railways or airlines that their rights have to be surrendered whenever employers invoke competitiveness or the national interest,” he said.

Ukraine lost another MiG-29 and its pilot on Thursday. It needs the jets to guard its cities, and almost none are left to replace them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:09:59 UTC
07:09:59 KST

- Ukraine has lost another Mikoyan MiG-29 fighter as well as its pilot
- The Ukrainian MiG fleet is slowly dwindling owing to combat losses and wear and tear
- The Ukrainian air force is acquiring new Western types to replace the MiGs and other ex-Soviet jets
Ukraine has lost another Mikoyan MiG-29 fighter and its pilot. The Thursday shoot-down extends the steady attrition of the Ukrainian air force MiG fleet, potentially drawing down the fleet to its pre-war strength.
That means Ukraine may have lost as many of the twin-engine, supersonic MiG-29s as it has received from its allies or restored from surplus stocks since February 2022.
It's an ominous milestone. The Soviet-vintage MiG-29 is no longer the Ukrainian air force's most important fighter. That honorific belongs to the air force's ex-European Lockheed Martin F-16s.
But the MiG-29 is still the air force's second most important fighter—and will remain so through 2027 as Ukraine awaits its first ex-Swedish Saab Gripens, due early next year, and French-made Dassault Rafales, due from 2028. Ukraine sorties MiG-29s for ground attack missions targeting Russian troop concentrations, strikes on Russian air defense systems, and air defense sorties over Ukrainian cities and ports.
The air force announced the loss of the MiG-29 and its pilot, Capt. Marat Mambetov, shortly after it occurred on Thursday. Mambetov, 25, was a flight commander in the 40th Tactical Aviation Brigade, known as the "Ghost of Kyiv" brigade. "Flying a MiG-29 fighter jet, [Mambetov] carried out missile and bomb strikes against Russian occupiers along one of the front-line directions," the air force stated. "During the mission, his aircraft was hit by an enemy missile. The pilot ejected, but tragically did not survive."
It's the 37th confirmed combat loss of a Ukrainian MiG-29 since Russia widened its war on Ukraine in February 2022, according to a tally by the Oryx open-source intelligence collective. Oryx has also registered damage to an additional three Ukrainian MiG-29s.
Thirty-seven write-offs, plus the likely grounding of several previously flyable MiG-29s owing to intensive wear and tear since 2022, may have reduced the Ukrainian air force's MiG-29 fleet to around three dozen active jets.
Fighter subtraction
The math is simple. The air force probably had between 30 and 35 MiG-29s in service when Russia attacked in February 2022. As losses cut into the fleet, Poland donated 14 surplus MiGs, Slovakia donated 10, and Azerbaijan reportedly donated three. Meanwhile, Ukrainian engineers tapped a global pipeline of spare parts to reactivate an estimated 20 grounded MiG-29s moldering in hangars at various Ukrainian airfields.
That's as many as 82 MiGs in and, as of Thursday, 37 out owing to Russian action—plus additional jets grounded due to airframe fatigue. The resulting active fleet should number around three dozen planes, around as many as Ukraine had on the eve of the wider war.
There aren't many more old MiGs that Ukraine could obtain to bolster the fleet. Poland still has as many as nine very tired airframes, but Kyiv and Warsaw have consistently failed to negotiate a transfer. There may yet be a few ex-Soviet MiG-29s, grounded for years or even decades, that Ukrainian engineers can restore to flightworthy status. Other than that, options are scarce.
Ukraine’s Swedish radar planes have flown inside Russian missile range for six months. None has been shot down.
The three dozen MiGs still in the inventory may have to last a little while alongside the few survivors of Ukraine's other Soviet-vintage warplanes, including Sukhoi Su-27s, Sukhoi Su-24s, and Sukhoi Su-25s.
Older Western types—the 80 or so F-16s European allies have pledged, about half delivered, as well as potentially a dozen or so ex-French Dassault Mirage 2000s—are steadily replacing the ex-Soviet jets. (So far, Ukraine has lost five F-16s and one Mirage.) Next year, the transformation of the Ukrainian air force from a largely Soviet-equipped force to a largely Western-equipped force will accelerate when the first of 32 Gripens arrive. Sixteen Rafales are to follow from 2028.
Barring catastrophic combat losses among Western types and assuming Ukraine can maintain and arm these new warplanes, by the end of 2027, the air force may not need its remaining MiGs and Sukhois, which by then could be very tired.
Russian missiles are steadily reducing the MiG and Sukhoi fleets, effectively forcing Ukraine to switch to new types.

Curious people tend to have more of the experiences linked to cognitive reserve, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:00:02 UTC
07:00:02 KST

A small study in the Netherlands found that people with a more curious personality tended to score higher on indicators of cognitive reserve, such as education and mentally stimulating leisure activities. However, neither curiosity nor these indicators of cognitive reserve were associated with performance on cognitive tests. The paper was published in Personality and Individual Differences.
As people age, many experience gradual cognitive decline. However, not everyone experiences this decline at the same pace or at the same age. While some individuals show marked cognitive decline relatively early, others maintain normal cognitive abilities into very advanced age. To help explain these differences, scientists developed the concept of cognitive reserve.
Cognitive reserve is the brain’s ability to maintain cognitive functioning despite aging, brain injury, or disease-related changes. It is thought to develop gradually across life through experiences that repeatedly engage the brain, such as education, intellectually demanding work, reading, learning new skills, and other mentally stimulating activities. In later life, greater cognitive reserve may help delay or reduce the cognitive effects of brain atrophy and other age-related changes, even though it does not necessarily prevent those physical changes from occurring.
One factor that may be of particular importance for building cognitive reserve is curiosity. Curious people are more likely to seek new information, explore unfamiliar experiences, and continue learning throughout adulthood. Activities encouraged by curiosity, such as reading books, learning languages, or exploring new places and ideas, may provide repeated cognitive stimulation over many years. Research has already linked the personality trait of openness to experience (a trait that also predisposes people to curious behaviors) to slower cognitive decline, suggesting that it may support resilience against it.
Study author Carolien Torenvliet and colleagues at Radboud University’s Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour explored the association between curiosity and various indicators of cognitive reserve. They also examined whether a curious personality (i.e., openness to experience and interest-based curiosity) was associated with cognitive abilities, and whether cognitive reserve might explain any such link.
Study participants were 106 adults recruited mainly from around Nijmegen in the Netherlands. They were between 40 and 85 years of age, with an average age of about 62, and 57% were women. People with current or past psychiatric or neurological disorders were excluded. Participants’ average estimated IQ was 118, well above the population average of 100.
Participants completed three questionnaires assessing curious personality: two measuring interest-based curiosity and one measuring openness to experience. They also completed the Dutch version of the Cognitive Reserve Index questionnaire, which estimates cognitive reserve from a person’s education, the complexity of their work, and their leisure activities. Finally, they completed three brief neuropsychological tests measuring memory, executive function, and processing speed.
Results showed that more curious individuals tended to score higher on indicators of cognitive reserve, specifically education and leisure activities, but not the complexity of their work. This association held after accounting for participants’ age. However, neither curiosity nor the cognitive reserve indicators were associated with performance on the cognitive tests.
“Although this study is limited by its cross-sectional design and relatively healthy sample, the results suggest that a curious personality may drive individual differences in cognitively stimulating experiences, but not cognitive abilities themselves,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of cognitive reserve. However, it should be noted that the design of the study does not allow any causal inferences to be drawn from the results. Curiosity may lead people to pursue more education and stimulating activities, but those experiences could also foster curiosity.
In addition, cognitive reserve was estimated from participants’ own reports of their past education, work, and activities rather than measured directly. Finally, participants were healthy and had higher-than-average estimated intelligence, and the sample was relatively small for a study of this type, which may have made it harder to detect links with cognitive performance.
The paper, “Curious people, resilient minds? The role of a curious personality in cognitive reserve and cognitive abilities,” was authored by Carolien Torenvliet, Dirk Bertens, Joukje M. Oosterman, and Iris Wiegand.

Israel could’ve ended Gaza war, freed captives sooner: Israel ex-negotiator
Retired General Nitzan Alon says more captives could have been returned alive and a deal was possible ‘maybe a year earlier’.
A former Israeli general who was the army’s point person for hostage negotiations at the beginning of the Gaza war says that a deal to return all Israeli captives could have been achieved “much earlier” than October 2025 but it was prolonged unnecessarily.
“I think that we could [have gotten to] this point much earlier, maybe a year earlier or so, without any major implication on the other strategic goals of the war,” Major General Nitzan Alon said on Friday. “We missed it, actually. The war was too long.”
He was speaking during a Washington Institute for Near East Policy webcast marking three years since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel preceding the genocidal war that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians.
Alon referred to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s claim that Israel must achieve “total victory” before signing a deal as “false”.
He called the October 2025 “ceasefire” a “strategic achievement” that has since curbed Hamas’s military power. But he said it could have been secured much sooner with “maybe some hostages that got killed or murdered during their captivity [coming] back home alive.”
Hamas and Israel carried out a prisoner exchange deal in October 2025 under a ceasefire agreement that saw the release of nearly 2,000 Palestinians imprisoned in Israeli jails and 20 Israeli captives held in the Gaza Strip.
“We could have – and we should have – shortened the war, brought all the hostages back, maybe a year earlier, and moved forward and maybe, you know, saved thousands of lives on both sides,” Alon told the panel discussion organised by the United States think-tank.
Alon had made similar comments in July, when he also criticised Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, saying Smotrich had opposed some of the agreements put forward at various stages and therefore could not take credit for the return of all the captives.
‘Not just a missed opportunity, it’s tragic’
Speaking to Al Jazeera on Friday, former Israeli diplomat Alan Pinkas said Netanyahu had stalled the end of the war.
“A deal was possible very soon after the Hamas attack in October 2023,” he said.
“It took almost two years before the hostages were returned, so it’s not just a missed opportunity, it’s tragic.”
Earlier this week, Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani said Israeli officials “rejected to entertain the idea” of a Hamas proposal to release all captives in exchange for a limited ceasefire soon after the attacks.
Al-Thani said Doha reached out to Israeli officials “on day one … Our message was very clear. They [Hamas leaders] are asking for a window of ceasefire to get the civilians out,” Sheikh Mohammed said in an interview with Piers Morgan. “And basically, they [the Israelis] were not interested to engage in the idea.”
Alon’s latest comments come less than a month before Israel’s October 27 legislative election, with polls showing the political battle remains at knife-edge.
Pinkas said Alon’s comments were unlikely to influence the outcome of the vote as polls already “reflect public anger” over the Netanyahu government’s failure to prevent the Hamas attacks.
A report by Israeli newspaper Haaretz claiming that United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan had warned Netanyahu about a possible attack also sparked outrage across Israel last month.
Netanyahu said he would sue the outlet over its report, which he described as “fabricated” and “false”.

Modi briefly spoke to him in Gujarati and said the country was eager to greet him after his recovery.Machchhar said work may keep him outside India but not away from its culture. He performs puja each morning and recites Hanuman Chalisa with his two-yearold son on his lap. Modi praised his family’s values and his parents’ composure

Roosters met with Rabbi Eli Schlanger days before Bondi attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:51:34 UTC
06:51:34 KST

Sydney Roosters met with Bondi victim Rabbi Eli Schlanger days before terrorist attack
On December 9, 2025, a group of Sydney Roosters players met with Rabbi Eli Schlanger and other leaders in the Eastern Suburbs Jewish community.
It was a Tuesday in the off-season for the rugby league club, months away from a ball being kicked or a tackle made.
They are a club on occasion tagged as well-oiled, representing the richest postcodes in Australia and lacking deep community ties.
But here were the Roosters, including Hugo Savala, Cody Ramsay and Billy Smith, eating kosher food, learning of Jewish customs at the Chabad of Bondi and walking along the beachfront and Bondi Pavilion.
Days later, metres away from that pavilion, the most devastating terror attack in Australian history occurred.
One of the 15 people killed in the mass shooting at Bondi Beach was Eli Schlanger.
Ten months on, and the Roosters are on the eve of a grand final against a Newcastle side almost universally cast as Sunday evening's community-minded underdog — but Easts' involvement and then support of their community during its darkest hour offers a glimpse into a story far more complex.
Rabbi Yehoram Ulman, Rabbi Shchlanger's father-in-law, was also on hand to meet with the players at the Chabad of Bondi Synagogue.
"They came to the synagogue, and they had a run-down of the different meanings and symbolisms," Rabbi Ulman told ABC Sport.
"And I remember they were very curious and very interested to understand everything that was going on."
Roosters CEO Joe Kelly, also present on the day, said the players took an immediate liking to Rabbi Schlanger — something that came as no surprise to Rabbi Ulman.
"Eli was a person who could connect with anybody," Rabbi Ulman said.
It was a "very happy occasion", according to co-CEO of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, Alex Ryvchin, who was also present.
"The Roosters came, they were incredibly charming, engaged, very articulate, very knowledgeable already about the Jewish community in this area," Mr Ryvchin told ABC Sport.
"And just really thirsting for more knowledge and understanding of Jewish customs and traditions … really left a very positive impression on everybody they met."
But the players also ended the day with a greater understanding of some of the darkness experienced by the community in the 12 months prior.
While walking down the promenade at Bondi Beach, Ryvchin explained to them how the uptick in antisemitic incidents had impacted the local community.
"They had a very high level of awareness already in terms of the fire bombings that were happening here routinely," Mr Ryvchin said.
"They were concerned about it, but at that point it was still probably abstract for them."
The events of December 14 were deeply impactful for the Roosters, as they were for the entire country.
And for those players who had broken bread with Rabbi Schlanger earlier that week, Joe Kelly said he could feel the enormity of their grief and shock.
"[It had] a real impact on those players, and on the wider club," Mr Kelly said.
"The fact that it was only five days, it was really close to home for us, and I know that that was felt more broadly across the community as well as across the country."
Rabbi Ulman, who spoke at Rabbi Schlanger's funeral at the very synagogue that had hosted the Roosters barely a week earlier, could understand their grief.
"When we see something that happens in the world that is wrong, we are affected by it, and we automatically feel how wrong this is," Rabbi Ulman said.
"But when it happens to somebody that we know, it affects us so much more because it's close to home.
"They saw Eli, they connected with him, and five days later, you know, what happened, happened."
Away on a training trip on the day of the attack, the Roosters players gathered to pay their respects on Bondi Beach as soon as they could, before hosting an open training session on the sand in January.
The Tricolours also had Summer, sister of the youngest victim, Matilda, toss the coin and deliver the ball ahead of the Roosters' first home game of the new year.
Mr Kelly said the organisation "got around the community as much as we possibly could" — while Rabbi Ulman said the reaction of the club, especially from those players he met at the synagogue just days before the attack, said a lot.
"That just shows you that they are good people. Because any good person would be deeply affected by what happened," he said.

The International Space Station may receive the Nobel Peace Prize; Ukrainians are also among the nominees – AP
Kyiv • UNN
The ISS, Mykola Kuleba, and Save Ukraine have been included among the potential nominees for the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. The laureate will be announced on October 9.
The International Space Station has emerged as one of the possible contenders for the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. Experts view the ISS as a unique example of international cooperation amid growing confrontation between states, Associated Press reports, writes UNN.
Details
The laureate will be announced on October 9 in Oslo. This year, the Norwegian Nobel Committee received 287 nominations, more than a quarter of them for organizations.
Håkon Gjørlöv, director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, included the ISS on his list of possible contenders. In his view, the project remains a rare symbol of global cooperation at a time when states are increasingly focusing on their own national interests.
A representative of Ukraine is among the possible contenders
Gjørlöv’s list also included Ukrainian human rights activist Mykola Kuleba and the organization Save Ukraine, which works to return and protect Ukrainian children.
Among the other possible contenders, the expert named U.S. President Donald Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms, and the Committee to Protect Journalists.
The International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court are also being named among the potential candidates.
At the same time, predictions regarding the Nobel Peace Prize remain speculative. The Nobel Committee does not publish the official list of nominees, so the laureate’s name will become known only on October 9.

====================================================================================================

America’s only major etrog grower is in survival mode amid global competition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:47:18 UTC
06:47:18 KST

On a small ranch in California’s Central Valley, below the foothills of the Sierra Nevada, an orchard grows an ancient and sacred fruit: the etrog, or citron.
At just 7 acres, the etrog grove at Lindcove Ranch in Exeter is a speck in Tulare County, where about 40% of California’s citrus crops are grown. But by another measure, the grove is giant: Lindcove Ranch is the only major commercial grower of kosher etrogs in the United States.
“This is my life — I really feel a calling to do this,” said Greg Kirkpatrick, 65, whose family has owned and operated Lindcove Ranch for more than 60 years.
The fruit looks like a strange lemon, with a knobby exterior, thick rind, and oblong shape. It exudes a sweet, fresh, lemony fragrance. It’s not a fruit you find in grocery stores. But for Jews, the etrog is crucial for fulfilling the commandments of Sukkot. During the holiday ritual, which includes a blessing, an etrog is held in the left hand while a bundle of palm, myrtle, and willow, called a lulav, is held in the right. Brought together, they are shaken in the four directions as well as upward and downward.
The Kirkpatrick family, who are not Jewish, began growing etrogs 46 years ago, when an Orthodox distributor from the East Coast reached out looking for a domestic grower. He wanted to avoid the costly import process of bringing in etrogs from any of the three major growing regions around the world: Israel, Italy, and Morocco.
Greg’s father, John, who was already a successful citrus farmer, decided to give the specialty crop a chance, and soon citrons became an important part of the ranch’s annual income. Its citron orchard is part of a larger specialty-citrus operation, which includes yuzu, finger limes, makrut limes and sour oranges on about 30 acres. The citron, however, has been the ranch’s top-earning crop.
The citron business is a difficult one that Kirkpatrick likens to the diamond industry, with single pieces of fruit selling for hundreds and sometimes thousands of dollars.
“It’s not so much how many we can grow. It’s the quality of the fruit,” he said.
An etrog must meet stringent requirements to be considered kosher for ritual use. It must be largely unblemished, retain its natural stem, called a pitom, and come from a documented lineage of trees that have never been grafted or crossed with another variety.
The requirements make growing them different from growing ordinary citrus, according to David Karp, a pomologist, citron expert and citrus researcher at UC Riverside.
“Many people have tried to grow citron in California,” Karp said, noting the financial allure of an etrog’s price tag. “But just because you can grow a lemon well doesn’t mean you can grow an etrog that’s right for Jewish ritual use. You can grow them, but you’ll end up selling them for $5 each, or feeding them to the cows.”
Karp said little in horticulture can compare to the scrutiny that etrogs undergo for physical appearance, all for the sake of religious ritual.
'Nothing remotely like this,' Karp says
“There’s nothing remotely like this,” Karp said. “In Japan and perhaps other countries in Asia … there’s a cultural predilection for perfect, extremely expensive fruit that would be given as a gift. But there’s nothing quite like the citron for Jewish ritual use.”
A typical crop may begin with 10,000 to 15,000 pieces of fruit, but perhaps only half will be suitable to bring to market, according to Kirkpatrick. His harvesters are trained to pick citrons carefully after inspecting them on the tree.
“Being able to judge on the tree if the fruit’s good enough to bring into the packing house or not is important, so we don’t have to spend hours wading through and washing and dealing with fruit that’s not going to make it to the market,” Kirkpatrick said.
Once picked, each fruit is placed in its own spot in a foam tray. The citrons do not touch one another through the picking or packing process because even minor bruising or scratches can reduce their value.
There are multiple grades of etrog, ranging from cheaper, wholesale stock sold in mail-order sets to exceptionally large and blemish-free fruit sought by elite buyers.
For decades, Kirkpatrick mostly sold his etrogs through a specialized marketing network to Orthodox Jewish customers on the East Coast, who seek citrons that are not only kosher but exceptional in size, shape and color.
“My partner sells to a very select group of Orthodox Jews in Lakewood, New Jersey, by appointment only,” Kirkpatrick said. “And if you don’t have appointment-grade fruit, they won’t come to buy your fruit.”
In 2023, the ranch received about 22 inches of rain and failed to get much of a crop. That same year, John died, leaving the grieving Kirkpatrick family to navigate the business without him. Then, in 2025, the ranch produced what Kirkpatrick thought was a successful crop, but his marketing partner was unable to sell enough of the fruit to recoup the $250,000 it cost to produce. Those years were the two worst for etrogs in the ranch’s history.
Distributors simply want more top-grade etrogs than the Kirkpatrick operation is able to supply.
Rabbi Menachem Sirota, a longtime etrog distributor based in Lakewood, New Jersey, who has purchased Lindcove Ranch citrons in the past, said he has opted to buy from larger growers who can supply more of the highest grade of the fruit.
“Personally, as a wholesaler, I need a very large quantity of nice ones,” Sirota said. “For a while I was getting them from California, but in recent years I was not so satisfied with the quality.”
As a result of the huge financial loss from this shift, one of the family’s homes on the ranch ended up in foreclosure earlier this year, Kirkpatrick said. With labor being one of the ranch’s biggest expenses, Kirkpatrick has had to cut back from eight full-time employees to five part-time workers.
One of the Lindcove Ranch etrogs that was delivered to Chochmat HaLev. (Aaron Levy-Wolins/J. Staff/Report For America)
The family is even thinking of selling the ranch.
But for now, Kirkpatrick is trying to save his business by becoming more of his own wholesaler.
“We’re reinventing ourselves,” he said.
The ranch is focused on selling bulk orders directly to congregations. Just before Sukkot began on Sept. 25, for example, Kirkpatrick delivered a shipment to Congregation Beth Emek in Pleasanton and Chochmat HaLev in Berkeley, California.
Etrogs grown without pesticides, chemicals
Kirkpatrick is also courting a new customer base with a pitch built on a genuine difference between his etrogs and those grown abroad. His etrogs are grown without pesticides or other chemical treatments, so after Sukkot they can be eaten or made into jam, candied peel or liqueur.
That sets them apart from etrogs grown overseas, according to Karp.
“Because a citron is of little worth unless it’s cosmetically perfect, they spray the heck out of these trees and fruit,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t advise eating etrogs grown outside the United States. “It wouldn’t be my first choice for a marmalade, let’s put it that way.”
Whatever Kirkpatrick’s hopes, the fate of Lindcove Ranch, and of California-grown etrogs, will depend on several factors, including the weather and how the next growing season plays out.
“I’m a farmer, I’m always optimistic,” he said. “You have to be in the farming business.”
This story was first reported by J. The Jewish News of Northern California and is reprinted with permission.
