J Street is trying to rescue Zionism in the battle over Israel’s future in the Democratic Party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
17:02:10 UTC
02:02:10 KST

The traditional pro-Israel wing of the Democratic Party, under the thumb of AIPAC and incapable of anything beyond the shallowest rhetorical empathy for Palestinians — if that — is clearly losing control. Its money and entrenched presence in Washington mean it will continue to be a problem for some time to come, but that wing has lost the support of an overwhelming majority of the Democratic base and cannot sustain its position of power.
The question is what comes next, and this week, there was a major development in how liberal pro-Israel forces are going to try to establish new guardrails around Israel policy.
J Street, the self-proclaimed “pro-Israel, pro-peace” lobbying group, announced the formation of a new advisory committee.
“The Jewish Communal Advisory Council will serve as strategic advisors for J Street staff and leaders in their engagement with American Jewish leadership and related institutions,” the group announced on its website.
The Council features some of the most prominent names in the recent history of so-called “mainstream” Jewish institutions. Some of them fit easily into J Street’s liberal-Zionist identity; others signal that J Street is expanding its leadership to the right, even as it has modified some of its rhetoric.
The more conservative names include two former chairs of the Conference of Presidents of Major Jewish Organizations; a former president of the American Jewish Committee; a former chair of the Jewish Agency for Israel; two former members of the House of Representatives, and more.
The significance of this move should not be underestimated.
A different future for Democrats
AIPAC has become a dirty word among Democrats. The Anti-Defamation League (ADL) is hemorrhaging credibility. Other major pro-Israel Democratic organizations are similarly seeing their impact diminish in the party.
This effect has largely been the work of Palestinian, Muslim, Arab, and anti-Zionist Jewish groups such as the Muslim Public Affairs Council, Americans for Justice in Palestine, the Arab American Institute, the U.S. Campaign for Palestinian Rights, and Jewish Voice for Peace.
Crucially, their work has been tremendously bolstered by lobbying and educational groups, most notably the Institute for Middle East Understanding, the Friends’ Committee on National Legislation, and, more recently, the Center for International Policy, among others.
J Street can certainly claim to be a part of this, but its efforts have been much more measured and mitigatory. For instance, they were eventually forced to grudgingly acknowledge the Gaza genocide, with J Street founder and President Jeremy Ben-Ami writing, “Until now, I have tried to deflect and defend when challenged to call this genocide. I have, however, been persuaded rationally by legal and scholarly arguments that international courts will one day find that Israel has broken the international genocide convention.”
But while J Street has also called for arms sales to Israel to be conditional and for the U.S.to stop selling some weapons to Israel, it remains dedicated, first and foremost, to preserving Israel’s existence as a Jewish state.
While many of the groups listed above do not specifically oppose that concept, in practice, it is at the very least not a priority, and is often seen as implicit in some of their policy stances.
This sets up a struggle over the direction of the Democratic Party, in which J Street starts with a distinct advantage.
Some of the leading figures in pushing for change among the Democrats are very comfortable in the J Street camp. An obvious example is Chris Van Hollen, senator from Maryland, who has been the most vocal proponent in the Senate for a different approach to U.S. policy in Palestine, and one of the clearest voices in defense of Palestinian humanity.
Van Hollen is an honored speaker at J Street conferences and a strong ally of the group. And while J Street doesn’t support Congressmembers like Rashida Tlaib, Ilhan Omar, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and other high-profile progressives, they also don’t act against them in most instances.
J Street gives Democrats a soft landing space where they can unload on Netanyahu, criticize Israeli settlements, and even call the assault on Gaza a genocide, all while affirming Israel’s ethno-state structure, which most supporters of Palestinian rights correctly call apartheid.
That soft landing spot is why pro-Israel figures who once wouldn’t have gone anywhere near J Street are now willing to join their board and engage in public advocacy—and, more importantly, lobbying—on behalf of the group. It’s either compromise or lose completely.
It’s a smart move. Unconditional support for Israel is dead among Democratic voters. Democrats, most Independents, and even a growing number of Republicans no longer want to be associated with Israel’s callous, racist, warmongering behavior, whether or not those people recognize how much that mirrors American activity in the world for much of the past century.
But will that extend to a true anti-apartheid policy? Democratic leadership and even most relatively progressive Democrats are not there and are not getting particularly close either. Advocates for full justice, like Rashida Tlaib or the sorely missed figures of Jamaal Bowman and Cori Bush, remain outliers in Democratic politics, even as so much has shifted.
J Street aims to keep it that way, as they must, especially in the face of several distinctly anti-Zionist voices either assured of a seat in Congress or with a very good chance of getting there in the next term.
J Street’s argument — which, unlike some Palestine solidarity activists, I believe is sincere — is that a secure, prosperous Jewish state requires a secure and prosperous Palestinian state next to it.
Yet, even if that is a sincere view, it still subordinates Palestinian rights to the maintenance of a Jewish ethno-state, albeit one — in J Street’s vision — with guardrails against the sort of extremism that Benjamin Netanyahu, Bezalel Smotrich, and Itamar Ben-Gvir represent.
And here is where J Street must be opposed.
The current Israeli election illustrates the problem with J Street’s approach as a whole. No Zionist party with significant support in Israel even endorses a two-state solution, let alone a solution that recognizes the reality that two states are no longer feasible, if it ever really was. (Note: The Israeli party, The Democrats, officially supports two states, but uses October 7 to say it is not “feasible” now.)
Whence the ‘liberal Zionists’?
Many Palestinians and supporters of Palestinian rights see liberal Zionists as little, if at all, different from hardcore, AIPAC zealots. I have never subscribed to that view, though I understand it. My own take has long been that those who fight for justice for Palestinians, who put the rights of all on an equal level, can find places where it is beneficial to work with liberal Zionists, and oppose them where that is necessary.
The moment for opposition is now.
One thing J Street and other liberal Zionist groups have in common with AIPAC is that they see their role, in part, as establishing boundaries around acceptable discourse. They simply draw the line in a different place.
Where AIPAC, ADL, and similar groups demonize all criticism of Israel and label it antisemitic, J Street and its fellows understand, correctly, that Israel will eventually lose U.S. support if it continues to act as it does. They know that the best way to secure Israel’s future as a Jewish state is to remove it from the role of maintaining a boot on the Palestinian neck.
Thus, they engage in criticism of Israel. They’re willing to see the U.S. and Europe exert measurable pressure on Israel, and for that pressure to bring about policy change. But it must always be, first and foremost, for the sake of preserving Israel as what they call a “Jewish state.”
Leaving aside that Israel is not and never was a Jewish state but a Zionist one, and that there is a huge difference between the two, that stance ultimately implies that Israeli interests remain paramount over Palestinian rights.
That is not going to change for J Street. Indeed, given the kind of people they have just recruited, it is more certain than ever that when Israel’s Jewish nature comes into conflict with any democratic aspirations regarding Palestinian rights, the Jewish nature will prevail.
I have often cited the late Israeli historian Ze’ev Sternhell, who highlighted this in his work. It was not, Sternhell argued, that there were no idealists among Zionist ideologues, both before and after the creation of the state of Israel. It was that whenever their ideals of socialism or egalitarianism clashed with their nationalism, nationalism always prevailed.
Democrats still don’t recognize Palestinian rights
The most powerful tool Palestinians have in the United States is the suffering they have endured under Israeli occupation. That includes the genocide in Gaza and the settler violence in the West Bank.
Yet while most Democratic voters have turned against Israel’s apartheid regime as a result of what they’ve seen in Gaza and the West Bank, many have not fully empathized with Palestinians as people rather than only as victims.
American views of Israelis have plummeted, but their view of Palestinians has remained largely steady. That will need to change, because it creates a playing field where pushing Israel to halt settlement expansion or to allow for some reconstruction in Gaza will be the ultimate goal rather than the full restoration of Palestinians’ legal, civil, human, and national rights.
J Street recently reacted to Israel barring two Jewish activists from claiming the Israeli citizenship that, according to Israeli law, is the birthright of any Jew in the world by saying: “A Jewish homeland must be one that welcomes all Jews. Including Jews who care about Palestinian rights and safety.”
It’s a noble sentiment. But it raises significant questions about who has the right to emigrate to that homeland on the basis of nationality. J Street defends the z’khut ha’shiva, the right to return for Jews, but opposes that right for Palestinians, and would never do so until there is a separate Palestinian state on a mere 22% of historic Palestine to which return would be limited.
J Street does not support a fully sovereign Palestinian state, either. To be sovereign, a state must have the ability to defend itself, and J Street explicitly calls for a “demilitarized Palestinian state” that would forever be helpless against an Israeli neighbor that has committed horrifying atrocities against the Palestinian people.
J Street would surely call it absurd to suggest that Palestinians require a demilitarized Israel. So, again, we see that they are not actually calling for equality.
Until now, and even going forward, there are places where it will be important that Palestine solidarity activists work with J Street and similar organizations. In restricting settlers, getting humanitarian aid to Palestinians who desperately need it, and reining in some of Israel’s worst excesses — as well as those of the AIPAC-ADL drive to label all criticism of Israel as antisemitism — there is much good that can be done together.
But we have, after a long and arduous struggle, arrived at a plac where we can change the face of a major political party as Americans. That face is, in fact, going to change, and in many ways it already has.
Earlier this week, the Senate defeated a bill that would have demanded a full accounting of Israel’s abuse of Palestinian-Americans in the West Bank and the killing of Palestinian children. It would have been a first step toward some significant sanctions. The bill failed on a mostly party-line vote, with the radical anti-Palestinian racist John Fetterman being the lone Democrat to vote with all Republicans (except Rand Paul) against the bill.
The list of Democrats who one could never imagine voting for such a bill is long, and it starts with Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. But they did, and whether that is because of a genuine change of heart (unlikely) or more cynical political calculations (almost certainly the case for most), it means there is real change.
J Street is determined that this change be one that still puts Israel first, but recognizes that it is not helpful for Israel if the United States simply indulges its and AIPAC’s every whim.
And J Street has a lot going for it. It is an organization that is well-liked and politically convenient for many in Congress. It allows for significant change, and many of its stances represent a real departure from American policy of at least the past 35 years.
More than that, J Street, especially with its new council, reaches into both the progressive Democratic world and the more corporate wing of the party.
But J Street, while certainly much closer to many Democratic voters than AIPAC, remains out of step with the forces in the party that have done the most to bring about this change. Those forces resist putting Israel’s interests first and have little sympathy for the state’s ethnocratic structure, whether they go as far as to call it apartheid or not.
The faces of Rashida Tlaib, Abdul El-Sayed, Ilhan Omar, Zohran Mamdani, Chris Rabb, Angie Nixon, and Darializa Avila Chevalier are the ones that Palestinians need to become the face of the party.
The first step was a huge one, showing the world the true face of Israeli apartheid, and Palestinians took that step.
But there is still work to do to get Americans to truly see the Palestinian people. There is a lot of racism — anti-Arab, anti-Muslim, anti-Palestinian, and simple xenophobia — to overcome. And that is the work of Americans, Palestinian and otherwise.
Democratic voters need to see Palestinian liberation, rather than mere opposition to Israel’s crimes, as their preferred policy. They’re not there yet. J Street would have the focus on stopping Israeli excesses. That’s important, but it is a step toward full Palestinian liberation, not as a way to protect Israel’s ethnocracy.
Democrats, I am convinced, can be brought around to support a policy that presses for justice, security, human rights, national rights, and equality for all, and that fully embraces the humanity of Palestinians. But that policy can only be promoted if the audience hasn’t already been convinced to support an ethnocracy, even one with a milder face.

Rheinmetall’s First Reconnaissance Satellite Launched into Orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:58:39 UTC
01:58:39 KST

On October 1, the first reconnaissance satellite developed by the German company Rheinmetall and the Italian company Argotec was successfully launched into orbit.
Rheinmetall reported that the satellite was launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.
With this launch, the German company, through its subsidiary Rheinmetall Italia S.p.A., is beginning the targeted development of an independent satellite constellation for military purposes. The focus is on airspace surveillance.
“The satellite program focuses on gathering intelligence rather than traditional mapping of ground targets,” Rheinmetall noted.
The satellite’s sensors detect signs of potential air threats on the ground, providing critical early warning and the data necessary for air defense.
The collected situational awareness data and imagery will be processed using artificial intelligence.
The system combines various capability layers — space-based surveillance, ground stations, and tactical networks — which will be managed through a command and control center.
“Together with Rheinmetall, we are transforming space technology into a valuable operational asset — scalable, networked, and ready to support complex defense scenarios,” said David Avino, CEO and founder of Argotec, regarding the satellite.
Building on this initial capability, the space component is planned to be gradually expanded into a more comprehensive satellite constellation.
The next satellite launch is already scheduled in the program’s roadmap for 2028.
Last year, Rheinmetall and satellite manufacturer ICEYE also signed a memorandum of understanding to establish a joint venture for satellite production.

Abu Shehadeh withdraws after Supreme Court signals disqualification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:58:32 UTC
01:58:32 KST

Sami Abu Shehadeh, chairman of Balad and the third-ranked candidate on the Joint List, withdrew from the October 27 election on Friday after a majority of the Supreme Court’s nine-justice panel appeared prepared to approve his disqualification.
The court nevertheless cleared the Joint List, Ra’am and MK Ofer Cassif to run, overturning the Central Elections Committee’s three other disqualification decisions. Abu Shehadeh was therefore the only target of the four proceedings ultimately removed from the ballot.
The four cases reached the court after the committee voted last week to bar Abu Shehadeh and Cassif and to exclude Ra’am and the Joint List, an alliance of Hadash, Ta’al and Balad.
The two lists appealed their disqualifications. The decisions against the two individual candidates automatically reached the Supreme Court because the committee cannot disqualify a candidate without its approval.
Otzma Yehudit and its chairman, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, brought the application against Abu Shehadeh. Likud sought the disqualification of Cassif and the Joint List, while three applications against Ra’am were submitted by Otzma Yehudit, Likud and the Choosing Life Forum.
At the heart of all four cases was Section 7A of Basic Law: The Knesset, which provides three grounds for barring a candidate or list: denying Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, inciting racism, or supporting an armed struggle by an enemy state or terrorist organization against Israel.
Supreme Court precedent reserves disqualification for extreme cases supported by clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence that the prohibited position is a central and sustained part of the candidate’s or list’s activity.
30 representatives voted to disqualify Abu Shehadeh
In Abu Shehadeh’s case, 30 committee representatives voted to disqualify him and four opposed the motion. Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg also took the unusual step of voting in favor, bringing the final tally to 31-4.
The Supreme Court convened on Thursday to consider all four cases. The panel comprised President Isaac Amit and Justices Dafna Barak-Erez, David Mintz, Yael Willner, Ofer Grosskopf, Alex Stein, Gila Canfy-Steinitz, Khaled Kabub and Yechiel Kasher.
Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara and State Attorney Amit Aisman urged the court to approve Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification solely on the ground of supporting armed struggle. Their position focused primarily on an article published on October 8, 2023, which Abu Shehadeh said he had written the previous day while the Hamas attack was still unfolding.
The article described the attack as an event of military, political and strategic significance and discussed its possible political “fruits.”
Adalah director-general Hassan Jabareen, representing Abu Shehadeh, argued that one article could not constitute the required critical mass when weighed against his decades of nonviolent political activity.
The Attorney-General’s representative responded that an exceptional case could be established through a single piece of “golden evidence,” even if the other material would not independently meet the threshold.
Barak-Erez asked how the court should reconcile what she described as an “objectively horrific article” with the far stronger evidentiary foundation ordinarily required to bar a candidate, and what weight should be given to Abu Shehadeh’s roughly 30-year public record.
Stein and Kasher focused on the article’s timing. They suggested that a text written spontaneously while the attack was taking place could reveal Abu Shehadeh’s genuine position more clearly than explanations offered years later.
Grosskopf asked whether the authorities had taken any action when the article appeared. The state said it had not been aware of it at the time. Canfy-Steinitz asked why Abu Shehadeh had not removed the article or issued a condemnation once the scale of the attack became clear.
Abu Shehadeh said the article was intended as a warning that Israel needed to reassess its policies and vulnerabilities, but acknowledged that one of its most disputed passages had failed to convey that meaning.
“The article contains things that were wrong,” he said. “I would not say them today, and I should not have written it that way.”
“I have never called for violence, and I never will,” he added. “I am against it. Those are not my tools.”
After the justices consulted during a break, Amit said they unanimously regarded Abu Shehadeh’s statements as “painful, outrageous and repugnant,” but disagreed on the legal result. He said an emerging majority appeared prepared to approve the disqualification.
All nine justices recommended withdrawal
All nine justices nevertheless joined a recommendation that Abu Shehadeh consider withdrawing, eliminating the need for a reasoned ruling in his case. Balad accepted the recommendation later that night.
Abu Shehadeh personally submitted an irrevocable resignation letter to the Central Elections Committee on Friday morning. Attorney Yifat Siminovsky, the committee’s legal adviser, certified his identity and that he was resigning of his own free will, and the committee notified the court that the letter had been received.
The resignation became effective once the court accepted the Joint List’s appeal and permitted the slate to run.
In his notice to the court, Jabareen wrote, “Nothing in this notice detracts from the arguments presented before the court or prejudices them.”
The court consequently dismissed the proceeding concerning Abu Shehadeh without deciding whether the evidence against him met the legal threshold for disqualification. The judgment noted that the justices disagreed but had been moving toward approving the committee’s decision; it did not reveal how they were divided.
Adalah, which represented all four candidates and lists, said the rulings confirmed that the applications against the Joint List, Ra’am and Cassif had relied on “old, irrelevant or distorted evidence” that fell short of the required “critical mass.”
The organization said Abu Shehadeh had been “unjustly pushed out of the elections in an unprecedented and dangerous move by the Supreme Court,” and accused those behind the applications of seeking to delegitimize Arab citizens and their parliamentary representatives.
Outcome sharpened concerns of disqualification cases
The outcome also sharpened concerns raised before the hearings that the campaign surrounding the disqualification cases could deter Arab voters even where the Supreme Court ultimately overturned the committee’s decisions.
In the other three cases, the court issued a summary judgment on Friday because of the statutory election timetable, saying its full reasons would be released separately.
The panel declined, by a 7-2 majority, to approve Cassif’s disqualification. Amit, Barak-Erez, Willner, Grosskopf, Canfy-Steinitz, Kabub and Kasher formed the majority, while Mintz and Stein dissented.
All nine justices expressed revulsion at some of Cassif’s statements and actions. The majority nevertheless found that the evidence did not satisfy the stringent tests established in previous rulings or form the critical mass required to prove either of the alleged grounds for disqualification.
Mintz and Stein concluded that Cassif’s conduct and statements directly and indirectly demonstrated support for armed struggle against Israel, particularly when considered alongside earlier remarks.
The court also unanimously accepted the Joint List’s appeal, finding that the material submitted to the committee did not meet the standards required to disqualify an entire slate.
It unanimously reached the same conclusion regarding Ra’am, which the committee had barred on all three statutory grounds.
Ben-Gvir claimed Abu Shehadeh’s withdrawal as a victory for his party, though he called it “regrettable” that a judgement had not ultimately been issued.

Riyad Albustanji, a Palestinian activist held in a high-security Italian prison on allegations of financing Hamas, praised fighters in Gaza, invoked martyrdom and called for divine punishment against Israel and its allies during a video call that later appeared on social media, Il Giornale reported Thursday. 
Albustanji, known among supporters as “the sheikh,” is detained in the high-security section of Bancali prison in Sassari, Sardinia. Italian prosecutors allege he belonged to a network that transferred money to Hamas through organizations formally operating as humanitarian charities. 
Il Giornale reported that Albustanji spoke with relatives in Arabic during the video call and delivered a religious sermon addressing the war in Gaza and the Palestinian struggle against Israel. People managing his social media accounts subsequently posted footage of the conversation, according to the newspaper, which said its publication may violate prison regulations. 
Albustanji appealed to God to grant victory to “Your fighters in Gaza, in Palestine” and to “guide their shots,” according to Il Giornale’s transcription. He also prayed for their wounded, martyrs, and prisoners and invoked martyrdom for himself and others “for Your cause.” 
Another passage called upon God to employ believers “for the liberation of Palestine and the Al-Aqsa Mosque.” Albustanji also sought divine punishment against “the criminal Zionists and all their allies” and called for fear and anguish among his enemies and the destruction of their possessions. 
Albustanji was arrested in 2025 over alleged financial support for Hamas
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Albustanji was arrested with Mohammad Hannoun and other suspects in December 2025 in a Genoa prosecutors’ investigation into alleged financial support for Hamas. 
ANSA reported September 18 that prosecutors had concluded their preliminary investigation into Albustanji, Hannoun and four other suspects. Albustanji, Hannoun, Yaser Elasaly and Raed Dawoud remained in high-security detention at that time. 
Prosecutors allege that charitable organizations collecting donations ostensibly for Palestinian civilians transferred funds benefiting Hamas. The defendants are presumed innocent unless convicted.

When journalism fails, democracy fails - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:58:05 UTC
01:58:05 KST

Imagine a family gathered outside an emergency room, anxiously awaiting news of a loved one undergoing lifesaving surgery. Will he survive? Was the operation successful? What decisions might still be required?
The surgeon emerges, only to discover that the entire family is drunk. In an attempt to manage their anxiety, they have shared a bottle of hard liquor. He approaches the eldest family member, seeking authorization for an urgent medical decision, but quickly realizes that nobody is capable of exercising sound judgment.
The patient is fighting for his life. Those entrusted with helping determine his future have incapacitated themselves.
Now imagine that the patient is Israel.
A country confronting extraordinary security, diplomatic, economic, and societal challenges requires an electorate capable of exercising critical judgment. But what happens when the very institutions responsible for informing that electorate increasingly substitute competing narratives for verified information?
What happens when we no longer know what to believe?
An epidemic without a vaccine
During COVID-19, Israel confronted an identifiable threat: a virus. People responded differently. Some vaccinated, others isolated, while many adopted combinations of preventive measures.
Today, we face another contagion: the erosion of our collective capacity for critical thinking.
Its symptoms include ideological tribalism, confirmation bias, selective reporting, sensationalism, and the increasingly blurred distinction between journalism and advocacy.
Unlike COVID-19, however, there is no convenient inoculation. Nor can we simply isolate ourselves from the information environment without surrendering our ability to participate meaningfully in democratic life.
Or can we?
During a recent visit to my brother-in-law’s sukkah, I encountered an unexpected perspective.
He is an ultra-Orthodox rabbi living a modest life in the Tel Aviv area. He has no television, radio, smartphone, or meaningful connection to the daily news cycle. When I asked why, he explained that he had no desire to contaminate his life with the hatred, accusations, and incessant disparagement dominating public discourse.
But how, I asked, could he make an informed electoral choice? His response was striking: Why should he dirty himself merely for the privilege of selecting a voting slip and placing it in a ballot box, when I am being briefed by those who do not value truth?
Initially, I found his position troubling.
Then I asked myself an uncomfortable question: Having consumed countless hours of news, commentary, analysis, and competing revelations, do I actually know substantially more about what is truly happening than he does? I was not entirely certain.
He has chosen isolation. I have chosen immersion. Yet neither approach necessarily guarantees an informed understanding of reality.
That is a frightening proposition for a democracy.
When everything is true and false
Another encounter brought the problem into sharper focus.
Haim, a politically right-wing acquaintance from my neighborhood, who is originally from America, frequently approaches me after morning prayers with philosophical questions.
Recently, he asked whether the new allegations that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had received advance warnings concerning the October 7 Hamas attack were true.
My answer surprised him. “They are 100% true and 100% false.”
I was not suggesting that mutually contradictory factual claims can both be correct. Rather, I was describing the predicament of the ordinary Israeli citizen.
Depending on which television channel, commentator, or newspaper one follows, the same allegations can emerge as established truth, malicious fabrication, selective disclosure, or politically motivated manipulation.
What was actually communicated? To whom? When? What evidence exists? What was understood at the time, rather than reconstructed afterward?
These are legitimate journalistic questions. They deserve documented answers. Instead, audiences are frequently invited to select their preferred reality.
The same challenge arises in reporting on the Qatar-related investigations, Netanyahu’s corruption trial, and the Sde Teiman affair. Allegations, evidence, prosecutorial decisions, contested interpretations, and judicial findings are distinct categories.
Yet in the public arena, these distinctions too often disappear beneath dramatic headlines and ideological certainty.
An accusation is not a conviction. Equally, the absence of a conviction does not establish that an allegation was fabricated.
Responsible journalism must preserve both principles.
Our media’s lack of a mutually assured destruction doctrine
Consider the increasingly adversarial relationship between Channels 12 and 14.
Both reach substantial Israeli audiences. Both have become associated with sharply contrasting political perspectives. Their competition reflects, and arguably reinforces, the divisions running through Israeli society.
The analogy that comes to mind is the Cold War nuclear arms race. The United States and Soviet Union eventually understood the logic of mutually assured destruction: Escalation without restraint could destroy both adversaries.
Israel’s competing media camps appear to lack an equivalent appreciation of the consequences of escalating their information warfare. Each side can become increasingly preoccupied with exposing the other’s failures, defending its preferred political actors and reinforcing the convictions of its audience.
But when the public concludes that journalism itself has become another political battlefield, the resulting damage extends far beyond either channel. The casualty is public capability for critical thinking.
This is not an argument for political neutrality in commentary. Journalists are entitled to opinions. Media organizations are entitled to editorial perspectives. But reporting and advocacy are different professional disciplines.
A journalist’s responsibility is not to establish that his preferred political narrative is correct. It is to establish what the available evidence supports, including when that evidence contradicts his own convictions.
The professional standards problem
The Worlds of Journalism Study, 2021-2023, whose Israeli research was conducted before October 7, 2023, provides an important insight.
Among the Israeli journalists surveyed, 57.7% supported applying professional ethical standards regardless of circumstances, while 60.7% considered departures from professional standards potentially justifiable in extraordinary situations.
These findings do not establish that Israeli journalists are less ethical than their Western counterparts. They do, however, illustrate the importance of examining how professional principles are interpreted and implemented.
Israel already possesses a comprehensive Press Council ethics code. It requires verification, accuracy, transparent identification of opinion, and appropriate correction of substantive errors. Publication urgency does not excuse inadequate verification.
Our problem, therefore, is not simply the absence of professional guidelines. It is whether those guidelines carry sufficient enforcement when political passions, competitive pressures, and commercial incentives collide.
Who guards the guardians?
Journalism is often described as democracy’s watchdog. But who holds the watchdog accountable when it confuses suspicion with proof, interpretation with fact, or a political objective with the public interest?
Israel needs a renewed commitment to independent professional accountability.
Major news organizations should publish transparent corrections, distinguish reporting from commentary, disclose relevant conflicts of interest, and explain their standards for relying on anonymous sources.
Independent professional audits should examine factual accuracy, source verification, correction practices, and editorial transparency across the political spectrum. Not to silence journalists. Quite the opposite.
A free press is indispensable. But press freedom without professional responsibility cannot adequately serve an informed electorate. Nor should government become the arbiter of acceptable journalism. That would replace one danger with another.
The responsibility must begin within the profession itself.
The real inoculation
I initially considered calling our contagion the woke virus. But that label risks reducing a much broader societal problem to yet another ideological argument.
The deeper infection is intellectual tribalism: the willingness to accept almost anything that validates our existing beliefs while dismissing almost anything that challenges them.
It afflicts the Right and the Left alike.
Its antidote is not censorship, withdrawal, or enforced consensus. It is the restoration of critical thinking, professional journalism, and the discipline to distinguish what we know from what we believe.
Israel cannot afford an electorate permanently intoxicated by competing versions of reality. We are confronting decisions affecting our security, democratic institutions, international standing, and national future.
This coming October 27, the surgeon will be standing outside the emergency room. The decisions cannot wait. The question is whether we are sufficiently informed and sober enough to make them.
The writer is a global strategist and a strategic adviser at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs. Follow him on X: @jeffkahn2020

Taiwanese boxer Lin Yu-ting won gold in the women’s 60-kilogram category at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Friday, two years after a gender eligibility controversy at the Paris Olympics.
Lin defeated China’s Yang Chengyu by a unanimous 5-0 decision at Nishio Gymnasium to claim her second Asian Games gold medal.
Lin and Algeria’s Imane Khelif both won gold medals at the 2024 Paris Olympics amid a dispute over their eligibility to compete in the women’s category.
Both boxers had been disqualified from the 2023 world championships by the International Boxing Association, which said they had failed eligibility tests.
The International Olympic Committee, which oversaw boxing at the Paris Games after stripping the association of its recognition, allowed Lin and Khelif to compete.
The committee criticized their 2023 disqualifications as “sudden and arbitrary.”
World Boxing, the governing body for Olympic-level boxing, introduced a new eligibility policy in 2025 requiring mandatory sex testing for athletes competing in its female category.
Lin was cleared to compete in the female category earlier this year following an appeal by the Chinese Taipei Boxing Association under World Boxing’s eligibility policy.

The Telegraph identifies Russian biker Oleg Levushkin as suspected organizer of Leipzig airport sabotage. It links the operation to a GRU unit whose officers are accused in the Skripal poisoning.
The British newspaper The Telegraph has identified the suspected organizer of a sabotage attack at Leipzig Airport. German media had previously reported on the suspect, citing German law enforcement authorities, without naming him.
The suspect is Russian national Oleg Levushkin, according to The Telegraph. He enjoys motorcycle trips, including through Europe. Agentstvo found photos of these trips on his social media accounts. Leaked data examined by Agentstvo indicates that he lived in Riga until at least 2018, moved to Russia’s Pskov region in 2019, and later moved to Sevastopol. The SPARK business database lists him as a co-owner of two companies in Pskov and another in Sevastopol.
Media reports say Levushkin has known Denis Smolyaninov for many years. Smolyaninov is a colonel in Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, and heads a department in its Special Activities Service. His department specializes in sabotage operations abroad. According to Süddeutsche Zeitung, cited by The Telegraph, the two met in 2007, when Smolyaninov mediated a financial dispute involving Levushkin’s business.
The Telegraph also identified the man who carried out the sabotage attack at Leipzig Airport as Andrei Karshakov. German media had previously reported only that he was a Belarusian citizen.
The Telegraph reported that the Leipzig sabotage attack, which Levushkin is suspected of organizing, is linked to military unit 29155. The unit is known for two former members, GRU officers Anatoly Chepiga and Alexander Mishkin, who are accused of poisoning Sergei and Yulia Skripal and carrying out sabotage in the Czech Republic. They used the names Ruslan Boshirov and Alexander Petrov, respectively. The unit has been part of the Special Activities Service since 2023.

He dreamed of a Kawasaki: boy killed in Russian strike on Kyiv Oblast laid to rest to the roar of bikes

The boy loved motorcycles dearly and dreamed of owning his own Kawasaki. That is why his family invited motorcyclists to the funeral to sound their horns for the teenager.
Source: Radio Liberty
Details: During the Russian attack, a missile hit the Honcharov family's house. The family had previously evacuated from the village of Yastrubshchyna in the Esman hromada A hromada is an administrative unit designating a village, several villages, or a town and their adjacent territories of Sumy Oblast due to constant attacks.
The boy's parents, Pavlo and Olena, as well as his younger sister Liza, were pulled from the rubble. Illia could not be saved.
The decision was made to bury the teenager in Vyshhorod. On the eve of the funeral, his relatives wrote on social media that Illia adored motorcycles.
Quote from one of his relatives on Instagram: "He simply lived for them. He started with a moped, then had a Viper, then a Shineray. He took great care of every single bike he had, looked after them, treasured them and constantly dreamed of a Kawasaki.
We want to say goodbye to Illiusha in a way that would be close to his heart, so we kindly ask everyone who has a motorcycle to join. When we lower him into the grave, we want motorcycles nearby – revving, idling and sounding their horns."
Several hundred people came to the church in Vyshhorod on 2 October for the memorial. Dozens of motorcyclists also arrived to pay their final respects to the teenager. They accompanied the funeral cortege to the burial site.
Background: In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, farewells were held for 15-year-old Ruslan Boreshchuk, who was killed as a result of a strike on a logistics company facility on 28 September.

The Guardian view on the Conservative conference: a party still searching for a purpose | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:51:19 UTC
01:51:19 KST

The Conservative party is far from the margin of British politics, but it has yet to recover the relevance to which it feels historically entitled. The Tories are flattered by their status as the official opposition in parliament. In the wider country, Reform UK has set the agenda on the right, overtaking Kemi Badenoch’s party in opinion polls and poaching MPs from her benches.
But Nigel Farage’s progress has stalled. Scrutiny of Reform’s finances has made its leader look shifty. Competition from Restore Britain, an extreme nationalist party, has denied Mr Farage the luxury of taking far-right votes for granted. Pandering to a hardcore audience makes it difficult for Reform to affect the moderation required to capture more Tory and Labour votes.
This creates an opportunity for Conservatives to reassert themselves as the mainstream opposition to Labour. Many Tories believe the available space has grown since Andy Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister.
Mr Burnham has a bolder agenda than his predecessor, and he communicates it well – qualities that have been rewarded with a poll-ratings recovery. It is also a programme with unapologetic left-liberal ambition – universal social care, free at the point of use; opening the door to public ownership of utilities; dissolving red lines in relations with the EU; electoral reform. Under new leadership, the party has risen out of the defensive crouch from which it fought the election, fearful of offending Conservative sensibilities. Conservatives are duly offended. The vision that Mr Burnham outlined at his party conference last week was a repudiation of Margaret Thatcher’s legacy, and there is no greater heresy in Tory doctrine.
Mrs Badenoch will not struggle to articulate a rebuttal at her party’s conference in Birmingham over the next few days. She is a devotee of the Conservative cult of the Iron Lady, committed to low taxes and a smaller state as axioms of political virtue. She believes there are voters who share that conviction, who will be repelled by Labour, and who are deeply wary of Mr Farage. This is the electoral audience she is targeting.
It isn’t an irrational strategy, but nor is it a well-developed one. Mrs Badenoch likes to debate the opponent she wants rather than the one she has. She accuses Mr Burnham of taking Britain back to the 1970s, without engaging with his analysis of what went wrong in the 1980s or considering that her own nostalgic ideology might need revision with reference to subsequent decades.
Her approach to Reform is even more blinkered. The Tories want voters to take a dim view of Mr Farage’s candidacy to be prime minister, but they are selective in their criticism. Mrs Badenoch joins the fray over opaque donations, but has less to say about Reform’s toxic rhetoric around immigration, largely because Conservative policy fits the Faragist mould. The traffic in defections has slowed, but the boundary between the two parties is porous.
To make her party competitive in British politics, Mrs Badenoch needs more serious arguments. She needs an answer to Mr Burnham that doesn’t retreat into lazy 20th-century political cliche. And she needs to reject Mr Farage’s brand of national populism in terms that give voters reasons to distinguish between their two parties on points of principle, when at the moment there are none.

American starts letting customers mix cash and miles for tickets

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:49:55 UTC
01:49:55 KST

American Airlines is joining carriers that allow customers to book with a combination of cash and miles, the latest change at the carrier as it tries to grow its lucrative loyalty program.
American said customers will see a slider bar allowing them to combine AAdvantage program miles with cash for their tickets at checkout.
The option could be useful when customers don't have enough miles for the entire ticket and are looking to shave some cash off the ticket price.
Other airlines, including American's chief rivals United Airlines and Delta Air Lines, currently allow customers to combine their frequent flyer miles with cash. For example, a one-way ticket on United from its Newark Liberty International Airport hub in New Jersey to Paris the first week of November was going for 40,000 United MileagePlus miles plus $5.60 in tax, $428.50 in cash, or $369 plus 6,000 miles.
The slider bar American plans to roll out in the coming days will give customers the option of using more miles for a bigger discount.
American's updated tool comes as airlines' battles for high-spending customers extend to new airport lounges, bigger premium cabins and in-flight Wi-Fi.

Top Americas diplomats back joint call for Nicaragua to restore civic liberties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:48:15 UTC
01:48:15 KST

Top Americas diplomats back joint call for Nicaragua to restore civic liberties
Oct 2 - The Organization of American States (OAS) on Friday approved a resolution that calls on Nicaraguan authorities to free political prisoners, restore civic liberties and carves a path for potential coordinated action.
The resolution establishes the creation of a group to follow up on and recommend potential action regarding a series of demands to Nicaragua, including that it establish conditions for fair elections, free political prisoners and disclose the whereabouts of people who have been forcibly disappeared.
The government of Nicaragua's Co-Presidents Daniel Ortega and his wife, Rosario Murillo, which has heavily restricted civil liberties since a wave of protests in 2018, last month banned its opposition from future elections.
The resolution was approved at the OAS' first meeting of foreign ministers in seven years, which saw most of the organization's 32 foreign ministers delegate attendance to deputies or ambassadors. Washington, which hosted and proposed the meeting, sent Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau.
"We all understand that the democratic crisis in Nicaragua isn't solely an internal matter; to the contrary, the dictatorship endangers the peace and security of our hemisphere," Landau said at the meeting.
"The dictatorship destabilizes Central America and our broader hemisphere by facilitating illegal immigration and embracing non-hemispheric security services, which support the repression," he added.
Earlier drafts of the resolution showed a rift between the US and aligned right-leaning governments, who pushed for stronger language and alleged foreign security presence in Nicaragua, and other countries including Brazil which said Nicaragua should not be considered a regional security threat.
Nicaragua, which left the OAS in 2023, has security cooperation agreements with Russia and China.
OAS Secretary-General Albert Ramdin told Reuters he hoped the meeting would lead to more than verbal condemnation over human rights abuses.
"That has been said many times already. It is good to say this again collectively, but that cannot be the only outcome," Ramdin said. "It must also be, what do we do next?" REUTERS

Polanski’s Greens look for their next opening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:47:59 UTC
01:47:59 KST

Green Party leader Zack Polanski delivers his speech during day one of the Green Party annual conference at Brighton Centre on October 2, 2026 in Brighton, England. | Alishia Abodunde/Getty Images
BRIGHTON, England — Green leader Zack Polanski has claimed credit for Andy Burnham’s recent arrival in No. 10. Now he’s trying to convince people that his party can still do more to move national politics.
In his second speech as head of the left-wing populist party — and less than a week before his personal brand is tested at the polls in Holborn and St Pancras, where he’s fighting to snag Keir Starmer’s recently vacated Westminster seat — Polanski positioned his party as a corrective, not a spoiler.
“Vote Green, and watch Labour move,” was his message. “Between general elections, we change the government.”
Advertisement
Polanski added: “Through our sustained pressure — and our historic wins — we have held the worst instincts of the Labour government in check. And started to move them in the right direction.”
The Labour washout in May’s local elections, courtesy of voter defections to right-wing populist Reform UK as well as to the Greens, accelerated Starmer’s exit as prime minister over the summer. Burnham has since promised many of the things that under Starmer were within the Greens’ sole purview — public ownership, care, and housing.
The task for the Green leader now is to decide where to push Labour next.
“It won’t surprise you to hear that I’m not hopeful about Labour’s backbone,” he told the crowd.
Hackney Mayor Zoë Garbett, who won her job in May’s local elections, said there were still “key differences” with the governing party, particularly on Gaza, climate and rent control — but conceded that Burnham had made it more difficult for the Green message.
She said: “People were so fed up in May, they were done with people making promises and not delivering, but we need to put forward what our vision is as well, that’s what this conference and Zack’s speech is about.”
Advertisement
Then there’s North London
Walking on stage to Calvin Harris’ Let’s Go, Polanski’s galvanizing energy seemed to convince even some of the skeptics.
“He brought the fire,” said one Green activist on exiting the conference hall, “in a way they’re not really bringing the fire in Holborn.”
Campaigners have been fretting that the Greens haven’t done enough to “bring Burnham back down to earth.” One told POLITICO that next week’s vote would force the party to grapple with its failure to reckon with the new prime minister.
Polanski’s speech went some way towards defining how he might do this. He went hard on rent caps, the proscription of Palestine Action, and new drilling in Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields. And in doing so, he took the first steps toward clarifying where the new battleground is.
More in Common pollster Luke Tryl said that after being hit by the Burnham bounce and Polanski’s tumbling ratings, the Greens “need to make sure they don’t lose sight of the environment.”
Polanski seems to agree. “Our differences with this Labour government could not be clearer,” he said in Brighton, “While they play politics with our planet — we stick to the science. While Andy Burnham barely whispers the word climate — we seek urgent action.”
Advertisement
That was the one time Polanski mentioned the new prime minister’s name, as he joked that the outcome of the post-wildfire government COBRA meeting was to ban outdoor grills.
The Green leader, currently a member of the London Assembly, also attacked Labour MPs for voting for the proscription of Palestine Action.
“Our MPs didn’t troop through the yes lobby. Our MPs were cowed by fear or malicious attacks in the press. They stood up for the principles we hold so dear,” he said.
Polanski is trying to position the party as the full-fat version of Burnham’s “end of neoliberalism” offering. This was set out in a strategy document earlier this summer, according to the Guardian,
“He is really speaking to what a lot of those disillusioned progressives wanted from Labour, and the reason why they left,” Tryl told POLITICO, arguing that the Greens should focus on the cost-of-living crisis and the environment as areas where they can claw back support.
A “timid budget” would “offer the opportunity for the Greens to come back in,” he said.
Tryl warned, however, about the “barnacles” on the party that may drive voters away, like a “Zionism is Racism” motion set to be debated Sunday.
Amid those debates on whether the party takes on a more radical agenda, Tryl said: “The question for Greens is do you want to be a pressure group that is pushing Labour to the left, or do you want to beat them outright.”

Why the Trump Administration Is Being Accused of Interfering in Brazil's Election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:47:14 UTC
01:47:14 KST

President Donald Trump on Thursday said he is following the upcoming Brazilian election “very closely,” referring to Brazil as a “very important" country. "The people of Brazil are fantastic people,” he told reporters outside the White House. “It’s a very important election.”
The U.S. State Department later announced the suspension of its consular services in Brazil ahead of the election taking place on Sunday, citing unspecified security concerns. “U.S. citizens seeking emergency assistance during this time should not come to the Embassy, the Consulates, or other U.S. diplomatic facilities,” the security alert advised.
Brazilians are heading to the polls for a set of federal elections spanning congressional and gubernatorial races, alongside the first round of the presidential election votes. It’s set to be a decisive moment for Latin America’s largest nation, as the region has seen a shift toward the right in recent years. An Oct. 25 runoff is expected, as polls show a tight contest between leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted last year for plotting a coup to overturn his 2022 election loss. Trump led the conservative voices denouncing the conviction, referring to the trial as a “witch hunt.”
While Trump has acknowledged his active interest as Brazil votes on its political future, there are concerns he could be too involved. Trump and his Administration have been accused of attempting to interfere with the high-stakes overseas election.
In a letter sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio in late September, Democratic lawmakers expressed “grave concern” over what they referred to as “the Administration’s coordinated effort to threaten our strategic alliance with Brazil and undermine the Western Hemisphere’s second-largest democracy ahead of its upcoming presidential election.”
“Over the course of President Trump’s second term, we have seen U.S. officials engage in a sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil,” the lawmakers said in the Sept. 24 letter, signed by 30 House Democrats and Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who caucuses with the Democratic Party.
In another letter sent to Rubio on Monday, three Democratic Senators voiced similar concerns about potential U.S. interference.
“This effort first escalated sharply during the summer of 2025, with the [U.S.] Administration deploying tariffs and targeted sanctions to attempt to shape the Brazilian Supreme Court’s verdict in the trial of former President Jair Bolsonaro on charges of attempting to foment a military coup to stay in power,” said the Senators, noting that the tariff pressure escalated in July this year when the Trump Administration moved to impose a new 25% tariff on many imports from Brazil—a decision labeled a “lamentable milestone” by Lula’s office.
The Senators argued that the “campaign directed at Brazil’s authorities resumed with the appointment of Darren Beattie as a senior advisor on Brazil issues in the State Department.” Beattie served as a White House speech writer in Trump’s first term, but was axed for attending a gathering of white supremacists. He returned to the fold early on in Trump’s second term. When serving as undersecretary for public diplomacy and public affairs last year, he called one of Brazil’s Supreme Court Judges a “key architect of the censorship and persecution complex directed against Bolsonaro and his supporters.”
Accusing the Trump Administration of using “diplomatic, economic, and political pressure in ways that risk weakening [Brazil’s] democratic institutions [and] undermining confidence in Brazil's electoral process,” the Senators closed the letter by asking the Administration to “commit to recognizing the certified outcome of Brazil's 2026 democratic elections.”
The White House has staunchly rejected claims of interference in Brazil’s elections.
“Conservative leaders are winning elections across the Western Hemisphere on their own merit because everyone sees the success of President Trump’s policies,” said White House spokesperson Anna Kelly in a statement to TIME. “These claims are nonsense.”
President Lula has also expressed concern over Trump’s interest in his country’s election. “I have already told President Trump it is very important that the U.S. do not interfere in Brazil’s elections,” he said in a Sept. 22 interview. “Brazilian elections are the concern of the Brazilian people. American elections are the concern of the American people.”
Lula added that he is “very worried about Marco Rubio,” claiming that the U.S. Secretary of State “is very closely connected to Bolsonaro’s people,” though he stressed that this was only “suspicion.” TIME has reached out to the State Department for comment.
How the Trump Administration has been accused of meddling in Brazil’s affairs
Trump has not formally endorsed either candidate in Brazil’s presidential race, but his defense of former Brazilian President Bolsonaro, who was last year sentenced to 27 years in prison, is well documented.
After Trump criticized the trial proceedings as a “terrible thing” in July 2025, the Trump Administration increased pressure on Brazil’s government by imposing punishing 50% tariffs— extended in part due to Bolsonaro’s treatment in the courts—and directing the office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) to investigate trade relations with the country.
The State Department added to the pressure later that same month, when Rubio called Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes’ actions a “political witch hunt against Jair Bolsonaro” and announced visa restrictions on Moraes, unspecified judicial allies, and their immediate families.
Feliciano de Sá Guimarães, an associate professor at the Institute of International Relations at the University of São Paulo, says Lula was able to turn the economic pressure into a political argument of his own.
“Lula realized that he could play [these threats] in his favor for electoral purposes,” he says, explaining that Lula used the concept of “rally round the flag,” meaning that once a country is targeted by another, “the incumbent President can rally the people and say, ‘look our sovereignty is under attack.’”
The theme of sovereignty has featured prominently in Lula’s 2026 government manifesto, which points to Trump’s tariffs as damaging the Brazilian economy.
Guimarães says the U.S. Administration has since slightly altered its strategy, favoring an approach that could instead benefit Lula’s opposition.
Flávio Bolsonaro met with Trump, Rubio, and Vice President J.D. Vance at the White House in May. Trump later described the Brazilian lawmaker as a “smart young man, who loves his country very much.” Shortly after that meeting, the U.S. Administration on May 28 designated Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho—two Brazilian gangs—as terrorist organizations, with Bolsonaro appearing to take credit for the move in the media.
Guimarães says the issue may have resonated in Brazil due to public concerns about crime.
“Brazilians are so desperate with the situation of crime in the country that they are resorting to support any initiative, whether it's coming from the federal government or a foreign power to fix the problem,” Guimarães explains, so the move could be seen to strengthen Bolsonaro’s chances with the electorate.
Economic pressure has continued as well. After ordering the USTR to investigate Brazil’s trade practices last year, the office imposed 25% tariffs on the country in July under Section 301, for what it described as unfair trade practices.
Other disputes have further heightened diplomatic tensions. At the end of July, Brazil denied visas to two U.S. State Department officials, accusing them of trying to interfere in the upcoming election. Shortly afterward, Brazilian Ambassador Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti had her U.S. visa revoked.
Is the Trump Administration influencing Latin America’s rightward-turn?
Since returning to office, Trump has sought to exert U.S. influence more directly across Latin America.
In November 2025, the Trump Administration released its National Security Strategy, which highlighted a return to U.S. dominance in the Western Hemisphere and the beginning of the implementation of the "Donroe Doctrine," an informal term for Trump’s reinterpretation of the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine.
“The corollary of the ‘Donroe Doctrine’ is trying to stop the influence of extra regional powers in Latin America, mainly China,” says Guimarães.
Trump has also showcased his support for right-wing candidates across the region.
In 2025, he endorsed close ally Javier Milei in Argentina’s midterm elections and supported Tito Asfura to become the next President of Honduras.
In June, he gave his “complete and total endorsement” to right-wing challenger Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia's June presidential election. (The Trump-backed populist went on to win the race.)
In response to Trump’s endorsement, House Democrats had sent a letter to Rubio expressing concern over what they said was “the brazen interference of senior U.S. officials, including President Trump” in Colombia’s election. “This interference involves the full-throated endorsement of Abelardo de la Espriella, a candidate with a profoundly troubling record that appears to run counter to U.S. interests and potentially to U.S. laws,” the lawmakers said.
But perhaps one of the most significant displays of American power came when the U.S. military captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife during an overnight operation in January and brought them to New York to face narco-terrorism and drug trafficking charges.
Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s acting president, has since adopted a friendlier posture toward the U.S. Administration, enabling access to the country’s oil. In an interview with TIME conducted in late September, Trump heralded the operation in Venezuela as an “incredible” feat and one of the “great things” he’s achieved in his presidency.
“The main reason the [U.S. Administration] will always prefer a right-winger more aligned with the United States, is so they can sell to domestic audiences that, at least in Latin America, Trump's policy is to some extent an effective foreign policy,” Guimarães says.
The State Department under Rubio’s direction has been key in the Trump Administration’s approach to Brazil, Guimarães says.
He cites the creation of the Shield of Americas, a U.S.-led security and political coalition launched in March to fight drug cartels and transnational crime across the Western Hemisphere, as an example. Brazil has not joined the initiative.
Guimarães calls it an “initiative launched by Rubio who wants to bring all Latin American countries under the yoke of the United States to fight organized crime,” and argues that Lula’s resistance could fuel Rubio’s interest in seeing a right-wing government take power, as Bolsonaro has promised to integrate Brazil into the security initiative if he wins the presidential election.

Greens' Polanski calls for UK Palestine Action ban to be lifted
Unknown

2026-10-02
16:43:54 UTC

Breadcrumb
'Not befitting of a democracy': Greens rally against UK Palestine Action ban
Green Party deputy leader Mothin Ali has backed Zack Polanski’s call to deproscribe Palestine Action, telling The New Arab on the sidelines of the party’s annual conference that Britain “can’t keep seeing grannies being carted off into meat wagons” for supporting the banned group.
Speaking exclusively to The New Arab at the Green Party conference in Brighton on Friday, Ali praised Polanski for speaking “powerfully” about Gaza, the cost of living and other issues facing the country.
“We can't keep seeing grannies being carted off into meat wagons by the Old Bill. We just can't have that anymore. It's not befitting of a 21st-century democracy,” Ali said.
Referring to calls for Palestine Action to be removed from the UK’s list of proscribed organisations, he added: “It's something that we're all wanting to see.”
His comments came after Green Party leader Zack Polanski used his conference speech to sharply criticise the Labour government over its approach to Gaza and the 2025 proscription of Palestine Action.
Addressing supporters at the Brighton Centre, Polanski also hailed the party's record-breaking achievements over the past year, including a surge in membership and a record number of councillors.
But some of his strongest criticism was directed at the government’s stance on Gaza, particularly Labour MPs' support for the proscription of Palestine Action.
“To a government so determined to crush dissent that it labels those with views it doesn't want to hear as terrorists. Terrorists,” Polanski said. “And hundreds of Labour MPs who were willing to troop through the voting lobbies to approve it.”
Polanski contrasted Labour's support for the ban with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's admission at the Labour conference earlier this week that the party had been wrong in its approach to Gaza.
He noted that while Miliband was delivering his speech in Liverpool on Monday, dozens of protesters, many of them pensioners, were being arrested for holding placards in support of Palestine Action.
“The sight of pensioners being put in handcuffs and bundled into police vans for holding up cardboard signs has been a stain on this country’s reputation for far too long,” Polanski said.
“And Greens, we stand with one voice now as we say: Drop the charges. End the Genocide. Deproscribe Palestine Action.”
Polanski also welcomed Miliband’s “long overdue” move to ban trade with illegal settlements, describing it as “necessary…but not nearly sufficient”.
Alongside Gaza, the Green leader used his speech to address climate change, the cost of living, housing and immigration.
‘It was very charismatic’
Speaking to The New Arab after the speech, Ali also praised Polanski's focus on domestic issues, including rent controls, council housing and water.
“It's so important to have someone speak so powerfully about the issues that concern us,” he said.
Green Party members and conference attendees who spoke to The New Arab also welcomed the speech.
“I thought it was very good. It was very charismatic,” Keith Garrett told The New Arab.
“But also, the things he said were very powerful and moving towards people and actually get to the nub of a lot of our problems, which is our societal ills and also the climate crisis and the wider issue of genocide and the genocide that's happening in Gaza.”
Garrett said Polanski's position on Gaza had strengthened his support for the leader.
“It really helps that the leader has taken a stand on [Gaza], on being essentially right, not just trying to be populist, but doing the correct things, which I think is the way forward with any modern party now.”
Another attendee, Conall Monaghan, described the speech as “compassionate”.
“You could see the influence the Holborn & St Pancras has had in thinking about the issues that really resonate in the community at the moment,” Monaghan told The New Arab.
“I felt like it was really, really powerful and the celebration of everything the Green Party has done in the last year… It felt really celebratory and positive and strong and really, really makes me feel hopeful about next week.”
The Green Party became the first political party in England and Wales to officially declare Israel’s war on Gaza a genocide at its September 2024 conference, while Polanski has been vocal in his support for Palestine since before becoming leader the following year.
This year’s conference comes days before Polanski contests the Holborn & St Pancras by-election on 8 October, following the departure of former prime minister and constituency MP Keir Starmer in September.
Polanski did not directly reference his campaign during the speech, other than joking that he had been knocking on a lot of doors “for some reason”.

Mecca pact defence committee meeting in Riyadh soon: Pakistan
Unknown

Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar has said that the Strategic Political Defence Committee (SPDC) established under the joint defence pact (Mecca pact) between Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia will meet “soon” in the Saudi capital Riyadh.
“Very soon, a meeting of the whole SPDC has been agreed to in principle to take place in Riyadh,” Dar said on Friday amid Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Later, according to the daily Dawn on Friday, he said that the meeting would take place “next week”.
Recalling his meeting with Iranians in New York last week, Dar said they had suggested in “good faith” that the Houthis should be engaged politically.
Both the Iranian president and foreign minister “wish” for the Houthi-Saudi conflict “to conclude", Dar said.
He said he “sensitised” the Iranian side about the trilateral pact signed in Mecca in August, adding that “as Muslims we have to honour it.”
Dar stressed, however, that any decision would be taken by all three members of the pact.
The Iranians “disassociate themselves from both Houthis as well as Iraqi militias," Dar said.
Dar said the committee has three members from each country: the foreign ministers, defence ministers and chiefs of General Staff.
The three military chiefs met in Riyadh on September 25 for a special meeting, while the foreign ministers met in New York on September 24.
Asked whether the Mecca pact would expand, Dar said, "At least more than six countries are keen to join the Mecca, which is defensive in nature.”
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August.
The agreement stipulates that an attack against any one of the signatory states will be considered an attack against all parties.
Houthi attacks
The Houthis claimed responsibility for other recent attacks in the kingdom, including strikes targeting Saudi Aramco facilities and military sites.
Saudi Arabia has also reported three Houthi attempts to target the holy cities of Mecca and Medina over the past nine years, including two incidents in September, drawing condemnation from Arab and Muslim countries.
Confrontations between Yemen's internationally recognised government forces and the Houthis have escalated since early July following years of relative calm.
The country has been engulfed in war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, before a Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.
The Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with government forces since Yemen's civil war reignited in July, when the group declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh and began targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
The group seized control of Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab al Mandab Strait last month, which has become vital as the wider US war with Iran chokes the Strait of Hormuz.
