Drones cannot replace jets in warfare, expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:28 UTC
01:38:28 KST

F-16C/D Block 70 jets remain relevant in modern warfare even as drones are playing an increasingly prominent role, an expert said, citing their ability to conduct combat air patrols (CAPs) and threaten conventional surface warships, including Chinese aircraft carriers deployed in waters off Taiwan’s east coast, an expert said.
Taiwan yesterday received two of the 66 F-16C/D Block 70 (or F-16V Block 70) jets it ordered from the US in 2019. The full order was due to be delivered by the end of the year, but supply chain disruptions and other issues have pushed back the schedule.
During wartime, Chinese forces would try to damage airbases’ runways to prevent fighter jets from taking off, Institute for National Defense and Security Research associate research fellow Shu Hsiao-huang (舒孝煌) said.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
While airbases in eastern Taiwan would less likely be targeted by Chinese ballistic missiles or long-range rockets, they would still be vulnerable to ship-to-surface and air-to-surface weapons, Shu said.
China could also deploy its aircraft carriers and other large surface vessels far away from Taiwan’s east coast to evade coastal missiles, and threaten shipping routes used to transport weapons, gas and fuel, Shu said.
Those threats are why drones cannot replace fighter jets, he said.
Drones cannot be deployed as effectively against large surface vessels, such as aircraft carriers, due to their limited payload capacity, Shu said, adding that the ability of drones to detect and track airborne targets is not as extensive as those of fighter jets, which provide more effective deterrence against airborne threats.
“The ability of fighter jets to conduct CAPs, generally speaking, cannot yet be replaced,” he said.
Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology policy analyst Cathy Fang (方怡然) said drones are meant to complement conventional fighter jets, not replace them.
“The value [of drones] is not that they replace conventional systems. It is that they add larger numbers of dispersed, lower-cost, and more replaceable sensors and shooters, increasing the density and resilience of Taiwan’s existing defense architecture,” he said.
Despite the F-16V Block 70’s larger fuel capacity, which allows the jets to remain airborne for longer periods, and their ability to carry more missiles, they would be at a disadvantage against China’s fifth-generation stealth fighter jets, such as the J-20, Shu said.
“They are not easily spotted, but they can see us,” Shu added.
The threat becomes more serious if enemy stealth fighters are equipped with beyond-visual-range missiles such as the PL-15 or PL-17, he said.
One system that could help overcome this capability gap is Lockheed Martin’s Legion-ES IRST21, also known as the Legion Pod, which can be integrated with F-16s, Shu said.
The pod uses infrared search and track technology to trace the thermal signatures of stealth fighter jets without activating a radar, and can support targeting for weapons such as AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles, he added.
“The enemy would not easily detect that we are monitoring it or firing at it,” Shu said. “This way, we could ambush the adversary and pose a substantial threat to enemy warplanes.”
While Lockheed Martin does not publicly disclose the Legion Pod’s detection range, the system is designed to detect and track airborne targets at extended ranges, with its effective range depending on factors such as the target’s thermal signature and environmental conditions.
Taiwan has agreed to purchase 55 Legion Pods for its F-16 fleet. The US Department of State approved the sale in August 2023, and the systems are scheduled to be delivered in full by June 2031.

Protecting teachers, improving education
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:25 UTC
01:38:25 KST

Amid nationwide teacher shortages, elementary and junior-high schools across Taiwan have managed to get through the first month of the school year relatively smoothly.
However, many schools are seeing the first waves of resignations from substitute teachers they painstakingly recruited over the summer, as some come to realize the demanding nature of the profession. Schools now have to recruit new substitute teachers to fill vacancies after this month. This turmoil is likely to remain a persistent nightmare for many schools throughout this academic year.
Two things are worth celebrating. One, the Ministry of Education is expected to announce its plan to improve school affairs committee procedures before the Double Ten National Day, and has guaranteed that teachers would feel a tangible impact.
Over the past two to three years, school affairs committees have had a serious chilling effect in the education field. Teachers, fearing frivolous complaints or lawsuits, have resorted to defensive teaching methods. This reluctance to discipline students has led to more chaos in classrooms, and contributed to waves of retirements and resignations.
The ministry’s reforms must genuinely protect teachers’ rights if they are to curb the culture of frivolous complaints, create a more supportive educational environment and encourage teachers to continue working in the field.
Second, a growing number of schools are introducing policies that require parents to respect teachers’ right to disconnect, allowing them to properly rest after work.
Since the advent of messaging apps, teachers’ work have been viewed as a responsibility-based system, requiring them to be available at all hours and respond to parents’ questions or needs. Teachers even face complaints for delayed replies. This has placed teachers under constant pressure.
That some schools are willing to take responsibility and establish rules protecting teachers’ right to “go offline” — allowing them to switch off after work without worrying about repercussions — is another positive step toward creating a more friendly educational environment.
If the government and the ministry place greater emphasis on protecting the rights and interests of teachers, call on parents to respect educators’ right to disconnect after work and institutionalize regular salary increases for teachers, Taiwan’s educational environment would improve, and ultimately, it would be the next generation that benefits from it.
Lee Chi-fu is a teacher.

Marking its centennial yesterday, the Chinese Taipei Alpine Association (CTAA) issued a white paper on government policy, and called for Cabinet-level coordination mechanisms and amendments to policy gaps.
The white paper, titled Mountain Taiwan White Paper (台灣國家山域治理政策白皮書), cited Control Yuan statistics of 531 mountain rescue operations involving 727 people, saying that self-organized groups and solo hikers accounted for a combined 77.31 percent of the cases.
The Executive Yuan should establish a cross-ministry task force with permanent staff to formulate policy guidelines for ministries and agencies to follow, the CTAA said.
Photo: Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
The Executive Yuan should also draft a legal framework for mountain governance, providing an overarching law to coordinate cross-sector and cross-ministry affairs, the CTAA added.
However, the proposed law should not replace existing sector-specific laws, including the Forest Act (森林法), the National Park Act (國家公園法), the Fire Services Act (消防法), the Tourism Development Act (發展觀光條例) and the Indigenous Peoples Basic Law (原住民族基本法), the association said.
Any proposed legislation should undergo reviews of its necessity and its potential effects on people’s rights, local autonomy, indigenous people, the environment, local finances and administrative capacity, the CTAA said.
The Control Yuan on July 16 issued a report addressing the need for a special law governing affairs and activities in mountainous areas, the eligibility of mountain guides, the management of indigenous villages and the integration of mountain guides into the commercial sector.
The report examined gaps in the government’s regulation of mountain activities. It also followed the Executive Yuan’s 2019 “Salute to the Mountains” policy (向山致敬), which sought to reverse the government’s restrictive approach to mountain access and make mountains and forests more accessible to the public.

Traffic fines to be fully allocated to road safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:22 UTC
01:38:22 KST

The Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC) yesterday announced amendments to the Regulations Governing the Allocation and Use of Road Traffic Fines (道路交通違規罰鍰收入分配及運用辦法) that would increase the proportion of revenue from traffic fines used to improve traffic safety and enforcement from “at least 12 percent” to 100 percent.
For traffic citations issued by special municipalities or city and county governments, 75 percent of the revenue goes to the local government.
In the six special municipalities, 99 percent of the fines are deposited into the municipal treasury according to regulations.
Photo: CNA
Another 24 percent is allocated to the issuing authority to cover operational costs and law-enforcement-related incentives, while the remaining 1 percent goes to the national treasury.
The system has often drawn criticism, with some saying that it creates an incentive for local governments to issue more traffic tickets as it boosts municipal revenue.
The issue is particularly pronounced in the six special municipalities, where nearly all traffic fines flow into the city’s coffers, critics said.
Department of Public Transportation and Supervision Director-General Hu Ti-chi (胡迪琦) said that with the changes, revenue from traffic violations would hopefully go toward ameliorating roads and financing law enforcement efforts.
The changes require city and county governments to issue a public report every six months on how they have used money generated from traffic fines, allowing auditors and the public to scrutinize their use, she said, adding that local governments must budget for and spend the funds in accordance with the Budget Act (預算法).
If the funds are not used for their designated purposes, competent authorities should demand local governments rectify the situation within a specified period, Hu said.
Official statistics show five of the special municipalities leading in collection of traffic fines: New Taipei City, NT$3.67 billion (US$115.3 million); Taipei, NT$3.15 billion; Taichung, NT$2.89 billion, Taoyuan, NT$2.5 billion; and Kaohsiung, NT$2.48 billion.
Citing the NT$20.5 billion in revenue generated by fines last year from all local governments, once the new regulations are implemented, an additional NT$18 billion should be available for traffic improvement and road safety, she said.
Local governments would be able to flexibly allocate the funds for infrastructure projects in accident-prone areas in their jurisdictions, including upgrading road signs, markings and traffic signals, renovating pedestrian overpasses and underpasses, and installing additional guardrails and traffic mirrors.
The new system would be implemented in line with local governments’ budget cycles, and is expected to take effect in 2028, she said.

INDONESIA
New islands appear
Two new islands have emerged in waters surrounding Mount Anak Krakatau following a major eruption last month that grounded flights for days, Rita Susilawati of the Centre for Volcanology and Geological Hazard said yesterday. The islands were spotted in satellite images of the water-filled caldera in which Anak Krakatau stands, she said. “Based on an evaluation of Sentinel satellite imagery, two formations resembling small islands can be seen around Mount Anak Krakatau” in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra islands, she added. One of the islands was about 760m northwest of Mount Anak Krakatau, the other about 495m southwest. Rita said it was too early to refer to the islands as “children” of Mount Anak Krakatau — which itself was formed by an underwater eruption in the caldera or depression left behind after the massive 1883 blowout of the original Krakatau volcano. “Anak” means child in Bahasa Indonesia. Rita said further research was needed to determine if the new islands were emerging from the base of the caldera in a similar way than Anak Krakatau did, or whether they were formed by deposits of volcanic material.

The movement, which began last week in the Paris region and rapidly spread nationwide, has seen teenage pupils at lycees in their final years of schooling block access to their establishments and clash with police. Labor funds rebound after fifth-largest monthly gain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:17 UTC
01:38:17 KST

Labor funds administered by the Ministry of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Funds totaled an aggregate gain of NT$366.7 billion (US$11.5 billion) in August, the fifth-largest monthly gain on record.
The sizeable gain was driven by a global stock market rebound in August after tech shares struggled in July due to fears of an expanding artificial intelligence (AI) bubble, the bureau said in a statement on Thursday.
The aggregate August gain, which followed an aggregate loss of NT$246.36 billion in July, trailed only previous monthly gains of NT$1.10 trillion in April, NT$586.0 billion in May, NT$418.4 billion in February and NT $394.6 billion in January.
Photo: Li Ching-hui, Taipei Times
Due to the August rebound, the bureau said, the accumulated gains in the value of assets in the funds’ portfolios and income on investments totaled about NT$2.32 trillion from January to August.
During the eight-month period, the TAIEX, the Taiwan Stock Exchange’s benchmark index, soared 59.26 percent and the MSCI World Index rose 14.31 percent, while the Bloomberg Barclays Global Aggregate Bond Index dropped 0.30 percent.
The eight-month gain translated into a rate of return of 29.45 percent from January to August for the labor funds, up from 25.03 percent during the January-to-July period, the bureau said.
The bureau said 53.82 percent of the funds’ investments from January to August were in overseas assets, while the remaining 46.18 percent were invested in the domestic market.
The labor funds managed by the bureau have various functions, mainly aimed at helping workers.
Specifically, the Labor Pension Fund collects contributions from employers and employees every month and is managed by the bureau to boost the value of the fund’s assets and stabilize funding for workers’ retirement.
The value of assets in the Labor Pension Fund, launched in 2015, totaled NT$5.98 trillion as of the end of August, the highest among all the labor funds, and its rate of return for the January to August period was 29.25 percent, the bureau said.
The Labor Retirement Fund, which has been in place since 1984, had about NT$1.20 trillion in assets as of the end of August, with a rate of return of 42.09 percent for the eight months, the bureau said.
Liu Li-ju (劉麗茹), deputy head of the bureau, said the labor funds are expected to report a gain for last month that would likely be smaller than in August, citing the TAIEX’s rise of 3.9 percent last month, compared with a 6.98 percent increase in August.
Meanwhile, the Bureau of Public Service Pension Fund said on Thursday that the Public Service Pension Fund, which the bureau manages, recorded NT$340.51 billion in gains in the eight months, equal to a rate of return of 24.93 percent.

Sea drones a Taiwan game changer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:17 UTC
01:38:17 KST

China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved.
Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising paths to forcing acceptance of a new “status quo.”
Taiwan cannot answer this daily assault with crewed warships and cutters of its own. They are expensive, few and prone to escalation. The tool Taiwan is reaching for instead is the uncrewed surface vessel (USV): autonomous craft that can contest coercion at scale, leverage home-field advantage and operate at a far lower cost, all without putting sailors in harm’s way.
The logic is straightforward. The outer, weakest rings — fishing boats and militia posing as trawlers — thrive on Taiwan’s reluctance to confront them, because China Coast Guard and PLAN vessels behind them can turn any Taiwanese response into an escalation. Send a crewed cutter and it is Beijing’s coast guard or navy that rams, escalates and narrates the encounter to the world. A USV changes that calculus: no sailor to intimidate, no crew to endanger, no martyr to manufacture. It can hold persistent presence, document illegal activity and shadow harassers — and if a Chinese hull rams it, the loss is a machine, not a man or his limb. Better still, a nimble USV fitted with spikes could leave that far more expensive Chinese hull worse for the wear just above the waterline, ensuring no captain rams one twice.
Ukraine’s naval drones, which crippled Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, already proved that small, expendable USVs can deny a superior navy freedom of maneuver; Taiwan’s opportunity is to apply that lesson daily, in peacetime, and help dissuade any invasion.
Analysts have begun making the case, and Taiwan has already moved away from matching China’s incursions ship for ship toward integrating uncrewed systems and reserving crewed vessels for enforcement. However, the harder question is, integration for what effect? The Philippines showed the limits of “assertive transparency”: publicizing provocations won sympathy, but cameras have not changed Beijing’s behavior.
Here USVs can do what a camera cannot. Fitted with long-range acoustic devices and directed-light systems, they can make sustained harassment genuinely punishing for militia and coast guard crews — and even for warships loitering inside 24 or 12 nautical miles — degrading morale and effectiveness over time, non-kinetically, without exposing sailors.
The acoustic options invite a distinctly Taiwanese flourish. For decades, Kinmen’s loudspeakers sent the ballads of Teresa Teng (鄧麗君) across the Strait to serenade — and needle — Chinese soldiers; a USV could revive the tradition with a wink: Teng by day to unsettle the militia with nostalgia, and AC/DC’s Thunderstruck at window-rattling volume once darkness falls — leaving Taipei free to joke that the racket is obviously the Australians’ doing.
Beneath the humor sits a serious target, the one variable Beijing cannot replace with more hulls: the willingness of fishers and militia to keep showing up once the cost-benefit calculus turns against them. Cost imposition, not documentation, is what turns presence into deterrence.
None of this exists yet, which is why the coming choices matter. Taiwan’s uncrewed effort spans two tiers. The Coast Guard Administration (CGA) is acquiring 25 high-end, ultra-fast, maneuverable 24-foot USVs — capable, but few — for the day-to-day “gray zone” fight. Separately, it is pursuing a proposed fleet of 1,320 attritable attack boats, cheaper and individually less capable, to saturate the Strait against invasion. Yet neither is in the water: the first of the 25 is unbuilt, and the 1,320 are nowhere near contract. Taiwan is deciding how to fight the “gray zone” before it has the hulls — making the doctrine the most urgent task of all.
Twenty-five boats, however capable, cannot be everywhere at once, and the daily fight demands mass — exactly what the 1,320 could provide, if Taiwan resists treating that fleet as an “in case of emergency, break glass” reserve mothballed until D-Day. A capability held only for the worst day atrophies before it arrives, as crews never gain proficiency, command-and-control goes untested, logistics stay theoretical and tactics never evolve against a real adversary. Worse, it cedes the very contest Beijing is waging now. At least a portion of the attritable fleet should rotate through daily “gray zone” operations alongside the CGA’s boats as it comes online.
Every patrol shadowing a militia boat or mapping a coast guard cordon doubles as a live rehearsal — sharpening operators, hardening datalinks against Chinese jamming and exposing failures far better found in peacetime than in war — while signaling to Beijing that the fleet and the resolve are real.
Critics will say USVs alone cannot resolve Taiwan’s security dilemma. True. No single capability can. However, in a contest defined by attrition, presence and narrative, they give Taiwan what it urgently needs: 24-hour coastal presence, without the political and human costs conventional platforms impose. Not a silver bullet, but a force multiplier for a democracy that cannot continue to cede its waters meter by meter.
Taiwan’s adversary is patient, its campaign built to erode political will and exhaust resources. The answer is not to match China ship for ship, but to field asymmetric, scalable tools — and to decide now that when they arrive, they serve the daily contest, not a war reserve. Taiwan’s ability to contest the war Beijing is already waging may ultimately decide whether D-Day ever comes.
Trey Meeks is a senior adviser to the Asia Group and senior defense fellow for the Center for a New American Security.

Donovan’s Deep Dives: Keeping Cheng at arm’s length
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:15 UTC
01:38:15 KST

Speculation started to fly last month that Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) candidates running in the November elections wanted to keep their distance from party Chair Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文).
That some in the KMT were concerned that Cheng’s firm ideological adherence to the “one China principle” is no secret. There had already been pushback from within the party on issues ranging from the budget to defense, as well as over some of her more hardline comments.
The timing made sense, however. The KMT party congress unity love fest wrapped up at the end of July. Through the primaries and up to that point, it was necessary to regularly appear with the party chair. Not so starting in August.
Photo: Weng Yu-huang, Taipei Times
In other democracies, candidates sometimes distance themselves from the party leader — especially in tough districts. In Taiwan, typically the party chair plays a role regardless, though how closely the candidates embrace them varies.
In 2018, however, there was a very public split between KMT candidates who preferred to appear with a trio of popular candidates and cut out the party chair from rallies and events, and a small handful of candidates that stayed loyal to the party chair.
Will Cheng face a similar marginalization? It is too early to say and the signs are mixed, but it will become glaringly obvious one way or the other in late October and into November as the rallies get into high gear.
Photo: Tsai Tsung-hsun, Taipei Times
Consider this from a candidate’s perspective. The June Formosa poll found that only 26.7 percent had confidence in Cheng, versus 56 percent who did not. Since then, a lot has happened that could have pushed those numbers both up or down, but it suggests that in competitive districts she could turn off independents.
Among KMT supporters, 69.2 percent trusted her, and among Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) supporters it was 49.1 percent. However, those picking “very confident” were only 12.4 and 9.5, respectively. That suggests she would not be a big draw for the base, either. Relations between the KMT and the TPP have soured in some parts of the country, so those TPP numbers could now be lower.
Of course, constituencies vary, and in some, Cheng is a positive, but broadly speaking, she is not a major asset. However, having the party chair as an ally comes with other benefits, and some candidates personally support her ideological stances.
Photo: Liao Hsueh-ju, Taipei Times
To research this, I set a start date of Aug. 1. I examined news stories about interactions between the candidates and Cheng, image searches of their public interactions, the Facebook photos posted by each candidate to see who they wanted to be associated with, and searched for campaign advertising. I examined all 19 KMT candidates for mayor and county commissioner, plus three KMT-backed independent and TPP candidates.
Some important broad patterns appeared. Most candidates in this cycle are not playing down their party affiliation, are proudly pan-blue and love being photographed with major party figures. Especially popular KMT figures to be photographed with include Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕), New Taipei Mayor Hou You-yi (侯友宜), Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) and New Taipei mayoral candidate Hammer Lee (李四川). Being pictured with TPP founder Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) is a popular choice in areas where KMT candidates hope to appeal to TPP supporters.
COUNTY COMMISSIONER RACES
At least three candidates are very keen to associate themselves with Cheng. Kinmen candidate Jennifer Chen (陳玉珍) and Cheng have a visibly warm relationship, and Cheng referred to Chen as a “cute little sister,” which is a far cry from Chen’s normal nickname, the “Kinmen tank.” The two are ideologically tight-knit.
In Changhua Wei Ping-cheng (魏平政) is widely disliked by the local KMT, and his two remaining major allies just got put in jail. He is desperately clinging to Cheng for dear life.
In Hsinchu County, Hsu Hsin-ying (徐欣瑩) also needs Cheng’s support in the wake of an ugly primary that split local KMT support. Then, relations with the TPP acrimoniously broke down over the Jhubei City mayoral race, with Hsu at the center of the controversy. Yilan’s James Wu (吳宗憲) faces the problem that the outgoing KMT administration was plagued by scandal and the DPP is looking strong this cycle.
Hsu Shu-hua (許淑華) in Nantou and Chung Tung-chin (鍾東錦) in Miaoli have also been welcoming of Cheng. Both are incumbents in deep-blue counties, so they do not need Cheng’s help, but they appear to appreciate it regardless.
KMT-backed former TPP-turned-independent Ann Kao (高虹安) in Hsinchu City and TPP Chiayi City candidate Chang Chi-kai (張啟楷) are playing a different game. They are welcoming of Cheng, but carefully balance her with appearances by Ko Wen-je and TPP Chair Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌).
Four candidates appear with Cheng in public, but do not emphasize it on social media.
In Pingtung, Su Ching-chuan (蘇清泉) lost in a tight race in 2022, and may hope Cheng will juice up voter turnout. In Taitung, Wu Hsiu-hua (吳秀華) is facing a DPP candidate that some think might actually have a chance in this deep-blue county, so she may be thinking along similar lines. Chiayi County KMT-backed independent Wu Pin-jui (吳品叡) will also need KMT voter turnout.
Though in a stronger position, Yunlin’s Chang Chia-chun (張嘉郡) may have similar considerations, but as a member of the powerful Yunlin Chang clan faction, she may have other motivations beyond electability in the direction of political influence.
The candidates for Lienchiang County (Matsu), Penghu and Hualien do not appear to have met with Cheng, but it is unclear if there is any political meaning, or they are simply too remote.
THE ‘BIG SIX’
Things got interesting examining the mayoral candidates for the “big six” special municipalities. Only three have met with Cheng publicly since July, but not one posted pictures on Facebook about it.
Tainan’s Hsieh Lung-chieh (謝龍介) met with her in August and again on Sept. 30 when Cheng moved the KMT’s central standing committee meeting to Tainan. On July 25 he was asked point blank if he would appear on campaign billboards with Cheng, and he replied he would not rule it out. However, so far it has not happened. Tainan is deep green, so that is not surprising.
In Taoyuan, Simon Chang (張善政) appeared with Cheng at an event on Sept. 2. Of the “big six” candidates, he has the least to lose by appearing with Cheng. He is far ahead in polling, and Taoyuan leans KMT.
On Sept. 12, Cheng and New Taipei candidate Hammer Lee (李四川) appeared at an event, but curiously two other attendees — Lu Shiow-yen and Hou You-yi — left before Cheng arrived. This could simply be scheduling conflicts, but regardless, it shows they did not prioritize being around Cheng.
A similar situation also took place the same day. Both Taipei candidate Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) and Cheng attended the same event, but not at the same time, so they did not appear together.
On Sept. 25, Kaohsiung’s Ko Chih-en (柯志恩) was sharing with the press plans to campaign with Ko Wen-je, but when asked whether she would invite Cheng to campaign with her, she simply said that everyone respects each other’s schedules and the pace of their respective campaigns. That enthusiasm gap is telling; she clearly calculates that Ko helps her gain supporters, but Cheng, not so much.
That Taichung’s Johnny Chiang (江啟臣) has not met with Cheng should surprise no one; the two are as far apart ideologically within the KMT framework as is possible. As if sending a message, he just announced that the exact same trio that cut out the party chair in 2018 — Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), Lu Shiow-yen and Hou You-yi will be attending his campaign headquarters opening on Oct. 4.

Council touts domestically developed AI vessel system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:15 UTC
01:38:15 KST

A domestically developed system combining artificial intelligence (AI)-powered autonomous navigation and federated learning has completed autonomous patrol tests using a medium to large-sized uncrewed surface vessel, the Ocean Affairs Council said yesterday, adding that it would help protect sensitive maritime data and improve vessels’ object-recognition capabilities.
The system is the result of the council’s “AI Navigation and Federated Learning for Maritime Object Recognition: Feasibility and Reliability Testing for Scalable Unmanned Surface Vessels” project, conducted under its Marine Technology Project Program.
The project was part of the council’s efforts to accelerate marine technology development and the application of smart maritime systems in Taiwan, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Ocean Affairs Council
Maritime imagery has been collected mainly as snapshots of individual incidents, while national and port security concerns limited access to broader datasets, restricting the amount of data available for AI training, the council said.
The use of federated learning allows AI models to be trained using data from multiple vessels without requiring ships to share sensitive data or imagery, it said.
Previously, uncrewed vessels trained their own AI models and could share the algorithms used in the training process, but not the underlying data, the council said.
The new system allows vessels across the fleet to improve their models collaboratively while keeping sensitive information and imagery on individual platforms, significantly improving their ability to recognize objects, it said.
To prevent “catastrophic forgetting,” in which AI models lose previously learned skills when acquiring new ones, the research team incorporated elastic weight consolidation.
The technology allows uncrewed vessels to learn to recognize new objects, such as newly introduced maritime warning buoys, without losing their ability to identify commercial vessels and fishing boats, the council said.
The vessels underwent stress tests in waters off Fengbitou (鳳鼻頭) near Kaohsiung Harbor.
Under real-world conditions, including sea states of force 2 or higher and challenging lighting, the vessel completed a series of demanding tasks, including point-to-point obstacle avoidance, hexagonal navigation, Z-shaped patrols and large-area “lawnmower” searches, the council said.
The system achieved a mean average precision of more than 90 percent for object detection, an inference speed of at least 15 frames per second and a forgetting rate of less than 10 percent, it said.
The project also established Taiwan’s first standard operating procedures for operating medium and large-sized uncrewed vessels in open waters, the council said.
The vessels are equipped with an emergency system that allows human operators to take control within three seconds of a communications failure, ensuring safe navigation, it said.
All of the system’s algorithms were developed domestically, the council said, adding that the project was designed to reduce reliance on foreign technologies subject to export controls and bolster Taiwan’s resilience in marine research and maritime security.

Return of moth swarms creates exciting spectacle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:14 UTC
01:38:14 KST

Moth swarms so thick they can blot out the stars are fluttering across Australia, heralding a migratory spectacle unseen since the creature’s brush with extinction nearly 10 years ago.
The great migration of the Bogong moth was once a yearly feature of the Australian spring, the insects humming down the nation’s east coast in their billions as they searched for cooler climes. However, drought, pesticides and habitat destruction triggered an unprecedented collapse that began in 2017, eventually wiping out an estimated 99.5 percent of the Bogong moth population.
While vast clouds of flying bugs might not be everyone’s cup of tea, scientists have been delighted to find that the Bogongs are back.
Photo: AFP
“There have been happy tears in my office because this is what nature should be,” conservation biologist Marissa Parrott said. “People are noticing those big swarms again. They can celebrate what I think is one of nature’s great spectacles.”
In a good year, 4 billion moths or more would escape the inland heat to seek shelter in the alpine caves of eastern Australia.
“So many Bogong moths would come through that they could block out the stars and the moon as they went overhead,” said Parrott, from Zoos Victoria.
Photos showed how the endangered moths clustered together so densely inside their caves, it was impossible to see the rock beneath.
“They get up into the mountains and into these caves, where they make this beautiful tiling pattern,” Western Sydney University insect researcher Eleanor Drinkwater said. “They cover the walls in this very dense mat of moths... They hang out there until the weather starts getting cooler, and they come back down to their breeding grounds.”
Their migration has long fascinated scientists, who have puzzled over how they found their way on a journey they only ever make once.
By placing a tether around captive moths and projecting stars on the wall, researchers last year showed how Bogongs used the Milky Way.
They were the first invertebrates — a broad group of animals including spiders, snails and worms — shown to use celestial navigation for such long trips.
Bogong moths are thought to help plants spread pollen and are also a key food source for the mountain pygmy possum, a critically endangered cave-dwelling marsupial.
“They are very, very important to Australian ecosystems,” Drinkwater said.
Drawn toward the blazing stadium floodlights, Bogong swarms caused havoc at the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney.
Forecasters warned that heavy rain was about to drench the event’s closing ceremony — only to realize the radar had picked up a cloud of Bogongs.
While the Bogong migration continued in the years following the population crash, scientists were aghast at how few moths were making the journey.
“People described going into the caves and finding barely any moths, and just kind of being in shock,” Drinkwater said.
Researchers are still working to better understand what contributed to the Bogong bounce-back, but believe a spate of wetter weather has helped.
With a severe El Nino forecast to send temperatures soaring over summer, scientists hope the rebound is not short-lived.
“It’s great they’re back, and we’re really excited they’re back,” Drinkwater said. “But we’re still worried about them.”

EDITORIAL More leave is not the birthrate fix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:14 UTC
01:38:14 KST

The government yesterday began fully subsidizing an additional six days of paid marriage leave, extending it from eight days to 14.
The Ministry of Labor’s Guidelines for Wage Subsidies for Marriage, Maternity and Paternity Leave under the Family-Friendly Workplace Program (友善育兒職場婚孕產假薪資補助要點) are part of an 18-point population strategy President William Lai (賴清德) announced earlier this year, aimed primarily at addressing the nation’s falling birthrate, which declined for the 32nd consecutive month in August.
However, the government’s proposed measures drew criticism from civic groups this week, who said that some could inadvertently reinforce gender inequality in the workplace.
Specifically, a proposal to extend maternity leave from eight weeks to 12 and marriage leave from seven days to 14 has been met with particular scrutiny.
The vast difference between the two types of leave would disadvantage female workers and deepen workplace discrimination, the groups said.
A study from Brazil cited by the Childcare Policy Alliance found that after maternity leave was extended without a corresponding increase in paternity leave, women’s overall promotion rate fell by 17 percent, their average income decreased by 3.5 percent and the proportion of women in high positions dropped by 5 percent. Meanwhile, the promotion rate for men increased from 3.35 percent to 6.23 percent.
Extending maternity leave without raising paternity leave could encourage employers to discriminate against women, because of the costs associated with the leave, the association said.
There is reason to expect this would happen, given that Taiwan already has significant gender disparities in the workplace.
After having a child, Taiwanese women work 8.7 fewer hours per week on average and their monthly income falls by nearly NT$9,000, reflecting a familiar pattern in which motherhood carries a much greater professional cost than fatherhood, a National Chengchi University study found.
However, there is another side to this issue that cannot be addressed simply by making leave equal for parents.
Women have historically taken more parental leave, not necessarily because the system forces them to do so, but because they continue to shoulder a disproportionate share of childcare and household responsibilities.
Women living with a spouse or partner spend an average 4.41 hours a day on unpaid care, 2.6 times the 1.72 hours spent by their partners, a Ministry of Health and Welfare survey found in 2024.
That disparity matters, especially when discussing why young people — specifically young women — are increasingly hesitant to have children. Equal leave might help reduce the career penalties associated with motherhood, but it would not by itself address the unequal division of domestic responsibilities.
For many young women, concerns about having children are not limited to the length of maternity or paternity leave. They must also consider that doing so would mean sacrificing their current lifestyle to permanently take on significantly more domestic responsibilities while facing expectations to maintain their careers.
This represents a much more complex hurdle for the nation’s population strategy. Marriage leave and parental leave would undoubtedly ease some of the burden faced by young couples who plan to have children, but the nation’s low birthrate is a result of more than just married couples being unable to afford a child.
Most married Taiwanese couples have children, but the proportion of people who marry has decreased significantly over the past few years. If young people perceive marriage and parenthood as having to surrender autonomy, career opportunities or an equal division of domestic responsibilities, additional leave would likely do little to change their minds.
The government’s new measures highlight a distinction that is easy to overlook: Making workplaces more family-friendly is only part of the equation; much of parenthood pressures begin at home.
Equal maternity and paternity leave might address part of the structural imbalance between working men and women who choose to have children. However, the deeper challenge lies in fundamentally shifting cultural expectations surrounding parental roles and the sharing of domestic responsibilities.
Taiwan’s demographic problem would not be solved by extending marriage and parental leave alone. If the government wants to address the birthrate, it must develop a population strategy capable not only of making parenthood more feasible, but also of changing the societal expectations that make marriage and parenthood increasingly difficult to reconcile with personal autonomy, career ambitions and a fair division of domestic responsibilities.

Amazon.com Inc is exploring a deal to shift about US$8 billion worth of top-end Nvidia Corp chips off its balance sheet, according to the Financial Times.
The move would offload thousands of Grace Blackwell chips across more than a dozen US data centers into a special-purpose vehicle which would be funded by outside investors, the paper said, citing people familiar with the matter. The structure would let Amazon keep using the hardware while adopting a more asset-light financing model. The vehicle could issue debt and sell up to a 10 percent equity stake to investors, the paper said.
Amazon and Amazon Web Services representatives did not immediately respond to e-mailed requests for comment outside of regular office hours.
Photo: Reuters
The deliberations reflect the elaborate financing the world’s big tech providers are resorting to as they spend hundreds of billions of US dollars to support the AI infrastructure buildout.
Under the proposed structure, Amazon would lease the advanced chips back from the entity. If the special-purpose vehicle receives an investment-grade credit rating, long-term investors like insurance companies and pension funds could join as backers.
AI infrastructure financing is broadening beyond the capex surge, as cumulative hyperscaler spending potentially nears US$9 trillion through 2031 and debt issuance possibly hits US$500 billion next year. Amazon.com’s obligations are rising, while Nvidia’s record buyback shows AI spending can coexist with shareholder distributions.
AI service providers including Alphabet Inc’s Google and Microsoft Corp are scrambling to address shortages in computing power, committing huge amounts of money on data center hardware and leases. AI tools are demanding climbing amounts of general-purpose computing power and memory as well as AI-focused graphics processing units.
Amazon has said it expects capital spending of US$220 billion this year, with most of the expenditures going to AI.
GPU-backed borrowing is already widely used by companies including CoreWeave Inc. Chips inside advanced data centers are estimated to need replacement every five years or so to keep pace with tech developments.

Workers at snack maker Kuai Kuai Co’s only production facility in Taiwan voted yesterday to continue their strike indefinitely following a one-day strike, as a dispute over the plant’s relocation and related labor arrangements remained unresolved.
Around 130 members of the Kuai Kuai union, which represents employees at the company’s Jhongli factory in Taoyuan, joined the strike, which began at 5 am yesterday following an announcement shortly after midnight.
The union said in a statement issued yesterday afternoon that an extraordinary members’ meeting held after the one-day strike approved extending the labor action indefinitely by “a near-unanimous vote.”
Photo: CNA
It called on Kuai Kuai and the San-Ti Group, which has owned Kuai Kuai since 2019, to begin negotiations as soon as possible.
The strike was initially described by the union as a one- day “warning strike.”
According to the union, workers only learned through news reports in July that the land and factory buildings at the Jhongli site, which is more than 57 years old, had been sold to Advanced Semiconductor Engineering (ASE).
The union subsequently sought talks with the company and applied for labor dispute mediation through the Taoyuan City Government. After two mediation sessions ended without agreement, 94 percent of members backed strike action in a vote held on Sept. 18.
The union has accused management of failing to engage in substantive negotiations and disputed company claims that most issues had already been agreed upon.
It said no agreement had been reached on arrangements for workers during the two-year transition period and after the relocation.
Under the property deal announced in late July, Kuai Kuai planned to immediately lease back the entire Zhongli site from ASE after completion of the transaction.
The west-side factory buildings were to be leased for six months and the east-side buildings for 24 months, giving Kuai Kuai up to two years to complete its relocation.
In response, Kuai Kuai spokesperson Chan Yi-kuo (詹益國) said the company regretted the strike but respected employees’ right to take industrial action.
Chan said the two sides had reached agreement on some issues, while discussions were continuing over arrangements for employees who leave the company during the two-year transition period before the relocation is completed.
He added that the company remains open to discussing the union’s demands and will continue negotiations.
The Ministry of Labor said it respects the union’s lawful exercise of its right to strike and reiterated that workers participating in union activities or the strike must not face “adverse treatment” by the company.
The ministry said the dispute has gone through two unsuccessful mediation sessions and multiple rounds of direct talks, but the two sides have yet to reach agreement on some demands.
It urged the company to negotiate with the union and workers with “the greatest possible sincerity and good faith.”
Kuai Kuai is one of Taiwan’s best-known snack brands, particularly for its eponymous puffed corn snacks.
Its green-packaged butter-coconut-flavored Kuai Kuai is also a familiar sight in Taiwan’s tech sector, where packets are often placed beside equipment in the belief they will help machinery “behave” and operate smoothly -- a play on the meaning of “Kuai Kuai” in Mandarin.

GOLF
China’s ‘Sherry’ wins in US
Xiaolong “Sherry” Zhong made a 15-foot birdie putt on the par-3 17th hole and matched pars on the final hole at Portland Golf Club to defeat Amandine Vincent of France and become the first player from China to win the US Senior Women’s Amateur. Zhong, who turned 50 in March and was low amateur at the US Senior Women’s Open, was the medalist in qualifying, won her final three matches on the 18th hole. Zhong built a 3-up lead through 10 holes until Vincent rallied by winning the par-5 15th with a bogey and the par-4 16th with a birdie. Zhong went with 8-iron on the 17th and it paid off with her birdie to take the final lead of the match. Zhong is the sixth player from China to win a USGA championship, and the first since Aaron Du and Sampson Zheng won the US Amateur Four-ball in 2023.

Burnham lifts Labour spirits, but detail lags
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:09 UTC
01:38:09 KST

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has restored some hope to his governing Labour Party with his vision for Britain, but how the new prime minister makes it a reality remains something of a mystery for businesses, lawmakers and even his most vocal supporters.
At the Labour Party’s annual conference in the northwestern English city of Liverpool, the mood was much more upbeat than the past two years of Keir Starmer’s administration, but there were nagging questions. It remains unclear when Burnham will plot a detailed route and allocate the funds to become the “circuit-breaker” for Britain’s recently unstable politics.
After promising to ease cost-of-living pressures and to spur economic growth through reindustrialization and devolving power to the regions, there is little detail on how Burnham will fund and implement his feel-good agenda in the near term, companies and lawmakers say. They say he is more focused on the future, specifically after the next national election, due in mid-2029.
Even his first conference speech as prime minister, in which he offered an “honest conversation” on the deepest problems afflicting Britain and the trade-offs involved in tackling them, posed more questions than answers on immediate policy decisions.
‘IN A HAZE OF DOPE’
Burnham himself concedes he is boxed in by Starmer’s earlier election promises, limiting not only his room to raise funds for his more ambitious aims before the next national election, but also preventing him from bringing in his own agenda.
“The whole conference feels like it is c,” said one business executive, speaking on condition of anonymity. “It is nice to be here. But it feels like everything is moving slowly.”
“The frustrating thing is some big ideas are being thrown about, but we don’t know enough about how they are going to work.”
Companies, which paid about ￡6,000 (US$7,924) to attend Labour’s business day and the wider conference, and lawmakers, nervously eyeing opinion polls, want answers — how will the government cut energy costs, borrowing and welfare, and is there money to spend on defense, health and education before the next election?
Burnham has promised to set out a 10-year plan later in the year, and has pushed back one major commitment — the reform of social care — saying he would only present proposals at the next election, due by mid-2029.
However, after offering some short-term “breathing space” to Britons struggling with cost-of-living pressures, Britain’s seventh prime minister in a decade has failed so far to offer, particularly to businesses, a blueprint of the government’s investment strategy and its plans to deliver lower costs.
The scale of the problems facing Britain has created some sympathy for Burnham, the former mayor who had been in parliament just a month when he became prime minister in July, after Starmer resigned earlier than expected.
Labour lawmaker Alex Sobel told Reuters Burnham had been dealt some of the trickiest challenges of any prime minister in modern history, including the rise of AI and wars in Iran and Ukraine pushing up Britain’s energy prices.
“You can’t say you have had three months, and everything should be sorted by now,” he said.
However, that understanding has its limits and the bounce in the opinion polls since Burnham took power could soon disappear.
John Curtice, Britain’s best-known pollster, said Burnham’s five-point bounce was very similar to that enjoyed by former Labour prime minister Gordon Brown and former Conservative prime minister Boris Johnson when they took on their roles mid-term.
Both lost their jobs about three years later.
“Things are better, but the party needs to do much more to win the next election,” Curtice said.
CLEAR SIGNALS
That means supporting businesses still angered by the tax and wage increases brought in by Starmer, and offering a clear signal about which sectors will benefit from government spending so they can increase investment.
One attendee of Labour’s business day on Monday said while the access to ministers was the best they had ever had, the real test would be the budget and the 10-year plan. They remain desperate for policy details.
However, Burnham must also convince voters he can ease cost-of-living pressures such as energy bills over the long term, start a mass house-building program and deliver higher defense spending and jobs, all without diverting spending on Britain’s struggling public services, such as health.
Businesses and lawmakers hope for more clarity in British Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey’s Oct. 28 budget, although his conference speech suggesting it would be business as usual made some worried that he was not yet ready to grasp the nettle.
“The grit is going to come,” said Claire Ainsley, director of the Project on Center-Left Renewal at the Progressive Policy Institute and a former Starmer adviser.
“The things that it’s going to take to reboot the economy are not necessarily the things that Labour members want to do,” Ainsley said.
At least eight Labour lawmakers canvassed by Reuters said that if the government fails to deliver, that could hand power to the populist Reform UK party, led by Brexit campaigner Nigel Farage.
The removal of Starmer for the more popular Burnham would have been all for nothing, one said.
“We have to deliver. We have no choice,” Labour lawmaker Chris Curtis said. “That is why we have to be bold and come up with solutions to those challenges.”

Kimi Antonelli would have to deal with an unfamiliar track and potentially heavy rain as he aims to recover from his “worst weekend” of his Formula 1 (F1) title challenge this year.
The unusually named Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia takes Antonelli and his rivals to a track F1 last visited in 2017 — when he was 11 — in a race hurriedly added to the calendar because of the disruption caused by the Iran war. It is to take place at the Sepang international circuit, about 60km south of central Kuala Lumpur.
With rain possible on all three days of on-track action, it could be the first real wet race since F1 shook up its regulations for this year’s season, and the abrasive asphalt tends to chew up tires, too.
Photo: Reuters
Antonelli still has a dominant 66-point lead over teammate George Russell, but that was trimmed from 81 last week after his crash in qualifying made for damage limitation in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. Antonelli scrambled from 16th on the grid to finish fifth, helped by plenty of incidents ahead of him, while Russell held off Max Verstappen for his first win in nearly three months.
“Last weekend was probably the worst weekend from me, from my side of the season,” Antonelli said.
“It was what I needed on Sunday, I needed a clean result after a very disruptive weekend. After the race, I wasn’t happy with the result and everything but I learn many things and the most important is that I need to always be 100 percent,” he said.
“I need to really do my best to achieve the best result because if I don’t do everything right, or I don’t try to do everything right in my power, then nothing is going to come my way,” he added.
Russell has made no secret of his struggles getting used to this year’s cars as he had to watch his younger teammate dominate.
After using the mid-season break to change his approach, a process he has likened to a golfer getting used to a new swing, Russell finally seemed comfortable in Azerbaijan. He went fastest by nearly a second in qualifying, and his narrow margin of victory over Max Verstappen in the race owed more to an unusual yellow-flag decision on track than anything else.
Mercedes has brought a package of upgrades to its car for this week, something Russell predicts could help him.
“I’m enjoying it more than I have done recently because I just feel more at one with the car and hopefully this new upgrade with a few characteristic changes that will also play into my favor a bit more,” he said on Thursday. “Bring it on.”
Lewis Hamilton said Ferrari remains united as he criticized attempts to “break our spirit” after the Italian brand confirmed it retains confidence in Fred Vasseur as team principal.
“Outside sources seem to be so negative towards us as a team and trying to break our spirit, but they’re not succeeding,” Hamilton said.
The latest speculation over Vasseur’s future came after former Red Bull boss Christian Horner told the Times of London last week that Ferrari was the only team in F1 he’d consider joining without an ownership stake, calling it “the dream” and a “sleeping giant.”
Ferrari is struggling on the track, with no podium finishes in the last five races for Hamilton or Charles Leclerc.
Meanwhile, Williams are caught in a “cost cap trap” that forces them to spend millions on basic factory systems rather than car development, team principal James Vowles said yesterday, calling for changes to F1’s financial rules.
Teams have a limit for spending on performance-related activities each season, with the cap at US$215 million for this year.
That, said Vowles, has created a “two-tier championship” where the top four teams — Mercedes, Red Bull, McLaren and Ferrari — have actually tightened their grip, rather than levelling the playing field.
“Cost cap has made it worse, not better. I’m probably unique because — it’s not a compliment — but I went from the best team to the worst team,” said Vowles, who has the unique perspective of moving from championship-winning Mercedes to struggling Williams.
“What I hadn’t appreciated or realized when you do that jump is just how little exists. When you make a cost cap, I’m not spending money on the car, I’m spending tens of millions just on basic systems just so you know where a part is in the factory,” he said.
“That’s not going to the car, that’s not going to an upgrade. It’s going on systems that I need to just do the basics, so we’re caught in a cost cap trap,” he added at a news conference.
However, he said the solution was not to scrap the cost cap entirely as the sport was financially stable as a result.
“But we do need to think about what mechanisms we have in there to make sure we all play with the same tools and the same mechanisms to be able to make things better,” he said.
Williams are ninth in the standings this year with 12 points and Vowles admitted that they have “gone backwards.”
“The reality is we’re too far away, which is what I was fearful of, and it’s still exposing those weaknesses. Those will not be addressed this year,” he said.

Taiwanese Olympic champion Lin Yu-ting (林郁婷) yesterday won her second consecutive Asian Games boxing gold, defeating her Chinese opponent in the women’s 60kg final.
Lin beat Yang Chengyu (楊成宇) by a unanimous 5-0 decision at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, adding the 60kg title to her 57kg gold from Hangzhou, China, in 2023.
“In this competition, I’m like a newborn calf ... or a little white rabbit that has wandered into a great forest,” Lin said.
Photo: Mohd Rasfan, AFP
“None of my opponents was ordinary. Every one of them was incredibly strong and powerful,” she said.
“I don’t think there was a single one of my four bouts where I didn’t end up on the ground at some point. That shows just how difficult this competition was,” she added.
Yang said she struggled to cope with the taller Lin’s style.
Photo: CNA
“She is really tall and, in training, we don’t often face someone of that height, so that distance can feel unfamiliar,” she said.
The victory gave Taiwan its fourth gold of this year’s Asian Games and was Lin’s first international title since moving up to the 60kg weight class following her gold-medal triumph at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
Lin had taken bronze at April’s Asian Boxing Elite Boxing Championships in Ulan Batar, Mongolia, before winning silver at the World Boxing Cup in Guiyang, China, in June.
Photo: Andy Chua, Reuters
In the event in Guiyang, Lin defeated former world champion Yang by a 4-1 split decision in the semifinals to reach her first World Boxing Cup final in the heavier division.
In the final, Lin was edged by Viktoriya Grafeyeva of Kazakhstan 3-2, but she avenged that defeat in the first round of the Asian Games competition with a 3-2 victory over the Kazakh boxer.
Lin said before the Asian Games that she had considered retiring after winning gold at the Paris Olympics, but wanted to carry on fighting in part to defy those who questioned her eligibility following a gender row that involved US President Donald Trump, Elon Musk and author J.K. Rowling.
Photo: AP
She said after her victory in Nagoya that she had been “waiting for that moment when the light breaks through.”
“It was really not easy at all,” she said.
“It’s rare to finally reach that point where you see the dawn, and I’m just so grateful to myself for making it through,” she added.
Photo: AFP
Winning at the Asian Games was different from her Olympic victory, Lin said, adding that its “significance is monumental.”
“I basically just felt like packing up my things and rushing back home — that was the kind of mindset I had,” she said of her previous experience.
“I didn’t hold on to any hope anymore. I am so grateful to the coach for always believing in me and always believing that good things would happen,” she said.
Lin was backed by a small pocket of vocal Taiwanese supporters in the cozy Nishio Gymnasium.
Lin declined confirming whether she planned to defend her Olympic title at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.
“I believe that in the future, we can also put on an even better performance, persevere all the way and laugh until the end,” she said.

Chinese construction on Antelope Reef gathering pace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:04 UTC
01:38:04 KST

Chinese construction of a runway on Antelope Reef (Lingyang Reef, 羚羊礁) in the Paracel Islands (Xisha Islands, 西沙群島), is well under way with analysts estimating it could be completed by the middle of next year, strengthening Beijing’s military control over the disputed South China Sea.
Satellite images reviewed by Reuters show grading work, piles of gravel and concrete, and compaction cranes in operation to build a full-scale runway that military attaches and security analysts say could be one of China’s most important offshore bases in the region.
The images, taken on Friday last week by commercial satellite imagery provider Vantor, also show a fully loaded gravel barge heading to a newly built wharf.
Photo: Screengrab from Damien Symon’s Instagram
A completed base at Antelope would be China’s most significant military expansion in the South China Sea in a decade, extending the reach of Chinese naval ships and military aircraft in a waterway that is an increasingly militarized arena of competition between Beijing and the US and its allies over Taiwan.
“If Fiery Cross [Yongshu Reef, 永暑礁] is the guide, I’d expect the runway paved in the first half of 2027 and a first landing by mid-2027, possibly earlier,” said Ben Lewis, founder of the open-source data platform PLATracker, referring to a 3km runway built on a reef in the disputed Spratly Islands (Nansha Islands, 南沙群島) further south in 2015.
“They’ve had 10 years to get faster at this,” he said.
Lewis said he had yet to note signs of excavation for possible ammunition and fuel storage, which a base of this scale would need.
The Chinese Ministry of National Defense did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.
China has yet to acknowledge construction of a new military base, while state media have said Antelope would serve civilian needs, such as weather forecasting and maritime and scientific research.
Vantor imagery analysts and open-source intelligence tracker Damien Symon, who first highlighted dredging at the reef in early January, also described the cranes as ones used to compact reclaimed or loose earth into foundations before paving.
In the northern part of the South China Sea, a future Antelope base would help extend deployments of a wide range of Chinese naval ships and military aircraft and help protect the approaches to Hainan Island, where China keeps its nuclear-armed ballistic missile submarines.
Reuters reported in late August that new installations have been sighted on a smaller islet near Antelope, but analysts have yet to gauge definitively the likely function of the three-pronged construction on Yagong Island (鴨公島).
The entire Paracels is also claimed by Taiwan and Vietnam. Taiwan’s defense and foreign ministries, as well as Vietnam’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters’ questions.
The progress on Antelope comes as China this week confirmed the creation of a new joint military support facility in Laos that could deepen Beijing’s presence in Southeast Asia.

The Philippine operation “disrupted the vessel’s unauthorized marine scientific research and compelled it to leave its loitering position,” said Jay Tarriela, Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson on South China Sea issues. The NHL Is Releasing Its Own ‘Hot’ Fanfic. Romance Lovers Hate It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:37:32 UTC
01:37:32 KST

For better or for worse, romance lovers have never been hornier for hockey. Now, the National Hockey League wants to cash in.
As part of its new “Hot for Hockey,” campaign, the NHL is rolling out romance novel-inspired short stories starring the league’s players on audiobook platforms. According to the Sports Business Journal, the league contacted popular hockey romance writers to write and narrate the 60 to 90 second stories, and will tap creators on BookTok, the romance-heavy literary subculture on TikTok, to promote the content.
The first batch of short stories, which dropped this week, feature players including the Philadelphia Flyers’ Trevor Zegras, the Carolina Hurricanes’ Sebastian Aho, and the Las Vegas Golden Knights’ Jack Eichel. They’re written by Pucking Wrong author C.R. Jane and more closely resemble back-cover summaries than actual romance novels. And, despite the nods to genre tropes, the players aren’t paired with romantic partners. Much more boringly, the stories appear to be a bid to get people to watch the actual games. The entirety of The Summer I Turned Gritty with Trevor Zegras is as follows:
“Trevor Zegras came to Philly looking for a fresh start. But after battling with Pittsburgh in the playoffs last year, he found out how gritty things could get. One heated summer later, Philly’s pretty boy is looking a whole lot grittier.”
Not all romance readers are thrilled about the campaign. Some argue that it makes players targets for sexual harassment. Others see the stories as cheap pandering that fails to engage with female and LGBTQ hockey fans’ concerns about homophobia and toxic masculinity in the sport.
“I cannot begin to describe the depths of my rage that this is actually happening,” Emily Rath, a best-selling hockey romance novelist, posted on Threads. “Yes, the NHL contacted me to participate. And I have never turned down an offer so fast.”
“They See Dollar Signs”
Romance novels focused on hockey players have been on the rise for years—the New York Public Library first highlighted the trend in 2019. Hockey romance burst into the mainstream with the massive success of romance novel-turned-streaming series Heated Rivalry, followed by Off Campus.
Jon Weinstein, a spokesperson for the NHL, tells WIRED in a statement that the campaign is a “playful nod to something that’s clearly going on in the cultural zeitgeist.”
“We were very proud to partner with real hockey authors, illustrators and voice actors in the space, and we’re grateful the players were willing to have a little fun with it too,” he says.
Yet many hockey romance fans applauded Rath and Chelsea Curto, the author of the steamy D.C. Stars series, for their refusal to participate in the campaign.
Rath, whose Jacksonville Rays series recounts a myriad of sexual relationships involving a fictional NHL team, said on Threads that the league’s slide deck for the campaign was filled with jokes she considered to be mockery of the genre, as well as what she alleged were AI cover renders. Curto also clocked the AI graphics, writing on Threads that it was probably for the best that she declined to be involved, as her books “can be very critical of the league.”
“They’re just encouraging the idea that women only care about hockey if it’s packaged like a romance novel,” Rath posted. “And they’re using popular authors and our credibility to launder their tarnished brand and lure in our readers.”
In Rath’s opinion, the NHL has failed to take accountability for or take action to address “racism, homophobia, and misogyny” in the league—a view shared by several hockey fans who spoke with WIRED. Lacey Conine, the founder of Double Hockey Stix—a clothing brand aimed at underrepresented hockey fans—says she initially thought news of the romance-centric campaign was satire.
“I had so many comments,” she says, “of people just being like, ‘This is disgusting. We hate this. What is this? How is the NHL this tone deaf?’”
In its current iteration, Conine says, the campaign feels like the NHL is “mocking you, and pandering to you, and making fun of you,” while failing to address fans’ concerns about aspects of hockey culture that can be hostile for fans that break the straight, white, male mold.
“I think that they see dollar signs,” Conine says. “They're trying to bring in Heated Rivalry fans—and then canceling Pride Nights. That tells you where they're at.”
While NHL commissioner Gary Bettman told reporters earlier this year that “every team does a Pride Night,” a handful of teams have moved away from themed nights that celebrate the LGBTQ community. That includes the Dallas Stars, which will not host a Pride Night this season, the team’s first time in five years without one. The Stars—which will host a night focused on romantic fantasy novel Iron Flame—did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. A portion of the Iron Flame event’s proceeds will go to the Trevor Project, a nonprofit focused on suicide prevention among LGBTQ youth.
The NHL banned players from wearing specialty-themed uniforms, such as Pride sweaters and tape, in June 2023. The decision on tape was later reversed, with the league emphasizing that it does not single out Pride specifically in its ban. The NHL also highlighted other partnerships with the LBGTQ groups, such as the annual Pride Cup.
Several female hockey fans say the NHL’s attempt to cater to romance readers falls flat because of how the sport’s governing bodies approach sexual assault allegations. Echo, a 35-year-old fan of the Montreal Canadiens who asked to be referred to by her first name to protect her privacy, says she believes the league aims to use “romanticized narratives to whitewash the insidious aspects of hockey culture and its players.”
The Globe and Mail reported in 2022 that Hockey Canada, the sport’s national governing body, had used players’ registration fees to build funds that covered certain expenses—among them, sexual assault claims, as well as other lawsuits. (A spokesperson for Hockey Canada, Jeremy Knight, said in an email that the organization has taken “considerable action to help drive systemic change” in the sport over the last four years.) Last year, five former Canadian Junior Hockey players were deemed eligible to play in the NHL after being acquitted in a high-profile sexual assault case. Three currently play in the league.
Players Can Face Sexual Harassment
NHL teams’ past hockey romance-centric campaigns have also raised concerns about the sexual harassment of players. In 2023, a player on the Seattle Kraken, Alexander Wennberg, and his wife, Felicia, posted about an influx in “predatory and exploiting” comments after the team’s social-media account published content aimed at BookTok.
The NHL said that players approved all content for the new campaign, which will be exclusively focused on hockey. (The NHL Players’ Association did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.) Still, Conine and other fans question if romance-inspired marketing focusing on specific players fuels an uncomfortable brand of sexualization and parasocial relationships.
“Fans are going to do what fans are going to do in their spaces and their time,” Conine says. But, when the league is “literally creating these narratives—I think there's a line there. And, I think they crossed it.”
Jess Rauchberg, a lecturer in the school of media and communication at the University of Leeds, notes that the campaign is essentially league-approved real-person fiction. Hockey RPF has existed since at least the late ’90s and often involves romantically or sexually coupling hockey players with other players.
“Breaking the fourth wall”—discussing RPF outside of fandom spaces or with players—has historically been seen as poor form. But as the NHL’s marketing efforts increasingly encourage fans to feel a personal connection with players, Rauchberg says, the division between RPF and marketing material has blurred.
A hockey fan herself, Rauchberg believes that hockey RPF and romance are popular because they allow fans to imagine a reality where their desires are represented. Sometimes that desire is for players to make out. Other times, it’s a league where players push back against rape culture and toxic masculinity.
“I describe them as fantasy novels,” Rauchberg says. “In real life, the players probably aren't like Ilya Rozanov, consent king.”
