What to Know About the Dengue Outbreak in the U.S.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:30:28 UTC
00:30:28 KST

This week, Hillsborough County in Florida, which includes Tampa, declared a state of emergency linked to a growing number of dengue cases. So far this year, around 485 cases have been reported in the state, according to the CDC. The disease, which is transmitted by mosquitoes, can cause serious flu-like illness, and one person in Florida has died in the outbreak so far this year, the state’s department of health told media outlets in September.
Seasonal outbreaks of the disease, which affects up to 400 million people worldwide annually, are not unusual in Florida, and they’re often linked to travelers. But this time is a little different, says Michael Johansson, an epidemiologist at Northeastern University. “This is the most locally acquired cases that we've seen in the state,” he says.
What is dengue?
Dengue, sometimes called dengue fever, is caused by a collection of viruses carried by mosquitoes, primarily Aedes aegypti. Dengue is endemic in a wide swath of the tropics, and usually, most Americans who have the infection acquire it outside of the U.S. during travel. Dengue symptoms can occur 5-7 days after being bitten and range from mild to severe. They may include painful body aches as well as fever and can last up to 10 days.
However, in parts of the U.S. where Aedes aegypti mosquitoes live, they can bite infected people and start to spread the disease locally. “The general pattern that we see—and we've seen this for more than a decade now—is that there are frequent travel-associated cases” in Florida, says Johansson. “We know we have the right vectors there, especially in southern Florida, where there's lots of Aedes aegypti, and there is some local transmission that occurs. Usually that looks like just one or two cases, but sometimes there are small outbreaks.”
In 2009, when two locally acquired infections were identified in Key West, public-health surveillance revealed that a substantial share of people in the town had markers in their blood showing a recent encounter with dengue, even if they hadn’t had symptoms. That suggests that in an outbreak, dengue is likely to be infecting more people than might immediately be clear from case counts.
One distinctive feature of dengue, however, is that the second time someone is infected is likely to be much worse than the first. Sometimes a second infection can progress to dengue hemorrhagic fever, which can involve bleeding and a drop in blood pressure, and is sometimes fatal.
This pattern, where the second exposure is more dangerous than the first, has complicated attempts to vaccinate people against the disease. In 2017, Sanofi Pasteur, the manufacturer of the dengue vaccine Dengvaxia, alerted the government of the Philippines that serious dengue infections might occur in people who had received the vaccine as their first exposure to the disease. No dengue vaccine is currently available in the U.S.; Dengvaxia was available starting in 2019 but in 2025 was discontinued by the manufacturer, which cited low demand.
Will dengue become endemic in the U.S.?
So far, dengue has not established a permanent foothold in the continental U.S., says Johansson. There are a few reasons why that might be: large numbers of people in Florida, where Aedes aegypti thrive, stay within air-conditioned spaces when they’re most active, which means chains of transmission tend to be short.
And the mosquitoes themselves are not particularly adventurous. They tend to stay close to home, within about a 100-meter range, so “it takes people to move the virus around,” says Johansson. If someone who’s infected doesn’t travel, the virus doesn’t either.
How can you protect yourself from dengue?
There is no cure for dengue; the only treatments are for symptoms. If you are in an area with mosquitoes that can carry dengue, the best way to protect yourself is to avoid mosquito bites. Keep windows closed or use screens, cover as much of your skin as possible with clothing when outdoors, and use mosquito repellent, says Johansson.
Keep yards free of containers that could fill with water and serve as breeding zones for mosquitoes. You’ll have to be vigilant: “These mosquitoes in particular, they can breed in a plastic bag that's collected a little bit of rainwater,” says Johansson.
Cooler weather brings relief. “We're getting to the time of year when things are cooling down, so we should expect a decrease in transmission,” says Johansson. “However, it's still hot in Florida right now”—so it’s not time to drop your guard yet.

Akhilesh Yadav's Rajya Sabha picks: Samajwadi Party's master strategy or 'PDA' contradiction?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:27:53 UTC
00:27:53 KST

SP chief Akhilesh Yadav has nominated Ram Gopal Yadav and Dhanraj Parimal Nathwani for the Rajya Sabha polls.
A 'family' man, a corporate executive, a possible third candidate and a high-stakes numbers game: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav's Rajya Sabha strategy has a bit of a test run for the 2027 UP assembly polls?His two picks have an element of continuity and also surprise. But then there is also an element of contradiction vis-à-vis the strong PDA pitch which has been the backbone of his 2027 poll strategy. Little wonder, then, that talk of a third nominee has begun even without the numbers, raising the stakes from a routine Rajya Sabha contest to an early test of Akhilesh's 2027 strategy.For the two sure-shot Rajya Sabha seats in Uttar Pradesh, Akhilesh Yadav has paired a familiar Samajwadi Party face with a distinctly unfamiliar political profile. Alongside his uncle Ram Gopal Yadav, the SP has nominated Dhanraj Parimal Nathwani, a senior Reliance Industries executive whose father, Parimal Nathwani, is a four-time Rajya Sabha MP backed by the BJP-led NDA. The choice immediately puts two very different images of the SP on the same ticket: its established family name and a corporate, professional profile from outside its traditional ecosystem.Nathwani's nomination also raises a larger question about the SP's direction as it prepares for the 2027 assembly election.
Is Nathwani's nomination an attempt to expand the SP's political appeal beyond its traditional social base, or does bringing a senior corporate executive into Parliament sit uneasily with a party increasingly building its politics for the 2027 polls around PDA, Pichhda, Dalit and Alpsankhyak? The question matters beyond the Rajya Sabha because the SP is simultaneously trying to project itself as the principal challenger to the BJP in Uttar Pradesh ahead of the 2027 assembly election.
Why Nathwani?
Akhilesh's second nomination is more than a surprise name on a candidate list. His corporate background gives the SP an opportunity to make a political argument it has not traditionally foregrounded. The party can present his candidature as evidence that its appeal is extending beyond its conventional political base and that people from the corporate and professional world now see the party as a credible political force.For a party preparing for 2027, that can also help reinforce a broader pitch around investment, jobs, industry and development alongside its social-justice agenda, which could become a significant part of the BJP and Yogi government's election campaign next year.Akhilesh, in fact, responded to queries over criticism of Nathwani's nomination by invoking Ram Manohar Lohia. "I think you should read about socialism again. I will give you a book by (Ram Manohar) Lohia," he said. He argued that socialist thought also talks about prosperity and equality and said governments across the country seek investment to generate economic growth."This time, it will be Lodhi vs Yogi (Adityanath)," he said on September 30.However, the same choice also produces a very different political reading.
Akhilesh's electoral strategy for the 2027 polls has been heavily identified with PDA, and Nathwani is not an obvious representative of the social coalition that phrase describes. That gives the opposition an opening to question why a party seeking votes in the name of backward classes, Dalits and minorities has chosen a senior corporate executive for one of its two Rajya Sabha seats.Mayawati, in fact, used the same charge against the SP. "SP wants votes in the name of PDA, but makes mostly its own family members and big capitalists MPs and MLAs," she said in a post on X.
State minister and Suheldev Bharatiya Samaj Party (SBSP) president Om Prakash Rajbhar also targeted Akhilesh, accusing him of repeatedly changing the framework for PDA. "Akhilesh Yadav keeps changing the PDA formula from time to time. Yesterday, he came up with the formula of a PDA family. 'P' now stands for 'Parivaar'," Rajbhar said, referring to Ram Gopal Yadav. "‘D’ stands for the 'Daulat', referring to Dhani Ram, who is affluent," Rajbhar said."Now, only 'A' remains, and he will bring in some criminal to represent it. The new PDA formula stands for 'Parivaar', 'Daulat' and 'Apradhi'," he added.The BJP, meanwhile, is watching Nathwani's nomination closely but has not mounted a similarly strong direct attack on the choice.
The third nomination suspense
The Uttar Pradesh assembly currently has 396 effective members after seven vacancies, putting the winning quota for a Rajya Sabha seat at 37 first-preference votes. The BJP has 255 MLAs, while the SP has 101 and Congress has two. The BJP's alliance partners include Apna Dal (S), RLD, SBSP and Nishad Party, giving the ruling camp a substantial numerical advantage. Broadly, the BJP-led camp is positioned to take the larger share of the 10 seats, while the SP-Congress combination has enough strength for two.The problem begins with the third candidate. The SP would need roughly nine additional first-preference votes to reach the quota for a third seat. That means Akhilesh cannot rely only on his existing alliance strength. He would have to attract support from outside it, potentially through smaller parties, independents or legislators willing to cross-vote.The suspense over that third candidate has now become central to the contest. SP MP Virendra Singh has said the party will field a third candidate, with the name to be decided and the nomination filed by October 5. Singh has also claimed that several BJP MLAs seeking SP tickets for the 2027 elections are in touch with the party.Akhilesh, meanwhile, has continued to leave room for political manoeuvring. Earlier in the day he described the Rajya Sabha election as "the time for coming together" and said it offered an opportunity to forget past mistakes and stand united with others on matters of principle.A day earlier, when asked whether the SP would field a third candidate, he declined to confirm the party's plans and said: "The BJP can do anything. They can field nine or even 10 candidates."The BJP, meanwhile, has made its own claims about SP legislators. Deputy CM Keshav Prasad Maurya has said that 25 SP MLAs are in contact with the BJP and warned that the party would "surprise" the SP.
A rehearsal for 2027
This Rajya Sabha election, along with the immediate parliamentary tally, will ultimately be about a strategic stress-test for 2027.In fielding Nathwani, Akhilesh Yadav is executing a high-stakes balancing act: attempting to reposition the Samajwadi Party as a pragmatic, investment-friendly government-in-waiting, without alienating the core PDA base that forms its electoral backbone. It is a gamble that risks handing opponents cheap ideological ammunition in exchange for broader institutional credibility and expanded corporate outreach.
Whether this move is remembered as a masterstroke of political expansion or a self-inflicted ideological contradiction will not be decided in the corridors of the Rajya Sabha. It will be decided by how effectively Akhilesh manages the cross-currents - maintaining the confidence of his grassroots voters while proving that his vision for Uttar Pradesh can accommodate both social justice and corporate capital. The upcoming floor vote, and the potential fight for a third seat, will offer the first real glimpse of whether that strategy can hold.

"The use of the term by private companies is not related to the state. Israelis staying in the Emirates are not stranded and do not need rescue."
UAE reactions to Israel's handling of Flydubai incident
In a separate report, Ynet cited a source close to the UAE government as saying that Israel was “exploiting the attack for political purposes” by delaying the return of Flydubai flights, adding that "The elections are managing the event, not logic."
“They are talking about ‘rescue flights,’ as if there is a war in the country,” the source said, adding that the UAE was willing to tighten procedures and conduct additional checks on flight crews.
“If passengers can be put on an Arkia flight, why not on a Flydubai flight?” the source said, according to Ynet.

The Omani co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities and later transferred to the UAE.
'Dangerous terrorist act'

North Macedonia Seeks Bulgaria’s Help to Unblock EU Accession
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:26:23 UTC
00:26:23 KST

North Macedonia will formally ask Bulgaria for a bilateral meeting next week in an effort to unblock its European Union accession process, Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski said after talks with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Skopje.
Mickoski said he had instructed Foreign Minister Timho Mucunski to send a diplomatic note requesting a meeting with his Bulgarian counterpart, Velislava Petrova, during his visit to Sofia for the Corridor 8 forum on Thursday, October 8.
The move follows von der Leyen’s call for Skopje to take a key step toward opening the first EU negotiation cluster, “Fundamentals.” She did not explicitly mention the constitutional amendments envisaged under the so-called French proposal, which would include Bulgarians in North Macedonia’s Constitution.
At a joint press conference with Mickoski, von der Leyen said the accession negotiations had started in 2022 after substantial work and dedication, but further progress depended on a new step by North Macedonia.
“North Macedonia has a place at the European table. I am aware of the sensitivities surrounding this, but I also want to be very clear: I want to state unequivocally the values Europe stands for. We welcome North Macedonia with its identity and language,” she said.
Von der Leyen added that Macedonian culture and language could enrich the EU, whose motto is “United in diversity.” She said the bloc took that principle seriously.
She also cited the Prespa Agreement as an example of political courage, saying North Macedonia had shown it could make bold decisions about its future. The agreement, reached by two countries that chose to turn the page and begin a new chapter together, paved the way for North Macedonia’s NATO membership, she said, describing the country as a valued ally.
At the beginning of her visit, von der Leyen said North Macedonia belonged in the EU and urged the country to act while the enlargement process was gaining momentum.
Mickoski said he and von der Leyen had discussed the challenges in North Macedonia’s relations with Bulgaria. He said Skopje wanted to address them through dialogue, goodwill and mutual respect, and expected EU institutions to help establish conditions for a sustainable solution without taking sides.
The prime minister said agreements and obligations should be clear and apply to everyone, while the accession process should not be reopened to new bilateral conditions, interpretations or demands. He said North Macedonia was not seeking to prolong the process but wanted it to proceed on a stable basis.
Mickoski also called for stronger political support from European institutions, saying his country wanted to join the EU and was working toward that goal. He said North Macedonia honored its obligations and carried out reforms, sometimes on time and sometimes with delays, but completed them.
Von der Leyen confirmed that the two sides had agreed on an initial step for the following week. She said a “pre-enlargement policy review” would also be presented during that week. The EU has roadmaps for countries that are already well advanced in accession talks and are opening and closing chapters, she said.
In her view, once the current impasse involving North Macedonia is resolved, the country could make rapid progress, although further work would remain.
BGNES reported that von der Leyen had told Skopje the country needed to take one key step to move forward and open the “Fundamentals” cluster. The agency also recalled that North Macedonia accepted the so-called French proposal in 2022, which was approved by all EU member states.
Under the negotiating framework, the inclusion of Bulgarians in North Macedonia’s Constitution is required for the country’s negotiations with the EU to begin. BGNES said the framework also requires Skopje to comply with the 2017 Treaty of Friendship, Good-Neighborliness, and Cooperation with Bulgaria and the two protocols attached to it.
The protocol from the second meeting of the Joint Intergovernmental Conference, signed three years ago by ministers Teodora Genchovska and Bujar Osmani, states that Skopje agreed to hold the next intergovernmental conference with the EU only after Bulgarians are included among the constituent peoples in the Constitution’s preamble and in two of its articles.
The same protocol records the North Macedonian government’s commitment that nothing in its Constitution may be interpreted as grounds to interfere in Bulgaria’s internal affairs in order to protect the status and rights of people who are not citizens of North Macedonia. BGNES said this provision means, both de facto and de jure, that Skopje will not seek recognition of a “Macedonian minority” in Bulgaria.
The protocol also covers measures against hate speech targeting Bulgarians and Bulgaria, the rehabilitation of victims of the communist regime in Macedonia, and the opening of the archives of the Yugoslav security services.

USA Imposes Sanctions on A7 Network, Which Supplied Components and Equipment to Russia’s Military-Industrial Complex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:26:00 UTC
00:26:00 KST

The U.S. Department of the Treasury has imposed sanctions against the A7 shadow banking network, which is linked to Russia and Iran.
This was reported on the department’s website.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) added the A7 network to its sanctions list as a transnational criminal organization.
According to the department, the network is headed by Ilan Shor, a Moldovan-Israeli oligarch who is already under sanctions and has been convicted, and the system itself was used to circumvent sanctions and launder money.
The A7 network was used to finance the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Hamas group, as well as to conduct transactions related to the sale of Iranian oil and the purchase of weapons.
The network used intermediaries in third countries, fictitious trade documents, and hidden VPN networks to funnel money through the international financial system.
All assets and property of the A7 network in the United States or under the control of U.S. citizens have been frozen, and any transactions involving them are prohibited under penalty of civil and criminal sanctions.
As a reminder, A7 developed a large-scale network of front companies that allows Russia to circumvent Western sanctions and purchase goods for its military-industrial complex
According to Western intelligence reports, Shor oversees these activities under the direct supervision of the Russian president’s administration.
Kyrgyzstan has long served as the main financial hub for the A7 schemes. Over $100 million in U.S. dollars and Chinese yuan passed through the bank accounts of local front companies.
To throw international oversight off track, the network created a special AI-based program that automatically forged invoices and customs documents. Instead of dual-use electronics, the documents listed civilian goods, such as car mats or light boxes.
Among the purchased goods, investigators discovered steel production equipment from the Chinese company Xi’an Heavy Equipment, which is used in the manufacture of ammunition and armor. Payments were also made for Nvidia servers for AI development and video components for Walksnail drones.

Trans-Caspian Corridor sea freight exceeds 4.5 mln metric tons in seven months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:25:27 UTC
00:25:27 KST

MINSK, October 2. /TASS/. The growth in sea freight along the Trans-Caspian Corridor has been impressive, with volumes exceeding 4.5 mln metric tons in the first seven months of this year, 60% more than in all of last year, Chairman of the Board of the Eurasian Economic Commission (EEC) Bakytzhan Sagintayev told reporters following a meeting of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council.
According to him, the heads of government discussed the development of transport infrastructure along the east-west and north-south routes, including in conjunction with China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Sagintayev noted that a common transport space is being actively developed within the EAEU, with the development of Eurasian transport corridors, including rail, road, and port infrastructure, among the key areas of this work. The EEC Board chairman noted that these corridors account for around 70% of transit freight traffic, making it crucial to synchronize the development of national sections of transport infrastructure in each country.
"In 2025, freight traffic increased in virtually all [EAEU] member states. In particular, 21.5 mln metric tons were transported along the North-South Corridor. The growth in sea freight along the Trans-Caspian route is impressive. In the first seven months of 2026, its volume exceeded 4.5 mln metric tons. For comparison, that is 60% more than in all of 2025. According to expert estimates, infrastructure modernization will increase the capacity of the eastern route of this corridor to 20 mln metric tons by 2030. This route has significant potential given our cooperation with China, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, and Mongolia," he said.
In addition, the second stage of introducing electronic document management at Russian and Kazakh seaports has been completed, with paper documents becoming a thing of the past, Sagintayev said. The EEC head noted that the introduction of digital tools simplifies procedures and reduces costs for businesses, while accelerating the movement of goods as much as possible.
The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor, runs through China, Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and onward to European countries. Container shipments along the route use both rail and maritime transport.

Damage to refineries decreasing — Novak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:21:44 UTC
00:21:44 KST

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Challenges arising in individual economic sectors, including oil refining, transport and logistics and agriculture, are in the sphere of higher attention and control by the government, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said when speaking in the Federation Council, the upper house of the Russian legislative assembly.
TASS put together key statements of the deputy prime minister.
Russian economy
The slowdown of national economy’s growth rates after high figures in 2023-2024 is an expectable phase. "Following high growth rates in 2023-2024, the economy moved to more moderate dynamic. This is an anticipated normalization phase after overheating and a condition for inflation decline at the same time," Novak said.
The current investment situation in Russia is the correction after the large-scale increase by almost 40% in 2021-2024. "Investments are definitely a factor of long-term growth. We forecast their decline this year, a minor increase by 0.2% next year, and growth by 2.5% and 3% in 2028-2029. This is the correction after the rise by almost 40% during the period by 2024," the official said.
The economy continues to be supported by revenues of households and the consumer demand. "In August, the GDP increased by 0.8%, and by 0.6% year-on-year during eight months of this year. According to the updated outlook, we expect approximately the same GDP level by the end of this year," Novak noted.
Requirements to efficiency of implemented projects have become more stringent currently. "The recent stage goes from a high base and increases efficiency requirements exactly for the new projects," said the deputy prime minister.
The unemployment rate in Russia remains historically low and equals 2.2%.
Government tasks
The task at present is "to restore sustainable growth rates of the economy and ensure further growth of citizens’ well-being," Novak said. "We plan to this end to expand domestic production, increase efficiency of resources utilization and create conditions for new investments," he added.
Difficulties arising in individual economic sectors are in the sphere of higher attention and control by the government. "Current objective difficulties are present in individual sectors," Novak said. "This refers to oil refining, transport and logistical sphere, and agriculture," the official said.
Fuel market situation
The government promptly took a wide range of measures to saturate the domestic market with fuel. "The temporary ban on gasoline and diesel fuel exports, organized imported fuel supplies, revised rules of exchange trading to restrain wholesale prices, and decision made on fiscal stimulation of extra production and import of fuel," Novak said.
The gasoline import measure is temporary as national fuel production is usually 10-15% higher than the demand. The diesel fuel market is now balanced.
Russia covered fuel needs of its northern region in full scope. "We supported fall field work of agricultural producers and fully supported northern import requirements of regions," said Novak.
Export fuel situation
Russia will partly authorize diesel fuel exports in case of overproduction. |Although we have just recently renewed the export ban for October, we will monitor the situation and in case of diesel overproduction, we will consider partial opening of exports," Novak said.
Russia will not accumulate too much fuel because it will lead to a decline in refining and output of other products. "It is a normal situation because since we produce 80% more diesel than consume in the domestic market, we support the domestic market and cannot accumulate more surplus than available tankage. Otherwise refining volumes have to be lowered, and this may adversely affect the output of other products enjoying demand," he added.
The country may return to gasoline exports when the domestic market situation stabilizes.
Operations of refineries
Authorities are currently exploring measures to support oil refineries and postpone their upgrade deadlines. "[Proposals] of the Russian Energy Ministry in cooperation with other federal executive authorities to are now being explored to support oil refineries that cannot currently meet the schedule and upgrade agreements signed with the Ministry of Energy, with the Federal Antimonopoly Service, due to objective reasons," Novak said.
Government agencies and oil companies completed a huge amount of work to protect oil refineries, which already led to a significant decline in damage. "We have seen lately that damage from continuous raids against refineries is much more mitigated. Passive protection was established, corresponding to threat models. Active protection by air defense assets was strengthened," the official said.
Oil companies managed to quicker put refineries into operation again after attacks. Four Russian refineries were attacked this night and only one refinery is currently estimating damage there. "We actually thwarted all the attacks against our plants," Novak noted.
Forecast
Inflation in Russia may total 6.8% as of the end of this year, the deputy prime minister noted. "Concerning inflation, it totaled 4.93% year-to-date. In annual terms, growth is 6.26% as of the end of September, we forecast 6.8% by the end of the year," Novak said.
The national GDP growth rate is expected to be 1.4% this year with gradual achievement of 2.4% in 2029.
Fuel prices and global demand
Non-oil and gas exports is expected to grow from $220 bln to $260 bln.
Global markets currently experience diesel fuel shortage. "Prices are exorbitantly high in global markets, exactly for diesel. We see diesel prices in Europe, in the United States of America break records," Novak said. Such situation has occurred due to sanction restrictions, attacks against the refining infrastructure and closing of logistical transport routes.
OPEC+ countries continue assessing maximal production capabilities of the states participating in the agreement. "This effort is still underway, as far as I know," Novak noted.

India: Authorities trampling on human rights in crackdown on electoral roll protests

Responding to the imposition of prohibitory orders, the detention of hundreds of protesters, and the suspension of internet and public transport services in Delhi and Mumbai amid peaceful protests demanding the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner of India, Aakar Patel, Chair of Board, Amnesty International India, said:
“The right to protest is not dependent on government approval. It is protected by the Indian Constitution and international human rights law.
“Prohibitory orders like Section 163 of India’s criminal procedure law, which grant temporary emergency powers to restrict gatherings in the name of public order, have become a convenient way for authorities to routinely prevent peaceful protests.
“Detaining people simply because they intend to protest is a blatant attack on the rights to liberty and freedom of peaceful assembly. Detentions must have a lawful basis and cannot be arbitrary or discriminatory. Those arbitrarily detained for solely exercising their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly must be released at once, and authorities must guarantee their right to protest.
The right to protest is not dependent on government approval
Aakar Patel, Chair of Board, Amnesty International India
“Cutting internet connectivity during a protest also raises grave human rights concerns. The internet is now part of how people exercise their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. Protesters use it to organize, communicate, share information, and document events. We urge the authorities to immediately restore online access.”
Background
The protesters led by Cockroach Janta Party, student unions and opposition parties are demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation amid controversy over the Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. More than 130 million people have been deleted from electoral rolls since 2025.
The protesters allege that the exercise risks wrongful removal of eligible voters and have questioned the transparency and impartiality of the process. The controversy intensified after reports that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections on 14 occasions over 10 months to decisions concerning voter additions, deletions and electoral systems.
The Election Commission claims that the revision is intended to verify voter eligibility and has denied allegations of political manipulation.

Russia Plans Up to 1,000 Strikes to Cripple Ukraine’s Energy Grid This Winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:20:55 UTC
00:20:55 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Plans Up to 1,000 Strikes to Cripple Ukraine’s Energy Grid This Winter
Russia is preparing what Ukrainian officials describe as its most ambitious campaign yet to cripple Ukraine’s power, heating, and water systems this winter, The New York Times reported on October 2.
The assessment is based on a document Ukrainian Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal recently presented to European partners in Paris. Two people familiar with the briefing told The New York Times that Shmyhal described it as an intercepted Russian plan for a methodical campaign against Ukraine’s energy system.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Last winter, Russian missile and drone strikes repeatedly targeted Ukraine’s energy and civilian infrastructure, leaving large parts of Kyiv without electricity, heating, and water in subzero temperatures. UNITED24 Media reported that one January attack alone left more than 1 million people without power and over 4,000 apartment buildings without heat.
According to the document obtained by The New York Times, Russia could use up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and guided bombs against electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants, boiler houses, and other infrastructure.
The plan also envisages attacks on electrical switchyards connecting Ukraine’s three operating nuclear power plants to the national grid. The facilities are located less than a mile from the reactors, The New York Times noted.
By striking those switchyards, Russia would seek to force the nuclear plants offline without directly attacking the reactors themselves.
The document also describes attacks on Ukraine’s water infrastructure, including pumping stations and wastewater treatment plants, using dozens of ballistic missiles and guided bombs. The New York Times wrote that Russia has not previously targeted such facilities on that scale.
Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa are identified as priority targets. The document outlines plans to reduce electricity and heating supplies in those cities by as much as 90% while severely disrupting sewage systems.
The New York Times could not independently authenticate the document, which is dated August and written in Russian. However, the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, has publicly threatened an expanded campaign against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure this winter.
“Our partners, like us, were struck by its cynicism, by this cold, terrorist calculation of how to destroy our energy sector,” Shmyhal stated previously when discussing the document publicly.
The apparent plan is divided into three stages, The New York Times reported. The first would target substations near Ukraine’s western border that allow the country to import electricity from Europe.
The second stage would focus on hydroelectric power plants, while the third would attempt to disconnect Ukraine’s three operating nuclear power plants from the grid. The document estimates that the campaign could eliminate nearly 15 gigawatts of generating capacity.
Ukraine has spent recent months strengthening critical infrastructure, repairing power plants and substations, and installing smaller distributed energy facilities that are harder to destroy. Authorities have also reinforced parts of the grid to reroute electricity when transmission infrastructure is damaged.
Those preparations remain vulnerable to renewed attacks. Energy analyst Maria Tsaturian told The New York Times that only a small number of major strikes could eliminate much of the five gigawatts of generating capacity Ukraine restored in recent months.
Russia has already begun renewed attacks on energy infrastructure ahead of winter. Before dawn on September 30, missiles and drones struck a major thermal power plant and other facilities, leaving parts of Kyiv without electricity and water, The New York Times reported.
Ukraine endured prolonged outages during the previous winter as Russian attacks repeatedly damaged power and heating facilities. In Kyiv, residents sometimes went 12 hours or more without electricity, while outages also disrupted water supplies, elevators, and heating systems in apartment buildings.
UNITED24 Media previously reported that Kyiv was stockpiling emergency food and drinking water ahead of the 2026–2027 winter, preparing for possible prolonged blackouts caused by renewed Russian strikes on energy infrastructure. The city also planned to expand emergency food reserves and support Points of Invincibility during extended outages.

Mexico to prohibit presidents from holding dual citizenship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:18:15 UTC
00:18:15 KST

Mexico to prohibit presidents from holding dual citizenship
MEXICO CITY, Oct 2 - A Mexican constitutional reform to require presidential candidates to renounce any dual citizenships is fast-tracking toward final approval, despite criticism that the measure backed by the ruling party infringes on political rights and aims to block opposition rivals.
President Claudia Sheinbaum has defended the initiative — which would also apply to state governors and the Mexico City mayor — as a safeguard against foreign interference.
"Presidents of Mexico can only have one flag, one homeland, one people to defend," Sheinbaum said during her daily news conference on Wednesday.
Its critics, however, say it erects hurdles for dual-national politicians and could hamper generational succession within Sheinbaum's ruling Morena party and those of its allies, where several figures hold foreign passports.
The constitutional changes were swiftly approved this week by a majority of Mexico's 32 state legislatures, backed by Morena lawmakers and their coalition after passing both chambers of the national Congress. Lawmakers must now issue a formal "declaration of constitutionality" before publishing the text in the official gazette.
Mexico's current constitution does not explicitly bar presidents and governors from holding dual citizenship. In Latin America, only two countries have such bans: Cuba and Venezuela.
The United States allows dual citizens to become president, but the issue has proven politically sensitive. Ted Cruz renounced his Canadian citizenship in 2014 ahead of his 2016 presidential run.
PATRIOTISM OR POLITICAL SUBTERFUGE?
Sheinbaum and her administration say that the citizenship proposal is part of the party's broader emphasis on defending national sovereignty amid mounting pressure from the administration of US President Donald Trump.
But its critics have questioned both the speed of its passage and its political intentions ahead of the 2030 presidential election. The requirement would take effect for prospective candidates in 2028, meaning it would not affect current state governors or candidates competing in the 2027 midterms.
Sheinbaum's office did not respond to requests for comment.
Mexican billionaire Ricardo Salinas, a prominent tycoon and fierce critic of the administration who has repeatedly hinted at political ambitions, has railed against the bill and suggested that it was designed specifically to thwart his possible run.
"Are they willing to screw over millions of Mexicans who migrated north... solely out of a sick desire to block a Mexican whom they fear and hate from the presidency?" Salinas wrote in a social media post in August.
On Monday, Salinas appeared to reverse course, writing on social media that he did not hold dual citizenship.
Reuters could not confirm whether Salinas holds a second citizenship. A spokesperson for Grupo Salinas declined to comment, describing his citizenship status as a private matter.
A source within the Morena party, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters the reform was aimed at hampering a possible run by Salinas.
Larry Rubin, president of the American Society of Mexico, who holds dual US and Mexican citizenship, has also condemned the measure.
"Having two nationalities does not make anyone less Mexican," Rubin said. "Do not turn your back on millions of dual nationals, migrants, and binational families."
Mexican ambassador to the United States, Roberto Lazzeri, however, said the measure is not a referendum on dual citizenship, but rather a specific tightening of the requirements for the highest political offices.
"Holding dual nationality does not make anyone less Mexican," he wrote on social media on Tuesday.
But, he added, "the greater the public responsibility, the greater the obligations toward the country." REUTERS

Turkish Aerospace Industries (TAI) is preparing to launch the second prototype of its fifth-generation fighter jet Kaan before the end of the year, while the craft is being tested for high-speed taxi maneuvers, the firm’s general manager told Anadolu.
Mehmet Demiroglu, speaking on the sidelines of the aerospace and tech event TEKNOFEST Southeast, stated that all system checks on the P1, the first Kaan prototype, have been completed and the craft is slated to fly within weeks, while the assembly and testing for the P2 prototype continue.
“We’ll launch the P1 and the P2 immediately after, if there are no setbacks or delays, since we’ve already done the slow taxi tests for the P2,” he said.

“We will sign new export agreements for both the training and the light-armed attack configurations of the Hurkus in the coming months and years,” he noted. “The production batch for the Azerbaijani delivery will be produced here, while we will deliver products that we’re making for the Turkish Air Force to ensure speedy delivery.”
“We’ve applied what we learned from the first aircraft to the new platforms and prototypes, and they’re nearly complete, as we’ve completed over 600 hours of flight time with two prototypes, while the third made its first flight last month and the fourth is on the way,” he said, noting that the first delivery of the mass-produced Hurjet units will be provided to the Turkish Air Force by late 2027 and will then be allocated to fulfill export deliveries to Spain by late 2028.
Demiroglu stated that the manufacturing architecture of the firm is being overhauled into a tiered subcontracting model to outsource up to 70% of part and subassembly fabrication, distributing structural workloads like wings, tails, and fuselages among seven to eight domestic partners to meet delivery deadlines while limiting production costs.
Efforts are also ongoing for the Air SOJ airborne electronic warfare project as well, with flight qualification trials currently underway for two specialized platforms.
TAI aims to deliver its first two operational Air SOJ platforms next year in coordination with Aselsan and the Defense Industries Agency (SSB).

generative code patterns trace across MM collective’s ceramic flower vases

generative code patterns trace across MM collective’s ceramic flower vases
mm collective is a dialogue between graphic and product design, unfolding through three ceramic vases inspired by the peony, lily, and tulip.
MMcollective: a series of three flower vases by MK Designers
MM Collective is a collaboration between graphic designer Michaela Zdeňková and product designer Marek Kounovský, MK Designers, that explores the relationship between graphic and product design through a series of three ceramic vases. The collection draws on the peony, lily, and tulip, with each flower carrying a personal significance for the two designers.
Each vase combines a physical form developed through product design with a graphic layer created through generative coding. A specific flower serves as the starting point for an original generative process, in which its natural form is translated into an abstract structure through digital code. The resulting pattern is then transferred onto the surface of the ceramic vase.
Flowers Become Abstract Patterns Through Generative Coding
The original floral motifs are not immediately recognizable in the finished objects. Instead, each flower functions as input data that moves through a sequence from natural form to digital code and finally to a physical object. This process creates a connection between the organic and the digital, while bringing graphic language into the three-dimensional form of the vase.
The selection of flowers is also connected to the relationship between the two designers and their shared habit of giving each other flowers. The peony represents the graphic designer’s favorite flower, the lily the product designer’s, while the tulip was selected by both. Together, the three vases connect this personal dimension with two distinct design disciplines, examining the relationship between graphic and spatial design, code and material, and natural form and digital transformation.

designer: MK Designers | @mkdesignersss
lead designers: Michaela Zdeňková and Marek Kounovský | @marek.kounovsky

Iraq: Authorities must guarantee fair trials for 5,700 detainees and protect child rights in mass trials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:15:14 UTC
00:15:14 KST

Iraqi authorities must guarantee full due process rights for more than 5,700 detainees transferred to Iraq from north-east Syria, and ensure the urgent protection of child rights, Amnesty International said today, ahead of an upcoming trial session on 5 October.
The transferred individuals are being prosecuted for their suspected affiliation with the armed group calling itself Islamic State, following their relocation to Iraq between late January and February 2026. The transferred group includes 5,704 individuals from 67 countries, including 16 Arab countries with thousands of Syrian nationals and hundreds of Iraqis, 19 from European Union countries, and 32 other foreign nationalities, and at least 157 juveniles under the age of 18.
”The opening of these trials places an enormous responsibility on Iraqi authorities to uphold international human rights law and standards of all those being prosecuted at every stage of judicial proceedings,” said Grazia Careccia, Deputy Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa at Amnesty International.
“While we acknowledge the security challenges and immense logistical strain this situation places on Iraq’s legal system, justice cannot be delivered through flawed procedures, forced confessions, or mass prosecutions. The Iraqi government must ensure that every single detainee receives a fair trial grounded strictly in individualized criminal responsibility, or else be released.”
In judicial proceedings, Iraqi authorities have said that prosecutions will move forward under Penal Code No. 111 of 1969 and Anti-Terrorism Law No. 13 of 2005. This counterterrorism framework has drawn long-standing criticism for its overly broad definitions of terrorist activity and for its provision of the death penalty, including for acts that encompass mere membership or support of a group.
The Iraqi government must ensure that every single detainee receives a fair trial grounded strictly in individualized criminal responsibility, or else be released.
Grazia Careccia, Amnesty International
In past proceedings, Iraqi courts have repeatedly demonstrated an over-reliance on confessions extracted under torture and ill-treatment. Amnesty International has documented widespread patterns where detainees transferred from north-east Syria were subjected to severe beatings, electric shocks, forced stress positions, and suffocation to compel self-incriminating statements.
“Iraq’s history of relying on torture-tainted confessions in terrorism cases makes strict adherence to international safeguards an urgent necessity,” said Grazia Careccia.
“The Supreme Judicial Council must exclude any evidence obtained through torture or ill-treatment and thoroughly investigate all allegations of human rights violations. Defendants must be granted prompt access to legal counsel, qualified interpreters, and public hearings. Crucially, given that trials in Iraq could result in the death penalty any failure to guarantee fair trial standards carries irreversible, fatal consequences. Amnesty International opposes the death penalty in all circumstances and calls on the Iraqi authorities not to impose or carry out death sentences, regardless of the offence or circumstances.”
The fact that at least 157 children are among the detainees standing trial also highlights the need for a child-rights-centered response that strictly adheres to international child rights and child justice standards, including the best interests of the child and child protection.
Many children and young adults were originally detained in north-east Syria under broad, indiscriminate circumstances. They include boys as young as 11 years old who were separated from their mothers in detention camps. International standards dictate that children recruited or used by armed groups must be recognized primarily as victims of human rights violations.
Criminal prosecutions of individuals for conduct allegedly committed while they were under 18 must remain an absolute exception, reserved only for credible allegations of crimes under international law or serious violent crimes under domestic law. In such cases, alternatives to judicial proceedings as well as community-based and noncustodial alternatives to detention must be considered, and sentencing options should support the child’s rehabilitation and reintegration, with detention used only as a measure of last resort and for the shortest appropriate period of time. Children should never be prosecuted for mere association with an armed group.
Background
The recent transfers follow years of arbitrary, indefinite detention in north-east Syria, where tens of thousands of men, women, and children were held without charge or trial in substandard facilities and camps following the military defeat of the Islamic State. Trial proceedings for the transferred individuals began on 20 September and will resume on 5 October.
As documented in Amnesty International’s 2024 report Aftermath: Injustice, Torture and Death in Detention in North-east Syria, detainees faced severe overcrowding, inadequate food and a complete lack of healthcare, leading to outbreaks of communicable diseases such as tuberculosis, which resulted in hundreds of deaths at facilities like Panorama prison in Hasakah.
Iraq continues to execute dozens of individuals annually, including following convictions under broad counterterrorism laws. In 2024, Iraqi courts issued more than 200 death sentences, and at least 63 executions were carried out, marking a four-fold increase from the previous year. Although executions slowed briefly following the passage of a General Amnesty Law in early 2025, judicial executions resumed in early 2026, raising severe international concern over systemic due process violations.

G7 agrees to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel after Trump pressure
Trump welcomed the announcement in a post on Truth Social
The Group of Seven major economies on Friday agreed to release 100 million barrels of crude oil and fuel from emergency reserves over four months to ease soaring fuel prices, following pressure from US President Donald Trump.
French President Emmanuel Macron announced the agreement on Friday and said participating countries had also agreed not to restrict oil exports.
The releases will begin immediately and be coordinated through the International Energy Agency, with a “substantial” release of diesel reserves within the first 20 days, according to a G7 statement.
The White House had reportedly asked Europe to unlock at least 100 million barrels and threatened to ban US diesel exports if European countries failed to comply.
Trump welcomed the announcement in a post on Truth Social.
“Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately. Thank you for your attention to this matter!” he wrote.
The agreement came as Trump sought to bring down high diesel prices ahead of November’s midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.
G7 leaders said the releases would take account of commitments already fulfilled under an earlier pledge made in March.
The Wall Street Journal reported that wars in the Middle East and Ukraine had disrupted shipments from regions that normally account for almost a third of global diesel exports, driving up costs for businesses, farmers and households. Analysts cited by the newspaper said restrictions on US exports would offer only temporary relief.

US Coast Guard says it intercepted ship carrying fuel to Cuba
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:13:23 UTC
00:13:23 KST

The US Coast Guard has announced that it intercepted a large cargo ship carrying fuel bound for Cuba, as the Trump administration’s crippling oil embargo against the island nation continued.
The vessel named Grace was stopped on 5 September in the Caribbean Sea between Cuba and Mexico while using tactics to evade authorities, the Coast Guard said. The New York Times reported that the ship was 91 metres (300ft) long.
“Grace was transiting to Cuba, carrying fuel, and was believed to be employing tactics common amongst the dark fleet,” the Coast Guard said in a statement.
A Coast Guard team boarded the ship and escorted it to Mexico, where a Mexican navy inspection team “confirmed the presence of large quantities of fuel in the vessel’s ballast tanks”. The vessel was also carrying several containers believed to contain illicit fuel, the statement said.
The Trump administration has openly stated that its goal is to change Cuba’s government. A US-imposed oil blockade implemented earlier this year has put the country under severe strain as it contends with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.
Oil shipments from Cuba’s traditional suppliers, Venezuela and Mexico, ended abruptly after the US ousted the Venezuelan president, Nicolás Maduro, in January. US Coast Guard cutters patrol the waters off Cuba, while sanctions and threats have dissuaded tankers from even setting sail.
“The high seas are not a sanctuary for lawlessness,” Adm Kevin Lunday, the commandant of the Coast Guard, said. “Dark fleet actors who employ deceptive tactics to engage in illicit activities will not evade justice.”
The statement did not say how authorities knew the fuel was headed to Cuba or how much fuel Grace was carrying.

Spanish lawmakers vote down affordable housing bills in blow to Sanchez’s government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:12:47 UTC
00:12:47 KST

Spanish lawmakers vote down affordable housing bills in blow to Sanchez’s government
Demonstrators protesting against Spain's housing crisis reacted with fury on Friday after the country's parliament rejected two bills put forward by the government that centre-left Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez hoped would address their concerns. Rents have doubled over the past decade, with average prices now almost equivalent to the average young person's monthly salary.
Spain's parliament on Friday shot down government bills aimed at quelling nationwide protests over a housing crisis that were sparked by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman.
The lawmakers' rejection of the two measures dealt a blow to Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and his centre-left government ahead of general elections scheduled for 2027.
"Shame!" yelled hundreds of protesters outside the parliament building as the bills were quashed. Fresh demonstrations were due to take place across Spain on Saturday.
Watch moreMaricarmen vs the 'vultures': A 'social tragedy' mobilising Spaniards
Spain has been gripped by protests for a week, including a tent city set up in the heart of Madrid, to rail against increasingly unaffordable housing for both tenants and buyers and demand swift action from the government.
Rents have doubled over the last decade with average prices reaching €1,176 ($1,323) a month, equivalent to 98.7 percent of the average salary for a young person, according to the Youth Council of Spain.
That grievance, which has repeatedly surfaced, was ignited on September 23 by the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid apartment she had occupied for around seven decades.
The investment company owning her building ended up reversing her eviction this week, but only after her case had become a symbol of growing frustration over housing affordability.
Protesters outside parliament said they backed calls for a general strike to pressure politicians after the rejection of the bills.
"We saw this coming, but even if we expected it we are going to have to fight on," said David Llamas, a 26-year-old living with his parents because of rents that were too high.
'Huge mistake'
Sanchez, just before the two votes, exhorted lawmakers to "forget for a moment political calculations" and urged them to back the measures in the parliament, where his coalition lacks a majority.
The bills included an automatic renewal of rental contracts when they expire and measures aimed at restricting the eviction of vulnerable tenants. They also targeted so-called vulture funds: investment firms that buy properties at low prices in pursuit of higher returns.
Passage of the government's bills was put in jeopardy on Thursday when the Catalan separatist Junts party said it opposed both measures. Sanchez's government relies on Junts's seven lawmakers to pass legislation.
With the opposition conservative Popular Party and far-right Vox party also rejecting them, the government bills failed on Friday.
The first was scuppered with 178 votes against and 172 in favour, and the second with 184 against and 166 in favour.
One minister, Pablo Bustinduy, in charge of social rights, said as he left the parliamentary chamber that the three parties voting against the measures "have made a huge mistake and will pay for this at the polls".
The government had negotiated the legislation with the business-friendly Junts party, but the Catalan party said Thursday it wanted the bills to be redrafted.
Junts argued that the proposals unfairly lumped small landlords who rely on rental income together with profit-driven real-estate companies, and could have "negative and irreversible" effects.
The Spanish Tenants' Union, which has organised many of the protests, has called for a general strike and for the tent camp set up in Madrid's central Puerta del Sol to remain until its demands are met.
Friday's defeat increases pressure on Sanchez's minority government and could intensify opposition calls for an early election.
The leader of the far-right Vox party, Santiago Abascal, said earlier Friday that "the sooner elections are held, the better".
Sanchez has repeatedly ruled out calling an early vote.
Recent opinion polls have generally placed the opposition Popular Party ahead of the Socialists.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

Israel's Supreme Court on Friday reinstated an Arab party to the election ballot, potentially giving it a pivotal role in the vote, hours after an Arab-Israeli politician withdrew his candidacy following court pressure.
An electoral committee made up of lawmakers in September had voted to disqualify from the Oct. 27 election candidates including those from the United Arab List, which had joined a motley government in 2021 that briefly removed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from power.
The Supreme Court unanimously overruled the lawmakers and allowed on the ballot the United Arab List, as well as another Arab party.
The justices, in a 7-2 vote, also reinstated the candidacy of Ofer Cassif, a far-left sitting Jewish member of parliament who is a relentless critic of Israel's mistreatment of Palestinians.
The two dissenting justices said that Cassif supported "armed struggle against the state of Israel" as grounds for disqualification.
The Supreme Court has nearly always overruled the committee of lawmakers who vote to ban candidates.
But at a hearing Thursday, justices suggested they would back the ban on Sami Abu Shehadeh, who heads the left-wing Palestinian Balad Party.
Abu Shehadeh late Thursday withdrew his candidacy in the face of near certain defeat in the court.
His party, in a statement, said that a court-ordered rather than voluntary removal of Abu Shehadeh from the election would have had "grave consequences for the country's political and parliamentary life".
A far-right ally of Netanyahu led the charge to disqualify Abu Shehadeh over an article after Hamas's attack on October 7, 2023, the deadliest in the history of Israel, which responded with a massive offensive in Gaza.
Abu Shehadeh in the article said that the attack was an "important historical event." He denied he was supporting the attack.
Israeli-Arabs, descendants of Palestinians who fled or were forced out when the state of Israel was created in 1948, make up about 20 percent of the country's population.
Most identify as Palestinians and until 2021 had stayed out of Israeli coalition politics.
The United Arab List, known by its acronym Raam, has taken the unprecedented step in the latest election of also running a Jewish Zionist candidate, Yoav Segalovitz, who earned popularity in Arab communities for his police work in curbing crime.

Leaked Video of Uruguayan Kingpin Triggers Mass Arrests Across Bolivian Justice System
Unknown

15:11:00 UTC
00:11:00 KST

Reported by
Even from inside an American prison cell, the Uruguayan drug kingpin Sebastián Marset managed to shatter the highest echelons of Bolivian justice this week.
The sudden release on Wednesday of two video recordings from Marset’s arrest in March sparked a sweeping law enforcement purge, leading to the detention of 14 high-ranking figures — including prosecutors, police commanders, the country’s attorney general, and the former national director of Bolivia’s special counter-narcotics unit.
The operation included raids on prosecutorial offices in Sucre, La Paz, and Santa Cruz after the newly surfaced video footage showed Marset claiming that the attorney general, Roger Mariaca, and other top law enforcement figures had shielded his criminal syndicate.
Bolivia’s Minister of Government, Marco Antonio Oviedo, described the operation as the dismantling of a “criminal organization entrenched in the justice system” that was dedicated to “protecting, encouraging, and supporting narco-terrorism.”
In the recording, captured at Viru Viru International Airport in Santa Cruz shortly before his extradition to the United States to face federal charges of drug trafficking and money laundering, a handcuffed Marset told agents, “I used to talk to Mariaca because he controls the Prosecutor’s Office.”
Within minutes of the video’s distribution on Wednesday night, law enforcement officers apprehended Mariaca and Alberto Zeballos, the departmental prosecutor for Santa Cruz, at the same airport.
Simultaneous raids followed nationwide, ensnaring senior prosecutors, including Martín Daniel Irusta Flores — a former attorney for former President Evo Morales — and Julio César Porras, an anti-drug prosecutor who had been assigned to lead the government's investigation into Marset.
The purge arrived just 48 hours after the U.S. State Department announced visa restrictions targeting Mariaca and other Bolivian officials over allegations of high-level corruption and illicit drug ties.
In the hours preceding his arrest, Mariaca had publicly vowed to press forward with a separate, politically sensitive investigation into Fernando Cerimedo, a political campaign consultant aligned with right-wing figures in the United States who had advised Bolivia’s newly elected president, Rodrigo Paz. Cerimedo is currently imprisoned in Bolivia in connection with the August attempted murder of his former partner, Nadia Beller.
The sudden collapse of the country's top prosecutorial office has sent shockwaves through Bolivia’s political and judicial institutions, thrusting the deep intersections of state power and transnational drug networks back into the national spotlight.

Zara removed a children's Halloween costume from sale after criticism over its resemblance to the clothing worn by prisoners in Nazi concentration camps. The company apologized.
Zara has found itself at the center of a scandal over a children’s Halloween costume that was compared to the uniforms worn by concentration camp prisoners, UNN reports, citing Bild.
Details
Spanish retailer Zara recently unveiled a "Children’s Halloween Groom Costume," which immediately sparked outrage on social media. The £39.99 blue-gray pinstriped suit, consisting of a jacket and shorts, reminded many people of the clothing worn by prisoners in Nazi concentration camps. The resemblance was emphasized by the vertical stripes, distressed appearance, and decorative elements reminiscent of barbed wire.
Some users disagreed, noting that the outfit more closely resembled the striped costume worn by the character from the film "Beetlejuice."
Following a wave of criticism, the costume disappeared from the online store. Zara said it regretted if the design had caused any misunderstanding and confirmed that the item was no longer being sold.
It should be added
This is not the first similar scandal for Zara. In 2014, the company withdrew a children’s striped T-shirt with a star from sale after it was compared to the clothing worn by concentration camp prisoners. And in 2007, a bag featuring an embroidered symbol resembling a swastika was removed from stores.

There has been an outcry in the United States over a decision by prosecutors not to file charges in the case at the Ivy League college two years ago, prompting the governor to appoint state Attorney-General Letitia James as a special prosecutor.

The alleged victim said in her lawsuit that in 2024 she was drugged with ketamine, assaulted and raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, a social club for male students.
“It should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a licence for sexual assault or gang rape. Period,” Hochul said.
“I support closing this loophole, and will work with the New York State Legislature to accomplish this.”
Hochul slammed the conduct of the initial investigation into the alleged victim’s claims.
“She sat for hours and told (police) exactly what happened to her. And according to new reports, she could not have been clearer that she was 100% confident that she had been raped,” Hochul said.
“In what world would the police learn from a victim that she’d been literally gang raped while intoxicated... in the fraternity house, and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney?”
James, a Democrat who has clashed repeatedly with US President Donald Trump, said on Oct 2 she would “review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses, and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions”.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said this week that he planned to file criminal charges against the seven men.
He said his office declined to prosecute in 2024 because the alleged victim’s testimony did not establish a lack of consent.
Following the allegations, Cornell closed the fraternity and temporarily suspended the students allegedly involved, several of whom were later expelled.
Cornell’s student body held a campus meeting on Oct 1 at which emotions ran high.
Speakers repeatedly attacked the college administrators for their handling of the case that has garnered nationwide attention.
“No public official gets to look the other way when the system breaks down and fails our young people. And as governor, I will not allow anyone to sweep this case under the rug,” Hochul said on Oct 2. AFP

IAEA's Grossi urges uninterrupted diesel supply for Zaporizhia NPP generators
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:09:14 EEST
00:09:14 KST

The Zaporizhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) is considering a further reduction in the number of emergency diesel generators (EDGs) kept in automatic standby as diesel fuel supplies at the site continue to be a concern, IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi said.
"The availability of sufficient and reliable emergency electricity generation capacity to supply safety-related equipment is essential for the safety of any nuclear facility. The continued lack of diesel deliveries to the ZNPP is exacerbating an already precarious situation," his statement was quoted as saying in an agency statement.
"The prompt delivery of fuel to the ZNPP would have a large positive impact on nuclear safety at the ZNPP. I call on all sides to work with the IAEA to achieve this goal," Grossi added.
According to the agency, diesel fuel reserves at the ZNPP remain low following an extended loss of off-site power in August and September, when the plant relied on EDGs for nearly three weeks. Efforts to replenish the reserves have been hampered by military activity in the area. The ZNPP has experienced 10 such losses since June alone and currently relies on a single off-site power line, the 330 kilovolt (kV) Ferosplavna-1 line.
On 29 September the IAEA team at the ZNPP was informed that planned maintenance of electrical equipment in the 750kV switchyard had been delayed due to the security situation. Maintenance of an EDG was also delayed due to the late arrival of contractors.
On 30 September the IAEA was informed of repair work required at the Zaporizhia Thermal Power Plant to increase the robustness of the power supply to the ZNPP. The IAEA is working with the Russian Federation and Ukraine on a ceasefire that should allow for the maintenance work to be carried out.
The ZNPP is Europe's largest nuclear power plant, with six VVER-1000 reactors. The plant has not generated electricity since September 11, 2022. All six ZNPP reactors are in cold shutdown.
The ZNPP is currently under Russian occupation.

G7 to release 100M barrels from emergency oil reserves over 4 months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:08:53 UTC
00:08:53 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
G7 leaders on Friday agreed to immediately begin a coordinated release of 100 million barrels from emergency oil reserves over four months in response to surging prices and growing volatility in global energy markets.
The release, coordinated through the International Energy Agency, will include a “frontloaded substantial diesel release” by G7 members and partners within the first 20 days, according to a statement issued after a virtual meeting of the group's leaders.
The G7 said it would meet within the agency's framework in the coming days to discuss possible additional diesel releases if necessary.
“We reaffirm our commitment to refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products between G7 countries and call on all producers to refrain from imposing bans that could exacerbate market tensions,” the statement said.
The group also agreed to coordinate maintenance schedules across G7 refineries to avoid simultaneous capacity shutdowns and temporarily increase utilization rates where possible.
The agency was asked to monitor the implementation and impact of the measures and deliver a follow-up report within 20 days, according to the statement.
The G7 also called for the “immediate and full restoration” of navigational rights in the Strait of Hormuz, expressing its “determination to redouble our collective efforts to that end.”
The group said it would maintain sanctions against Russia while working with the International Energy Agency and other partners to limit spillovers into fuel, gas and other commodity markets.
EU welcomes release of emergency reserves
European Council President Antonio Costa welcomed the coordinated measures, saying EU leaders would discuss the energy situation at their Oct. 15-16 meeting.
"I welcome today’s G7 coordinated measures in response to the global energy situation: a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels, beginning immediately and continuing over four months, with the release of diesel front-loaded, by G7 members and partners; a commitment to refrain from imposing export restrictions on energy and energy products between G7 countries, and a call on all producers to refrain from imposing bans that could exacerbate market tensions," Costa said in a post on the US social media platform X.
He said EU leaders will address “how we can alleviate the impact of rising energy prices on European citizens, businesses and industry” during the European Council meeting in October.
According to Costa, the crisis also highlighted the need to reduce dependence on fossil fuels and accelerate the transition toward homegrown energy sources.

Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:07:19 BST
00:07:19 KST

Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87
- Published
Spain's Congress has rejected a series of measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis, in a defeat for the government of Pedro Sánchez that increases pressure on him to call a snap election.
Lawmakers voted on two decree-laws presented by the government in response to nationwide protests that have followed the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, from her home.
The decrees, which introduced a series of initiatives aimed at protecting tenants in the rental market, required parliamentary approval in order to remain in place.
MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.
Hundreds of demonstrators had gathered outside Congress as the debate took place and there were angry scenes.
Protesters chanted "shame on you" and "your profits, our misery", after the results were announced.
The government's defeat underlines the fact that Sánchez, a Socialist, does not command a congressional majority and it has heightened speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.
Sources told Spanish media that the government would spend the weekend deciding its next step, and whether to dissolve parliament.
Sánchez's beleaguered government had already been mired in a series of scandals and judicial cases affecting his Socialist Party and close allies.
Abascal was evicted after she was unable to pay a sharp rent increase introduced by Urbagestión, the company that owned her flat in central Madrid.
Hundreds of protesters gathered to oppose the eviction last week and the case triggered a broader movement across the country demanding affordable rentals, which have soared in recent years.
The social backlash has seen Urbagestión negotiate the return of Abascal to her flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued, with people occupying squares in Madrid and other cities, pitching tents in squares and with a series of marches scheduled for this weekend.
The Sindicato de Inquilinas (Tenants' Union) activist association which has been co-ordinating protests, announced during the congressional debate that it was abandoning the tent protest in central Madrid. It said it wanted to "take the struggle to all the neighbourhoods, residential blocks and homes of Madrid, wherever there are rental increases, expulsions and abuses each day, and turn the energy of the last few days into a permanent organisation".
Protesters are also calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.
The left-wing coalition government responded to the social anger by hurriedly drawing up the two decree-laws in an effort to defuse the protests.
The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds".
The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Sindicato de Inquilinas.
The conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.
However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.
Friday's debate was fierce and at times angry, as supporters and opponents of the decrees clashed in Congress.
"I don't ask you, I beg you to be brave and consistent," Sánchez said, moments before the two votes took place. "Because they are not just ambitious measures, they are necessary".
He appealed to lawmakers "to put order and humanity into [the housing] market, because if we don't, it will bring down our society".
Social Affairs minister Pablo Bustinduy, of the Sumar alliance, the junior partner in the governing coalition, presented the debate in dramatic terms.
"Today is about defending an international oligarchy which is extracting the rent from salaries earned with the effort of working classes of this country in order to share it out with dividends and they don't even pay taxes in Spain," he said.
"Voting against these decrees today means defending the interests of this oligarchy and turning your back on your own people."
However, Miriam Nogueras, of JxCat, said the decrees had been hastily drawn up and lacked rigour.
She said the decrees "will allow [vulture] funds to keep buying, keep speculating and evictions to keep happening… these two decrees would provoke the opposite effect of what they aim to achieve."
The political right has argued that the government's attempts to intervene will frighten homeowners, causing them not to put their properties on the rental market and pushing prices up further.
Juan Bravo of the PP said "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes".

Ukraine could become a major storage and distribution hub for American natural gas in Central and Eastern Europe, according to an analysis published by the Atlantic Council.
Stephen Blank, a senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, argues that western Ukraine’s storage facilities near the European Union could support expanded US supplies, provided security and logistical obstacles are addressed.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine’s underground gas storage operator, Ukrtransgaz, puts the network’s total capacity at 30.95 billion cubic meters (1.09 trillion cubic feet). That figure represents storage capacity, not the amount of gas currently held.
The proposal comes as Russian attacks increase Ukraine’s reliance on imported gas. According to Blank’s analysis, strikes knocked out up to 60% of domestic production capacity in 2025.
Ukraine contracted about 456 million cubic meters (16.1 billion cubic feet) of US liquefied natural gas (LNG) in 2025 and another 381 million cubic meters (13.5 billion cubic feet) in the first quarter of 2026, the analysis said. Naftogaz has developed supply routes through terminals in Poland, Lithuania, Germany and Greece.
In November, Naftogaz announced a deal with Poland’s ORLEN for 300 million cubic meters (10.6 billion cubic feet) of US gas, scheduled for delivery in the first quarter of 2026. In February, it announced its first US LNG supply through Germany’s terminal on Rügen.
‘We Can No Longer Pretend’: Kyiv Faces Fight for Survival, Klitschko Warns
LNG arriving at European terminals is converted back into gas before entering pipeline networks.
Blank argues that Ukraine could become a major gas storage partner for the Three Seas Initiative, helping redistribute American gas across the region and meet seasonal demand. He cautions that this would require investment and sustained US institutional support.
The Trump administration, however, doesn’t show signs of willingness to do that.
Security remains a constraint. Deep underground reservoirs offer protection for stored gas, but the infrastructure serving them remains exposed. A Russian attack on a Naftogaz storage facility in March 2024 damaged equipment, although the company said storage services would continue.
