Ukrainian Grandmother Detained in Alleged FSB Trap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:50:36 UTC
22:50:36 KST

Kazakh authorities detained Ukrainian citizen Liubov Rozhanska at Astana airport at Russia’s request after she traveled there to collect her grandson, in what her lawyer described as a possible operation organized by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).
Rozhanska was detained while passing through border control after arriving from Istanbul to Kazakhstan on Thursday, Oct. 1, her lawyers Alexei Pryanishnikov and Riza Nurbayeva told Deutsche Welle (DW).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Russian request was reportedly transmitted through the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), a Moscow-led security alliance that includes Kazakhstan.
Rozhanska is being held in a detention center in Astana. Her lawyers said a court hearing was expected within three days and warned that she could be sent to Russia despite being a Ukrainian citizen.
Neither Kazakhstan’s authorities nor Ukraine’s foreign ministry had publicly commented on the case at the time of publication.
Grandmother traveled to collect child
According to the lawyers’ account, Rozhanska traveled to Kazakhstan to collect her grandson, who was supposed to be brought there from Russia and returned to his father in Odesa.
The boy was born in Odesa in 2018 to a Ukrainian family. His parents later separated, and in 2021 his mother moved with him to Russia’s Kaliningrad region, where her new Russian husband lived.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the mother applied to renounce Ukrainian citizenship for herself and the child, both receiving Russian citizenship in 2022, according to DW.
Kremlin Urges US-Russia Deals Before Ukraine Settlement
The child’s father began legal proceedings in Ukraine and in March 2025, Ukraine’s Supreme Court determined that the boy should live in Odesa with his father.
Russian case opened before proposed handover
Pryanishnikov said that the mother’s new husband, Vitaly Andreyev, and Andreyev’s father contacted Rozhanska in July and proposed handing over the boy to his Ukrainian father and grandmother.
Negotiations over the transfer intensified in late August.
At the same time, however, Russian authorities were pursuing a criminal case against Rozhanska over the alleged attempted abduction of the child.
Nurbayeva said the case had been opened in Russia in 2023, even though Rozhanska had never entered Russian territory and was allegedly unaware of either the investigation or an arrest order.
“When she arrived in Kazakhstan, she was detained under a ruling by a Kaliningrad court,” Nurbayeva told DW.
Documents sent by Russia reportedly show that investigators from the FSB’s Kaliningrad regional branch were preparing to place Rozhanska on a wanted list and seek her extradition while negotiations over the child’s transfer were continuing.
Lawyer alleges FSB provocation
Pryanishnikov described the arrest as a “rather clearly planned operation” and an FSB provocation, arguing that the invitation to collect the child may have been used to lure Rozhanska to a country where Russia could seek her detention.
“Despite the seemingly family nature of this case, I clearly see a political context connected with the war between Russia and Ukraine,” he said.
Pryanishnikov’s allegation has not been independently confirmed, and neither the FSB nor the relatives involved in the proposed handover have publicly responded.
Kazakhstan has previously transferred people wanted by Moscow to Russia. In February, Kazakh authorities deported IT specialist Oleksandr Kachkurkin, who was detained upon arrival in Russia, and charged with treason over alleged financial transfers to Ukraine.

Can India’s ‘cockroach’ movement oust Modi’s election chief?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:50:06 UTC
22:50:06 KST

Can India’s ‘cockroach’ movement oust Modi’s election chief?
India’s youth protests return to streets, eyeing PM Modi’s prized bureaucrat who oversees the world’s biggest elections.
New Delhi, India – Central parts of the Indian capital turned into a ghost town on Friday as Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s police detained hundreds of protesters, as the ‘cockroach’ movement that ousted the country’s education minister this past summer joined opposition parties in demanding the resignation of India’s elections chief.
The government shut down metro stations leading to central Delhi and suspended internet services. Heavily deployed government forces blocked all entries to Parliament Street and the Jantar Mantar protest strip – the stage of the youth movement that forced out Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan just two months ago.
Saurav Yadav, a 24-year-old musician from Gwalior, a city in central India nearly 335km (210 miles) from New Delhi, took an overnight bus to join the protest, called by the cockroach movement and joined by a spectrum of opposition parties and unions.
But as Yadav approached the site – his first time in the Indian capital – he was dragged away by two policemen, even as he held the tricolour national flag in his hands. “This government is managing the elections. Just imagine, the only thing that gives them power is managed!” Yadav told Al Jazeera, sitting startled in the back of a police van.
“We are just cosplaying democracy,” he said, sweating profusely. “We cannot keep pretending this.”
The cockroach movement is taking the street protests to several Indian cities in the coming days, including in the country’s financial capital, Mumbai, later on Friday. But youth protest leaders, emboldened by their success against the education minister, face a new set of challenges as they set their sights on the Modi government’s most politically prized bureaucrat.
‘Gyanesh Kumar needs to go’
Last week, India was shaken by new revelations showing divisions within the supposedly autonomous body that is in charge of conducting its elections over controversial policies that critics say have disenfranchised tens of millions of people.
India’s Election Commission chief, Gyanesh Kumar, frequently overruled concerns raised by the two other election commissioners about the integrity of ongoing changes in the voter database, an investigation by the Indian Express reported.
The commission has not refuted the investigation, but indicated, since the revelations, that it was acting to address concerns raised by the other two election commissioners.
The revelations came after a months-long struggle by India’s opposition parties to bring what they have described as the “sabotaging” conduct of the election commission to the fore, which they say is dictated by Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) for its electoral benefit.
Since June last year, the commission has been revising and updating the voters list statewide. It has struck off more than 130 million names during the exercise since then, which the critics say targeted economically weaker sections, minorities and other vulnerable groups in Indian society disproportionately.
The cockroach movement leaders moved fast to tap into the growing calls for Kumar’s resignation, terming it the “last call to save democracy”.
The leader of the opposition, Rahul Gandhi, has called for the election chief to be tried for treason against India.
N Sai Balaji, a senior leader of All India Students’ Association (AISA), the student wing of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation that was at the centre of youth protests earlier this year, said that “people have been suspecting the election commission for a long time – and different people have been flagging a range of issues”.
“We do not need to build a movement this time. We just need to come out on the streets, and there will be no opposition to the central demand: Gyanesh Kumar needs to go,” Balaji told Al Jazeera.
The success of the youth protests that ousted the education minister was credited to the unifying platform of education in India’s otherwise deeply divided society. “Then this is perhaps the most secular issue in India,” said Balaji. “Who is a bureaucrat to decide who gets to vote and who doesn’t?”
Balaji said that there is “a unanimous understanding across the opposition’s spectrum that the elections are managed and staged.” If Kumar stays as the chief, he said, “no one will trust any electoral outcome in the so-called world’s largest democracy.”
‘Bigger blow: Bureaucrat of choice’
Kumar, India’s 62-year-old election chief, is a trusted lieutenant of PM Modi, and his career has intersected with several of the government’s most consequential and controversial decisions.
Currently, Kumar is spearheading the highly contested revision of the voters’ list.
In 2016, he was tapped as a joint secretary in the Home Ministry’s Kashmir division, which oversees the Indian-administered Kashmir. Three years later, Kumar was entrusted with drafting the legislation that sliced the state of Jammu and Kashmir into two federally controlled territories, stripping the contested region of special rights in August 2019, as the Modi government clamped down on the region with a months-long curfew and a communication blackout.
Within a few months, Kumar was moved to the Modi government’s next flagship project: the construction of a controversial Ram Temple.
On December 6, 1992, a far-right Hindu mob tore down the 16th-century Babri Mosque, triggering religious riots across the country that killed over 2,000 people, mostly Muslims. After years of legal battles, the top court awarded the site to Hindus. Kumar led the team overseeing implementation of the Supreme Court’s verdict, including the formation of a trust tasked with managing the new temple that has now come up at the site.
“Gyanesh Kumar has been the bureaucrat of choice to get these things done for the ruling government. If he is forced out, it is going to be a much bigger blow for the Modi government,” said Neelanjan Sircar, a senior fellow at the Centre for Policy Research, a think tank in New Delhi.
“The cost of losing Kumar would be higher: it would be a much bigger signal to the larger ecosystem if you can’t protect a man like that,” Sircar added.
Asim Ali, a political analyst in New Delhi, said he doesn’t expect the government to cave in. “Kumar’s resignation would be seen as a fatal admission of guilt, and it would undermine the legitimacy of elections, and hence their power,” he told Al Jazeera.
Taking a jibe at Kumar, India’s opposition leader Gandhi called on him to become a state witness, saying PM Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah would eventually face prosecution for “treason”.
‘Experienced protest leaders’
The swift crackdown on protesters on Friday suggests the Modi government will not let the protest movement take charge of Jantar Mantar this time around, say analysts.
“Lessons that the government learned from earlier youth protests are in terms of strategy,” said Sircar, adding that the Modi government would want to avoid a confrontation with protesters. “They do not want any visuals like the last time. The goal will be to prevent any kind of assembly from an earlier stage.”
On July 20, the cockroach movement staged a sit-in at Jantar Mantar, then called on thousands of protesters to march peacefully towards Parliament. They were met with police brutality, leaving more than 100 students injured.
The visuals then galvanised a wider Gen Z uprising in the national capital, with protesters choking key streets in central Delhi, and eventually forcing the removal of the education minister.
But Ali, the political analyst warned that the protest leaders are more experienced now. The cockroach movement, which grew into the Gen Z uprising, was born out of a casual joke on X after the chief justice of India equated unemployed youth to “cockroaches”.
None of the central leaders had experience of organising a mass movement at the time. Now, they are returning to the streets “as experienced protest leaders, who have developed a following.”
“There are no assured brakes,” Ali said. “And that makes this situation more explosive.”

Global life expectancy approaches pre-pandemic levels — WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:49:25 UTC
22:49:25 KST

GENEVA, October 2. /TASS/. Average life expectancy has reached 73.3 years, approaching the 2019 pre-pandemic figure, the World Health Organization (WHO) reported.
"Following the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, global life expectancy has returned to close to pre-pandemic levels. At the same time, noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) account for an increasing share of deaths," the WHO noted. In 2023, global life expectancy "reached 73.3 years, close to the 73.4 years recorded in 2019." However, healthy life expectancy "has recovered more slowly, reaching 62.8 years in 2023, still 0.4 years below its 2019 level."
At the same time, according to WHO estimates, "the long-term shift towards NCDs continues." In 2023, NCDs accounted for 74% of all deaths worldwide, whereas in 2000, this figure was 58%.
Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death. In 2023, ischemic heart disease caused approximately 9.5 million deaths. It also accounted for a total of "210 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), measured in years of healthy life lost.".

Competitors in the Formula 1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix held practice sessions at the Sepang International Circuit in Malaysia Friday, marking the return of Formula 1 racing to the Southeast Asian country after nine years.
The three-day event runs through Sunday with practice sessions beginning Friday, qualifying scheduled for Saturday and the main race set for Sunday.
The Grand Prix was moved from Bahrain to Malaysia after the race in Sakhir, originally scheduled for April, was cancelled due to geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, Bernama News reported.
The relocation followed an agreement between Formula 1, the motorsport governing body FIA and the governments of Malaysia and Bahrain, allowing the Bahrain Grand Prix to remain on the 2026 calendar.
Formula 1 teams and drivers are participating in the event, with reigning four-time world champion Max Verstappen among those taking to the 5.543-kilometer (3.44-mile) Sepang circuit.
Verstappen topped Friday’s opening practice session for Red Bull, ahead of Mercedes driver George Russell and Racing Bulls’ Isack Hadjar. Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc finished fourth, followed by Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli.
Sunday’s Grand Prix is scheduled to begin at 3 pm local time and will be contested over 56 laps, covering 310.417 kilometers (192.88 miles).
Malaysia last hosted a Formula 1 Grand Prix at Sepang in 2017. Around 95,000 three-day passes had been sold ahead of this weekend’s event, according to Bernama.

Deidan described the capture as an important step in the army’s efforts to cut the RSF’s supply lines, saying the town serves as a link between North Kordofan and West Kordofan states.

The army has recently reported sweeping advances across much of North Kordofan following battles with the paramilitary group, announcing control of 11 areas in the state.
North, West and South Kordofan have witnessed clashes between the army and the RSF since Oct. 25 last year.
Sudan has been engulfed in war between the army and the Rapid Support Forces since April 2023. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Representatives of the Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS) and the State Emergency Service (SES) discussed response algorithms for radiation, chemical, biological and nuclear threats with officials in charge of radiation and chemical protection in regional military administrations, the URCS said on Facebook on Friday.
"The Ukrainian Red Cross, together with the SES, held a meeting with representatives of regional military administrations responsible for organizing radiation and chemical protection of the population and territories. Kalashnikov unveils boats for operations in Caspian Sea at exhibition in Baku

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Russia’s Kalashnikov Group has presented a high-speed assault boat, a high-speed transport and landing craft, and a unique civilian passenger and cargo vessel at the ADEX 2026 Defense Industry Exhibition in Baku, the company told TASS.
"As part of the 6th International Defense Exhibition ADEX 2026 taking place in Azerbaijan, the Kalashnikov Group’s shipbuilding division is presenting to experts and guests of the forum ready-made, effective solutions for the most complex and diverse tasks that arise in the waters of the Caspian Sea," the group said.
It noted that three key products are on display in Baku: the BK-10E high-speed assault boat, the BK-16E high-speed transport and landing craft, and the unique civilian passenger and cargo hovercraft Khaska.
The BK-16E is an 18-meter armored boat, proven by time and extensive operational experience, designed to transport and land troops on unfortified shores and provide them with fire support, Kalashnikov reported. An undeniable advantage of the boat is its combination of high combat performance, survivability, and a top speed of 45 knots. Its cruising range is 400 nautical miles.
The BK-10E assault boat, on the other hand, is a simpler and more mobile platform for transporting and landing troops. It is equipped with 7.62-mm machine guns and a grenade launcher. The assault boat has a draft of 0.6 m and can reach speeds of up to 40 knots, which could be tactically advantageous in the shallow waters of the Caspian Sea and the river deltas of Azerbaijan.
"Since the start of the special military operation, the BK-10E and BK-16E have been continuously modernized based on experience gained from their combat use. For example, the BK-16E’s bridge and troop compartment are reliably armored thanks to modern, high-strength composite materials, and its two engines are also thoroughly protected," Kalashnikov noted.
Passenger-cargo vessel
The third shipbuilding product presented is the Khaska hovercraft with flexible skegs. The main feature of the Khaska is its ability to carry up to 20 metric tons of cargo, including passengers, troops, and vehicles. When fully loaded, the vessel can travel at a speed of 40 knots, is capable of navigating extremely shallow waters, and beach landing. The vessel is 23.7 meters long and can clear obstacles up to 1.2 meters high.
"The Khaska can serve as a higher-capacity and more economical alternative to helicopters for supplying oil and gas fields in the Caspian Sea, rotating personnel at remote outposts, or conducting rescue operations. The Khaska can also be used for amphibious operations," the company added.

Labor market faltered in September as jobs increased by just 29,000, unemployment rate rose to 4.2%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:45:58 UTC
22:45:58 KST

The U.S. economy created far fewer jobs than expected in September, pointing to a surprising soft spot in the labor market and broader economy.
Nonfarm payrolls rose a seasonally adjusted 29,000 for the month while the unemployment rate increased to 4.2%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for job growth of 84,000 and an unemployment rate of 4.1%.
In addition to the weakness in September, the August jobs count was revised lower to reflect a gain of 133,000 while July switched from a gain to a loss as payrolls fell by 10,000. The revisions in total showed 60,000 fewer jobs than previously reported.
Market reaction was swift to the report, with traders interpreting the soft jobs numbers as good news as they likely further cemented the Federal Reserve staying put at its October meeting.
Stock futures rose sharply after the release while Treasury yields slumped after recently rising to levels not seen since the early part of the century. Market-implied odds that the Fed will hold rates steady at its Oct. 27-28 meeting jumped to 82.8%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
"For the Fed, this number should be the nail in the coffin for an October hike," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a note.
"The payroll data surged in August, and we had expected the momentum to continue this month, given the historically low prints on jobless claims in recent weeks," he added. "However, it now appears that the August number was nothing more than a rebound from very weak hiring in June and July."
Fed officials more closely watch the unemployment rate than the headline payrolls numbers.
The household survey, which is used to calculate the jobless level, was considerably better than the establishment survey, which is used to derive the payrolls count.
Household employment rose by 406,000 for the month, while the labor force swelled by 485,000 and the participation rate, which counts those working or actively searching for a job as a share of the total labor force, increased 0.2 percentage point to 61.8%, its highest since May.
An alternative measure of unemployment, which includes discouraged workers and those holding part-time jobs for economic reasons, edged down to 7.6%, its lowest since January 2025.
The report comes with Federal Reserve officials weighing the state of the economy and how it should affect their next interest rate move.
Following statements in recent days from central bank policymakers, markets have recalibrated expectations and now expect the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee to hold off until December for its next hike. The FOMC raised benchmark rates a quarter percentage point in September.
Policymakers largely see inflation as a larger threat to the economy than the labor market, which had shown resilience in recent months. The data has painted a picture of a low-hire, low-fire economy, with weekly jobless claims low and one indicator showing layoffs at their lowest rate in four years.
Inflation, though, has held well above the Fed's 2% target. The most recent indicator of the central bank's preferred gauge showed core inflation at a 3% annual rate.
Wages, though, continued to show signs of disinflation.
Average hourly earnings increased just 0.1% in September, putting the 12-month gain at 3%, the lowest since May 2021. Wall Street had been looking for readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, respectively. The average work week was unchanged at 34.6 hours.
"Americans are frustrated by the lack of opportunities right now," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "Wage growth fell to a new 5-year low and is being wiped out entirely by inflation. That stings heading into the holidays."
However, Long described the labor market as "stable" and said she doesn't think the Fed will be dissuaded from hiking in December.
Most of the monthly job gains came from healthcare, which added 17,000 workers. Construction was up by 11,000, and manufacturing added 9,000.
Government employment fell by 17,000, while temporary help services saw a decline of 11,000, and information services lost 10,000 amid worries over the impact artificial intelligence may have on the jobs picture. Financial activities also saw a drop of 7,000 jobs.
The weak job growth comes despite signs of strength elsewhere.
On a macro level, economic growth has been strong.
Earlier this week, the Commerce Department revised its count of both first- and second-quarter gross domestic product growth, to 2.5% and 2.2%, respectively. The Atlanta Fed is tracking third-quarter GDP at 3.7%.

Japan has imposed new sanctions against the russian federation — the "shadow fleet" was affected
Kyiv • UNN
Japan has expanded sanctions against Russia, freezing the assets of 42 individuals and restricting transactions involving 35 vessels. Exports to four companies have also been banned.
Japan announced the introduction of additional economic sanctions against Russia over its invasion of Ukraine, including measures targeting 35 vessels of the "shadow fleet." The Japanese Foreign Ministry reported this on October 2, UNN writes.
Details
"In view of the current international situation surrounding Ukraine and in order to contribute to international efforts to achieve international peace aimed at resolving this issue, in accordance with measures taken by other major countries, the Government of Japan has introduced the following measures pursuant to the Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act, based on the Cabinet decision entitled ‘Freezing of Assets of Individuals and Entities of the Russian Federation and Other Measures’ (as of October 2, 2026)," the statement said.
According to the report, these include:
-  asset-freezing measures. Restrictions on payments and capital transactions will take effect for legal entities and individuals of the Russian Federation (33 legal entities and 9 individuals; 
-  a ban on exports to certain entities in countries other than the Russian Federation and the Republic of Belarus. A ban will be introduced on exports to 4 specific entities in countries other than the Russian Federation and the Republic of Belarus; 
-  restrictions on service transactions involving certain vessels. Restrictions on service transactions and capital transactions will take effect for 35 specific vessels; 
-  a ban on exports to the Russian Federation of goods that could contribute to strengthening Russia’s industrial potential. 
As Nippon notes, the sanctions also target 35 vessels from the so-called shadow fleet that transport Russian oil and help Moscow evade sanctions. This is the first time the Japanese government has imposed sanctions on vessels. In particular, the measures will restrict the provision of services such as repairs and insurance for the sanctioned vessels.
In addition, according to the report, to counter attempts to circumvent sanctions through third countries, Japan recently banned exports to four organizations in Turkey and the United Arab Emirates.

Hundreds of schools closed as fiery French student protests spread
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:41:14 UTC
22:41:14 KST

France student protests spread from Paris, with violent clashes forcing hundreds of high schools to close
Paris — French high school students lit fires outside schools and faced off with police on Friday as a protest movement that has forced the closure or disrupted education at more than 560 establishments showed no sign of abating.
The movement, which began last week in the Paris region and rapidly spread nationwide, has seen teenage pupils in their final years of high school block access to buildings and clash with police.
The students say their school hours are excessively long, conditions inadequate including overheated classrooms and dilapidated buildings, and that there are too many staff absences.
"For a whole year, we didn't have a science teacher. We don't have any textbooks," said Simon, a 15-year-old who declined to give his surname outside the Turgot high school in central Paris. "And still, we're the lucky ones. It's even worse in the suburbs."
The government says the grievances are legitimate but has condemned what it calls "urban violence."
Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing tear gas canisters to disperse the protests.
In Paris on Friday, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools, with the fire brigade called to extinguish the blazes, an AFP photographer said.
"Held hostage by ultra-violent fringe groups"
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said "the high school student movement is being held hostage by ultra-violent fringe groups."
His ministry said Friday that education had been disrupted at more than 560 high schools out of the 3,700 in the country. More than 1,000 high schools were affected Thursday, the interior ministry has said.
Many high schools have planned to conduct classes remotely, particularly in the southern city of Marseille.
At least 65 staff members have been injured, including 40 high school principals, since the start of the movement, Geffray told BFMTV, while about 170 students have been wounded and over 100 high schools have suffered "severe damage."
"Parents must clearly step up and tell their children not to go" to the protests, he said. "What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger."
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said he has asked prosecutors to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children during the protests and "pay for repairs."
 Since the start of the movement, around 2,000 people have been taken into police custody "90% of whom were minors," Darmanin told RTL.
"We've won — our school is closed"
In the western city of Rennes, the tension was already palpable outside the Jean-Mace high school with students dressed in black and wearing balaclavas standing not far from a heavy police presence.
"As far as we're concerned, we've won — our school is closed this morning," said Lola, 16, who declined to give her last name.
She condemned what she said was police violence.
"It makes us even angrier — the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us," she said.
Police used tear gas at the Kerichen high school in Brest, in western France, an AFP photographer said.
The protests have also made a strong political echo just over half a year before presidential elections, with the government accusing the hard left France Unbowed (LFI) — whose firebrand leader Jean-Luc Melenchon is again standing for the presidency - of being behind the movement.
But senior LFI official Manuel Bompard accused the government of "descending into conspiracy theories."

Israeli court pressure pushes Israeli Arab leader to quit election race
JERUSALEM, Oct 2 - The head of a left-wing Arab party has dropped out of Israel's election after the country's Supreme Court advised him that a majority of judges supported disqualifying him if he did not voluntarily withdraw.
It was the first time the Supreme Court had signaled it might uphold a bid by the Central Election Commission to disqualify an Israeli Arab politician. The rights group Adalah said the court decision set different standards for political participation for Jewish and Arab citizens.
Israel's Central Election Commission, a political body, had sought to disqualify Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Balad party, over an article in which he described the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel as "an important historical event".
Far-right parties accused him of supporting the attack, which he denies.
The October 27 election is Israel's first since that attack, which killed about 1,200 people, according to Israeli tallies.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's ruling coalition, the most right-wing in the country's history, has been stoking fears against parties representing Israel's Arab minority of Palestinian heritage.
SHEHADEH ALLEGES DISCRIMINATION
Shehadeh told Reuters he had a long record of supporting peace and human rights, which he said the court had ignored.
"The margins for political activity, for freedom of speech for the Arab-Palestinian minority in Israel are becoming narrower," said Shehadeh, adding, "I think the decision shows that in the Jewish state, there are two different laws for citizens according to their identity."
Israel's Central Election Commission voted in late September to bar from the election Shehadeh, Ofer Cassif, and four parties which aim to represent Israel's 20% Arab minority.
On Friday, the Supreme Court said it had overturned the bans on Cassif and the four parties.
Adalah, a Palestinian legal rights centre based in Israel that represented Shehadeh and the other defendants, said he had withdrawn his candidacy to avert a dangerous legal precedent.
"They (the court) would disqualify on the basis of one article, or more specifically one sentence in an article, which is unprecedented," said Suhad Bishara, Adalah's legal director.
Shehadeh has said his singling out was part of a racist campaign that aimed to reduce the influence of the parties representing Israel's Arab minority.
"The same Central Election Committee that disqualified me for an article refused to disqualify all the extreme right-wing racist politicians with all the serious files that were against them," he told Reuters on Friday.
"Committing a genocide is considered acceptable and legitimate, but talking about ending the occupation (of Palestinian land) and peace is considered illegitimate."
Following the Hamas attack on Israel, Israeli forces launched an offensive in Gaza in which more than 74,000 people have been killed, according to local health authorities. The campaign has displaced most of Gaza's population, caused a hunger crisis, and charges of genocide from scholars, rights groups, and an independent UN commission.
Israel denies committing a genocide in Gaza.
In an interview with national media in August, Israel's far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called for the killing of "30 to 40" Gazans nightly, saying there were people in Gaza "not worthy of life". REUTERS

Trump regales supporters in Alabama with familiar tales, some imaginary
Donald Trump is regaling supporters in Alabama with a version of his rally speech that includes many of his familiar boasts and grievances, a number of which are based on entirely imaginary claims.
To take one example, Trump once again claimed that he was instantly blamed for high prices by the media after just one day in office.
“I took over and in my first news conference on January 21st … a day after that beautiful day we had in quite cold weather, the inauguration. A day later, I had a news conference and they said, ‘affordability’. I said, ‘I just got here. What do they mean?’” Trump insisted, despite the fact that he was, in fact, asked no questions about affordability at all during that news conference.
In the first weeks of his administration, Trump repeatedly claimed that prices were dropping and then, at a cabinet meeting two months into his second term, claimed for the first time that he had been unfairly blamed for high egg prices. “When I came in, after one week, they were screaming at me about eggs. Eggs had nothing to do with me,” the president said on 24 March 2025. He has repeated the false claim that reporters blamed him for high food prices dozens of times since.
Later in the address, Trump said, as he has dozens of times since he visited Saudi Arabia in May 2025, that the Saudi king had praised him for almost instantly turning around the US economy.
“Less than two years ago, our country was dead,” Trump told supporters in Alabama on Friday night. “Remember that? I told you, the king of Saudi Arabia was talking to me. He said, you know, ‘Sir, just a short time ago, your country was dead. The whole Middle East, the whole world was laughing at you. And now you have the hottest country anywhere in the world.’”
As the Guardian has reported previously, Trump did not meet the Saudi king, who is elderly and not often seen in public, during his visit last year. Instead, he was hosted by the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. There is also no evidence that the Saudi prince made this statement to Trump, but there is video of Trump making a version of that claim to bin Salman during an address to a US-Saudi investment event in Riyadh on 13 May 2025.
“The days of economic misery under the last administration are rapidly giving way to the greatest economy in the history of the world,” Trump said before directly addressing the crown prince in the audience. “We are rocking. The United States is the hottest country, with the exception of your country, I have to say, right? … No Mohammed… You’re hotter. At least as long as I’m up here, you’re hotter. But groceries, gasoline, energy and all other prices are down with no inflation. We have no inflation.”
Two weeks after his return to the US, Trump began saying that this observation had been made not by him, but to him. “I went to Saudi Arabia,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on 28 May 2025. “The king told me, he said, ‘you got the hottest com-’ we have the hottest country in the world right now.,” Trump said. “Six months ago this country was stone cold dead. We had a dead country.”
As he repeated the story, again and again, Trump began to also attribute his own claim, that the US was “dead” under Joe Biden, to the Saudi king as well. In remarks at the Nato summit in the Hague in June 2025, Trump insisted that the Saudi king had told him: “A year ago, your country was dead. You had a deadhead running it. Since then, Trump has repeated the tale dozens of times.

In August, crews contracted by US Customs and border protection (CBP) began bulldozing at the mouth of Big Bend National Park’s famed Santa Elena Canyon. The plan was to construct new border security infrastructure, which was dubbed the “smart wall”.

Donald Trump personally directed the use of $20m in taxpayer funds to purchase advertising time on national television to air a series of political ads that celebrate his presidency in the run-up to the midterm elections, the New York Times reported on Friday.
The campaign, which has featured four pro-Trump ads so far, has been called illegal government propaganda by critics.
“The money for the ads was freed up on Sept. 19, when the Office of Management and Budget shifted $20 million in Customs and Border Protection funds to a budget category called One Big Beautiful Bill Commemorative Events,” the Times reported, citing anonymous sources familiar with the spending.
The first pro-Trump ad, broadcast on Fox News last week, uses audio of Trump telling supporters in Las Vegas last month: “Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America,” and a rapid-fire montage of images of Trump beneath the onscreen text: “America will never be a communist country,” as a chorus sings the words “love me”, taken from a song of that name by JMSN. The last 10 seconds of the ad included text at the bottom the screen saying: “Paid for by the US government.”
The second ad was a White House produced highlight reel of Trump’s address at Mount Rushmore on the weekend of 4 July.
The third ad was a recycled 2024 Trump campaign ad showing a moody, black-and-white shot of Trump staring into the camera as the soundtrack plays the closing riff of a campaign speech he gave dozens of times in 2023 and 2024. The ad was played on giant screens during the 2024 Republican national convention before Trump’s speech accepting his party’s nomination.
The most recent ad, first broadcast this week, is a celebration of Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran, and features audio taken from the president’s 28 February declaration that the United States military had begun major combat operations there. That ad concludes with images of Iranians in New York celebrating the initial strikes the next day. It makes no mention of the fact that the war is ongoing, seven months later.

Environmental groups sue Trump administration for slashing fuel economy rules
A group of environmental organizations have sued the Trump administration over its recent move to slash clean-car rules that had been aimed at reducing planet-heating emissions and boosting electric vehicles.
On Monday, the administration relaxed the Corporate Average Fuel Economy (Cafe) standards that regulate how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline.
Donald Trump said last week that the less stringent mileage requirements would “take the waste out of building cars in America” and save families “thousands on a new, beautiful and safe car”, while boosting auto production in the US.
Trump has repeatedly pledged to end what he falsely calls an EV “mandate”, referring incorrectly to Joe Biden’s target that half of all new vehicle sales be electric by 2030. No federal policy has mandated auto companies to sell EVs.
Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, hailed the new initiative – called Freedom Means Affordable Cars – which the agency said would reduce the average cost of new vehicles by $1,300, and save consumers $138bn over the next five years.
The lawsuit is currently a petition to review the Department of Transportation’s move.

Ukraine Tests Five High-Speed Drone Interceptor Models to Counter Russia’s Jet-Powered Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:31:25 UTC
22:31:25 KST

Ukraine is testing five high-speed interceptor drone models designed to shoot down Russia’s increasingly common jet-powered attack drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times published Friday.
One of the five models could reach production of around 400 units by the end of October, while the other four remain under testing, Zelensky said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Jet-powered drones, which blur the line between drones and missiles, have been increasingly used by Russia against Ukraine in recent attacks, posing challenges for Ukrainian air defenses as current interceptor drones struggle to catch up with their higher speeds.
Zelensky said Russia launched around 500 drones against Ukraine in a recent 24-hour period, about half of them jet-powered. Ukraine is currently destroying about 57% of the jet-powered drones, compared with 85% to 90% of conventional drones, he told the FT.
The faster drones have created a new challenge for Ukraine’s layered air defenses. Reuters reported in September that some Ukrainian interceptor prototypes struggled to remain controllable at speeds exceeding 400 kilometers per hour during testing, showing the technical difficulty of developing drones capable of chasing and destroying the new Russian weapons.
Ukrainian manufacturers have nevertheless begun developing interceptors specifically for the threat. One model unveiled in September, the Zorelit v5, has a reported top speed of 416 kilometers per hour and a range of up to 47 kilometers.
Kyiv Grinds to a Halt as Russian Strikes Shut Bridges, Force People to Walk
Its manufacturer says it can be used against both conventional Shahed-type drones and faster jet-powered variants.
The biggest obstacle to rapidly scaling production is not only technology but supply.
“Engines are key,” Zelensky told the FT. “We really import a lot of engines.” He said Ukraine produces some engines domestically but does not have enough to meet demand. He also cited a shortage of budget funding for the development and mass production of air-defense weapons.
Ukraine has been working to expand domestic production of the technology. Zelensky said last week that new decisions had been made to establish production of several types of jet engines inside Ukraine, following tests of interceptor drones against Russian jet-powered Shaheds.
The interceptor program has become increasingly urgent as Russia intensifies its aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities ahead of winter.
The new interceptor drones are intended to provide Ukraine with a cheaper and more scalable layer of air defense against the faster weapons, reducing pressure on scarce surface-to-air missiles and fighter jets.
Zelensky said US-made F-16s have proved effective against the new Russian drones, but argued that too many Ukrainian aircraft are undergoing lengthy maintenance in Europe. Kyiv wants more repair work moved inside Ukraine so the fighters can return to service faster.
What changed in Russia’s drone war in Ukraine?
Since Aug. 27, Kyiv has been living under a near-continuous drone campaign.
Russia shifted its long-range drone tactics that day, replacing the large swarms once or twice a week that Kyiv residents had become accustomed to with repeated waves across Ukrainian airspace.
The change was particularly noticeable in the capital, where attacks have increasingly continued into daytime hours.
As of Friday, Oct. 2, there has been no clear let-up. Repeated drone attacks have disrupted life in Kyiv, while strikes on warehouses, businesses and other civilian infrastructure have increasingly affected economic activity.
Russia has also sharply increased its use of jet-powered drones.
Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said Russia launched 3,177 jet-powered UAVs in September as of Sept. 29, compared with 2,850 drones of all types in August.
“We have already had more drones this month than in the previous month overall,” Ihnat said, adding that Russian forces were continuing to attack in waves.
Kyiv and the Kyiv region remained the main focus, he said, while Kharkiv, Odesa, Mykolaiv, Sumy, Kherson and Dnipro were also repeatedly targeted.
The increase marks a dramatic escalation from earlier in the summer. Ihnat previously said Russia used about 350 jet-powered drones in June, 1,500 in July and 2,850 in August.
The new drones are significantly faster than the older piston-engine Shahed variants, making them harder for Ukraine’s existing low-cost interceptors to catch.

With the assistance of the Ombudsman’s Office and partner organizations, 41 Ukrainian citizens returned this year in August–September through the "Mokrany–Domanove" crossing point in Volyn. They included four children and five teenagers
In addition
The Ombudsman also shared several stories of Ukrainians who managed to return from the occupation:
-  one family was able to return after the father was released from captivity. Their eldest son has remained in captivity since April 17, 2022. The woman and her younger son were under the constant supervision of the occupying authorities’ medical and law-enforcement services. According to them, they had previously been placed in a place of detention under the pretext of providing medical assistance, where they were held against their will and subjected to forced treatment. Now they were able to return to Ukraine; 
-  among those who returned was also a young female medic. She was evacuated on the eve of her actual mobilization into the armed formations of the aggressor state. A little more time, and her life could have followed a scenario imposed on her in the occupation; 
-  another man in the temporarily occupied territories was detained several times and held in basements. His Ukrainian citizen’s passport was confiscated. For him, returning meant not only crossing the border, but also once again having the opportunity to freely manage his own life. 
Lubinets emphasized that such stories show that occupation is not merely territory on a map. It is the loss of freedom, documents, housing, work, contact with loved ones, and a sense of security.
He recalled that the situation remains particularly acute in Oleshky and the surrounding settlements of the Kherson region. Elderly people, people with disabilities, the sick, and families living amid constant danger and limited access to food, water, medicine, medical care, and communications remain there. Safe evacuation remains extremely difficult for them.
The Ombudsman’s Office receives daily appeals from people who want to leave the occupation. We process every appeal, look for routes, engage government and international partners, and work through third countries. Because behind every appeal is a specific person and their right to return home. Volyn is one such route today. The "Mokrany–Domanove" crossing point is a place where, after months or years of occupation, people begin their return to free Ukrainian soil and subsequent recovery

A court in Germany denied the operators of the Nord Stream pipelines access to the case concerning the explosions on the gas pipelines
Kyiv • UNN
Nord Stream AG and Nord Stream 2 AG were not admitted to the proceedings as injured parties. The court in Hamburg will hear the sabotage case on October 14.
The operator Nord Stream AG and the company Nord Stream 2 AG will not be able to act as injured parties with the rights of the prosecution in the proceedings concerning the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines for now. The Higher Regional Court of Hamburg made this ruling. Bild reports, writes UNN.
Details
The court found that the companies had suffered losses as a result of the explosions, but saw no grounds for their participation in the proceedings as injured parties supporting the prosecution. The claimed losses, amounting to hundreds of millions of euros, were not deemed existential by the court: these are companies backed by multibillion-euro investments in the pipelines.
The court separately emphasized that the task of criminal proceedings is to establish whether the accused committed a crime. The court does not intend to examine the entire history surrounding Nord Stream within these proceedings, identify other possible perpetrators, or lay the groundwork for future compensation claims.
If accusations are made against the companies themselves during the proceedings, they will be able to reapply to participate in the proceedings as injured parties.
The controlling stake in Nord Stream AG belongs to Russia's Gazprom, while Nord Stream 2 AG is fully under its control. Charges have already been brought against an alleged participant in the sabotage, a Ukrainian citizen; another suspect was previously detained abroad. Both deny involvement. The trial itself in Hamburg is scheduled to begin on October 14.

From papads to pitches: NCERT brings startup lessons to Class IX
Unknown

2026-10-02

22:30:22 KST

A new chapter on startups and entrepreneurship has been introduced for Class IX students in NCERT textbooks.
NEW DELHI: Seven women, Rs 80 in borrowed capital and a Mumbai terrace. That was how Lijjat Papad began in 1959. More than six decades later, the story will be used to teach Class IX students how an idea, however small, can grow into an enterprise.NCERT’s new social science textbook has introduced a dedicated chapter on startups and entrepreneurship, taking students through the basics of identifying business opportunities, understanding markets and preparing a workable business plan.The chapter is built around three broad questions — how entrepreneurship affects society and the economy, what the main functional areas of a business are, and how an effective business plan is prepared.It also places these lessons in the context of India’s startup journey. The book says the country had only around 350-400 startups about a decade ago, while the ecosystem has now expanded to nearly 2.3 lakh enterprises, making India the world’s third-largest startup ecosystem. The broader policy push, it says, is to bring research, industry, startups and entrepreneurship onto a common platform.Students are introduced to the building blocks of running a business — understanding market activity, spotting opportunities, assessing performance and planning before committing resources.
The chapter also brings artificial intelligence into the discussion, explaining how AI can assist in market analysis and business decision-making.Alongside contemporary startup concepts, the book uses stories of Indian entrepreneurs to make the subject relatable.
One of them is Mohan Singh Oberoi, who began his working life on a salary of Rs 50 and went on to become a pioneering figure in India’s hospitality industry. Born in Punjab in 1898, Oberoi mortgaged his wife’s jewellery to buy his first hotel and later built a major hotel business.The Lijjat Papad story, meanwhile, illustrates entrepreneurship at the other end of the scale. Seven homemakers living in a Mumbai chawl started making papads with borrowed supplies and a traditional recipe. With no factory, each woman took dough home in the morning, rolled papads while managing household work and returned the finished product by evening.The lesson highlights how quality, organisation and persistence helped turn the modest venture into a widely recognised brand.

Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportage—both reflective and news-driven—adds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.

American supercarrier heads in for multi-billion refit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:30:17 BST
22:30:17 KST

The U.S. Navy has awarded Newport News Shipbuilding a $5.1 billion contract to carry out the Refuelling and Complex Overhaul of the aircraft carrier USS Harry S. Truman (CVN 75), with the ship due to return to the fleet in November 2031, according to the service.
The contract with the HII division uses a Fixed Ceiling Incentive structure, which the U.S. Navy says shares risk between the service and the shipbuilder while rewarding improved performance against required delivery dates. It is the first carrier RCOH contract awarded since the establishment of Portfolio Acquisition Executive (PAE) Maritime.
Rear Admiral Casey Moton, Acting PAE Maritime, said in the release: “This award is the latest example of how we are leveraging innovative contracting approaches to drive improved outcomes.” He added: “Our program management and contracting teams have worked side by side to arrive at a contract that incentivises schedule performance, addresses key lessons learned, shares risk appropriately so that we can re-deliver Truman to the Fleet on budget and on schedule.”
An RCOH involves refuelling the carrier’s two nuclear reactors alongside the modernisation, upgrade and repair of the ship’s systems. The U.S. Navy describes the work as a full recapitalisation intended to keep the ship relevant through the second half of a service life of more than 50 years, and says the availability accounts for nearly a third of the maintenance and modernisation the carrier will receive over its lifetime.
Truman will be the eighth Nimitz-class carrier to go through the process at Newport News, following Nimitz, Dwight D. Eisenhower, Carl Vinson, Theodore Roosevelt, Abraham Lincoln, George Washington and John C. Stennis. Recent overhauls have run beyond their planned durations. George Washington spent close to six years in its RCOH before returning to the fleet in 2023, and the John C. Stennis availability, which began in 2021, has also experienced significant schedule delays.
The carrier’s overhaul was itself once in doubt. In its fiscal 2020 budget request, the U.S. Navy proposed skipping Truman’s RCOH and retiring the ship early to free up funding for other priorities, a plan that was reversed weeks later following opposition in Congress.
Commissioned in 1998, Truman has deployed repeatedly to the Mediterranean and Middle East. Its most recent deployment, which ended in June 2025, saw the carrier strike group conduct strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen. During that cruise, the ship was involved in a collision with the merchant vessel Besiktas-M near Port Said, Egypt, in February 2025, after which its commanding officer was relieved. The carrier also lost three F/A-18 Super Hornets during the deployment, including one shot down in a friendly fire incident involving the cruiser USS Gettysburg.
According to the U.S. Navy, Truman will rejoin the fleet as the most technologically advanced carrier of the Nimitz class when the overhaul is completed.

Around 79,000 children displaced in western Yemen in less than a month: UNICEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:30:13 UTC
22:30:13 KST

Mohammed Sameai and Lina Altawell
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Around 79,000 children have been displaced in western Yemen in less than a month amid escalating fighting between government forces and the Houthis, UNICEF said late Thursday.
“Across western Yemen, renewed hostilities and shifting frontlines have deepened an already devastating humanitarian crisis,” the UN children’s agency said in a report.
It said fighting in Taiz and Al Hudaydah provinces, the western coast and surrounding areas have forced families to flee once again, leaving behind their homes, belongings and livelihoods.
“Between 3 September - 30 September, more than 145,000 people have been displaced, including an estimated 79,000 children,” UNICEF said.
The agency warned that the latest escalation comes amid an already severe humanitarian situation in a country where needs are among the highest in the world.
“More than 12 million children in Yemen require humanitarian assistance,” it said.
UNICEF said some displaced families are staying in overcrowded camps with limited access to clean water, healthcare and other essential services, while many arrived with little more than the clothes they were wearing.
The agency said it continues to support affected communities while calling for safe humanitarian access to children most in need.
On Thursday, UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg called for an end to fighting in Taiz province and for civilians and civilian infrastructure to be protected.
Yemen has witnessed its broadest military escalation in three weeks between government forces and the Houthis in recent hours.
The developments are part of an escalation that began in July, the most intense since the relative calm that followed an April 2022 truce.
Fighting accelerated in September, leading to Houthi control of several key locations in Al Hudaydah and Taiz provinces, including the strategic city of Mokha, and extending to Mayun Island overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, before a Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of the Yemeni government.

Amnesty International France has voiced alarm over the use of police violence against French high school students during protests over better learning conditions that have been under way for several days.
"The images of high school students being subjected to violence by law enforcement are extremely concerning. Many of them are minors, children. They must be protected, not beaten with batons," Amnesty wrote on X on Thursday.
The group also voiced concern over the high number of arrests while acknowledging that there had been violence by some protesters as well, which it described as "unacceptable".
"But even in these situations, including during arrests, the use of force must remain proportionate," it added.
The rights group further reported that a 14-year-old was hit by a grenade to the jaw on Monday and lost several of his teeth as a result.
It said grenade launchers should only be used in cases of widespread violence, when no other means are available, and never fired directly at people.
Amnesty also reported that a 14-year-old girl was violently grabbed by the neck by a police officer outside her high school on Tuesday, stressing that chokehold techniques in law enforcement are prohibited.
It also said that many arrests and detentions had been made since the beginning of the blockades, citing 164 on Monday, 440 on Tuesday, and 625 on Wednesday.
"Under international law, the arrest of minors should be a last resort," Amnesty wrote.
It called on authorities to prioritise dialogue and de-escalation, rather than the use of weapons.
Schools shut
Hundreds of schools have closed and been disrupted, while mass arrests and injuries were reported across France as student protests over better learning conditions continued.
The Ministry of National Education said 564 schools across France were affected on Friday.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told BFMTV that 1,207 high schools were disrupted or blocked at some point during the student mobilisation that has been ongoing for days.
Geffray warned Thursday that the movement “changed in nature” and was being “hijacked by violent groups".
Strasbourg protests
Tensions particularly rose in Strasbourg during the early hours of Friday when the protests outside a high school advanced towards a campus of the University of Strasbourg after protesters were pushed back by law enforcement.
During the protest, numerous mortar fireworks were reportedly heard while gasoline was used to start a fire.
Clashes were also reported between the crowds and police close to campus, with security forces dispersing protesters with tear gas.
Around a dozen rioters dressed in black were reportedly present, while high school and university students were also among the crowd.
Many protesters reportedly threw street furniture or other projectiles at the police.
Paris protests
In Paris, firefighters intervened at fires ignited at the entrances of several schools.
Police in Loire reported arrests of several individuals carrying dangerous objects, including a firework stick and a glass-breaking hammer.
The prefect of Bouches-du-Rhone told BFMTV that the situation was "incomparable with yesterday", with “far fewer protesters” on the streets of Marseille.
A total of 11 schools were “more or less affected” Friday morning, with some blockades cleared by riot police.
Prefect Jacques Witkowski said 55 high schools had switched to remote learning in the morning.
The Auvergne-Rhone-Alpes region estimated that damage linked to the student mobilisation amounted to $28 million to $33 million. The region reportedly recorded 180 blockades over three days and 90 attacks on high schools.
Protests in Aude
Protests also broke out near several schools in the Aude region, where projectiles were launched and rubbish bins set on fire.
At least seven arrests for possession of explosives and throwing projectiles took place in the department.
Meanwhile, an investigation was opened for attempted murder in Belfort after an off-duty police officer was reportedly beaten until he lost consciousness.
Top government officials held an emergency meeting on Thursday afternoon.
Several organisations representing the student movement, together with left-wing and far-left political groups, have called for a second round of mobilisation on October 6 against what they described as police “repression.”

UK's Manchester City formally appeals guilty verdict in Premier League financial case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:29:15 UTC
22:29:15 KST

Dilara Hamit
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Manchester City have formally appealed an independent commission’s finding that the club committed extensive breaches of the Premier League’s financial regulations, the club announced Friday.
City said the appeal was lodged at 7 pm local time Thursday, ahead of Friday’s deadline.
The club maintained its innocence and argued that the commission’s opinion contained “clear material errors, of law, principle and fact.”
It also said it had submitted a “comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence” supporting its position.
The Premier League announced Tuesday that the commission had found City guilty of all charges relating to serious financial breaches across nine seasons between 2009-10 and 2017-18. Three of four charges concerning the club’s failure to cooperate with the league’s investigation were also upheld.
According to the commission, City used “sham” contracts with sponsors and other commercial partners to inflate its reported revenue and reduce the expenses recorded in its accounts.
The panel found that some sponsors paid only part of the fees attributed to them, with the remainder provided by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment and Development Ltd., which owned the club.
The arrangements allowed City to overstate revenue and understate costs by more than £900 million ($1.2 billion), enabling it to appear compliant with Premier League and UEFA spending limits, the league said.
The commission also concluded that City filed misstated accounts, concealed the true condition of its finances from auditors and football regulators and sought to obstruct the Premier League’s four-year investigation.
Premier League Chief Executive Richard Masters said the decision established that City had “systematically” broken the competition’s rules for nearly a decade.
No sporting punishment has yet been imposed. Sanctions will be considered separately and could include fines, points deductions or other sporting penalties.
The appeal will be considered by a three-member Appeal Board appointed through the Premier League’s independent judicial process. The board may uphold or dismiss the appeal, vary the commission’s findings or issue another order.
Separately, the Football Association (FA) warned Friday that the commission’s verdict had “significant implications for the integrity of the game.”
In a statement published on its official website, England’s football governing body said it was carefully considering the decision and would take action where appropriate.
The FA said it would not comment further while the proceedings between the Premier League and City remained active but would continue monitoring developments.
The case has also attracted scrutiny from British lawmakers. Treasury Committee Chair Meg Hillier has asked Her Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC) whether it had examined the commission’s findings or requested an unredacted copy of its report.
Hillier also sought information about HMRC’s work concerning the taxation of remuneration and potential tax avoidance within football clubs.
Her intervention followed an analysis by Tax Policy Associates estimating that approximately £12 million ($15.2 million) in income tax and National Insurance may not have been paid in connection with what the commission described as a sham consultancy arrangement involving former City manager Roberto Mancini.
The group said the potential liability could reach £23 million ($30.42 million) to £24 million ($31.75 million) once interest and penalties were included. It stressed that its assessment was preliminary and did not accuse Mancini or any individual of committing a criminal offense.

An Ebola treatment center was burned down in Congo amid more than 4,000 deaths during the outbreak

Unknown Publisher

An Ebola treatment center was burned down in Congo amid more than 4,000 deaths during the outbreak
Kyiv • UNN
In the DRC, 4,018 people have died from Ebola out of 8,300 confirmed cases. Efforts to contain the disease are hampered by strikes, violence, and community distrust.
The Ebola outbreak in Congo has claimed the lives of more than 4,000 people, according to authorities, amid efforts to contain the spread of the virus. UNN reports this, citing AP.
Details
The latest figures published by the Ministry of Health on Thursday showed that 4,018 people had died, accounting for nearly half of the 8,300 confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
On May 15, Congo declared an outbreak caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there is no known treatment or vaccine.
Frontline workers have gone on strike several times since the outbreak began, further hindering efforts to contain the disease.
Some healthcare workers gathered in Bunia, the capital of the northeastern province of Ituri and the epicenter of the outbreak. They demanded payment of overdue wages but were quickly dispersed by officials. Among the protesters were members of a monitoring group who identify people who have come into contact with infected patients. They waved signs reading: "No money, no data!" and "No payment for months."
A senior UN official said that soldiers burned down an Ebola treatment camp containing a transit center for infected patients earlier this week while searching for weapons in Kigonze, on the outskirts of Bunia, forcing 19,000 people in the camp to flee.
"The enormous challenge of stopping the spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) became even more difficult after a key transit center for patients requiring treatment burned down in Ituri province," the United Nations said.
Julien Harneis, the UN's senior Ebola coordinator, said that establishing Ebola transit and treatment centers had been a challenging task requiring money and personnel, both of which are in short supply.
"When we lose a center, it means we lose capacity, we lose investments, and we have to start all over again. And above all, it means that people are not gaining access to the medical care they really need," Harneis said.
Infected aid worker evacuated to the Netherlands
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) contracted the Ebola virus while working in Congo, the organization said in a statement.
The worker arrived late Thursday evening after being transported to the Netherlands on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, according to a statement from Leiden University Medical Center.
"The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, where communities are facing the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the country," MSF said.
More than 50 healthcare workers have died after contracting the virus.
Danger and community resistance hinder containment efforts
The World Health Organization recently raised the alarm over the rapid spread of the virus into new healthcare zones, draining limited resources.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said at its latest press conference that the number of new confirmed cases is declining, but this could be explained by danger and difficulties in engaging communities to cooperate in some hotspots. Although the spread of the disease has slowed in some areas, it has accelerated in others, creating what experts consider a delicate situation.
The number of confirmed cases slowed in recent weeks, from approximately 850 cases and 470 deaths per week in mid-July to an average of 490 cases and 230 deaths in September. Overall, the outbreak also saw a similar 33% increase in both confirmed cases and deaths by September.
Earlier this week, a Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death for defending government measures to combat the outbreak, highlighting the tensions that have overwhelmed both the medical community and local resources.
The attack on Marie-Celestine Karondwa, a local official of Congo’s ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern province of North Kivu. His house was set on fire afterward, and he died in hospital from his injuries.
Widespread distrust of health workers and the authorities has hindered efforts to slow the 17th Ebola outbreak in the Central African country.
Last month, the authorities introduced a village-focused approach, but these efforts are facing resistance from residents who believe Ebola is a hoax. There is also deep distrust of the country’s government for reasons ranging from its handling of past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption, the publication writes.

BRUSSELS, 2 October. /TASS/. Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken has acknowledged that European countries do not have the necessary resources to conduct combat operations or respond to various types of threats, as they have focused only on social benefits and soft power for many years.
"Europe has been very good at investing in soft power, in social security, and it's beautiful to have a pension system, to have social welfare systems," Francken said in an interview at Euronews' Defence and Space Summit.
"When somebody gets sick, when somebody has lost his job, we have everything. But when there's war or when there is a hybrid threat, we don't have anything."
His words came amid European NATO member states’ efforts to increase defense spending and Brussels’ implementation of policies to strengthen the defense industry. In 2025, the EU set a course for large·scale militarization. For instance, at an emergency summit in Brussels in March, the ambitious 800 billion euro ReArm EU rearmament plan was approved; it envisages joint weapons purchases and the use of funds from the program for depressed regions. Later, the EU Council approved the creation of a 150 billion euro Security Action for Europe militarization fund as part of a long·term military construction program until 2030. Last year, at a NATO summit in The Hague, it was decided to increase European states’ defense and security spending to 5% of GDP by 2034.
Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that the alliance is following a path of "reckless militarization," and the image of Russia as a "threat" is being used to justify the decision to increase the defense spending of the bloc’s member countries to 5% of GDP.

Russia has increased repression against its citizens abroad eightfold — intelligence
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:19:34 EEST
22:19:34 KST

Russia has increased repression against its citizens abroad eightfold — intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
After 2022, the number of documented cases of Russia’s repression abroad increased eightfold. Moscow is persecuting critics and their relatives.
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin has intensified the persecution of its citizens abroad. Over three years, the number of documented cases of transnational repression has increased eightfold. This was reported by the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, citing a report by Mariana Katzarova, the UN Special Rapporteur on human rights in russia, UNN writes.
Details
The document "Nowhere to Hide: Exporting the 'Rule of Fear' Beyond the Country’s Borders – Transnational Repression by the Russian Federation" cites nearly 400 cases of russia persecuting citizens living abroad, as well as other people whom the Kremlin considers its opponents.
Before the beginning of the full-scale war, an average of 29 such cases per year were recorded over an eight-year period. After 2022, the average increased to 89 cases.
According to Katzarova, russia has created a state system for monitoring, intimidating, and punishing critics of the regime who have left the country. The pressure also extends to their relatives who remain in russia.
Leaving russia does not mean leaving Russian repression behind
The methods of persecution listed in the report include killings, assassination attempts, attacks, and poisoning. According to the document, at least nine FSB units are involved in such operations, along with Russia’s military and foreign intelligence services, the prosecutor’s office, and federal ministries.
In addition, moscow uses international mechanisms to search for and detain people abroad. In particular, russia actively submits so-called Red Notices to Interpol. At the same time, about half of such requests submitted in 2024 were canceled by the organization’s headquarters.
Cooperation between russia and partner states remains a separate instrument. According to the report, through such mechanisms moscow is attempting to persecute abroad people whom it considers disloyal to the Russian regime.
