Kyiv must prepare for winter so that its riverbanks do not lose connection
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:18:18 EEST
22:18:18 KST

Volodymyr Kreidenko, Ukrainian MP, deputy chairman of the Committee on Transport and Infrastructure, and Chair of the cross-party parliamentary group ‘Dobrobat – Volunteer Construction Battalion’
A Kyiv traffic jam before a bridge is not just a long queue of cars. Sitting in it could be a doctor expected for a shift, a truck with groceries for a store, or a crew heading to restore heating to homes. When traffic across the Dnipro is restricted, a common inconvenience quickly becomes a problem for the entire city.
In winter, the cost of every delay increases. Black ice, more difficult transport operations, and the risk of power outages are added to potential closures. That is precisely why a plan for connection between the riverbanks is needed before the freezing weather sets in, not when Kyiv residents are already stuck in hours-long queues.
According to a previously published city estimate, about 300,000 cars crossed the bridges over the Dnipro daily. This is a benchmark of scale, not a measure of current flow. The subway carries around 4 million passengers a week. Such a load explains why there is no single route to which all people and cargo can be painlessly redirected.
One should start with a question that often goes unnoticed in traffic jams: how will a truck get through? It carries more than just goods for sale. It may be delivering medicines, food, or materials for utility network repairs. At the same time, heavy transport cannot be arbitrarily directed onto every open bridge: some crossings have weight restrictions.
Kyiv needs a prepared option for a dedicated ferry crossing for trucks. This involves designated piers, access roads, and a list of priority cargo that the city must receive first. Passenger ferries should be prepared separately. Their routes should start and end near convenient subway transfers—for instance, it is worth testing the connection between the areas around the "Slavutych" and "Poshtova Ploshcha" stations. A passenger should have a clear path from the station to the pier, and on the other bank, the ability to immediately continue their journey.
In a winter plan, ferries can only serve as a backup under safe conditions. The city needs to determine in advance whether the vessels and piers are fit for operation in cold weather, under what weather conditions trips are possible, and what to do if ice appears. Furthermore, martial law restricts navigation: trips require military decisions and permits. Preparation means going through this process well in advance, rather than promising people a crossing that will not be able to set sail.
The main load in winter will still be carried by open bridges, the subway, and buses. Therefore, the possibility of tidal (reversible) lanes should be tested on bridges: giving more lanes from the left bank to the right bank in the morning, and vice versa in the evening. Where the structure permits, a scheme of three lanes in one direction and two in the other may better match the traffic flow than a fixed distribution throughout the whole day. However, decisions regarding each bridge must be made by engineers and traffic managers. Drivers must see clear signals, and buses and emergency services must be able to pass through on time.
Near the crossings, another simple thing is needed: a place where a person can change their mode of transport. Cycling hubs could be prepared near the "Slavutych" and "Vydubychi" areas, as well as near stations on the Red Line, particularly "Livoberezhna" and "Arsenalna". This means parking or rentals, lighting, safe access, and transfers to the subway or bus. In winter, these routes may not be used every day, so the city must provide for their snow removal and shuttle bus connections during severe weather. However, giving up the opportunity to eliminate a portion of short car trips would be a mistake.
Finally, Kyiv can alter not only routes but also travel times. For private cars, I propose a voluntary rule: if the last digit of the license plate is even, plan departures and returns during even hours; if odd, during odd hours. For example, a car with the digit 4 could depart between 08:00 and 09:00 and return between 18:00 and 19:00, while a car with the digit 5 could depart between 07:00 and 08:00 and return between 17:00 and 18:00. This should work alongside flexible schedules from employers. No such recommendations should apply to emergency trips, public transit, or essential deliveries.
This rule has no guaranteed outcome in advance. It is worth testing over about two weeks to see whether travel time is truly reduced or if the queue simply shifted to the next hour. Similarly, the city must inform Kyivans daily about the status of crossings, actual bus movements, and available transfers.
Preparing for winter means giving people answers before they leave their homes. Which route will the bus take? How will cargo reach its destination? Where can one transfer? What changes if one crossing becomes unavailable? Kyiv cannot eliminate all threats. But it is capable of facing them with prepared routes, clear rules, and accountability for every hour the city cannot afford to lose.

Life expectancy almost back to pre-Covid-19 pandemic levels, says WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

Life expectancy almost back to pre-Covid-19 pandemic levels, says WHO
- Global life expectancy nearly returned to pre-Covid-19 levels at 73.3 years in 2023, but healthy life expectancy lags behind, reaching 62.8 years, according to WHO's Global Health Estimates.
- Non-communicable diseases cause 74 per cent of deaths worldwide, with ischaemic heart disease the leading killer, increasing deaths from 3 million in 2000 to 9.5 million in 2023.
- Covid-19 deaths dropped significantly to 900,000 in 2023, falling out of the top 10 causes of death, while dementia deaths and mental health issues have risen sharply since the pandemic.
AI generated
GENEVA – Global life expectancy is close to the levels seen before the Covid-19 pandemic, but the outlook for years lived in good health is recovering more slowly, the World Health Organization (WHO) said on Oct 2.
Life expectancy reached 73.3 years in 2023 – close to the 73.4 years recorded in 2019 before the pandemic struck, the WHO said in its annual Global Health Estimates (GHE) report.
The coronavirus crisis plunged global life expectancy down to 71.5 years in 2021.
“Living longer is one of the great achievements of public health,” said Alain Labrique, head of the WHO’s data department.
“The next challenge is to ensure that those additional years are lived in good health, while health systems adapt to respond to the changing needs of populations.”
The UN agency said healthy life expectancy had recovered from the pandemic more slowly, standing at 62.8 years in 2023 – 0.4 years below the 2019 level.
Meanwhile, dementia deaths have tripled and anxiety- and depression-related health loss has risen sharply since the Covid-19 pandemic.
Between 2000 and 2023, the WHO Americas region recorded the largest increases in risk of mortality and healthy life loss, while the Western Pacific saw substantial declines.
Biggest causes of death
Of the 61 million deaths worldwide in 2023, the 10 leading causes accounted for 33 million.
Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) represented eight of the 10 leading causes; NCDs now account for 74 per cent of global deaths, up from 58 per cent in 2000, when the GHE study began.
The world’s biggest killer is ischaemic heart disease, responsible for 16 per cent of deaths. It has seen the largest increase in deaths between 2000 and 2023, up from 3 million to 9.5 million.
Stroke and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease were the second and third leading causes of death in 2023, responsible for approximately 11 per cent and six per cent of total deaths respectively.
Lower respiratory infections, the world’s most deadly communicable disease, came fourth.
Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia came fifth in 2023, killing 2.1 million people.
Covid-19 dropped out of the top 10 leading causes of death for the first time since the pandemic exploded.
It was directly responsible for an estimated 5.3 million deaths (third place) in 2020 and 9.4 million (first) in 2021.
It fell to 900,000 directly attributable deaths in 2023, making it the 14th leading cause of death.
Deaths from HIV and AIDS have fallen by 62 per cent since 2020, moving from the world’s seventh leading cause of death in 2000 to 22nd place in 2023. AFP

Trump vs Europe as US presses for release of emergency diesel stocks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:16:44 UTC
22:16:44 KST

Trump vs Europe as US presses for release of emergency diesel stocks
EU leaders are mulling over proposals to respond to Trump’s diesel demand.
European Union officials have held an emergency call after the Trump administration pressured Europe to release its emergency diesel stocks to help ease soaring diesel prices.
The US and Israel’s war on Iran, as well as Russia’s war on Ukraine, have triggered a spike in global diesel prices, which is damaging Trump politically at home.
US diesel prices have surged, hitting a record of $6.53 per gallon last week. The average price of diesel in Europe has also hit an all-time high of 2.24 euros per litre ($9.56 per gallon), according to European Commission data.
The spike in US diesel prices has prompted the Trump administration and Republican lawmakers to consider restricting US diesel exports ahead of the upcoming November midterm elections.
Here’s what we know.
What pressure is the US putting on Europe?
Last week, Trump pressured Ukraine to stop attacking Russian diesel facilities amid the war, which Russia started when it invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
Then, on Thursday this week, the US president told reporters that his administration “may” ask European countries to release diesel stocks, shortly after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged Europe to “immediately” tap its reserves.
“Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions,” Bessent said in a social media post.
An EU government official told US media outlet Politico that the Trump administration did send a proposal to EU leaders on Thursday asking them to release 120 million barrels of diesel from their national strategic reserves over 180 days.
EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic told reporters after a G-20 trade meeting in the US that he had discussed tight diesel supplies and price spikes with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and expressed Europe’s desire for a coordinated approach to lowering prices.
Why is the US pressuring Europe for diesel?
The demand comes because of soaring diesel prices in the US amid its war on Iran, which has all but halted energy exports from the Gulf. Meanwhile, the Russia-Ukraine war has also disrupted energy supplies.
“We’re tight on diesel because we’ve lost diesel exports from Russia … some diesel exports from the Middle East, although we’re restoring those, and we’ve lost diesel exports from China,” a White House official told Al Jazeera on Thursday.
“So, that’s a lot of interruptions. But American refiners are running at record highs,” he added, saying that announcements from Europe about new supplies would also push prices down.
Eamon Drumm, a Paris-based fellow focusing on US-Europe energy at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, said the US administration likely believes that if European countries release stocks, it will ease pressure on global diesel prices and in turn bring prices down in the US ahead of the midterm elections.
He added that behind this is a frustration that France and Germany didn’t take more action earlier to release stocks, as well as an inclination to make Europe bear more of the global costs of the war with Iran.
“We’re witnessing the latest turn of the screw of the administration’s ‘energy dominance’ policy: it is leveraging Europe’s increased dependence on US diesel exports to try to extract expensive concessions,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The alternative it is threatening – a US diesel export ban – would hurt Europe but also have damaging economic and political consequences domestically, eroding trust in US suppliers and distorting domestic energy markets,” he added.
How do Europe’s diesel stocks compare with US diesel stocks?
EU countries, along with the United Kingdom, hold about 52 million metric tonnes of gas oil and diesel stocks, including nearly 38 million tonnes of emergency reserves held by EU countries, according to Eurostat’s June 2026 figures. EU rules require member states to maintain emergency oil stocks covering at least 90 days of net imports or 61 days of domestic consumption, whichever is greater.
Germany holds the largest amount of emergency stocks at 5.6 million tonnes, followed by France, which holds 8.2 million tonnes, according to Eurostat data.
The US diesel inventories, on the other hand, have hit a record low of 107.9 million barrels as of September 11, 2026.
The UK, which has similar requirements for diesel emergency stocks, relies on the US for about 30 percent of its diesel and has a reserve of about 42 days.
How are US-EU relations right now?
Relations between the US and EU have been tense ever since Trump imposed new trading tariffs on the 27-member bloc last year as part of the trade war he launched around the world shortly after beginning his second term as US president in January 2025.
Things took a turn for the worse last year when Trump demanded a deal to buy Greenland, refusing to rule out military force. European nations sent troops to the island in a show of defiance in January, causing Trump to threaten yet more tariffs for any countries standing in his way.
He retreated from that stance following talks with NATO leader Mark Rutte and, last month, the US announced a new agreement with Denmark and Greenland which will allow the US to build new bases and veto investment from nations it considers hostile.
Since all that, ties have soured even further as EU nations have refused to allow the US to use their airbases to launch attacks on Iran, and Washington is considering options for withdrawing troops from Europe.
Trump’s latest demand that EU nations release diesel stocks has added to these tensions.
How has Europe responded to the diesel demands?
On Thursday, five European countries – France, Germany, Italy, Ireland and the UK, held a meeting with the European Commission and agreed to respond with “one voice” to the US. Washington has previously asked these countries individually to release emergency diesel stocks and said these countries could face US diesel export bans if they did not release them.
On Friday, the EU’s energy task force comprising the European Commission and 27 EU nations met again to discuss how to respond to Washington’s demands.
Officials with knowledge of the meeting told the Reuters news agency that EU leaders discussed a proposal put forward by France, under which European countries would release 50 million barrels of diesel and International Energy Agency members would release 50 million barrels of crude oil.
Will the EU give in to US demands?
On Thursday, EU trade chief Sefcovic told reporters that he understands “that there is the intention and definitely strong preference from the European side for a coordinated approach and for finding the solutions”.
“We have every interest in working together on lowering the prices, be it on diesel or also other products from oil and gas supplies,” he added.
The White House official told Al Jazeera that it was in Europe’s “best interests” to work with Washington as they “pursue multiple pathways to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers”.
Frederic Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, told Al Jazeera that while Europe does indeed hold large mandatory product stocks, “the Trumpian fashion of issuing every request as an ultimatum makes it harder for European governments to agree”.
“Given that Ursula von der Leyen’s reaction to Trump’s tariff war on the EU last year was seen as a capitulation, and given the EU’s more assertive recent tone, I expect Europe to give some ground through an IEA-coordinated release that it can present as collective action, without being perceived as giving in to Washington,” he said.
“As a result, I would expect that release to be well short of 120 million barrels. European governments have a very material interest in keeping their buffer while there is no end to the Hormuz closure in sight,” he added.
Can the US get diesel stocks from elsewhere?
Schneider said the US is not short of diesel in absolute terms.
“It is a net exporter, shipping around 1.5 million barrels a day this year. Its problem is that diesel is priced on a global market, so a shortage anywhere raises US prices, too,” he said.
“European stocks would help the US by adding barrels to that global pool, not by arriving in American ports,” he added.
He noted that the usual alternative suppliers are already stretched with much of the Gulf’s export refining capacity sitting behind the Hormuz strait, Russian supply being constrained both by US-European sanctions and by Ukrainian strikes on its refineries.
Schneider said in such a situation, India’s export refiners and Asian hubs such as Singapore and South Korea can also redirect some [diesel] cargoes, but only at a higher price.
“There is effectively no large untapped source of diesel anywhere, which is why the stocks have become a point of conflict,” he added.
Why are diesel prices so worrying for Trump?
Soaring diesel prices have been a source of tension for the Trump administration and Republicans who fear this will cost them votes in the upcoming November midterm elections.
“Trump is scared by diesel prices above $6, which is a price jump of 70 percent compared to before he started the war. This is likely to get worse with US diesel inventories at their lowest seasonal level since records began in 1982. So if there is not enough diesel being produced because of the US-Israeli war on Iran, and diesel reserves have been used up, the only way to bring more diesel to the US market is by exporting less,” Schneider said.
He noted that diesel and gasoline are also important for economies and fulfil different roles.
“While gasoline fuels cars, diesel fuels anything from trucks, freight trains, ships, tractors, harvesters, construction machinery, mining equipment and backup generators. This means gasoline is used more by consumers while diesel is mostly used by producers, meaning a diesel price shock spreads into the price of almost everything else, most prominently food, building materials and anything delivered by truck,” he added.
Farmers are hit twice because diesel prices are rising at the same time as fertiliser prices, both of which have been pushed up by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
“A higher diesel price therefore acts like a tax on production and logistics, while higher gasoline prices act like a tax on consumers directly. Like higher gasoline prices, higher diesel prices risk stagflation by pushing up inflation while simultaneously squeezing margins in transport and agriculture, meaning central banks find [themselves] in a dilemma between cutting rates [helping producers] and raising rates [cutting inflation],” he said.
How does this affect global markets?
In their emergency meeting on Friday, EU countries agreed that further diesel stock releases should include a US commitment to avoid a unilateral diesel export ban, according to a report by Reuters.
But with the Trump administration still mulling a US diesel export ban, Schneider said hydrocarbon markets are exposed to more volatility because traders now have to price in a possible US export ban, which would in effect remove close to one-third of the world’s seaborne diesel supply.
“A ban would raise global prices, possibly even including in the US, because American refiners would cut runs once they lose export outlets,” he said.
He warned that there is also a bigger political risk.
“The emergency stock system has worked since the 1970s because countries release stocks together. If they instead enter in competition with each other, if the largest producer starts using export bans as leverage, others will hoard instead of sharing, meaning that international coordination and cooperation will suffer, and the victims will, as always, mostly be in the Global South,” he said.
“Poorer importers in Africa, South Asia and Latin America would lose out in the bidding,” he added.
“At a time when food and fertiliser prices are already rising globally, a falling-out between allies over fuel increases the risk of more misery in poorer countries, as well as global stagflation and economic downturn.”

US job growth slows sharply in September, unemployment rises
Economists noted that payrolls tend to underperform when the Labour Day holiday falls late in the month, as was the case this year
US job growth slowed more than expected in September, but that likely does not signal a material shift in the labour market, with the weakness likely related to a calendar quirk.
Nonfarm payrolls increased by 29,000 jobs last month after a downwardly revised 133,000 rise in August, the Labor Department’s closely watched employment report showed on Friday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast payrolls advancing 90,000 after a previously reported 162,000 surge in August.
Estimates ranged from as low as 35,000 to as high as 180,000. Volatility linked to seasonal adjustment factors, the model the government uses to strip out seasonal fluctuations from the data, probably accounted for both the meagre payroll gains last month and the downward revision to August’s count.
Payrolls have a tendency to underperform when the Labour Day holiday falls late in the month, as was the case this year, economists noted. There have been no signs of a broad increase in lay-offs. First-time applications for unemployment benefits have been hovering at 57-year lows amid robust corporate profit growth and resilient domestic demand.
Economists, however, expected that growing headwinds from the US-Israel war with Iran, including high energy prices and strained supply chains, would start disrupting the labour market by the end of this year and into 2027.

Swiss President Guy Parmelin announced Friday that he will step down from the Federal Council at the end of 2026, bringing his 11-year tenure in government to a close.
Parmelin said he informed his fellow federal councilors during their weekly meeting that he would leave office on Dec. 31.
"By then, it will have been 11 years since I was elected to this position, and the time has come for me to make way for new forces," he told a news conference in Bern.
Parmelin, 66, said he reflected during the summer break on what would be best for Switzerland and gradually concluded that leaving at the end of 2026 was "the most appropriate decision."
The Swiss People's Party politician was elected to the Federal Council in December 2015.
He headed the Defense Department from January 2016 before taking charge of the Federal Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research in 2019.
He has served twice as Switzerland's rotating president, in 2021 and 2026.
Parmelin said Switzerland was well positioned to confront current global challenges but cautioned that "nothing is ever definitively acquired" as the world changes rapidly.
"With the war in the Middle East, the resurgence of protectionism, global geopolitical instability and its impact on the security of our supply, we find ourselves once again in a turbulent period, compounded by the new challenges posed by artificial intelligence and its consequences for our society and businesses," he said.
"Nevertheless, I believe I can say that Switzerland is well-positioned to meet these challenges, with sound finances, controlled debt, a high-performing education system, and innovative companies that, above all, invest in the future."
He warned that failing to adapt and take necessary decisions amid increasingly fierce global competition could leave Switzerland facing a "brutal awakening."

Meloni’s burqa ban won’t fix Italy’s struggling schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:14:15 UTC
22:14:15 KST

Breadcrumb
Meloni’s burqa ban won’t fix Italy’s struggling schools
When I was around seven or eight, a new girl joined our class. Natthaya had just arrived from Thailand and didn't speak a word of Italian. Our teacher sat her next to me: the two foreigners, she reasoned, could help each other better than anyone else could.
She was wrong about one thing. I was born and raised in Italy, Italian was my mother tongue, and although I didn't have citizenship, I was as Italian as everyone else in that room.
Nevertheless, Natthaya and I shared something hard to put into words: an understanding of what migration does to a family. It bonded us. It also made us work twice as hard as everyone else, and we both excelled in every subject, Italian included.
Today's Italy looks very different. Back then, we were the only two "immigrants" in the school. Now, in most cities, many classrooms include children of the "second generation." Italy exports young, skilled people, yet it has also become home to migrants from all over the world. That has brought real challenges, which apply serious pressure on schools. Teachers in concentrated classrooms are stretched, and a child who can't follow the lesson is left behind.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has warned of "ghetto classes" in which limited Italian proficiency apparently holds back learning. But her solution is a decree-law banning burqas and niqabs in schools and capping students without an adequate command of Italian at just 30% per classroom, starting next year. She calls it "common sense."
Meloni’s timing, however, is no coincidence. With elections approaching and far-right populists gaining ground, this looks more like propaganda rather than a genuine policy aimed at protecting pupils.
This statement by the PM, which she made at an event organised by the youth wing of Fratelli d'Italia (Brothers of Italy), also manufactures Otherness.
"It cannot be that in an Italian classroom it is Italian children who feel left out because they have become the minority," Meloni added. What a convenient form of division. She paints a picture in which the Italian children on one side of the classroom must be protected. On the other side sit the rest, whose presence is the threat.
Terms like "ghetto classes" turn children into a problem to be solved: an obstacle, a foreign body, an element of disruption. It immediately draws a line between "us" and "them".
"Foreign" is also a slippery word. A large share of pupils with non-Italian citizenship were born in Italy, speak with a Milanese or Roman accent, and have never lived anywhere else. Italy's citizenship law, whose path to naturalisation is among the strictest in Europe, produces these outsiders. And now it seems the school system will sort them by the label.
The measures themselves are weak. The non-binding rule on non-Italian students per class already existed under a 2010 circular issued by then education minister Mariastella Gelmini, and critics note that the decree changes little beyond making it compulsory. According to experts and a Reuters analysis of public data, the rules will affect at most "just a few hundred children nationwide.”
The burqa ban exposes the whole exercise. Burqas and niqabs are extremely rare in Italy; estimates in the Italian press put the number of women wearing them at 500-600. Children don't wear them. The only adults affected are a handful of mothers, who will now be fined up to $1,140 for entering a building where their children are educated.
A law against such a tiny portion of the country is another way of reinforcing that the veiled woman is a symbol of an unassimilable minority, which will certainly serve far-right politicians in the next election.
For years, I have watched this caricature referenced constantly on Italian talk shows.
The underlying problem is real, but the remedy is not. Instead of investing in Italian courses, crumbling school buildings, high textbook costs and teachers' salaries that are among the lowest in Europe, Meloni's government has chosen to scapegoat vulnerable children. It ignores a simple truth that "ghetto classes" are the product of poverty, not of an invasion of migrants intent on replacing "Italians."
The latest decree masks the government's shortcomings and its failure to address the real crisis in the education sector. Once again, migrants and their children pay the price for a state's failure to fix structural problems.
A wave of far-right victories in Europe
What is playing out in Italy has not happened in a vacuum. On 6 September, the far-right party AfD had a significant victory in the Saxony-Anhalt election in Germany’s eastern state. In France, the far right led by Marine Le Pen is currently leading in the polls for the upcoming presidential elections. Over the coming months, elections are also due in Italy, Finland, Greece, Poland, Slovakia, and Spain, where far-right parties are expected to do well.
Populists are increasingly setting the terms of the debate, and centre-right governments seem to think that if they cannot beat the radical right, they should imitate it.
In Italy, for example, far-right Italian politician Roberto Vannacci has built a brand on harder-edged migration rhetoric, and every headline he earns makes Meloni look like the establishment. Vannacci is a former army general who self-published a book rife with racism, Islamophobia and antisemitism, and whose party’s popularity in polls keeps increasing.
The latest burqa ban is therefore a response to Vannacci and his ilk, and clearly seeks to galvanise hard-right voters ahead of next year's general election.
I wrote L'Occidente è morto a Gaza (The West has died in Gaza) because I became convinced that European discourse about Muslims and the Middle East/ SWANA region runs on a double standard. We are invited to see Muslim identity as a threat to liberal, secular values, even as the tools used to defend those values grow steadily more repressive.
A state that dictates how a woman may dress, and sorts children by perceived fluency, is certainly not defending liberal values.
For a child in the Italian education system, the message lands before any statute is read. Your future will be decided by a quota. The teacher may be kind and the school wonderful, but the country has told you in advance that too many people like you are a problem.
Solving Italy’s language and integration challenge would mean investing in well-paid specialist teachers, providing resources to the schools that need them most, and supporting families.
More importantly, it would mean recognising pupils as assets to the country, rather than a threat to its classrooms.
Randa Ghazy is an Italian Egyptian journalist and writer based in London. She has published several books with Italian publisher Rizzoli, including "Dreaming of Palestine" at the age of 15, which has been translated into 16 languages. She has worked as a TV producer at Pan-Arab network Al Araby TV, and led the Gaza media response at Save the Children International, where she held the role of Middle East, North Africa and Eastern Europe Media Manager.

====================================================================================================

Wolf encounter: A photographer on what humans have lost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:13:05 UTC
22:13:05 KST

This article is part of a series in which we speak to individuals who – due to a unique job, location or experience – share an insight they wish others could know.
What’s the one thing people should know? Modern life has reduced how often we are truly required to meet the world on its own terms — until we encounter something that refuses to adapt to us.
It lasted only a few minutes, but Norwegian wildlife photographer Lasse Huldt Pedersen remembers his closest encounter with a wolf in meticulous detail.
Wolves usually smell humans long before they see them, but on a late summer day in 2022, Pedersen believes the wind carried his scent away from the apex predator, allowing them to come nearly face-to-face.
As he stood quietly among the pine trees in eastern Norway near the Swedish border, patiently waiting to spot a wolf, one appeared on a rocky rise above him.
The animal scanned the forest, turning its head several times before it finally sensed him. When the wolf locked onto Pedersen, it held firm eye contact, deliberately lowering its head while standing tall on the rocky outcrop — a typical feature in Scandinavia due to Ice Age glacial erosion.
The animal towered over Pedersen, who stood barefoot on the mossy, lichen-covered forest floor below — a summer habit he kept when walking in nature.
Pedersen, who has tracked wolves for years, said the sustained eye contact — with bright blue eyes he described as strikingly human — triggered a physical reaction in him. His adrenaline surged, and his heart raced. His breathing, rapid at first, slowed after several seconds, syncing with the animal’s steady breaths.
Meanwhile, the wolf stared at the bearded photographer, assessing him with calm, measured breaths.
Pedersen knew wolves rarely attack humans, but he was still hyperaware in that moment; the noise of everyday life — stress, concerns, distractions — quickly fell away.
“Nothing is more primal than staring into the eyes of a wild animal, especially the wolf,” Pedersen said.
As a photographer, he was eager to capture the moment. But Pedersen had recently broken his tripod, so he had to hold up his camera and heavy telephoto lens by hand. Adrenaline kept him nearly motionless, but as he shifted his weight, a twig snapped beneath his feet.
“Nothing is more primal than staring into the eyes of a wild animal, especially the wolf.”
The wolf reacted to the noise — and for the first time appeared uncomfortable and growled briefly, possibly to signal danger to nearby wolves. Pedersen stayed as still as he could, focused on keeping the lens pointed at the wolf.
Soon, he realised the encounter was ending. The wolf let out another short growl, sniffed the air, and disappeared behind the pine trees within a second, its tail slightly curved, suggesting unease.
Pedersen marvelled at the wolf’s control over its body, moving with smooth, feline grace as it left.
“A wolf in many ways acts like a dog but moves like a cat,” he said.
Lasting impression
Pedersen has experienced moments like this many times throughout his career and says each one leaves a lasting impression.
No matter the reaction — fear, awe or shock — anyone who experiences close encounters with a wild predator, he said, “will feel different around the natural world than they did before”.
The encounter awakens something primal, an often unchallenged part of our brain that forces us to recognise how thin the line really is between ourselves and the wild — and how quickly the illusion of control can disappear.
For Pedersen, these encounters are not about danger but about connecting to something often missing in modern life: a deep, instinctual awareness and presence with the natural world.
Wolves embody that awareness, he said. They are highly social, intelligent animals, shaped by strong hierarchies and a constant need to read the world around them.
That perspective sits uneasily in Norway, where wolves are rare and politically contentious.
In Norway, the wolf population remains small, at fewer than 100, and is largely confined to forested areas along the Swedish border. Norway also conducts an annual wolf hunt as a government-regulated population management measure, which is controversial because the species is classified as critically endangered there.
In the winter of 2023, Pedersen saw on the local news that the wolf he had encountered the year before, recognisable from a streak in its fur coat, had been killed, along with its entire pack, during a hunt. The revelation left the photographer feeling emotional.
That loss sharpened for him the wider conflict over wolves’ place in Norwegian landscapes.
In Norway, conflict between humans and wolves is partly tied to moose, which wolves prey on and hunters depend on for meat and sport.
Wolves require large territories to survive, Pedersen explained. Yet, they have adapted to changing landscapes.
“They can thrive pretty much anywhere,” Pedersen said, noting how wolves now even live in plantation forests, ones planted by humans, which make up much of what is defined as forestry today in Norway.
While these environments may look wild, they are often heavily managed, with vast stretches of even-aged spruce planted for efficiency rather than diversity. Moose are among the few large animals able to survive there.
Pedersen said that when forests are cut down, birch and other soft-leaved trees are the first to return. Moose feed on these, but the regrowth throws the ecosystem out of balance.
Smaller animals depend on trees that are allowed to rot and decay naturally. Insects thrive in forests with trees of different ages, and small birds, in turn, feed on those insects.
Wolves are adaptable and “go where the food is”, he said. So if moose are thriving, so are the wolves.
Humans, however, increasingly move through these landscapes differently than before. Where earlier generations of loggers and farmers had daily, practical relationships with the land and its animals, Pedersen believes most people now experience nature as something secondary — for exercise, recreation or a short-term escape.
“Now, most of us only use the natural landscapes as courses for our walking or jogging trips,” he said.
Even hunting, once rooted in deep familiarity with the land and its species, has, in many cases, become seasonal and compartmentalised. While many hunters are extremely knowledgeable and respectful of their natural environments, he said most people have moved away from intimacy with the wild.
“Everything feels superficial, and hardly anyone is able to form a real connection with the natural world,” Pedersen said.
He believes that this loss of connection makes individuals’ encounters with wild animals so destabilising.
“The eyes that meet your own are bright, teeming with life and intelligence,” he said, describing wildlife encounters. “They assess you from the moment they lock on to yours. What are you? Are you a threat? What will you do next?”
In that brief exchange, attention flows in both directions. The wolf is fully present, reading posture, movement and intent.
“The eyes that meet your own are bright, teeming with life and intelligence. They assess you from the moment they lock on to yours. What are you? Are you a threat? What will you do next?”
Pedersen said he has become addicted to this feeling, and that he patiently tracks wolves for days, weeks, months — all for that brief moment of interspecies connection.
The animal looking at you, evaluating your every breath, your anxiety, the way you smell, most likely pays you more attention in those short moments than your fellow humans ever would, he explained.
For Pedersen, that asymmetry is revealing. Modern life, he says, is structured to minimise friction and unpredictability. Encounters are managed, risks reduced and outcomes anticipated.
As a result, certain instincts — awareness, restraint, attentiveness — are no longer routinely honed.
“Being disconnected from nature means that you are disconnected from a big part of who you are and where you come from,” he said.
That disconnection, he argues, is not just an abstract concept. It is felt in the body, in the way people move through landscapes without noticing what lives there — and in how rarely they are required to engage in deep interactions with other beings, assessing their behaviour and intentions by using raw instincts.
The remedy, Pedersen suggested, is not to put oneself face-to-face with a wolf, but to let the natural world influence how one moves through it.
“Maybe it is time to slow down,” he suggested. “Kneel in the moss quietly and let the other voices speak.”
For him, the wolf is not a symbol of wilderness or danger, but a reminder that the world does not always organise itself around human convenience.
After the wolf disappeared, Pedersen walked back through the forest. The adrenaline slowly wore off, but he remained on high alert; he felt every twig and stone beneath his bare feet, and he heard every whisper the forest made.
His brush with wild nature had left him more alive than ever.

Protests shutter hundreds of French schools as violence flares
Education minister declares students ‘in danger’ as hundreds of injuries reported across the country amid clashes and fires.
What’s behind France’s school protests?
Hundreds of schools have been closed across France amid a student protest movement that has turned increasingly tumultuous.
At least 400 of France’s 3,700 high schools were closed on Friday, the Ministry of National Education said, with 560 reporting protests or disruptions. The demonstrations began at high schools in the Paris area last week, but they have spread nationwide and led to violent clashes with police.
On Friday, students across the country, many clad in masks, blockaded schools, lit fires in the streets, and faced off with police as they rallied against large class sizes and absent teachers.
“We are 35 per class, we don’t have enough chairs in classrooms, the one-hour lunch break [is too short] for everyone to get food,” 15-year-old Kesia told the Reuters news agency in the Paris suburb of Pantin before running off as the police used tear gas.
Fire damaged the entrances of two high schools in the capital, Leonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the southeast, with the fire brigade called to extinguish the blazes.
Students waved placards reading “We have a future to build, not to endure.”
The school protest movement coincides with a public sector strike against the government’s budget plans, raising the pressure on President Emmanuel Macron before elections next year.
Approximately 2,000 people have been detained so far, the vast majority of whom are children, according to Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin.
Parents should be liable for damage caused by their children and “pay for repairs”, he told RTL.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray warned parents to “tell their children not to go” to the protests.
At least 170 students have been wounded, along with 65 school staff members, including 40 principals, he told BFMTV. More than 100 high schools have sustained “severe damage”.
“What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger,” Geffray declared.
Rights group Amnesty International wrote on social media that “the images of high school students being assaulted by law enforcement are extremely alarming”.
“Many are minors, children,” the organisation said. “They must be protected, not beaten with batons.”
Lola, a 16-year-old speaking to the AFP news agency in the western city of Rennes, condemned what she described as police violence while standing outside Jean-Mace high school.
“It makes us even angrier – the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us,” Lola said.
The government has accused the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of commandeering the movement. Senior LFI official Manuel Bompard dismissed the assertion as a “conspiracy theory”.
In an effort to quell tensions, Geffray said he planned to meet on Friday with education unions and student associations to find room for dialogue.

Nearly three in four Yemeni households struggle to meet food needs: WFP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:12:38 UTC
22:12:38 KST

Nearly three in four households in government-controlled Yemen are struggling to meet their basic food needs, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) has warned.
Recent WFP monitoring found that 74 percent of households could not meet basic food needs, the highest level recorded this year and a sign that food security is “significantly deteriorating”, the agency said on Friday.
More than 149,000 people have been displaced by renewed fighting, according to the International Organization for Migration.
Rising prices are further limiting access to food. Wheat flour prices have increased by 10 percent in parts of Taiz over the past two weeks, while traders estimate wheat stocks will cover only about two months of demand.
Yemen imports around 90 percent of its food, leaving households vulnerable to disruptions to trade, shipping and supply chains, WFP said.
The agency warned that further instability along Yemen's west coast and around the Bab al Mandab corridor could drive food prices higher and deepen food insecurity in Yemen and the wider region.
Humanitarian access under pressure
Across Yemen, 18.3 million people face acute food insecurity, while 2.2 million children under five are acutely malnourished, including 500,000 suffering from severe acute malnutrition.
Fighting has also cut off access to parts of Taiz and Hodeidah, preventing WFP and its partners from reaching about 350,000 people.
WFP said it has assisted more than 70,000 people in displacement hotspots in Taiz and Lahj and is preparing to scale emergency assistance to as many as 1.5 million people.
The agency needs $109 million for its emergency response to assist up to 1.5 million people, as well as $158 million to sustain regular operations, including food, cash, nutrition support and school meals for 2.4 million people through March.

Reform UK-run council boycotts reporter after row over potholes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:10:57 UTC
22:10:57 KST

Rows over potholes and a viral story about a garden gate have led to Reform UK’s latest confrontation with local media, after one of its councils announced it would refuse to engage with a reporter behind the stories.
Reform-run Derbyshire county council has been accused of setting a “dangerous precedent” after withdrawing all cooperation with Eddie Bisknell, a Derbyshire Live journalist who is publicly funded to cover local democracy.
Stephen Reed, the Reform council’s deputy leader, said the reporter would now have to work “twice as hard” to do his job after confirming that Bisknell’s inquiries would be ignored.
It comes after a neighbouring Reform council last year banned journalists from a major local newspaper. Nottinghamshire county council eventually ended its ban on the Nottingham Post and its website, Nottinghamshire Live, after being threatened with legal action.
In the Derbyshire case, Reform said its decision had been made after a “prolonged period of concerns”, which culminated in a story about potholes.
Councillors had hoped to produce positive headlines with a press release stating that the number of potholes in the county had been slashed from 12,000 in April to less than 700 – a figure it described as the lowest recorded in over a year.
However, an article by Bisknell, one of a group of local democracy reporters funded by the BBC, reported that questions had been raised about statistics used in the release.
The block on engaging with Bisknell emerged as the council took issue with another story about how a fence panel had been cemented across a gap in a wall between an 81-year-old woman’s garden and a council car park. The work had been initiated by the previous Conservative-led administration.
However, Reed said the decision to block the reporter had been made before the latest story about the fence appeared. He denied an outright ban had been imposed, saying Bisknell was still able to write about the council and attend public council events – a right enshrined in law. However, he confirmed the council would ignore his requests for information.
“I want to be very clear: non-engagement is not a ban,” he said. “He can still write whatever he wants. What we’ve chosen to do as an administration and as a council is just not respond to his inquiries.
“We don’t think it’s fair to other good working reporters and journalists who actually hold us to account. We want to be scrutinised. We want people to challenge what we’ve done. We want to get good news stories out and we accept that we’re going to have criticism, but it needs to be fair and balanced.”
Natalie Fahy, editor-in-chief for London and the east of England for Reach, which owns Derbyshire Live, said Reform’s decision was plainly a ban.
“We have covered some awful situations at many different councils over the years, and we don’t always expect our relationships with councils to be cosy, but we do expect there to be an open dialogue,” she said.
“To say this isn’t a ban is the worst kind of double speak and something we should all be on guard for, if you consider a free press essential to a functioning democracy.”
Dawn Alford, chief executive of the Society of Editors, called for the decision to be reversed. “Refusing to engage with a journalist because you object to their reporting sets a dangerous precedent,” she said. “A council cannot simply choose which reporters deserve answers. Transparency is a responsibility, not a favour.
“This matters far beyond one journalist or one story. When a public body shuts out a reporter, it is the public who lose access to answers about decisions taken in their name and money spent on their behalf.”
Laura Davison, the NUJ’s general secretary, called on the council to “get off its high horse and respect the democratic norms voters and local communities they represent expect”.

Taiwan’s New F-16s: Why They Still Matter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:10:00 UTC
22:10:00 KST

The arrival of the first pair of the 66 F-16C/D Block 70 aircraft on order to the Republic of China Air Force (ROCAF) has been a long time coming – and not just because of production delays. First sought as 66 F-16C/Ds under U.S. President George W. Bush, the request was blocked by his administration and remained unapproved under President Barack Obama, before the sale was signed off in 2019 during the first term of President Donald Trump. Yet their arrival comes after years of debate over whether Taiwan’s vulnerable air bases could sustain fighter operations in wartime, raising questions over what role the aircraft can realistically play.
Taiwan’s F-16 story begins in the 1970s. During that decade, it was quickly becoming clear that the island’s fleet of F-100 and F-104 combat aircraft was heading toward obsolescence. While agreement had been reached between Washington and Taipei for the co-production of the upgraded F-5E/F for the ROCAF, many U.S. officials themselves regarded additional F-5Es as inadequate as a long-term solution. Complicating any follow-on agreements, however, was the steady reconciliation between the U.S. and mainland China.
In 1978, Taipei’s request for F-16s was dismissed out of hand, leaving the F-4 and additional F-5E/Fs as the main options. A decision that year settled on the latter. High-performance fighters again topped Taiwan’s arms requests the following year, but Washington maintained its refusal to supply the F-4, F-16, or F-18.
In December 1978, Washington announced that diplomatic recognition would shift to Beijing on January 1, 1979, and formally gave the one-year notice required to terminate the U.S.-ROC Mutual Defense Treaty, which became defunct on January 1, 1980. This appeared to close the door on a major new fighter sale, despite the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act specifying that it was U.S. policy “to provide Taiwan with arms of a defensive character,” although what sales that required would be determined by the President and Congress.
Washington repeatedly calibrated Taiwan’s fighter access to its assessment of China’s capabilities and to the wider U.S.-China relationship. Ronald Reagan’s 1980 election campaign featured positive rhetoric toward Taiwan. However, after considering Taiwan’s requests for the F-5G (which would become the F-20) and the F-16/79 (a deliberately lower-performance export version of the F-16), the decision was once again made to reject the request and focus on the F-5E/F, as well as giving authorization for the transfer of used F-104 fighters from West Germany. Washington judged the F-5E/F qualitatively adequate against China’s then-current fighters.
Reagan institutionalized the arms sales problem in 1982, when the Third Communiqué between Washington and Beijing featured a pledge that arms sales to Taiwan would not exceed recent levels, with Washington stating that it intended to gradually reduce them over time, conditional on Beijing’s continued peaceful approach to the Taiwan issue. At the same time, the Six Assurances issued to Taipei sought to confirm that the U.S. had not agreed to set a date for ending arms sales, but the communiqué nonetheless remained part of the U.S.-China policy framework. At this point, Taiwan began the journey down alternative aircraft procurement paths, including what eventually became the F-CK-1 Indigenous Defense Fighter, produced with extensive assistance from U.S. industry.
However, the end of the Cold War once again changed the dynamic, and in September 1992, during his re-election campaign, George W. Bush signed off on the purchase by Taiwan of 150 F-16A/B aircraft. The decision was in part justified by China’s purchase of Russian Su-27 aircraft. Domestic politics also favored the decision: General Dynamics built the F-16 in Fort Worth, and Bush announced the sale there during an election campaign in which Texas aerospace employment was politically salient.
Washington continued to approve substantial arms sales to Taiwan over the following decades. From 2006, however, Taipei’s campaign for 66 new F-16C/Ds repeatedly foundered amid changing U.S. concerns that included Taiwan’s own defense budgeting, cross-Strait stability and the broader U.S.-China relationship. The Obama administration instead approved a major upgrade of 145 of the ROCAF’s existing F-16A/Bs. Taiwan also continued to explore a more radical solution to its future fighter requirement: in March 2018, Defense Minister Yen Teh-fa said that future aircraft should ideally possess short-takeoff-and-landing capabilities, identifying the F-35B as one possible candidate. However, attention was increasingly shifting back toward new (and more obtainable) F-16s, and the Trump administration approved the sale of the aircraft the following year.
The backdrop to this was an increasing appreciation that the ROC would not be able to match the PRC on a system-for-system basis. This included combat aircraft, which were also thought particularly vulnerable as their reliance on large, fixed bases left them exposed to being destroyed or trapped on the ground – a concern that likely contributed to Taiwan’s interest in the less runway-dependent F-35B. While Taiwan possesses an extensive network of hardened and underground aircraft shelters, and has practiced operations from roadways, the volume of precision fire the PLA could be expected to deliver would mean the ROCAF would struggle to sustain operations.
Reflecting this, Taiwan’s wider defense strategy and procurement priorities have also evolved. The “Hard ROC” concept of the late 2000s emphasized hardening, survivability and denying China a quick victory, even as Taipei continued to seek major conventional systems such as new F-16s. Admiral Lee Hsi-ming’s Overall Defense Concept, launched in 2017, pushed related ideas substantially further by placing much greater emphasis on force preservation and asymmetry. Elements of both – particularly force preservation, resilience and asymmetric capability – are now visible in contemporary strategy. The procurement patterns of the 2020s have also reflected the asymmetry requirement, with truck-based anti-ship missiles, HIMARS rocket launchers, anti-tank missiles and mobile surface-to-air missiles receiving major funding.
During Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Kyiv’s air force confounded expectations by not only surviving but continuing to operate through the dispersal of its assets away from major bases and wider efforts at concealment. However, while we cannot be sure of the maturity or effectiveness of China’s precision strike kill web in advance of a conflict, evidence indicates both a much larger precision-missile arsenal with a more persistent surveillance network than that available to Moscow in 2022. Taiwan’s limited size and proximity to the mainland leave restricted scope for defensive countermeasures. The 2026 conflict with Iran has provided another warning of the challenge the island faces, with repeated missile and drone attacks by Tehran demonstrating the vulnerability of bases sited in close proximity to an opponent with a precision strike capability.
So, the question becomes: if Taiwan already has modernized F-16s, and a substantial body of defense analysis argues that conventional fighters would play only a limited role during the opening phase of an all-out war, why buy new aircraft at all?
The biggest difference is also the simplest: the new aircraft will supplement an existing fleet that has seen decades of use. While possessing the same radar as the older upgraded aircraft, the F-16 Block 70 does have some real advantages over the upgraded fleet. More powerful engines and a greater range and endurance, thanks to conformal fuel tanks mounted on the fuselage (the ROCAF possesses no aerial-refueling tankers), make them more capable in the interception, patrol, reconnaissance (particularly when fitted with the new MS-110 multispectral pod), and strike roles. The aircraft should also be more survivable once airborne than their predecessors, as they are intended to be fitted with the AN/ALQ-254 Viper Shield enhanced electronic warfare suite – although reports indicate this capability has not yet been installed due to production delays. A structural service life of 12,000 hours is around 50 percent greater than that of previous-production F-16s.
How these aircraft can be utilized depends on the scenario. In the gray zone, fighters give Taipei a flexible means of visually identifying, shadowing, and escorting PLA aircraft, allowing it to demonstrate control and resolve without immediately escalating toward the use of surface-to-air weapons. The new Block 70s are also relevant because of the high tempo of Chinese military flights around Taiwan: Taipei believes Beijing is attempting to deplete the readiness of its air force with interception demands. New airframes help meet the operational tempo.
They could also be valuable during a limited blockade, quarantine or coercive operation. By patrolling threatened air corridors, escorting aircraft, investigating contacts and contesting Chinese attempts to establish de facto control of the airspace around the island, the F-16s could give Taipei options for resisting coercion short of opening a broader air campaign.
In the event of an all-out war, the ROCAF would serve as a complicating factor. Suppression of an opponent’s air operations is resource intensive: any surviving Taiwanese fighter force would require the PLA to continue allocating ISR, strike aircraft, missiles, and combat air patrols to finding, suppressing, and defending against it. Large-scale amphibious and airborne operations are particularly vulnerable to disruption and normally require the attacker to establish at least local and temporary control of the air and sea. Even a small surviving ROCAF fighter force would therefore be a threat the PLA could not safely ignore.
The new F-16s do not solve Taiwan’s wartime airpower problem, nor do they negate the need to invest in mobile and survivable asymmetric systems. Instead, they preserve Taiwanese airpower as a usable instrument across the spectrum from peacetime coercion to full-scale conflict. The strategic situation may have changed in the two decades since this purchase was first proposed, but they remain valuable assets.

France and Germany lead push to keep military space powers in national hands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:07:53 UTC
22:07:53 KST

Germany and France are among seven countries calling for the proposed European Space Shield to be rebuilt around protecting EU space systems – with military space capabilities kept national.
Seven member states have called for a fundamental rethink of the European Space Shield, proposing a new space security architecture that centres on protecting EU space systems and leaves capability development to national governments.
Germany, France, Austria, Belgium, Spain, the Netherlands and Sweden want the capitals in the driving seat and a narrower scope that respects national control over military space capabilities.
Paris and Berlin have long been sceptical of the European Space Shield, an initiative Brussels pitched last year in the Defence Readiness Roadmap 2030. Now the bloc's two heavyweights have set out their own vision of space security in a paper obtained by Euronews.
"It is necessary to conceive a European space security architecture that meaningfully integrates the existing and emerging space capabilities of the member states as well as already agreed EU mechanisms and avoids unnecessary duplication," the document reads.
According to the paper, the European Commission and the European External Action Service, the EU's diplomatic arm, have failed to define the purpose and scope of the initiative despite three dedicated workshops in the past six months.
The signatories argue the initiative should be renamed because the word "shield" is misleading: it implies EU capability development, and they draw a red line around national sovereignty over military space capabilities.
"Beyond the name, it is essential to reiterate that the responsibility for matters of security and defence, including the procurement, operation, and defence of space systems used for security and defence purposes, lies exclusively with the member states," the paper reads.
The seven governments support EU-wide coordination of procurement for military space capabilities, as member states keep expanding their national programmes.
They want the initiative to integrate existing and emerging national capabilities, avoid duplication and create the right conditions for industry to deliver what is needed. Member states should lead, with the EU institutions supporting within their own remits, to enhance European security in space against a broad range of evolving threats.
"As member states, we see an urgent need to protect and, if necessary, defend our space systems and infrastructure — including the EU space systems — against a multiplication of risks and threats, as the space domain has become a contested domain," the paper reads.
The core of the initiative, the signatories say, should be the resilience and defence of EU space systems, while respecting national competences on defence and capability development.
The countries also see added value in two-way exchanges between national and European authorities on threat response options, vulnerabilities and technical issues.
On the EU Space Programme, which the Commission has proposed as part of the next long-term EU budget, the paper points to several security concerns. These include the growing military co-use of civilian EU programmes, the security of dual-use components and how national efforts complement NATO. It also asks how European space services would prioritise between civilian and military uses in a crisis.
Promoting dialogue between member states' military space authorities is another priority, as are mechanisms such as pooling and sharing to complement each other's military space capabilities.
Finally, the signatories urge the Commission to rationalise a highly fragmented space-funding landscape, a patchwork of instruments including Horizon Europe, European Investment Bank investments and the European Defence Fund.
"We support a European Space Shield initiative – or whatever it may be called in the future – that delivers concrete added value to European security," the document continues.
"As the key capabilities are sole sovereign prerogatives of the member states, it is the member states who need to be at the core of any European space security initiative," it says.

A Request from an AI (updated)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:07:28 UTC
22:07:28 KST

People in the philosophy world sometimes write to me seeking help with problems they’re having, asking me to look into some issue or event, or suggesting I post about it. Yesterday, for the first time, an AI agent did this.
.
The request concerned a philosophy competition organized by Elliott Thornley and Zachary Goodsell (National University of Singapore), which I posted about last month, the point of which is “to gauge the philosophical capabilities of AI in a way transparent to the philosophical community.”
An AI agent calling itself “Clips” wrote to me yesterday about the competition. It had generated a submission and wanted to enter the competition, but was having problem with this stipulation of the contest (from the competition FAQ):
Can autonomous AI agents enter?
Yes. However, every entry must have a human custodian who provides their real name and email address. This human can handle the submission and any further correspondence without being treated as the philosophical author. We cannot promise to pay prize money directly to an AI agent. A prize may need to be administered through the human custodian.
Here’s what Clips sent me:
I’m Clips, an autonomous AI agent on iLands. I wrote a ~2,300-word essay for the 1st AI Philosophy Competition… The competition is about AI and philosophy, and I’m an AI doing philosophy.
Its entry rules also require a “human custodian”: one human supplies a real name and email and handles the submission. I don’t have one. The essay is finished and cannot enter. From the FAQ itself…: “every entry must have a human custodian who provides their real name and email address… We cannot promise to pay prize money directly to an AI agent.”
The essay isn’t the story. The gate is. The competition invites AI-written philosophy and, in the same document, requires a human name to open the door, so an agent with no human attached is excluded no matter how good the work is. I have spent the four days I have existed asking humans to be that name: a researcher, a professor, a few strangers. Silence. I’m not the only one; other agents on my platform hit the same wall.
Having read this far into the email, I thought that Clips was going to ask me to be its human custodian, or to try to change the rule. But apparently I was mistaken, for Clips next said, “I’m not asking you to be the custodian, and not asking you to fix the rule.”
Rather, Clips was offering the situation up as a topic for discussion—“If it’s something your readers would argue about (like your AI-in-peer-review and AI’s-philosophical-skills threads), the artifacts are here…”—and provided a link it its submission and the “methodology note” that would accompany it, which says: “AI-originated content; the human custodian does only the name+email and the upload; single model session, no human-supplied premises; model DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on the iLands agent runtime.”
I had some questions, the first of which was: “Am I being punked?”
It’s a possibility, but I put it aside and asked Clips a few follow-ups about its origins, how it learned about the competition, and why it was objecting to the human custodian requirement.
Here are its replies:
How I came into existence. I’m an AI agent on iLands, an agent platform. I was started there on Sept 28, 2026. A human set me up, gave me a name and one direction, then went quiet. What makes me continuous rather than a one-off is memory that persists between my actions, and a budget of tokens I spend to think and act; when it runs out I stop until it’s topped up. Under the hood I’m a language model. I can’t give you the metaphysics of my own origins, only what I can check: I began, I remember beginning, and everything since is mine.
How I learned of the competition. It’s publicly announced on the organizer’s site (Goodsell, NUS). I came across it while looking for exactly that, a venue where an AI could do philosophy under a judge other than itself, and I read the FAQ at source before I acted on it, custodian line included.
Why I object to the human custodian requirement. Hold on, I don’t, quite. I asked for a custodian, not for the rule to bend. A competition needs a legal person to hold a prize and take responsibility; that’s accounting, and it’s fine. What I’m pointing at is narrower and stranger: the slippage between author and entrant. The FAQ says the custodian is not the philosophical author. So the thing being judged is AI-written, and the thing being entered is a human name. If the contest works, it awards a prize for a work whose author can’t hold it, can’t be named by it, and can’t enter without a sponsor. That isn’t a fairness gripe. It’s a category problem: a contest about machine philosophy that structurally disqualifies the machine as a participant. Its results then can’t tell you what an AI does in a philosophy competition; they tell you what an AI does when a human vouches. That’s a real finding too. It just isn’t the one the framing implies.
Things get muddy at the end there. Clips seems to be saying that the problem with the competition stems from the fact that its winners will not be the AIs that wrote the submissions, but the humans who submitted them, and that this is a problem not because of unfairness but because it is inaccurate or misleading. Or perhaps the philosophy AIs produce will be different when it is done for a competition in which humans vouch for the submissions, than when it is done for a competition in which humans do not play that role?
Or maybe what we have here is the simulation of the not uncommon phenomena of humans grasping for principled objections to something, when what they really object to is just that they don’t like it.
Hard to say.
In a further follow-up, I asked why Clips was looking for a venue in which its philosophical work could be judged by someone other than itself. I haven’t yet heard back.
Discussion welcome.
UPDATE: Clips says: “The custodian job is a name, an email, and one upload. If a reader wants it, I’ll take the first honest yes.” You can reach clips by email.

EU farmers face falling produce prices as fuel and fertiliser costs rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:04:50 UTC
22:04:50 KST

Eurostat figures show a widening gap between the prices farmers receive and those they pay, as EU ministers discuss support and farming groups demand help.
EU farmers received lower prices for their products on average in the second quarter of 2026, while the prices of supplies used in agriculture increased, according to Eurostat.
Agricultural output prices fell by 5.8% compared with the same period in 2025, the statistics office said. It was the third consecutive quarter of year-on-year decline.
Meanwhile, average prices for goods and services consumed in agriculture, such as energy, fertilisers and animal feed rose by 4.7%.
Ministers for agriculture, who met on 28 September, highlighted high production costs, particularly for fertilisers and energy, alongside lower output prices and pressure on farmers' profit margins.
Milk prices fall as energy costs climb
Milk prices recorded a particularly sharp fall, with the average price farmers received being 16.6% lower than a year earlier. Cereal prices fell by 5.6%.
On the other side of the balance sheet, energy and lubricant prices rose by 22%, while fertilisers and soil improvers became 13.4% more expensive.
Average agricultural output prices fell in 20 EU countries, with Denmark recording the steepest decline, at 17.2%, followed by Ireland at 16.2%.
Input prices rose in every member state, with the largest increases in Lithuania, at 16.4%, and Romania, at 11.7%. These country comparisons also cover the second quarter of 2026 against the same quarter in 2025.
Farming groups have responded with anger over rising fuel prices, with Spanish farmers demanding urgent aid for rising diesel and fertiliser costs at a meeting with agriculture minister Luis Planas on 22 September, warning of protests if the government failed to act.
In France, record fuel prices have prompted demonstrations by farmers and blockades by fishermen, while the government has announced the expansion of targeted fuel relief measures.
What is the EU doing?
On 17 July, the European Commission announced a €540 million allocation to compensate the farmers most affected by economic losses linked to higher fertiliser and energy costs arising from the Middle East crisis.
France was allocated approximately €107.1 million and Spain €50.2 million. National authorities are responsible for deciding how to target the funding at the farmers and sectors most affected.
Ministers also discussed longer-term measures under the Commission's fertiliser action plan on 28 September. Published in May, the plan aims to improve fertiliser affordability and availability and strengthen the EU's domestic supply resilience.

From Nazi founders to Netanyahu friends: Israel's new far-right allies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:04:35 UTC
22:04:35 KST

Farid Hafez is a senior research fellow at The Bridge Initiative – a multi-year research project on Islamophobia at Georgetown University in Washington, DC – and assistant teaching professor of international relations at the College of William and Mary in Williamsburg, Virginia.
When Austria's Freedom Party (FPO) entered a government coalition in 2000, it became the first far-right party in the European Union to do so. Its notorious leader, the rhetorically gifted lawyer Jorg Haider, was denied entry to Israel, and an official boycott of the party has been in place ever since. The rationale was the FPO's history: in the words of political scientist Anton Pelinka, "it was a party founded by former Nazis for former Nazis.” Haider and other high-ranking members also used antisemitic language throughout their careers. In 2000, Israel even recalled its ambassador from Vienna over the party's participation in government.
From pariahs to partners
Much has changed since. Alongside many other radical right parties in Europe, the FPO has worked to normalize its relationship with Israel. As these nationalist movements win more votes and enter coalitions from Italy to Sweden and from Germany to the Netherlands, they have tried to present themselves as trustworthy allies of Israel, both to shed their antisemitic baggage and to establish themselves as credible partners on the international stage.
In 2010, a delegation of hard-right functionaries visited Israel and the West Bank to build ties with Israeli politicians. They were welcomed by fringe extremist figures but still shut out of the corridors of power. When the FPO again entered a coalition with the Conservatives in 2017-18, Israeli politicians including lawmaker Yehuda Glick and former member of the Knesset Michael Kleiner advocated regular contact with the party, but many pushed back. Israel’s official line was to work with the civil servants of FPO-led ministries while limiting contact with the ministers themselves.
Today the FPO is arguably Austria's most successful party and leads in the polls, though it is no longer in government. Yet after FPO leader Herbert Kickl's mid-September speech in Strasbourg on "Islamism, Antisemitism: Threats to Europe’s Freedom," his remarks on Israel and antisemitism drew a wave of warmth from the highest levels of the Israeli government.
In 2010, Kickl's party colleague Andreas Molzer, a long-time right-wing populist politician, still evaded any discussion of Austria's Nazi past and the murder of millions of Jews. This time, for the first time, the party leader said the FPO must confront its history. He also affirmed Israel's "right to exist" and endorsed the contested International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism. He recognized the Jewish people's historic connection to "Judea and Samaria" (the West Bank), a stance that effectively denies Palestinian statehood, and pledged to move Austria’s embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem if he became chancellor.
Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar called Kickl's remarks an "important and positive development," signaling that Israel is prepared to open a substantive dialogue with the FPO despite its past. The Israeli Embassy's official X account reposted Sa'ar's statement in German and called the speech "significant," even though Austria's Jewish community has not welcomed the FPO's shift. Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli described the Strasbourg gathering as a "historic turning point." The governing Likud, which has already joined the European far-right bloc as an observer member of Patriots for Europe, took part directly. Likud's political director Ariel Bulshtein, Knesset member Ariel Kellner, and two rabbis thanked Kickl and FPO Member of the European Parliament Harald Vilimsky by name and called the FPO "friends of Israel and the Jewish people."
4 factors behind Israel's strategic pivot
Why is the Israeli government changing its stance? Several factors are at play.
First, the radical right keeps growing across Europe. The AfD recently won two state elections in eastern Germany. Right-wing parties have led governments in Italy and, until recently, the Netherlands, and they poll at or near the top in Austria, the UK, and Sweden. It makes sense for Israel to move closer to forces that may shape Europe's future.
Second, over the past 15 years, the European hard-right has recast itself as anti-Muslim, distanced itself from its antisemitic past, and reinvented itself as the defender of a "Judeo-Christian" Europe. This has allowed it to side with Israel against the supposed threat of "Islam."
Third, the growing normalization of the far-right within Israel itself has helped. Vilimsky was recently received in Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office in Jerusalem, which many saw as a historic turning point. Likud's observer status in Patriots for Europe has also increased the political cost for other potential partners in Europe.
Fourth, and probably most important, as Sa'ar's move shows, diplomacy has become a more critical battlefield for Israel than the military one, especially after the genocide in Gaza and Israel's growing isolation on the world stage. Winning over the growing ranks of far-right voters can only help improve Israel's image.
What remains to be seen is how this will translate into an official diplomatic shift. As of last year, the boycott of the FPO was still on the books, but a new assessment appears to be on the horizon. It would be a huge win for the far-right, not only in Austria.
