Greens see red-hot anger as an opportunity to take on Hanson, Labor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:33:41 UTC
21:33:41 KST

analysis
Greens leader sees red-hot anger as an opportunity to take the battle to Hanson, Labor
David Shoebridge has big ambitions for the Greens, but his party is still wrestling with how to turn voter disillusionment into greater support.
The new leader wants to harness the anti-establishment anger rife in Australia, declaring the Greens will fight and ultimately seek to "replace" Labor.
That won't be easy at a time when the populist right is capturing much of the voter anger here, though Shoebridge is not alone in seeing widespread economic frustration as an opportunity for the left.
Insurgent political movements in Britain, the United States and Germany have built support around everyday frustrations like rent, wages and living costs, and directed voters' anger toward inequality and concentrated wealth rather than the targets favoured by their opponents on the right.
Zack Polanski took the Green party in the UK and explicitly embraced "eco-populism" to achieve extraordinary membership growth and a surge in the polls.
In New York, Zohran Mamdani defeated an establishment Democrat and won the mayoral election by relentlessly translating socialism into rent, buses, childcare and groceries.
While a revitalised Die Linke party in Germany has almost doubled its vote through young supporters with a pitch on rent, wages and inequality.
Loading...
All three have embedded climate, minority rights and other progressive causes inside a simple economic story.
Their circumstances and politics differ significantly, but each has demonstrated the potential for the left to turn economic dissatisfaction into electoral support.
If some of that sounds familiar, it's because the strategy is hardly new to Australians.
Long before Polanski or Mamdani became globally recognised names, the Greens here were trying to harness economic frustration with a pitch centred on inequality and the cost of everyday life.
Particularly under former leader Adam Bandt, the Greens consciously broadened beyond environmentalism.
Housing, inequality, free childcare, dental in Medicare, taxing billionaires and corporations and cost of living were all brought to the fore.
The strategy delivered the party four lower house seats and a 12.25 per cent primary vote nationally in 2022.
But three years later the Greens got a taste of just how fragile success can be.
Greens' changing strategy
The 2025 loss of three lower house seats — including Bandt's — showed the limits of a strategy that had produced spectacular gains, even as the party's national vote barely moved.
The Greens' attempts to extract concessions from the Albanese government on housing and climate were ultimately presented by Labor as blocking progressive outcomes rather than achieving them.
When Larissa Waters became leader of the party last year, she instead promised to be "firm but constructive" with Labor — to "get shit done".
The party's strategy basically went from "Labor isn't good enough so fight them and force them further left" to "Labor isn't good enough so negotiate and show voters what Greens leverage delivers".
But that leverage has yet to translate into a significant boost in the polls.
Shoebridge has now swung the emphasis back towards confrontation, though in a dramatically different political environment.
"We're not here to make the Labor Party any better. The Greens are here to replace them," he said.
He's also vowed to fight One Nation but blamed Labor for the rise of the populist right party.
Radical change, but how?
Meanwhile, Shoebridge's rivals for the leadership have ended this week emphasising markedly different priorities.
The rare, contested ballot against Mehreen Faruqi and Sarah Hanson-Young on Wednesday exposed a party still grappling with how to translate its ambitions into greater political power.
While they broadly share a vision of radical change, there is a live argument about who the Greens should fight and what voters should hear from them first.
Faruqi used a post-ballot statement to suggest she had not sought the deputy role so she could have the freedom to pursue "bold politics and radical action" from outside the leadership team.
Expressing her disappointment at the result, Faruqi appeared to imply she would have succeeded had the party held a membership-wide vote for the leader.
Her reaction contrasted starkly with Hanson-Young, who not only managed to congratulate Shoebridge but also kept her sights trained firmly on the populist right.
She cast the Greens as a progressive force to take on Pauline Hanson, rather than sharpen the fight with Labor.
It's been a week of free advice from outside the party room, too, with ousted MP Max Chandler-Mather also calling for a membership ballot — something Shoebridge has guaranteed would happen by 2028.
Meanwhile, Bandt told the Insiders On Background podcast politicians could either choose "division and fear" or to "offer hope", working to "get good things done for people, for nature for climate".
When pushed on the idea that using the power of government to achieve those goals sounded "quite different" to the pitch from Shoebridge, Bandt replied, "well, that's right".
Loading
Opponents, allies and message
There is strong agreement inside the Greens about the problems they want to solve. But consensus on who exactly is their main opponent, which allies they need and what message will grow the party's support remains elusive.
For now, Labor and the Greens have a relatively reliable path to passing legislation through the Senate when they agree.
That arithmetic could look very different after 2028.
Shoebridge evidently believes there are gains to be made in chipping away at Labor, perhaps even more so if Labor is preoccupied fighting One Nation.
But it's unlikely Anthony Albanese would ever lose focus on a perennial political foe to his left.
That makes the Greens' message as important as the opponents they choose.
Each leadership hopeful offered a different strategy for success and while Shoebridge prevailed on the day, the battle for the future of the party is ongoing.

A winegrower by trade, Parmelin is from the French-speaking western canton of Vaud. He is from the hard-right Swiss People's Party (SVP), which is the biggest in the country.
Swiss President Guy Parmelin announced on Friday that he will quit the government at the end of the year, in a sudden move after more than a decade of ministerial service.
Switzerland's presidency rotates annually among the seven members of the government, called the Federal Council, of which Parmelin was the longest-serving minister.
Parmelin told a press conference in Bern that he had informed ministerial colleagues of his decision to step down on 31 December.
"By then, it will have been 11 years since I was elected to this role, and the time has come for me to make way for new energy in these times of great uncertainty," he said, admitting to feeling "a certain weariness" while insisting he was not stepping down for medical reasons.
Tariff tussle with Trump
A pragmatist, Parmelin seemed to make more headway with US President Donald Trump than his predecessor Karin Keller-Sutter.
Trump shocked Switzerland in August 2025 when he announced 39% duties on imports of Swiss goods, among the highest in his global tariff blitz.
Parmelin, the economy minister, went to Washington three times in a bid to reduce the rate.
Eventually, Switzerland and the United States announced a declaration of intent to cut tariffs to 15%, with the Swiss vowing to invest $200 billion (€178 billion) in the United States.
A winegrower by trade, Parmelin is from the French-speaking western canton of Vaud. He is from the hard-right Swiss People's Party (SVP), which is the biggest in the country.
Parmelin was previously president in 2021 and took centre-stage as Switzerland hosted a summit in Geneva between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Joe Biden.
The president of the Swiss Confederation is first among equals on the Federal Council, chairs its meetings and typically represents the country in major domestic and international matters.
The position goes to whoever has had the longest run on the council without being president.
Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis will become president in 2027.
Parmelin joined the Federal Council in 2016 as defence minister and has held the economy brief since 2019.
The Federal Council seven seats are shared 2-2-2-1 among the four main political parties under a decades-old tacit agreement known as "the magic formula."
Parmelin's successor will come from the SVP. Candidates have until 23 October to come forward and parliament will choose on 9 December.

US Navy to buy 30 medium drone warships from three firms
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:30:56 BST
21:30:56 KST

The US Navy plans to buy 30 Medium Unmanned Surface Vessels (MUSVs) from Galliano Marine Services, HII and Saronic Technologies after completing the first phase of at-sea testing, with the first vessels due for delivery before the end of fiscal year 2027, according to the service.
Each of the three companies has been awarded a production Other Transaction Authority agreement covering 10 vessels, at an average procurement cost of $40 million per boat. Across the three agreements, that amounts to roughly $1.2 billion. Three other firms that took part in the prototype phase, Leidos, PAC MAR and Sea Machines, were judged to have completed the work set out in their prototype agreements and will each receive a $15 million award under the terms previously agreed.
All six companies will be accepted onto the Maritime Marketplace hosted by Drones.mil, the Navy said, making them eligible for follow-on production agreements from acquisition authorities across the Department of War. On 23 September the service also released a Phase II Integration and Testing Call for Solutions, which it says is intended to widen the pool of offerings and meet future MUSV mission sets.
According to the Navy, Phase I testing assessed the vessels’ ability to perceive and understand the surrounding maritime environment, their autonomous navigation in line with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, and their capacity to carry out long-duration missions.
Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said in the release: “Our warfighters don’t have time to wait on bureaucracy while our adversaries pace forward.” He added: “Our message to the defense industrial base is simple: build fast, deliver on time, and match the urgency of the threat. This MUSV award is a prime example of how we are streamlining acquisitions to ensure our Sailors and Marines have the capabilities they need to fight, win, and come home safe.”
The Navy’s interest in medium-sized uncrewed surface vessels dates back several years, with earlier efforts including DARPA’s Sea Hunter, the Overlord programme and a 2020 MUSV prototype contract awarded to L3Harris. The three production awardees take different approaches. HII has developed its ROMULUS family of autonomous vessels, Saronic has expanded from small autonomous boats towards larger designs, and Galliano Marine Services comes from the Gulf Coast offshore vessel sector.
The Chief of Naval Operations was quoted in the release as describing MUSVs as part of the hedge strategy set out in the service’s Fighting Instructions. “They give commanders a Tailored Offset — additional capacity and capability that can be rapidly adapted to the threat, distributed across the battlespace, and placed at risk without placing Sailors at unnecessary risk,” the CNO said. “Just as importantly, MUSVs give us a platform for rapidly integrating new sensors, weapons, and other mission payloads as technology and operational requirements change. This is about moving beyond experimentation and putting reliable, combat-relevant capability into the hands of our Sailors at the speed the Fleet requires.”
Fielding will be led by the Direct Reporting Program Manager for Robotic and Autonomous Systems, working alongside the Robotic and Autonomous Systems Warfighting Development Center, which is responsible for developing tactics, training and operational experience for the vessels. Under the Navy’s Containerized Capability Campaign, the service intends to use modular payloads so commanders can fit sensors, weapons and other mission equipment to the boats according to the task at hand.

Ethiopian gov’t-aligned group claims close to full control of Tigray region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:27:52 UTC

Ethiopian gov’t-aligned group claims close to full control of Tigray region
Claim comes as violence flares across northern Ethiopia, provoking diplomatic spats amid a deteriorating humanitarian situation for millions.
Eritrea severs diplomatic ties with Ethiopia in row over Tigray
An armed group aligned with the Ethiopian government has said it is close to gaining full control of the conflict-stricken northern Tigray region.
The commander of the Tigray Peace Forces (TPF) declared on social media late on Thursday that Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) forces had been wiped out.
The claim, which could not be immediately verified by Al Jazeera, came after fighting resumed between Ethiopian federal forces – including the TPF – and an opposition alliance led by the TPLF in September.
Residents told the Reuters news agency on Friday that Ethiopian government forces were closing on the region’s capital Mekelle.
TPLF chairperson Debretsion Gebremichael acknowledged on Thursday that federal forces had occupied some parts of the region but said his forces would counter-attack “in due course”.
Pro-government forces have made quick advances into Tigray since fighting erupted last week. The return of the hostilities follows the apparent collapse of a 2022 peace deal that ended the war between the federal government and forces from the Tigray region.
Seven armed and political groups announced an alliance on September 20 aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s administration and establishing an inclusive transitional government.
The African Union reported last month that Tigrayan forces had seized airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire and detained federal personnel, disrupting civilian air services.
Fighting has also spread from southern Tigray to the neighbouring Amhara and Afar regions.
The remarks from the commander of the Tigray Peace Forces “shed light on a new phase of this conflict,” reported Al Jazeera Arabic Ethiopia Bureau Chief Mohammed Taha Tawakel.
The federal army is clearly providing full support to the TPF, yet the original TPLF still holds several towns, he said, but maintains a strong link with Eritrea along more than 800 kilometres of frontier.
“That raises the prospect of the conflict increasingly becoming an internal struggle among Tigrayans themselves,” Tawakel noted.
Ethiopian military officials have accused Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of supporting the Tigrayan-led fighting alliance. That has led to tit-for-tat expulsions of diplomats between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt.
The African Union has called for “maximum restraint” between the three countries and for them to “refrain from actions or statements that could further escalate tensions and undermine regional peace”.
Eritrea and Egypt have denied accusations that they are backing efforts to destabilise Ethiopia.
Meanwhile, the conflict is provoking a worsening humanitarian situation in Tigray.
”The region is home to between six and seven million people, living amid electricity cuts, internet blackouts and a total lack of communications,” Tawakel said.
Some civilians, fearing the fighting could move into major urban centres, have already begun fleeing to Amhara and Afar, he reported.
Aid agencies, including the United Nations, have managed to relocate some operations to newly secured areas, he added, in an effort to maintain a minimum level of humanitarian access.

EU current account surplus drops to $90B in Q2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:27:38 UTC
21:27:38 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
The EU current account balance recorded a surplus of €80.2 billion ($90 billion) in the second quarter of 2026, shrinking from the previous quarter, according to official data.
This figure accounted for 1.6% of the bloc's gross domestic product, decreasing from a surplus of €98 billion, or 2% of GDP, in the first quarter, Eurostat announced on Friday.
In the second quarter of 2025, the EU recorded a current account surplus of €91.7 billion, which also represented 2% of GDP.
The surplus in the goods account fell to €62.9 billion in the second quarter, down from €63.6 billion in the previous three-month period.
The services account surplus also dropped to €41.7 billion during the same period, compared to €48.1 billion in the first quarter.
Eurostat data showed the primary income account surplus narrowing to €0.8 billion from €15.7 billion.
The secondary income account deficit decreased to €25.2 billion from €29.3 billion in the preceding quarter.
The capital account deficit widened significantly to €16.2 billion in the second quarter, up from €1.7 billion in the first quarter of the year.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

21:24:00 KST

Annual inflation in the eurozone rose to 3.8% in September, above market forecasts and at its highest level since September 2023, CNBC reported.
The rate increased from 3.2% in August, while analysts had expected September inflation to reach 3.6%. The latest figure puts inflation further above the European Central Bank’s 2% target.
Core inflation, which leaves out more volatile components, came in at 2.5%, in line with market expectations.
Energy costs were the biggest contributor to the headline inflation rate, with energy inflation reaching 18.8% in September, its highest level since January 2023. The continuing conflict in the Middle East is adding to upward pressure on energy prices.
Harry Ullman, a global capital markets analyst at Validus Risk Management, said energy was still the main source of inflationary pressure, but the September acceleration suggested price increases were spreading beyond the energy sector.
He said this would increase the significance of the ECB’s next meeting on October 29. “Markets have scaled back expectations for consecutive interest rate hikes in recent days after President Lagarde stated that higher bond yields are already providing some of the necessary monetary policy tightening. Today's inflation data makes that argument harder to sustain,” Ullmann commented.
He added that a central bank drawing lessons from 2022 would not want to delay action until secondary inflation effects had intensified and become entrenched.

US halts consular services in Brazil ahead of election, increasing tensions
WASHINGTON/SAO PAULO, Oct 2 - Citing security concerns, the United States suspended consular services on Friday, prompting Australia to also close its embassy two days before the country's presidential election, fueling an already uneasy environment ahead of the high-stakes vote.
Brazil's Federal Police said on Friday afternoon they had carried out preventive searches in Sao Paulo and near Brasilia, but had so far found no evidence of a threat or identified any suspects linked to criminal organizations.
The State Department did not elaborate on the security issues or link them to Sunday's election, which has been marked by tensions over alleged foreign interference and strains between Washington and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's government.
"We are working closely with our Brazilian counterparts to address the security concerns," a department spokesperson said in an email.
The department did not say when the consular services would resume.
"Consular Services in the US Embassy and Consulates in Brazil will be suspended starting Friday, October 2 due to security concerns," it said in a statement Thursday. "US citizens seeking emergency assistance during this time should not come to the Embassy, the Consulates, or other US diplomatic facilities."
Australia's ambassador to Brazil, Sophie Davies, said on social media that the Australian embassy in Brasilia would also be closed on Friday due to security concerns, citing the alert issued by the US and advising Australians to avoid US embassies and consulates in Brazil.
Brazil's foreign ministry declined to comment on the matter.
ELECTION TENSIONS
The State Department made the announcement at a tense moment for US-Brazil relations.
Brazilians will vote for president on Sunday in a race that will determine whether Latin America's largest nation follows the conservative shift that US President Donald Trump has often cheered on from Washington.
Lula and his allies have warned of foreign interference in the election, pointing to tariffs and an effort by Washington to send officials to Brazil to "discuss electoral integrity."
Edinho Silva, president of Lula's Workers' Party, called Friday's closures "unprecedented" in a press conference.
"It makes no sense at all. It's one of Trump's ways of trying to influence Brazilian public opinion," Silva said.
Though he has publicly praised Lula's main right-wing opponent Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, Trump has not formally endorsed a candidate, and the State Department has rejected claims of election meddling, but the issue has hovered over the race.
Brazilian intelligence officials this month briefed a French and German delegation in Brasilia on what they described as US and Russian interference before Brazil's election. The visit underlined growing concern on both sides of the Atlantic over Trump's efforts to support like-minded candidates.
Violent crime has also dominated the list of voter concerns in Brazilian election polls, prompting candidates to pledge tougher security measures. REUTERS

The exhibition running until mid-August next year also features works spanning his stellar career.
His Türkiye photographs, commissioned by Borusan Contemporary under the heading Time Space Geometry, depict nine archaeological sites in Türkiye, including Ephesus, Aphrodisias, Hierapolis and Laodikeia.
Barbieri, born in Carpi, Italy, in 1954, now lives in Modena. He is known in international art circles for challenging how we look at images.
He has photographed around the world, from China to the US, from the Alps to Capri, from New York to Istanbul, and from Niagara Falls to Victoria Falls, always finding something new for viewers to notice even if we think we already know the subject of the photograph.
His Time Space Geometry is one of two exhibitions currently running at Borusan Contemporary, housed in Perili Kosk – or “Haunted Mansion” – and serving as Borusan Holding’s headquarters during the workweek and an art space at weekends.
Rather than hanging in a sterile gallery with bare white walls, Barbieri’s photographs are scattered around office spaces overlooking the Bosphorus.
Borusan Contemporary is concurrently hosting Haunted. A single ticket provides access to both exhibitions.
The exhibition also includes a photograph of Istanbul taken from a helicopter in 2011, part of Barbieri’s site specific_ series.
“Istanbul is an ancient city rich in historical vestiges. It is a place of connection between East and West – or West and East – and a potential point of equilibrium in dialogue with Rome, New York, and Shanghai,” he says.
‘Image of reality’
Curator Firat Arapoglu says Barbieri’s photographs “begin with recognizable subjects—a city, an archaeological site, a mountain, a waterfall—but very quickly turn into questions about perception”.
According to Arapoglu, Barbieri connects the geographically distant locations of the different series he has produced “through a single question: How is the world transformed by the way we look at it?”
Barbieri says it all goes back to the late 1990s, when he was “annoyed” by claims that suggested photography was a depiction of reality, “something that was almost never true”.
So he set out to prove them wrong.
“Using the technique of selective focus, I devised a process that allowed me to indicate the starting point for reading the image, much like a page of text,” he says.
“It was only then that I realised the image of reality was transforming into a scale model, a maquette.”
His technique, perfected over the years, has resulted in “a novel way of interpreting the visible world”. Barbieri says he later started using helicopters “to see what would happen from a floating vantage point”.
When asked what he would say to a visitor encountering Barbieri’s work for the first time, Arapoglu says: “I would first tell the visitor not to concentrate only on what Barbieri has photographed, but on how he makes us look at it. That distinction is fundamental.”
Arapoglu believes that describing Barbieri’s manipulation of “focus, scale, perspective, and colour, particularly through the selective-focus strategies associated with his site specific_ project” simply as a “miniature effect” would be misleading.
He brings up the ancient sites in Türkiye that Barbieri was commissioned to photograph: “What he gives us is not a ‘better view’ of antiquity. He gives us an unfamiliar view of something excessively familiar.”
When asked whether he makes any modifications or corrections to the images before he prints them on a massive inkjet printer, Barbieri says: “I never intentionally alter the form of the object or subject being depicted. These interventions serve only as tools to subliminally emphasize potential hidden meanings within the image.”
He adds: “Very often, I do nothing.”
Does Barbieri have an idea of the final image in his head as he takes a photograph, or does the initial output guide him?
The photographer says: “I always have an ideal image in mind that I want to create, but it is rarely the right one. During the shooting and selection process, I almost always discover something unexpected that surpasses my initial intent.
“This is the most interesting aspect of the practice.”
Olivo Barbieri’s Time Space Geometry exhibition, so named because “the sites depicted were built according to precise mathematical laws”, can be viewed at Borusan Contemporary on Saturdays and Sundays from 10 am to 7 pm.
Barbieri adds that these laws, “in the form of artworks, appear as technological images, algorithms from the past” and are “the necessary completion of the site specific_ project” that he began in 2003.

Lithuania Deploys Ukrainian SkyFortress Acoustic Drone Detection System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:18:52 UTC
21:18:52 KST

Lithuania is deploying a pilot version of the Ukrainian SkyFortress system to detect low-flying drones using acoustic signatures or radio signals.
The Ministry of National Defence of Lithuania reported this on October 2.
The Lithuanian Defence Minister explained thatLithuania is adapting solutions already in use in Ukraine to strengthen the entire air-defense chain – from surveillance to the interception and neutralization of threats.
“Instead of creating everything from scratch, we are adapting systems that are already operating in Ukraine,” said Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas.
Using artificial intelligence, the system detects and tracks low-flying drones and cruise missiles. It can classify objects in real time based on their acoustic or electromagnetic signatures.
The deployment is covered by a contract signed in the summer of 2026. The agreement also includes sensor data processing, the use of acoustic and radio-frequency signature libraries based on unclassified information, and personnel training.
There is still little detailed public information available about SkyFortress. According to UNITED24 Media, as of July 2025, Ukraine’s Sky Fortress network consisted of around 14,000 acoustic sensors. Each device cost approximately $400–$1,000.
The acoustic data collected by the sensors is combined with radar information and transmitted to mobile fire teams equipped with tablets. In the early versions of the system, mobile phones were used to process the data, helping speed up development. The team later developed dedicated hardware with its own processors and sound cards.
A project engineer told the publication that the developers had reached the third generation of the devices by mid-2025.
As Militarnyi previously reported, the Commander-in-Chief of the Lithuanian Armed Forces announced that the Ukrainian acoustic system would be deployed in Lithuania starting in 2026. He said preparations had been delayed by bureaucratic procedures and the need to adapt the Ukrainian system to U.S.-made equipment.
Reports of NATO countries showing interest in Ukraine’s Zvook and Sky Fortress acoustic monitoring systems first emerged in July 2024.
At the time, Sky Fortress was demonstrated to representatives from 11 NATO member countries at a European military training ground. During the demonstration, the system detected and tracked simulated cruise missiles and drones.

From Ottoman 'rocket man' to lunar mission: How did Türkiye’s long road into space begin?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:18:01 UTC
21:18:01 KST

On a festive night in 1633, as Istanbul celebrated the birth of Kaya Sultan, the daughter of Ottoman Sultan Murad IV, an inventor known as Lagari Hasan Celebi is said to have mounted a seven-branched rocket packed with gunpowder paste on the shores of the Bosphorus.
When the powder burned out, as the story goes, he opened a pair of wings he had built himself, descended into the sea in front of the Sinan Pasha mansion and swam back to shore.
The episode is recorded by 17th-century Ottoman traveller Evliya Celebi in his Seyahatname, or Book of Travels.
Nearly four centuries on, the “rocket man” gives his name to a satellite and space museum operated by Turksat, Türkiye’s state-owned satellite operator.
Decades earlier, in 1577, the Ottoman astronomer Takiyuddin established the landmark Istanbul Observatory, where he conducted astronomical observations and developed instruments for measuring celestial movements. Equipped with a large armillary sphere, mechanical clocks capable of measuring time in seconds, and other precision instruments of his own design, the facility ranked among the most advanced of its age.
From observatories and early experiments in flight to satellites and human spaceflight, Türkiye’s relationship with the sky has evolved dramatically.
From Oct. 5 to 9, the country’s space program will be on show before the global space community, when the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) opens in the Turkish resort city of Antalya.
It is the first time the annual gathering, organized by the International Astronautical Federation (IAF), is being held in Türkiye.
The 1990s brought Türkiye's first major step into satellite communications.
Turksat 1B was launched in August 1994, becoming Türkiye's first communications satellite, followed by Turksat 1C in 1996.
The country's ambitions increasingly shifted from operating satellites made elsewhere toward designing and building spacecraft itself.
RASAT, launched in 2011, was the country's first domestically developed Earth-observation satellite, while GOKTURK-2, launched in 2012, became Türkiye's first high-resolution Earth-observation satellite.
In 2023, IMECE, a high-resolution Earth-observation satellite designed and built by TUBITAK UZAY, the country's space research institute, was launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 from California. According to the institute, it featured Türkiye's first space-compatible electro-optical camera, along with domestically developed electric propulsion, star trackers, reaction wheels and other key systems.
TURKSAT 6A, launched in 2024, became Türkiye's first domestically developed communications satellite, putting the country among 11 countries with the capability to build their own.
The turning point came on Dec. 13, 2018, when a presidential decree set up the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) under the Ministry of Industry and Technology. Its mandate included preparing and implementing the National Space Program and setting longer-term priorities for space and aerospace science and technology.
That program was unveiled in 2021 with a 10-year vision.
Its goals included reaching the Moon, developing a globally competitive commercial satellite brand, establishing a regional positioning and timing system, creating independent access to space and a spaceport, improving astronomical observation and space-object tracking capabilities, as well as developing a domestic space industry and technology-development zone. A human space mission was also included among the program's objectives.
The first major public milestone arrived sooner than some of the longer-term goals.
In 2024, Alper Gezeravci became the first Turkish citizen to travel to the International Space Station, spending 18 days in orbit as part of Axiom Mission 3. He carried out 13 scientific experiments prepared by Turkish universities and research institutions.
Four months later, Tuva Cihangir Atasever conducted a suborbital research flight, carrying out seven scientific experiments.
The most ambitious item on that list is now within reach.
In mid-September, Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir announced that production, assembly and system integration of Türkiye's first lunar spacecraft had been completed.
The roughly 3.5-ton vehicle was developed under the leadership of TUBITAK UZAY as part of the Lunar Research Program, known by its Turkish acronym AYAP. It has been handed over to the Space Systems Integration and Test Center (USET) at Turkish Aerospace (TUSAS) for system-level environmental testing.
According to Kacir, more than 80% of the vehicle was produced domestically, and all of its software was written in Türkiye.
Once testing is over, it will be shipped to the Kennedy Space Center in the US for launch, as the lift-off is planned for the first months of 2027.
After a journey of about two months, the spacecraft is expected to settle into a circular polar orbit some 100 kilometers above the lunar surface and operate there for at least three months. A hybrid propulsion system developed in Türkiye is to handle its maneuvers, including a controlled descent to the surface at the end of the mission.
Kacir said the program, launched in early 2022, had reached 77% completion, with more than 200 engineers contributing.
Noting that only eight countries have so far carried out a Moon mission, the minister said: "With our Lunar Research Program, which we will carry out with our own engineering capabilities, we aim to become the ninth."
Under the 2021 road map, this mission is the first phase. A second phase envisages a launch on a national rocket and a soft landing on the Moon.
Türkiye also wants to be able to put its own satellites into orbit from its own launch site.
Last year, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan announced that Türkiye plans to build a spaceport in Somalia under agreements signed between the two countries. He made the announcement at a joint news conference in Istanbul with Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud.
Minister Kacir said feasibility studies had identified Somalia as the most suitable location. He cited its proximity to the equator, its ocean coastline, weather that allows launches year-round and low air and sea traffic.
The feasibility and design work had been completed and first-phase construction had begun, he said, adding that the site would serve both national needs and the commercial launch market.
As for rockets, defense company Roketsan is developing a Micro Satellite Launch System designed to place satellites of at least 100 kilograms into a 400-kilometer orbit.
The country's space ambitions is being backed by a growing budget. Under the 2026 central government budget, Türkiye allocated a record 8.729 billion liras to space and aviation activities this year, up from 5.052 billion liras in 2025.
In December 2025, TUA President Yusuf Kirac was unanimously elected council chair of the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization (APSCO) for 2026-2027. He is the first Turkish representative to hold the post.
Ankara has also stepped up its space diplomacy. On Aug. 31, Kacir signed the Artemis Accords at NASA headquarters in Washington. That made Türkiye the 71st signatory to the US-led set of principles for peaceful and sustainable exploration of the Moon and beyond.
The signing came just weeks before Türkiye hosts its first International Astronautical Congress.
From Oct. 5 to 9, Antalya will host the 77th International Astronautical Congress, the world’s largest space gathering, marking the first time the event has been held in Türkiye.
Organizers expect more than 10,000 registered participants, including space agency chiefs from around the world, industry executives, engineers, scientists and students. This year's theme is The World Needs More Space.
The event is hosted by Türkiye's national space agency TUA and co-hosted by SAHA, a Turkish defense and aerospace industry cluster.

DUBAI – An Indian pilot attacked by his co-pilot aboard a flight from the UAE to Israel said on Oct 2 that he “could not let all those people die”, in his first public remarks after he helped stop the plane from crashing.
His actions on Sept 30 helped avert disaster when he managed to open the cockpit door despite suffering injuries, allowing passengers and crew to take control of the plane and make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
The co-pilot has been returned to the United Arab Emirates, where the incident is under investigation to determine any “terrorist activity or intent”.
The mostly Israeli passengers on the flight have been flown back to Israel on a replacement plane.

“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push, that the door was right there,” he said.
“I was being hit even then, but I just opened the door and everyone came in.”
Machchhar, who has 17 years of aviation experience – 11 as a captain – described the moment he realised the plane was going down while he was lying injured.
He told Modi that during the ordeal, he had recited a Hindu devotional prayer dedicated to the deity Hanuman.
“I know God himself saved me,” he said.
He said years of aviation experience allowed him to understand what was happening even while he was wounded.
‘Kill me, kill me’

Passengers described rushing into the cockpit and a fight for control after the plane suddenly plummeted – losing around 17,000 feet of altitude in the span of a minute, according to the Flightradar24 website.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu earlier also credited Machchhar, as well as the flight’s passengers, with averting catastrophe.
US President Donald Trump warned on Oct 1 that if Iran was found to be linked to the attack the country would be “hit very hard”.
Netanyahu has said the suspect had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination”.
“The attacker, he calls out to the aircrew, ‘Kill me, kill me’,” Netanyahu told US media, adding it was “clear he was suicidal”.
The Israeli leader identified the co-pilot as an Omani national and said Israel would check how he had been cleared to work on flights to the country.
“We have constraints that say that you can’t have pilots from countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. Obviously he was able to go through that,” Netanyahu told Fox News.
Flydubai has suspended flights to and from Israel since the attack, leaving some Israelis stranded in the UAE.
Israel’s flag carrier El Al is planning replacement flights to bring them home but was forced to cancel them on Oct 2, saying the Emirati authorities had not given landing permission.
“As soon as approval is received from the authorities, we are prepared to carry out the special flights to Dubai and return the Israelis home as soon as possible,” El Al said in an online notice. AFP

Global food prices hit four-year high in September: FAO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
20:16:11 CST
21:16:11 KST

ROME, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Global food prices rose in September to their highest level in nearly four years amid disruptions to logistics and concerns over weather conditions, the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said Friday.
The FAO Food Price Index averaged 136.0 points in September, up from a revised 134.0 points in August and reaching its highest level since November 2022.
The FAO benchmarks for cereal, sugar and vegetable oil prices all increased last month, while meat and dairy prices declined.
FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero said disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea, combined with climate shocks, were putting pressure on energy, transport and key food commodities.
If sustained, such pressures could eventually be passed on to consumer food prices, particularly in countries dependent on food and energy imports, Torero said.
Concerns over a severe El Nino weather pattern pushed international sugar prices to an 18-month high, while disruptions to Black Sea trade amid the conflict drove wheat futures to a three-year peak in early September, according to the FAO.
The FAO forecast global cereal production in 2026 at 2.979 billion metric tons, broadly unchanged from its previous forecast. The figure is 2.1 percent below the 2025 level but would still be the second-highest on record.
The FAO also cut its forecast for global cereal trade in 2026/27 by 0.7 percent from September, citing lower expectations for wheat and maize exports amid constrained shipping routes in the Black Sea. ■

Just four minutes into Friday's bronze medal match, South Korea earned a free kick on the right. After a series of headers inside the box, Noh Jin-young headed the ball home to give South Korea an early lead.
Both teams struggled to establish control in a scrappy first half. China's best chance came in the 17th minute when Wang Yanwen won possession and crossed into the middle of the box, but Shao Ziqin's shot sailed over the crossbar.
After the break, China head coach Ante Milicic brought on forward Wurigumula to replace midfielder Wang Aifang in an attempt to increase the tempo and strengthen the attack.

South Korea came close to doubling its lead in the 88th minute when its forward broke through for a one-on-one opportunity, but China's goalkeeper Xiao Zitong came off her line to avert the danger.
South Korea held on for a 1-0 victory.
China had 10 shots, three on target, and 46 percent possession, compared with South Korea's nine shots, two on target, and 54 percent possession.
Asked about China's repeated concessions from set pieces, Milicic blamed the quality of training, the players' defensive ability and luck.
"When a team concedes in the same way repeatedly, it is inevitable that the defense will become nervous. This has taught all of us a very good lesson about the importance of set pieces. At the same time, we created many chances but failed to turn them into goals," said Milicic.
"If you understand football, we absolutely shouldn't have lost this game. But we were punished by a set piece at the very beginning and failed to take our chances. That's football, and that's the frustrating part. We will learn from this and make sure the same mistakes don't happen again," he added.
Chinese captain Wu Haiyan said: "Failure to finish on the podium this time is a regret. I just told the younger players that I hope this can become a valuable experience for them, because the road ahead may be even tougher for them than it has been for us." ■

France weighs emergency oil release as US pressure mounts ahead of G7 call
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:15:49 UTC
21:15:49 KST

France is set to present a plan to release emergency oil stocks following US pressure, with Paris considering a combined release of crude oil and diesel. President Emmanuel Macron will hold a G7 call on Friday.
France is considering releasing emergency oil stocks to ease soaring diesel prices and address supply concerns, according to three EU diplomats.
The idea was floated at a meeting between the European Commission and EU countries on Friday morning, shortly after French President Emmanuel Macron spoke with US President Donald Trump about the global energy situation.
According to the diplomats, France has not yet made a formal proposal but suggested releasing 50 million barrels of diesel alongside another 50 million barrels of crude oil from the International Energy Agency's (IEA) emergency stocks.
"The US demanded 100 million barrels, but the EU is not accepting, and France proposed the 50 + 50 formula," one EU diplomat told Euronews.
The US has been pressing European countries to release more strategic oil reserves as Washington seeks to contain rising fuel prices ahead of November's midterm elections, with the Trump administration also considering a diesel export ban.
US energy secretary Chris Wright previously suggested the EU release 120 million barrels from its stockpiles over three months as an alternative to a dramatic US diesel export ban.
Macron has previously described a potential US diesel export ban as "catastrophic", with France among the countries expected to be most affected.
Brent crude prices rose above $100 a barrel on 1 October, driven by the deployment of a third US aircraft carrier to the Middle East and China's suspension of fuel exports.
Following Friday's energy meeting, the European Commission said the EU was "ready for collective action", while stressing that the IEA would be responsible for organising any potential stock release.
The proposed split between diesel and crude is significant because diesel can reach consumers more quickly, while crude would first need to be refined into fuel.
Any release would also require coordination among countries participating in the IEA's emergency stock system.
A G7 leaders' videoconference will take place on Friday afternoon, with France currently holding the group's presidency.
"The aim is to coordinate measures to help ease price pressures and guarantee supplies of crude oil and refined products — both among G7 nations and globally," the Elysée said.

ZAGREB, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Croatia's inflation accelerated to 4.7 percent year-on-year in September, mainly driven by energy price hikes, the Croatian Bureau of Statistics said on Friday.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices rose 0.9 percent, up from 0.3 percent in August. Energy prices were the main driver of inflation, rising 20.5 percent year-on-year amid supply disruptions linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
Prices of services increased 7.6 percent, while prices of food, beverages and tobacco edged up 0.2 percent.
According to Eurostat, Croatia's annual inflation stood at 4.3 percent in September, up from 3.7 percent in August. Meanwhile, inflation in the euro area as a whole accelerated to 3.8 percent in September from 3.2 percent in August.
Croatia's inflation has been among the highest in the euro area in recent years, but the gap has narrowed in the last few months. Finance Minister Tomislav Coric said earlier that the government expects inflation to match the euro area average in the first quarter of 2027. ■

Kyrgyzstan's first national satellite launched into orbit

21:15:36 KST

BISHKEK, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Kyrgyzstan's first national satellite was launched from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, the United States, on Oct. 1 local time, according to a statement published by the official website of the president of Kyrgyzstan on Friday.
Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov attended the satellite's launch ceremony during a working visit to the United States. The satellite was launched aboard a Falcon 9 rocket operated by the U.S. company SpaceX, the statement said.
The satellite was launched into orbit as part of a group of spacecraft carried by a single launch vehicle. The satellite will be controlled from a center in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, it said.
Data obtained from the satellite will enable the monitoring of agricultural land, glaciers, water bodies, forests and pastures, as well as changes in natural ecosystems, the statement said.
Satellite technologies will be particularly important for the monitoring and early detection of natural hazards, it added, noting that the data obtained will enable the faster detection of signs of droughts, floods, landslides, mudflows and forest fires, creating additional opportunities for timely response and mitigation of potential damage.
In the future, satellite data will be integrated into the country's government digital systems and used to create spatial maps and analytical models. This will enable the use of objective data in government decision-making, investment planning and monitoring the implementation of state programs, the statement said. ■

America moves guided missile destroyer to Europe
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:15:33 BST
21:15:33 KST

The U.S. Navy destroyer USS John Basilone (DDG-122) will move its homeport from Naval Station Mayport, Florida, to Naval Station Rota in southern Spain this autumn, according to U.S. Fleet Forces Command.
The Flight IIA Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer is described by the U.S. Navy as capable of ballistic missile defence, anti-submarine warfare, maritime interdiction operations and integrated air and missile defence. Built by General Dynamics Bath Iron Works in Maine, the ship was commissioned in November 2024, making it one of the newest destroyers in the fleet to be forward deployed to Europe.
At Rota, John Basilone will join the U.S. Navy’s Forward Deployed Naval Forces-Europe, a group of destroyers permanently based in Spain and operating under U.S. Sixth Fleet. The arrangement began in 2014 and 2015 when four destroyers, USS Donald Cook, USS Ross, USS Porter and USS Carney, moved to the Andalusian base as part of the U.S. contribution to NATO ballistic missile defence under the European Phased Adaptive Approach. Their Aegis combat systems and Standard Missile interceptors were intended to provide sea-based protection for Europe against ballistic missile threats from the Middle East.
In June 2022, during the NATO summit in Madrid, Washington and Madrid agreed to increase the number of U.S. destroyers based at Rota from four to six. The expansion has been accompanied by a gradual rotation of ships, with older destroyers returning to the United States and newer hulls taking their place. Ships based at Rota spend more time on station in the Mediterranean, the Black Sea region before 2022, the Baltic and the High North than destroyers deploying from the U.S. East Coast, as they avoid the lengthy Atlantic transit at either end of each patrol.
Naval Station Rota is a Spanish naval base at which U.S. forces operate under a bilateral defence agreement between the two countries. Located near the Strait of Gibraltar, it gives ships quick access to both the Atlantic and the Mediterranean and also supports U.S. Navy logistics and maritime patrol aircraft.
The ship’s namesake, Gunnery Sgt. John Basilone, received the Medal of Honor for his actions defending Henderson Field on Guadalcanal in October 1942, when his machine gun section held off repeated Japanese assaults. After returning to the United States to promote war bond sales, he requested a return to combat and was killed on the first day of the landings at Iwo Jima in February 1945. He was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for his actions there, making him one of the most highly decorated Marines in U.S. history, the U.S. Navy noted. A Gearing-class destroyer, USS Basilone, previously carried his name and served from 1949 to 1977.
U.S. Fleet Forces Command, which announced the move, is responsible for manning, training and equipping more than 125 ships and 1,000 aircraft and supplying combat-ready forces to numbered fleets and combatant commanders around the world.

Türkiye’s Fund Coordination Board reviews payment schedule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:15:32 UTC
21:15:32 KST

Türkiye’s Fund Coordination Board, chaired by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz, held its second meeting on Oct. 2 to discuss the payment schedule for fund accounts and a draft amendment to the Capital Markets Law.
On Sept. 30, the Capital Markets Board (SPK) approved interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras per eligible investor in funds established by Tera, Pusula, Atlas and Hedef portfolio management companies that are undergoing liquidation.
According to a statement issued after the meeting, the Coordination Board reviewed the work being carried out by relevant institutions on the calculation methodology for net investment amounts under the SPK’s Sept. 30 decisions.
The board also assessed secondary regulations and the payment timetable related to the SPK’s decision on payments.
In addition, the board discussed a draft law amending the Capital Markets Law, which has been under preparation for some time. The statement said instructions had been conveyed to relevant institutions and organizations to finalize the draft.
“The necessary efforts regarding the resolution of problems that have emerged in a specific and limited segment of the fund market will continue swiftly and effectively within the framework of capital markets regulations, with due regard for fairness and justice,” the statement said.
The SPK said on Oct. 30 that payments will be made to investors whose account reconciliations have been completed and will be treated as advances against final liquidation proceeds.
The payments will be calculated based on each investor’s net investment amount determined by the Central Securities Depository (MKK). Investors with net investments below 1 million liras will receive the full amount, while payments for investors with net investments of 1 million liras or more will be capped at 1 million liras.
The liquidation process will begin with money market funds, while other funds will be liquidated according to investor numbers.
According to the SPK, 131 investment funds designated for liquidation hold approximately 826 billion liras in assets across 455,758 investors.
On Oct. 1, Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said in a social media post that stronger macroeconomic fundamentals and the measures being taken would limit the impact of recent developments on the financial system and the real economy.
The measures would also give Türkiye’s capital markets a stronger, healthier and more resilient structure, he said.
Meanwhile, speaking online at S&P Global Ratings’ 6th Annual Global Emerging Markets Conference on Oct. 1, Şimşek said authorities had moved swiftly.
“We acted very quickly. We “quarantined” the troubled portfolio management companies and the relevant funds,” he said.
Şimşek said the main objective was to prevent the problem from spreading to the rest of the financial system.
“Our aim here was to stop the contagion from spreading to the rest of the system, and I believe we have been largely successful in doing so,” he said.
“There has, of course, been a limited impact, but we are not talking about a systemic problem. We will continue to deepen the capital markets,” Şimşek added.

A second strike by EasyJet cabin crew is scheduled for Dec. 19-23. ■

EU rejects potential US diesel export ban, warns it could undermine trust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:15:15 UTC
21:15:15 KST

Melike Pala
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
The European Commission on Friday rejected any potential US ban on diesel exports, saying such a measure would benefit no one and could undercut the European Union's trust in the US as a "reliable partner."
"We fully reject any ban on diesel. A ban would not be beneficial to anyone. It would undermine our trust in the United States as a reliable partner," European Commission spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen told reporters in Brussels.
Itkonen said the EU is ready to act collectively through the International Energy Agency (IEA), which she said was responsible for organizing any possible release of oil stocks.
She stressed that the bloc's role is to coordinate member states' positions within the IEA, rather than independently decide on a stock release.
Her comments came after US President Donald Trump said he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves as his administration considers restricting US diesel exports amid pressure on global refined-fuel supplies.
Itkonen said member states had coordinated their positions at an Energy Union Task Force meeting on Friday and that discussions are continuing with international partners.
She said the EU would remain united in whatever further steps are taken, while declining to specify whether the bloc is considering "retaliatory" measures against Washington.
"We take one step at the time," Itkonen said.
She added the EU currently sees no immediate security-of-supply problem, with oil supplies stable for the time being, but warned that high energy prices are creating an affordability crisis for households and industry.
Paula Pinho, another spokesperson, said France, which holds the G7 presidency this year, intends to convene a video conference of G7 leaders "as soon as possible" to coordinate measures aimed at easing energy price pressures and guaranteeing supplies of crude oil and refined products.
She said EU coordination groups had been closely monitoring energy markets for months and that gas prices in Europe had risen by 140% since the end of February, when the US and Iran launched their war on Iran, while diesel prices had doubled.

Ethiopia: African Union must convene emergency session on Ethiopia as new conflict expands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:14:42 UTC
21:14:42 KST

The African Union must convene an emergency session on the situation in northern Ethiopia as the latest armed conflict which broke out in the Tigray and parts of Afar and Amhara regions on 21 September expands, Amnesty International said today.
Since the outbreak of fresh fighting, the organization has continued to receive credible reports of destruction of civilian objects through shelling and air strikes, intensified forced conscription, and other acts that may constitute violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law.
“The African Union’s Peace and Security Council cannot wait for mass atrocities to unfold or for a surge in civilian casualties before placing Ethiopia, its host country, on the agenda. The AU, which was one of the guarantors of the ceasefire agreement that has now effectively collapsed, must learn from past mistakes and urgently activate its response mechanisms and mobilize its member states before it is too late,” said Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa.
“The starting point is for the Peace and Security Council to urgently convene an emergency session on the situation in Ethiopia. This is especially critical as fears of regionalisation of the conflict are on the rise”.
The African Union’s Peace and Security Council cannot wait for mass atrocities to unfold or for a surge in civilian casualties before placing Ethiopia, its host country, on the agenda. The AU, which was one of the guarantors of the ceasefire agreement that has now effectively collapsed, must learn from past mistakes and urgently activate its response mechanisms and mobilize its member states before it is too late.
Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa
The fighting between Tigrayan forces and their allies on one side, including Amhara Fano forces, and the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) and its allies, on the other, has significantly intensified across southern Tigray and the Northern Amhara and Western Afar regions since it began a week ago. In addition to the extensive use of heavy weaponry, the renewed hostilities have involved intensified aerial attacks across Tigray including in the town of Axum and the regional capital Mekelle.
Amnesty International is particularly alarmed by reports that civilian infrastructure, including several schools, has been damaged or targeted during aerial attacks. Fighting involving heavy weapons in and around the towns of Maychew and Alamata has reportedly resulted in civilian casualties and further endangered critical civilian infrastructure.
The disruption of communication services across Tigray, and parts of Afar and Amhara regions combined with increasing restrictions on civic space by the Ethiopian government, raises serious concerns that grave human rights violations could occur under the cover of darkness, hidden from independent monitoring.
“Disrupting communications in conflict-affected areas is a well-documented pattern in Ethiopia’s armed conflicts. Such restrictions have frequently concealed atrocities and isolated civilians from the outside world. We call on all relevant authorities to immediately restore access to communications services and ensure civilians are not cut off from life-saving information and assistance at this critical time,” said Tigere Chagutah.
The current outbreak of conflict in Tigray and the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions comes on the backdrop of six years of persistent armed conflict across Ethiopia, including in the Oromia region. These armed conflicts have devastated communities across the country with most of the armed actors involved in the fighting linked to serious violations of international human rights and humanitarian law. Yet, despite the scale and gravity of these abuses, meaningful and independent accountability remains largely absent.
Disrupting communications in conflict-affected areas is a well-documented pattern in Ethiopia’s armed conflicts. Such restrictions have frequently concealed atrocities and isolated civilians from the outside world. We call on all relevant authorities to immediately restore access to communications services and ensure civilians are not cut off from life-saving information and assistance at this critical time.
Tigere Chagutah
“Regional and international actors, including the AU, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), and the UN, must address the deeply entrenched accountability crisis in Ethiopia. They must take urgent measures to protect civilians from harm, renew efforts to restore independent investigations into serious violations committed by all parties to Ethiopia’s conflicts, and ensure unhindered access for journalists, humanitarian organizations, and human rights monitors,” said Tigere Chagutah.
Background
The Peace and Security Council (PSC) is AU’s standing decision-making body for the prevention, management and resolution of conflicts in Africa. During the 2020-2022 armed conflict in Tigray and parts of Afar and Amhara regions, the PSC held its first session on the situation in Ethiopia in November 2021, one year after the conflict began.
The conflict was described by the UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia (ICHREE) as ‘one of the deadliest conflicts of the twenty-first century.’ Reports indicate that hundreds of thousands of people died, millions were displaced, and thousands of women and girls were subjected to conflict-related sexual violence and other grave violations.
The conflict was marked by an unprecedented communications blackout as civilians in Tigray were largely cut off from telephone services, internet access, and other forms of communication for more than a year.
Although hostilities formally ended in November 2022, the consequences of the conflict continue to be felt. Hundreds of thousands of displaced people remain unable to return home. Victims of serious violations continue to await truth, justice, and reparations.

UN rights chief calls for 'decisive shift' toward de-escalation, peace in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:12:40 UTC
21:12:40 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Friday called for a “decisive shift” toward de-escalation and peace in Ukraine, urging renewed negotiations as he warned the war has become a “human rights catastrophe” that is intensifying by the week.
“The conduct of this war to date cannot be allowed to dictate its future. We need a decisive shift towards de-escalation and peace,” Turk told the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva.
He said rebuilding momentum toward negotiations was key, calling for confidence-building measures that could reduce the impact of hostilities on civilians.
Such measures could include an agreement to end attacks on economic targets and energy infrastructure, local ceasefires along the frontlines, enabling civilians to leave Oleshky, and a full exchange of prisoners of war, he said.
Turk urged the international community, particularly states with influence, to take “urgent action to push for a negotiated peace now, before this tragedy becomes even worse.”
The rights chief said his office verified some 15,280 civilians killed and injured across Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026 -- an average of more than 400 every week and 55% higher than during the same period in 2025.
Calling Ukraine a “laboratory for drone warfare,” Turk urged international action to address the “carnage” caused by such weapons worldwide.
He said Russian aerial glide bombs alone killed or injured nearly 2,500 civilians in the first eight months of the year in the Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia regions, up 62% year-on-year.
Turk also accused Russian forces of increasing attacks on energy infrastructure, supermarkets, food companies and transportation networks.
In Russia, Ukrainian forces have reportedly struck warehouses and logistics centers belonging to major e-commerce companies, as well as oil refineries, he said.
Turk also cited a recent report documenting more than 1,000 cases of conflict-related sexual violence, of which "89% were attributed to Russian authorities and 11% to Ukraine." Most victims were men, particularly in detention, though women and children were also affected, "primarily in occupied Ukrainian territory," according to Turk.
“Alongside peace, there must be accountability,” he said.
The UN rights chief also voiced alarm over human rights violations linked to the presence of fighters from third countries in the war, noting his staff had interviewed "prisoners of war from 29 countries who are held by Ukraine; many said they were deceived into joining the Russian forces."

‘West Bank is Israel’s weak point’: US sanctions pressure grows ahead of Israeli election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:12:37 UTC
21:12:37 KST

Little is expected to change before Israel’s election and the formation of its next government. What follows, according to sources familiar with Israel’s relations with Washington, could depend heavily on the composition of that government.
If the current coalition returns to power, they say, the U.S. approach toward Israel could harden further, potentially including sanctions. They also warn that after the U.S. midterm elections, declining public support for Israel could increasingly translate into concrete congressional action.
“The West Bank is Israel’s weak point in Washington today,” one source familiar with the issue said, citing anger in the United States over settler violence and a growing number of congressional initiatives targeting settlements and individuals involved in them.
Two such initiatives came close to advancing this week.
Six Democratic members of the House of Representatives introduced the Stop the Settlements Act: Joaquin Castro, Madeleine Dean, Don Beyer, Greg Casar, Sara Jacobs and Veronica Escobar.
The legislation would impose sanctions on foreign individuals and entities involved in establishing or expanding settlements and outposts in the West Bank and Gaza, while also banning imports of goods produced there.
According to information provided to Ynet, the initiative has support from nearly 40 Democratic lawmakers, including figures associated with the party’s mainstream rather than only its progressive wing.
Other supporters include Stephen Lynch, Bennie Thompson, Rosa DeLauro, Ro Khanna and Pramila Jayapal.
The bill would require sanctions against foreign actors involved in establishing new settlements or outposts, developing infrastructure for their expansion, construction in the E1 area or facilitating the transfer of civilians into settlements.
Potential penalties include asset freezes, visa restrictions and bans on entry into the United States.
The bill could also apply to individuals involved in maintaining or expanding existing settlements, including through financial and banking sanctions. Under the language described, people who attempt to facilitate such activity or are indirectly involved could also fall within its scope, potentially including officials responsible for planning approvals.
Ministers in the Israeli government, and potentially even the prime minister, could be affected. Provisions concerning infrastructure and E1 construction contain no stated starting date, raising the possibility that they could apply to earlier activity.
U.S. citizens, including settlers with dual citizenship, are exempt. The legislation does not explicitly define the term “settlement,” does not specifically mention East Jerusalem and leaves the final sanctions list to the president.
The proposal is not expected to pass the current Congress, where Republicans hold the majority and President Donald Trump remains in office. Its sponsors, however, are already looking toward the next Congress.
A senior Democratic source told Ynet that the ability of party leaders to prevent such measures from advancing would depend heavily on Israel’s election.
“If the same coalition returns, these proposals will pass Congress,” the source said, presenting that as the source’s assessment of the political trajectory in Washington.
At the same time, a separate resolution led by Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen was narrowly defeated in the Senate this week, 51-47.
The measure invoked Section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act and would have required the State Department to submit a report within 30 days on the deaths of nine U.S. citizens in incidents involving Israeli settlers or security forces since 2022, as well as on the detention of Palestinian children.
Had the resolution passed and the administration failed to provide the required report, most covered U.S. security assistance to Israel could have been suspended until the report was submitted.
All Senate Democrats except John Fetterman supported the measure, along with Republican Sen. Rand Paul. Two senators did not vote.
Dr. Kobi Barda, an expert on U.S. politics, reacted to the developments on X: “I don’t even want to think about the blood bath waiting for us after the midterms. I don’t believe we’ve reached the bottom yet.”
Another source of tension is Lt. Gen. Sean M. Salene, the U.S. security coordinator responsible for strengthening security cooperation between Israel and the Palestinian Authority.
According to sources familiar with the matter, Salene has been sending Washington troubling reports about what he views as lawlessness in the West Bank and failures by the IDF and police to address it. Israeli officials dispute that characterization, arguing that information reaching Washington is one-sided and reflects the Palestinian narrative.
The same sources said there is anger within the current U.S. administration over the Israeli government’s handling of the West Bank. They added that U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee should not necessarily be viewed as the best indicator of broader administration policy, arguing that his positions are particularly close to those of the settlement movement.
Another indication cited by the sources is Washington’s muted official response to settlement-related sanctions announced by Britain and other Western governments, as well as British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s accusations of “ethnic cleansing” in parts of the West Bank.
U.S. officials had drafted a statement sharply criticizing the measures, but it was never issued after failing to win support from senior White House and State Department officials. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would not join the sanctions but stopped short of condemning the countries that imposed them.
For Israeli officials watching Washington, that silence was viewed as a troubling signal.
According to the sources, possible U.S. measures against Israeli military units accused of serious violence against Palestinian civilians also remain under discussion.
The Biden administration previously considered action against the Netzah Yehuda battalion but ultimately declined to impose sanctions after sustained Israeli pressure.
A more severe option described by the sources would restrict the use of U.S.-supplied weapons by particular units or in certain areas.
Another possibility would be placing IDF or police officers on lists of officials with whom the United States would cut contact over alleged involvement, or possible involvement, in settler violence.
“That does not necessarily mean it will happen,” one source said. “But it is on the table.”
The source added that the political situation in Congress surrounding Israel is now “far more serious” than in the past.

Russia’s Drevoch camouflage suit upgraded based on special op experience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:12:34 UTC
21:12:34 KST

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Russia’s Drevoch camouflage suit has been modernized based on experience gained in the special military operation, enhancing its ability to reduce visibility in the thermal imaging spectrum, the Zavoz.pro company told TASS.
Drevoch was introduced about a year ago as a camouflage suit for units that need to maintain mobility. Unlike capes and ponchos, the suit consists of a jacket and pants and is designed for active movement. Its design allows for movement across rough terrain and through vegetation, while the fine mesh of the base fabric reduces the likelihood of snagging on equipment. "The product was improved based on feedback from Russian service members fighting in the special military operation zone," the company reported.
It noted that one of the main changes was the decision to add a shielding layer made of metallized fabric to the design, which will make the suit easier to use in cold temperatures.
Previously, Drevoch already combined several types of camouflage. For example, its camouflage pattern and three-dimensional 3D texture help conceal a person’s silhouette in the terrain, while the material with infrared properties reduces visibility when observed through night vision devices and thermal imagers.
In addition, Zavoz.pro reported that over a thousand Drevoch suits were delivered during the first year of production. "The upgraded version was released later - about three months ago. During this period, about 500 suits with improved design were delivered," the company stated.

Media reveal information about Russian who may have organised sabotage at Leipzig airport
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:10:00 EEST
21:10:00 KST

Media reveal information about Russian who may have organised sabotage at Leipzig airport
Russian biker Oleg Lyovushkin, who is linked to a Russian military intelligence officer, may have organised an attempted sabotage at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany.
Source: a joint investigation by The Telegraph and Welt am Sonntag, as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to the investigation, Lyovushkin presumably organised the attempt to plant explosives at the airport. German investigators believe that Belarusian intermediary agent Andrei Karshakov was supposed to carry out the plan.
Journalists analysed intelligence documents from Germany, Lithuania, and Poland, and also spoke with representatives of Western secret services. According to their data, Lyovushkin and Karshakov arrived in Germany to carry out the sabotage operation.
German investigators suspect that Lyovushkin conducted reconnaissance of the airport shortly before the attack, after which he instructed Karshakov to execute the plan.
Investigators also found similarities between the incident in Leipzig and other attempted Russian sabotage operations in Poland, Lithuania, and Germany.
Specifically, the explosive device seized in Leipzig was reportedly similar to devices used in other sabotage operations in Europe.
Lyovushkin, who holds a Russian passport and is an avid motorcyclist, is also linked to Denis Smolyaninov, a man Western secret services consider to be one of the coordinators of Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
According to Lithuanian intelligence, Smolyaninov headed the Ukrainian desk in Russian military intelligence and specialised in psychological operations, among other things. Documents also link him to secret sabotage campaigns in Europe.
It is noted that Lyovushkin and Smolyaninov met back in 2007. Reportedly, they have kin repeated contact over the many years.
German security agencies link the Leipzig attack to GRU Unit 29155, which, according to German intelligence assessments, plays a key role in Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
German security agencies assess that the goal of such operations could be to create a sense of insecurity among European society due to its support for Ukraine and to influence the debate on further assistance to Kyiv.
Lyovushkin himself publicly leads an inconspicuous life. He takes part in motorcycle races, travels around Europe, fishes, and skis with his family.
At the same time, journalists claim that this lifestyle may conceal his involvement in Russian sabotage operations in Central Europe.
According to German intelligence, he travelled to Germany via Türkiye this summer to prepare an attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport. Investigators stated that Lyovushkin rented a car at Berlin airport a week before the attack and over the next few days drove it to several locations where weapons were suspected of being stored.
They believe that the explosives used in the operation were transported to Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia, hidden in the cavities of trucks, and were likely temporarily stored along the route.
The journalists say that Lyovushkin's links to the GRU were known at the time he entered the country. However, he was not placed under surveillance upon his arrival.
Background:
- On 1 September, Germany directly accused Russia of a hybrid attack at Leipzig airport in early August and announced countermeasures.
- On 6 September, it was reported that German Interior Minister Nancy Faeser was planning a set of measures to cover protection against drones, sabotage of critical infrastructure, and cyberattacks, as well as the detection of spies and potential terrorists.

The UAE’s Technology Innovation Institute (TII) will showcase some 23 demonstrations from its nine applied research centers, as well as sector-specific innovations in energy, marine infrastructure, aerospace and autonomous systems.
