The Telegraph Names Suspected Organizer of Leipzig/Halle Airport Attack, Links Him to Russia’s General Staff Main Directorate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:44:49 UTC
19:44:49 KST

The Telegraph has identified the suspected organizer of the drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport and linked the sabotage attempt to Unit 29155 of Russia’s military intelligence agency, the Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces.
The investigation by the outlet states this, based on investigative materials and information from European security agencies.
The suspect has been identified as Oleg Levushkin, a Russian and Latvian citizen who, according to investigators, provided logistical support and helped prepare the attack.
At the end of July, Levushkin traveled via Turkey to Berlin Brandenburg Airport, and rented a car on July 27. On July 31, the vehicle was recorded near Leipzig/Halle Airport, where he allegedly conducted reconnaissance ahead of the attack.
According to a journalists’ source in the German security services, the explosives may have been transported to Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia, concealed in truck voids.
Levushkin had maintained ties with the Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces’ Colonel Denis Smolyaninov for about two decades. As WDR, NDR, and Süddeutsche Zeitung previously discovered, European security agencies knew him as a suspected Russian agent even before the attack, but he was not placed under close surveillance after arriving in Germany.
Investigators also found similarities between the explosive device on the drone in Leipzig and devices recovered from caches in Lithuania. In both cases, tin cans filled with explosives and metal plates with circular indentations were used. This similarity is being considered alongside data on the suspects’ movements and other intelligence information.
According to sources involved in the investigation, the Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces’ Unit 29155 plays a key role in Russia’s sabotage campaign in Europe, in the context of which they are considering the attack in Leipzig. At the same time, Levushkin’s affiliation with the unit has not been established.
Levushkin did not respond to the journalists’ request for comment. The Russian Embassy in Berlin denied Russia’s involvement in the attack and other acts of sabotage in Europe.
As Militarnyi reported, on the night of August 5, 2026, a drone carrying an explosive device was found near Ukrainian An-124 Ruslan transport aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport. The work of bomb disposal experts led to a temporary suspension of flights. Antonov uses the airport as a temporary base following the destruction of the airfield in Hostomel by Russian forces.
A subsequent analysis of video footage showed that on August 4, the drone had struck the wing of an An-124 near the fuel tanks but failed to detonate and fell to the ground.
The investigation revealed signs that at least three drones were involved. During the suspension of flights, a DHL cargo aircraft aborted its landing and collided with an unidentified object at an altitude of about 400 meters, believed to have been another drone. A third drone was found on August 14 in a field near the western part of the airport.
In August, Militarnyi reported on an assessment by U.S. intelligence that pointed to the involvement of the Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces. An ABC News source described the drone’s design and the explosives as typical of equipment used by Russian military intelligence.
On September 1, the German government officially held Russia responsible for the attack. In response, Berlin announced the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the termination of the agreement under which the Russian House operated in Berlin.
Later, investigators identified two suspects: Oleg L. and Belarusian national Andrey K., who also holds a Russian passport. The second man’s DNA was found on one of the drones, inside a container with explosives, and on an antenna near the airport. The matches were found in databases in Lithuania and Finland.
According to preliminary investigation findings, Oleg L. left Germany two days before the attack. Andrey K. entered the Schengen Area on a tourist visa issued by the Italian mission in Minsk.
One of the suspects in the attempted sabotage was located in Finland. However, local police failed to detain him, as he left the country before a decision to detain him was made. Finnish law enforcement did not comment on the details, citing an ongoing pretrial investigation in another country.

Nearly 3 in 4 households unable to meet basic food needs in parts of Yemen: UN food agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:42:48 UTC
19:42:48 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Nearly three in four households in accessible areas of government-controlled Yemen are unable to meet their basic food needs as renewed fighting drives displacement and disrupts markets and humanitarian access, the UN’s World Food Program (WFP) warned Friday.
Recent WFP monitoring found 74% of households were unable to meet basic food needs, the highest level seen this year and an indication that food security is “significantly deteriorating,” the UN agency said in an operational update.
More than 149,000 people have been displaced by renewed fighting, according to the International Organization for Migration.
The deterioration comes as conflict and rising prices further constrain access to food, the WFP said.
Wheat flour prices have risen by 10% in just two weeks in parts of Taiz, while traders estimate wheat stocks are sufficient to cover only two months of demand. Disruptions to vegetable oil supplies are putting further pressure on already elevated food prices.
According to the WFP, Yemen imports around 90% of its food, leaving households particularly vulnerable to disruptions in trade, shipping, and supply chains.
The agency warned that further instability along Yemen's west coast and around the Bab al-Mandab corridor could push food prices even higher and deepen food insecurity in both Yemen and across the wider region.
Across Yemen, 18.3 million people face acute food insecurity, while 2.2 million children under 5 are acutely malnourished, including 500,000 suffering from severe acute malnutrition.
The WFP said conflict has also cut off access to parts of Taiz and Hodeidah, preventing it and its partners from reaching approximately 350,000 people.
The agency has already assisted more than 70,000 people in displacement hotspots in Taiz and Lahj and is preparing to scale emergency assistance to as many as 1.5 million people, according to the operational note.
The WFP said it needs $109 million for its emergency response in Yemen to assist up to 1.5 million people, while the agency needs $158 million to sustain its regular operations, including food, cash, nutrition support, and school meals for 2.4 million people through next March.

French leader Emmanuel Macron urged G7 nations to work together to bring down fuel prices in a call with US President Donald Trump on Friday, as Washington pressures Europe to tap its strategic diesel reserves and threatens curbs on US exports.
The US war on Iran has sent energy prices skyrocketing, coming back to bite Trump at home with high fuel costs a key issue in the run-up to midterm elections next month.
"The president stressed that G7 countries had a common interest in acting in a coordinated way, without export restrictions," the French leader's office said after his exchange with Trump.
The appeal came as the European Union's 27 countries were holding crisis talks in Brussels with the European Commission to develop a unified response to US pressure.
"Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a post on social media on Thursday.
"American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden of a global diesel shortage."
Macron's office said France intended to convene a video call of leaders of the G7 group of nations — which also include Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan and Britain — "as soon as possible" to ensure coordination on the matter.
Earlier this week, the head of the International Energy Agency (IEA), Fatih Birol, said European nations were yet to release part of the stocks they had agreed to in an earlier bid to ease prices in March.
"A big chunk of the stocks have been released, but still some remain, both in terms of crude oil and products," Birol told reporters on Tuesday after a meeting of EU energy ministers in Dublin.
'Dramatic consequences'
The 32 members of the IEA agreed to unlock 400 million barrels of oil from reserves — their largest release ever — in March.
About a third was yet to come to market, Birol said, adding further releases were possible with 80 percent of overall IEA stocks "still in our pocket".
Diesel prices in the United States have hit record highs due to the US-Iran war, with Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure also blamed for pushing up prices.
The issue has emerged as a major drag in the upcoming midterm elections for Trump's Republican Party, which risks losing control of Congress.
The president on Wednesday floated the possibility of banning exports of diesel, which is used in trucks and other hauling vehicles — something the EU, which relies heavily on fossil fuel imports, has slammed as a "bad idea".
EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic told reporters on Thursday on the sidelines of the G20 trade ministers gathering in Milwaukee that any move by the US to ban diesel exports would be "unexpected for Europeans."
"It would have very dramatic consequences for our economic performance," Sefcovic said.
Reports said the Trump administration wants France and Germany in particular to tap their stockpiles of diesel to try to curb prices.
"It is in Europe's best interest to work with the United States as we pursue multiple pathways to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers," a US official told AFP.
At G20 trade talks in Milwaukee, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer struck a conciliatory tone, saying there was an "eagerness on both sides to work together" on the diesel issue.
Average US diesel prices have surged more than 70 percent to $6.39 a gallon since the start of the Iran war, according to data by the American Automobile Association.

====================================================================================================

Ukraine is preparing to resume flights, but domestic airlines may not wait for it
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:40:09 EEST
19:40:09 KST

Ukraine is preparing to resume flights, but domestic airlines may not wait for it
Kyiv • UNN
The authorities are working on the safe resumption of civil flights without setting a timeline. The aviation industry faces the risk of leasing being taxed as royalties.
The authorities are already preparing for the possible resumption of civil flights and are working out scenarios for airport operations amid security risks. At the same time, civil aviation itself, which is supposed to be the first to return to Ukraine’s skies, continues to operate under extremely difficult economic conditions and is facing additional pressure because of the treatment of aircraft leasing from non-residents as royalties for tax purposes, UNN writes.
Details
Is there a task to open the skies? There is. What are the priorities here? People’s safety. Will we prepare for the opening? This work is already under way! We have calculated all the algorithms to prevent, God forbid, an emergency. It is better to forecast 5, 15, or 100 action plans in advance. And that is what we are doing now
At the same time, Kalashnyk did not name any specific timeframe for reopening the skies.
The minister drew attention to the experience of Israel and African countries, where civil aviation continues to operate despite wartime risks. According to him, Ukraine is studying the experience of these countries and will also exchange experience with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), which regulates flight procedures.
He clarified that work is currently under way to organize safe spaces and shelters, provide alternative sources of electricity, and so on.
So this work is being carried out. It will definitely happen. It is simply a matter of time. Either the hostilities will end earlier with our great Ukrainian victory and peace will come, or civil aviation will resume during the period in which we are preparing for this
While airports are being prepared, the aviation industry is trying to survive
Obviously, reopening the skies is not enough. There must be those who return to them. After the airspace is reopened, Ukrainian carriers will have to compete with major foreign airlines. But Ukrainian airlines themselves have the potential to quickly return to the domestic market, restore jobs and increase tax revenues, as well as provide the country with its own aviation capacity.
Therefore, alongside the preparation of airports, shelters, and security procedures, another question arises: what condition will Ukrainian civil aviation itself be in by the time the skies reopen? This is where the situation remains difficult. Because of the war, Ukrainian civil aviation was forced to relocate abroad, where international contracts enable it to retain its personnel, certificates, and the airworthiness of its aircraft.
At the same time, the aviation business traditionally operates with low profitability and significant fixed costs. Aircraft require maintenance regardless of how intensively they are used, while carriers incur expenses for insurance, aircraft leasing, crew training, maintaining certificates, and compliance with international requirements.
Against this backdrop, another risk has emerged for the industry – an unexpected change in the approach of government bodies to the taxation of aircraft-leasing transactions with non-residents, without any change to the legislative framework.
More than 80% of Ukrainian airlines’ aircraft are leased
The issue of leasing is not a problem for an individual airline; it is systemic. As an earlier analysis by UNN of data from the State Register of Civil Aircraft showed, as of July 29, 2026, 27 private airlines operated 152 aircraft. Of these, 131, or 86%, were leased, while only 21 airplanes and helicopters (14%) belonged to the airlines themselves.
It is worth noting that all leased commercial aircraft are owned by foreign owners.
International leasing is one of the fundamental mechanisms on which global commercial aviation is built, and Ukraine is no exception. It is aircraft leasing that allows carriers to use expensive airplanes and helicopters without spending tens of millions of dollars purchasing them.
Under international law, in particular double taxation avoidance conventions, taxes on leasing are paid in the country where the lessor company is a resident, that is, abroad. In Ukraine, airlines pay other taxes and fees.
In particular, according to Danyil Menshikov, Head of the State Aviation Service of Ukraine, aviation industry companies paid almost UAH 27 billion in taxes and fees to the budget in 2022–2025, despite the closure of Ukrainian airspace.
Leasing began to be interpreted as royalties
Representatives of the aviation industry have long been drawing attention to the problem of the new interpretation by government authorities of leasing payments made to non-residents, which emerged without any amendments to tax legislation or international double taxation avoidance conventions. As UNN previously reported, since 2024 the Bureau of Economic Security has begun interpreting transactions involving the leasing of air transport from non-residents of Ukraine as the use of equipment. According to the investigators’ version, Ukrainian air carriers were supposed to pay royalties for the rental of aircraft and helicopters. Based on this approach, the BES opened criminal proceedings against at least five air carriers, including UIA, Constanta Airline, Windrose, H3Operations, and Skyline Express. According to UNN, another airline—Urga—may also feature in a similar case.
The criminal cases were opened despite the fact that almost all air carriers had successfully undergone tax audits, and the tax authorities’ comments concerning leasing applied to only one company.
Representatives of the aviation industry insist that the problem arose because of an ambiguous interpretation of legal provisions and requires the establishment of a unified state approach. Moreover, interpreting aircraft leasing as royalties—a practice that does not exist in any other country in the world—makes Ukrainian carriers uncompetitive in the international market.
The average profitability of airlines today is only 7–10%, while additional taxation of leasing payments may reach 10–15%, depending on the lessor’s jurisdiction.
Earlier, in response to a request from UNN, the Ministry of Finance reported that the taxation of aircraft leasing transactions is carried out in accordance with the Tax Code and Ukraine’s international treaties. At the same time, the Tax Code of Ukraine does not provide for the possibility of taxing aircraft leasing as royalties.
Therefore, representatives of the aviation industry call the Bureau’s approach of interpreting aircraft leasing without amending tax legislation pressure that could destroy the entire passenger and freight transportation sector.
To resolve the situation, the issue of aircraft leasing was submitted for consideration by the Committee on Tax Policy, Accounting and Auditing of the Public Council under the Ministry of Finance. Following the first meeting, it was decided to initiate the creation of a working group under the Ministry of Finance, which is to develop a draft general tax consultation on the taxation of leasing payments made to non-residents.
This mechanism could regulate the situation regarding the taxation of leasing and establish uniform, clear rules of the game for the aviation business that would comply with the Tax Code of Ukraine and international law.

India’s Foreign Minister Jaishankar Openly Calls Out the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:39:00 UTC
19:39:00 KST

On September 28, India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi had a telephone conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump to review progress in bilateral cooperation. In a post on X, Modi described the conversation as “productive.” “We reviewed our bilateral cooperation in trade, defence, energy, critical technologies and other areas. We agreed to maintain close engagement to take our Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership forward,” he said.
While Modi’s post about his conversation with Trump was not negative, it was far less effusive than in the past, even bland. As Yashraj Sharma observed in an article in Al Jazeera, it was a “cold and formal depiction far removed from his description of the US president as a ‘good friend’ in previous years.”
The Trump-Modi phone call came at a time when already fraying bilateral relations hit yet another difficult phase.
Ten days earlier, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (SRIA) of 2026, which gives the U.S. president the authority to impose up to 100 percent tariffs on countries that continue to purchase Russian oil and gas. India, which is among the largest buyers of Russian energy, could potentially be impacted.
India-U.S. cooperation has deepened and widened over the past two decades. Despite “complexities,” ties were expected to grow under Trump; the outlook was upbeat.
However, Trump 2.0 has not been good for the partnership. Within weeks of the inauguration of Trump’s second presidential term, ties began unravelling not only over tariffs and immigration but also Washington’s cozying up to Pakistan on a raft of issues, including terrorism, an issue that Delhi is highly sensitive about.
India was among the countries that were hit the hardest by Trump’s “reciprocal tariffs” announced last year. Adding insult to injury, India was then slapped with another 25 percent “punitive tariffs” for buying Russian oil.
Should the U.S. press ahead with imposing SRIA on India, it would hit India’s oil imports and, consequently, its energy security.
Over the past 19 months, although Indians took note of Trump’s abrasive remarks and insensitive tweets, they took it in their stride. The diplomatic establishment seemed to have adopted a patient wait-and-watch policy. India, after all, needed the U.S and benefited from economic and security cooperation with Washington. The current uncertainty was seen as temporary.
However, that mood in Delhi is changing. Its patience with Trump seems to be wearing thin. Officials and analysts are calling on the government to be more realistic in its assessment of the current India-U.S. relationship.
In an article in The Week, Navtej Sarna, a former Indian ambassador to the U.S., wrote: “We need to accept, without caveats, that the relationship has cratered significantly. In America’s eyes, India is not the strategic partner that we believed we were.”
A change is evident not just in Delhi’s mood but also, in its approach.
“India has reached the end of its tether with Trump,” a former official in India’s MEA told The Diplomat. “In the past we abhorred megaphone diplomacy, preferring to sort out nettlesome issues with friends quietly and only via diplomatic channels. That was India’s approach towards Russia’s intervention in Afghanistan in 1979, and its invasion in Ukraine in 2022, for example. But that is clearly changing,” he said. “India today is not averse to calling out, even friends, on difficult matters if core concerns are being undermined.”
This change was on full display last week during India’s Minister for External Affairs S. Jaishankar’s visit to the U.S.
At an event at the Asia Society in New York, Jaishankar did not hold back in drawing attention to Washington’s lack of “understanding or appreciation or empathy” for Delhi on issues of concern and sensitivity to the latter. He was referring to Washington’s courting of Pakistan despite the latter’s support for anti-India terrorism. “If one of my primary concerns is not fully appreciated by my partner, then clearly there is an impact of that on the relationship,” he said. Although he did not mention the U.S. by name, it was evident who he was referring to.
Strong India-U.S. relations have enjoyed bipartisan support in the U.S. over the past two decades. Whenever differences surfaced or ties frayed, Indian officials would avoid airing grievances to the media. They seemed willing to bide their time in the hope that this was a mere hiccup, a troubled phase that could be navigated. India being important to the U.S. in its strategy to contain a rising China, it was widely believed that the strategic partnership was solid.
But with the U.S.-China relationship seemingly moving to a phase of competitive coexistence rather than confrontation, India’s role in Washington’s containment strategy against China could decline. As Indian academic Atul Mishra pointed out, “If balancing China is no longer a priority, then India’s importance within America’s strategic calculus goes down.”
Especially after the recent meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, cracks are visible in the once-solid belief that India is important to the U.S. Apprehensions have deepened further amid Trump’s courting of Pakistan.
There are other reasons why the current troubled phase in India-U.S. ties may not be as temporary as Delhi believed over the past year. There is a growing perception that the fraying partnership may survive the end of Trump’s term.
According to Sarna, the current downturn in India-U.S. relations cannot be attributed to Trump alone. “Economic nationalism, racial supremacism, moral poverty, naked aggression and wanton disregard for international law and norms are trends which will outlast Trump; on many issues the centre has moved in American politics,” he argues, pointing out that Trump’s successor, be it U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio or even a Democrat politician, “may not be much different [from Trump], though a tad predictable.”
Meanwhile, all eyes in India have turned to India’s Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal’s ongoing visit to the U.S. Many rounds of talks have taken place so far, and while India and the U.S. reached a framework for an interim trade agreement in February 2026, a final Bilateral Trade Agreement remains elusive.
Ahead of his U.S. visit, Goyal said that the India-U.S. trade pact was “almost done and dusted.” Should the two sides firm up an agreement soon, that could lighten the gloomy mood in Delhi somewhat. Of course, much will depend on what the final agreement brings India.
An agreement that is heavily weighted against Indian interests can be expected to deepen the prevailing pessimism in Delhi over its ties with the U.S.

Iran vs Guinea-Bissau friendly cancelled
TEHRAN - Despite efforts by the Iranian Football Federation to arrange the match, the proposed friendly between Iran and Guinea-Bissau has been canceled.
As a result, Iran’s national football team will conclude their current schedule with two matches against Uzbekistan and Russia.
In recent days, there had been considerable speculation over the identity of Iran’s third opponent, with Guinea-Bissau emerging as one of the leading candidates. The Iranian Football Federation was working to organize the match in either Turkey or Qatar and, as part of those efforts, proposed hosting the game in Istanbul to the Turkish Football Federation.
However, the Turkish Football Federation rejected the proposal, citing a congested schedule and its existing calendar of fixtures and activities. The decision by Turkey was only one of several obstacles that ultimately prevented the match from going ahead, as further complications emerged during the process of arranging the fixture.
One of the main challenges involved the Guinea-Bissau team’s travel arrangements. Flight restrictions and financial difficulties resulting from sanctions imposed on Iran made it difficult for the Iranian federation to arrange air tickets for members of the Guinea-Bissau squad.
International financial transfers are also a complicated and time-consuming process under the existing restrictions. As a result, the Iranian Football Federation was unable to purchase the necessary tickets for the Guinea-Bissau delegation through foreign companies.
Consequently, even after efforts were made to move the proposed match to Turkey, the travel and logistical problems facing the visiting team remained unresolved. With the administrative and logistical arrangements unable to be finalized, the friendly was eventually cancelled.
Iran will therefore finish this stage of its preparations with matches against Uzbekistan and Russia, without adding a third fixture to their schedule.

MADRID – Protesters said they would return to the streets across Spain and press on with their encampment in Madrid after a government bid to answer their complaints about a mounting housing crisis was rejected by Parliament on Oct 2.
Crowds gathered outside the assembly chanting “your profits, our misery” as lawmakers voted down the minority government’s decree that had been drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman.
The legislation had sought to ban evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, impose a two-year rent freeze extension for existing leases and introduce tighter rules for short-term rentals.
‘We’re aiming for a general strike’
It failed after lawmakers from Catalan separatist party Junts – a sometime ally of the left-wing government – joined the opposition in voting it down, arguing that the proposals would exacerbate matters by reducing housing supply.
The Tenants’ Union, which had driven the protests, said it would press on with plans for more mass rallies on Oct 3, piling pressure on the coalition. The decree failed with 178 votes against and 172 in favour.
The eviction of pensioner Maricarmen Abascal last week triggered protests across Spain. Young people pitched tents in Madrid’s central square and other cities for almost a week, bringing back memories of anti-austerity sit-ins in 2008-12 sparked by the global financial crisis.
“The encampment will continue and will continue expanding to other neighbourhoods. We’re aiming for a general strike,” Tenants’ Union spokeswoman Alicia del Rio said.
Abascal’s eviction unleashed anger over the cost of housing, with many young people past 30 years of age living with parents.
Rents have doubled over the last decade, with average prices reaching €1,176 (S$1,700) a month, equivalent to 98.7% of the average salary for a young person, according to the Youth Council of Spain.
“People have said ‘enough is enough’; this cannot go on. The housing problem must be resolved, structural measures must be taken, and this cannot continue,” Abascal’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said in an interview with Reuters on Oct 1.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s coalition government has 147 seats in the 350-seat chamber and relies on smaller parties, including Junts, to pass legislation.
Junts parliamentary spokesperson Miriam Nogueras said the decrees would have the opposite effect of their intended aims. “Finding housing will become more difficult every day. Our responsibility is to provide certainty, not uncertainty.”
She urged the government to work on a new decree.
The opposition People’s Party also voted against the measures.
“Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees. It becomes more affordable by building more homes. We’re not going to lie to you – it’s not going to be easy, and it’s not going to happen quickly,” said PP lawmaker Juan Bravo.
Before the vote failed, Emilio Anton, a protester camped in Sol, said earlier that the protests would continue.
“I’m almost certain we’ll carry on like this until there’s a final agreement or until they kick us out,” he said. REUTERS

Türkiye’s national defense minister said Friday that the security of the Caucasus cannot be considered separately from the security of Türkiye, Azerbaijan, and Georgia, stressing the importance of trilateral cooperation for regional peace and stability.
Expressing pleasure at being in the Azerbaijani city of Shusha, which he called the heart of the country’s culture, for a trilateral defense ministers' meeting, Yasar Guler said Türkiye, Azerbaijan and Georgia are three friendly neighboring countries connected by a shared history and geography, mutual trust, and strong bonds of friendship.

"Ensuring the security of these projects is the shared responsibility of our countries," he said.
Guler said joint military exercises, training and exchanges of experience among the three countries' armed forces are practical reflections of this responsibility.
"The security of the Caucasus cannot be considered separately from the security of Türkiye, Azerbaijan and Georgia," he said.

French high school students lit fires outside schools and faced off with police on Oct. 2 as a protest movement that has forced the closure of some 400 establishments showed no sign of abating.
The movement, which began last week in the Paris region and rapidly spread nationwide, has seen teenage pupils at lycees in their final years of schooling block access to buildings and clash with police.

The government says the grievances are legitimate but has condemned what it has described as “urban violence.”

Education Minister Edouard Geffray said “the high school student movement is being held hostage by ultra-violent fringe groups,” adding that nearly 400 high schools out of the 3,700 in the country were expected to be closed on Oct. 2.
Many high schools have also planned to conduct classes remotely, particularly in the southern city of Marseille.
At least 65 staff members have been injured, including 40 high school principals, since the start of the movement, Geffray told BFMTV. Some 170 students have been wounded while over 100 high schools have suffered “severe damage.”
“Parents must clearly step up and tell their children not to go” to the protests, he added. “What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger.”
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said he has asked prosecutors to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children during the protests and “pay for repairs.”

China's railway network handled 25.204 million passenger trips on October 1, the first day of the week-long National Day holiday, setting a new single-day record, China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) said on Friday.
On October 2, the railway network is expected to handle 20.39 million passenger trips, with 1,462 additional trains scheduled to accommodate the high demand, the company said.
Passenger ticket pre-sales show that Friday's popular departure cities include Beijing, Guangzhou, Shanghai, Chengdu, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou and Nanjing, while popular arrival cities include Beijing, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Hangzhou, Shanghai, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou, Nanjing and Changsha.
Routes such as Xi'an-Chengdu round trips, as well as Beijing to Shenyang, Zhengzhou and Qingdao, are among the busiest.
Railway authorities across the country have strengthened transport organisation and implemented measures to ensure safe, convenient and comfortable travel.
The China Railway Taiyuan Group has coordinated with local transport departments and scenic spots to add shuttle buses linking Datong South Station with the Yungang Grottoes, a Unesco World Heritage site featuring over 50,000 Buddhist stone sculptures, and the Hengshan Mountain scenic area in north China's Shanxi Province.
The China Railway Hohhot Group has added 11 multiple-unit trains on the Baotou-Wuhai section of the Baotou-Yinchuan high-speed railway.
The China Railway Wuhan Group, tapping the newly opened Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway, has launched a promotion campaign with local governments in Yichang and Xingshan, offering passengers exclusive discounts at scenic spots, hotels and homestays with their train tickets.
China Railway expects some 284 million passenger trips during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, which extends from September 23 to October 8.
On October 1, a total of 329.5 million cross-regional passenger trips were made across China, down 1.9 percent year on year, according to the Ministry of Transport.
Specifically, railway passenger trips reached 25.204 million, up 9 percent year on year; road passenger trips stood at 300.36 million, down 2.8 percent; waterway passenger trips totalled 1.416 million, up 7.2 percent; and civil aviation passenger trips came in at 2.515 million, up 0.5 percent, according to the ministry.
China's total cross-regional passenger trips are expected to reach 308.19 million on October 2, up 2.1 percent year on year, the ministry added.
On Friday, the National Energy Administration reported that, based on statistical analysis of 62,700 highway charging facilities included in the national charging infrastructure monitoring service platform, the first day of the National Day holiday saw a total highway charging volume of 28.05 million kilowatt-hours nationwide.
This represents a 60.4 percent increase compared to the first day of last year's National Day holiday, setting a new single-day holiday record for charging volume. (Xinhua)

As the olive harvesting season gets underway, farmers in Tarom County, Zanjan Province, are busy picking and preparing the crop for processing.
After being transported to local processing workshops, the harvested olives are sorted according to the size and dimensions of the fruit. They are then cracked using specialized machinery to prepare them for subsequent stages of processing.

The activity plays an important role in the local agricultural economy and provides livelihoods for a large number of farming households in the county.

The county has around 18,000 hectares under olive cultivation, and local agricultural officials have forecast production of about 50,000 tons of olives in the current year. Olive cultivation is therefore a major component of Tarom’s agricultural economy, while the development of processing facilities has further strengthened the crop’s role in local employment and value-added production.

The System That Failed Cornell’s Jane Doe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:35:05 UTC
19:35:05 KST

On Sept. 16, a student at Cornell University filed a lawsuit against the university, fraternities, and sororities after she was allegedly drugged and gang-raped by seven fraternity brothers in 2024. The allegations are horrifying. But just as troubling is what the lawsuit describes afterward: a survivor seeking help from the systems meant to protect her and finding, again and again, that she was failed.
In 2026, we are still asking how this happened. The Cornell case is not only about the conduct alleged in one lawsuit. It is about a broader failure of prevention, investigation, and accountability—one that survivors of sexual violence encounter far too often, on campuses and far beyond them.
For nearly a decade, I have worked alongside survivors who made the extraordinarily difficult decision to share their stories. Some became public faces of national reckonings. Many more remained anonymous, fearful of backlash, retaliation, disbelief, or the permanent consequences of public exposure. Their names did not make headlines. Their pain was no less real.
What I have learned is that survivors are often failed more than once: first, by the person who harms them, and then by the very systems that are supposed to prevent, investigate, and respond to sexual violence.
The allegations in the complaint involving Cornell's campus are deeply disturbing, and new ones continue to emerge hour by hour. Just as disturbing is how this young student was reportedly failed afterward. According to her lawsuit and news accounts, the alleged assault involved drugs, multiple perpetrators, and digital evidence. The complaint has raised serious questions about whether the case was thoroughly investigated after it was reported. That should concern every parent, student, university administrator, and public official, not simply because it occurred at an elite university, but because these failures can occur anywhere.
We must start with prevention. Consent is not a box to check. It must be voluntary, informed, ongoing, and freely given. It cannot exist when a person is incapacitated, and it can be withdrawn at any time.
So how did young men come to believe this was acceptable? As a society, we have failed to educate young people about consent, respect, and the gravity of sexual violence. That education must begin before college; we cannot wait until they arrive on campus.
College students need more than a single orientation presentation they forget by October. Schools should provide sustained, practical education about consent, coercion, alcohol and drugs, healthy relationships, and bystander responsibility.
But education and prevention alone are not enough. Institutions must have protocols to ensure justice when prevention fails.
On Sept. 18, 2026, in response to recent community outrage over how the case was handled, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten issued a statement explaining why his investigation resulted in a lack of criminal charges. Jane Doe’s credibility “was never in question,” he wrote, explaining that the initial sworn statement shared with the DA, which was reviewed by “multiple prosecutors and criminal investigators,” did not include the full information provided in Jane Doe’s 2026 civil suit.
Transcript records, obtained by CBS News New York, from a November 2024 interview with Cornell campus police indicate that Jane Doe told officials, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."
Van Houten has since stated that he was never shown the transcript. "If she had said those words, we certainly would want to have explored that more," he told CBS. "Like I said, that wasn't provided to me."
This demonstrates why the response to reports of sexual assault must be trauma-informed and evidence-based. Survivors may not disclose everything at once. Their recollections may emerge in fragments. They may hesitate, change the order of events, or struggle to articulate what happened. Those are not automatic signs of deception; they can be well-recognized effects of trauma. I have seen it firsthand, personally and professionally with Weinstein survivors.
Prosecutors and investigators handling sexual assault cases must receive mandatory trauma-informed training. They must know how to preserve evidence, interview witnesses, assess digital records, and investigate without allowing outdated assumptions about how a “credible” victim should behave to dictate the outcome.
Universities have an equally urgent responsibility. A sexual-assault report cannot be treated as a public-relations problem to contain quietly. Institutions need independent investigators, clear procedures, meaningful support for complainants, and processes that are fair to all parties while prioritizing campus safety. When an impartial process finds a student responsible for sexual assault, the consequences must be serious enough to protect the community and demonstrate that violence will not be tolerated. And Title IX policies and procedures should likewise be reviewed and strengthened to ensure that complaints are handled fairly, promptly, and effectively.
Public accountability also matters. When survivors decide that speaking publicly is right for them, they deserve legal, communications, and institutional support. This creates a powerful transformation. They are no longer isolated voices. Their experiences, amplified through journalism and public discourse, create pressure that institutions cannot ignore. They become part of a movement.
This is how cultural change happens. A survivor speaks publicly. Her story resonates. Others find courage to come forward. Lawmakers, university administrators, and prosecutors suddenly face inescapable public scrutiny. The conversation shifts from whispered allegations to national headlines, from institutional cover-ups to criminal investigations.
No survivor should have to go public to be believed. No survivor should have to become a national story to receive a competent investigation. And no college should wait for headlines to do what it was obligated to do from the start.
The alleged events at Cornell remind us that awareness alone is not action. We have spent years talking about sexual violence, consent, and institutional accountability. We know more about trauma than we did a decade ago. We have policies, resources, and legal frameworks that can make a difference.
What has been missing is the will to use them consistently.
Survivors deserve institutions that prevent harm where possible, respond effectively when harm occurs, and refuse to protect reputations at the expense of safety, dignity, and justice. We should not still be here in 2026, asking why.
We cannot continue to let survivors down.
We all must do better—institutions and individuals alike.

Cotton Queen: Sudan's colonial past meets its cinematic future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:34:47 UTC
19:34:47 KST

Breadcrumb
Cotton Queen: Suzannah Mirghani's Sudanese story of women, cotton and colonialism
Proclaimed the first Sudanese female filmmaker after her debut feature Cotton Queen premiered at the 2025 Venice Film Festival’s Critics' Week programme, Suzannah Mirghani disputes the description, saying the fragile Sudanese film industry doesn't keep good track of its history, so there must be other women before her.
Building on her previous short film Al-Sit (2020, available on Netflix Middle East), Cotton Queen won the ArteKino Award at L’Atelier de la Cinéfondation at Cannes in 2022 before heading to Venice, and it celebrates its UK premiere on October 2.
The film follows Nafisa, a teenage girl growing up in a cotton-farming village in Sudan. When a businessman arrives promising to modernise the local cotton industry with genetically engineered seeds and asks for Nafisa’s hand in marriage, she finds herself caught between tradition, modernity, and her own emerging sense of independence.
Cotton Queen draws on Suzannah's childhood memories of Sudan, where she lived until she was a teenager, as well as her later research into the history of cotton and British colonialism in the country.
The original intentions were to shoot in Sudan, with many of the same actors and crew who worked on Al-Sit. But the outbreak of the Sudanese civil war in 2023 forced Mirghani to relocate production to Egypt.
Suzannah Mirghani speaks to The New Arab about making a film rooted in Sudanese memory, the complicated relationship between cotton and colonialism, the country’s interrupted cinematic history, and why she wanted her teenage protagonist to challenge both tradition and modernity.
The New Arab: You have been described as the first female Sudanese feature filmmaker. What does that mean to you?
Suzannah Mirghani: It’s a big, big responsibility. But I always say someone somewhere must have made a feature film; it just didn’t get publicity.
I’m always hesitant to say I’m the first because I truly believe other women have written and directed films, and we simply don’t know about them.
Maybe their work wasn’t properly archived. In Sudan's history, there isn’t a documented female feature filmmaker before me, but women have been writing for television and working in other forms of filmmaking. So I don’t really like to make that claim about myself.
How did Cotton Queen begin? Is it based on real events?
I lived in Sudan until I was a teenager, about the same age as the protagonist. Then my family left, and we moved to Qatar.
My recollections of Sudan are a mixture of memories of my grandmother, life on the cotton farms and my extended family, who had cotton fields. I remember it all as magical, romantic and nostalgic.
But as I got older and read more, I started learning more about Sudan's history, especially the history of cotton. I learned about the dark and violent history of British colonialism.
So the film is really taking two tracks. On the surface, it’s a happy, light-filled, enchanting story. But underneath lurks a very harsh reality. In this regard, Cotton Queen brings my two lives together: my childhood memories and my adult research brain.
What is interesting about the film’s visual language is that the cotton fields usually associated with struggle and exploitation are depicted here beautifully, not necessarily in the context of physical hardship or poverty.
Was that a conscious choice? Absolutely. Whenever we see cotton on screen, especially for audiences around the world, it’s usually associated with the American South, slavery and a horrible history.
In Sudan, yes, we had a violent and horrible history around cotton, but we also had a community relationship with the crop. There was a loving and caring connection between the communities that grew cotton and the cotton itself.
People used cotton directly for their own needs, for clothes and bedding. Women especially had a close relationship with cotton, using raw cotton for menstruation, while grandmothers spun it into thread and turned it into fabric.
We also have a strange situation in some Sudanese rural communities where grandmothers can be financially independent because they make money selling thread, while other household members may be unemployed.
The grandmother in Cotton Queen has enormous authority. What does she represent within Sudanese society?
Sudan has a very strong matriarchal cultural identity, even though the country is extremely patriarchal at the governmental, economic, and macro levels.
It is patriarchal, militaristic and dictatorial. But inside the home, things are very much guided by women, and especially by the grandmother. She can be at the top of the household power structure.
I’m talking about specific rural communities, of course, not every Sudanese grandmother.
In some communities, grandmothers have traditionally had a say in who and when gets married, and other important family decisions.
They also hold tradition and, in some cases, control the income from cotton. Even going back to ancient times, women could rule alongside men. That respect for older women has continued.
I remember very funny situations from my childhood where my grandmother would discipline my father in front of us. We would be dying of laughter because my father was a very patriarchal man, and yet there was this old woman telling him what to do.
But, as I said, that power is usually contained within the household. For me, it was important to ask: what happens when a girl or a woman takes that power beyond the home?
The main character, Nafisa, is at the centre of the film’s conflict between tradition and modernity. What did you want her to represent?
She is part of a new generation that questions everything: tradition, modernity, and their families. But at the same time, they are still trying to hold on to some of those customs.
It’s about picking and choosing what is good rather than simply accepting everything – the good and the bad.
Sudan has beautiful customs, but also harmful ones, such as female circumcision, where Nafisa’s sceptical view on marriage emerges from.
These are things that have to change through action, and the process is very difficult to do in tight, conservative communities.
So, for me, the film is about Nafisa rejecting what is bad and taking what is good from both the modern and traditional worlds.
The film also introduces a new kind of outsider and coloniser – a businessman arriving with genetically modified cotton. How did that storyline emerge?
I came up with it through my research. When I first started writing, I made a proof-of-concept short film in 2020, Al-Sit. At that point, I hadn’t done all the research that I eventually did for the feature.
The short was more about love, poetry, cotton, beauty and nostalgia. I shot it in Sudan and promised everyone I would come back and make a feature. I was telling the children: don’t grow up, stay exactly as you are!
But when I began developing the feature, I started reading much more about genetically modified seeds and their introduction into Sudanese agriculture.
That made me think about another cycle of dependence. Foreign agricultural companies introduce seeds, farmers become dependent on external systems, and the cotton ultimately becomes part of an international economic structure that can leave farmers in a weaker position.
That is where the colonial history of cotton becomes connected to the present, and colonisation actually keeps going.
You initially intended to shoot the feature in Sudan. What happened?
I had always wanted to shoot in Sudan. There was no question about it. The plan was to use the same actors and crew who had worked on Al-Sit. Then the Sudanese civil war began in 2023, and all of those plans were destroyed.
We eventually moved the production to Egypt. It was the practical choice: Arabic-speaking, culturally similar, with cotton fields and the Nile.
But I really didn't want to shoot my first feature anywhere other than Sudan, because it is about the land.
So, I refused at first. I waited for a year, and the war kept getting worse. Meanwhile, the actors had fled Sudan and gone to Egypt.
At a certain point I thought: what am I doing in Sudan on my own? And I inevitably had to take the film to Egypt.
The fact that Cotton Queen is fiction helped me make it in another country. I tried to put a positive twist on the situation: we were recreating Sudan at a time when the country was being destroyed.
I’m still sad about it, to be honest. But you have to make compromises in times of war.
You cast non-professionals and theatre actors rather than established screen actors. How did you find them?
The young actors were doing their first major screen roles, apart from the experience they had with my short film. We auditioned in Sudan because this was originally the same cast as Al-Sit. There were only one or two different characters, but we still held auditions.
The funny thing is that when we auditioned for the young businessman, we had more than 100 candidates. While for Nafisa, the main role, we had only five girls from the whole country.
That tells you something about how families support young girls becoming actors – or rather, how they don’t. They don’t necessarily see acting as a possible future career for their daughters.
For many of them, it is just something fun that they do. They don’t imagine it as a profession.
Within the fragile Sudanese reality you are describing, Sudan has produced several important films in recent years. How come?
We have a very unfortunate history with filmmaking. Every time the industry starts growing, something happens politically that shuts it down. It’s like every decade has a bloom and then a destruction.
The 1960s and 1970s were amazing. Then in the 1980s and 1990s, there was almost nothing because the government outlawed many forms of art and culture.
Then in 2019, we had the revolution, and suddenly the arts became the darling of the country. Music, singing, dancing, filmmaking – everything.
It was only a short period, between 2019 and 2021, but we saw films like You Will Die at Twenty, Talking About Trees and Khartoum Offside. Those films gave us a lot of hope.
When I saw Talking About Trees, I immediately went to Sudan to shoot my short film.
All you need is for someone to tell you that something is possible. We worked with some of the same crew, asked people for information, and shared knowledge. That’s how you grow a community and eventually a film industry.
But now everything has gone back to zero. I do know that some people have returned and are shooting short films, sometimes almost in secret. There is still a desire to make films.
Will Cotton Queen eventually be shown in Sudan?
Right now, the situation is very bad. But even before the war, we didn’t have functioning cinemas in the way you would expect. So, there wasn’t really an obvious place to screen the film.
But I would say that it doesn’t matter where I screen this film in the world. There is a Sudanese audience.
You describe yourself as a Sudanese-Russian filmmaker. What does that identity mean to you?
I grew up in Sudan and never lived in Russia. However, my mother met my father in Russia when Sudanese students were sent to the Soviet Union in the 1970s on scholarships to study there, in Moscow, Rostov, and other cities.
There are thousands of people like me with Russian-Sudanese citizenship in both countries, as well as Russian-Congolese, Russian-Palestinian, and many other communities that emerged from that period. It was part of the Cold War project.
My father has a similar story to Suleiman, one of the character-filmmakers in Talking About Trees. He is a doctor, but he also studied in the Soviet Union.
What the Soviet government probably didn’t anticipate was that all these students would bring Russian wives back home.
Finally, what does the title Cotton Queen stand for?
While researching the film, I came across a brief reference to something called the Cotton Queen beauty competition.
In the 1930s, the British had a beauty competition called the Cotton Queen. It took place in northern England, in places like Manchester and Lancashire, for British women working in cotton mills and turning cotton into thread.
What they didn’t necessarily realise was that the cotton they were working with could have come from Sudan.
Then I discovered that there had also been a Cotton Queen competition in Sudan. But those women never received the same headlines, crowns or publicity.
I learned about it by talking to older people. And immediately I thought: that’s the title of my film.
Those two words capture everything I wanted to say: cotton, industry, colonialism. Both British colonialism and Sudan.
But I also wanted to take the idea of the Cotton Queen away from its original meaning of beauty, girls and a patriarchal industry.
To turn my character into a real queen – a woman with real power.
Mariana Hristova is a freelance film critic, cultural journalist, and programmer. She contributes to national and international outlets and has curated programs for Filmoteca de Catalunya, Arxiu Xènctric, and goEast Wiesbaden, among others. Her professional interests include cinema from the European peripheries and archival and amateur films

WHO representative highlights need for integrated, person-centered care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:34:14 UTC
19:34:14 KST

WHO representative highlights need for integrated, person-centered care
TEHRAN - The WHO Representative in Iran has highlighted the importance of strengthening intersectoral collaboration and promoting integrated, person-centered care, while underscoring the need to expand community-based rehabilitation services and foster age-friendly environments to better respond to the needs of older people.
“Longer lives should not simply mean adding years to life. They should mean adding health, dignity, participation and meaning to those years,” Dr Jean Jabbour said on Thursday in a ceremony to commemorate the International Day of Older Persons.
WHO remains committed to supporting national programmes in the Islamic Republic of Iran through technical cooperation, capacity-building, knowledge exchange and stronger connections with international experience and networks.
As people live longer, health and social support systems must evolve to meet their needs throughout the life course.
On 14 December 1990, the United Nations General Assembly designated October 1 as the International Day of Older Persons. This was preceded by initiatives such as the Vienna International Plan of Action on Ageing, which was adopted by the 1982 World Assembly on Ageing and endorsed later that year by the UN General Assembly.
The 2026 United Nations International Day of Older Persons, under the theme "The Age of Longevity: Rethinking Systems for Longer Lives," calls on Governments, civil society, the private sector, researchers and older persons themselves to examine how societies can ensure that the additional years gained translate into healthy, productive, dignified and equitable lives for all.
Humanity is living longer than ever. Global life expectancy has risen steadily for over seven decades, yet the gap between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy reached 9.6 years in 2019, reflecting the growing burden of noncommunicable diseases. Longer lives are drawing greater attention to how health, social and economic conditions, and human rights are experienced across the life course.
Longevity intersects with health systems, labour markets, social protection, education, housing and fiscal sustainability in ways that cannot be addressed in isolation. Where years are lived in good health and supported by inclusive labour markets and effective social protection, longer lives can generate a longevity dividend. Conversely, without improvements in healthy life expectancy, older persons may spend more years in poorer health, limiting their functional ability, well-being, autonomy and participation.
The number of older people (defined as those aged 65 years or older) tripled from around 260 million in 1980 to 761 million in 2021. Between 2021 and 2050, the global share of the older population is projected to increase from less than 10% to around 17%.
Rapid growth in the number of people reaching older ages underscores the significance of promoting health, preventing, and treating illnesses throughout the entire course of life.
In societies with aging populations, it becomes imperative to adjust to the increasing number of elderly individuals who possess a diverse range of functional capacities. The capability to carry out essential functions and partake in everyday activities is influenced not solely by an individual's inherent capacity but also by the social and physical environments in which they reside. Supportive environments play a pivotal role in assisting older individuals to maintain their activity levels and independence as they progress in age.
Elderly to account for 30% of Iran’s population by 2050
With older adults already accounting for 13 percent of Iran’s population and the country’s fertility rate continuing to decline, demographic shifts are accelerating. Current projections indicate that within the next 25 years, nearly one-third of Iran’s population will be aged 60 and above.
Iran is aging, and this demographic shift will place significant pressure on the healthcare system, pension funds, social support agencies, and the national economy. To prevent the consequences of an aging population, the country is pursuing policies aimed at boosting the youth population and incentives for childbearing.
According to Marzieh Vahid-Dastjerdi, the secretary of the National Population Headquarters, the young population is one of the indicators that has to be paid attention to. The young population is the share of the population aged less than 15 years old. In Iran, it forms 21.5 percent of the total population, that is, 21.5 out of 100 individuals are below 15 currently. However, it is declining with falling birth rates.
Fortunately, Iran is in a population window of opportunity – a period when a large proportion of the population is of working age; the country has 15 to 20 years before the demographic window begins to close.
Alireza Raeisi, an official with the health ministry, says that “Population decline is itself a consequence rather than a cause; therefore, to reverse the trend, the various economic, social, cultural, and familial factors that have led to reduced fertility must be identified, analyzed, and addressed. Furthermore, even if we succeed in increasing the population, we must bear in mind that population aging is inevitable.”

Ukrainian Mirage 2000-5F Shoots Down Banderol Missile With Cannon for First Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:33:36 UTC
19:33:36 KST

A French Mirage 2000-5F fighter jet has, for the first time in history, shot down a Russian S8000 Banderol small-sized cruise missile using its aircraft cannon.
France transferred aircraft of this type to Ukraine from the stocks of its Air and Space Force in 2025, according to French Aid to Europe.
The aircraft’s primary cannon armament consists of two 30 mm DEFA 554 automatic aircraft cannons, which are integrated into the fuselage.
The fighter carries 125 rounds of ammunition for each cannon, with a rate of fire of up to 1,800 rounds per minute. The guns use 30×113 mm high-explosive fragmentation and armor-piercing incendiary ammunition, with a muzzle velocity of approximately 815 m/s.
The S8000 Banderol was developed by the Russian company Kronstadt. Its maximum speed is 620–650 km/h, while its cruising speed is 520–560 km/h.
The missile is powered by a Chinese-made Swiwin turbojet engine weighing 8.5 kg. At a maximum rotational speed of 65,000 rpm, the engine produces up to 81.6 kgf of thrust. With these engine characteristics, the missile’s stated range is up to 500 km.
The missile is equipped with an OFBC-150 high-explosive warhead with a total mass of 114.3 kg, of which 49.5 kg is explosive filler.

BRUSSELS, Belgium — Ukraine received 2.9 billion euros ($3.3 billion) from the European Union on Oct. 2, after Kyiv passed several key reforms.
"As Ukraine defends itself against Russia's aggression, it also continues to deliver comprehensive reforms under the Ukraine Plan," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in a press statement.
The payment was greenlit by the EU on Sept. 23.
"European solidarity means concrete support. Europe will stand by Ukraine's side for as long as it takes," von der Leyen said.
"This is very timely support, which will help ensure Ukraine's macro-financial stability and strengthen our defense capabilities," said President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Kyiv reaffirmed that it would carry out previously agreed-upon reforms, and Brussels clarified the amount of support available.

Among the approved reforms were changes to judges' integrity declarations, the appointment of a new electricity market operator, a plan to address the gender pay gap, and laws to improve traffic safety.
More reforms are expected to be passed when the parliament reconvenes on Oct. 12, which could unlock some of the more than 20 billion euros ($23 billion) of financial support available for 2026.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi stressed that "the need for funding remains critical."
"We are speeding up the adoption of all government decisions as much as possible. We are also working with the parliament to pass the necessary bills as quickly as possible."

DiscoverEU applications now open: Thousands of free travel passes for young Europeans up for grabs

Applications for the scheme are open until 15 October, giving eligible young Europeans the chance to explore the continent by train and other sustainable transport, with discounts on accommodation, culture and more.
If you’re 18 years old, living in an EU or Erasmus+ country, and are keen to explore Europe, you may be able to do just that – for no cost.
Applications are now open for the European Union’s DiscoverEU scheme, which offers more than 40,000 free travel passes for young Europeans. The application process will close at midday Brussels time (CET) on 15 October 2026 and you can apply at youth.europa.eu.
Here’s everything you need to know about the DiscoverEU programme.
Thousands of passes for free travel will be awarded
If you were born between 1 January 2008 and 31 December 2008, and are a citizen or resident of the EU, Overseas Countries and Territories associated with the EU or third countries associated with the Erasmus+ programme, including Iceland and Türkiye, you’re able to apply to the scheme
If selected, you’ll receive a travel pass for the most environmentally friendly means of transport, including trains.
You'll be able to travel for up to seven days within a one-month period, any time between 1 March 2027 and 31 May 2028.
Lucky passholders will also receive a DiscoverEU discount card, which will offer numerous discounts on accommodation, culture, sports, local transport, and other services, making trips significantly more affordable.
If you’re keen to travel with friends, that’s doable, too. If a group submits the application together, they may all be given the chance to travel for free.
Where could your journey take you?
The DiscoverEU Culture Route is a pre-planned itinerary covering destinations across Europe, with stops for everything from architecture, music and fine art to theatre, fashion, folk art and local food.
Some of the cities featured have received European Commission recognition, including Cork in Ireland and Valletta in Malta, both named European Capitals of Culture.
Others, such as Lyon in France, have been recognised for their efforts to improve accessibility for everyone, regardless of age, ability or mobility.
Young travellers can also use DiscoverEU as a starting point for planning their own routes and exploring destinations that interest them.

Police seize over 250 tons of narcotics since March

Unknown Publisher

19:32:04 KST

Police seize over 250 tons of narcotics since March
TEHRAN – The Iranian anti-narcotics police have seized more than 250 tons of narcotics in the first six months of the current Iranian year (started on March 21), indicating a 20 percent increase compared to the same period last year.
The anti-narcotics police have disbanded 780 drug trafficking gangs across the country, IRNA quoted, Iraj Kakavand, the head of anti-narcotics police, as saying.
The official made the remarks at a press conference in Tehran on the occasion of the ‘national law enforcement week’, which is being held from October 2 to 8, under the theme ‘committed police, mobilized people, proud Iran’.
Over 7,000 smugglers were arrested and six were killed, more than 330 weapons, and 8,000 vehicles were confiscated, he added.
Monitoring social media, the police managed to arrest 196 individuals, seize over 460 kilograms of narcotics, more than 420,000 pills containing illicit drugs, and dismantle 14 gangs operating online, Kakavand further noted.
Supporting Iran’s counter-narcotics work pays off beyond its borders: UNODC
In August, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) released a report, emphasizing the need to support Iran in the battle against narcotics.
Supporting Iran’s counternarcotics work pays off beyond its borders, the report highlighted, saying it keeps drugs from reaching other regions, cuts into the money that funds the organized crime and supports public health by slowing the spread of addictive synthetic substances.
The main seizure of methamphetamine in and around Middle East and South-East Asia over the past few years has been reported in Iran, according to the report which was published on Thursday.
Iranian seizure of methamphetamine increased from 30,393 kilos in 2022 to 40,453 kilos in 2025, placing the country at the forefront of the fight against drugs trafficking.
In the first quarter of 2026 alone, Iranian authorities have intercepted 3,663 kilograms of methamphetamines destined for Europe and the Persian Gulf.
These weren’t just street-level busts. These were five intelligence-led operations targeting industrial-scale shipments originating in Afghanistan, evidence that trafficking networks in the region are shifting toward synthetic drugs.
While international attention has primarily focused on the vast region’s declining opium production, advanced criminal drug trafficking networks have successfully shifted toward manufacturing and exporting synthetic drugs such as methamphetamine, commonly known as meth. West Asia is now the epicenter of a synthetic drug boom.
Iran is strategically positioned along the “Afghanistan-West Asia corridor,” which serves as the primary trafficking route for these illicit commodities. The clear signal from Tehran is that these substantial shipments are being intercepted before they can reach international markets. Yet, sustained success will require enhanced international cooperation and support.
Each interception reduces the illicit financial flows that fund organized crime and slows the spread of synthetic drugs into new markets. These shipments are not merely statistics. Each seizure disrupts a supply chain that would otherwise put methamphetamine on the streets of Europe and the Persian Gulf, while cutting into the earnings of organized criminal networks.
Through its Country Partnership Programme as well as the Cooperation Framework with the Islamic Republic of Iran, UNODC supports the country efforts in advancing border technology with procurement of detection scanners, strengthening labs forensic capabilities in identify new synthetic compounds as well as regional intelligence sharing.
Sustained donor investment is critical to prevent this route from becoming a gateway for synthetic drugs. However, the scale of the challenge demands more than financial contributions—it requires a collective and sustainable approach by the international community. By supporting UNODC’s work in Iran, donor nations are investing in regional stability and international security, while also protecting their own borders from the flow of illicit substances.

Fact check: What's going on with Spain's 'Maricarmen' housing protests?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:30:25 UTC
19:30:25 KST

Spanish protests against the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen have led to misleading claims about Spain's housing activists and the wider rental crisis.
Thousands of people are protesting across Spain after authorities evicted Maricarmen Abascal from her home in Madrid.
Maricarmen, who is 87 years old, had been living there for over 70 years. Images of police forcibly removing her from the flat on a stretcher have now turned the legal dispute into a symbolic fight for housing activists.
The protesters marched through Madrid, camped out in Puerta del Sol, and organised demonstrations in other Spanish cities.
They are using Maricarmen's case to protest the wider housing crisis: rising rents and a shortage of affordable homes, which are fuelling fears that tenants can no longer afford to stay in major cities.
The situation has become a very politicised debate, fuelling several false, misleading, and selectively edited claims.
A legal decision
One of the most prominent claims circulating online is that Maricarmen’s eviction was "illegal". This is false: courts authorised the eviction after a years-long dispute over a protected rental contract dating back to the 1950s. It was carried out under a valid court order, despite the backlash it received.
Maricarmen's father originally held the lease, which later passed to her mother and then to Maricarmen herself. The courts ruled that this second transfer could continue for only two years unless Maricarmen had a recognised disability above 65%; authorities recognised hers at 50%.
Spain's Supreme Court upheld the owner’s position, which meant the old, protected tenancy had legally expired and the company could recover the flat. The eviction was therefore lawful.
The goal of the protests
So, contrary to what some misleading headlines imply, protesters are not arguing whether the eviction was lawful, but whether it was fair.
This is partly because, under Francisco Franco’s dictatorship laws, married women could not legally sign financial contracts or property leases independently.
Maricarmen's mother could inherit the lease only by subrogation upon her husband's death. Had she been a co-owner or co-signer from the start, Maricarmen's inheritance of the lease would have counted as the first subrogation, legally protecting her right to stay in the home for life.
Protesters also point out that Maricarmen is 87, has lived in the property for more than seven decades, and continued paying her protected rent.
After the old tenancy ended, property management company Urbagestión proposed a rent of around €1,650 a month, far above the roughly €440 to €500 she had previously paid. This is higher than her monthly pension of around €1,350, therefore forcing a vulnerable long-term tenant out because she cannot afford the new rent.
Protesters are asking for stronger protections against evictions of vulnerable tenants, longer or automatically renewed rental contracts, and tighter limits on rent increases.
Some groups also want tougher rules on speculative housing practices and greater public intervention in the rental market. They are now pressing parliament to approve new protections for vulnerable tenants and longer lease terms.
Other false and misleading claims
Another disputed claim going around online is that the Sindicato de Inquilinas, Spain's main union for tenants, prevented Maricarmen from reaching an agreement with the owner before the eviction.
Urbagestión says the union made it hard to contact Maricarmen directly, while Maricarmen’s lawyer says the opposite: that the company had refused repeated attempts to negotiate.
Urbagestión has also accused people involved in the dispute of coercion, extortion and hacking phones and email accounts. However, the company did not provide evidence for these claims in reporting reviewed by fact-checkers like Spain's Maldita.es.
Another misleading assertion comes from a shortened video of Maricarmen herself. In the clip, she appears to blame left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez specifically for her situation, but the full interview adds more names: she also criticises Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso, Madrid mayor José Luis Martínez-Almeida (both members of the right-wing Popular Party) and Urbagestión itself. The clip therefore uses a genuine quote but removes the wider context of her answer.
A separate false claim involved two protesters called "Irene and Pablo" who spoke to elDiario.es at a protest camp at the Puerta del Sol square in Madrid. Some social-media users suggested they were Pablo Iglesias, former leader of far-left party Podemos, and MEP Irene Montero, from the same party.
However, a quick look at the article itself shows us that they are actually a different 28-year-old woman and 37-year-old man, with no indication that they were the politicians in question.
The next steps
Maricarmen has now accepted an agreement that will allow her to return to the apartment once she leaves hospital. Under the new arrangement, she will pay roughly the same as her previous rent, around €500 a month, capped at 30% of her income. The agreement creates a new tenancy; it does not overturn the court ruling that ended her old, protected lease.
Meanwhile, Spain's government has proposed measures that would extend some eviction protections and lengthen rental contracts, but parliament still needs to approve them. Protesters are therefore continuing their campaign and pushing politicians to adopt those measures while demanding broader reforms to Spain's housing system.
