Tehran to host 2nd national ‘youth, innovation, health technology festival’
TEHRAN –The second national youth, innovation, and health technology festival, focusing on artificial intelligence (AI) in the health sector, is scheduled to be held from October 14 to 16 in Tehran.
Hosted by Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, the festival will be centered around ‘AI and machine learning in health’, ‘digital health and telemedicine’, ‘emerging technologies in rehabilitation’, ‘biotechnology, regenerative medicine, and pharmaceuticals’, ‘law and ethics in digital health’, ‘medical devices’, ‘nutrition and the food industry’, ‘psychology and psychotherapy’, and ‘environmental health’, ISNA reported.
The event provides a great platform for students from schools and universities, innovators, technologists, and experts in health sectors, as well as researchers to showcase their innovative ideas. It will also contribute to networking between owners of the innovative ideas, experts, and specialized organizations, paving the way for supporting and implementing these ideas.
The participants can also focus on ways to make health services more intelligent, enhance the quality of healthcare, develop digital tools, and develop innovative ideas to address challenges faced by the healthcare system.
Opportunities, challenges of digital health in Iran
Modern communication technologies have fundamentally changed people’s lifestyles, social interactions, and access to information, with the health sector going through digital transformation, being no exception.
The emergence of tools such as health applications, telemedicine, electronic health records, and online health platforms has made digital health an important part of the health system. Digital health provides advantages, but it also brings challenges.
Digital health refers to the use of information and communication technologies to promote health, improve access to health services, and enhance the quality of health care. Bridging the distance between the patient and the service provider, digital health makes it easier for different groups in society to receive health services.
It plays a pivotal role in raising public awareness, preventing diseases, and improving health-oriented behaviours.
Despite these benefits, digital health faces some challenges. The most important one is the digital gap, which refers to inequality in accessing and using communication technologies. The gap can be caused by different reasons such as income, place of residence, age, and literacy level.
Researchers at Tehran’s Allameh Tabatabaei University have studied digital health in the country to identify its strengths, shortages, opportunities, and threats, ISNA reported.
 
The research findings show that digital health in Iran has significant strengths, including national healthcare platforms, the growing use of artificial intelligence tools in healthcare services, and online healthcare services.
Meanwhile, a lack of a comprehensive legal framework for health data protection, integration among digital platforms, digital literacy, and communication infrastructure, as well as structural resistance to technological change, are among the main weaknesses, which highlights that digital health needs both new technologies and reforms in structures and laws.
To realize the healthcare system transformation goal, the health ministry has developed eight projects with a focus on smart e-health using artificial intelligence.
The projects include improving health literacy and self-care, designing a smart referral system, launching a national health observatory, changing health data into operational knowledge, managing the healthcare supply chain of subsidized medicines using AI, establishing a diagnosis-related groups (DRG) payment system, designing a productive smart hospital, and integrating online insurance processes.

Your Driverless Cab Is Spying on You
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

One afternoon this past summer, a self-driving Waymo pulled into a parking lot in San Mateo County, California, and stayed there until the police arrived. Local cops had gotten a 911 call from Waymo staffers—humans, it should be said—who were viewing the car’s passengers through cameras installed inside the vehicle. It looked like two teens were shooting a black handgun out the window of the vehicle, playing with it and drinking between shots, a police report said.
The story has a happy(ish) ending: The gun was shooting water-filled Orbeez, not bullets. But the incident drew attention to Waymo’s surveillance system. The cars are equipped with automated tech that can flag the presence of a firearm inside, the company said.
The outsides of self-driving cars are studded with cameras, which help them “see” the world around them. (Most also use other sensors, including radar and lidar.) Less appreciated are the cameras inside the vehicles, which companies say are essential to keeping riders safe and enforcing their rules. Earlier this year, Waymo said it used its cabin cameras to do both after some California passengers, many in their twenties or older, reported that Waymo employees suddenly took over the vehicles’ intercoms mid-ride to make sure they were old enough to ride on their own. (One 35-year-old told WIRED he thought his backpack sent up red flags.)
Still, robotaxi privacy policies can be broad. They suggest that footage captured inside vehicles can be used for many innocuous and commonsense reasons—to check cleanliness between rides, to detect lost items—but also to improve their products or services. These catch-all terms could cover many uses. Experts say that in the US, few clear rules govern this sort of surveillance, especially because riders often must agree to lengthy “terms of service” printed in minute fonts before they use ride-hailing apps. That leaves riders to trust that the companies are handling their information responsibly.
“We are being essentially abandoned by our lawmakers when it comes to consumer privacy and what companies can do with information after they’ve collected it,” says Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, where he works on surveillance and policing issues. His advice? “Just because you’re alone in the car doesn’t mean you’re alone in the car. You should behave as if there’s a jumpy person in the front seat.”
In general, robotaxi companies including Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla say that human staff view interior cameras only when needed. All say personal data, including recordings, may be sent to law enforcement or regulators. (A Waymo support page says that government agencies seeking data “are directed to follow valid legal processes in making such request.”)
But that doesn’t mean the interior cameras aren’t on and working. Waymo spokesperson Julia Ilina says the company uses “automated technology to support our teams in identifying potential violations.” A 2025 patent held by Waymo describes a system in which vehicles’ interior camera systems conduct automated "predetermined ride checklists” before, during, and after rides. (Ilina did not say whether that system is in use.)
Zoox’s website says its interior cameras “record the entirety of your ride.” This sort of personal data can be used to help operate rides, but also to develop and improve Zoox’s product. The company—owned by Amazon—says it might record conversations between riders and its support employees, but that it doesn’t save recordings. Zoox spokesperson
Whitney Jencks said the company had nothing more specific to share about its privacy policies.
Online documents for Tesla’s Robotaxi service say a green indicator shows up on the vehicle’s central touchscreen when the camera is activated. Riders can opt in to sharing in-cabin video and audio with the company through a toggle menu in the “data and privacy” section of its app. The documents also say riders in the company’s “early access” program automatically opt in to data sharing. The company didn’t respond to questions for this story, including whether that early access program has technically concluded. The company opened its Robotaxi app to the public in a handful of Texas and Florida cities in early September.
Cameras inside robotaxis make plenty of sense. “You need some kind of check on what people do in a car with no driver,” says Justin Brookman, who directs technology policy at Consumer Reports. “People are going to have sex in Waymos if there are no cameras.” (Media reports suggest that the cameras don’t always stop them.)
But the law hasn’t yet fully contemplated what companies should be able to see, save, and use. “These vehicles are relatively new, so there are no expectations around what’s appropriate,” Brookman says. “There should be some check in place.”
Auto companies don’t have the best record on data privacy.
In 2023, Reuters reported that groups of Tesla employees had, over several years, shared sensitive videos and images captured by owners’ cars. Shared recordings reportedly included a video of a man approaching a car while naked, and a violent collision between a car and a child on a bike. Tesla boasts that its years-deep repository of data from personal vehicles gives it an edge in developing autonomous vehicle software, and its privacy policy says camera recordings are kept anonymous. But former employees told Reuters that the system easily revealed where the images were recorded, which could have allowed them to link recordings to specific owners’ garages or driveways.
Earlier this year, General Motors paid California motorists nearly $13 million in penalties after the company was found to have sold driving data to brokers and eventually insurers without their consent.
“My big concern is that automakers love to collect data,” Guariglia says. “With autonomous vehicles, there’s even more data to collect. And the more data they collect, the more they’re going to find reasons to sell it.”
In the meantime, his privacy-related advice? Behave.

Three CGTP unions have called a strike for Friday, disrupting schools, public services, councils and rubbish collection. An easyJet cabin crew walkout is also causing flight delays nationwide.
More than 350,000 public administration workers are covered by the strikes called by three CGTP-affiliated unions for this Friday in Portugal. The biggest effects are being felt in education, with dozens of schools closing their doors due to a lack of staff.
"We have schools closed from the north to the south of the country, in the Azores and Madeira as well," explained Sebastião Santana, speaking to TVI. Outside the Francisco Arruda School in Lisbon, which kept its gates shut this morning, the coordinator of the Common Front highlighted the "strong turnout" for the protest.
The union leader was speaking at the Francisco Arruda School in Lisbon, which did not open because of the 24-hour stoppage.
The protest was called by the National Federation of Public and Social Service Workers' Unions (FNSTFPS), the National Union of Local and Regional Administration Workers, Public Companies, Concessionaires and Related Entities (STAL) and the Lisbon Municipal Workers' Union (STML), covering operational assistants, technical assistants and senior technicians.
As well as school closures, the strike may also cause disruptions to social security services, registry and notary offices, the justice system and rubbish collection.
The walkout may also have some impact on local health units and other bodies under the Ministry of Health.
Dozens of people have gathered in Lisbon for a march between Praça da Figueira and the Ministry of Finance.
The unions are calling for the immediate upgrading of these professionals' career structures.
EasyJet: union reports strong support and hundreds of flights cancelled
easyJet cabin crew launched a five-day protest action on Friday, with the strike continuing until Tuesday. The National Union of Civil Aviation Flight Personnel (SNPVAC) reports strong participation and expects 80% of flights to be cancelled during the five days of stoppage.
Speaking to the Lusa news agency, SNPVAC president Ricardo Penarroias said that 443 flights have already been cancelled for the coming days at Lisbon, Porto and Faro airports.
Also speaking to Lusa, an official easyJet source said it expects to operate around 55% of its schedule during the strike period, through minimum services and flights operated from other European bases.
"The company will carry out the minimum services, which are compulsory, and the other flights it has not cancelled (...) are flights it will operate illegally," said the union president.
The workers' demands include more stable rosters, pay progression based on seniority and the conditions proposed as part of the negotiations for the company agreement.
A second stoppage has been scheduled for 19 to 23 December.

Tories warn Burnham’s EU ‘pandering’ will shred post-Brexit trade deals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:28:42 UTC
19:28:42 KST

Tories warn Burnham’s EU ‘pandering’ will shred post-Brexit trade deals
Three former ministers tell POLITICO of “grave consequences” if the U.K. moves closer to the EU under prime minister’s bid for a revamped relationship.
LONDON — The architects of Britain's first post-Brexit trade deals have warned that the country's independent trade policy is under threat after Andy Burnham pledged a major review of its relationship with the EU.
Their intervention marks the latest salvo in a political fightback against Burnham's EU policy as the Conservative Party conference gets underway in Birmingham this weekend.
Burnham this week vowed to discuss a revamped relationship with Europe, including rejoining the EU's customs union, moving closer the bloc's single market — or even pushing to outright rejoin the bloc. It marks a fundamental shift from a Labour Party that has previously ruled out all three.
Advertisement
Customs union membership — a popular option among some members of Burnham’s Cabinet — would ease trade between the U.K. and its largest trading partner, but require Britain to sacrifice the trade deals it has struck since leaving the bloc six years ago.
Greg Hands, who served as trade minister four times between 2016 to 2024 under Conservative governments, said that all options presented “grave consequences for Britain's independent trade policy.”
“Depending exactly on what is agreed, it is likely to invalidate or make very difficult most — if not all — of those existing trade agreements, or many of those existing trade agreements,” he said.
Since Brexit, the U.K. has negotiated free trade deals with nations including Australia, New Zealand, Japan and — more recently — the Asia Pacific trading bloc CPTPP, India, the Gulf states, as well as upgraded deals with South Korea and Switzerland.
Although the U.K. could technically copy-and paste EU versions of trade deals, Hands warned that the terms might not be so favorable, highlighting that the U.K.-Japan deal he had helped to negotiate “has got much more liberal rules on data” than the EU equivalent.
As a non-EU member, the U.K. would also surrender its ability to negotiate the terms of any new trade deals, Hands argued. “Why would the EU prioritize the U.K., which is not a paying member of the EU, over paying full members of the EU when it does trade agreements?”
Advertisement
But the issue goes further than free trade agreements, he said, pointing out that entering a customs union with the EU would affect the U.K.’s global tariff — the independent system of taxes and duty rates applied to goods imported from other countries. This would be a “huge diminution of the U.K.'s influence in the world to align or take the EU's customs tariff,” Hands added.
Moreover, by signing up to a customs union, the U.K. would also lose its ability to erect its own trade defenses and be forced to implement EU measures like tariffs on steel and electric vehicles, Hands warned.
He also cautioned that closer alignment could complicate relations with the U.S., which has been critical of U.K. ambitions for closer alignment with the EU. “The U.S. is our single largest bilateral trading partner and I don’t think it would be in the U.K.’s interest to mess up that relationship.”
End of CPTPP membership
Liam Fox, a self-proclaimed “staunch euroskeptic” who served as trade secretary in the immediate aftermath of the referendum, between 2016 and 2019, said rejoining the EU or customs union would “mean an end to Britain’s independent trade policy and any strategy influence we have from membership of organizations such as [the Asia-Pacific trade bloc] CPTPP.”
“This vague language from Andy Burnham is all about keeping the Labour left quiet whatever the consequences,” Fox added. “Rejoining the EU would mean being part of Schengen with free movement of people and adoption of the Euro. If that is what Andy Burnham wants, let him make the case for it, stop his mealy-mouthed pandering to his own party and start acting like a real prime minister.”
A third former Tory trade minister — granted anonymity to speak frankly — told MTUK the risks to Britain’s new trade deals was “real” and would “undermine new relationships with some of the fastest growing middle-class economies in the world.”
“As the mature EU markets continue to be a smaller part of U.K. export opportunities, the prime minister should be focusing on supporting U.K. businesses to win export contracts where huge new markets exist,” the former minister argued.

Record numbers going hungry in Yemen amid escalating conflict, WFP says

Three in four families go hungry in parts of Yemen from new fighting
GENEVA, Oct 2 - Three-in-four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry from the "absolutely devastating" impact of a surge in fighting, which has displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said on Friday.
Yemen is experiencing the most serious escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthi group since a UN-brokered truce largely halted cross-border attacks in 2022. The renewed conflict could reshape control in Yemen, with implications for Red Sea shipping lanes.
Within just a few weeks, the fighting has driven the share of households without sufficient food to 74% in government-controlled areas accessible to WFP, the UN hunger body's Assistant Executive Director for Programme Operations told reporters in Geneva. The total population of government-held areas is estimated at around 10 million people.
“The effect of this latest flare-up of insecurity on the food security situation threatens to be absolutely devastating,” Hollingworth told reporters in Geneva via video link from Rome.
The Houthis, who already control most of northern Yemen including the capital Sanaa, seized the country's entire Red Sea coast last month from Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government, based in the southern port of Aden.
Displaced families are arriving outside Aden and around the mountain city of Taiz without any water or food, as many had to leave everything behind, WFP said.
Prices of basic food staples such as wheat flour and vegetable oil are rising in a country that imports around 90% of its food.
“We are looking at a hunger crisis that is going to grow as it persists,” Hollingworth said, adding that frontline areas like Taiz were increasingly hard to access due to the fighting.
WFP said it was scaling up its response but unless it gets around $109 million in funding within a few weeks it will run out of food stocks and money to help the 152,000 newly displaced persons inside the country, as well as the 1.4 million people it is already supporting.
Hollingworth also pointed to the potential ripple effects of disruption to two major chokepoints in the Middle East: the Bab el-Mandeb Strait near Yemen at the mouth of the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula.
That, as well as disruption in the Black Sea due to the Ukraine-Russia conflict, risk driving up food and fuel prices and deepening food insecurity globally.
A new analysis published by UN Women on Friday said an additional 11.7 million women and girls across 28 countries including Yemen, Sudan and Lebanon could face food insecurity by the end of the year, due to escalation in the Middle East and disruption to the Strait of Hormuz. REUTERS

Researchers create "mini brains" to advance MS research
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:27:18 CST
19:27:18 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Researchers from Australia and New Zealand have developed 3D "mini brains" that they hope will speed up the search for treatments for multiple sclerosis (MS), an autoimmune condition affecting almost three million people worldwide.
The research team used reprogrammed adult stem cells to engineer a human-like central nervous system cell model about the size of a grain of rice, according to a statement released Friday by Australia's Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health.
The "mini brains" cell model provides a detailed cellular view of myelin destruction and regeneration in human cells, and would allow researchers to see drugs working in near-real time on human cells, according to the study published in Nature Neuroscience.
Myelin is a fatty sheath that covers and protects nerve fibers and allows messages, via electrical impulses, to travel quickly around the brain, spinal cord and body. In MS, the immune system mistakenly attacks myelin, causing nerve damage and disability, researchers said, adding that existing MS medications can only treat symptoms and slow progression, with no therapies currently available to repair the damage.
The study's senior author Associate Professor Samantha Barton of the Florey Institute said the cell model, which took more than six years to develop, allows researchers to introduce immune cells to trigger injury similar to MS and study myelin repair.
"This model can help researchers better understand what drives myelin damage and repair in MS and it also gives us a new platform to screen drugs that protect or restore myelin," Barton said. ■

Passenger ticket pre-sales show that Friday's popular departure cities include Beijing, Guangzhou, Shanghai, Chengdu, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou and Nanjing, while popular arrival cities include Beijing, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Hangzhou, Shanghai, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou, Nanjing and Changsha.

The China Railway Hohhot Group has added 11 multiple-unit trains on the Baotou-Wuhai section of the Baotou-Yinchuan high-speed railway.
The China Railway Wuhan Group, tapping the newly opened Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway, has launched a promotion campaign with local governments in Yichang and Xingshan, offering passengers exclusive discounts at scenic spots, hotels and homestays with their train tickets.

Specifically, railway passenger trips reached 25.204 million, up 9 percent year on year; road passenger trips stood at 300.36 million, down 2.8 percent; waterway passenger trips totaled 1.416 million, up 7.2 percent; and civil aviation passenger trips came in at 2.515 million, up 0.5 percent, according to the ministry.
China's total cross-regional passenger trips are expected to reach 308.19 million on Oct. 2, up 2.1 percent year on year, the ministry added.

"World's supermarket" Yiwu gets robot security guards
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:26:34 CST
19:26:34 KST

HANGZHOU, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- As the Yiwu International Trade Market falls quiet at 10 p.m., a legion of four-legged robots step out of automatically opening doors to begin their nightly patrol.
Since last month, the sprawling market in Yiwu, a major foreign trade hub in east China's Zhejiang Province, has started using 16 robot dogs as its new "security guards," according to the market's management.
As the world's largest small commodities market, the Yiwu International Trade Market features a labyrinth of crisscrossing aisles and tens of thousands of stalls packed into an operational area of over 6.4 million square meters. Patrolling a complex of this scale has been a grueling task, at least for humans.
"The robots never get tired. When their batteries run low, they automatically return to their docking stations to recharge," said Zhu Weijie with the market's management company.
It takes a quadruped robot 1.5 hours to patrol an area that used to take human patrollers 2.5 hours to cover, Zhu said, also praising the robots' ability to "leap over steps, navigate through complex passageways and reach into blind spots that are difficult for humans to inspect."
Equipped with infrared thermal imaging devices and high-definition cameras, the robots help staff monitor crowd flow during daytime patrols. At night, they can detect abnormal heat sources such as fires or intruders.
"Beyond the novelty, it truly feels like an added layer of security," Xu Yan, a merchant at the market, remarked on the newly-employed robot security guards.
Yiwu is known as the place where the world buys small goods. In 2025, the city's foreign trade value hit 836.5 billion yuan (about 124 billion U.S. dollars), and its export value ranked first among Chinese county-level regions.
The market management said they would continue to use robotic patrols to train recognition algorithms and upgrade the equipment, while also improving the coordination between the robots and security personnel.
China has been accelerating the deployment of robots in real-world settings, especially for repetitive, strenuous and high-risk tasks where human labor is in short supply.
Earlier this year, Chinese authorities jointly launched a special action plan for real-scene training of humanoid robots and embodied AI, aiming to identify more than 100 high-value application scenarios.
Chinese-developed quadruped robots accounted for nearly 70 percent of global sales in the first half of 2026, according to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. ■

Radev Defends Shipka Monument Renovation in Parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:25:42 UTC
19:25:42 KST

Prime Minister Rumen Radev said in Parliament that the Shipka Freedom Monument is a sacred symbol of the Bulgarian nation and that its renovation is necessary to preserve it for future generations.
Radev rejected allegations that the monument was being improperly dismantled and said the restoration would leave its appearance unchanged. He made the remarks while answering a parliamentary question about the renovation.
"There are 1,000 pages of documentation, material you ought to be familiar with, as it is publicly available. It was prepared by Bulgarian architects, designers, and builders, ensuring the monument will be restored to its exact original state, preserving the legacy left for those who follow," Radev said.
He said the monument had become dangerous, with areas cordoned off, stones falling, mortar joints disappearing and moisture penetrating its interior, while the exhibition was also being damaged. Radev said the government had decided to assume the risk of carrying out the repairs to ensure that the monument would remain for future generations.
The government and the Revival parliamentary group have clashed over the Shipka renovation, with the party questioning the way the work is being carried out and who should finance it. Radev said the monument belongs to all Bulgarians and argued that claims it was being “gutted” were speculative.
"Shipka is not in the best condition, and you know that very well. Weather conditions have been extremely harsh in recent years; the steps have shifted, and there are gaps and moisture issues. Until now, no one cared about the monument, and no one provided any funding for it. The monument's appearance after the renovation will remain exactly the same," the prime minister said.
Radev stressed that his government had initiated the repair project with the aim of preserving the monument for future generations.
Revival MP Angel Yanchev responded that the monument’s staircases were not covered by the renovation project and called on the government to abandon the plan.
Radev said Culture Minister Evtim Miloshev had inspected the Shipka Monument and, together with the museum director, had decided that progress reports on the renovation would be submitted every ten days.
BTA reported additional details from Dr. Chavdar Angelov, director of the Shipka-Buzludzha National Park-Museum. Angelov said the reinforcement work would not affect the monument’s structural integrity and that its appearance would be exactly the same after the renovation.
He said the conservation and restoration project for the Monument of Freedom on Shipka Peak was progressing according to schedule. Construction and installation work is planned to take 642 calendar days, with the timetable spread from April 1 to October 31 over three consecutive years because of the extreme weather conditions typical of the Shipka Pass area.
Work began on September 3 and is currently being carried out six days a week. Angelov said the aim was to use the remaining period this year when work at the site can be performed.
He also explained the removal of the stairs leading to the monument’s northern entrance. Under the approved project scheme, the cladding slabs and steps were removed, numbered, arranged and stored within the construction site area on the monument’s western and southern sides.
The staircase is being dismantled so a new foundation can be poured before the structure is rebuilt. Angelov said the decision was based on two considerations: the staircase was in poor condition, and its presence prevented full access to the northern base of the monument.
Assessments showed that the cladding had been installed over a stone foundation that had settled over the years, causing the steps to sag and creating gaps between the individual cladding elements. The staircase also substantially conceals the northern base of the monument, which needs to be fully exposed so its stone masonry can be treated under the approved conservation and restoration methodology.
Angelov said a stone-concrete foundation would be poured after restoration of the northern façade base, matching the original staircase in both proportions and volume, before the cladding slabs were returned to their original positions.

Mathematicians Name 50 of the Highest-Stakes Problems in Math
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:24:33 UTC
19:24:33 KST

Mathematicians love to collect elegant, profound questions that defy proof: the longer the holdout, the better. And one day in June, groups from around the world gathered to do just that. The goal was a new list of 50 high-stakes questions with an important caveat: there had to be a way to automatically check solutions to the problems. Workshops took place in six cities: London, Toronto, Los Angeles, New York City, Berkeley, Calif., and Cambridge, Mass.
That morning Yang-Hui He, a mathematician at the London Institute for Mathematical Sciences, was accompanied by a very young guest. His son was on school break, so He brought him along to the workshop. The two entered a room full of mathematicians who were well supplied with lunch, snacks, and coffee and got to work. Under the watchful eye of his cake-munching son, He collaborated with others to submit three problems that touched on fields from knot theory to algebra, topology and number theory. “There’s a big culture in mathematics, which is solving open conjectures,” He says. “Many people get Fields Medals because they solve open conjectures. This is very big.”
The event was held at the request of Epoch AI, an organization that benchmarks the progress of artificial intelligence systems. Epoch AI senior researcher Greg Burnham says the problems cover a broad spectrum of topics. Lately AI models from various companies have been cutting through a large swath of math’s biggest challenges. Earlier this month, for instance, OpenAI claimed a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the towering Millennium Prize Problems.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
As of late September, a few of the problems from the new list have been solved, including some landmark ones. The official list still remains peppered with unsolved problems, although OpenAI recently announced that its unreleased internal AI model has solved more than 100 open questions. “My guess is that it likely contains at least a few [of these],” Burnham says.
Here are a few of the critical problems the mathematicians identified.
The Sum of Three Cubes
Status: Open Mathematicians would like to find integer solutions to polynomial equations that contain three different cubes. “It’s strongly suspected that there are integer solutions to the equation x3 + y3 + z3 = 114,” Burnham says. “But it’s suspected that the smallest solutions have something like 30 digits in them.”
In 2020, Andrew Booker of the University of Bristol and Andrew Sutherland of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology settled the case for when the sum of x3 + y3 + z3 totals 42. Their efforts consumed 1.3 million computing hours, distributed across volunteer home computers. The next total is 114. Burnham estimated that the same strategy for 114 would cost perhaps $100 million or more, making such a blunt approach unrealistic. Checking the solution simply requires evaluating the equation with the new values.
Lo Apéry-Style Irrationality Proof
Status: Rumors swirl that this has been solved
Irrational numbers are decimals that can’t be rewritten as a fraction of two integers. Pi and √2 are familiar examples. Although the idea is simple, proving that a number is irrational is notoriously difficult—it took two millennia to prove that pi was irrational.
In 1978 the eccentric French mathematician Roger Apéry proved that a number known as zeta(3) was irrational. The zeta numbers originate from Riemann’s famed zeta function, which describes intriguing statistical patterns in the arrangement of the prime numbers. Apéry’s discovery has shaped modern number theory.
Evaluating the zeta function at 3 gives the sum of the series 1⁄n3: 13 + 1⁄23 + 1⁄33 + 1⁄43+ .... The idea that this series should sum to an irrational number might be come as a surprise, but centuries ago Euler proved that all the even values of the zeta function are tied to powers of pi, making them irrational. This led mathematicians to suspect that the odd values were also likely irrational.
To find the proof for zeta(3), Apéry sandwiched the function between two infinite series that converged at just the right speed to ensure zeta(3) must be irrational. Mathematicians were baffled: How did he find the two series? Frustratingly, Apéry replied that he found them in a flower pot. The mystery of how he located them remains outstanding today. If anyone can reconstruct Apéry’s reasoning, the odd values of zeta may finally be proven irrational.
“A credible solution to Apéry-style irrationality—for one of the relevant numbers, the one called zeta(5) —has been circulating,” Burnham says.
The Lonely Runner Conjecture
Status: Open
Like the previous two problems, the “lonely runner conjecture” seems simple but has deep ties to many fields. On a circular track, place a group of runners, all of whom run at unique, constant speeds. The lonely runner conjecture predicts that, at some point, a runner will be maximally distant from all the other runners—the saddest, loneliest phase of the race. Mathematicians want to rescue this runner with a counterexample: some number and combination of speeds that will break the pattern. The problem has stood since 1967.
The Jones Unknot Conjecture
Status: Open
Take a tangled loop of string. Can you tell whether it’s truly knotted or just a circle in disguise?
In 1984 the late mathematician Vaughan Jones introduced a new way to assign polynomials to knots, thereby tangling the two fields together. He later won a Fields Medal for the discovery. If two knots have different Jones polynomials, they’re different knots. But the reverse doesn’t hold—different knots might be linked to the same polynomial. In fact, mathematicians already know that knots of two or more links have ambiguous polynomials. But what about the simplest knot, a circle? In knot theory, a circle is known as an “unknot” and has the trivial Jones polynomial 1. Mathematicians strongly suspect that there is a genuinely knotty loop that also has a Jones polynomial 1. It would only take a single example to show that the Jones polynomials can’t reliably detect whether a knot is there at all.
The Core in Approval-Based Committee Elections
Status: Recently solved by humans and AI
Imagine a town of 1,000 people elects a 10-member council. Each citizen can vote for as many candidates as they like. What would make the election fair? One natural answer is proportional representation of the town’s people. For instance, a group of 300 people should wind up with three seats’ worth of influence.
How do you tell whether a particular voter is well represented? Count how many of the candidates they voted for that end up winning seats.
Now suppose the group of 300 proposes its own three-person slate. Take a resident who voted for only one of the 10 winners but for two of the slate’s three candidates. The council gives her only one representative. But the slate would give her two. If every member of the group likewise ends up with more of their picks on the slate than on the council, the group has a legitimate reason to complain. With just the three seats the group is owed, it could serve every one of its members better than the entire council.
A council that no group can object to is said to be in the “core,” a term borrowed from game theory. In a 2016 preprint paper, a team of computer scientists asked whether every election has at least one council in the core.
For nearly a decade, progress was slow. Certifying a council as fair means comparing it against every possible group of voters and every slate of candidates that group can claim. As election sizes grow, the number of such combinations explodes. Researchers managed only smaller cases, for instance, 15 candidates in 2025.
On September 10 three researchers based in Germany, France and England posted a preprint on arXiv.org that settled the question: every election has a fair council, and there’s an efficient method for finding one. The method doesn’t need to check every group because the proof guarantees that the council it produces is fair. The researchers employed AI as an assistant, alongside their own mathematical intuition, and verified their result using the proof assistant Lean.

Alexis Nikole Nelson, aka Black Forager, reveals the wild foods hiding outside your door
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:24:22 UTC
19:24:22 KST

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. And normally I’d tell you who today’s guest is but she described herself so delightfully that I want you to hear it in her own words:
Alexis Nikole Nelson: Alexis Nikole Nelson, field botanist, eater of things off ground?
Feltman: Even if you don’t know Alexis by name, you’ve almost certainly seen some of her work on social media as Black Forager. Millions of followers devour her videos about finding and eating wild foods, from fruits to flowers to seaweeds. She’s here today to talk about her debut book, Happy Snacking, Don’t Die!
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Thank you so much for coming on to chat with us today.
Nelson: Oh, my gosh, I’m so happy to be joining you.
Feltman: So let’s talk about your new book a little bit and how you got to be writing it. I would love to just go back in time a little bit and hear how you first got into foraging.
Nelson: So I began foraging at, like, the ripe old age of five with my mom. I used to love tagging along when she was working in the garden on the weekends. And I don’t know if you know this, famously, five-year-olds, not the most helpful genre of human. Motor skills not fully downloaded yet. And so whether it was an act of love and sharing knowledge or an act of trying to keep a small child busy, my mom pointed out some onion grass that was growing in our back lawn, and I had never noticed it before.
I asked her when she put it there. She said she didn’t, it was just there on accident, and that there were lots of plants that were just there minding their own business that were also edible and medicinal. And to me, a small child, that blew my mind. I was like, “What do you mean you didn’t put it here? And why isn’t everyone talking about this? Alert the presses. Alert the masses.” And that just sparked my love of knowing all things edible that happened to be growing in my general vicinity, which, you know, has now spread to just a love of the natural world in general.
Feltman: You know, speaking of the love of the natural world and, you know, how foraging feeds that for you, tell me about, you know, what you love about foraging and why it feels so important to share with other people.
Nelson: I think it’s two main things that I really love about it. One is: It’s really meditative. It’s a beautiful way to force your brain to slow down and to notice tiny details about the world around you, to participate in your local ecosystem. And I think that does my brain a whole world of good. I know I’ve been traveling a lot lately, so I haven’t been able to, and I can definitely tell the difference in brain when I am outside in the woods every day and brain when I’m not.
And additionally, I think especially this past summer, we have recognized how fragile some of our food systems are and how maybe we have created such a big food system in which we’re so separated from the food that ends up on our plates that maybe we’ve taken a bridge too far. So it’s really nice to have some things in your pantry, on your dinner plate, that you know the entire trajectory of its travel from being in the ground to being on your plate.
I think it’s a good skill to have. I don’t think it’s ever gonna replace the grocery store for anybody, but there’s something really fulfilling about being responsible for some of the things you’re eating. You know, people who have hobby vegetable gardens will say the exact same thing.
Feltman: So in doing this work publicly including on the Internet, what kinds of questions do you get from the people who are watching what you’re creating?
Have you been surprised at all by what kinds of feelings come up in people when they, they see you sharing stuff about foraging?
Nelson: Yeah, absolutely. I think the two most surprising questions that I still get with some amount of frequency is always a question of where I’m foraging and the legality of me as an individual foraging there.
Feltman: Interesting.
Nelson: And there’s a lot to unpack in that particular question, ’cause sometimes it is really coming from a place of, like, earnest curiosity. A lot of times, some people are also kind of telling on themselves with some of their own inherent biases, and I try to talk through that with people to the best of my ability, ’cause a lot of our feelings about trespass and who has access to wild spaces ends up becoming, like, a classism conversation, I think, a lot faster than people necessarily expect it to.
And I also don’t think a lot of people realize that the origin of a lot of trespass law lies in purposefully cutting off poor people and people of color from being able to access wild foods, be they plants, fungi, fish, squirrels, on land that doesn’t belong to them.
The other question very much in that same vein is “Well, what happens if everyone starts foraging? What’s gonna be left?” People think everyone’s gonna see one of my videos, and then it’s just going to be, like, a cartoon desert with a tumbleweed going by—except maybe no tumbleweed, ’cause, you know, that’s a brassica. Somebody might try to eat that, too. And the first thing that I love to assure people is everyone’s not gonna become a forager.
I know, ’cause I try. I can’t even get my whole family to go foraging with me. And that’s okay. Choose your own adventure, like the books at the library in the ’90s. Choose your own adventure. I am not here to yuck anybody’s yum, and sometimes people are city mice and inside mice, not country mice, and that’s fine.
Second of all, I think, to assume some sort of, like, capitalist intent behind every single person who is foraging is also kind of telling on yourself if that’s the frame of mind you’re going into asking the question with—because I do honestly and earnestly believe that if people were just foraging for the sake of being able to take care of themselves, their family and the community in which they live, and that includes your human neighbors and your not human neighbors, too, then they will make an informed choice while they are gathering.
You know, there are a lot of different global cultures that have rules and rituals to follow, whether that is, you know, some of the Indigenous bands here in the United States taking a moment to pause, lay down tobacco, because that moment of mindfulness helps you from going overboard. You know, globally there’s a lot of also, you know, never take the first thing that you see of a specific species. You know, never take a noticeable amount of a specific species—because not only would that be bad for the thing you’re gathering, but in the long run, it’s also bad for you.
Feltman: Right.
Nelson: You know, foragers are constantly having to be future-focused. We are constantly in a conservationist mindset, not just because we also want to keep having that experience, but we would love people a generation down the road, seven generations down the road, to also get to foster these relationships with our nonhuman neighbors, with the trees and the plants and the fungi and the animals that we happen to be lucky enough to live near.
I think foraging becomes poaching when you start putting money into the equation. I live in a part of the country that is, you know, in the ramp belt. And if you’re not a foodie, a ramp is a very pungent wild onion that is in season for about a month in the Midwest.
Feltman: And people lose their minds.
Nelson: They lose their minds. People lose their ever plant-loving minds over them.
Martha Stewart wrote one article about them two decades ago, and the ramps have not recovered since. And you will see people, in order to be able to stock, like, farmers markets in Manhattan and in order to be able to stock, you know, the kitchens of Michelin-starred restaurants around the country, coming into places like southeast Ohio, coming into West Virginia, and filling up trash bags with this plant that frequently can take nearly a decade to reach maturity. You know, [it] can sometimes take 10 years before it is at a point where it can be procreating, creating seeds. Those seeds take an additional two years then to break down their seed coat and germinate. So you, you do have to be using your noggin when you’re going out and gathering.
And if you’re just gathering enough for you and your family to have a mess of greens for a couple nights in the spring and to pickle a couple jars of bulbs, that’s totally fine. I’m not the person who’s gonna be, like, pick-shaming people for going and gathering ramps. They’re a wonderful springtime treat. But yeah, the second that you put money into the equation and start putting more steps in between the gathering and the consuming of the plant, the muddier the waters become, the less careful the people doing the gathering suddenly start to be because you have this magical dollar sign hovering over your head that you’re chasing.
Feltman: Yeah. So let’s talk about your book. Who is it for, and what are they going to come away with after reading it?
Nelson: My book is for current and future foragers. I think people assume you have to be at my level to be considered a forager, and I think if you just go and dig up the dandelions in your backyard, congratulations, you are a forager. Your laminated name tag will be in the mail shortly, I promise. And I want this book to help people recognize that and also help them recognize that you don’t have to live in the middle of the woods on an expansive piece of land in order to become a forager.
There are so many opportunities. I live in the middle of a city. I love getting—you know, another question I get a lot is “Oh, where do you live where you find all of the”—Columbus, Ohio. We often don’t take stock of the plants that do exist around us. Even if you feel like you’re living in a concrete jungle, odds purslane is still coming up out of the sidewalk cracks. There you go. That’s a snack that you could be foraging. Make sure it’s not in a place where a dog could have peed on it, but you know, that’s still something forageable in the heat of summer, surrounded by nothing but industry and concrete.
Feltman: Yeah, very cool. What are some other of your favorite sort of like gateway-drug foraging things that, like, are more abundant than people realize, that they’re gonna love once they try them, and then they won’t be able to stop picking stuff?
Nelson: Ooh, my favorite is actually a throwback for both of us, Rachel, and that is serviceberries, which secretly have a million names. If I don’t call them by the name that you at home specifically call them, I’m so sorry, but we don’t have time....
Feltman: And you can go listen to my other show,The Weirdest Thing I Learned This Week, if you want to hear, still probably not literally every name for the serviceberry, but many more of them.
Nelson: They’re such a popular planting for parks and lining city streets because they’re resilient, their foliage is beautiful in the autumn, and their fruits are so good. Amelanchier arborea is the species that I see used in parks globally the most. I saw an Amelanchier arborea in the middle of Tokyo earlier this year.
So when I say that there is one hiding near you, that is not a joke. Unless you live right around the equator, where it’s a little too toasty for them, you will probably find a park close to you that has these guys, and they are such a springtime treat. You might have to fight some birds for them. I have an uneasy truce with the robins in my neighborhood. They’re like, “You don’t bring out the berry rake, we don’t poop on you. That’s the deal.”
Feltman: Well, and so as an experienced forager, I would also love to hear, to inspire our guests for their future foraging endeavors: What are some of the more surprising or challenging things that you have foraged yourself?
Nelson: Ooh. Well, I was in Glacier National Park last summer and just hanging out on a mountainside, eating alpine strawberries. That was fun and worth it. I mean, that hike did kick my whole butt. But also, if you’ve never had a wild strawberry, I need you to pencil it in for next summer because the amount of flavor that gets packed into one of those little guys is insane. They’re so good.
Feltman: Well, another one that I would love to hear more about, I think you recently did some ocean pickling, uh, which of course, so much interesting science there. So for our listeners who don’t follow you yet online, it would be great if you could tell us a little bit about that one.
Nelson: So I love food history, especially when it comes to things like foraging and fermentation and older food preservation methods. And there is a pretty strong bit of evidence for humans discovering lacto-fermented pickles through preserving things in saltwater, because frequently, so long as it hasn’t rained super recently, ocean water is right around the salinity that you want to make a good sour lacto-fermented pickle—like, high 2 percent to high 3 percent range, enough that you get some good salty flavor but also not so salty that the lactobacteria can’t get really active and create that delicious lactic acid that we love, that wonderful crisp acidity that we love from a good pickle.
So to showcase this, while I was visiting some of my family on Martha’s Vineyard—far away from industry, I promise, that’s always everyone’s biggest fear—I checked the water quality levels before I did this. I gathered up a bunch of seawater, put it through multiple layers of filtration. We filtered out the bits, big and small, brought it up to a rolling boil for just a moment, just to kill off anything too small to be able to be filtered out.
And then I have pickled beets, jalapeños, garlic. They all pickle beautifully. And due to the fact that our ocean water, it’s not just sodium making a salt in the ocean, we also have some magnesium salts in there, too, which I think add to the flavor profile of the pickles. They are pretty slammin’, if I may say so myself. And I love an excuse to sneakily shove some science education into my videos.
Feltman: Amazing. Well, thank you so much for coming on to chat with us. This has been wonderful.
Nelson: Thank you so much for having me.

UK diesel price hits record high of £2 a litre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:20:26 UTC
19:20:26 KST

British motorists face more pressure at the pumps after the average price of diesel climbed to a record £2 a litre.
The price of a litre at UK forecourts has risen 40.5% since late February, when the US-Israel war on Iran began disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf, leading to cost increases across the economy.
The RAC motoring group said on Friday that the average price had reached 200.01p a litre, meaning the cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war.
Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC, said: “This is a pump price threshold that no one wanted to cross.”
The RAC figures measure the average cost of fuel, but in reality many forecourts have been selling diesel above £2 a litre for some time.
Petrol prices are also continuing to rise, with a litre of unleaded costing 174.1p on average, a 31.5% increase since 28 February, taking the cost of a typical tank to £96, just over £23 more than before the US-Iran conflict.
Earlier on Friday the transport minister Keir Mather sought to avert panic at the pumps, insisting the UK was not facing a diesel shortage, after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel.
The Trump administration has told Germany and France to release their diesel stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban.
On Thursday, the UK opened talks with European allies over releasing emergency supplies, and Dan Jørgensen, the EU commissioner for energy, said on Friday that Europe was discussing the diesel reserves issue with all members of the International Energy Agency (IEA), not only the US.
In a video conference with G7 leaders, chaired by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, attenders discussed a proposal from the French government that European nations release 50m barrels of diesel from reserve supplies, and for members of the IEA to release 50m barrels of crude oil, Reuters reported.
The UK relies on the US for about 30% of its diesel, with the vast majority coming from mainland Europe, and has reserve supplies for 42 days.
Motorists and small businesses have been struggling with the increasing cost of filling up.
Williams added: “This will be very challenging for households and companies that drive a lot of miles, from commuters, haulage and delivery firms, businesses with large fleets all the way through to sole traders.
“In a cruel twist, it’s diesel vehicles, which were once considered the most cost-effective option for lengthy journeys, that are now burning a hole in people’s pockets.”
Capital Economics estimated that a ban on US exports of diesel could raise UK diesel prices from £2 a litre to £3 a litre and push inflation up to 5%, from 3.1% in August.
The fresh high was recorded after record fuel prices across Europe in recent weeks, which have ignited calls for political leaders to take action to protect consumers against rising cost pressures.
Inflation in the cost of road fuels has outpaced the surge in global oil markets due to a sharp drop in output from refineries damaged by war in the Middle East and in Russia.
Before the Ukraine war, Russia provided between 10% and 15% of the world’s diesel supplies. Another 10% of global diesel supplies transited through the strait of Hormuz from Gulf nations before Iran responded to the US-Israeli attacks by disrupting the strait.
Trump has pushed his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to cease Kyiv’s drone and missile attacks on Russian refineries so they can help to relieve the global fuel squeeze.
The Middle East war has also pushed up household energy bills. This week the quarterly price cap rose by 4%, meaning a typical household in Great Britain will pay £1,723 a year. The cap is forecast to increase by a further 16%, equivalent to adding £276 to the average annual dual-fuel bill, to take it to £1,999, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight.
Reports of talks among European nations to potentially release diesel and oil reserves fuelled a 2.5% fall in the price of Brent crude to $99.78 a barrel.
“This highlights that the main stress in the energy market is no longer crude availability, with Middle East flows recovering,” said Ole Hansen, the head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank. “But rather refined product supply, constrained by reduced refinery capacity and output across the Middle East and Russia.”

Ten members of the Gradient production team from the Kotlas Electromechanical College worked more than 2,600 hours at the Baltic Shipyard in St. Petersburg, doing electrical work on the Chukotka nuclear icebreaker that is under construction there. Another 15 students from the region's construction teams worked on the construction of the Moscow - St. Petersburg high-speed highway, one of the country's major infrastructure projects. Additionally, construction teams' twelve members worked at port infrastructure facilities in the Krasnoyarsk Region's Dudinka.
"In the year of our movement's 60th anniversary, the students have demonstrated that they can work at the country's most important facilities," the Arkhangelsk Regional Branch's leader Egor Ivanov said. "A nuclear icebreaker, a high-speed highway, and an Arctic port are projects that determine Russia's future."
From Kaliningrad to Sakhalin
The student teams worked at enterprises in the Russian Federation's 15 regions. Construction teams (65 people) worked at strategic sites in the Murmansk, Moscow, Novgorod and Krasnoyarsk Regions, as well as at defense facilities in the Arctic and in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Region. The Artel restoration team's 14 members spent the labor season restoring the 19th century's Chapel of Elijah the Prophet in the village of Novaya Derevnya, in the Vologda Region. Service teams (68 people) worked at hotel complexes in the south of Russia and at the Pulkovo Airport. Medical teams (29 people) practiced at hospitals in Arkhangelsk and participated in national projects - the Academy Project in Novosibirsk, and the Parma Project in Perm.
It was for the first time that the movement had fishing season teams (28 people) - students worked at fish processing enterprises of the Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands. Agricultural teams (13 people) worked on the AgroNero and ChistoYagoda projects in the Leningrad Region. Several teams (56 people) worked on special projects: an archaeological team worked at the Russian Academy of Sciences' Institute of Archeology, a search team participated in expeditions, a career guidance team participated in the admission campaign at the Northern Arctic Federal University (NArFU), and a media team conducted photo and video support at the national Arctic Project and at children's camps.

In 2026, the Arkhangelsk Region's student teams have celebrated their 60th anniversary. Over the years, more than 135,000 young people have taken part in the movement. Presently, in the region's 14 municipal districts operate 55 student teams and 32 teenager labor teams. The youth labor movement's development continues under the Youth and Children National Project.

Could the future of AI data centres be in space? Google wants to find out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:19:48 UTC
19:19:48 KST

The tech giant has launched a prototype satellite carrying its AI chips to explore whether solar powered infrastructure in orbit could one day support large-scale computing.
Google launched a prototype satellite into orbit loaded with its AI chips on Thursday as part of the first phase of a project to explore if space could be the best place for powering large-scale AI infrastructure.
The satellite, built by Planet Labs and launched on SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare, is loaded with Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) to see how they perform in space and deal with the physical stress of spaceflight, radiation and extreme temperature conditions.
The thinking behind the initiative, aptly named 'Project Suncatcher', is to place satellites in low-earth orbit where they can benefit from near-constant sunlight to capture up to eight times more solar energy than on Earth.
Google wants to see if large-scale machine-learning infrastructure can survive in space and benefit from abundant solar energy.
The amount of energy data centres consume is growing rapidly, driven in no small part by the massive surge in artificial intelligence workloads. Globally, data centres consumed an estimated 415 to 485 terawatt-hours (TWh) last year.
This accounts for 1.5% to 2.5% of the world’s total electricity generation, according to the European Commission, a figure that is set to double by 2030.
Many data centre projects around the world are facing growing public opposition amid concerns that they drive up energy bills; therefore, building data centres in space far away from the general public is an appealing prospect.
Google is not the only company exploring the possibility of sending AI into space. Nvidia-backed startup Starcloud trained an artificial intelligence model from space for the first time last December.
In June, Elon Musk unveiled SpaceX's AI1 satellite, also known as Starmind, a new satellite class designed as a flying GPU (graphics processing unit) cluster rather than a communications relay.
And in September, Mistral announced a partnership with Marlan Space and Loft Orbital to develop artificial intelligence satellite infrastructure, with the first satellite launch this October.
What is Google testing?
The launch marked the first phase of Google's test with a 10-minute climb into low Earth orbit. The spacecraft endured intense vibrations and sustained acceleration of up to 10 times the force of gravity, while the TPU chips on board were hit by brief shocks of between 50 and 100g.
In anticipation of these hardy conditions, the Suncatcher team carried out vibration testing on the satellite to mimic a rocket launch, with the craft and TPU chips passing test.
Now that Google has safely launched the TPU chips into orbit, the next phase of the experiment begins as the team assesses how the TPU chips deal with the higher levels of radiation outside the Earth's atmosphere, as well as solar events and cosmic rays, which can also disrupt electrical systems.
Data centres infamously require an inordinate amount of energy and water resources, but in the vacuum of space this is a different problem entirely. The mission will be an opportunity for the research team to test a number of different solutions, including a combination of heat pipes and radiators to cool the chips.
In future Suncatcher missions, satellites carrying dozens of TPU chips will be tested with the aim of moving from the current approach of low bandwidth across large distances to high bandwidth over extremely short distances to maintain connectivity.
The technology already exists in space. However, Google will test ways of maintaining a high bandwidth connectivity over shorter distances with greater accuracy when it launches further satellites next year.

Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Giant Samara Oil Hub—Fire Erupts at Europe’s Largest Tank Farm
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck an oil-industry facility in Russia’s Samara region overnight on October 2, as explosions were followed by a fire at what open-source analysts believe was the massive Samara oil pumping and dispatch complex.
Russian outlet ASTRA, after analyzing eyewitness imagery, reported that the blaze likely broke out at the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station, or LPDS Samara.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Residents across the region reported drones overhead during the night, while a missile alert was declared in the city of Samara at 5:51 am. A particularly powerful explosion was reported at around 6:30 am.
Authorities did not publicly confirm the weapons used in the operation or the immediate cause of the fire.

Ukrainian OSINT project Exilenova+ separately reported a fire at LPDS Samara and published coordinates pointing to the site.

LPDS Samara is part of Russia’s Transneft pipeline network and functions as a major storage, pumping, and crude-blending hub.

The facility also incorporates the Samara-1 and Samara-2 pumping stations and a separate crude-blending station.
Four major trunk pipelines converge at the hub, carrying oil from Western Siberia, Tatarstan, the Orenburg region, and Kazakhstan before it moves farther through Russia’s pipeline system.

Taiwan's Chen Nien-chin wins Asian Games silver in women's boxing

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwanese boxer Chen Nien-chin (陳念琴) won silver in the women's 65-kilogram division at the Asian Games on Friday, losing to India's Parveen Hooda by a 2-3 split decision in the gold-medal bout.
Chen battled back from a first-round deficit to level the fight in the second round, but three of the five judges scored the decisive third round for Hooda, per ETtoday. The silver medal marks the best Asian Games result of Chen's career.
Chen advanced to the final after defeating Thailand's Suwannapheng 5-0 in the quarterfinals to secure a medal. She then edged North Korea's Hwang Hyo-sun 3-2 in a split decision in the semifinals, reaching an Asian Games final for the first time.
Under the 10-point system, each of the five judges scores every round independently, typically awarding 10 points to the winner and nine to the loser. Each judge totals the points across all three rounds to determine the winner on their scorecard.
In the opening round, all five judges scored Hooda 10-9, leaving Chen trailing 0-5 on the scorecards, ETtoday reported. Chen responded in the second round, with all five judges awarding her a 10-9 win to level the fight at 19-19 on every scorecard.
The gold medal came down to the final three minutes, with the five judges split on the decisive round. Two scored it 10-9 for Chen, while the other three gave Hooda the same margin, resulting in a 3-2 split decision in the Indian boxer's favor.
Chen finished with a 29-28 advantage on two scorecards but trailed 28-29 on the other three, according to ETtoday. The decision gave Hooda the gold and Chen the silver, one judge's vote short of her first Asian Games title.

Flydubai hijacking: Israel is a nation of heroes - time for the gov't to show courage too - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:17:56 UTC
19:17:56 KST

Israelis are a nation of heroes. That might sound like a slogan, but every so often something happens that reminds us how true this is.
Of all the extraordinary stories to emerge from Wednesday’s flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, the one that stands out is the courage of the passengers who realized something had gone terribly wrong, forced their way into the cockpit, and helped subdue the co-pilot, who had allegedly stabbed the captain and appeared to be trying to bring down the plane.
The aircraft plunged thousands of feet; there was chaos onboard, and the passengers had no way of knowing exactly what was happening or whether they had minutes, seconds, or no time at all.
And they acted. They didn’t wait for someone to rescue them or see if everything would resolve itself on its own. They took the initiative and saved lives: not only of the passengers on board, but whatever else the plane could have taken down with it.
When we remember aircraft that have been hijacked or crashed over the years, it is difficult not to appreciate what happened aboard this flight and how there is something deeply Israeli about it.
It is part of this country’s culture: not to stand by and watch events unfold, but to run headfirst into the fire, battle, or the storm and do whatever can be done to save lives.
We have now heard some testimony from passengers aboard the flight. It is frightening and disturbing, particularly as investigators are still trying to understand what exactly happened and what the co-pilot’s motive was. But there is also something heartwarming in hearing how people responded in those terrifying moments.
They literally took charge, and, when we think about it, it is a characteristic we know all too well. Next week, Israel will mark three years since October 7. That terrible day will be seared into our collective memory as one of the greatest failures and tragedies in Israeli history. But, like with the airplane, it too was filled with stories of some of the greatest courage this country has ever seen.
There are many different kinds of heroism, and there is no need to rank them.
But it is impossible to forget the people who woke up that morning, heard that something incomprehensible was happening in the south, understood that people were in desperate need of help, and got into their cars. They took whatever weapons they had, if they had any, and drove straight into the battle.
They did not know what they would find. They did not know how many terrorists had crossed the border, where the army was, or whether they themselves would make it home. They just went.
That, to a large extent, is the story of Israel: a small country whose people are repeatedly confronted with danger and who, when the moment comes, stand up, fight and lead the charge.
A nation prepared to fight
It is worth thinking about that now, just weeks before Israelis go to the polls on October 27.
This election will help determine the direction Israel takes after three extraordinarily difficult years. And whichever government ultimately emerges, it will inherit a country confronting a series of strategic challenges, almost none of which have truly been resolved.
Hamas still controls part of Gaza and retains weapons and military infrastructure. Hezbollah remains a threat to Israel’s north. And Iran remains locked in confrontation over its nuclear program and its wider regional capabilities.
It is true that three years after October 7, Israel has achieved amazing accomplishments, but victory, as we know too well by now, is not measured only by what an army destroys – it is also measured by what a country builds in its place.
And that is where a striking discrepancy has emerged.
Israel’s leaders have been given an extraordinary gift: a population willing to fight, to endure difficult years, and send its children to war knowing the risks and knowing, painfully, that some will not return.
Consider the family of Israel’s ambassador to Washington, Yechiel Leiter. His son Neria was seriously wounded last week in a ramming attack on Route 443 while serving in the reserves. His brother, Moshe, was killed fighting in Gaza in 2023.
Neria had every reason not to continue serving: his brother had been killed, and his family had already sacrificed enough. He could have remained home with his wife and children. He could have spared his parents the anguish of once again worrying about a son fighting on the front.
But he did not. He continued putting on his uniform. He continued reporting for reserve duty. And he continued serving.
Without people like that, Israel would not survive. But courage cannot only be demanded of soldiers and civilians; it must be demanded of politicians as well.
Political courage is different. It is not about charging a cockpit or running toward gunfire. It is about making difficult decisions, accepting risk, challenging traditional assumptions and, most importantly, telling the public where you actually want to take the country.
That is the question Israelis should be asking as they prepare to vote: What is the vision?
Is the future being offered to us simply one of hunkering down, a kind of super-Sparta, stronger and better armed than everyone around us but condemned to fight one war after another?
Or is there another possibility, one that recognizes the threats Israel faces, takes them seriously, and preserves overwhelming military strength, but also searches for a path toward greater security, stability, and eventually something else?
Israel looking for brave leaders
Last week in New York, for example, the US-backed Board of Peace unveiled an ambitious plan for Gaza. Senior officials acknowledged the enormous obstacles standing in the way, including the unresolved dispute over how Hamas will disarm and how Israel will withdraw.
Considering everything that would have to happen for this plan to succeed, skepticism is more than understandable. Is it ambitious and hard to imagine? 100%.
Three years after October 7, with the situation in Gaza still dire – both for its residents and for Israel’s security – this is a thoughtful plan that offers a real chance to change reality on the ground. Considering all the alternatives, isn’t it worth a shot?
But here is the catch: Israelis were not even in the room.
That is what this election campaign should be about. Instead, too much of Israeli politics remains focused on what candidates are against. This person will sit with that party; that person cannot be trusted; this bloc is dangerous, and that bloc is illegitimate.
But what are these politicians for? Where do they want Israel to be in five years?
What is their plan for Gaza? For Lebanon? For the Palestinians? For Israel’s increasingly strained relationship with parts of the Western world? What does victory realistically look like?
Israelis have demonstrated time and again that they are prepared to take extraordinary risks for this country.
The people who stormed the cockpit this week did not wait to be asked. Neither did the Israelis who drove south on October 7. They saw danger. They understood that someone had to act. And despite having no guarantee of what would happen next, they moved forward.
Israel’s political leaders do not need to storm a cockpit. But they do need to show some of the same courage. Instead of spending the next few weeks telling Israelis what they will never do, whom they will never sit with, and why everyone else is dangerous, they should tell us where they want to take this country.
The Israeli people have already shown that they are prepared to be brave. Now they deserve leaders brave enough to offer them a future.
The writer is a co-founder of the MEAD policy forum, a senior fellow at JPPI, and a former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post. His newest book is While Israel Slept.
