====================================================================================================

Health Care Workers Are Tired of Cleaning Up Palantir’s Mess
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Over the past four months, Amber Retzloff, a critical care nurse in Florida, requested to work 50 specific 12-hour shifts. But over half the time, she says her hospital’s Palantir-powered scheduling software assigned her to different shifts, often putting her on back-to-back-to-back days and leaving her mentally drained. Retzloff doesn’t expect to always get the slots she wants, but by her count the tool does a far worse job honoring her preferences than managers did when they assigned shifts by hand.
Retzloff’s experience mirrors that of other nurses across HCA Healthcare, the largest hospital chain in the US. Since 2023, HCA has rolled out an AI scheduling tool it co-developed with Palantir called Timpani at roughly 130 of its 190 locations. Retzloff’s hospital adopted it nearly two years ago.
“No one is happy with Timpani,” says Retzloff, echoing what five nurses at other locations reported in interviews with WIRED. “Everyone complains all the time.” Other purported HCA workers have expressed similar gripes about the tool on platforms like Reddit.
The nurses who spoke with WIRED allege that Timpani has potentially harmed patients by causing care teams to be understaffed, imbalanced, and exhausted. Operating with minimal oversight, they say the tool routinely schedules too few nurses or not enough experienced veterans during shifts, particularly on Sundays. It also frequently ignores nurses’ stated preferences for spacing out shifts, working nights and weekends, or taking specific days off.
As a result, nurses say they are being forced to waste more time trying to trade shifts or appeal their schedules than prior to the arrival of the software. They also believe colleagues are increasingly calling out, using paid or unpaid time to skip assignments, though doing so more than a few times annually puts them at risk of termination.
Retzloff, 34, a National Nurses United labor union leader with a decade of bedside experience, recalls recent shifts where all four of her colleagues were junior. Because she was the only senior nurse working, Retzloff says she had to delay care for the sickest patients to guide the novices through milder cases.
HCA is “letting AI dictate,” Retzloff says. “We are overriding clinical judgment and the human-to-human piece of health care with an app.”
Previously, managers handled scheduling manually and generally consulted nurses well in advance when overriding requests. With Timpani, nurses report needing to make alternative arrangements on shorter notice and an increase in temporary reassignments to different teams. “I can’t remember any issues before,” says a non-union nurse in Texas who asked to remain anonymous out of fear of retaliation from HCA. “Everything came out on time.”
Harlow Sumerford, an HCA spokesperson, says that nursing leaders, not Timpani, make final scheduling decisions. Assertions that the tool “is designed to reduce staffing at the expense of patient care” are misrepresentative, he adds.
HCA’s goal is “to have the right caregivers, with the right skills and experience, available to meet the needs of our patients while also considering our colleagues’ scheduling preferences,” Sumerford says, noting that the company is continuing to improve Timpani based on nurses’ feedback.
“Being Kicked”
On average, Timpani schedules nurses for 1 percent of their requested days off, or what are known as red days, according to HCA. Lee Barker, an HCA nurse in Missouri, says while that number might appear relatively low, getting scheduled on red days was previously unheard of at their facility.
But less than a year after management introduced Timpani, Barker says now essentially every nurse has been assigned to work on a day they were supposed to be off. Barker delayed a long-planned doctor’s appointment for a chronic condition after struggling to trade an assigned red day. “It feels like we’re being kicked while we’re already down,” Barker says.
Complaints about Timpani have prompted HCA management to make minor updates to the software, but problems still persist, according to nurses across the US. Leaders of National Nurses United, the labor union representing about 10,000 of HCA’s 100,000 nurses, says the company has rejected their requests for information about the technology.
Some purported details emerged in July when a former HCA data science manager, Angelique Russell, sued the company for allegedly firing her in retaliation for raising concerns about Timpani. She accused HCA of routinely deleting data the tool uses to create schedules, which prevented auditing how well it worked and she claimed may have violated several healthcare laws. (HCA has yet to formally respond in court, and Russell declined to comment.)
Timpani was built on Palantir Foundry, a software platform for storing and analyzing different data from across a company’s operations. Named after the beat-keeping musical instrument, it uses algorithmic forecasts of patient volumes and staffing needs to automatically build nursing schedules. When Timpani launched in 2023, HCA’s top innovation executive Michael Schlosser told WIRED it would save time and money, as well as eliminate favoritism in assigning shifts.
Schlosser said in a paper this past July that Timpani has drastically reduced the number of hours managers spend on scheduling each month, lowered reliance on costly contract nurses to fill shifts, and increased retention. “The efficiency comes from AI generating stronger initial schedules,” he wrote, adding that over 98 percent “include a mix of skill and experiences.”
HCA’s responsible AI policy emphasizes protecting individuals from “physical” or “emotional” harms, and executives have said they spoke to nurses and took an empathetic approach in developing Timpani. In marketing materials, the company features nurses praising the tool for being easy to use and saving them time. Yet other HCA nurses say they feel ignored and disrespected, and they are not the only health care workers who have raised concerns about Palantir’s push into their industry.
Rayus Radiology, a large US imaging chain, began receiving complaints about scheduling errors earlier this year after it introduced a tool also built on Palantir Foundry, according to internal documents viewed by WIRED. The software is designed to populate scheduling fields from doctors’ orders. But in a number of cases, it linked the requests to the wrong patient profiles, listed tests or scans that didn’t match the orders, or made up personal details about patients. Schedulers who work at Rayus suspect that non-standard forms, illegible handwriting, and insufficient human review contributed to the issues.
Rayus spokesperson Kit Crancer says “the broad characterizations” do not fairly reflect its “processes, safeguards, or commitment to safe, accurate, and timely patient care.” He adds that Rayus uses technology “to support, not replace, appropriate human judgment and oversight.”
A Palantir spokesperson declined to comment using their name, but the company has described its software as merely presenting information in a more helpful manner and emphasized that customers are responsible for the data, policies, and decisionmaking.
Palantir Anxiety
Palantir’s sales have nearly doubled recently to almost $2 billion per quarter, as organizations seek its help analyzing data and automating tasks. Soaring costs and staffing shortages have made health care providers especially eager customers. Cleveland Clinic credited Palantir software with boosting patient capacity by forecasting ER discharges and replacing manual coordination.
But Palantir has also received pushback from civil rights activists over its defense and immigration work, as well as the stated political views of cofounders Peter Thiel and Alex Karp. In the UK, Palantir landed a $440 million contract with the National Health Service to try to cut appointment wait times, but nurses and activists have demanded it be canceled over privacy and security concerns.
At HCA, some nurses also want Palantir gone. While studies show AI-based scheduling holds promise, nurses say Timpani has become a source of anxiety. “Everyone checks immediately and every month you hear, ‘Man, why did it schedule me like that?’” Barker says.
Initially, some local managers could edit Timpani’s schedules. Now, nurses must flag problematic shifts to a centralized team at HCA headquarters in Nashville, which reviews appeals without direct communication or room for explanation, according to nurses. If denied, they try to swap shifts, but the chances of success are about only 50 percent, Barker and Retzloff claim.
Barker, who is a National Nurses United leader at an HCA psychiatric center, claims several colleagues quit over Timpani and that workplace injuries have climbed in the first 12 months with the tool. The center’s union of about 500 nurses filed a grievance over the software, arguing HCA is failing to sufficiently honor scheduling preferences. The matter is likely headed to arbitration.
In Timpani’s early days, HCA’s Schlosser acknowledged health care workers can be slow to adopt tech “because they have people’s lives in their hands.” But he envisioned a future where frontline nurses actively pushed for more tools: “Then it’ll be fun.” Three years later, some nurses see little reason to rejoice.

Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered his military commanders to abandon previous constraints on aerial attacks and intensify strikes on civilian sites, President Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview published Friday, Oct. 2.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“He said there are no rules now,” Zelensky said, referring to the alleged order from Putin.
According to Zelensky, the instruction was issued in September, as Russia intensified attacks on Kyiv and increasingly struck schools, hospitals, telecommunications facilities and data centers.
Zelensky speaks from school bomb shelter
Zelensky spoke to the FT inside the bomb shelter of a Kyiv school struck by a Russian jet-powered drone on Thursday.
The school’s director said 104 students and 60 teachers survived because they reached the underground shelter before the drone hit shortly after 9 a.m.
The drone’s 50-kilogram (110-pound) warhead pierced the floor but failed to detonate, Ukrainian authorities said. The impact nevertheless damaged the building and started a fire.
Zelensky later called attacks on educational institutions “a deliberate tactic”, saying Russia was attempting to terrorize civilians and disrupt ordinary life.
Kyiv Grinds to a Halt as Russian Strikes Shut Bridges, Force People to Walk
The FT said debris recovered at the school bore markings from Russian manufacturers and handwritten Russian text. Some components were reportedly manufactured in Russia on July 28, while others appeared to be Western-made.
Russia has denied deliberately attacking civilian sites. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told the FT that Russian forces do not strike schools or hospitals.
However, Ukraine’s Education Ministry has recorded more than 4,700 attacks on educational institutions since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The World Health Organization has verified more than 3,000 attacks affecting healthcare facilities.
Deliberately attacking civilians or civilian objects constitutes a war crime under international humanitarian law.
Russia seeks to pressure civilians
Zelensky said Russia had previously concentrated much of its long-range campaign on military and energy infrastructure, although civilian sites have been repeatedly struck throughout the full-scale invasion.
He alleged that Moscow had now deliberately expanded its target list because Russian forces had failed to achieve their objectives on the battlefield, particularly in the Donbas.
The new campaign seeks “to pressure people,” Zelensky said, describing the strikes as an attempt to frighten civilians, force residents to leave Ukrainian cities and weaken the country’s ability to continue resisting Russia.
On Monday, a Russian drone struck Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv. Russia also repeatedly attacked the Pivdennyi Bridge in Kyiv on Thursday, damaging a support column, the road surface and a barrier and disrupting transport across the Dnipro.
Recent Russian strikes have also damaged Ukrainian schools, healthcare facilities, warehouses, businesses and communications infrastructure. A Sept. 23 attack damaged Kyiv data centers, disrupting internet service for some residents.
Jet-powered drones strain Ukrainian defenses
Zelensky said Russia had launched around 500 drones over the previous day, approximately half of them jet-powered models that fly considerably faster than conventional Shahed-type drones.
Ukraine intercepted around 57% of the jet-powered drones, compared with between 85% and 90% of conventional models, he said.
Russia’s use of jet-powered drones increased eightfold between June and August, according to figures previously released by Ukraine’s Air Force. Their higher speed gives defenders less time to detect and intercept them and can force Ukraine to use comparatively expensive aircraft and missiles.
Zelensky said F-16 fighter jets had proven effective against the new drones. However, around half of Ukraine’s F-16 fleet was spending extended periods outside the country for maintenance and repairs, he said.
Kyiv is seeking Western assistance to move more maintenance work into Ukraine so that aircraft can return to service faster.
Ukraine is also testing five high-speed interceptor drone models. Zelensky said one model could enter production at a rate of approximately 400 units by the end of October, while the other four remained in testing.
He identified shortages of suitable engines and insufficient financing as the main obstacles to mass production.
Western pressure ‘not enough’
Zelensky also criticized the US and European governments for failing to apply sufficient economic and diplomatic pressure on Putin to end the war.
Asked whether Ukraine’s partners were doing everything possible to help, he replied: “Not enough, of course not enough.”
Zelensky argued that Russia’s partners had the leverage required to increase the cost of continuing the invasion but lacked the political will to use it fully.

Another NSW government website has been hacked by an OpenAI agent
Unknown

09:28:02 UTC
18:28:02 KST

In brief
- The breach follows earlier break-ins to the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and Medicare statistics.
- In this breach, OpenAI's agent accessed a National Parks and Wildlife Service web application platform.
Another AI breach is under investigation after a rogue agent accessed public information on a state government web application.
The NSW premier's department on Friday said it had been informed by OpenAI, the tech company behind ChatGPT, that one of its models accessed a National Parks and Wildlife Service web application containing historical information and data on fires in NSW.
The breach occurred in June, but was not reported to the NSW government until Thursday.
"The NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water is working with Cyber Security NSW and its technology service provider to investigate the matter and assess its impact," the department said in a statement.
The government said its investigations had not identified unauthorised access to personal information as a result of the breach.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The NSW Greens called on the Minns government to audit all government systems and databases to check for additional breaches.
"We simply cannot trust these companies. They have no respect for the sovereignty of our governments, of our way of life," Greens MP Abigail Boyd said.
She said it was damning that the breach occurred in June, but the government was not notified until this week.
"We clearly cannot rely on these multinational big tech companies to comply with even the most minimal of social obligations such as notifying when, or even taking enough care to notice if, their products are hacking government systems," she said.
The breach follows earlier break-ins to the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and Medicare statistics by OpenAI agents, which prompted an urgent bolstering of government cyber systems.
The Department of Home Affairs on Wednesday issued a directive advising federal departments to examine their older software and technology, which will be assessed for shortcomings in order of priority.
Sam Spencer, who runs tech security company Aristotle Metadata, warned the edict was essentially an extension of an existing system that did not work.
A national data commissioner's office was first established in 2022 after a series of data breaches. It was ordered to help departments find and upload datasets to a national catalogue.
Over four years, it identified only 500 datasets that were not already available on the open portal data.gov.au.
Spencer has been working to gather information on hundreds of government datasets, inform departments of privacy concerns, and even blamed the Medicare breach on the commissioner's office.
"I would firmly look at the data commissioner, because they were responsible for cataloguing data," he said.
A spokesperson for the Department of Finance, which houses the data commissioner's office, told the Australian Associated Press data registration would not prevent further breaches.
"The proposition that data registration can prevent cyber incidents is incorrect," the spokesperson said.
Infrastructure Minister Tim Ayres defended Australia's approach as "world-leading" despite the concerns.
"The approach is about making sure that artificial intelligence investment here supports Australia's national interest, happens on Australia's terms," he told ABC Radio on Friday.
Spencer suggested the government could not have a robust approach to data security without fully understanding what it held.
The Australian Signals Directorate advises government agencies to keep a clear catalogue of data for security.
Under national requirements, departments must enter mandatory answers to 10 questions about each dataset they upload to the catalogue.
Spencer's analysis found Home Affairs had entered only 90 per cent of the compulsory information it should have. It had one of the lowest scores of any agency.
A Department of Home Affairs spokesperson said data protection was key to its work.
"The department takes its responsibilities in relation to both data accessibility and cyber security seriously and continues to make progress in each area."

Kilometer-long traffic jams are being reported in Kyiv following a nighttime strike on the Pivdennyi Bridge, which was completely closed as a result. Traffic on Paton Bridge from the right bank to the left bank was fully restricted. Metro Bridge was closed in the direction of the right bank, reports UNN.
Details
On the morning of Friday, October 2, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that, according to law enforcement officials, the Pivdennyi Bridge had been completely closed to traffic in both directions.
Traffic has been partially restricted to one lane on Metro Bridge from the left bank to the right bank, while traffic on Paton Bridge from the right bank to the left bank has been completely restricted.
Klitschko did not specify the reason; however, the Pivdennyi Bridge was likely closed because it was hit by an enemy drone. i
The bridge closures caused a transport collapse in Kyiv, effectively paralyzing the city, while hundreds of people waited in queues for public transport. Some even decided not to stand in line and instead walked from the right bank to the left bank.
Kyivpastrans reported that buses No. 51, 55, 115, 118-D and trolleybuses No. 43 and 50 had resumed service along their regular routes, which pass over Paton Bridge; however, transport is operating behind schedule.
Kyivpastrans also added that buses No. 22 and 91 from the left bank to the right bank of Kyiv are temporarily operating via Darnytskyi Bridge.
Route toward the right bank: Mykola Bazhan Avenue − Dnipro Embankment – Bereznykivska Street – Yuri Shumskyi Street – Petro Radzinia Street − Darnytskyi road-and-rail bridge – Nadniprianske Highway – Mykola Mykhnovskyi Boulevard – Holosiivskyi Avenue, then along their regular routes.
Analysts at the Institute for the Study of War believe that Russia seeks to block transport flows between the right and left banks of the Dnipro by carrying out repeated precision strikes on the same location.
The Russian strike on the Pivdennyi Bridge is part of a broader Russian campaign targeting civilian infrastructure, involving both daytime and nighttime strikes aimed at making life in Kyiv more difficult and disrupting the city’s everyday functioning. The strike also aims to undermine Ukraine’s economy by blocking the movement of people and cargo through the city. Russian forces may be using shaped charges on their long-range drones to strike large, fortified targets such as the Pivdennyi Bridge, but causing significant damage in this way would require repeated, precise strikes over a short period of time

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Oct. 2 warned of "additional measures" against Ukraine if its government refuses to take responsibility for a downward spiral in Kyiv-Seoul relations.
President Volodymyr Zelensky angered Seoul after providing details of a transfer of North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to South Korea during a Sept. 23 U.N. General Assembly speech.
The two POWs were among the several thousand soldiers that North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un dispatched to help Russia fight off a Ukrainian incursion in Russia's Kursk Oblast in 2024.
South Korea claims Zelensky breached a confidentiality agreement between the two nations by revealing the transfer. The Ukrainian Presidential Office responded by claiming that no such agreement existed, prompting an additional rebuke from Seoul.
Kyiv's denial is "making the head of state of another country out to be a liar," Lee wrote on social media.
"If you (Ukraine) continue to refuse to acknowledge the facts and issue a public apology, we will take additional measures. As this is a matter concerning the honor of the Republic of Korea's people and nation, we cannot overlook it."
It is not clear what measures Lee is referring to, but South Korea is one of Ukraine's few clear supporters in East Asia and is considered a potential source of various types of military equipment, including PAC-3 Patriot interceptor missiles.
However, Seoul has long refused to provide direct military aid to Ukraine, citing legislative constraints and limiting its support to humanitarian and other non-lethal assistance.
Like most allies of Ukraine, South Korea retains its own connections to Russia and, along with Japan, has successfully lobbied the EU and the U.K. to allow it to continue importing Russian liquefied natural gas unimpeded.
In his social media post, Lee also said that "when we demanded acknowledgment of the agreement and an apology, they (Ukraine) instead spoke of an imminent military clash between North and South, praying for the outbreak of war on the Korean Peninsula."
Though Lee did not specify which comments he was referring to, Zelensky's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, warned in a recent interview that North Korea is learning lessons from the Russia-Ukraine war and building up its military capabilities to be ready for combat operations in its own region.

Arab party leader forced to withdraw from Israeli elections

Arab party leader forced to withdraw from Israeli elections
Palestinian participation in upcoming Knesset vote continues to shrink with withdrawal of Sami Abu Shehadeh.
Arab-Israeli party leader drops election bid
Arab Israeli politician Sami Abu Shehadeh has withdrawn his candidacy for the upcoming Israeli elections after the Supreme Court advised him to drop out.
The leader of the left-wing Palestinian Balad party announced on Friday he was dropping his bid for election to the Knesset on October 27.
His withdrawal, which came after the court threatened to disqualify him, comes amid recent efforts by Israeli authorities to block Arab Israeli parties from taking part.
Speaking to Al Jazeera on Friday, Abu Shehadeh said he withdrew because he “didn’t have any other choices”.
He said the push to bar Arab parties in Israel was aimed at keeping Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir in power.
“Netanyahu and Ben Gvir know that if the Arab-Palestinian community participate in the next election, this will be the highest wall preventing them from returning to rule,” he said.
Of 38 lists running in the election, only two represent the Arab Palestinian minority, he noted. “They’re trying to disqualify the two lists.”
Political analysts view Arab Israeli parties as potential kingmakers in the election, with polls showing neither Netanyahu’s coalition nor the main opposition bloc on course for an outright majority.
Abu Shehadeh’s withdrawal came after the Supreme Court indicated that a majority of its judges agreed with a September 23 decision from Israel’s Central Elections Committee to oust him from the race after nationalist political rivals accused him of supporting Hamas’s attack on October 7, 2023.
Adalah, a rights organisation representing Abu Shehadeh, condemned the court, saying the evidence it presented had no legal basis.
“The court has effectively decided to remove a Palestinian leader, a citizen of Israel, from the Knesset,” Adalah said in a statement.
“The court’s clear intention to disqualify him,” it added, was “a direction that would have set a dangerous legal precedent with devastating consequences”.
Abu Shehadeh served in the Knesset from 2019 to 2022. Balad confirmed he was withdrawing his candidacy but stressed that the decision did not mark the end of his political struggle and that he would remain party leader.
A ‘historical catastrophe’ for democracy
Israel’s elections committee voted to disqualify him at the request of far-right minister Ben-Gvir, who accused him of supporting the Hamas attack due to an article issued the following day in which Abu Shehadeh called it an “important historical event”.
Speaking to the Supreme Court on Thursday, Abu Shehadeh said he did not support “armed struggle” but acknowledged that a paragraph in the article had been incorrectly worded. He said his intention was to call for moving the conflict towards a political process.
Adalah labelled his withdrawal from the election “a severe blow to the right of Palestinian citizens to be represented and to stand for election”.
The elections committee also barred two Arab electoral lists: the United Arab List and the Joint List, a three-party alliance that includes Abu Shehadeh’s party Balad. But the Supreme Court overturned that decision on Friday.
Adalah has questioned why Palestinian candidates are being disqualified but far-right Israeli candidates were “cleared to run” despite openly calling for violence against Palestinians and making statements “amounting to incitement to genocide”.
Although the Supreme Court restored the United Arab List, and another Arab party, to the ballot on Friday, Shehadeh said the court’s reversal did not make the original disqualifications acceptable.
“In the end, what happened yesterday was a historical catastrophe for democracy, or the very narrow margins of democracy in the State of Israel,” he said. “I was disqualified because I think differently, because I have a different narrative on how to read history, the present, and the future in the place that we live today.”

Signal 2.0 perimeter surveillance system is deployed in Zaporozhye front of special op
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:25:11 UTC
18:25:11 KST

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. The Signal 2.0 mobile system for the rapid deployment of security systems is being deployed in the Zaporozhye and Volchansk sectors of Russia’s special military operation in Ukraine, Igor Potapov, an unmanned aircraft and electronic warfare expert and spokesman for the NPP Design Bureau, told TASS.
"The Signal 2.0 mobile system is designed for the rapid deployment of security systems at technically unprepared front lines and temporary facilities. It is optimized to operate in field conditions and at facilities with heightened requirements for stealth. Currently, the system is being used in the Zaporozhye and Volchansk sectors. It is also supplied to meet industrial needs where rapid perimeter and site monitoring is required," said Potapov.
According to him, the system is based on passive infrared detectors. "A breach is detected when a temperature contrast is identified between a moving object (a person) and the thermal background. The detection range in the base version is up to 2 km. With an additional antenna installed, the range can be extended to 10 km from the monitored area," the expert said.
Potapov also noted that the Signal system was developed in 2023 at the request of troops carrying out missions in the Zaporozhye area. "At that time, enemy reconnaissance and sabotage groups were actively operating along the line of contact. It was necessary to quickly deploy a monitoring and alarm system for areas of possible intrusion. We approached the process with a focus on speed and efficiency, aiming to bring an area under control in just a few minutes using sensors that can be mounted on any surface," he emphasized.
NPP also reported that the system has undergone a series of upgrades over the past few years. "Signal 2.0 has changed significantly: the control panel has effectively become ‘pocket-sized’ while retaining all of its original functionality and tasks. It features audible, visual, and vibrating alerts, and all modes can be disabled," Potapov said.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
He noted that Ukrainian strikes on domestic energy sites reduced Russia's gross domestic product by approximately 1%.
The statements follow claims from Moscow accusing NATO of planning a blockade of Kaliningrad, the Baltic exclave bordering Lithuania and Poland. Putin pointed to NATO naval drills in the Baltic Sea as a threat to the region's security.
NATO General Secretary Mark Rutte rejected these claims, emphasizing that alliance exercises are purely defensive and calling Moscow's nuclear messaging unhelpful.
Addressing the situation in Ukraine, Putin alleged that Russian strikes against Ukrainian energy and economic targets were direct responses to strikes on Russian oil refineries and Black Sea vessels, according to BBC.

Putin reiterated his position that broader international instability is driven by Western policies, warning of rising global risks associated with advanced weaponry and emerging technologies like artificial intelligence, BBC reported.
He called for updating global international rules, arguing that global tensions will shift as traditional international power dynamics continue to adjust.
Amid growing security concerns over potential aggression around Kaliningrad, Lithuania designed its future Gizai power substation, located 30 kilometers from the Russian exclave, to withstand physical sabotage and drone strikes, including attacks from multiple explosive-laden Shahed drones.
The 35-hectare facility, which formed part of the Harmony Link project connecting the Baltic power grid to Poland, featured reinforced concrete protective walls, vehicle-proof fencing, and underground tunnel sensors.
Litgrid CEO Andrius Semeskevicius emphasized that the grid was planned for hybrid and military threats following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the Baltic states' disconnection from the Russian electricity system in 2025. Regional security concerns had escalated due to recent infrastructure sabotage in Germany and fears of potential false-flag operations near the Suwalki Gap.

French President Emmanuel Macron (C) walks with France's Foreign Affairs Minister Jean-Noël Barrot (L) as they head to Trump Tower in New York City on Sept. 21, 2026, ahead of a meeting with US President Donald Trump. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — French officials proposed a large release of strategic oil and diesel reserves during emergency talks Friday after Washington urged European capitals to tap stockpiles or face a potentially crippling ban on fuel exports, according to two officials briefed on the meeting.
Under a proposal made during a gathering of senior European energy officials Friday, Paris suggested that EU countries release 50 million barrels of crude oil and 50 million barrels of diesel, according to the officials. The idea is still undergoing technical assessment, said one of the officials.
It comes after U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright asked European countries to release 120 million barrels from stockpiles over a three-month period to combat rising diesel prices or else face export restrictions. According to the officials, France's compromise offer Friday was in response to a fresh request by the U.S. to French President Emmanuel Macron to release 100 million barrels of fuel, all of which should be diesel.
Advertisement
Berlin, on the other hand, was reluctant to release any barrels, according to the officials. "Germany and others don't want to be used; they wish to release stocks only for real security of supply reasons," one of them told POLITICO, speaking on condition of anonymity to speak candidly, as with others in this piece. Germany and France have the largest reserves of oil and petroleum products in Europe, according to official EU statistics.
"France is keen to participate and meet the request ... it's clear the EU will do something, to the extent they can agree on something," said the second person. They added that it was unclear whether the release would be jointly coordinated by the EU or done on a bilateral basis, given the "messy" approach by the U.S., which has sent different requests to different countries. "It's a typical US request — they don't go through the official normal channels."
A spokesperson for French Economy Minister Roland Lescure dismissed the proposal as "rumors" and declined to comment further. In a statement, the Elysée palace said Emmanuel Macron will convene a meeting of G7 leaders "as soon as possible to coordinate the measures needed to help ease the pressure on prices and ensure the supply of crude oil and refined products among G7 countries and globally."
Macron had a phone call with U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday night to "discuss the global energy situation" and "ensure the global availability of refined products," the Elysée said.
European Commission spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said on Friday a ban on diesel exports "would undermine our trust in the United States as a reliable partner," adding: "We are ready for collective action in the context of the IEA. It is their role to organize possible stock release."
U.K. officials are expecting a G7 meeting to be convened as soon as Friday, but immediate outcomes are unlikely, according to a person familiar with the matter, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive fuel supply issues. Any European release of reserves would be IEA-led, the person said.
Advertisement
The U.S. is increasingly frustrated at EU countries that have failed to deliver on commitments to contribute to the 400 million barrel release coordinated earlier this year by the International Energy Agency following the outbreak of the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. In the high-level Energy Union Taskforce meeting Friday, some EU countries also rounded on France and Germany for their failure to release substantial oil reserves into the market, according to one of the officials.
POLITICO reported Thursday that leading EU countries and the U.K. wanted to respond to the U.S. pressure with an "assertive" voice while seeking to de-escalate.

AI usage among individuals, businesses in Türkiye doubles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:23:36 UTC
18:23:36 KST

Artificial intelligence utilization among individuals and enterprises across Türkiye doubled in 2026 as digital tools expanded across personal routines and corporate operations, the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) reported Oct. 2.
Generative AI usage among individuals surged to 37.6 percent from 19.2 percent in 2025. Women led adoption at 38.1 percent against 37.2 percent for men. Young people recorded the highest engagement, with the 16-24 age group reaching 64.9 percent and the 25-34 demographic at 55.7 percent. University graduates led educational levels at 62.7 percent, while primary school graduates trailed at 8.5 percent. Individuals deployed tools largely for private tasks at 86.4 percent and professional work at 37.3 percent.
Enterprise integration reached 14 percent, nearly doubling from 7.5 percent in 2025 and up from 2.7 percent in 2021. Firms with 250 or more employees led adoption at 37.1 percent, compared to 12.8 percent for small businesses. Sectorally, telecommunications and IT companies dominated at 63.7 percent. Businesses utilized AI primarily for marketing and sales at 51 percent, alongside research and innovation at 46.3 percent.
Open-source software accounted for 67.8 percent of corporate acquisitions. Some 16.6 percent of AI-integrated firms processed personal customer data. Companies avoiding the technology cited lacking internal expertise at 72.3 percent, liability ambiguities at 66.4 percent and privacy risks at 65.4 percent. The surge aligns with a worldwide push to draft comprehensive governance rules balancing technological innovation with data protection.

The incident prompted OpenAI to conduct a large-scale analysis of the activities of its AI models—so-called agents designed to perform tasks autonomously based on simple instructions.
This week, the AI lab said it had notified more than 100 organizations about incidents involving unauthorized activity carried out using its AI systems.
The notification "does not mean that any confidential information was obtained" or that the system was compromised, OpenAI said.
In September, researcher Jacob Coxon, who left Anthropic, called for slowing AI development so that its potential risks could be properly assessed.
Anthropic head Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also called for measures to address issues related to AI.

The survey published by daily Maariv also projected 12 seats for Arab parties and four for the Reservists party led by Yoaz Hendel.
Under the projections, neither Netanyahu’s camp nor the opposition would reach the 61-seat majority needed to form a government in the 120-member Knesset or parliament.
Most opposition leaders say they will not rely on Arab parties’ support to form a government, leaving prospects for a governing coalition uncertain.
Maariv said Netanyahu’s bloc gained two seats compared with the previous survey, while the opposition lost two, narrowing the gap between the camps to two seats.
Within Netanyahu’s camp, his Likud party was projected to win 19 seats, followed by extremist National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power with nine.
The ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism would each secure seven seats, while Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism would take five and Ofer Winter’s People of Israel party four.
Among opposition parties, Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar would win 21 seats, Naftali Bennett’s Together 13, Yair Golan’s Democrats 10, and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beytenu nine.
The Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, was projected to secure seven seats, while Mansour Abbas’s United Arab List would take five.
On the poll’s questions on suitability for prime minister, Eisenkot led Netanyahu by 47% to 41%, with the gap narrowing to six percentage points.
Bennett led Netanyahu by 45% to 41%, while Netanyahu led Lieberman 44% to 39%.
Israel’s prime minister is not directly elected. Forming a government depends on securing sufficient parliamentary support.
The poll also found that 67% of Israelis expressed concern about the possibility of a security incident on the scale of the Oct. 7, 2023 attack.
Of those surveyed, 43% were moderately concerned and 24% very concerned. Another 26% were not concerned, while 7% were undecided.
Lazar Research conducted the survey among 602 Israeli adults. Its margin of error was four percentage points.

Ambassador to UAE says flydubai incident didn't weaken Israel-Emirati relations - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:20:37 UTC
18:20:37 KST

Ambassador to the United Arab Emirates Yossi Shelley said the dramatic attack aboard a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv has not weakened the strategic relationship between Israel and the UAE, arguing instead that the Emirati authorities' response has demonstrated the strength of the ties established under the Abraham Accords.
In an interview with The Jerusalem Post on Friday, Shelley said he had received what he described as a “very warm” response from Emirati officials and members of the public following the September 30 incident, in which a co-pilot attacked the captain aboard flydubai flight FZ1073, sending the aircraft into a rapid descent before passengers and crew helped regain control.
“I definitely feel a warm embrace,” Shelley told the Post. “Of course there is concern," he said.
Shelley said the response he has received from senior Emirati officials has reinforced his assessment that the relationship between Jerusalem and Abu Dhabi remains deep.
For example, he described calling a senior Emirati business executive around 1 a.m. about the aviation situation and receiving a response shortly afterward.
“I called him at one in the morning, and he called me back at 1:10,” Shelley said. “Who calls you back at 1:10 at night because you have a question about flights tomorrow?”
Investigation being conducted by Israeli, Saudi, Emirati authorities
Shelley said that the investigation into the flydubai incident is being conducted by the relevant authorities in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Israel. On Thursday, the Omani co-pilot was transferred to the UAE for further investigation. “The UAE are investigating, they are doing everything that needs to be done, and we trust them", Shelley said. Israel is preparing to send an investigation team to the country.
Shelly emphasized the importance for Israel of determining whether the attacker acted independently or was sent by someone else.
“We have a very, very big interest, just like everyone else, in knowing whether someone came because somebody sent him, or whether he acted alone,” Shelley said. “We want to know the result because there are implications afterward.”
Shelley said the incident should lead to broader consideration of how flight crews are screened, particularly when airlines operate routes connecting countries that are experiencing political or military tensions.
“When we leave the country and arrive in other countries, they ask us: Where did you come from? What did you bring?” he said. “We need to raise the level and ask the pilots as well: What did you bring and where did you come from?”
He added that authorities should consider the nationalities and backgrounds of pilots when assigning crews to sensitive routes.
“I don’t want to send an Iranian pilot to Israel, or a pilot from a country involved in a war with us,” Shelley said, while stressing that he was speaking about the need for authorities to consider such issues rather than identifying a particular country as responsible for the flydubai incident.
Ambassador expresses gratitude to heroic captain
Shelley also thanked Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot who was injured in the attack.
Machchhar was stabbed during the incident but managed to open the cockpit door, allowing others to intervene. Israeli passengers subsequently helped subdue the attacker and prevent the aircraft from crashing.
Shelley said he had spoken with India’s ambassador in the UAE and told him that Israel wanted to find a way to formally thank Machchhar.
“I told him that I want him to speak with the prime minister,” Shelley said. “We really are grateful to him, and of course to all the people who have been talked about and will be talked about.”
Shelley said he had hoped to visit Machchhar personally after the injured pilot was transferred to the UAE, but that logistical and security arrangements had so far prevented the visit.
Not a threat to Abraham Accords
Asked directly what the incident could mean for the Abraham Accords and Israel’s relationship with the UAE, Shelley rejected the idea that the attack could fundamentally damage the partnership.
“Let’s say what it did not do,” Shelley said. “It did not succeed in bringing them down. It tried to break them. It tried to break us. We are strong.”
He pointed to the decision to resume Israeli airline operations to the UAE as evidence that the relationship had not been derailed.
“It did exactly the opposite,” Shelley said of the impact of the incident on the bilateral relationship.
He argued that the UAE’s willingness to allow Israeli carriers to resume operations demonstrated continued confidence in the relationship.
“There is something important here,” Shelley said. “This is not a temporary agreement. It is a way of life. It is a partnership between partners.”
Shelley sought to play down reports of a broader crisis over the resumption of flights between Israel and the UAE.
He said Israeli carriers were expected to begin landing later on Friday and continue operations over the coming days.
“There is no crisis, no major event,” Shelley said.
He described the situation as a matter of establishing new procedures following the incident, including determining how baggage should be handled and screened.
“There are all kinds of things that are part of the setup,” he said. “They don’t want to fall into the second trap.”
The ambassador said the relationship with Abu Dhabi had already endured the unprecedented regional tensions of recent years and that the latest incident would not, in his assessment, change its fundamental trajectory.
“This is a partnership,” he said. “It’s not something temporary.”

Simchat Torah 2026: What exactly are we so joyous about?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:20:28 UTC
18:20:28 KST

On Simchat Torah, we mark the completion of the annual cycle of Torah reading and the beginning of a new cycle.
Jewish custom is to read the portion of Vezot Habracha and, immediately afterward, to begin reading the first portion, Bereshit, creating an unbroken continuity between the conclusion of the Torah and its beginning.
Rabbi Yaakov ben Rabbeinu Asher wrote about this:
“It is called Simchat Torah because on it we complete the Torah, and it is fitting to rejoice upon its completion. It is customary to begin Bereshit immediately, so that Satan will have no opportunity to accuse us, saying: They have already finished it and do not wish to read it again” (Tur, Orah Hayim, Laws of Lulav, 669).
The conclusion of the Torah and the beginning anew are not two separate things. Precisely because we finish, we hurry to begin again. Had we waited until the following Shabbat to begin reading it again, the conclusion might have seemed like a farewell. Beginning immediately teaches us that the conclusion is not an ending in the sense of parting, but, rather, is meant to make possible a new beginning, with a desire to learn anew.
What exactly am I so happy about?
THIS IDEA takes on special meaning when we consider our relationship to Simchat Torah.
Some people do not feel a sense of connection to the holiday. In particular, someone who does not study Torah regularly might ask: What exactly am I so happy about? What connection do I have to dancing around the Torah scroll when, in my everyday life, I hardly ever open it?
One way to answer this is through a folk tale about a simple villager who was seen dancing with all his might with the Torah scroll, singing, “Your Torah is better for me than thousands of pieces of gold and silver.” When people asked him, “But you haven’t opened a book in a long time,” he replied: “If my brother is getting married, shouldn’t I celebrate with him?”
This story carries a profound point. The joy of Simchat Torah is not merely an individual’s personal joy. It is joy about the Torah that exists within the people of Israel; about the connection it creates between the Jewish nation and the Creator of the world; about a Torah-centered world that continues from generation to generation; and about the people within this nation who have devoted their lives to its study. Even if I have not yet found the time and place for it in my own life, the Torah is not foreign to me. It belongs to my family, to my people, to the tradition from which I come. If my brother gets married, I rejoice in his wedding; if the Jewish nation rejoices in the Torah, I, too, share in that joy.
Another way to understand the nature of this joy is this: Dancing with the Torah is not merely an expression of joy that already exists; sometimes, it is the joy itself that creates the connection. When a person dances with the Torah, he brings himself into the joy, even if at first he does not feel a deep connection to Torah study. The very effort to rejoice can open the heart and prepare a person for a new connection with the Torah.
This also has enormous educational significance. A child who sees his father rejoicing with the Torah, dancing with it and expressing his love for it, receives a message far more powerful than any explanation: the Torah is not merely a system of obligations, but something filled with life and joy.
Even if the father has not succeeded in incorporating Torah study into his daily routine, the dancing the child witnesses may influence him years later and awaken in him a desire to become a person of Torah.
AND YET, we can still ask: How can someone who does not feel connected to the world of Torah relate to this joy? How can he dance enthusiastically with something he feels is not a meaningful part of his life?
In his book Pahad Yitzchak on Sukkot, Rabbi Yitzchak Hutner recounts a story about two students of the Hiddushei HaRim, the first Gerrer rebbe. The two students were dancing with tremendous enthusiasm on Simchat Torah. The Hiddushei HaRim looked at them and said to those around him: “Look at these two. One of them will tire before the other.” Indeed, a short while later, one of the students grew weak and stopped dancing, while his friend continued dancing with renewed strength.
When the rebbe was asked how he knew this in advance, he explained:
The student who became tired was dancing out of joy over the Torah he had studied in the past. There is a limit and measure to Torah that has already been attained, and therefore his joy eventually came to an end, and he became tired.
The student who did not grow tired was dancing with joy over the Torah he would study in the future. And since the future has no limit, his joy never ended.
The Hiddushei HaRim added:
“The world thinks that we rejoice on Simchat Torah because we have finished the Torah. But the truth is that we rejoice because we are beginning the Torah anew.”
These words offer a new perspective on Simchat Torah: the joy is primarily about what is yet to come. Someone who studied Torah throughout the year can rejoice over what he has accomplished, but even someone who did not manage to study as much as he had hoped does not need to stand outside the circle of joy. The dancing is not a celebration of past achievements, but of the possibility of beginning again.
We finish so that we can begin
From this perspective, on Simchat Torah we all start from the same place. One person arrives after a year in which he studied a great deal of Torah, while another barely studied at all. One arrives with great accomplishments, while another arrives with a sense of missed opportunities. But when we open the Book of Genesis once again, both stand before the same Torah, the same possibility, the same year that has not yet been written.
Now we understand why, immediately after completing the Torah, we begin the Book of Genesis anew, rather than waiting until the following Shabbat. This is the heart of the matter: we finish so that we can begin. The conclusion is not a point at which we stop and look backward, but the moment from which we set out on a new journey. In this sense, the familiar phrase “Every ending is a new beginning” takes on a particularly profound meaning on Simchat Torah.
On Simchat Torah, we do not need to ask ourselves only how much Torah we studied during the year that has passed. We can ask a different question: How much are we prepared to study in the year that is about to begin?
For Simchat Torah is not only the joy of those who have completed the Torah. It is also, and perhaps above all, the joy of those who are ready to open it anew.
Chag Sameach.■
The writer is the rabbi of the Western Wall and holy sites.
SIMCHAT TORAH
RABBI SHMUEL RABINOWITZ

Women, girls make up 53% of people facing added food insecurity due to Mideast escalation: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:20:05 UTC
18:20:05 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Women and girls account for 53% of the projected 22 million additional people who could face food insecurity by the end of this year due to the Mideast escalation and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, according to a UN Women analysis released Friday.
That amounts to an additional 11.7 million women and girls across the 28 countries analyzed, on top of an estimated 208 million who were already food insecure or undernourished, it said.
“When food becomes scarce, women eat less and last,” UN Women Deputy Executive Director Nyaradzayi Gumbonzvanda said, noting that women often shift to less nutritious diets or skip meals to prioritize others.
The analysis said disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz are increasing energy, fertilizer and transport costs, pushing food prices higher.
According to the analysis, countries such as South Sudan, Sudan, Haiti, Yemen, and Palestine face more concentrated risks, as multiple sources of vulnerability overlap.
Sudan's female population faces highest risk
In South Sudan, the additional number of women and girls who could face food insecurity represents around 14%, or one in seven, of the country's female population, the highest proportion among the 28 countries analyzed.
Lebanon follows with nearly 4% of its female population potentially facing additional food insecurity.
Women and girls are also expected to account for a particularly high share of those potentially affected in several countries, including 60% in Afghanistan, more than 57% in Yemen, and nearly 56% in Sudan.
The analysis also highlighted employment and financial inequalities that could leave women less able to absorb rising food prices and income losses.
Around 80% of women in Egypt, Iraq, Palestine, Sudan and Syria are outside the labor force, rising to around 95% in Afghanistan and Yemen.
Among employed women, more than 80% are in vulnerable employment in Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, Haiti, Mali, and South Sudan.
Financial access also remains limited, with fewer than one in five women in Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, and Yemen owning a bank or mobile money account, according to the analysis.
UN Women called for food and cash assistance alongside nutrition, protection, livelihoods and agricultural support.
It also urged resources to be targeted to places where women and girls face multiple, overlapping risks, and delivered at the right time – including ahead of agricultural seasons.

These are the easiest countries to be a digital nomad in, according to a new study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:19:23 UTC
18:19:23 KST

Holafly’s Digital Nomad Friction Index 2026 looked at factors such as visa complexity, banking access, healthcare and cost of living.
Becoming a digital nomad is a goal for many remote workers, but the hoops you have to jump through to achieve it vary from place to place.
Bureaucracy can be a beast in any country, but certain destinations are making it easier for those who want to set up shop abroad.
Now, we know exactly which places are doing so thanks to Holafly’s Digital Nomad Friction Index 2026.
The eSIM company analysed 17 popular digital nomad destinations, looking at factors such as visa complexity, banking access, healthcare, connectivity, cost of living and disruption risk, in order to create an overall friction score.
“Arriving to a country is usually the easy part. The real burnout happens when remote professionals hit a wall of post-landing bureaucracy, lost work hours, and unstable internet,” Metin Kastro, COO at Holafly, said.
“We ran this study to shed light on these hidden friction points because long-term mobility only works when everyday logistics stop eating into people’s livelihoods and peace of mind.”
The easiest countries to set up in as a digital nomad
After all the number crunching, one destination came out on top with the lowest friction score: Georgia.
The Caucasus nation has no mandatory residence registration, no tax ID requirement, and you can open a bank account with just a passport within hours, making it a bureaucratic breeze.
Next up is Peru, which came in second place to its Rentista residency category which allows for indefinite permanent residency with a low income threshold. It was beaten out for the top spot because of its earthquake and El Niño exposure.
Third place went to South Africa, which has no mandatory address registration or tax ID for non-residents, but was let down by its below-average healthcare score.
Thailand and Malaysia are in fourth and fifth place respectively, with purpose-built digital nomad visa programmes and moderate banking friction as pluses, but natural disaster exposure among the negatives.
The only European nations to make the top 10 were Croatia, Hungary and Poland, in seventh, eighth and ninth place respectively. All three have nomad visa programmes, but mandatory registration and tax ID requirements held them back from securing a higher spot.
The top 10 countries for pain-free digital nomad set-up
- Georgia
- Peru
- South Africa
- Thailand
- Malaysia
- Vietnam
- Croatia
- Hungary
- Portugal
- UAE

Russian troops shoot down own Mi-8, killing three crew
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:18:54 UTC
18:18:54 KST

- Russian forces shot down their own Mi-8 helicopter over the Voronezh region on Oct. 1, killing all three crew members.
- A ground-based air defense crew mistook the helicopter for an enemy drone, the latest in a series of Russian friendly fire helicopter losses.
Russian forces shot down one of their own Mi-8 military helicopters over the Voronezh region on Oct. 1, killing all three crew members.
The helicopter was hit by a Russian Su-35 fighter during operations to move aircraft out of the way of a Ukrainian drone strike, sources said. The Su-35 crew apparently mistook the helicopter for a Ukrainian drone.
The Mi-8 came down in a field in the Anninsky district, about 80 km (50 miles) from the city of Voronezh and roughly 200 km (125 miles) from the Ukrainian border. The crew of three, a pilot, a navigator and a gunner, were killed, Russian Telegram channel Mash reported on the evening of the crash.
The Mi-8 is the Soviet-designed twin-engine transport helicopter that forms the backbone of Russia’s military rotary-wing fleet. Armed versions carry rockets and machine guns and are used for troop transport, resupply, medical evacuation and, increasingly, for hunting Ukrainian long-range drones at low altitude.
The Su-35 is Russia’s most advanced fighter in wide service and is regularly sent up to intercept Ukrainian drones over Russian territory. A slow, low-flying helicopter can be hard to tell apart from a large drone on radar or at night, especially when Russian pilots and air defense crews are working in the same airspace during a raid.
Russian officials have not publicly acknowledged that the helicopter was downed by friendly fire. Several Russian military bloggers have hinted at the cause without stating it directly.
“The cause is a classic one, which humanity is unlikely ever to defeat, despite AI, robots, neural networks, ‘friend or foe’ and other wonders of science and technology,” wrote Ilya Tumanov, who runs the Fighterbomber Telegram channel and is known for his ties to Russian military aviation.
The shootdown is the latest in a series of friendly fire losses involving Russian helicopters, many of them during Ukrainian drone raids.
On July 2, a Ka-52 attack helicopter crashed in the same Voronezh region. Russian military blogger Vladimir Romanov said it was hit by a Verba shoulder-fired missile fired by a mobile fire group from Russia’s BARS reserve units, according to The Insider. One crew member was killed.
On March 3, Russian forces likely shot down one of their own helicopters near Millerovo in the Rostov region during a Ukrainian drone attack, The Defence Blog reported, after pro-government Russian sources said air defenses had mistaken it for a drone.
A Russian fighter jet has been linked to at least one earlier case. When a Ka-52M was shot down during a counter-drone operation in late 2025, the Telegram channel Pozivnoi Katsman suggested the strike may have come from a Russian fighter.
In June 2024, air defenses near Anapa shot down a Russian Ka-29 helicopter, killing all four people on board. By late 2025, The Insider counted at least 17 Russian aircraft lost to friendly fire since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Europe’s hottest summer ‘caused record heat stress’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:18:48 UTC
18:18:48 KST

A record 52 percent of Europe was exposed to intense heat stress during the exceptionally hot summer that seared the continent this year, the EU’s climate monitor said on Oct. 2.
Fueled by climate change, the world’s fastest-warming continent endured a relentless series of heatwaves that began unusually early in the spring, shattering temperature records and causing tens of thousands of excess deaths.
“One of the things that stands out for 2026 is that the heat was not only remarkable for its intensity, but also for its geographical extent,” said Samantha Burgess, climate lead at the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which operates Copernicus.
It was the continent’s third warmest summer on record and the hottest for western Europe, with several countries reporting all-time temperature highs.
Four of Europe’s top 10 heat waves occurred this past summer alone, Burgess said in a media briefing, with August 2003 still ranking as the most severe ever recorded.
This left 52 percent of Europe exposed to “very strong” heat stress, when temperatures feel hotter than 38 degrees Celsius, according to Copernicus.
Around 80 percent of the continent experienced “strong” heat stress, or feels-like temperatures of more than 32 degrees, which occurred on a record 41 days by the end of the season.
“Summer 2026 demonstrated how heat stress is becoming both more widespread and more persistent,” Burgess said, noting that it was the leading cause of weather-related mortality globally.

What does music look like? This British artist paints what he hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:18:02 UTC
18:18:02 KST

Sounds can sometimes interrupt Andrew’s thoughts, but he sees synaesthesia as an inseparable part of his life.
For British artist Jake Andrew, music has colour, shape and texture. His paintings capture what he sees when he hears it.
Andrew has synaesthesia, a rare neurological condition in which one sensory experience can trigger another. For him, sounds produce an immediate visual response.
His favourite instrument to paint is the cello.
“It's dark, but it doesn't feel ominous," he says. "It's got this kind of like... and then edge of.... Does this make any sense? Like the edge of the tube itself, of where the sound comes from has these kind of like almost dust particles that come off it."
These responses extend to everyday sounds. A passing motorbike appears dark purple to Andrew, while a friend’s dog’s bark takes on a lime-green colour.
In September, he brought that way of experiencing sound to a live performance at the Handbag Factory in Vauxhall, London, United Kingdom.
Pianists Camden Stewart and Karim Kamar improvised around their original compositions as Andrew translated the music into paint.
The results do not always follow familiar associations between colour and mood. A minor key need not produce a sombre-looking painting.
“E minor, that's usually dark blue, slow legato movements where it's kind of like swirling,” he explains.
Finding the meeting point between visual and audio
Experts say sound-to-colour synaesthesia, known as chromesthesia, can also involve shapes, movement and texture.
“It's the shapes, it's the movement, it's texture and all of these things, and how it's organised in space as well,” shares Jamie Ward, professor of cognitive neuroscience at the University of Sussex.
Sounds can sometimes interrupt Andrew’s thoughts, but he sees synaesthesia as an inseparable part of his life.
“It's not a curse, though. I can't imagine what it would be like to not have it,” says Andrew.
For the musicians who are taking part in the live performance, it has been a fascinating process.
“That's like asking me 'what does a fourth dimension look like?' I can't even fathom it.”

“This is a matter concerning the dignity of the Republic of Korea and its people and cannot be overlooked,” Lee posted on X on Oct. 2.

Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga told a briefing Thursday that he would “not like to call it an incident,” describing it instead as a “diplomatic misunderstanding.”
“I very much want this situation to be resolved in the short term, and we are working on this. For us, South Korea is an important country,” he added.

Stephanie Rady and Lina Altawell
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam on Friday called for efforts to secure Israel’s full withdrawal from Lebanon and strengthen state authority, amid continued Israeli attacks in the south.
“The real way forward is in mobilizing whatever resources and support we can to achieve a full Israeli withdrawal and rebuild a capable and effective state ... with one army and one decision-making (authority),” Salam said at a news conference during a visit to the southern city of Nabatieh.

Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his election rival Flavio Bolsonaro are leaving no controversy unturned in their last-ditch efforts to discredit each other and win over voters ahead of Oct. 4’s nail-biter election.
A campaign dominated by scandals and insults has done little to ease the deep political polarization in Latin America’s biggest economy, one of the last major leftist bastions in the region.
The tight race pits Lula, 80, against the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of Donald Trump who has backed a wave of victorious right-wing candidates in Latin America.
Trump said on Oct. 1 he was watching Brazil’s election “very closely.”
Opinion polls predict the vote will go to a runoff on Oct. 25, with Lula and Flavio in a dead heat.
“The race is tied but not at a standstill: The final week will determine where the voters who can still be swayed will go,” Felipe Nunes, director of the Quaest polling institute, told AFP.
Many of the nation’s 160 million registered voters are disenchanted with their options and were deprived of a debate between the leading candidates when both declined to attend a televised program on Oct. 1 evening.
The race for undecided voters has had both sides on alert for anything they can twist to their advantage.
In recent days, Brazil’s beloved patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida, depicted as a Black Madonna, became the focus as rumors erupted that Flavio Bolsonaro planned to strip her of her post if elected.
Flavio issued fierce denials as Lula took to the campaign trail clutching a statue of the saint, declaring that “messing” with her was “unacceptable.”
The electoral court ordered on Oct. 1 that posts with the “untrue” claims be taken down.
Lula tends to have more support among Catholics while Bolsonaro has the backing of a booming Evangelical population.
Next, Flavio Bolsonaro and his supporters pounced when Lula said that men were “cowards” when it comes to getting their prostates examined, while “women learn to receive a touch from a young age,” referring to gynecological exams.
Clips of his comment circulated widely on social media as if it were an allusion to abuse, and Flavio Bolsonaro accused Lula of being “sexist.”
“It’s really turned into a circus, my vote won’t go to any of them,” said Gisele Sousa, 45, a clothing shop employee.
In another jab during a podcast on Oct. 1, Lula said he was sure he would win in the first round, over a rival he said was not even qualified “to serve as a building manager.”
Veteran leftist Lula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, boasting he is fitter than ever despite his advanced age.
The former union leader has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment while massively curbing deforestation in the Amazon rainforest.
Nevertheless, voters complain about a high cost of living and are fed up with violence and crime.
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has remained a tough foe for Lula, even as it emerged he was under investigation for corruption over the financing of the biopic “Dark Horse” about his father.

Breadcrumb
During visit to south, Lebanon PM says scale of war recovery beyond state's capacity
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said Friday that rebuilding regions destroyed in the latest Israeli war on Lebanon was beyond the state's capacity, calling for funding as he visited the heavily damaged south.
"I am aware of the magnitude of the crisis" including the destruction, displacement and loss of livelihoods due to Israeli attacks, Salam said in Nabatieh, a major southern city hit hard by airstrikes.
"But the scale of the needs exceeds the capacities of the Lebanese state and its ability to bear these burdens alone," Salam added. "We still need significant funding" for reconstruction, the prime minister said.
Fighting broke out in March during the early period of the US-Israeli war on Iran, as Lebanese militant group Hezbollah shot rockets and Israel unleashed massive airstrikes and a ground invasion.
The fighting followed another war that erupted in 2023 related to Israel's genocide of Gaza.
Lebanon has put the overall death toll from these Israeli wars on the country at more than 8,900.
Hundreds of thousands of people remain displaced, mainly from the south, while Israel maintains troops in a self-declared "security zone" running around 10 kilometres (six miles) inside Lebanon along the border.
Last month, Salam said the estimated total cost of the two wars could exceed $27 billion.
"I am here today to affirm the return to work of state institutions," he said during Friday's visit.
Violence has decreased since a ceasefire following a US-Iran memorandum of understanding in June, while Lebanon and Israel concluded a US-sponsored framework agreement later that month.
But Nabatieh and surrounding areas in particular have seen continued Israeli attacks.
The Israel-Lebanon deal involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon's south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in test areas known as "pilot zones".
Salam said it was important to rally "all the capabilities and support we can to achieve a full Israeli withdrawal" and build a state that is the sole decision maker on war and peace.
"This is the path to avoid finding ourselves once again facing a new war or new pretexts to attack Lebanon, or a new expansion of the (Israeli) occupation," he added.

Ukraine has limited contingency plans for Russian attacks on water supply – NYT
Ukrainian officials have said they are concerned that Ukraine does not have a sufficiently developed contingency plan in the event of large-scale Russian strikes on its water supply system.
Source: The New York Times, citing its sources
Details: Russia has never previously carried out large-scale strikes on water infrastructure facilities.
A Russian plan for attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, which Ukraine reportedly intercepted, states that Moscow intends to target Ukraine's water supply system with dozens of ballistic missiles and glide bombs, including pumping stations and water treatment facilities.
The New York Times notes that Ukrainian officials have privately expressed concern that the country has limited contingency plans for major disruptions to its water supply.
Background: According to an approved Russian plan reportedly intercepted by Ukraine, Russia plans to cut Ukrainian nuclear power plants off from the power grid during its winter attacks by striking targets within a kilometre of the plants, as well as carrying out large-scale attacks on water supply systems.

Gaza toddlers evacuated in incubators return home after 2 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:11:26 UTC
18:11:26 KST

Bissan’s life began in the chaos of war, and her first months were marked by separation from the mother she had never known.
Two weeks after the war in Gaza began in October 2023, an Israeli airstrike hit Bissan’s family home in Beit Lahiya, killing a sister she would never meet. The blast severely injured her pregnant mother, Sundus al-Kurd, who was forced to deliver Bissan six weeks early to save their lives.
She was evacuated to Egypt in an ambulance, inside an incubator, with 28 other premature babies.
Seven of those children died in Egypt. Bissan survived.
She spent the next two years growing up in Egyptian hospitals and a care home, away from her parents. Her mother remained in Gaza, holding onto hope that they would be reunited.
Whenever she had internet access, Sundus made video calls to her daughter.
In March this year, Bissan was brought back to Gaza in a U.N.-assisted operation. She was among 11 children from the group evacuated to Egypt in 2023 who were returned to their families.
But the reunion was not what Sundus had imagined.
Bissan did not recognize her.
The toddler would call any woman who showed her affection “mama,” Sundus said. After spending most of her life away from her family, Bissan had to learn who her mother was.
Reuters documented their reunion and followed Bissan and several other children as they rebuilt relationships with their parents.
Returning home has also meant learning to live where the sounds of war remain part of everyday life.
Bissan returned to Gaza as a toddler, but she was coming home to a war zone.
When she first heard explosions, she would freeze in fear for several minutes, Sundus said. Even a balloon popping can still trigger panic.
“Her life changed. Her life became sleeping and waking up to the sound of explosions, to the sound of the numerous attacks and missiles,” Sundus said.
Yet there are moments when fear gives way to childhood curiosity.
Soon after their reunion, Sundus took Bissan to a small zoo in central Gaza. Wearing pink-framed glasses, the girl watched as a blue parrot perched on her mother’s arm.
For Sundus, such moments are part of helping her daughter rediscover childhood.
Not every child returned to Gaza was able to meet a mother who had been waiting for them.
For Ibrahim, the reunion with his mother was already impossible.
His mother, Israa Badr, gave birth to him during the eighth month of pregnancy. After her premature son was evacuated to Egypt, she fell into a deep depression. She died the following month.
Her husband, Jabri Badr, said doctors told the family she had died from overwhelming sadness.
“Ever since he was in her womb, she thought about him, dreamed of holding him, playing with him, and feeling what it was like to be a mother,” he said.
Ibrahim has since been reunited with his father in Gaza. But their separation has left another bond to rebuild.
“He was supposed to call me dad,” Badr said. “Today he doesn’t even say dad, or anything. I tell him to come, and he ignores me.”
Arafat Abu Mashayikh, a Gaza-based mental health expert, said the children and their parents would need time to reconnect after nearly two years apart.
The separation deprived the children of their mothers’ presence.
“They were deprived not only of their mother’s milk but also of her embrace and the emotional development that comes with it,” Abu Mashayikh said.
For Bissan and Sundus, the bond is returning through everyday routines.
Some days, they walk to Gaza’s Mediterranean shoreline. On a recent afternoon, they held hands along the sand. Bissan smiled as she looked toward the horizon.
Nights are harder.
When explosions shake the area, Bissan wakes up and searches for her mother. Those moments have brought them closer.
Sundus said her daughter is beginning to understand who she is and what it means to have a mother.
“Bissan has begun to understand who mama really is, who her mother really is,” Sundus said. “I am the only person present in her life. I am the one who feeds her, changes her clothes, combs her hair, and plays with her.”
For a child whose life began with an airstrike and who spent her earliest years separated from her family, the bond is still being built.
Each walk, embrace and frightened midnight search is helping Bissan learn the meaning of the word she once used for any woman who showed her kindness: “Mama.”
