Pete Hegseth creates Pentagon Office of Religious Affairs reporting directly to him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:51:33 UTC
17:51:33 KST

Hegseth has infused his evangelical Christianity into his leadership of the Pentagon, hosting worship services for employees and often speaking of the United States as a Christian nation.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is launching an office of religious affairs, the latest of his faith-related reforms at the Pentagon.
He announced in a speech on Wednesday that the office will help offer “first-class religious support” and will report directly to him.
“Our department is, you might say, putting on the full armour of God, because while we wage physical war, we all know the real battle is spiritual,” he said.
Hegseth has infused his evangelical Christianity into his leadership of the Pentagon, hosting worship services for employees and often speaking of the United States as a Christian nation.
The Office of Religious Affairs (ORA) will advocate for military chaplains and religious support “at the highest level of the Department,” according to a Pentagon statement.
It will not “compel religious participation, favour one faith, or diminish the rights of personnel of any faith or lack thereof.”
Some criticism of the initiative surfaced quickly.
The Pentagon “owes it to the nation’s service members to defend religious freedom,” said Rachel Laser, head of Americans United for Separation of Church, which has sued the Pentagon over its worship services.
“Hegseth’s latest announcement violates that promise by elevating Christianity to an even higher role in shaping US military policy.”
Other federal agencies have had religious or faith-based offices, which were established under President George W. Bush and were continued in different forms under the Obama and Biden administrations.
President Donald Trump established a White House Faith Office and had a similar effort during his first term.
Shaun Casey, a religion scholar, led the State Department’s Office of Religion and Global Affairs during the Obama administration.
The office did not promote religion or spiritual well-being, he said. “It was there to understand what were the political implications of lived religion in the various hot spots around the world.”
The leader of the new office has not been named. A Pentagon memo said the religious affairs director will coordinate spiritual resources, including “faith-based homeschool support for military families.”
Hegseth has also pushed the military school system to introduce more coursework that draws from conservative and Christian influences.
The memo mentions “faith-based initiatives supporting Department-wide suicide reduction.”
In recent years, the military has become increasingly dependent on chaplains to help address the growing numbers of troops in mental health distress.
Hegseth has said he wants chaplains to focus more on God and less on therapeutic “self-help and self-care.”
The secretary has pushed other changes within the military’s chaplain corps, which provides spiritual care to troops.
He ordered chaplains, who are commissioned officers, to no longer wear their rank on their uniform but instead be identified by religious insignia.
The Defence Department also slashed the number of religious affiliations it officially recognises, down to 31 from more than 200 previously recognised traditions.
The list no longer includes atheists, Unitarian Universalists, pagans and Wiccans.
Hegseth spoke directly to chaplains in his address at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia. Using Christian-inflected language, he said: “Live your calling. Stand firm. Preach truth. Minister to the flock.”
He then quoted from the Bible: “The Lord is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do unto me?”

Asian Games | Wu Yibing reaches Asian Games tennis men's singles final
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:49:11 CST
17:49:11 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Despite battling a cold, China's Wu Yibing advanced to the men's singles final at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games here on Friday, defeating Japan's Hayato Matsuoka 6-3, 6-2.
Wu said after the match that it was the second day of his illness. "My physical condition is actually worse than yesterday. My throat felt quite sore when I woke up today, and I also had a runny nose. But once I got into the match, I felt fine," Wu said.
Wu was broken early in the first set but quickly broke back to level at 3-3. He broke Matsuoka again in the eighth game before holding serve to close out the set 6-3.
In the second set, Wu broke serve in the third game when Matsuoka sent a return long. Wu broke his opponent again in the fifth game to extend his lead and went on to seal the victory.
"I was a little more consistent than my opponent today. On the key points, I made some small adjustments to disrupt his rhythm. I also changed my positioning when returning serve to put more pressure on him," Wu said.
"I handled the important points better. Even after building a lead in the second set, I stayed calm. I wanted to keep applying consistent pressure throughout the match," the third-seeded Chinese player added.
Wu will face Coleman Wong of Hong Kong, China, in the final.
The two have had a series of memorable encounters in recent years.
At the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou, Wu lost to Wong in a grueling match lasting two hours and 48 minutes. Wu squandered five match points in the deciding-set tiebreak and was eliminated before the quarterfinals.
The pair met again in the semifinals of China's 15th National Games in 2025, where another tense tiebreak proved decisive. This time, Wu rallied to win 2-1 after two hours and 47 minutes.
"I lost to him at the last Asian Games on home soil, and eight years ago was also the last time I reached the Asian Games final. It feels like fate has brought us together again. I hope I can perform well tomorrow and win the gold medal," Wu said. ■

Congo Ebola death toll hits 4,000 as violence hampers response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:49:00 UTC
17:49:00 KST

The Democratic Republic of the Congo's Ebola outbreak has killed nearly 4,000 people and infected more than 8,200, with violence and mass displacement in the country's east making it increasingly difficult for health workers to track infections and contain the virus.
The health ministry reported 8,224 confirmed cases and 3,982 deaths as of Sept. 29, putting the crude case-fatality rate at about 48%. More than 2,200 patients have recovered, while hundreds remained hospitalized or in isolation.
The outbreak, declared May 15, is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, a species of Ebola for which there is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment.
It has spread across 63 health zones in seven provinces, with Ituri remaining the epicenter and cases also reported in North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, Bas-Uele, Tshopo and Sud Ubangi.
The scale of the outbreak has made it the deadliest Ebola epidemic in Congo's history, surpassing the 2018-2020 outbreak caused by the Zaire species.
It is also the second-largest Ebola outbreak recorded globally, behind the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic, which infected more than 28,000 people and killed over 11,000.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has warned that the virus is continuing to reach new health zones, stretching an already heavily pressured response.
WHO has classified the risk inside Congo as very high and the risk to neighboring countries as high, particularly as infections have appeared in areas near international borders.
Bundibugyo virus is a zoonotic disease believed to have a natural reservoir in fruit bats. It can initially spread to humans through contact with infected animals and then pass between people through blood, secretions and other bodily fluids.
Health facilities with weak infection-control measures and burial practices involving close contact with the dead can accelerate transmission.
Symptoms usually appear within two to 21 days and can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat before progressing to gastrointestinal problems and, in severe cases, organ failure and bleeding.
Without an approved vaccine or specific therapy for Bundibugyo virus, the response depends heavily on early diagnosis, isolation, contact tracing, safe burials and supportive treatment.
Health authorities have expanded laboratory capacity and treatment facilities, but insecurity and difficult terrain continue to limit access to affected communities.
The latest setback came at Kigonze, a displacement camp near Bunia in Ituri province that had housed about 19,000 people.
Security forces entered the camp searching for weapons and people suspected of links to armed groups, according to Congolese and health officials.
Clashes followed, prompting thousands of residents to flee over several days and leaving the camp largely abandoned.
The exodus has created a major problem for Ebola surveillance. Two health officials familiar with the situation told Reuters that about 1,000 people identified as Ebola contacts were living at the camp. Only about one-fifth had been traced after residents fled, according to one of the officials.
An Ebola transit center at Kigonze, where suspected patients could be isolated, tested and treated, was also burned down.
Julien Harneis, the U.N.'s senior Ebola coordinator in Congo, said the developments had made an already enormous challenge even harder, with surveillance, contact tracing and access to health care disrupted.
The camp had already experienced a deadly wave of illness. Reuters reported in June that more than 30 people had died there in just over a month, with many deaths linked to Ebola.
The U.N. refugee agency has recorded 88 confirmed Ebola cases and 56 deaths across displacement sites in Congo, including Kigonze, while warning that the actual toll is likely higher. The International Organization for Migration said fatality rates among Ebola patients in other displacement sites had exceeded 80%, compared with roughly 50% across the wider outbreak.
The crisis is unfolding in Ituri, North Kivu and South Kivu, regions that have endured decades of armed conflict and are home to more than 5 million displaced people. Crowded settlements, limited sanitation and frequent population movement create additional challenges for disease control.
Transmission has not followed a uniform pattern. WHO has reported declining cases in parts of Ituri, while North Kivu has experienced increases. New infections in border areas have also raised concerns that the outbreak could spread beyond Congo.
The response has expanded through cooperation between Congo's Health Ministry, WHO, Africa CDC and international partners. Teams are working to strengthen surveillance, laboratory testing, treatment, community engagement and cross-border coordination.

Column: Strategic stability, a new framework for China-U.S. relations
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:48:55 CST
17:48:55 KST

by Lyazid Benhami
As Chinese President Xi Jinping makes his second state visit to the United States, 11 years after his first, China-U.S. relations are entering a new phase. A new expression has appeared in the diplomatic vocabulary: "strategic stability." Can it offer a new approach to managing differences between the world's two major countries?
Xi's state visit to the United States from Sept. 23 to 25 came as the two countries seek to develop a new framework for their relationship.
There remain differences between the two sides, but high-level contacts continue. The notion of "building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability," deserves to be examined as a possible new way of thinking about relations between major countries.
The first characteristic of this approach is that it does not seek to eliminate competition. China and the United States have different interests and each seeks to preserve its economic, technological and strategic influence. The challenge, therefore, is less about eliminating competition than about preventing it from becoming uncontrollable.
Some differences between major countries cannot be resolved quickly and must be managed. This requires maintaining channels of communication, including during periods of tension, and distinguishing between areas where compromise is possible and those where positions remain far apart.
Dialogue does not necessarily signal convergence of positions. It is first and foremost an instrument for preventing and managing crises. This is the difference between seeking to immediately resolve every disagreement and creating the conditions to live with certain differences.
International relations have long been viewed primarily through the lens of the balance of power: defending one's interests, strengthening one's influence and containing that of the other.
Strategic stability introduces another dimension: the ability to manage the balance of power constructively. Strength then lies not only in the ability to exert influence, but also in the ability to prevent a crisis from crossing a threshold beyond which neither side would retain control.
The notion of "strategic stability" should therefore be understood as a framework for managing differences, rather than as the elimination of competition between the two countries.
This is what gives high-level dialogue its importance. The Xi-Trump summit does not mean the two countries' positions have converged. It means that the political channel remains sufficiently important to allow the two sides to address the most sensitive issues directly.
A diplomatic expression, however significant, is not always enough to transform an international relationship on its own. It must be accompanied by decisions, consultation mechanisms and practices that can prevent misunderstandings and contain crises.
Stability, moreover, cannot rest on the declarations of one actor alone. It requires a degree of reciprocity: each side must be able to take the other's interests and concerns into consideration.
The evolution of China-U.S. relations concerns not only the two countries themselves. If Beijing and Washington can maintain their competition while reducing the risks of escalation, the consequences could be significant for the international economy and security as a whole.
The notion of strategic stability could ultimately go beyond the China-U.S. framework alone to become a process to be maintained. This requires dialogue, predictability, mechanisms for crisis prevention and the ability to distinguish competition from confrontation. This may be the real significance of the Xi-Trump summit.
From this perspective, the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability would not mean the absence of competition. It would mean the ability to organize coexistence despite competition. This conception could become one of the major diplomatic endeavors of the 21st century.
Editor's note: Lyazid Benhami is a member of the Paris Association of French-Chinese Friendship.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

China Focus: Crime drama inspired by renowned trace-evidence expert leads China's holiday box office
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:48:50 CST
17:48:50 KST

by Xinhua writers Zhang Yunlong and Zhang Xiyue
BEIJING/HARBIN, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Crime drama "Traces of Justice" led China's box office on Thursday, the first day of the weeklong National Day holiday, emerging as the early front-runner in a release calendar short on traditional blockbuster fare.
According to ticketing platform Maoyan, China's box office totaled 180 million yuan (about 26.73 million U.S. dollars) on Oct. 1. "Traces of Justice" generated 71 million yuan, accounting for 39 percent of total ticket sales.
The film was followed by comedy "Mr. & Mrs. Pardon," which earned 48 million yuan. Together, the two titles accounted for nearly 66 percent of opening-day revenue.
Directed and co-written by Chen Sicheng, "Traces of Justice" is based on the life and work of Cui Daozhi, a renowned trace-evidence expert. The film stars Zhang Yi as Cui Xun, a trace-evidence specialist, alongside Ma Li as a forensic pathologist and Chen Minghao as a veteran detective.
Rather than focusing on action-driven police work, the film centers on forensic science and evidence analysis. Drawing inspiration from a series of real criminal cases dating back to the 1970s, it follows investigators solving seemingly unsolvable crimes through bite marks, fingerprints, fibers, firearms evidence and other overlooked clues. The story traces the development of Chinese forensic techniques over several decades.
The film's strong opening suggests audiences may be responding to a genre mix that differs from the patriotic epics and effects-heavy spectacles that have often dominated China's National Day holiday in recent years.
Maoyan analyst Lai Li noted that this year's National Day lineup offers a broad range of genres but lacks a clear tentpole release capable of driving the market on its own. That dynamic may have worked in favor of "Traces of Justice," which entered the holiday with recognizable creative talent and a distinctive crime-investigation premise.
The film kicked off its nationwide roadshow Thursday in Harbin, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, where Cui spent much of his professional life and where portions of the story are set.
Cui joined the provincial public security department in 1955 and has spent more than six decades working in criminal forensic science, participating in over 1,200 major cases and examining thousands of pieces of evidence.
Director Chen said Cui's life story offered a unique lens through which to examine the evolution of Chinese criminal investigation. Star Zhang Yi described the film as not only a portrait of one investigator but also a tribute to generations of police officers whose work has largely remained out of public view.
Whether "Traces of Justice" can maintain its lead over the remainder of the seven-day break remains an open question. The market is expected to become more competitive as additional titles are released, including crime sequel "Go for Broke 2" on Oct. 3 and imported horror title "Resident Evil" on Oct. 5.
These staggered openings, along with sustained demand for family moviegoing during the holiday, are expected to support the market throughout the latter half of the holiday period, according to Chen Jin, an analyst at film data platform Beacon. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's Taravadee Naraphornrapat and Worapeerachayakorn Kongphopsarutawadee beat China's Xia Xinyi and Yan Xu 2-1 on Friday to win the women's beach volleyball gold medal at the Asian Games.
The victory gave Thailand its first Asian Games women's beach volleyball title since 1998 and ended China's run of six consecutive titles in the event.
Thailand took the first set 21-17 before China responded with a 21-13 win in the second. The teams were tied 5-5 in the decider before Thailand took control, winning 10 of the next 13 points to close out the match 15-8.
"For the whole year, I worked for beach volleyball. This is the time to go back and spend time with my family and just eat dinner with them," Naraphornrapat said.
Xia was seeking her fourth Asian Games gold medal with a fourth different partner, but the Thai pair denied her bid by pulling away in the deciding set.
"This tournament exposed some of our problems, such as our lack of consistency on court and some roughness in our basic skills," she said.
Earlier Friday, the Philippines' Khylem Harl Progella and Sofiah Shanine Pagara came from behind to beat China's Dong Jie and Cao Shuting 2-1 in the bronze-medal match, earning the Philippines its first Asian Games medal in beach volleyball.
The men's beach volleyball final and bronze-medal match are scheduled for Saturday. ■

E. Japan experiences wettest, least sunny September on record
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:48:23 CST
17:48:23 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Eastern Japan recorded the most rainfall for September since data became available in 1946, as well as the fewest hours of sunshine for the month, the country's weather agency said Thursday.
According to the Japan Meteorological Agency's report on the month, precipitation in the region was more than double the September average, while sunshine hours were only about half the norm.
The agency attributed the weather conditions mainly to frequent approaches by typhoons and a stagnant autumn rain front.
The prolonged rain had a wide-ranging impact on daily life and economic activity.
In particular, Typhoon Dujuan, which approached the Pacific coast of eastern Japan last week, brought record downpours, triggered landslides and river flooding, and left 14 people dead in areas near Tokyo.
In central Tokyo, rain has fallen every day since Aug. 27, extending the streak to 37 consecutive days as of Friday, the longest on record.
The weather agency, however, predicts a far sunnier October for most of the country. ■

The midnight rescue of Karachi's Mahatma Gandhi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:48:14 UTC
17:48:14 KST

Gandhi statue outside the Sindh high court, Karachi (Picture credit: Haider Sherazi)
One of the first things I did when I returned to Pakistan in early 2000, this time as the Indian High Commissioner, was to pay my respects to an imposing bronze statue of Mahatma Gandhi. One of only two Gandhi statutes in Pakistan, Bapuji stands tall at the lobby of the Indian High Commission in Islamabad, famed walking stick in hand, gazing into the distance.The tale of how a pre-Partition statue found its way to its eventual home in the Indian High Commission is a fascinating saga reflecting the tangled tumultuous history of our two countries. It is a journey in which I was honoured to have played a small part.
Gandhi statue in the Indian High Commission, Islamabad (Picture credit: Haider Sherazi)
According to several accounts, the statue originally stood outside the Sindh high court on what was known as Kings Way in Karachi. It had been commissioned by the Indian merchant association sometime in the 1930s to commemorate the historic Karachi session of the Indian National Congress. The plaque underneath the life-size monument apparently read: “Mahatma Gandhi – the reputability of freedom, truth and nonviolence.
”Partition brought the inevitable dislocation. With communal riots engulfing Karachi in 1948, there was fear that the statue would be torn down amidst mob fury. Accounts vary on what exactly happened, but apparently after the intervention of Jamshed Nussranwanji Mehta, a Parsi and former Mayor of Karachi, the statue was surreptiously taken down and moved quietly to the home of the Cowasjees, a leading Parsi family of Karachi.And there it lay for more than thirty years…A few months into my first stint in Pakistan as Consul General in Karachi, a middle aged Parsi gentleman approached me. He was a well known Karachi businessman, activist and columnist whose name I am withholding. Over the course of several meetings he told me his incredible tale. How he as a young man along with several of his school chums insouciantly removed the Gandhi statue in the dead of the night armed with some basic tools and a lorry – all while Karachi seethed with fear and hatred. It was then ferried to his father’s home, initially meant as a temporary abode until a handover to Indian representative could be organised. Unfortunately, the then Indian High Commissioner to the Dominion of Pakistan could not assure a safe passage and refused. And that was how the Cowasjees became the involuntary guardians of Gandhi in PakistanThe Parsi gentleman was clear that his part in the story had to come to an end. We were now in the early 1980’s. General Zia’s Islamisation project was well underway. Sharia laws had been introduced into the legal system. Strict Islamic punishments were to be meted out for crimes like adultery, theft and drinking of alcohol. Educational curriculums were being rigorously overhauled to promote religious studies and conformity with orthodox Islamic principles. Dress codes, especially for women, were being enforced. The sari, once common amongst upper class Pakistani women, was fast disappearing. An ongoing media clampdown weeded out content deemed as un-Islamic.Though historically Parsis, unlike other minorities in Pakistan, have enjoyed a somewhat protected status and though Ardeshir was and continued to be a fearless and outspoken critic of the political establishment, he was no longer comfortable with his role as the statue’s custodian. He asked me if the long delayed handover of the statue could finally take place.I immediately agreed. I was determined that the statue, now a priceless historical artifact, should come home on my watch. There was, however, a tricky logistical issue to navigate. Constant surveillance by Pakistani intelligence was a fact of life. So how could we transport the statue without compromising the Cowasjees.After clearance from Delhi, we decided to replicate the original midnight run. A non-descript truck, organised by the Consulate, picked up a large wrapped item from the Cowasjee residence and quietly brought it to the Indian mission late one summer night.I personally inspected the precious cargo. Through all its travails, the statue had endured some damage. One hand was broken and the glasses were cracked, but otherwise Gandhiji stood tall. We arranged for some minor repairs, and after a few weeks, the statue took pride of place in the Chancery reception. Suddenly confronted with this majestic but serene statue, surprised Pakistani visitors were often curious about its origins, but we remained tightlipped.Eventually, once the statue was properly restored, we arranged for its transportation to the High Commission in Islamabad. In hindsight, that last trek from Karachi to Islamabad turned out to be as consequential as the original journey in 1948. In 1993, following the demolition of the Babri Masjid, furious mobs in Pakistan attacked over 30 Hindu temples and in Karachi ransacked both the Consulate and the Consul General’s residence in which I had once lived.
Valuable art was vandalised, including a beautiful painting by B. Prabha.Post the 1993 attacks, the Indian consulate in Karachi closed down. It remains shut to this day. In Islamabad, however, the Gandhi statue still stands, an enduring testament to “freedom, truth and non-violence” true to its original plaque.G. Parthasarathy has served as India’s Consulate General in Karachi and as India’s High Commissioner in Islamabad.

A recent lobbyist for the controversial $450bn US tech company Palantir played a senior role in helping Andy Burnham become prime minister, it has emerged.
Martha Dalton, whose company Lodestone worked for Palantir in 2024 and 2025, campaigned for Burnham in the Makerfield byelection that secured his return to parliament. She worked closely with his team on strategic communications and rebuttals, and was among supporters who clapped him into Downing Street in July.
Lodestone, which Dalton co-founded, worked for Palantir on projects including promoting its software at events in parliament where its engineers demonstrated AI-powered systems for use in British public services to MPs.
Dalton previously worked on the autumn 2025 deputy leadership campaign for the current education secretary, Lucy Powell, a few months after Lodestone stopped working for Palantir.
Her role emerged as Palantir fights to retain its £330m contract with NHS England to run the federated data platform, a national medical data system.
Burnham’s government is under pressure to scrap the deal. Campaigners are angry about Palantir’s work for the Israeli military in Gaza and Donald Trump’s ICE immigration crackdown. They have also raised concerns, acknowledged by NHS England’s chief executive, Jim Mackey, that the benefits to public health may not be as significant as has been claimed.
Lodestone’s work for Palantir and Dalton’s subsequent role with Burnham is the latest link between Labour and the tech firm, which also works for the US and UK militaries and was co-founded by the Trump-supporting tech billionaire Peter Thiel.
The Labour peer Tom Watson took a full-time job lobbying for Palantir earlier this month after a period as a member of Lodestone’s “strategic advisory council”. Palantir previously employed Peter Mandelson’s lobbying firm, Global Counsel, before it collapsed over the former Labour trade secretary’s links to Jeffrey Epstein.
Dalton wrote on her LinkedIn account that it had been “an absolute honour to work on Andy Burnham’s campaign to become Labour leader and prime minister”. She took six weeks’ unpaid leave from Lodestone to spend time in Makerfield “supporting on strategic comms and rebuttals”.
A spokesperson for Lodestone said: “She had no contact with clients during that time and did so because she believes Andy Burnham is the best person to lead the Labour party and the country. Lodestone had previously worked with Palantir on various projects – all focused on helping them to explain their technology to those who rightly hold them to account.”
Health workers who want ministers to scrap Palantir’s NHS deal protested at the Labour party conference in Liverpool on Tuesday. Labour members had earlier tabled a motion calling for the deal to be axed, claiming Palantir was “facing numerous allegations of involvement in serious breaches of human rights”, citing its development of technology for Israel’s military.
Palantir’s executive vice-president for the UK and Europe, Louis Mosley, has said its technology was used to locate hostages but not to identify military targets in Gaza. That appears to contradict an earlier statement by the firm’s chief executive, Alex Karp, who was challenged last year by a protester alleging “Palantir kills Palestinians” in Gaza. He replied: “Mostly terrorists, that’s true.”
Palantir’s fortunes in the UK are intertwined with the Labour government. A break clause in the NHS England contract looms in February 2027. The Labour mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, is also in a legal battle with Palantir after he blocked the Metropolitan police from awarding it a £50m contract to supply AI tools to assist criminal investigations. The firm also has a £240m contract with the Ministry of Defence and has been selling its services to other police forces and councils.
Mosley recently said that people who don’t recognise the positive impact the firm’s technology has on cutting treatment waiting times and speeding up hospital discharges were suffering from “Palantir derangement syndrome”.
Tom Brake, the chief executive of Unlock Democracy, a not-for-profit campaign group, said candidates should observe Cabinet Office advice on secondments before adding volunteers or secondees to their campaign teams.
“This requires successful secondees to declare relevant outside interests, clarify that potential conflicts will be explored and ensure appropriate mitigations are put in place,” he said.
A Labour spokesperson said: “There are robust rules and procedures to manage any potential conflicts, whether that be in government or in campaigns, and those were followed.”
A Palantir spokesperson said: “Lodestone has worked with us on a range of projects to explain how our software is used to deliver public services – for example parliamentary events that enable MPs to see demonstrations of our software and ask our engineers questions around data privacy and security.”

Arab party leader agrees to drop out of Israeli election race under court pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:44:37 UTC
17:44:37 KST

Israel’s Arab Balad party on Thursday evening decided to withdraw its leader's candidacy from the October 27 general elections after the Supreme Court indicated that a majority of its judges supported his exclusion.
Channel 12 reported that Balad, formally known as the National Democratic Assembly and running as part of the Joint List, agreed that its leader Sami Abu Shehadeh would accept the court’s proposal to withdraw from the parliamentary (Knesset) election.
The decision followed a hearing earlier on Thursday during which Supreme Court President Yitzhak Amit told Abu Shehadeh that most judges on the panel favoured upholding his disqualification.
The court gave him until Friday to withdraw voluntarily, warning that otherwise it would issue a ruling barring his candidacy, according to Israeli public broadcaster KAN.
Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted on September 23 to disqualify Abu Shehadeh and Joint List lawmaker Ofer Cassif.
The committee also voted to exclude the Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas, from the election.
The case against Abu Shehadeh centres on an article he published on October 8 2023, a day after a Hamas-led attack on Israeli communities near Gaza.
Right-wing Israeli groups, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party, sought his disqualification, alleging that the article expressed support for the attack. Abu Shehadeh denies the allegations.
Speaking before the court on Thursday, Abu Shehadeh said he did not support “armed struggle” and acknowledged that a paragraph in the article had been incorrectly worded. He said his intention was to call for moving the conflict towards a political process.
KAN reported that the judges considered some passages in the article to provoke “displeasure and revulsion.”
Exclusion protested
Adalah, the rights group representing Abu Shehadeh, argued that the request to bar him relied on a single article that contained no explicit call to support armed struggle.
Israel’s attorney general supported disqualifying his candidacy.
Arab lawmakers and supporters held a demonstration outside the Supreme Court in West Jerusalem as hearings on the disqualification decisions began.
Ben-Gvir arrived at the scene and waved an Israeli flag in front of the protesters, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
Under Israeli electoral rules, a decision to disqualify an individual candidate takes effect only after High Court approval. Decisions barring electoral lists can be appealed before the court.
The High Court has previously overturned Central Elections Committee decisions excluding Arab candidates and parties.
Palestinian citizens of Israel make up about 20 percent of the country’s population. Voters will elect members of the 120-seat Knesset on October 27.

World food prices near four-year high in September, UN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:43:20 UTC
17:43:20 KST

World food prices near four-year high in September, UN says
- World food prices reached their highest level in nearly four years in September due to logistics issues and weather concerns, as reported by the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).
- Sugar prices hit an 18-month high and wheat futures peaked at a three-year high, driven by El Nino fears and disruptions in Black Sea trade.
- FAO forecasts global cereal production for 2026 to be slightly lower than in 2025 but still the second-largest ever, while world cereal trade is expected to decline due to shipping constraints.
AI generated
PARIS – World food prices rose in September to their highest in nearly four years as logistics disruptions and weather concerns affected crop markets, the United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said.
Fears about a severe El Nino weather pattern have pushed international sugar prices to an 18-month high, while a war-related collapse in Black Sea trade pushed wheat futures to a three-year peak early in September.
The FAO Food Price Index, which tracks monthly changes in international prices for a basket of food commodities, averaged 136.0 points, up from a revised 134.0 for August and the highest reading since November 2022.
FAO’s benchmarks for cereal, sugar and vegetable oil prices all rose in September, though meat and dairy quotations fell.
“We are seeing a persistent and increasingly broad-based build up in global commodity prices, as disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea combine with climate shocks, putting pressure on energy, transport and key food commodities,” FAO chief economist Maximo Torero said.
“If sustained, these pressures will soon pass through to consumer food prices, especially in food and energy import-dependent countries,” he said in a statement.
In a separate report, FAO kept its forecast for global cereal production in 2026 almost unchanged at 2.979 billion metric tons, 2.1 per cent below the previous year’s peak but still the second-largest harvest on record.
FAO cut its forecast for world cereal trade in 2026/27 by 0.7 per cent from September, citing lower wheat and maize export expectations due largely to constrained Black Sea shipping routes. REUTERS

‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:39:40 UTC
17:39:40 KST

The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.
“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.
The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him.
Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation.
Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.”
“You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.”
The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone “Islamic radical indoctrination”.
The attacker is to be sent back to the United Arab Emirates, where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation.
Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives.
The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi.
He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi.
“I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”

The U.S. Navy has awarded a $24.4 billion contract to accelerate the production of air defense and missile defense interceptors
Kyiv • UNN
The U.S. Navy and Raytheon have signed a five-year agreement worth up to $24.4 billion for the production of SM-6 missiles. The contract may be extended for another two years.
The U.S. Navy and Raytheon, a company within RTX Corporation, have signed a $24.4 billion contract to accelerate production of Standard Missile-6 (SM-6) missiles. UNN reports this, citing Raytheon and the U.S. Navy.
Raytheon, an RTX business, has signed a five-year contract, with options for an additional two years, worth up to $24.4 billion to supply Standard Missile-6 (SM-6) interceptors, which will significantly increase stocks of critical munitions capable of carrying out both offensive strikes and missile defense missions
The SM-6 supply contract is the latest in a series of major munitions contracts that the Pentagon has awarded this year in an effort to push contractors to ramp up production more quickly. It follows a previous multiyear agreement worth $20.7 billion for the supply of Raytheon’s AMRAAM air-to-air missiles, signed in late September, and a $58.6 billion contract for the supply of Patriot interceptors, which was awarded to Lockheed Martin.
The company said that the SM-6 is the only combat-proven weapon capable of conducting air defense and anti-ship warfare while also providing missile defense.
It has been successfully tested from various U.S. Navy ship platforms and ground-based launchers, providing the fleet with a versatile and highly reliable weapon to counter the full spectrum of kinetic threats faced by modern naval forces.
Acting U.S. Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said: "Maritime power requires weapons that are produced quickly and in large quantities."
This investment expands production and provides the firepower our military needs to fight, win, and return home safely

The U.S. Department of Defense signed a seven-year, $22.9 billion contract with RTX’s Raytheon business to significantly increase production of Tomahawk cruise missiles.

Taiwan health officials urge women to prevent bone loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:35:34 UTC
17:35:34 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Health officials on Friday urged women to take steps early to protect their bone health and reduce the risk of fractures later in life.
The Health Promotion Administration's national survey found that one in 10 women aged 50 and older has osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become thinner and weaker due to a loss of bone mass. The proportion increased to one in six among women aged 65 and older, according to UDN and Min-Sheng General Hospital.
Taiwan Association of Obstetrics and Gynecology Secretary-General Huang Jian-pei (黃建霈) said women’s bone density generally peaks at around age 35 before gradually declining. Bone loss accelerates after menopause, which typically occurs around age 50, as female hormone levels fall, according to CNA.
Clinical data shows that hip fractures among people aged 80 and older are often associated with osteoporosis, Huang said. More than 50% of those who suffer a hip fracture die within six months, while those who become bedridden or lose their ability to care for themselves may place significant caregiving and financial burdens on their families, he added.
Huang stressed the importance of addressing bone loss before it becomes a serious problem. Those at higher risk include people with smaller body frames, limited exposure to sunlight, insufficient physical activity, or inadequate calcium intake, as well as those with certain conditions that can accelerate bone loss.
Huang advised people with risk factors to seek medical evaluation early and follow their doctor’s treatment and regular follow-up recommendations if abnormalities are detected.
To help prevent bone loss, the Health Promotion Administration recommended at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise each week. Director-General Shen Ching-fen (沈靜芬) said calcium-rich foods such as dairy and soy products, fish, and dark green vegetables are important for bone health. She also recommended sufficient protein and vitamin D intake.
Taiwan Dietitian Association Vice President Chang Huei-ping (張惠萍) said one simple approach is to include a source of calcium in every meal. People with osteoporosis can also drink an additional cup of sesame milk or sesame soy milk each day to increase their calcium intake, Chang added.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Taichung-based Aerospace Industry Development Corporation said Friday it will exhibit drone technologies at the Taichung AI & Smart Manufacturing Show, including prototype drones and guidance systems.
A press release said the trade show is a four-day event running from Thursday to Sunday. Highlights include AIDC's prototype Raven X munitions drone, counter-drone system, and the AIxVNAV autonomous flight system co-developed with US-based drone systems firm Vantor.
AIDC said its Raven X is a fixed-wing loitering munition drone designed to locate and lock onto moving ground and seaborne targets within a 100-kilometer radius for precision strikes. AIDC added that Raven X can be configured to suit different mission requirements managed by an AI pilot system. AIDC is doing further flight tests to optimize the working prototype.
A loitering or kamikaze drone is designed to hover or fly in holding patterns over a designated area for minutes or hours waiting for threats to appear. Once it identifies a target with its onboard cameras, it will use precision missile strikes or dive-bombing to destroy it.
AIDC said its counter-drone system can quickly acquire target data such as aircraft type, altitude, and speed, then target it with signal jamming or laser takedown. AIDC noted it can guard key installations such as power plants, ports, and airports. AIDC said that it saw action at the recent 15th Chin An exercise in September held by the Ministry of Justice's Agency of Corrections.
AIDC said AIxVNAV is an alternative when GPS signals fail. It added that drone cameras would send ground images that Vantor's AI algorithm compares with its database to estimate coordinates. AIDC completed a series of round-trip flights during the Presidential Cup in August and plans to deploy it for defense, public safety, and disaster relief.
AIDC also displayed a miniature replica of its Spearhead drone for one of its overseas clients. The aerospace firm signed an agreement with French aerospace company I-See to design and manufacture multiple drones.

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Russia’s oil and gas revenues will decline from 3.3% of GDP in 2026 to 2.7% of GDP in 2029 amid stabilizing price conditions and a shrinking share of the oil and gas sector in the economy, according to the main guidelines for budget, tax, and customs tariff policy for 2027 and the planning period of 2028 and 2029, reviewed by TASS.
"After reaching 5.5% of GDP in 2024, oil and gas revenues have been steadily declining, taking into account exchange rate trends, global energy prices, as well as the structure of hydrocarbon production and export volumes, and are estimated at 3.3% of GDP in 2026, followed by a further decline relative to GDP over the forecast horizon, to 2.7% in 2029, amid stabilizing price conditions and a declining share of the oil and gas sector in the economy," the document said.
In addition, a significant increase in federal budget revenues excluding oil and gas from key taxes is expected over the forecast horizon due to growth in the tax base, improved tax collection, and implemented and proposed changes to tax and other legislation.

The Saudi-led coalition said a drone hit the Taibah electricity distribution station, which supplies power to the Prophet's Mosque, one of Islam's holiest sites. The Houthis denied the claim, stating it was a "lie" to back previous allegations against the group.
The Saudi-led coalition accused Yemen's Houthis of striking a power station in the holy city of Medina in Saudi Arabia, a claim the Iran-backed group denied.
The alleged attack came as fighting intensified in Yemen, where forces of the internationally recognised government said they carried out attacks on Houthi targets and witnesses heard explosions in the Houthi-held capital Sana'a.
The Saudi-led coalition said on Thursday a drone struck Medina's Taibah electricity distribution station, which provides power to the Prophet's Mosque.
Medina, the burial place of the Prophet Mohammed and home to the Prophet's Mosque, is one of Islam's holiest cities alongside Mecca.
Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said a drone struck the Taibah electricity distribution station at 5:11 am (3:11 am CEST) on Tuesday.
"The investigation and evidence gathered by the competent authorities have confirmed the involvement of the terrorist Houthi militia in planning and executing this cowardly terrorist act, based on after-action review and the wreckage of the drone used," he said in a statement.
The coalition said one transformer was taken out of service without affecting the wider electricity network. Al-Maliki said the facility supplied electricity to the Prophet's Mosque.
"This cowardly terrorist act, targeting a civilian facility providing electricity to the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, is a continuation of this extremist militia's attempts to target the Two Holy Mosques," he said.
On Thursday, a senior Houthi official again rejected allegations that the movement had targeted Islamic holy sites, stating they were a "lie" to further back previous claims, according to Houthi-run news agency Saba.
The group had firmly rejected Riyadh's accusations in mid-September of a drone attack on Mecca, Islam's holiest site.
"Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said at the time, adding that "fabrications and lies propagated by the criminal al-Saud regime cannot deceive anyone."
Mecca is Islam's holiest site, home to the Kaaba — which Muslims worldwide turn toward for prayer — and the destination of the Hajj pilgrimage, one of the faith's Five Pillars or main tenets.
The accusation came as fighting intensified in Yemen, as the internationally recognised government's military said it had carried out strikes on Houthi targets in Sana'a, Saada and Taiz.
A spokesman said the military had conducted a "high-value targeting operation" in Sana'a and struck 11 targets in Saada.
He added that 27 air strikes had targeted an "integrated military system" belonging to the Houthis in Taiz.
The Houthis, who control Sana'a and much of Yemen's Red Sea coast, have repeatedly launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia since the kingdom intervened in Yemen's civil war in 2015.
Any confirmed attack on either Mecca or Medina would put the perpetrators beyond the pale in the eyes of virtually the entire Muslim world, Shia and Sunni alike.
Ankara blasts 'provocative attacks'
Turkey strongly condemned the alleged attack and voiced support for Saudi Arabia.
"We strongly condemn the Houthis' attack on civilian infrastructure" in Medina, the foreign ministry said.
"These provocative attacks, which threaten Saudi Arabia's sovereignty and security and target the sacred values of the Islamic world, must cease immediately and unconditionally."
Turkey said it reiterated its "strong support for Saudi Arabia" and called for steps to prevent further escalation.
Qatar also condemned the attack. In a statement, Doha said it was "a grave assault on the sanctity of Islamic holy sites", a violation of Saudi sovereignty and international law.
It reaffirmed its "full solidarity" with Riyadh and said the kingdom's security was integral to Gulf security.
The League of Arab States joined the condemnation, calling the attack "an unacceptable transgression".
The organisation said the attack "provokes the sentiments of Muslims worldwide" and represented a dangerous escalation.
Al-Azhar, the Cairo-based institute of Sunni Islamic learning, also denounced the incident, stating that "targeting Medina provokes the sentiments of Muslims worldwide".
The Houthis are Zaydi Shia Muslims, a specific branch of Islam historically rooted in northern Yemen that is theologically distinct from both the Twelver Shia Islam dominant in Iran and Saudi Arabia's Wahhabi-influenced Sunni tradition.
The group formally known as Ansar Allah is tied to Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

How the US went from ‘a position of strength’ to ‘gung-ho’ on China
Years of decoupling showed that independence was an economically ruinous illusion while pragmatic bargaining yields vastly superior returns
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Jianlu Bi is a senior fellow at the Foreign Policy in Focus think tank at the Institute for Policy Studies in Washington, DC, and a research fellow at the Charhar Institute in Beijing. 
Not so long ago, Washington’s approach to relations with Beijing was anchored by a single assertive phrase: dealing “from a position of strength”. It was rooted in a unipolar mindset: a belief that the United States could dictate terms, manage competition unilaterally and demand compliance from a distance.
Yet, at their recent summit, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump formally established a new strategic framework: a “constructive strategic stability relationship based on respect, fairness and reciprocity”.
The shift in the American mindset was visible in the reception of Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, from the moment their plane landed in Washington. Trump and first lady Melania Trump took the extraordinary step of welcoming the couple on the tarmac. Accompanied by a 21-gun salute, full military honours from every service branch and a dramatic fighter jet flyover above the White House, Washington sent an unmistakable signal that it acknowledged China as an equal on the global stage.

Saudi Arabia has reported three Houthi attempts to target the holy cities of Mecca and Medina over the past nine years, including two incidents in September, drawing condemnation from Arab and Muslim countries.

According to an Anadolu review of official Saudi statements, the latest alleged attacks targeted Medina and an area south of Mecca, while the first reported attempt occurred in July 2017.
Mecca and Medina are home to Islam’s holiest sites, the Grand Mosque and the Kaaba in Mecca and the Prophet’s Mosque in Medina.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government against the Houthis since March 2015. The Yemeni group has controlled the capital Sanaa and several provinces since September 2014.
Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia intensified in September after the group announced what it called a “maritime blockade” on the kingdom in July and later claimed ballistic missile and drone attacks on Saudi sites and vessels.
Two incidents in September 2026
On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said a drone attack it attributed to the Houthis had targeted a power station in Medina.
Coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al Maliki said the attack occurred early on Tuesday and knocked a transformer out of service without affecting the electricity grid.
Maliki accused the Houthis of targeting civilian infrastructure providing electricity services to the Prophet’s Mosque, describing the incident as an “extension of this extremist militia’s approach in attempts to target the Two Holy Mosques.”
“Investigation findings, operational data and examination of debris from the drone used in the attack proved the Houthi militia’s involvement in planning and carrying out this act,” he said.
The coalition would continue taking measures to deter the Houthis and protect the Two Holy Mosques and pilgrims in Mecca and Medina, he added.
On September 16, Maliki said Saudi air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca before it entered the city’s restricted airspace.
Saudi Arabia’s foreign ministry said at the time that it was the second alleged Houthi attempt to target Mecca after an earlier incident in July 2017.
Saudi King Salman bin Abdulaziz condemned the Houthis’ attempt to again target Mecca, saying the incident had drawn international condemnation because violating the sanctity of holy sites provoked the feelings of Muslims around the world.
Abdul Mohsen al Qasim, an imam at the Prophet’s Mosque, also said during a Friday sermon that attacking Mecca and Medina was “a grave offence before God.”
2017 allegation
On July 27 2017, the Saudi-led coalition announced that it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards Mecca over Taif province, around 69 kilometres from the holy city, without causing damage.
Saudi Arabia’s foreign ministry accused the Houthis at the time of violating the sanctity of Mecca in “a desperate attempt to disrupt the Hajj season.”
The Houthis did not immediately deny the latest accusation involving Medina.
The group, however, swiftly rejected the Saudi accusation concerning the September 16 incident near Mecca.
Houthi leader Abdul Malik al Houthi and Hizam al Assad, a member of the group’s political bureau, denied the allegation.
The Houthis also rejected the July 2017 accusation, saying their missile forces had targeted only the Taif military base and had not targeted Mecca.
Saudi announcements concerning the alleged attempts to target Mecca in July 2017 and September 2026 prompted condemnation from a number of Arab and Muslim countries and organisations.
The statements condemning the Houthis were issued by Türkiye, Qatar, Egypt, Yemen, Jordan, Morocco, Palestine, Syria, Bahrain, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Sudan, the United Arab Emirates and Somalia.
The Gulf Cooperation Council, Arab League and Organization of Islamic Cooperation also issued condemnations, with several statements warning that attacks involving Mecca would offend Muslims around the world.

In a strongly-worded letter to Burnham the Lib Dems’ spokesperson for culture, media and sport, Anna Sabine, criticised his apparent defence of City as “extraordinary” and invoked Gianni Infantino’s aborted World Cup sell-off scheme in what she described as a difficult year for football.
“As you will know, an independent commission has found Manchester City guilty of 114 charges of breaching financial rules over a timeframe of nearly a decade, including the use of ‘sham contracts’ and schemes to disguise more than £830m of funding,” Sabine writes in a letter seen by the Guardian.
“Despite this, your response was to thank the club’s owners for their work and describe the findings as ‘contested’ and that it was ‘wrong to jump to a conclusion’. It is extraordinary that a prime minister would use his position to call into question the findings of the independent investigation, and risk undermining trust in the Premier League’s processes.
“This has been a difficult year for football’s reputation. Fifa’s conduct around the World Cup has already raised serious questions about integrity in the game we love. At a moment like this, fans expect their prime minister to stand up for the rules in place, not to appear to side with a club found guilty of breaking them.”
Sabine also told the Guardian that Burnham’s ties to ADUG should be scrutinised and is planning to write to Downing Street and the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to demand details of their meetings.
Rows over potholes and a viral story about a garden gate have led to Reform UK’s latest confrontation with local media, after one of its councils announced it would refuse to engage with a reporter behind the stories.
Reform-run Derbyshire county council has been accused of setting a “dangerous precedent” after withdrawing all cooperation with Eddie Bisknell, a Derbyshire Live journalist who is publicly funded to cover local democracy.
Stephen Reed, the Reform council’s deputy leader, said the reporter would now have to work “twice as hard” to do his job after confirming that Bisknell’s inquiries would be ignored.
In the Derbyshire case, Reform said its decision had been made after a “prolonged period of concerns”, which culminated in a story about potholes.
Councillors had hoped to produce positive headlines with a press release stating that the number of potholes in the county had been slashed from 12,000 in April to less than 700 – a figure it described as the lowest recorded in over a year.
However, an article by Bisknell, one of a group of local democracy reporters funded by the BBC, reported that questions had been raised about statistics used in the release.
Polanski: Burnham's Labour 'bending to the whims of fossil fuel giants'
Zack Polanski uses the conclusion of his keynote speech to set out the differences between the Greens and Andy Burnham’s Labour party.
He says:
Our differences with this Labour government could not be clearer. While they play politics with our planet, we stick to the science. While Andy Burnham barely whispers a word about climate, we seek urgent action.

He goes on:
One of my political heroes, Tony Benn, he once said ‘hope is the fuel of progress and fear is the prison in which you put yourself’.
Over the last year, we’ve seen just how powerful hope with a plan can be. It has fuelled our membership to record levels, propelled our party to amazing electoral success but more importantly, it’s changed our country for the better. But we in this room all know we are just getting started.
Polanski concludes:
And so when times get tough, when our opponents attack us, or smear us, or try to put obstacles in our way, we remember that fear will get us nowhere. Only being brave – being bold – will take us where we need to go.
And when I’m in need of hope all I need to think of is what is in front of me right now … The movement that has brought us so far already because only with real hope and real change can we build the country and the world we can be so proud of.
That brings his speech to a close, to rapturous applause from the delegates in the audience.
“The sight of pensioners being put in handcuffs and bundled into police vans for holding up cardboard signs has been a stain and a shame on this country’s reputation for far too long,” Polanski says in reference to the Palestine Action arrests.

To a Labour government so determined to crush dissent that it labels those with views it doesn’t want to hear as terrorists. Terrorists. Terrorists.
Hundreds of Labour MPs who were willing to label people terrorists to troop through the voting lobbies to approve it.
You know something? Our MPs didn’t troop through the yes lobby. Our MPs were cowed by fear or malicious attacks in the press. They stood up for the principles we all hold so dear.
Those principles? Free speech. Civil liberties. The right to dissent, which has won us our most precious freedoms. And Greens? We stand with one voice now as we say: Drop the charges, end the genocide, deproscribe Palestine Action.
Polanski makes the case for the electorate to back the Greens in elections by suggesting only the Greens can guarantee affordable rents.
He says:
And that’s why we are needed, people need an alternative. Only by voting Green can voters be sure that they will back a real plan for shaking up the housing market.
Only by voting Green can they put an end to the rental rip-off and guarantee affordable rents.
And only by voting Green can they choose a future where houses don’t sit empty as mere investment assets but as the safe place to rest our heads at night that we all need. That’s what a Green vote gets.
Polanski calls for triple lock-style guarantee to limit rent rises
The Greens leader calls for a triple lock-style guarantee to ease young adults’ housing costs.
Polanski says:
Today we are calling on this government to put in place a three-year emergency brake on private rents. No rent rises above CPI, wage growth or 2% – whichever is lower. No sudden hikes. No evictions under the guise of rent rises. No more uncertainty, no more fear.
That emergency brake would give renters vital breathing space. Let wages begin to catch up with the rents that have outstripped them for far too long.
And in the long term, we’ll put in place a national Fair Rents Guarantee – to keep rents affordable for everyone, forever. That doesn’t just mean cheaper homes, it doesn’t just mean government savings.
It will mean that people can stay in the places they love, close to their family and friends. It will mean young people can take those first amazing, exhilarating steps into independence and have full lives waiting for them on the other side.
Young families able to live around the corner from the in-laws, not crammed into their spare room.
Polanski says the Greens main priorities are to “tax the very richest, bring our public services back into public hands and end rip-off Britain”.
Speaking in Brighton, he says:
I am always guided by three essential questions: how do we make life more affordable? How do we back the caring majority over a tiny wealthy elite? And how do we protect our planet for generations to come?
Now, I’ve been knocking on lots of doors lately for some reason. Particularly in an area I’ve known for a long time. Lived there, worked there, seen it change.
Some of the changes are really visible. Luxury high-rises springing up on spots that used to be green space for council estates. Porches out the front of what used to be family homes – stuck all over with lock boxes for Airbnb keys.
But some of these changes are subtler. Many of the doors I’m knocking on look the same as they did ten or twenty years ago.
He goes on:
But behind those doors something has shifted. It doesn’t matter whether it’s council homes, or terraced houses – I hear one thing again and again. Mums answer the door, and tell me ‘I’ve still got my kids living at home with me.’
Nineteen year olds who can’t afford student housing, so they’re living with their parents and commuting to uni. But they’re missing lectures because they can’t afford the train in and out. Missing out on living with strangers who could have become friends for life.
Or there’s the twenty five year olds who can’t find a job, no matter how many tens or hundreds of applications they send. Who can’t imagine ever being able to afford to rent even a room of their own, never mind having a whole place of their own. That feels like an impossible dream.

Ukraine to lose 30 mln tonnes of agri exports - minister
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:26:44 EEST
17:26:44 KST

Ukraine's agricultural exports amounted to up to 50% of potential at the end of September and start of October amid Russia's continued blockade of Black Sea ports, Agrarian Policy and Food Minister Taras Vysotsky told reporters on Friday.
"Without the existing deep-water Black Sea ports, we can export about half of the products we have grown that are export-oriented. As for the consequences, it is the inability to export about 30 million tonnes of agricultural products worth about $30 billion in the current marketing year," he said.
Ukraine exported 2.4 million tonnes in September, or 46% of what should have been exported, the minister said. Grain accounted for 1.4 million tonnes, or 38%, oilseeds for 444,000 tonnes, or 83%, vegetable oil for 311,000 tonnes, or 64%, and meal for 280,000 tonnes, or 46% of the potential required exports.
"These 46% have essentially not changed since Sept 20. That is, we are reaching what we forecast: 45-50% is the objective maximum within the current routes," Vysotsky said.
Rail carried 41% of exports, or 993,000 tonnes, in line with forecasts, the Danube 54%, or 1.3 million tonnes, and road transport 5%, or 120,000 tonnes, he said.
"In September we increased both rail and the Danube compared with August," he said.

Israel's airline El Al cancels Dubai evacuation flights after UAE withdraws landing permits

Rania R.a. AbushamalaAbdel Ra'ouf Arnaout and Rania Abushamala
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Israeli flag carrier El Al announced Friday that it had canceled flights scheduled to bring Israelis home from Dubai after the United Arab Emirates withdrew landing permits for Israeli carriers.
“Due to the cancellation of approval for Israeli companies to land in Dubai, as was reported by the authorities in Israel, we are forced to cancel, at this stage, our rescue flights … for tomorrow, Friday, October 2,” the airline said on Facebook.
El Al said it remains fully prepared to operate charter flights to Dubai to bring Israeli citizens home as soon as official approval is received.
The airline added that flights set for next Sunday, Monday, Wednesday and Thursday remain on its timetable, but are fully booked.
El Al did not explain why the landing permits had been withdrawn, and there was no immediate official clarification from Emirati authorities.
Israel’s Channel 7 reported that the announcement followed a last-minute UAE decision to withdraw landing permits for the evacuation flights.
Israeli carriers had been preparing special flights to repatriate stranded Israelis after flydubai suspended services following an incident Wednesday aboard a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
Israeli authorities said that during the incident, the flydubai co-pilot stabbed the plane’s captain and tried to crash the aircraft before passengers and crew managed to restrain him.
The plane made an emergency landing in the Saudi city of Tabuk.
Emirati authorities ordered an investigation to establish the circumstances and motives behind the incident. Flydubai urged against speculation.
Air travel between Israel and the UAE has been disrupted in recent months by Israeli attacks on Iran.
Israel and the UAE established diplomatic relations in 2020 under a US-brokered normalization agreement.

US delivers F-16V fighter jets to Taiwan as island eyes threat from China

US delivers F-16V fighter jets to Taiwan as island eyes threat from China
Amid threats from China, Taipai is growing concerned about the Trump administration’s commitment to arming the island.
The United States has delivered two F-16V Block 70 fighter jets to Taiwan as the island seeks to build its defence capabilities to deter a feared attack by China.
The aircraft, built by US defence contractor Lockheed Martin, are part of an $8bn deal for 66 F-16Vs approved during President Donald Trump’s first term. They landed on Friday following months of delay due to repeated requests from Beijing to the US to stop arming Taiwan.
The jets, which flew via Hawaii and Guam, touched down at noon (04:00 GMT) local time. They arrived a week after Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.
Taiwan is eyeing a rising military threat from Beijing, which claims the democratically governed island as its own territory.
“Of course we won’t only have delivered these two [F-16Vs] by the end of the year,” Minister of National Defence Wellington Koo said.
The arrival of the planes comes amid growing concern in Taiwan about the Trump administration’s commitment to arming Taipei.
The US is bound by law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, but the two have no formal diplomatic relations.
Trump said in May, after meeting Xi in Beijing, that he was holding out on a new $14bn package for Taiwan, though he did approve one worth $11bn in December 2025.
Washington has said there has been no change in policy.
“We continue standing with friends and allies across the Indo-Pacific to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values — that includes Taiwan,” a US State Department spokesperson said when asked about the delivery.
The F-16Vs, which received an upgrade in 2023, have advanced avionics, weapons and radar systems to better counter the Chinese air force, including its J-20 stealth fighters.
However, Washington has been unwilling to provide Taiwan with its most advanced fighters, such as the F-22 or F-35.
