Last-Minute Push for Russia Sanctions Bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:21:00 UTC
17:21:00 KST

The American Coalition for Ukraine’s (ACU) fall Ukraine Action Summit arrived at a pivotal moment: the final days before the House vote on the Russia sanctions bill.
As lawmakers weighed their positions, advocates for Ukraine met with them as constituents, in some cases becoming the last people to make a direct appeal before the vote.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Interviews with participants offer a close-up view of those tense hours: lawmakers’ hesitation, advocates’ arguments, and the effort to turn uncertainty into support and a “yes” vote.
Sen. Lindsey O. Graham (R-S.C.) had spent more than a year pressing Congress to adopt sweeping new sanctions against Russia. Weeks after his death in July, the Senate renamed the legislation in his honor and passed it 86 to 11, an overwhelming bipartisan vote that sent the measure to the House.
But trouble quickly emerged in the House, where some Democrat lawmakers were not prepared to embrace the Senate-passed bill without changes.
Within hours of its passage, Rep. Gregory W. Meeks (D-N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) warned that they had “fundamental concerns” about the bill’s tariff provisions. The measure, they said, granted Trump “sweeping new tariff authorities that the president could weaponize with abandon.”
For Ukrainian advocacy, the bill became the top legislative priority, prompting a nationwide campaign to mobilize supporters and press lawmakers for its passage. By mid-August, most House Republicans appeared prepared to support the bill, encouraged by signals that the White House had given the legislation a green light.
646 Drones Swarm Russia as Fires Hit Europe’s Largest Tank Farm, Oil Facilities
That forced Ukrainian American advocates to shift their strategy: after months of concentrating on reluctant Republicans, they now had to persuade skeptical Democrats to support the bill.
“Now, support from Democrats and representatives of the Democratic Party is very important to us, because without them, we see that this bill will not move forward in Congress,” said Maryna Baydyuk, president and CEO of United Help Ukraine.
A month-long ACU advocacy campaign helped build support among House Democrats, as advocates argued that the bill represented Ukraine’s last realistic opportunity before the midterm elections to intensify economic pressure on Russia and push Moscow toward ending the war.
“Many House Democrats changed their minds after our delegates met with them. They were shown exactly how this bill would reduce Russia’s funding, that its tariff provisions are limited to Russia’s biggest sponsors, that the legislation gives Congress more control, not less by codifying executive orders, and that the bill received broad support from Ukraine, the European Union and the Senate,” said Eugene Goncharov, director of policy at the American Coalition for Ukraine.
Ambassador Erin McKee, CEO of Nova Ukraine urged lawmakers to keep the bill’s broader purpose in view.
“I hope lawmakers remain focused on the larger objective: reducing the revenues Russia uses to finance its war against Ukraine,” she said.
Many Democrats were prepared to support the bill, but not all, leaving its passage in jeopardy.
The vote before the vote
The next obstacle was the rule – the procedural vote required before the sanctions bill could reach the House floor.
The House had only four scheduled voting days before lawmakers left Washington to campaign for the midterm elections. Speaker Mike Johnson shortened that window further, ending the session Sept. 16 and sending members home until after Election Day.
If House Democrats, including Rep. Gregory W. Meeks (D-N.Y.), succeeded in amending the bill, it would have to return to the Senate for another vote, effectively closing the narrow path to passage before the recess. The only realistic way to complete action in time was for the House to approve the Senate version without changes.
Marianna Tretiak, president and chair of the board of the American Coalition for Ukraine, said waiting could mean losing the only viable path forward. “If this doesn’t pass, we go back to zero,” she said.
But first, the House had to adopt a procedural rule allowing that vote and Republicans needed Democratic support to pass it.
The two democratic votes that kept the bill alive
On Tuesday, Sept. 15, the House adopted the rule 214 to 211. Republicans supplied 211 votes, and independent Rep. Kevin Kiley (I-Calif.) added another, leaving the measure one vote short.
Democratic Reps. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Wash.) and Jared Golden (Maine) broke with their party and voted yes.
A last-minute push by Ukrainian advocates
The rule vote concluded at 5:27 p.m. on Tuesday, Sept. 15. About five hours earlier, a six-member Washington state delegation had met with the legislative director to Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.), according to Katya Sadova, who co-led the delegation.
“We met with her office on Tuesday, just ahead of the rules vote,” Sadova said. “We asked how she felt about voting for the rule to put the bill on the floor, and we got a sense that anything could happen.”
With the bill’s fate hanging in the balance, Sadova and her fellow advocates made a direct appeal, emphasizing what the vote and the sanctions it would unlock meant for Ukraine.
“It gave us a little note of optimism that she might be willing to vote for the rule to put this act on the House floor,” Sadova said.
By Tuesday evening, the path was clear: The House would hold its final vote on the sanctions bill the next day, Wednesday, Sept. 16.
On Wednesday, the delegation returned to Gluesenkamp Perez’s office to thank her in person.
                                                                                                                                                                         Photo Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) with the Washington State ACU delegation. (Credit: Katya Sadova)                             
“After the vote on the rule, we reached out to the office and asked whether we could come in and thank her,” Sadova said. “When we arrived with the whole delegation, the congresswoman was there. She sat down with us for 15 minutes, asked us about our stories and teared up when we talked about how important this was to us.”
How constituents made their case to a New York Democrat
On Tuesday, Sept. 15, at about 2:30 p.m., Yuliia Nevmerzhytska, co-leader of the New York state delegation, and other advocates met personally with Rep. Paul Tonko (D-N.Y.). Tonko immediately told them that he could not support the sanctions bill because he did not trust the Trump administration to use its tariff authority responsibly.
“The first thing he said was that he was not supportive of the bill,” Nevmerzhytska said. “He felt that the president would abuse this tariff authority, and therefore he could not support it. He straight up said that.”
                                                                                                                                                                         Photo Rep. Paul Tonko (D-N.Y.) with the ACU New York delegation. (Credit: Yuliia Nevmerzhytska)                             
The delegation responded with both personal appeals and detailed arguments about the legislation. Fourteen-year-old Nicole Hnatiuk, a constituent Tonko knew through the local Ukrainian community, spoke about Russia’s abduction of Ukrainian children. Nicole asked Tonko to imagine her in their place.
“What if it were me?” she asked, according to Nevmerzhytska. “If the United States could not provide the support our people need, I might not even be here.”
                                                                                                                                                                         Rep. Paul Tonko (D-N.Y.) and Nicole Hnatiuk. (Credit: Yuliia Nevmerzhytska)                             
In that tense, uncertain moment, the constituents felt they had to be equally direct. “Our community would not be able to support you anymore if we did not see a ‘yes’ vote on this bill,” Nevmerzhytska recalled Nicole saying. “It was so urgent and such a pressing issue.”
Other delegation members explained that the tariff authority was limited, that the administration would have to report its actions to Congress and that lawmakers would retain oversight of waivers and termination decisions. They also argued that the bill was Ukraine’s last realistic opportunity to secure stronger sanctions before the midterm elections.
Rep. Paul Tonko (D-N.Y.) voted yes.
A final-hours appeal to a Texas Democrat
Wednesday offered Ukrainian advocates one final chance to persuade wavering House Democrats to support the bill.
Five hours before voting.
At 12:15 p.m. Wednesday, the ACU Texas delegation met with Rep. Marc Veasey (D-Texas), a longtime supporter of Ukraine, for a hurried conversation as he walked between meetings on Capitol Hill.
Veasey’s concerns about the tariff provisions were serious enough that advocates feared he might vote against the bill.
“It was a 10 minute meeting and we actually had to walk down the hallway with him. He was very concerned about some components of the bill, specifically the tariffs,” said Olena Jacobs, who co-led the delegation.
Jacobs said Veasey had long supported Ukraine and had voted for every previous Ukraine-related measure. On Wednesday, advocates argued that after nearly five years of war, the United States needed to demonstrate global leadership and use severe sanctions to force Russia toward serious negotiations.
“Thankfully, the big picture prevailed,” Jacobs said. “He saw the good in sanctioning Russia and just how important it was.”
                                                                                                                                                                         Photo Rep. Marc Veasey (D-Texas) with the ACU Texas delegation. (Credit: Olena Jacobs)                             
When Veasey left, the advocates continued their appeal with his legislative assistant. Jacobs said the delegation’s relationships with staff members, developed over several previous summits, allowed them to keep pressing their case after the congressman departed.
“I spoke with her [Rep. Marc Veasey legislative assistant] twice, first when we arrived and were waiting for the congressman, and then I returned to the office and pleaded again,” Jacobs said of a senior staff member. “I reminded her of my personal story, my losses, and how many people want this war to end as soon as possible.”
Some Republicans began to doubt
Wednesday, Sept 16. 6 hours before voting.
Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Mich.) had been expected to provide a reliable Republican vote for the sanctions bill. Nellie Petlik, an ACU delegate from Michigan and a constituent in Huizenga’s district, arrived at their meeting expecting an easy commitment.
“Honestly, I expected him to be in favor of the bill,” Petlik said. “I was expecting him to say, ‘Yes, no problem. I plan to vote for the bill.’ I was a bit surprised when we met with the representative himself and he said, ‘I’m actually not sure how I’m going to vote today.’ He seemed skeptical that the president would implement the sanctions as written, and he mentioned that the bill gave the president authority to waive them.”
The advocates pushed back. Petlik said sanctions experts in the group argued that presidential waivers were common in sanctions legislation. More importantly, they told Huizenga that enacting the measure would give Congress greater authority to oversee how the sanctions were carried out instead of leaving them under executive orders controlled largely by the White House.
“We made the argument that by passing this bill, he would have more power to make sure the sanctions were implemented as designed,” Petlik said.
Huizenga did not fully explain what was driving his hesitation. Petlik wondered whether the approaching midterm election also weighed on him, particularly the risk that an opponent could portray his support for new tariffs as a vote to raise consumer prices. Other House Republicans had expressed similar concerns about potential political blowback from tariffs.
“I do wonder if he was concerned about the tariff authority and worried that an opponent could say he voted to basically raise prices for the American people,” Petlik said. “He didn’t say this to us in the meeting. That’s just a pure guess.”
Petlik and other advocates met with Huizenga late Wednesday morning, about six hours before the final vote. With the congressman still undecided, the meeting carried unusual urgency. They were probably among the last constituents to speak with him before he entered the chamber, Petlik said.
“I told him, ‘I just came from my hometown in the district. It’s a town of 10,000 people, and I see Ukrainian flags everywhere,’” Petlik recalled. “There’s not a huge Ukrainian community there. These are Americans of Polish, Lithuanian, and German descent who care about this issue because their families, mine included, came from Europe after World War I and World War II.”
Petlik delivered a direct message: Support for Ukraine reached well beyond Ukrainian Americans, and voters back home would be watching.
“We were probably the last people who talked to him, so I like to think that we made a difference,” she said.
Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Mich.) ultimately voted for the bill.
The most difficult target
Even before the summit began, Rachel Smith, head of the Louisiana delegation, had identified Rep. Clay Higgins (R-La.) as its most difficult target and expected the meeting to unfold in hostile territory.
“His track record until Wednesday had been 100 percent voting against anything to help Ukraine. It didn’t matter what it was, he was a no,” she said.
Smith had met Higgins once before, in the spring of 2025, and remembered the encounter as unusually confrontational.
“He saw that we were on schedule and came out and spoke to us with the intent of sending us out of his office crying,” Smith said. “But we ended up changing his mind enough that he stopped repeating Kremlin propaganda on social media.”
By the time Smith’s delegation returned to Higgins’s office during the 2026 summit, however, the political landscape had shifted. During a scheduled meeting Tuesday morning, Smith said a staffer told the group that Higgins had spoken with President Donald Trump about the bill during the weekend.
                                                                                                                                                                         Photo The Louisiana delegation with Henry Keating, a staffer for Rep. Clay Higgins (R-La.). (Credit: Sofia Poliakova)                             
“We left the office cautiously optimistic that his loyalty to the president would lead him to vote yes on the bill,” Smith said. “And that’s exactly what happened.”
Smith was unequivocal in her interpretation of Higgins’s decision.
An unexpected opening with a Ukraine skeptic
Rep. Paul Gosar (R-Ariz.), a MAGA-aligned Republican and longtime Trump ally, has been one of the most vocal opponents of US aid to Ukraine. Yet he had never personally met with the ACU’s Arizona delegation. Oli Nevinska, the delegation’s co-leader, had advocated on Ukraine since 2022 and contacted Gosar’s office twice a year, but the meetings had always been with members of his staff.
That relationship began to change after the office hired a new legislative aide, Louis, whom the delegation first met at the April 2026 summit.
Nevinska said the new aide was better informed about Ukraine, making subsequent discussions with the office more productive. At the September summit, the delegation was waiting for its scheduled meeting with Louis when Gosar unexpectedly emerged from his office.
“I saw him come out of his office and realized that I was not going to simply let him walk away,” Nevinska recalled.
Nevinska introduced herself and made the delegation’s case for the sanctions bill. Gosar stayed, turning a routine staff meeting into an impromptu 15-minute conversation with the Arizona advocates.
“He said he was glad to meet us and would join the meeting, even though it had not been scheduled,” Nevinska said. “He asked us about Ukraine, about the war, the Russian attacks and the drones. We shared what we knew, including firsthand accounts from our families in Ukraine. And, of course, we asked him to support the sanctions bill.”
The meeting ended with an unexpected gesture. Gosar showed the delegation a collection of rocks from space displayed in his office. When Nevinska joked that she intended to keep one, the congressman told her he could not surrender the entire meteorite but he could give her a piece.
“He knelt down in front of our delegation and used one stone to break a piece from another,” Nevinska recalled. “Then he gave me the meteorite fragment as a keepsake.”
Nevinska carried the fragment back to Ukraine, a small reminder of a meeting neither side had planned.
An ally who needed no persuading
In Rep. Michael McCaul’s office, the ACU Texas delegation found an ally who needed no persuading. The Republican had introduced the House version of the sanctions legislation and was working to secure its passage.
The advocates were unable to meet directly with Rep. Michael McCaul as he was on the House floor preparing for the vote when the delegation arrived, said Anna Berezniak, who led the group. His senior legislative assistant had just five minutes to spare.
“She assured us that they were continuing to work until the last minute to get the bill passed,” Berezniak said. “They considered it one of the strongest pieces of legislation supporting Ukraine that could realistically pass Congress.”
                                                                                                                                                                         Photo ACU Texas delegation at the office of Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas). (Credit: Olena Jacobs)                             
McCaul’s senior legislative aide asked the delegation to provide public statements endorsing it. The advocates later shared statements from the Ukrainian Cultural Club of Dallas and 50 States for Ukraine.
They came to be heard
After clearing both chambers, the bill became the first pro-Ukraine measure enacted by this Congress when President Donald Trump signed it into law on Sept. 18.
Goncharov said what had begun as an urgent effort to secure enough votes ended with nearly twice as many Democrats supporting the bill as he had initially counted. He accredited that shift in part to sustained advocacy and arguments that directly addressed lawmakers’ reservations about the bill.
“Over 363 meetings with Congressional offices, I feared we would not have sufficient votes for the first procedural vote, and counted we had the support of about 30 Democrats for final passage,” said Eugene Goncharov, director of policy at the American Coalition for Ukraine. “In the end the sanctions bill passed with the support of 58 Democrats, many of them convinced directly through meetings with constituents. Furthermore, as the votes kept coming on the House floor, additional Democrats felt comfortable voting to pass the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, resulting in a resounding 262-159 final vote.”
Behind the roll-call tally was a basic act of representative democracy: constituents sitting across from their elected officials, explaining what was at stake and asking them to act. For ACU’s delegates, support for Ukraine was a priority they carried to Washington from the districts those lawmakers represented.

After botched execution attempt, Tennessee must commute Christa Pike’s death sentence as a first step
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:20:36 UTC
17:20:36 KST

In response to the state of Tennessee’s senseless pursuit of the death penalty and the attempted execution of Christa Pike, Justin Mazzola, Deputy Director of Research with Amnesty International USA said:
“Tennessee’s attempted, but botched, execution of Christa Pike was an extreme display of cruelty and the latest reminder that the death penalty is the ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment.
“Governor Lee had the power to stop this execution before it reached this point. Yet he appallingly chose not to. To make matters worse, the state of Tennessee rushed toward the execution even after a circuit court issued a temporary stay to give time to look into claims that the severe childhood sexual abuse and trauma Ms. Pike experienced were not adequately presented during her trial. It shouldn’t have gotten this far.
“This is the second time in less than five months that Tennessee has botched an execution, with Tony Carruthers having a similar experience in May. Not only does Tennessee have an extended history of botched executions, but its authorities have pursued executions also by shrouding in secrecy its lethal injection process. The extraordinary display of cruelty is emblematic of why the death penalty must be immediately abolished. There is no humane way for the state to kill someone. The death penalty system is broken beyond repair. It is a violation of human rights, and no government should have the power to carry it out.
“Governor Lee has said he will pause all executions, but that does not go nearly far enough. He must grant both Ms. Pike and all those on death row clemency and commute their sentences. He must also establish an indefinite moratorium on all executions, not just for a few months. Yesterday’s harrowing spectacle must spark a new determination to work to move the state of Tennessee to abolish the death penalty once and for all.
“As the death penalty continues to decline around the world, the United States remains increasingly isolated. It is long past time for Tennessee and the United States to stop executing people under the guise of justice and banish this cruel punishment to the history books.”
Notes to editors
Amnesty International opposes the death penalty in all cases without exception – regardless of who is accused, the nature of the crime or if they are guilty or innocent.
In 2025, the U.S. carried out 47 executions in 11 states, reaching the highest they’ve been since 2009. Florida drove the spike with 19 executions. South Carolina, Texas, and Alabama followed with five executions in each state. Other states that used the death penalty were Tennessee (3), Arizona (2), Indiana (2), Mississippi (2), Oklahoma (2), Missouri (1) and Louisiana (1). The U.S. was among the top five highest executing countries of 2025.
So far in 2026, there have been 29 executions in the U.S. Tennessee has executed 11 people since 2018. As of today, 113 countries have abolished the death penalty for all crimes and 145 are abolitionist in law or practice.

The story of a Mariupol surgeon who returned from abroad to serve in the army
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:20:00 EEST
17:20:00 KST

"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here": the story of a Mariupol surgeon who returned from abroad to serve in the army
Mariupol-born Dmytro Hetmanov was used to medicine, with all its difficulties and losses: his entire family works in healthcare, and he himself had barely taken off his white coat since 2013.
But on 24 February 2022, his life was divided into "before" and "after". Suddenly, the civilian urological surgeon found himself having to try and save dozens of people who had been wounded in Russian attacks – many of them fatally.
One of the most challenging cases of Dmytro's life was a teenager who died on the operating table. It was March 2022. A father carried in his wounded son, a boy of 14 or 15.
At first the teenager's wound appeared minor – just a small hole in his chest. But before long, his blood pressure began to drop and his heartbeat slowed. The doctors tried to resuscitate him, but nothing worked.
Dmytro performed a thoracotomy, opening up the boy's chest to carry out direct cardiac massage. It was then that he saw that the heart and blood vessels had been torn apart. There was no way to save him.
The boy's father was waiting outside the theatre.
"I couldn't talk to him. I just couldn't bring myself to do it. I turned around and moved on to the next patient," Dmytro recalls.
At the time, Dmytro was working at Mariupol City Hospital No. 1. People had been bringing wounded civilians in from the early days of the full-scale war. For three weeks, he saved lives in a city where fighting was raging.
When it became almost impossible to continue working, Dmytro left the besieged city with his parents and neighbours. He then spent two years working as a urological surgeon at a university hospital in Poland, but eventually he returned to Ukraine to join the military.
Today, Dmytro is operating on wounded people once again, this time as a military surgeon with the 4th Medical Battalion of the 3rd Army Corps. Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia tells his story.
"I don't remember even a single one of my patients' faces." Surviving Mariupol
Dmytro Hetmanov, who now goes by the alias Hetmani, was born into a family of doctors in Mariupol. Medicine has been his passion since childhood, he says.
In 2013, he graduated from Kharkiv National Medical University and began a urology internship in Donetsk. When the city was occupied by the Russians in 2014, he collected his documents and transferred to a hospital in Kharkiv. After completing his internship in 2015, he returned to his native Mariupol.
Shortly before the start of the full-scale invasion, Dmytro suspected that the war might reach his city. On 23 February 2022, he called his ex-wife and asked her to pack her things.
Dmytro went to his parents' home that night. At around 05:00 on 24 February, he heard the first explosions. His ex-wife left the city with their six-year-old daughter, and Dmytro went to work.
"Everyone was in utter despair, except for some of our junior medical staff. There were some pro-Russian people among them who were delighted that it was happening. They were like, 'The Russians will come now, Putin will hand out money,'" Dmytro recalls.
Some of the doctors left the city during the first few days of the full-scale war. Of the 11 or so urologists working at the hospital, only three initially remained. Later one of them stopped coming in: he lived in another part of Mariupol and could no longer get to work.
The remaining medical staff worked alternate shifts: 24 hours at the hospital, 24 hours off.
"We had a team there: about three or four surgeons stayed. There were two trauma surgeons and two anaesthetists, although in fact there was only one, because the other one took over the running of the hospital," Dmytro says.
The number of wounded patients increased dramatically when Russian forces entered the settlements near Mariupol, including Sartana and Talakivka. More and more casualties began arriving from those areas.
In the early days the emergency services were still able to take the wounded to hospital. Once they stopped operating, people had to find their own way to safety – driving in their own vehicles or walking, sometimes carrying wounded people in their arms.
"It was mostly shrapnel wounds. There weren't any drones back then, but there was a lot of tubed artillery, so it was shrapnel from the shells. And there were penetrating wounds – to the abdomen, chest and so on. We stabilised the patients, then operated on them and continued to care for them afterwards," Dmytro recalls.
Around 30-50 people would arrive at the hospital every day, and around a third of them would need surgery.
"A lot of desperate people whose homes had already been destroyed came to us," Hetmani recollects. "They were looking for shelter and protection in the hospital. The hospital reception was on the ground floor of our surgery building. People used to gather in the corridors.
At first the Russians tried not to hit the hospital. But by mid-March we'd started getting hit too. The hospital was near the Illich Steelworks, where marines from the 36th Brigade were holding the defence. They were under fire from everything, and so were we – tubed artillery, multiple-launch rocket systems, ballistic missiles, mortar fire. Eventually, small-arms fire started up nearby as well. There was close-quarters fighting not far from the hospital."
The doctors were working with no electricity or running water and insufficient medical supplies. By early March, petrol stations, pharmacies and shops had been almost completely emptied.
At home, Dmytro's family shared food with their neighbours. They ate whatever anyone had left – preserves, tinned food and supplies from their freezers. At the hospital, meanwhile, the medical staff prioritised feeding the wounded.
"We didn't eat much. The portions were very small. The wounded were given food first. We'd just grab a little something ourselves and carry on working," Dmytro recalls.
Water was also hard to come by. After his shifts, Dmytro and his family would go to a well near Petrovskyi Park, not far from the cemetery. They boiled the water from the cemetery area and drank it. They collected snow for washing dishes and other household needs. Fortunately, State Emergency Service workers were at least able to deliver non-potable water to the hospital.
Eventually the medical staff ran out of anaesthetics, sutures and dressing materials. Worst of all, however, the hospital had no blood for transfusions. As a result, the post-operative mortality rate was very high, Hetmani recalls.
"Of course the situation in Mariupol was terrible. I've forgotten a lot of it. The mind pushes the bad things away. For example, I can't remember a single face of any of the patients we helped in Mariupol. I don't remember them at all," he says.
There were some lighter moments, however. Dmytro recalls one risky expedition to find diesel.
"I'd come home from a shift and my parents were cooking outside. We'd had a bit to drink – I was stressed. Then some guys we knew came over and said, 'Everyone's looting the petrol stations. You can get some diesel there.'
And I thought, 'We've got a generator at the hospital. Let's grab some containers, go and get some diesel and take it to the hospital,'" Dmytro recalls.
Dmytro drove to a petrol station near the Illich Steelworks. To the sound of artillery fire booming all around him, he drew off the diesel and poured it into plastic containers. He took it to the hospital, then collected some empty containers that had been used for dialysis water and made several more trips.
"When the fuel there ran out, we went to another petrol station where the marines were handing out diesel. I said, 'Guys, let me through, it's for the hospital.' I hadn't even changed yet – I was still wearing my scrubs. And one of the marines says over the radio, 'There's some half-drunk doctor here demanding diesel,'" Dmytro smiles.
Dmytro managed to obtain around 300 litres of diesel – enough to keep the hospital running for four or five days. When he finally returned home, his mother was crying. She had thought he had been killed somewhere in the city.
"The Drama Theatre was burning before my eyes." The escape
On 15 March, Dmytro and his colleagues had an especially hard shift. Many wounded people were brought to the hospital, and the surgeons operated until late into the night. When the work was finally over, Dmytro went to sleep, only to be woken the next morning by an explosion nearby.
"A FAB [a high-explosive aerial bomb – ed.] had landed somewhere nearby. I woke up and went to the stairwell to have a smoke. You could see the village of Volonterivka from a nearby window, and there was already small-arms fire there. I thought, another day or two and the Russians will be here [in the hospital]. We have to do something," the doctor recalls.
That day, the medical staff gathered to discuss how they would continue working. Several older colleagues who could not leave because they were taking care of sick family members decided to stay at the hospital, while the rest of the team decided to try to escape the city.
Dmytro decided to leave as well. He says he realised that once Russian forces were established there, someone might snitch on him because of his pro-Ukraine views.
Back home, Dmytro told his parents they needed to pack immediately. The family also took some neighbours with them whose cars had been destroyed.
"There were seven people and a cat in my car. And my parents had another two or three people in theirs," he says.
To leave in the direction of Berdiansk and then on to Zaporizhzhia, they had to cross Mariupol. Dmytro lived in the Kalmiuskyi district, so their route took them through the city centre, where intense fighting was underway. There was no humanitarian corridor at the time – the family set off at their own risk.
On the way, Dmytro drove past the Drama Theatre. That day, 16 March, Russian forces had bombed the building, where hundreds of civilians had been sheltering.
"It was still burning before my eyes," he recalls.
Dmytro and his family headed west through the port towards the road to Manhush. They managed to avoid the fighting. A convoy of cars had already formed on the road, full of other people trying to escape Mariupol.
Then came the Russian checkpoints. At a checkpoint in Manhush, Russian soldiers nearly confiscated Dmytro's car. He was eventually allowed through after giving money to one of them.
At around 01:00, they reached Tokmak, where they met some of Dmytro's colleagues. Another Russian checkpoint lay ahead, but no one was being allowed through at night.
"There was this huge line of refugees. It was bitterly cold, around -10°C. And I had hardly any petrol left, so I couldn't turn on the heater. Nobody slept that night," Dmytro says.
At around 06:00, the barrier was raised. After being checked, the convoy continued on its way. Dmytro says they passed through around 10 checkpoints in Tokmak alone. Beyond Vasylivka, he saw signs of fighting and burnt-out military vehicles, both Ukrainian and Russian.
Near the line of contact, Russian troops stopped the convoy of civilian vehicles and used it as cover.
"There was a Russian armoured personnel carrier in front, people moving in formation on either side, and all this whistling and roaring overhead – mortar rounds, artillery fire. And they stopped us and used us as cover. They kept us there for about 40 minutes.
I'm sitting behind the wheel thinking, 'Well, that's it. We survived Mariupol, the Russian shells didn't get us, and now our own guys are going to finish us off,'" Dmytro admits.
But the Ukrainian troops did not fire when they saw the civilian vehicles. Eventually, the Russian soldiers allowed the convoy to continue. A bridge on the road to Zaporizhzhia had been destroyed, so the drivers had to take other roads around it. Finally, Dmytro and his family reached Ukrainian-controlled territory.
"I saw the Ukrainian flag and our police officers. I'd never been so happy to see the police in my life. We were home," he recalls.
The police met the evacuees and helped them reach a hub for displaced people in Zaporizhzhia which had been set up in a hypermarket. Dmytro and his family had left Mariupol with almost no food or water, so the first thing they did was look for something to eat.
"I got a can of Coca-Cola and a fresh, warm French baguette. It was the best thing I'd eaten in two weeks," the doctor recalls.
Shortly after Dmytro escaped, Russian forces razed the Mariupol hospital where he had worked to the ground.
"Friends were joining the Armed Forces while I was sitting here. It really ate away at me." Poland
Dmytro's ex-wife and daughter found refuge in Kraków, staying at the home of a Polish woman who was also a medical professional. She invited Dmytro to join them – as the father of a child with a disability, he was entitled to leave Ukraine.
"To be honest, I thought I'd go back straight away. I thought I'd have a month off, then return and join the Armed Forces. Because the guys I'd worked with joined up almost immediately. Most of them went into the Medical Forces. But my ex-wife said to me, 'Why would you go off to fight? You have a child, and you can work as a doctor in Poland. Give it a try.'
So I thought, all right, I'll give it a try. I started going around hospitals and looking [for jobs] online. I was told to get lost a few times. Then I found Professor Andrzej Paradysz in Katowice. He's an amazing person, a very empathetic doctor. I told him my story and he took me on straight away. He has a soft spot for Ukrainians because his family has roots in Lviv. He treated me extremely well," Dmytro recalls.
Later his ex-wife and daughter moved to the US, while Dmytro stayed in Katowice with his parents. At first he assisted doctors during operations. He later obtained his licence and began operating independently. Within six months, he had learnt Polish fairly well and become close with his colleagues. But he says he was plagued by guilt.
"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here. Some of my friends had joined the Armed Forces, while I was sitting here enjoying life. It just gnawed away at me. I was constantly watching the same Dvizh footage [a YouTube project by the 3rd Assault Brigade – ed.] on social media or military videos.
Then my parents went to Kyiv. They'd been really homesick and had neither the energy nor the inclination to settle in Poland. I told them, 'If that's how you feel, then go.' Once everyone had left, I was on my own. I became terribly depressed. And eventually I couldn't take it any more," Dmytro recalls.
After two years in Poland, Dmytro handed in his resignation to the professor and left a few days later. He obtained a letter of recommendation for a military unit, took it to a military enlistment office, completed basic military training and signed a three-year contract as a soldier.
Dmytro decided to take a break from medicine and joined one of the regiments in Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces.
"I wanted a bit of a break from medicine. I was also interested in working with maps and spatial orientation. I've been interested in military equipment and geography since I was a child," he says.
He spent around six months working in Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv oblasts, and occasionally in Luhansk Oblast. But eventually he began to miss military medicine. His original crew was also starting to be disbanded, as the regiment was being expanded into a brigade.
"I'd done enough 'flying', put it that way. I realised I missed medicine. I was already starting to forget a lot of things, and my hands weren't getting any practice. It's like being a guitarist or a pianist – you've got to keep your hand in," he says.
In 2025 Dmytro saw an ad on social media for the medical battalion of the 3rd Assault Brigade. He applied for a position.
"I didn't want to work in some hospital in a town or city. I like working closer to the battlefield. I wanted to be nearer the action," he says.
"What I probably like most is the camaraderie." Serving with the 3rd Army Corps
Dmytro is once again working as a surgeon with the 4th Separate Medical Battalion of the 3rd Army Corps, but his range of duties is now considerably broader than when he worked as a urologist. For one thing, he has taken part in brain surgery for the first time.
"I'd never operated on someone's head in my life. But Vahus, our neurosurgeon, said to me, 'Come along with me and get some practice.' I assisted him and sutured the dura mater. I have general surgical skills, but I'd never worked in that area before. With his help, though, it was interesting to try something new," Dmytro says.
Dmytro had also never performed an amputation in civilian practice, but he can now take part in such operations as well.
The medical team most often treats soldiers with limb injuries. Many have minor shrapnel wounds or gunshot fractures. Trauma surgeons primarily handle these cases, with Dmytro assisting them.
Dmytro himself most enjoys operating on penetrating abdominal wounds.
"I like operating on the abdomen. I used to work in endourology, so I'm not afraid to go in there now," he says.
Not all of his work in the battalion involves combat injuries. Soldiers also come to Dmytro with ordinary urological conditions. He performs ultrasound scans, gives medical advice and sometimes operates on them. On days when there are few wounded soldiers, he devotes his time to routine procedures.
"I've been with the battalion for almost a year now, and we've all learned to work really well together. We have a great team. We're all very close, we work well together and communicate well with each other. What I probably like most is the camaraderie, the sense that we're all brothers," he says.
Hetmani says he hasn't regretted his decision to serve for a single day, although he does miss his daughter.
"I can see she's upset that I'm not there with her," he says. "Maybe she sees other children's dads picking them up from school, and she doesn't have that. She doesn't talk about it, but I can tell it bothers her.
But this is my duty. I volunteered, so ultimately it was my decision. I need to finish what needs to be done here, and then I can think about what comes next."
Olena Barsukova, Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life)

Over 65 participants join URCS Intl Humanitarian Law School
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:17:33 EEST
17:17:33 KST

Over 65 participants joined the Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS) September School on International Humanitarian Law (IHL).
“International humanitarian law consists of rules that must work in real life and protect real people. This is particularly important for Ukraine today. IHL is part of our daily reality. Behind its rules are civilians, the wounded and sick, medical personnel, humanitarian workers, families waiting for their loved ones and other people protected by IHL,” stated Maksym Dotsenko, President of the Ukrainian Red Cross Society.
As URCS said on Facebook, this year’s School brought together more than 65 participants, including members of the Interagency Commission on the Application and Implementation of International Humanitarian Law in Ukraine. Over four days, participants discussed current IHL issues, worked through practical cases and exchanged experiences with representatives of Ukrainian government institutions and the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement.
The School’s programme covered the fundamentals of IHL and its practical application, including the protection of civilians; means and methods of warfare; the treatment of prisoners of war; the protection of the natural environment and cultural property; humanitarian assistance; and the use and protection of the Red Cross emblem.
Particular attention was paid to contemporary challenges, including the use of unmanned systems, information and communication technologies, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence during armed conflict. Participants also discussed the implementation of IHL in national legislation, accountability for violations of IHL, the Platform for the Progressive Development of IHL, the Global Initiative to Galvanise Political Commitment to IHL, and the Register of Damage for Ukraine (RD4U).
Ukrainian and international IHL experts, representatives of Ukrainian government institutions, the Ukrainian Red Cross, the Danish Red Cross, the Norwegian Red Cross, the British Red Cross, the Canadian Red Cross, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and other organizations contributed to the training sessions.
The IHL September School is part of the Ukrainian Red Cross’s ongoing work in its auxiliary role to government authorities in the humanitarian field. It provides a space for professional exchange and the practical application of IHL knowledge.

Zelensky: Russia launched over 100 attack drones at Ukraine overnight, nearly 50 of them jet-powered
According to Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in a Facebook post.
"Last night, the Russians launched more than 100 attack drones at Ukraine, nearly 50 of them jet-powered. Our warriors neutralized most of them, but unfortunately, there were also hits. In Kyiv, 'Shaheds' struck the Pivdennyi Bridge several times. In the morning, a residential high-rise was hit. Tragically, one person was killed. My condolences to their family and loved ones. In Kherson, the Russians 'defeated' a kindergarten; in Kharkiv, they attacked a grocery store, and an institute and critical infrastructure were damaged," Zelensky said.
According to him, enemy strikes also hit apartment buildings in Kramatorsk and Sumy. The Dnipro, Odesa, Kharkiv, Kyiv, Poltava, and Rivne regions also came under attack. As of now, four people have been reported injured in the overnight Russian attack. Emergency services are working wherever they are needed.
"No matter how hard Moscow tries to fully localize the production of its drones and missiles, its ability to escalate remains critically dependent on foreign components. These are supply chains running from Europe, the United States, China, Japan, and many other countries. Most of these companies are well-known manufacturers, but their components still make their way to Russia," Zelensky said.
He stressed that every Russian drone can in fact be stopped while it is still on the production line.
"What is needed is the political will of these countries. If the Kremlin has chosen more strikes, sanctions must work and must be strengthened. Thank you to everyone who is helping.," Zelensky added.
As reported, public transport traffic on some bridges in Kyiv has been temporarily restricted due to overnight enemy attacks.

Today, Dmytro is operating on wounded people once again, this time as a military surgeon with the 4th Medical Battalion of the 3rd Army Corps. Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia tells his story.
"I don't remember even a single one of my patients' faces." Surviving Mariupol
Dmytro Hetmanov, who now goes by the alias Hetmani, was born into a family of doctors in Mariupol. Medicine has been his passion since childhood, he says.
In 2013, he graduated from Kharkiv National Medical University and began a urology internship in Donetsk. When the city was occupied by the Russians in 2014, he collected his documents and transferred to a hospital in Kharkiv. After completing his internship in 2015, he returned to his native Mariupol.
Shortly before the start of the full-scale invasion, Dmytro suspected that the war might reach his city. On 23 February 2022, he called his ex-wife and asked her to pack her things.
Dmytro went to his parents' home that night. At around 05:00 on 24 February, he heard the first explosions. His ex-wife left the city with their six-year-old daughter, and Dmytro went to work.
"Everyone was in utter despair, except for some of our junior medical staff. There were some pro-Russian people among them who were delighted that it was happening. They were like, 'The Russians will come now, Putin will hand out money,'" Dmytro recalls.
Some of the doctors left the city during the first few days of the full-scale war. Of the 11 or so urologists working at the hospital, only three initially remained. Later one of them stopped coming in: he lived in another part of Mariupol and could no longer get to work.
The remaining medical staff worked alternate shifts: 24 hours at the hospital, 24 hours off.
"We had a team there: about three or four surgeons stayed. There were two trauma surgeons and two anaesthetists, although in fact there was only one, because the other one took over the running of the hospital," Dmytro says.
The number of wounded patients increased dramatically when Russian forces entered the settlements near Mariupol, including Sartana and Talakivka. More and more casualties began arriving from those areas.
In the early days the emergency services were still able to take the wounded to hospital. Once they stopped operating, people had to find their own way to safety – driving in their own vehicles or walking, sometimes carrying wounded people in their arms.
"It was mostly shrapnel wounds. There weren't any drones back then, but there was a lot of tubed artillery, so it was shrapnel from the shells. And there were penetrating wounds – to the abdomen, chest and so on. We stabilised the patients, then operated on them and continued to care for them afterwards," Dmytro recalls.
Around 30-50 people would arrive at the hospital every day, and around a third of them would need surgery.
"A lot of desperate people whose homes had already been destroyed came to us," Hetmani recollects. "They were looking for shelter and protection in the hospital. The hospital reception was on the ground floor of our surgery building. People used to gather in the corridors.
At first the Russians tried not to hit the hospital. But by mid-March we'd started getting hit too. The hospital was near the Illich Steelworks, where marines from the 36th Brigade were holding the defence. They were under fire from everything, and so were we – tubed artillery, multiple-launch rocket systems, ballistic missiles, mortar fire. Eventually, small-arms fire started up nearby as well. There was close-quarters fighting not far from the hospital."
The doctors were working with no electricity or running water and insufficient medical supplies. By early March, petrol stations, pharmacies and shops had been almost completely emptied.
At home, Dmytro's family shared food with their neighbours. They ate whatever anyone had left – preserves, tinned food and supplies from their freezers. At the hospital, meanwhile, the medical staff prioritised feeding the wounded.
"We didn't eat much. The portions were very small. The wounded were given food first. We'd just grab a little something ourselves and carry on working," Dmytro recalls.
Water was also hard to come by. After his shifts, Dmytro and his family would go to a well near Petrovskyi Park, not far from the cemetery. They boiled the water from the cemetery area and drank it. They collected snow for washing dishes and other household needs. Fortunately, State Emergency Service workers were at least able to deliver non-potable water to the hospital.
Eventually the medical staff ran out of anaesthetics, sutures and dressing materials. Worst of all, however, the hospital had no blood for transfusions. As a result, the post-operative mortality rate was very high, Hetmani recalls.
"Of course the situation in Mariupol was terrible. I've forgotten a lot of it. The mind pushes the bad things away. For example, I can't remember a single face of any of the patients we helped in Mariupol. I don't remember them at all," he says.
There were some lighter moments, however. Dmytro recalls one risky expedition to find diesel.
"I'd come home from a shift and my parents were cooking outside. We'd had a bit to drink – I was stressed. Then some guys we knew came over and said, 'Everyone's looting the petrol stations. You can get some diesel there.'
And I thought, 'We've got a generator at the hospital. Let's grab some containers, go and get some diesel and take it to the hospital,'" Dmytro recalls.
Dmytro drove to a petrol station near the Illich Steelworks. To the sound of artillery fire booming all around him, he drew off the diesel and poured it into plastic containers. He took it to the hospital, then collected some empty containers that had been used for dialysis water and made several more trips.
"When the fuel there ran out, we went to another petrol station where the marines were handing out diesel. I said, 'Guys, let me through, it's for the hospital.' I hadn't even changed yet – I was still wearing my scrubs. And one of the marines says over the radio, 'There's some half-drunk doctor here demanding diesel,'" Dmytro smiles.
Dmytro managed to obtain around 300 litres of diesel – enough to keep the hospital running for four or five days. When he finally returned home, his mother was crying. She had thought he had been killed somewhere in the city.
"The Drama Theatre was burning before my eyes." The escape
On 15 March, Dmytro and his colleagues had an especially hard shift. Many wounded people were brought to the hospital, and the surgeons operated until late into the night. When the work was finally over, Dmytro went to sleep, only to be woken the next morning by an explosion nearby.
"A FAB [a high-explosive aerial bomb – ed.] had landed somewhere nearby. I woke up and went to the stairwell to have a smoke. You could see the village of Volonterivka from a nearby window, and there was already small-arms fire there. I thought, another day or two and the Russians will be here [in the hospital]. We have to do something," the doctor recalls.
That day, the medical staff gathered to discuss how they would continue working. Several older colleagues who could not leave because they were taking care of sick family members decided to stay at the hospital, while the rest of the team decided to try to escape the city.
Dmytro decided to leave as well. He says he realised that once Russian forces were established there, someone might snitch on him because of his pro-Ukraine views.
Back home, Dmytro told his parents they needed to pack immediately. The family also took some neighbours with them whose cars had been destroyed.
"There were seven people and a cat in my car. And my parents had another two or three people in theirs," he says.
To leave in the direction of Berdiansk and then on to Zaporizhzhia, they had to cross Mariupol. Dmytro lived in the Kalmiuskyi district, so their route took them through the city centre, where intense fighting was underway. There was no humanitarian corridor at the time – the family set off at their own risk.
On the way, Dmytro drove past the Drama Theatre. That day, 16 March, Russian forces had bombed the building, where hundreds of civilians had been sheltering.
"It was still burning before my eyes," he recalls.
Dmytro and his family headed west through the port towards the road to Manhush. They managed to avoid the fighting. A convoy of cars had already formed on the road, full of other people trying to escape Mariupol.
Then came the Russian checkpoints. At a checkpoint in Manhush, Russian soldiers nearly confiscated Dmytro's car. He was eventually allowed through after giving money to one of them.
At around 01:00, they reached Tokmak, where they met some of Dmytro's colleagues. Another Russian checkpoint lay ahead, but no one was being allowed through at night.
"There was this huge line of refugees. It was bitterly cold, around -10°C. And I had hardly any petrol left, so I couldn't turn on the heater. Nobody slept that night," Dmytro says.
At around 06:00, the barrier was raised. After being checked, the convoy continued on its way. Dmytro says they passed through around 10 checkpoints in Tokmak alone. Beyond Vasylivka, he saw signs of fighting and burnt-out military vehicles, both Ukrainian and Russian.
Near the line of contact, Russian troops stopped the convoy of civilian vehicles and used it as cover.
"There was a Russian armoured personnel carrier in front, people moving in formation on either side, and all this whistling and roaring overhead – mortar rounds, artillery fire. And they stopped us and used us as cover. They kept us there for about 40 minutes.
I'm sitting behind the wheel thinking, 'Well, that's it. We survived Mariupol, the Russian shells didn't get us, and now our own guys are going to finish us off,'" Dmytro admits.
But the Ukrainian troops did not fire when they saw the civilian vehicles. Eventually, the Russian soldiers allowed the convoy to continue. A bridge on the road to Zaporizhzhia had been destroyed, so the drivers had to take other roads around it. Finally, Dmytro and his family reached Ukrainian-controlled territory.
"I saw the Ukrainian flag and our police officers. I'd never been so happy to see the police in my life. We were home," he recalls.
The police met the evacuees and helped them reach a hub for displaced people in Zaporizhzhia which had been set up in a hypermarket. Dmytro and his family had left Mariupol with almost no food or water, so the first thing they did was look for something to eat.
"I got a can of Coca-Cola and a fresh, warm French baguette. It was the best thing I'd eaten in two weeks," the doctor recalls.
Shortly after Dmytro escaped, Russian forces razed the Mariupol hospital where he had worked to the ground.
"Friends were joining the Armed Forces while I was sitting here. It really ate away at me." Poland
Dmytro's ex-wife and daughter found refuge in Kraków, staying at the home of a Polish woman who was also a medical professional. She invited Dmytro to join them – as the father of a child with a disability, he was entitled to leave Ukraine.
"To be honest, I thought I'd go back straight away. I thought I'd have a month off, then return and join the Armed Forces. Because the guys I'd worked with joined up almost immediately. Most of them went into the Medical Forces. But my ex-wife said to me, 'Why would you go off to fight? You have a child, and you can work as a doctor in Poland. Give it a try.'
So I thought, all right, I'll give it a try. I started going around hospitals and looking [for jobs] online. I was told to get lost a few times. Then I found Professor Andrzej Paradysz in Katowice. He's an amazing person, a very empathetic doctor. I told him my story and he took me on straight away. He has a soft spot for Ukrainians because his family has roots in Lviv. He treated me extremely well," Dmytro recalls.
Later his ex-wife and daughter moved to the US, while Dmytro stayed in Katowice with his parents. At first he assisted doctors during operations. He later obtained his licence and began operating independently. Within six months, he had learnt Polish fairly well and become close with his colleagues. But he says he was plagued by guilt.
"It was eating away at me that my country was at war while I was here. Some of my friends had joined the Armed Forces, while I was sitting here enjoying life. It just gnawed away at me. I was constantly watching the same Dvizh footage [a YouTube project by the 3rd Assault Brigade – ed.] on social media or military videos.
Then my parents went to Kyiv. They'd been really homesick and had neither the energy nor the inclination to settle in Poland. I told them, 'If that's how you feel, then go.' Once everyone had left, I was on my own. I became terribly depressed. And eventually I couldn't take it any more," Dmytro recalls.
After two years in Poland, Dmytro handed in his resignation to the professor and left a few days later. He obtained a letter of recommendation for a military unit, took it to a military enlistment office, completed basic military training and signed a three-year contract as a soldier.
Dmytro decided to take a break from medicine and joined one of the regiments in Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces.
"I wanted a bit of a break from medicine. I was also interested in working with maps and spatial orientation. I've been interested in military equipment and geography since I was a child," he says.
He spent around six months working in Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv oblasts, and occasionally in Luhansk Oblast. But eventually he began to miss military medicine. His original crew was also starting to be disbanded, as the regiment was being expanded into a brigade.
"I'd done enough 'flying', put it that way. I realised I missed medicine. I was already starting to forget a lot of things, and my hands weren't getting any practice. It's like being a guitarist or a pianist – you've got to keep your hand in," he says.
In 2025 Dmytro saw an ad on social media for the medical battalion of the 3rd Assault Brigade. He applied for a position.
"I didn't want to work in some hospital in a town or city. I like working closer to the battlefield. I wanted to be nearer the action," he says.
"What I probably like most is the camaraderie." Serving with the 3rd Army Corps
Dmytro is once again working as a surgeon with the 4th Separate Medical Battalion of the 3rd Army Corps, but his range of duties is now considerably broader than when he worked as a urologist. For one thing, he has taken part in brain surgery for the first time.
"I'd never operated on someone's head in my life. But Vahus, our neurosurgeon, said to me, 'Come along with me and get some practice.' I assisted him and sutured the dura mater. I have general surgical skills, but I'd never worked in that area before. With his help, though, it was interesting to try something new," Dmytro says.
Dmytro had also never performed an amputation in civilian practice, but he can now take part in such operations as well.
The medical team most often treats soldiers with limb injuries. Many have minor shrapnel wounds or gunshot fractures. Trauma surgeons primarily handle these cases, with Dmytro assisting them.
Dmytro himself most enjoys operating on penetrating abdominal wounds.
"I like operating on the abdomen. I used to work in endourology, so I'm not afraid to go in there now," he says.
Not all of his work in the battalion involves combat injuries. Soldiers also come to Dmytro with ordinary urological conditions. He performs ultrasound scans, gives medical advice and sometimes operates on them. On days when there are few wounded soldiers, he devotes his time to routine procedures.
"I've been with the battalion for almost a year now, and we've all learned to work really well together. We have a great team. We're all very close, we work well together and communicate well with each other. What I probably like most is the camaraderie, the sense that we're all brothers," he says.
Hetmani says he hasn't regretted his decision to serve for a single day, although he does miss his daughter.
"I can see she's upset that I'm not there with her," he says. "Maybe she sees other children's dads picking them up from school, and she doesn't have that. She doesn't talk about it, but I can tell it bothers her.
But this is my duty. I volunteered, so ultimately it was my decision. I need to finish what needs to be done here, and then I can think about what comes next."
Olena Barsukova, Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life)

Drones connection to ERA-GLONASS system may help to ease flight restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:14:55 UTC
17:14:55 KST

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Drones identification via the ERA-GLONASS infosystem could pave the way for a gradual easing of flight restrictions in Russian regions, Maxim Chizhov, the Board Chairman of Kitoglav company engaged in the production and operation of agricultural drones, told TASS.
"Such transparency is precisely what is needed for a gradual transition from case-by-case permits and restrictions to broader industrial applications of drones, in agriculture, infrastructure monitoring, forestry, aerial photography, and logistics. The more operators will work in good faith within a clear and controlled digital environment, the more grounds will be for easing flight restrictions on unmanned aerial systems in the regions," he said.
The requirement for a verified connection to the system when submitting a flight plan integrates aircraft identification, operator accountability, and airspace use planning into a single digital environment, Chizhov said.
"For drone owners compliant with the law, this is not an additional formality but a tool that confirms the legality of the flight and makes operating in the airspace more predictable. In turn, for government authorities and regulatory agencies, identification provides a transparent picture of who is flying, where, and on what legal grounds," he noted.
More than 1,000 users have connected to the system, with over 1,200 drones registered. The users pool includes around 750 legal entities, including 50 drone airlines. The system underwent testing across 40 regions before its launch, allowing its performance to be checked under various conditions and drone application scenarios.
Earlier, the Russian Ministry of Transport said that drone flight plans would only be accepted if connected to the ERA-GLONASS system since October 1.

‘They are crying’: Refugees in Malaysia in fear amid Myanmar deportation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:14:18 UTC
17:14:18 KST

‘They are crying’: Refugees in Malaysia in fear amid Myanmar deportation
Shrinking financial and operational resources for refugee support groups in Malaysia collide with increasing hostility towards them, particularly stateless Rohingya.
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – The phone hasn’t stopped ringing in recent days. Raf*, a leader of refugees from Myanmar who are living in Malaysia, receives more than 100 calls a day, and they follow a common pattern.
“They are crying, asking me to do something,” Raf told Al Jazeera.
The Malaysian government on Tuesday deported nearly 1,500 refugees, part of its stated plan to send back at least 5,000 refugees as part of a deal with the military government of Myanmar. That move, from a country that had long taken in the refugees, has sparked fear among the tens of thousands of other refugees from Myanmar in the country, who have one question at the top of their minds: Who might be next?
The deportation was carried out during escalating raids on refugee communities by immigration officials, which have led to the detention of more than 50,000 refugees this year alone. Those working with refugees in Malaysia said the frequency of the raids has increased since June when Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced the repatriation agreement with Myanmar.
“[We’ve seen] a sharp increase. Raids are happening every single day. There’s up to 50 raids or more happening every day,” said Heidy Quah, founder and executive director of the Malaysian nonprofit Refuge for the Refugees.
Minister of Home Affairs Saifuddin Nasution told local media that the government has conducted more than 9,700 such operations from the beginning of this year until September 17. That’s an average of 37 operations a day.
There are now more than 10,000 Myanmar nationals in Malaysia’s immigration depots, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs.
In all, Malaysia is home to more than 215,000 refugees, according to the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). Nearly 194,000 are from Myanmar. There are more than 126,000 Rohingya refugees in Malaysia, where they have been the target of widespread hate speech on social media in recent months. Apart from the Rohingya, the Myanmar refugees in Malaysia include nearly 16,000 from the Chin community and 33,000 from other Myanmar communities. The non-Myanmar refugees in Malaysia include small numbers of Pakistanis, Yemenis, Somalis, Afghans, Syrians, Sri Lankans, Palestinians and Iraqis.
The Myanmar refugee community in Malaysia has yet to identify any Rohingya among the first nearly 1,500 people deported on Tuesday, community leaders told Al Jazeera. Instead, many are from Myanmar’s other ethnic minorities, who are more likely to have valid national identification documents, community leaders said.
“The Rohingyas are a problem for deportation because Myanmar denies their citizenship,” Raf said. “So I don’t think that Myanmar will agree and accept all those Rohingyas.”
Myanmar officially treats the Rohingya as Bangladeshi immigrants despite the community’s long roots in Myanmar and their distinct ethnic identity. The Myanmar army has repeatedly cracked down on the Rohingya minority, including a wave of violence in 2017 that many rights groups have described as genocide. It set off a major refugee crisis when hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled to Bangladesh, Malaysia, India and other neighbouring nations.
Myanmar community leaders also said the raids this year appear to have targeted locations highlighted in anti-refugee videos on social media in which content creators filmed refugee-populated areas, portraying them as hubs of chaos. These videos have been shared thousands of times on platforms such as Threads, TikTok and Facebook.
Al Jazeera contacted the Immigration Department to verify the link between the videos and raids but had not received a response at the time of publication. Accounts that had posted and shared antirefugee sentiment also did not respond to requests for comment.
Decline in resources
The increase in hostilities towards refugees in Malaysia coincides with a sharp decline in the capacity of local and international aid groups to support them, especially since the closure of the United States Agency for International Development in July 2025.
In Malaysia, this severely shrank resources for organisations helping refugees with basic needs, such as healthcare, Quah told Al Jazeera.
“Then slowly, United Nations organisations were being defunded, and even within the UN High Commissioner for Refugees in Malaysia, they lost a lot of staff,” Quah said. The job cuts reflected global retrenchments by UNHCR last year.
The agency continues to struggle with a funding crisis, saying on Tuesday that it faces a $5.79bn funding gap and, as of July, has received 32 percent of the funds it needs this year.
In Malaysia, this has led to even less protection for refugees and higher rates of exploitation, Quah said.
“Even UNHCR cardholders are arrested and remanded for about 14 days [while the] cards are verified,” she said.
For instance, an asylum-seeking woman who had scheduled an appointment to meet UNHCR representatives this month was recently detained, and immigration authorities demanded a letter from the organisation to prove that she was an asylum seeker, Quah said.
Although UNHCR confirmed the woman was seeking asylum, she remains in detention, Quah said.
Ongoing violence in Myanmar
UNHCR and rights groups in Malaysia have urged the Malaysian government to stop the deportations as violence continues in Myanmar.
A day before Malaysia’s deportation of the refugees on Tuesday, an air strike by Myanmar’s military was reported to have killed at least 33 people in Rakhine state, the historical home of the Rohingya. The Arakan Army group said the victims included vendors, shoppers and pedestrians. In June, the UN said Myanmar’s military was responsible for more than 700 civilian deaths over a six-month election period that started in August last year.
The Human Rights Commission of Malaysia (SUHAKAM) said that while Malaysia is not a party to the Refugee Convention of 1951, the principle of nonrefoulement has become part of customary international law and Malaysia, therefore, is bound to abide by it. The principle protects people from being returned to a place where they face a real risk of persecution, torture or other serious harm.
Particular attention should also be given to children, SUHAKAM said, highlighting that Tuesday’s deportation included 27 children, some reportedly as young as eight years old.
“No child should be returned to danger. Their safety, dignity and best interests must come first,” it said.
Myanmar community leaders in Malaysia told Al Jazeera the ships that departed on Tuesday will arrive in Yangon on Sunday.
“After that, we will [learn] whether they are allowed to leave the port safely [or are detained],” said one community leader who requested anonymity due to the increase in violence towards refugees in Malaysia.
Still, even those who are allowed to leave the port may need to spend months or years in Yangon because it is unsafe to travel across the country, the community leader said.
Call for independent access
Rights groups further criticised the Malaysian government’s framing of the deportations as “voluntary”, saying individuals should have sufficient information about conditions in their home countries before making such a decision.
“While authorities say the returns are voluntary, those returned had been held in immigration detention. This raises serious questions about whether decisions to return were genuinely free and informed,” UNHCR Assistant High Commissioner for Protection Edem Wosornu said.
The Malaysian government said people were selected for deportation based on a list of names shared by the Myanmar government in an official diplomatic note.
“Such [a] ‘voluntary’ decision must be determined by an independent authority, such as the UNHCR, and not by the Immigration Department,” SUHAKAM said .
UNHCR told Al Jazeera that it was not involved in the latest return process and did not have access to the individuals concerned. “[We were,] therefore, not in a position to independently ascertain the voluntariness of their decisions to return,” it said.
“We continue to encourage the government to ensure that return processes include individual assessments, access to protection procedures and safeguards to ensure that any decision to return is free, informed and genuinely voluntary,” it said.
Malaysia registering refugees
The deportations come at a time when Malaysia is simultaneously positioning itself as welcoming to refugees and their needs.
In 2015, the Malaysian government launched a Refugee Registration Document (DPP) programme. On paper, it is supposed to help register refugees, giving them official documentation.
Raf welcomed the DPP as long as the registration and documentation of refugees in Malaysia leads to access to work, education and healthcare.
“If these three things are provided, I think that’s a good solution for temporary refugees staying here.”
But the Malaysian branches of Amnesty International and Asylum Access said the latest deportations raise profound concerns about the purpose of the DPP. The programme should not be used to fast-track unlawful deportations, the groups said in a joint statement.
*Name changed to protect the individual’s identity

BAKU, October 2. /TASS/. The Unmanned Systems Group is updating the production of Supercam S350 drones to meet new customer demands, taking into account the situation on the battlefield, the company’s Spokeswoman Yekaterina Zgirovskaya told TASS at the ADEX 2026 International Defense Exhibition in Baku.
"Our main focus now is on effectively adapting to the demands of the military and civilian markets. We are streamlining our production processes, developing our in-house capabilities, and expanding our network of suppliers. This enables us to quickly implement new solutions and support the entire product lifecycle, including new operator training programs and after-sales service.

"At the start of the special military operation, the Russian Army needed a stealthy and quiet tactical reconnaissance drone with an electric motor. As we can see, the Supercam S350 performed this task successfully," Zgirovskaya said. "However, over time, the enemy learned to counter them using its electronic warfare systems. That’s when the upgraded S350M version appeared, featuring improved protection against such systems. Then anti-aircraft drones came into play and began shooting down the reconnaissance aircraft. As technology evolved, reconnaissance aircraft began to be targeted by drones capable of flying faster than a quadcopter, and so on.".

SP to field third candidate in UP Rajya Sabha polls? How move would trigger contest with BJP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
08:13:46 UTC
17:13:46 KST

The SP has so far announced two candidates, both of whom are assured of win
NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party (SP) MP Virendra Singh on Friday announced that the party will field a third candidate in the upcoming Rajya Sabha elections in Uttar Pradesh, despite only two SP candidates being assured of victory.If the SP fields a third candidate, it would set up a contest with the ruling BJP for one seat. Seven BJP candidates are assured of victory. Polling for 10 vacant Rajya Sabha seats from the state is scheduled for October 16.“We will decide our third candidate today and the nomination will be filed by October 5,” Singh told PTI.The Chandauli MP further remarked that the SP would adopt the “same strategy” the BJP used to secure the election of its candidates in the previous Rajya Sabha polls.“We will get all three of our candidates elected through the same route by which the BJP had got its candidates elected in the last Rajya Sabha elections,” Singh added.He also claimed that several BJP MLAs seeking SP tickets for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections were in touch with the Akhilesh Yadav-led party.Singh’s remarks came a day after Akhilesh Yadav declined to confirm whether the SP would field a third candidate, suggesting that the BJP could put up “nine or even 10 candidates.”
The SP on September 30 nominated veteran party leader and Akhilesh Yadav’s uncle, Ram Gopal Yadav, and Reliance Industries executive Dhanraj Parimal Nathwani for the elections. Both subsequently filed their nomination papers in Lucknow.
The arithemtic
The number of first-preference votes required to win a Rajya Sabha seat in Uttar Pradesh depends on the number of vacancies and the number of MLAs eligible to vote. With 10 seats up for election this time, the winning benchmark is likely to be around 37 first-preference votes.The BJP currently has 255 MLAs in the 403-member Uttar Pradesh assembly, while its NDA allies have another 33, taking the alliance’s combined strength to 288.The SP has 101 MLAs. Three legislators who defected to the BJP are currently unattached, while rebel MLA Puja Pal remains listed with the SP despite having joined the BJP. The Congress, an SP ally, has two MLAs.
In the 2024 Rajya Sabha elections in Uttar Pradesh, the BJP won all eight seats it contested, while two of the SP’s three nominees were elected. The SP’s third candidate, Alok Ranjan, lost.Rajya Sabha elections are conducted through proportional representation using the single transferable vote system. Under this system, surplus votes received by winning candidates can be transferred to other candidates based on voters’ subsequent preferences.As a result, if more than 10 candidates enter the fray, the contest could hinge on the distribution and transfer of votes, making electoral arithmetic and strategy crucial.(With PTI inputs)
