France closes 400 schools as education protests spiral into unrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:51:00 UTC
16:51:00 KST

About 400 schools and other educational institutions in France were expected to remain closed Friday after student protests over teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating school buildings escalated into violence in several cities.
The protests, which began in the Paris region last month, have spread across the country and increasingly involved clashes with police, arson and vandalism.
French authorities said nearly 2,000 people had been detained since the unrest began, including more than 600 on Wednesday alone.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said Thursday that slightly more than 400 schools and other educational establishments would remain closed Friday and offer distance learning.
"These are a little over 400 schools and other educational establishments that I know of that will be closed," Geffray said in an interview with France 2.
Geffray said 170 students and 65 education-sector employees had been injured since the protests began. He called for calm and said the government would hold talks with student representatives.
The Interior Ministry said 1,949 people were detained Thursday, while 305 police officers and gendarmes were reported injured. Authorities said most of those detained were suspected of violence, including attacks against police.
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said Friday that about 2,000 people had been arrested since the protests began, with roughly two-thirds placed in police custody.
"We have gone from high-school student demonstrations to a public-order disturbance," Darmanin said in an interview with RTL radio. "When people target buses and set schools on fire, it is no longer simply a protest issue."
Darmanin also questioned whether all those involved in the violence were students, describing an "active and violent minority" among the protesters.
The demonstrations have centered on complaints about teacher shortages, deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms. Many students have continued to protest peacefully, but violence has been reported in a number of cities.
In Marseille, in southern France, officials said teachers were inadvertently splashed with petrol at a school where protesters were involved in an incident. A fire engine was also set alight in the city.
At least two high schools were set on fire Thursday, while a car was torched in Strasbourg in eastern France.
In Toulouse, in the southwest, riot police clashed with youths. Rubbish bins were set ablaze, firecrackers were thrown and the entrance hall of a secondary school in Nantes was set on fire, according to local reports.
Police used tear gas against demonstrators in some locations, while attacks on buses and bus stops were also reported.
The protests also spread to universities Thursday, with blockades reported at about 30 campuses, according to the Union Etudiante student union.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu convened a crisis meeting Thursday as the unrest spread.
According to a source close to the prime minister, intelligence agencies told the meeting that hard-left politicians, including members of La France Insoumise, had helped initiate the protest movement.
LFI lawmaker Louis Boyard rejected the allegation in comments to French broadcasters.
The Interior Ministry said the violence had moved beyond the legitimate expression of grievances and described the unrest as resembling urban disorder.
The government faces pressure to address the students' complaints while restoring order around schools and other educational institutions. Geffray said authorities would engage with student representatives as officials sought to contain the unrest.
The demonstrations have also drawn attention beyond France. Students in Liege, Belgium, began protesting Thursday over education-related issues, and local media reported that schools in the city were expected to close Friday.
A municipal spokesperson did not immediately confirm the reported closures.

Regular power outages in Ukraine — will there be a blackout this year?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:48:46 EEST
16:48:46 KST

Regular power outages in Ukraine — will there be a blackout this year?
Kyiv • UNN
The power system has spare capacity, while demand is forecast to be lower. Massive Russian strikes could cause a deficit and localized outages.
As the cold weather approaches, the question of the energy system’s stability is once again becoming one of the key issues for Ukrainians. The situation in winter will be affected by air temperature, consumption levels, the condition of generation facilities and networks, as well as damage to the energy system caused by strikes by the Russian Federation. At the same time, individual regions may find themselves in different circumstances due to the specific features of the energy system’s architecture. Journalist UNN was told more about whether blackouts should be expected in the near future by Andrian Prokip, head of energy programs at the Ukrainian Institute of the Future.
Details
According to the expert, several factors will simultaneously affect how quickly outages occur. It is not only a matter of how much of the energy system has been repaired, but also of other factors.
The need for outages is determined by the balance between the capabilities of the energy system (the availability of sufficient capacity to generate, transmit, and distribute electricity), on the one hand, and demand, on the other. As of the end of September, there is sufficient capacity under various weather scenarios. This winter is also expected to be warmer than last winter. And it is Russian shelling that may critically change this balance—either across the country as a whole or in individual regions. In other words, the critical factor in determining the need to introduce outage schedules will be how effectively we protect ourselves—the effectiveness of our air defense
Another factor that will affect the scale of potential outage schedules is the reduction in electricity consumption. And this is not only about the expected warmer weather.. According to Andrian Prokip, this is related, in particular, to strikes on energy-intensive enterprises and problems with product exports, as well as consumers installing their own electricity generation facilities.
We have another factor that will reduce the potential deficit in the energy system—the decrease in electricity consumption by industry. Primarily because of Russian strikes on energy-intensive consumers, such as the metallurgical industry. And because of these enterprises’ problems exporting their products via the Black Sea. These enterprises are effectively halting production. Another factor reducing demand for electricity from the integrated energy system is self-generation: consumers are actively installing their own generation facilities, including solar power plants, while industry is also installing gas-fired generation
Thus, according to him, a significant reduction in electricity demand is expected this year, which may also affect the scale of a possible deficit. However, the final situation will depend primarily on the course of Russian attacks.
Ultimately, we expect a significant reduction in electricity demand this year. That is, even if a deficit arises, assuming the same pattern of shelling as last year, it should occur later and its scale should be smaller. But despite all this, there may be a situation in which there is a deficit in some regions and not in others. In other words, there will be outages in some places and no outages in others
Attacks on facilities that ensure the transmission of electricity between regions remain a separate problem. As a result, the situation may differ in different parts of the country. Andrian Prokip emphasizes that it is currently impossible to predict a specific scenario.
We do not have information about how they will strike, when they will strike, what they will strike, or how we will be able to repel the attacks. Accordingly, it is impossible to say what the outages will be like or when they will begin. At the same time, if we do not take into account the possibility that we may have problems with air defense due to a shortage of missiles, then, essentially, we are much better prepared for winter—we are in a better position than we were last year
According to the expert, the energy system currently has reserve generation capacity compared with peak consumption, but this may change in the event of new large-scale attacks on energy facilities, as happened last year.
As of October 1 last year, our power system had enough capacity that we should have gone through the entire winter without outages. In principle, we should have been exporting electricity in winter, but starting on October 10, a new wave of massive attacks began. And remember the situation we found ourselves in in January and February. In other words, based on the capacity balance that existed before the shelling, everything was fine for us, but the shelling changed this situation
In addition, individual regions may face a deficit earlier due to the specific features of local generation and networks.
Right now, our surplus of generation over peak consumption is even greater. No one will tell you exactly what the outages will be or when they will begin. Among the cities facing such a risk, the expert specifically named Kyiv and Odesa, because their own generation does not cover the entire demand, so they depend on electricity transmission from the integrated power system. Strikes on substations that provide this connection may create local problems.
For example, Kyiv, and Odesa, for example. We do not have enough of our own generation to cover demand. And what the Russians are doing is trying to strike the substations that connect these cities to the integrated power system. Remember Odesa and how this used to happen. But everything was restored, we all pulled together, and everything fell back into place
Thus, it is currently impossible to determine the specific period when the nearest outages will occur. At the same time, according to the expert's assessment, Ukraine is entering this heating season in a better position than last year.

Christa Pike in critical condition after Tennessee botched execution, lawyer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:48:27 UTC
16:48:27 KST

Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.
A condemned female murderer who survived two lethal injections during a botched execution by the US state of Tennessee is in critical condition and receiving "life-saving care," her lawyer said on Thursday.
In an extraordinary chain of events, Christa Pike, 50, was whisked from a prison execution chamber to a hospital on Wednesday night, still alive despite two deadly doses of pentobarbital.
"What we have been told is that she is in critical condition, receiving life-saving care," Randy Spivey said in a virtual news conference on Thursday afternoon, declining to provide further details.
He urged Governor Bill Lee, who had denied a clemency request earlier in the week, to scrap Pike's death sentence.
"After having endured solitary confinement for more than 20 years and a full attempt to kill her by lethal injection, Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty. The governor must commute Christa's sentence now."
Experts on the US death penalty said the case was unprecedented.
"This failed attempt is the worst we've ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," said Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Centre.
The centre counts seven inmates whose executions could not be carried out because medical staff were unable to establish IV lines, but "Pike is the first person to survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs."
Late on Thursday, US President Donald Trump questioned how an execution like Pike's could fail, telling reporters that it "shouldn't be very difficult."
'Loudly snoring'
The case had already attracted scrutiny as Pike would have been the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
Kim Chandler, a media witness with the Associated Press, told CBS News that "Pike appeared notably awake as the execution began" at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.
"A couple of times she looked around the room. At one point she looked towards prison officials and asked if it was supposed to feel that way," Chandler said.
Pike later began snoring and witnesses listened from the viewing area for about an hour before being ushered out.
The condemned woman was "loudly snoring, clearly very alive" as journalists left, Chandler told CBS.
Pike's legal team had previously objected to the execution IV protocol, saying it would have caused needless suffering due to her small veins and a blood condition.
"I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone, one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt" to start an IV line, Spivey said.
Lawyer Stephen Ferrell said medical experts had warned of needles becoming dislodged or piercing through the vein, causing lethal drugs to flow into Pike's arm instead of the bloodstream.
"It sounds like that is likely to have occurred," he said.
Media witnesses said Pike told execution staff her arm felt like it would "burst open," and Spivey said he saw her right arm turn purple, especially after the second lethal injection.
Pike had not been scared to die, Ferrell said.
"It was a fear of a prolonged, painful, traumatic death, and that's what happened, minus the death."
'A mess'
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol," adding that Pike was subsequently taken to an "off-site medical facility."
Governor Lee called for a "comprehensive, third-party review" of the failed execution.
The state's remaining scheduled execution, convicted killer Gary Wayne Sutton is scheduled to die on 3 December, would not be carried out this year, Lee added.
Pike's case had sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals. She was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp.
The killing gained national attention after Slemmer's body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, told NBC News the botched execution was "a mess."
Pike's lawyers had argued she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of Slemmer's killing. They also cited her history of childhood sexual assault and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Following a flurry of legal filings that delayed the execution by several hours, the US Supreme Court on Wednesday night cleared the way for the punishment to go ahead.
In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
UN rights chief Volker Turk urged Tennessee not to make a new attempt to execute Pike.
"The case of Christa Pike lays bare multiple reasons why the death penalty should be abolished," his office said on X.

Breadcrumb
UN urges more US action on Marshall Islands nuclear fallout legacy
The United States needs to take additional steps to remedy the nuclear legacy in the Marshall Islands by providing healthcare and releasing secret archives, according to a UN report presented to its human rights body on Thursday.
The US, which administered the Pacific islands after World War Two, conducted 67 nuclear weapons tests in the Marshall Islands from 1946 to 1958, including "Castle Bravo" at Bikini Atoll in 1954
The human cost of these tests has been "severe and lasting", the UN human rights office report said, adding that there has not yet been a just settlement of the claims
"The damage needs to be repaired," Awa Dabo, Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, told the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva
The UN cited examples of the ongoing impact, such as elevated levels of cancer, displacement from contaminated areas and lasting social stigmas affecting exposed persons who are referred to as "poison people"
The report called for the US to provide remedy in the form of healthcare and to declassify all information pertaining to the nuclear legacy
The US State Department said it had already reached a full and final settlement of all claims with the Marshall Islands in 1986 and said it continues to provide medical and cancer assistance and environmental monitoring programmes for those affected
"The United States has recognised the effects of its nuclear testing program and has accepted and acted on its responsibility to the citizens of the Republic of the Marshall Islands," the State Department said.
Marshallese residents, including Alson Kelen who was displaced from Bikini and lost both parents to cancer, addressed the council and called for a meaningful resolution to the legacy
The Marshall Islands' representative, Senator David Anitok, told the UN body: "The continued denial of an effective remedy has forced us to come before this Council to ask for help"
Washington disengaged from the UN Human Rights Council last year, alleging an anti-Israel bias, and its seat was left empty on Thursday

U.S. Air Force buys weather data from smart balloons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:45:18 UTC
16:45:18 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded WindBorne Systems a sole-source contract worth up to $48.7 million for global atmospheric data through Sept. 30, 2033.
- Only $1.7 million was obligated at award under the first task order, meeting the contract's required minimum purchase.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded WindBorne Systems, a California startup that flies a fleet of self-steering weather balloons, a contract worth up to $48.7 million to supply atmospheric data for military weather forecasting and mission planning.
The contract, awarded on Sept. 29, covers continuous, global and targeted vertical profiles of the atmosphere, from the surface up to the stratosphere, according to the Department of War. The work runs until Sept. 30, 2033. The U.S. Air Force obligated about $1.7 million in fiscal 2025 and 2026 research and development funds under the first task order, which meets the contract’s required minimum purchase, so the rest of the $48.7 million ceiling will only be spent if the service places more orders.
The contract was awarded without competition by the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Hanscom Air Force Base, Massachusetts. The notice does not say how much data the U.S. Air Force will buy, which regions it will focus on, or whether it will cover WindBorne’s own forecasts as well as its raw measurements.
WindBorne, founded in 2019 by Stanford University graduates and based in Redwood City, builds what it calls Global Sounding Balloons. Each weighs less than 1.4 kg (3 pounds) at launch and carries solar-powered sensors that measure temperature, humidity, pressure and wind. Unlike standard weather balloons, which rise for a couple of hours over their launch site before bursting, WindBorne’s balloons stay aloft for weeks and repeatedly climb and descend between about 1 km and 20 km (12 miles), sending data back by satellite.
The balloons have no engines. They steer by changing altitude to catch winds blowing in the direction they need, which lets the company send them toward specific areas. That is what the contract means by targeted profiling: measurements over places the U.S. military cares about, including oceans and remote regions where few weather stations exist and traditional balloons cannot be launched.
The company says it keeps about 600 balloons in the air at any time from 20 launch sites around the world, TechCrunch reported in August, when WindBorne raised $37 million in new funding at a $250 million valuation. It also runs WeatherMesh, an artificial intelligence forecasting model trained partly on its own balloon data.
WindBorne has worked with the U.S. military for several years. The U.S. Air Force gave it a contract in 2021 to help build its balloon constellation and feed the data into the service’s weather cloud, and the Defense Innovation Unit and the U.S. Air Force picked it in 2022 as one of five companies for a commercial weather data prototype project. The company has also had research contracts with the U.S. Navy, and the National Weather Service buys its data, which feeds into NOAA’s main global forecast model.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Cabinet Spokesperson Michelle Lee (李慧芝) on Friday defended the legality of the government's NT$607.6 billion (US$19 billion) supplementary budget after the Legislative Yuan Budget Center raised concerns that the proposal could break budget rules.
The center said Thursday that the Cabinet's proposal to submit a supplementary budget before the 2026 central government budget takes effect could violate the Budget Act, per Mirror Daily. It noted that agencies may apply for supplementary funding when a major event requires spending beyond their allocated budgets.
The center also questioned the Cabinet's inclusion of increases to national pension and elderly farmers' welfare allowances in the supplementary budget. It said changes to benefit levels require authorization.
The Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics responded that the benefit increases are being pursued in parallel with legislative work, per Rti. It said the move was intended to allow recipients to receive the increased benefits as soon as the relevant amendments are passed by the legislature.
Responding to the Budget Center, Lee cited Article 51 of the Budget Act, which stipulates that the legislature should receive the central government budget one month before the start of the fiscal year, per CNA. She noted that the 2026 budget was instead passed on Aug. 14.
Lee said the Cabinet submitted the supplementary budget after the 2026 budget completed its third reading to prevent further delays, stressing that the move complies with Article 79 of the Budget Act.
The review of the 2026 budget was delayed after the Cabinet refused to implement laws concerning pay raises for military personnel, pension increases for retired police officers and firefighters, and a halt to cuts to civil servant and teacher pensions. The legislature eventually agreed to send the budget to committees after the Cabinet promised to implement previously passed funding for new initiatives and submit bills related to the pay and pension increases.
The Budget Center has repeatedly criticized the Cabinet's budget decisions. It previously questioned the government's use of supplementary budgets to increase defense spending as a share of GDP, warning that repeated use could normalize employing flexible measures for defense needs, per China Times.
More recently, the center raised concerns about the inclusion of NT$10,000 cash handouts in the 2027 budget, per UDN. It argued that major policies require new legislation or authorization under existing laws to be implemented.
The center also said the fluctuating nature of securities transaction tax revenue makes it an unstable funding source for the handouts.

Taiwan optical suppliers eye orders as US moves to restrict Chinese-made transceivers

Unknown Publisher

16:40:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s optical communications industry could benefit from potential order shifts as the US moves to restrict Chinese-made components used in AI infrastructure, CTEE reported Friday.
A Morgan Stanley report said the US could add Chinese-made optical transceiver modules to its list of controlled products as early as October. The move would not initially amount to a blanket ban, with restrictions potentially starting with next-generation 3.2-terabit products.
The policy could create opportunities for Taiwanese suppliers as US customers seek to diversify their supply chains. Industry sources said local optical communications companies could become second-source suppliers as orders shift away from Chinese manufacturers.
Potential beneficiaries include LandMark Optoelectronics Corp., Elite Advanced Laser Corp., Fiber Optic Communications Inc., LuxNet Corp., Browave Corp., and Ezconn Corp.
LandMark and Elite Advanced Laser are developing components for high-speed optical communications. Fiber Optic Communications and Browave, meanwhile, have expanded into optical fiber components for AI data centers and co-packaged optics.
LuxNet has been developing high-speed optical transceivers. Ezconn is targeting high-speed fiber-optic connectivity products.
As AI data centers handle growing volumes of data, conventional electrical signals face greater signal loss and power consumption at higher transmission speeds. Optical communications address these limitations by using light-based signals to transmit data, enabling higher bandwidth and lower losses over long distances, according to Pocket Securities.
Optical transceivers are key components in data centers and AI infrastructure. They convert electrical signals into optical signals for high-speed, long-distance data transmission, using lasers to transmit signals and photodetectors to receive them, according to Moomoo.
As AI computing requirements grow, optical transceivers have advanced from 100G to 400G and 800G, with 1.6T products increasingly being deployed. Morgan Stanley said the proposed rules would have limited near-term impact on widely used 800G products and the growing 1.6T segment, as they would primarily target 3.2T products.
The 3.2T products are expected to begin ramping up in 2028 and see broader adoption in 2029, suggesting any impact on orders and revenue would emerge gradually.

The SpaceX crew set a record by reaching the ISS in less than 8 hours
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:38:41 EEST
16:38:41 KST

The SpaceX crew set a record by reaching the ISS in less than 8 hours
Kyiv • UNN
Crew-13 arrived at the ISS in a record 7 hours and 55 minutes for the United States. Jessica Watkins became the first Black woman to command a crew.
Four astronauts arrived at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday after an eight-hour flight that set a speed record for the United States and also made history with the first Black woman to lead a crew during orbital insertion. The Guardian reports, writes UNN.
Details
SpaceX launched the spacecraft with commander Jessica Watkins and her crew on behalf of NASA after a three-week delay caused by the need to fix a leak in the Dragon capsule’s fuel system. Thick clouds threatened to disrupt the countdown throughout the morning, but the skies eventually cleared enough to allow a safe launch from Cape Canaveral at 11:10 (15:10 GMT).
Seven hours and 55 minutes later, the SpaceX Dragon "Grace" capsule docked with an ISS port, setting a record for the fastest flight by an American spacecraft to the station.
During a live broadcast on NASA TV, the capsule could be seen smoothly approaching the stationary ISS, while both spacecraft sped through space at about 17,500 mph (28,100 km/h).
The newcomers—Americans Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian Joshua Kootrick, and Russian Sergei Teteryatnikov—floated into the space station through the pressurized transfer compartment and spoke with colleagues on Earth late Thursday evening.
The duration of the flight largely depends on the distance between the ISS and the spacecraft at the time of launch. The previous crew to launch from US territory took more than 30 hours to reach the station.
During the late-morning launch, Watkins became the first Black woman to lead a crew during orbital insertion. Watkins, a geologist who worked with NASA’s Curiosity rover ten years ago, traveled to the space station for the second time after an extended stay there in 2022.
Although they will spend six months aboard the ISS, the journey to the station was the fastest not only for Elon Musk’s company but also for any American organization, including NASA.
This was the 13th crew launched by SpaceX for NASA, not counting the 2020 test flight. The Crew-13 designation on the mission patch pays tribute to "Apollo 13"—the dramatic 1970 lunar mission that ended with the astronauts’ safe return.
Three hours after the Crew-13 launch, SpaceX launched a Falcon rocket from California carrying more than 100 small satellites. Another Falcon rocket was scheduled to launch late Thursday evening from Florida, carrying a secret satellite for the US National Reconnaissance Office. All of this is taking place in the same week that the company’s giant Starship rocket reached orbit for the first time.

Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot of the Flydubai flight who was transferred Thursday to a hospital in the United Arab Emirates, appeared publicly for the first time Friday in footage from the hospital, speaking by video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
“I had so many injuries that I collapsed. I’ve been a captain for 11 years. I know, even with my eyes closed, what is happening with the aircraft. When I fell, I felt the plane descending, the nose going down, and I knew these were the final seconds. I tried to crawl. I opened the door, and everything else happened immediately after that. People in Saudi Arabia and here in the UAE took care of me, and I could not have received better treatment or medical attention,” Machchhar said.
He added: “I realized that if I didn’t show courage, 170 passengers would lose their lives.”
Modi praised the captain, telling him: “The entire country is praying for you. The courage, composure and calm you showed saved many lives. The country can proudly say Indians are not people who take lives, but people who are prepared to risk their lives to save others.”
Machchhar replied: “I never thought I would have the opportunity to speak with you.”
Indian media reported Thursday that Machchhar, who was stabbed by his Omani co-pilot, underwent emergency surgery at a hospital in the Saudi city of Tabuk, where the aircraft landed. His family was making its way from Mumbai to Dubai.
The government of the Indian state of Gujarat said it would honor Machchhar with an award. Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel praised the pilot’s “unwavering courage,” saying his actions saved the passengers’ lives.
Israeli investigators have still found no link between the Omani co-pilot and Iran, despite U.S. President Donald Trump suggesting Thursday that there could be a connection. The Omani co-pilot was also transferred Thursday from Saudi Arabia to the UAE.
Israel is seeking to send a team to the UAE in the coming days, though the move requires prior coordination. Emirati officials have conveyed anger to Israel over what they viewed as a premature Israeli conclusion that the co-pilot acted out of terrorist motives aimed at undermining the Abraham Accords, before the investigation had been completed.
An Israeli official said the word “terror” is particularly sensitive for the Emiratis because it could suggest a lack of control. Abu Dhabi therefore prefers not to get ahead of the investigation and, for now, is being cautious in drawing conclusions about the Omani pilot’s motives.
A senior Israeli official said the pilot most likely acted alone. After Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News that the Omani had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination,” the official said Israel was examining the suspect’s activity on social media. At the same time, Israeli assessments are increasingly leaning toward a nationalist and religious motive rather than a suicide attempt.
Israel had asked to participate as an observer in the investigation in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, but Riyadh did not agree. Now that the co-pilot has been transferred to the UAE, Israel is counting on its close ties and cooperation with Abu Dhabi to become as involved as possible in the investigation, even if only as an observer.

Heat deaths in Western Europe top 34,600 during warmest summer ever

Heat deaths in Western Europe top 34,600 during warmest summer ever
- More than 34,600 heat-related deaths occurred in five Western European countries during the hottest summer on record, with Spain, France, Germany, Britain, and Belgium all severely affected.
- Spain recorded 5,805 excess deaths with 61 heat wave days, while Germany saw about 16,000 heat deaths, the highest in a decade, including a record June wave.
- Western Europe experienced temperatures 2.5 deg C above average, with 52 per cent of the continent facing extreme heat stress, surpassing previous records and challenging healthcare systems.
AI generated
MADRID – More than 34,600 people died in five Western European countries due to heat this summer as the region posted its hottest June, July and August on record, according to a Bloomberg compilation of mortality estimates from different agencies.
Spain saw its deadliest summer since records began in 2015, with 5,805 excess deaths attributable to heat between May 15 and Sept 30, according to data from the Instituto de Salud Carlos III that was made public on Oct 1.
In France, three heatwaves led to an estimated 7,824 deaths, the highest toll since at least 2015, according to provisional figures from the national public health agency. Germany, Britain and Belgium also recorded elevated heat-related mortality.
“Spain has recorded 61 heatwave days over the summer, with four heatwaves, a fifth in September and extreme heat episodes in May,” said Diana Gomez, head of the mortality monitoring system at ISCIII. “All of that has resulted in an increase of deaths attributable to heat.”
Heat can exacerbate existing illnesses and is particularly dangerous for vulnerable people including young children, the elderly and workers exposed to high temperatures over long periods of time.
Western Europe faced extraordinary heat throughout the summer, with average temperatures for the region 2.5 deg C above the average between 1991 and 2020, according to the latest monthly report by Earth observation programme Copernicus.
European data indicates temperatures over the summer were the highest since at least 1979 across virtually all of England, Wales and Belgium, as well as most of France, Spain, Italy, Switzerland and Austria.
The previous record was set in 2003, when countries including Britain, France and Germany recorded tens of thousands of heat deaths, and healthcare services struggled to cope with cases of heat stroke, forcing the authorities to improve emergency responses and hot-weather services.
On 17 days in 2026, at least 60% of Western Europe experienced temperatures above 30 deg C, according to a Copernicus report released on Oct 2. That compares with 11 days under the same conditions during the summer of 2003.
A record 52% of the European continent experienced temperatures of 38 deg C or higher during the summer, which qualifies as “very strong” heat stress under the Copernicus ratings system.
In Spain, the 2026 summer’s heat deaths exceeded the previous record of 2022 by more than 1,000, the ISCIII found.
The worst day was July 10, according to the public health research institute, which calculates excess mortality by comparing the daily total of deaths to average mortality rate in previous years and factoring in temperature thresholds for each of the country’s 50 provinces.
“Thresholds have been surpassed in every province for many days,” Gomez said. “Ours is the only system that issues daily estimates and, since we have a lot of experience in this field, several European countries have been in touch with us over the past few days.”
In Germany, deaths reached the highest level in at least a decade, with about 16,000 heat-related deaths between April 6 and Sept 13, according to the Robert Koch Institute, the federal government agency responsible for disease control. About 9,600 people died as a result of the heatwave at the end of June, which was the worst on record for Western Europe. The country’s previous record was about 9,000 heat deaths in 2018.
Preliminary data from Sante Publique France indicate heat deaths in France this summer hit the highest number since at least 2015 due to three major heatwaves in June, July and August. The government agency is expected to publish a definitive mortality report in early 2027.
That compares with 5,700 estimated deaths in 2025. In 2003, researchers at the University Paris 5 found that devastating temperatures that year led to 14,800 excess deaths in August alone.
In Britain, heatwaves caused an estimated 2,877 deaths in May and June, according to the British Health Security Agency, which is due to release a final mortality report covering the whole season in 2027. In Belgium, 2,112 people died between June 18 and July 12, according to Sciensano, the country’s public health institute. BLOOMBERG

Taiwan Coast Guard hoses Chinese fishing boat off Dongsha
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:35:59 UTC
16:35:59 KST

- Taiwan's Coast Guard used a water cannon on the Chinese fishing boat Jin Sha after it refused to leave waters near Dongsha Island.
- The patrol vessel Yunlin later gave the crew 35 hot meals and towed the boat out, handing it to a Chinese vessel early Oct. 2.
Taiwan’s Coast Guard used a water cannon on a Chinese fishing boat that refused to leave waters near Dongsha Island in the South China Sea, then warned its crew they would be arrested and their boat seized before finally towing it out of the area.
The Coast Guard Administration said its Dongsha-Nansha Branch spotted an unidentified boat around 11 a.m. on Oct. 1, about 15.5 nautical miles (29 km) northeast of Dongsha. It sent the 4,000-ton patrol vessel Yunlin (CG-5003), which around 3 p.m. found two Chinese fishing boats, the Yue Hui Dong Yu 75066 and the Jin Sha, fishing about 27 nautical miles (50 km) east of the island inside waters Taiwan controls, Taiwan’s Central News Agency reported.
The Yue Hui Dong Yu 75066 left after the Yunlin’s warnings. The Jin Sha did not. After three radio warnings went unanswered, the Yunlin fired its water cannon for 30 seconds from about 200 meters (660 feet) away, and when that failed it moved closer and sprayed the boat for another 90 seconds.
Coast Guard personnel then approached the fishing boat again and told the crew to leave or face arrest on the spot and seizure of the vessel. Footage released by the agency shows one Coast Guard officer holding a firearm at the ready during the encounter.
The standoff ended without arrests. At the crew’s request, the Yunlin gave the Jin Sha’s crew 35 hot meals, then towed the boat out of Taiwan’s restricted waters and handed it over to a Chinese work vessel early on Oct. 2. The Coast Guard said its use of the water cannon followed standard procedures, and urged Beijing to stop illegal fishing in the area.
Dongsha, also known as Pratas Island, lies about 450 km (280 miles) southwest of Kaohsiung and is one of two island groups Taiwan controls in the South China Sea, along with Taiping Island in the Spratlys. About 300 Coast Guard personnel are stationed there, and the surrounding atoll is a marine national park where all fishing is banned.
Taiwan defines two zones around its territory. Its prohibited waters are its territorial sea, normally 12 nautical miles from shore, and its restricted waters are a contiguous zone extending to 24 nautical miles. Around Dongsha, the lines can reach farther because they are measured from surrounding reefs.
The waters around Dongsha have seen repeated encounters this year. In May, the 5,500-ton Chinese coast guard ship CCG-3501 entered Taiwan’s restricted waters there and spent more than a day in a standoff with the Taiwanese patrol vessel Taichung, with each side radioing the other to leave. The Coast Guard said at the time it was the sixth time this year a Chinese coast guard ship had approached the island. In June, Taiwan reported the first entry by a Chinese government vessel into the restricted waters around Taiping Island.

louvre-lens turns cuteness into an art history of pink, plush toys and kawaii
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:30:55 UTC
16:30:55 KST

so cute! louvre-lens exhibition unpacks the art of happiness from ancient times until today
through more than 300 works, from ancient cats to rebellious soft toys and the history of pink and glitter, the show examines art's ability to bring us joy and comfort.
LOUVRE-LENS TRACES THE ART AND AESTHETICS OF CUTENESS
Cuteness gets the museum treatment at Louvre-Lens with So Cute! The Art of Happiness, an exhibition tracing how artists and cultures have produced — and occasionally weaponized — the feeling of ‘aww’ from antiquity to the present. Bringing together around 300 paintings, sculptures, photographs, films, objects and installations, the show moves between animals, babies, the color pink, soft toys, glitter and kawaii culture to ask why certain shapes, gestures and materials trigger affection, comfort and the instinct to protect. In other words, the museum is taking cute seriously, without pretending it has always behaved itself.
Curated by Annabelle Ténèze, director of Louvre-Lens, and Émilie Girard, director of the Musées de la Ville de Strasbourg, the exhibition places works from radically different periods into deliberately unlikely conversations. Egyptian cats and ancient babies meet Théodore Géricault, Auguste Renoir, Nicolas Poussin, Jeff Koons and Philippe Katerine, while Cindy Sherman, Rosa Bonheur, Agnès Varda, William Wegman and Pierre et Gilles expand the story through portraits, pets and pop culture. Rather than defining cuteness as a fixed aesthetic, the exhibition treats it as something that shifts with time, geography and whoever happens to be doing the looking.
FROM KAWAII AND PINK TO CUTENESS WITH A DARKER SIDE
One section follows kawaii back well beyond its contemporary overload of mascots and merchandise. The Japanese term emerged centuries ago before developing into the visual vocabulary of rounded forms, oversized heads, large eyes and soft colors now embedded in manga, fashion and advertising. Takashi Murakami appears among the artists extending that language into contemporary art, while an adjacent chapter looks at South Korea’s own culture of cuteness. Elsewhere, pink gets its historical due, alongside works by Cindy Sherman and Ettore Sottsass, whose Ultrafragola mirror makes a fairly convincing case that a color can be both sweet and spectacularly self-aware.
The sugar rush does not last uninterrupted. So Cute! also examines the relationship between adorableness, consumer culture, propaganda, war imagery and social critique, showing how supposedly innocent visual codes can comfort, persuade or unsettle depending on their context. Soft toys move from childhood companions to artistic tools for addressing memory and vulnerability, while the mischievous expressions of characters such as Labubu complicate the idea of the perfectly behaved plushie. The exhibition ends this line of thinking with Pascal Lièvre’s glitter-covered reinterpretations of Louvre icons, where sequins and drag aesthetics turn familiar masterpieces into something brighter, stranger and considerably less reverential.
MATHIS BOUCHER BUILDS A PINK, INTERACTIVE DREAMWORLD
Architect-scenographer Mathis Boucher translates the theme into an environment conceived somewhere between a story and a video game. Visitors pass through a rounded pink entrance into a sequence of dreamlike rooms linked by curves, soft edges and tactile materials including fur, mirrors, bouclé and carpet. Rabbit-shaped magnifying glasses and other ‘treasure objects’ are tucked into the route, while a chapter dedicated to cuteness’ darker side interrupts the fantasy before the exhibition heads towards what the museum describes as a happy ending in a puff of glitter. Argile developed a custom powder tone, dubbed Louvre-Lens Pink, specifically for the scenography.
The visitor is not expected to remain entirely passive in all this softness. A 2.7-meter-wide wheel of emotions greets the public before entry, while interactive labels, a kawaii guide character named Momo, a manga library and a multisensory ‘Symphony of Emotions’ room invite different ways of moving through the show. At the end, visitors can even vote for the work that affected them most. The cheerful scenography also hides a pragmatic layer: almost 90% of its display cases and 80% of its hanging system come from the museum’s reuse program. So Cute! The Art of Happiness runs at Louvre-Lens through January 18, 2027.

‘I have not lost my dreams’: Refugee education funding cuts threaten millions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:30:36 UTC
16:30:36 KST

‘I have not lost my dreams’: Refugee education funding cuts threaten millions
A teenage girl who fled war-torn Sudan for neighbouring Egypt and hopes to pursue a technology degree is an example of why countries must ensure that young refugees can continue to learn.
“When we left Sudan, I was worried that my education would stop,” said Jamila Mostafa, 19, one of the estimated 13.1 million refugee children of school age worldwide in 2025.
Yet nearly half – 5.8 million – remain out of school as funding cuts threaten to roll back years of progress in educating children and adolescents forced to flee their homelands due to war, conflict, violence or persecution.
A generation at risk
The warning comes in a new report by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR.
“At a time of severe pressure on humanitarian and development financing, cuts to education risk reversing decades of collective investment and closing opportunities for a generation of young people,” said UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih, a former refugee from Iraq.
The transition to secondary education remains one of the biggest challenges for refugee children, according to the report. Only 32 per cent were enrolled in high school in 2025, compared to 65 per cent at the primary level.
However, many young refugees arrive at primary school unprepared. Two in three lack the foundational learning that prepares them for the classroom.
Gender gap, enrollment goals
Even though refugee girls and boys attend primary school at similar rates, the gap widens sharply in secondary education. Increasing numbers of adolescent girls leave school due to poverty, early marriage, safety concerns and other pressures.
Meanwhile, progress in higher education underscores the value of sustained investment. Refugee enrollment at the tertiary level reached a record 11 per cent in 2025, with more than 450,000 students attending university or undertaking technical and vocational training.
This means UNHCR and partners are on track to ensure that 15 per cent of refugee youth can access higher education by the end of the decade, known as the 15x30 pledge.
Faiza Qudrati from Afghanistan grew up in Kazakhstan and studied medicine before switching to psychology.
“For me, higher education gives me a chance to grow, learn and one day help other people in the same way that support was once provided to me,” she said.
Unequal access
Although higher education can significantly improve the lives of refugee women and girls, providing them with access to skills, qualifications, employment and greater financial independence, access is still deeply unequal.
Refugee enrollment remains below the national average in more than 80 per cent of reporting countries. In low-income and conflict-affected countries, only two per cent of refugees were enrolled in higher education, compared to 13 per cent of nationals.
UNHCR stressed that improving refugee education also means strengthening national education systems by investing more in teachers, classrooms, learning materials and financing to benefit both refugees and host communities.
Shaping their own future
UNHCR called for the international community and development partners to safeguard education funding and invest in the national systems of countries hosting refugees.
“Education gives young people the tools to shape their own future,” said Mr. Salih. “Our responsibility is to make sure they have that chance.”
Jamila, the young Sudanese woman in Egypt, is continuing her high school education through UNHCR-backed support. She has developed a particular interest in artificial intelligence (AI) and how it can help address social and economic challenges. She hopes to study technology at university.
“School gives me confidence,” she said. “It reminds me that even though I lost my home because of the war, I have not lost my dreams.”

Why Indian pilots struggle to take jobs abroad

A sand sculpture for Captain Smit Machchhar by artist Sudarshan Pattnaik in Puri, Odisha
NEW DELHI: At a time when pilots’ mental health has emerged as a key concern post some recent events, with flydubai cockpit fight being the most recent one, India’s restrictive rules for cockpit crew to leaves domestic airlines only after serving long notice periods could be adding to their stress. The rule for a co-pilot to serve six months’ notice and a captain a year (which has been challenged legally), has made it difficult for foreign airlines to hire Indian aviators as they mostly want people to join in three months. Now with Captain Smit Machchhar proving his mettle in flydubai, the budget arm of Dubai’s mega carrier Emirates, Indian pilots hope foreign airlines — primarily in Gulf and other places like Sri Lanka and South Korea — keep the Indian reality in mind while giving them offer letters.“We usually don’t hire direct from India and prefer if a pilot has worked in a second country before onboarding them,” a senior official of a leading West Asian airline had recently told TOI. The reasons are two-fold: India’s notice period requirement, which remains binding for pilots even if the employer in India defaults on contractual obligations like paying on time, and then informal tie-ups with big Indian carriers against “poaching.
A senior official of an airline here said: “Because of the notice period requirement, some pilots here give ‘fake resignation’ in advance and then look for jobs so that they can leave in three months of getting a job abroad. And if they don’t get a job, they take the fake resignation back.”The notice period rule has been challenged by pilots in court and the matter is sub judice. “There are concerns about pilots’ state of mind due to what could be going on in their personal lives. This notice period rule, meant to ensure schedule integrity of airlines by preventing sudden mass resignations, has outlived its utility. Today India has two big and well-funded airline and a few emerging ones. Now it is only protecting airlines that are unable to pay,” said a pilot.

Climate, Density, and Spatial Layers: 18 Houses Shaping Contemporary Vietnamese Architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

Contemporary Vietnamese residential architecture stands out for its deep sensitivity to local microclimates and context. Detailed studies of weather patterns consistently drive strategic design decisions, resulting in buildings that act as adaptive shelters. Facing conditions that range from scorching summers to dry, cold winters, along with frequent exposure to heavy rains, storms, and floods, architects adopt protective facade elements and multi-layered spatial configurations to shield interior spaces from harsh environmental factors.
A central feature across these projects is the presence of vegetation. Greenery is deployed dynamically: either across outer facades as an active filter against heat, heavy rain, and urban noise, or embedded deep within central courtyards and green terraces. These internal gardens act as the environmental heart of the home, allowing natural light and airflow to penetrate into the floor plans while significantly enhancing the residents' quality of life. By relying on bioclimatic architecture and passive strategies, such as wide eaves, breathable dynamic skins, double facades, and buffer zones, these houses achieve optimal thermal comfort while substantially reducing the reliance on artificial air conditioning.

Hungary welcomes Ukraine's bill strengthening Hungarian minority rights
BUDAPEST, Oct 2 - Hungary welcomed on Friday Ukraine's move to submit draft legislation to parliament that strengthens the education rights of its ethnic Hungarian minority.
A long-running dispute over minority rights had strained ties between Budapest and Kyiv and complicated Hungary’s support for Ukraine’s ambition to join the European Union.
"The bill strengthens the legal guarantees of education in the Hungarian language, and the network of educational institutions," Prime Minister Peter Magyar said in a Facebook post.
Magyar has taken a less confrontational stance towards Kyiv than his predecessor Viktor Orban, but he too has said that progress on boosting the rights of some 100,000 ethnic Hungarians in Ukraine is a prerequisite for Budapest's backing of Ukraine's EU accession.
Hungary's Foreign Minister Anita Orban - no relation of the former prime minister - said on Friday that Ukraine's Deputy Prime Minister Vsevolod Chentsov had informed her that the bill on education rights would be submitted to the Ukrainian parliament with a decision expected this month.
"We welcome this step, which was preceded by bilateral Hungarian-Ukrainian expert-level talks in recent weeks and consultations with representatives of the Transcarpathian Hungarian community," Orban wrote in a Facebook post.
This step follows a June announcement from Magyar that Hungary and Ukraine had reached an agreement on the language, cultural and educational rights of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine.
At the time Magyar said that once Ukraine enshrines the terms of that agreement in legislation, as well as its action plan for its EU accession talks, Hungary would support the opening of the first cluster of Ukraine's accession talks.
Magyar has repeatedly said his government does not support accelerated membership talks for Ukraine. REUTERS

Captain Smit Machchhar: A steady hand, in and out of the cockpit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:26:58 UTC
16:26:58 KST

Long before he was the captain who held a cockpit together despite stab wounds, Capt Smit Machchhar was the pilot who interacted with loaders, engineers, ground staff, catering people, all with equal respect.“Smit is the most calm, composed and down-to-earth person you could ever meet,” said Capt Dharav Gosalia, a friend since his flying school days.On Wednesday, that steadiness was tested at altitude. flydubai flight FZ1073 was carrying 174 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv when, according to Israeli officials, Machchhar’s co-pilot stabbed him and tried to crash the aircraft. The jet reportedly dropped nearly 14,000 feet in under 30 seconds. Seriously wounded, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, letting passengers and crew overpower the attacker. The plane landed in Saudi Arabia.Those who know Machchhar, 39, are not surprised by how he behaved. What shocks them is that it was ever required. “He is one of the calmest and most fun guys possible,” said a friend, a B737 pilot who requested anonymity. “Maybe it is his upbringing. He is always in fun mode, but he is family-oriented too.”
.
Machchhar earned his commercial pilot licence at Mainland Aviation College in New Zealand in the late 2000s, where he became the classmates’ go-to person for hard subjects. “Anyone with a problem in air navigation, aircraft technical or any subject went to him,” the pilot said. “Becoming a line trainer at flydubai was the best thing that could have happened to him.”The instinct to help was visible earlier, too. At M D Bhatia School, where he passed Class 10 in 2003, school friend Bhavin Jethva remembers him as “straightforward, bindass”. “He didn’t like to lie,” Jethva said. “He was never fake and he couldn’t pretend.” Amit Soni, a childhood friend who played cricket with him, called him cheerful and lively.At Swastik Heights in Mumbai’s Tilak Nagar, where Machchhar lived until about 2022, neighbour Laxmikanth Joshi remembers practical kindnesses. After returning from Kenya, Joshi realised he had bought too little coffee to share with friends. Machchhar arranged for a pilot colleague to bring back more. Joshi also remembers Machchhar going straight to the hospital after landing in India when his father underwent bypass surgery about six months ago. He stayed through the treatment. Then there were the Independence Day and Republic Day celebrations. He recalls Capt Machchhar taught them to tie the rope into a knot just right. “One pull and the flag unfurled,” recalled Joshi.
Akshay Joshi, his immediate neighbour, recalls tense moments at his place when his parents learned about the attack. Late in the evening, though, Machchhar’s parents informed the society’s WhatsApp group that their son was recovering.Capt Machchhar moved to Dubai around 2022 after leaving SpiceJet, and flies the Boeing 737 as a captain and line trainer at flydubai. He and his wife, Sonal, have two children: Krishay, 2, and Ziva, 9.Friends and colleagues tried to reconstruct the sequence. A B737 commander said the co-pilot would most likely have used the ‘crash axe’, which is carried on the flight deck for use during emergencies, such as cutting through panels and debris, or the cockpit window to exit the aircraft after an accident. “At the Dubai airport, even shoes and belts are removed at security,” he said. “There’s no way the co-pilot could have got onboard with a pocket knife.”
Another colleague said the co-pilot “apparently stood up and hit Machchhar on the side of the head”. This colleague added that the captain was also struck in the chest, before he regained control after the dive. A third pilot said Machchhar appeared to have squawked ‘7500’, the hijack transponder code. A B737 commander also pointed to a gap: “We have SOPs for a hijack scenario, but not for a cockpit where the aggressor is inside.
” He noted that Capt Machchhar’s bravery boils down to two acts: first, he managed to get the aircraft straight and level after that precarious dive, despite being attacked; second, though he had lost a lot of blood, he managed to open the cockpit door before he passed out.At M D Bhatia School, former classmates have been posting prayers for his recovery on their WhatsApp group. “We are proud of him,” Jethva said.

U.S. anti-ship missiles head to Japan’s westernmost island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:26:16 UTC
16:26:16 KST

- The U.S. military will deploy its NMESIS anti-ship missile launcher to Japan's Yonaguni Island during the Keen Sword exercise, Kyodo News reported.
- Keen Sword is set to begin Oct. 19 and run 11 days, NHK reported, marking NMESIS's first deployment on Yonaguni.
The U.S. military will deploy its NMESIS anti-ship missile launcher to Yonaguni, Japan’s westernmost inhabited island and about 107 km (66 miles) from Taiwan, during a major U.S.-Japanese exercise this month, Japan’s Kyodo News reported on Oct. 2, citing the Yonaguni town government.
The launcher will take part in Keen Sword, a large joint exercise held every two years. Japan’s public broadcaster NHK reported that this year’s live field training will start on Oct. 19 and run for 11 days, with both countries bringing their newest ground-based anti-ship missiles, and that it will be the first time NMESIS is deployed on Yonaguni, SBS reported.
Neither government has said how many launchers will go to the island, how long they will stay, or whether any missiles will be fired.
NMESIS, short for Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System, is a U.S. Marine Corps weapon built on an unmanned Joint Light Tactical Vehicle that carries two Naval Strike Missiles. The missiles can hit ships at ranges of more than 185 km (115 miles), and the remotely driven launcher is designed to move between islands and hide, so it can threaten enemy warships from shore while staying hard to find.
The system belongs to the 12th Marine Littoral Regiment, a unit based on Okinawa that the U.S. Marine Corps reorganized to defend and hold key islands in a conflict. The regiment formally received NMESIS, along with the MADIS counter-drone system, in June 2026. Its Hawaii-based sister unit, the 3rd Marine Littoral Regiment, was the first to field NMESIS in late 2024 and took it to the Philippines for the Balikatan exercise.
NMESIS first arrived in Japan in July 2025. During the Resolute Dragon exercise that September, Marines moved a launcher to Ishigaki, about 240 km (150 miles) from Taiwan, and displayed it alongside Japan’s Type 12 anti-ship missile at the Japanese base there, though no missiles were fired. Yonaguni is closer to Taiwan still.
Japan has stationed troops on Yonaguni since 2016, when a Ground Self-Defense Force coastal surveillance unit and radar began operating there. Tokyo announced in February 2026 that it plans to place surface-to-air missiles on the island by 2031. The 12th Marine Littoral Regiment has also used the island before, deploying its AN/TPS-80 G/ATOR radar to the Japanese base there during Resolute Dragon in 2024.

"We are giving justified responses to Russia’s escalation with our own long-range sanctions. Important results are achieved practically every day,” he said.
He said “successful operations” were carried out in the Black Sea and in Russia’s Voronezh, Nizhny Novgorod, Volgograd, Samara, and Krasnodar regions, targeting airfields, industrial facilities, oil refineries, a missile and space center, and an ammunition depot belonging to Russia.

An assessment of the damage is currently underway at just one of the plants," he said.

Independent verification of the claims from both sides remains difficult due to the ongoing war.

Protesters in Denmark rally against last EU shipyard servicing Russia-linked tankers
A coalition of civil society organizations protested against Danish shipyard Fayard's continued servicing of vessels transporting Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG), at a rally held in Copenhagen on Oct. 1.
Fayard is the last known EU shipyard that is still maintaining a fleet of specialized Arc7 tankers that export LNG from Russia's Arctic north.
"Fayard's service of the LNG fleet is a blemish on Danish support for Ukraine. We will continue to pressure Fayard to stop," Jens Alstrup, the chairman of the NGO Freedom for Ukraine, said in a statement shared with the Kyiv Independent.
Fayard has faced scrutiny from NGOs, European lawmakers, and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen for servicing Russian-linked tankers. Critics say that aiding Russian energy trade contradicts Denmark's support for Ukraine.
The shipyard has serviced four Russian-linked LNG tankers since late June, with the fourth, Nikolay Yevgenov, undergoing service at the yard on Sept. 24, according to the sanctions-monitoring NGO Urgewald.
An EU-wide ban on Russian LNG imports will take effect from Jan. 1, 2027, and countries are already weaning themselves off Moscow.
However, sanctions pressure began to slacken when the bloc decided to grant an exemption to Greek shipping company Dynagas, which will allow it to keep transporting Russian LNG to third countries even after 2027.
Likewise, the EU has repeatedly failed to agree on a maritime services ban, which would make it illegal for Fayard to provide maintenance services to Russian vessels. The bloc has instead said such a move should be done with the agreement of the G7.
"Enough is enough. Denmark faces a growing security threat from Russia, yet Fayard continues to repair tankers that keep Russian Arctic LNG moving while also servicing Danish naval vessels," said Alexander Kirk, a protest organizer and a sanctions campaigner at Urgewald.
"That is a glaring security contradiction. Fayard should stop servicing the Arc7 fleet now."

Saudi Arabia says Houthis attempted to target Mecca, Medina 3 times over 9 years: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:20:28 UTC
16:20:28 KST

Hussien Elkabany and Lina Altawell
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
- Houthis have denied targeting Mecca, while Iran dismissed one Saudi accusation as an unsubstantiated claim
Saudi Arabia has reported three Houthi attempts to target the holy cities of Mecca and Medina over the past nine years, including two incidents in September, drawing condemnation from Arab and Muslim countries.
The Yemeni group has denied some of the accusations.
According to an Anadolu review of official Saudi statements, the latest alleged attacks targeted Medina and an area south of Mecca, while the first reported attempt occurred in July 2017.
Mecca and Medina are home to Islam’s holiest sites, the Grand Mosque and the Kaaba in Mecca and the Prophet’s Mosque in Medina.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government against the Houthis since March 2015. The Yemeni group has controlled the capital Sanaa and several provinces since September 2014.
Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia intensified in September after the group announced what it called a “maritime blockade” on the kingdom in July and later claimed ballistic missile and drone attacks on Saudi sites and vessels.
2 incidents in September 2026
On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said a drone attack it attributed to the Houthis had targeted a power station in Medina.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said the attack occurred early Tuesday and knocked a transformer out of service without affecting the electricity grid.
Maliki accused the Houthis of targeting civilian infrastructure providing electricity services to the Prophet’s Mosque, describing the incident as an “extension of this extremist militia’s approach in attempts to target the Two Holy Mosques.”
“Investigation findings, operational data and examination of debris from the drone used in the attack proved the Houthi militia’s involvement in planning and carrying out this act,” he said.
The coalition would continue taking measures to deter the Houthis and protect the Two Holy Mosques and pilgrims in Mecca and Medina, he added.
On Sept. 16, Maliki said Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca before it entered the city’s restricted airspace.
Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry said at the time that it was the second alleged Houthi attempt to target Mecca after an earlier incident in July 2017.
Saudi King Salman bin Abdulaziz condemned the Houthi militia’s attempt to again target Mecca, saying the incident had drawn international condemnation because violating the sanctity of holy sites provoked the feelings of Muslims around the world.
Abdul Mohsen al-Qasim, an imam at the Prophet’s Mosque, also said during a Friday sermon that attacking Mecca and Medina was “a grave offense before God.”
2017 allegation
On July 27, 2017, the Saudi-led coalition announced that it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward Mecca over Taif province, around 69 kilometers (43 miles) from the holy city, without causing damage.
Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry accused the Houthis at the time of violating the sanctity of Mecca in “a desperate attempt to disrupt the Hajj season.”
Houthi denials
The Houthis did not immediately deny the latest accusation involving Medina.
The group, however, swiftly rejected the Saudi accusation concerning the Sept. 16 incident near Mecca.
Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi and Hizam al-Assad, a member of the group’s political bureau, denied the allegation.
The Houthis also rejected the July 2017 accusation, saying their missile forces had targeted only the Taif military base, and had not targeted Mecca.
In September, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said on US social media company X that any attack targeting Mecca should be condemned, but described reports of an intercepted drone over the city as “merely a claim” that could not serve as a basis for accusing any party.
Arab, Muslim condemnation
Saudi announcements concerning the alleged attempts to target Mecca in July 2017 and September 2026 prompted condemnation from a number of Arab and Muslim countries and organizations.
According to an Anadolu review, statements condemning the Houthis were issued by Türkiye, Qatar, Egypt, Yemen, Jordan, Morocco, Palestine, Syria, Bahrain, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Sudan, the United Arab Emirates and Somalia.
The Gulf Cooperation Council, Arab League and Organization of Islamic Cooperation also issued condemnations, with several statements warning that attacks involving Mecca would offend Muslims around the world.

The European Commission has suspended nearly $20 million in aid to Sierra Leone’s 2026 budget due to the West African country’s harboring one of Europe's most wanted fugitives, alleged cocaine kingpin Joseph "Jos" Leijdekkers, Dutch Justice Minister David van Weel said Thursday.
Posting on social media from the EU’s Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting, van Weel wrote: “At the JHA Council meeting in Luxembourg, discussions are focusing on European security, the EU sanctions regime for organized crime. A positive development in this context is that the EU will no longer provide budget support to the authorities of Sierra Leone this year.”
Later in the day, he told Dutch public broadcaster NOS that the EU had suspended 18 million euro (roughly $20 million) in aid to Sierra Leone because the West African country is not cooperating with the Netherlands’ extradition request of Leijdekkers, a Dutch citizen.
Courts in the Netherlands and Belgium have handed Leijdekkers more than 100 years in prison sentences in absentia in convictions for a range of crimes, including drug trafficking, assault, armed robbery, and attempted murder.
Leijdekkers’ lawyer Guy Weski has in a phone conversation with OCCRP denied his involvement in large scale cocaine shipments from Sierra Leone.
The suspension of the funding, which does not include overseas development and humanitarian aid, was a “clear signal from the EU Commission that Sierra Leone must stop sheltering this criminal,” van Weel told NOS, adding the Sierra Leone government "can resolve this within 24 hours by arresting and extraditing this man."
However the Sierra Leone government refuted van Weel’s assertions in a press statement issued Thursday by its Ministry of Information and Civic Education. Sierra Leone had been informed by EU representatives that support for the country’s budget had been delayed by procedural issues, not talks with the Netherlands or any individual case, and disbursements were now proposed for 2027 and 2028, it said.
“Sierra Leone remains committed to international cooperation against transnational organized crime and to constructive judicial cooperation with all partners. At the same time, attempts to instrumentalize development cooperation or exert pressure on Sierra Leone through public threats and media campaigns are unhelpful,” it added.
At a Thursday press briefing following the high-level meeting of EU justice and home affairs ministers, Magnus Brunner, the EU Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration, said the suspension of aid “was due to technical reasons,” not for Sierra Leone’s alleged harboring of Leijdekkers.
“I think what we need is action against third countries that harbor drug traffickers [...] We are concerned as a European Union about drug trafficking and transnational crime and organized crime trends in Sierra Leone,” he told reporters, but added: “When it comes to the suspension of the support, that's due to technical reasons.”
Van Weel ’s office did not respond to an OCCRP request for further comment, and he did not release a statement after or speak after the official press conference after the Luxembourg meeting, where discussions focused on migration, the EU drugs strategic framework, and the impact of the geopolitical environment on European security.
However, a Dutch diplomat with the delegation in Luxembourg backed the justice minister’s assertion that the suspension of aid to Sierra Leone was tied to its harboring of Leijdekkers.
The diplomat, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said to confront similar challenges in the future, van Weel would push for the European Commission to fast-track the adoption of a new proposed sanctions regime targeting organized crime.
“Organized crime networks operating across borders can be very effective being based in a third country where local authorities might be unwilling to cooperate or extradite them,” the delegate told OCCRP in a telephone interview.
The new sanctions regime aimed at tackling organized crimes such as migrant smuggling, human, firearms and narcotics trafficking and money laundering was proposed by the EU Commission and High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy in July.
In Sierra Leone, the news that the EU aid to the country’s budget may have been suspended over the alleged harboring of Leijdekkers raised concerns that it would affect livelihoods.
“Justice and accountability for transnational crimes are non-negotiable, but they must be pursued through strengthened partnership and rule of law, not by withdrawing support from the people of Sierra Leone,” Abdul M. Fatoma, a human rights activist and anti-corruption campaigner in the capital of Freetown told OCCRP.
Additional reporting from Saidu Bah in Sierra Leone.
