How the fighting in Ethiopia spread beyond Tigray, in maps and charts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:17:02 UTC
16:17:02 KST

How the fighting in Ethiopia spread beyond Tigray, in maps and charts
Old rivalries, territorial disputes and new alliances are reshaping the conflict in Ethiopia’s north.
Fighting is intensifying across northern Ethiopia, almost four years after a peace deal ended a devastating two-year war in the country’s Tigray region.
The conflict has also spread into the neighbouring Amhara and Afar regions. Government-aligned forces say they captured the strategic town of Alamata, Tigray, on September 28, while Tigrayan forces have pushed into Afar.
Telecommunications have been cut across much of Tigray and commercial flights have been suspended, separating families and hampering humanitarian operations.
Ethiopia’s army chief has accused Eritrea, Sudan’s army and Egypt of backing the armed groups, raising fears of a wider regional war. All countries have denied the allegations, with Egypt adding that it strictly respects the sovereignty of neighbouring states.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera maps where the fighting is, who is involved and how Ethiopia got here.
Where is the fighting happening?
Fighting is concentrated in three regions in northern Ethiopia: Tigray, Amhara and Afar. There are several active fronts rather than a single battlefield.
In southern Tigray, government forces and their allies have taken Alamata, a strategic town about 120km (75 miles) south of the regional capital, Mekelle.
The town is a supply hub for troops, fuel and food near Tigray’s border with Amhara.
On September 22, between 15 and 17 drone strikes hit Alamata, including several schools and a hospital, according to the conflict monitor ACLED.
To the west, a separate front has opened near the Tekeze River in western Tigray, an area disputed between Tigray and Amhara.
Fighting has also spread into northern Amhara, around Kobo and Gidan in North Wello zone and Sekota in Wag Hemra zone, which government forces retook on September 27.
Further east, Tigrayan forces and the Afar armed group Ugugumo have advanced into Afar, where fighting has been reported along the Tigray-Afar border and around Erebti and Abala.
The advance matters because it could threaten the Semera-Djibouti corridor, Ethiopia’s main route for imports, including fuel.
Which main groups are fighting?
Seven Ethiopian armed and political groups announced an alliance on September 20 aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and establishing an inclusive transitional government.
The group is called the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, or the Alliance for Survival. Its members include:
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF): The alliance’s main military force, whose fighters launched the latest offensive. It dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018. War broke out between the TPLF and federal forces in November 2020.
The Amhara Fano National Movement: A coalition of Fano factions that turned against Abiy’s government in 2023, after fighting alongside federal forces during the Tigray war.
The Oromo Liberation Army (OLA): It has fought federal forces in Oromia since 2018, seeking greater self-determination for the Oromo.
The other groups named in the alliance are the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), the Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (also known as Ugugumo), the Benishangul Peoples’ Liberation Movement and the Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement. On September 25, the Sidama National Liberation Front announced that it would also join.
The alliance’s membership is contested. According to Jalale Getachew Birru, senior East Africa analyst at ACLED, the Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement has denied joining, saying it has no armed wing. The ONLF is split: one faction backs the alliance, while another says it is not part of it. The OLA has indicated that its main interest is removing the government rather than joining coordinated military operations.
ACLED says only three members, the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement and Ugugumo, were actively fighting federal forces as of September 26.
In its founding statement, the alliance accused the government of “dictatorial rule”. It said a transitional government would end the country’s wars, protect rights and open a national dialogue.
What are the regions of Ethiopia?
Ethiopia is a landlocked country in the Horn of Africa, bordered by Eritrea, Sudan, South Sudan, Kenya, Somalia and Djibouti. With about 139 million people, it is Africa’s second-most populous country after Nigeria.
It is also one of the world’s most ethnically diverse countries, with more than 80 groups. The Oromo are the largest, making up about 35 percent of the population, followed by the Amhara at about 24 percent. Other major groups include Somali (7 percent), Tigrayan (6 percent) and Sidama (4 percent).
Ethiopia is divided into 12 regional states and two chartered cities, Addis Ababa and Dire Dawa. The federal system, introduced in 1992 and formalised in the 1994 constitution, largely follows ethnic and linguistic divisions.
How did we get here?
The renewed fighting stems from political and territorial tensions left unresolved following Ethiopia’s 2020-2022 Tigray war. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and the federal government remain divided over political control, security and disputed territory.
Tensions have been building for months. According to the conflict monitor ACLED, clashes between Tigrayan and federal forces began near the Sudanese border on August 1, followed by federal drone strikes and Tigrayan troop deployments.
In September, Tigrayan forces moved tanks and artillery south. There were also reports of renewed recruitment and forced mobilisation in Tigray.
On September 20, the TPLF and six other armed and political groups announced the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, which aims to overthrow Abiy’s government and install a transitional administration.
Three days later, on September 23, fighting escalated sharply. Tigrayan forces seized the airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire and pushed into neighbouring Afar and Amhara. The government says the TPLF launched an “all-out offensive”. The TPLF says it is fighting a “defensive war” and accuses federal forces of attacking with aircraft, drones and artillery.

Türkiye, Ukraine free trade agreement takes effect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:16:20 UTC
16:16:20 KST

The free trade agreement between Türkiye and Ukraine came into force to establish a predictable framework and boost the bilateral trade volume to $10 billion in the short term.
The Turkish Trade Ministry announced via the Turkish social media platform NSosyal that the Türkiye-Ukraine Free Trade Agreement entered into force on Oct. 1, 2026.
Türkiye and Ukraine aim to develop commercial relations within a more predictable framework.
Customs duty regulations regarding the trade of goods will take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.
The agreement aims to contribute to maintaining trade between the two countries under more predictable rules in current conditions.
The deal, signed on Feb. 3, 2022, creates a framework to develop commercial relations in line with the joint goal of reaching a bilateral trade volume of $10 billion in the short term.
The agreement, prepared by considering the sensitive sectors of the parties, includes regulations on services, investments, electronic commerce, trade facilitation and customs cooperation, in addition to the trade of goods.
Regulations for conducting quota-free bilateral and transit transportation between Türkiye and Ukraine aim to support commercial flows.
As Ukraine’s economic integration with the EU advances, the agreement offers a framework to maintain preferential trade opportunities for Turkish and Ukrainian businesses while providing a competitive advantage against third-country suppliers.

Russia Sets 2026 Conscription Target at 261,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:14:08 UTC
16:14:08 KST

Russia intends to draft 120,000 men for compulsory military service between October and December, with Moscow once again promising that conscripts will not be sent to fight in Ukraine, despite previous assurances that were later contradicted.
Col. Gen. Yevgeny Burdinsky, head of the Russian General Staff's mobilization department, said recruits would start leaving assembly points for their assigned places of service on October 10. He maintained that they would not be deployed for combat operations in Ukraine or in the four partially occupied Ukrainian regions that Moscow claims to have annexed.
Russia has issued similar assurances in the past. President Vladimir Putin repeatedly said in interviews in early March 2022 that conscripts would not be required to take part in the invasion or sent to the battlefield. However, just days later, Russia's Defense Ministry acknowledged that some conscripts had been deployed to Ukraine and taken prisoner.
The Kremlin subsequently said Putin had instructed military prosecutors to investigate and punish officials accused of disregarding his orders to keep conscripts out of the war.
Russian conscripts were also directly caught up in the fighting during Ukraine's 2024 incursion into Kursk Oblast, even though they had not been deployed to Ukraine, with some captured by Ukrainian forces.
Human rights organizations and independent media reports have additionally documented instances in which conscripts were pressured into signing military contracts, making them legally eligible for deployment to combat zones.
The upcoming draft is not a new mass mobilization and involves fewer recruits than Russia's previous autumn conscription campaign.
Moscow plans to enlist 120,000 men this autumn, down from 135,000 in autumn 2025. The spring 2026 campaign saw more than 141,000 people called up for compulsory military service.
A decree signed by Putin in December established a total target of 261,000 conscripts for Russia in 2026.
Russia introduced a year-round conscription system on January 1, 2026, enabling authorities to process recruits throughout the year. However, their actual transfer to military units continues to take place during the traditional spring and autumn draft periods.

The court extended the preventive measures for Odrex doctors accused of medical negligence

The court extended the preventive measures for Odrex doctors accused of medical negligence
Kyiv • UNN
The Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa upheld the preventive measures against Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska in the case of medical negligence that may have caused the death of Adnan Kivan.
On October 1, the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa extended the preventive measures imposed on doctors at the private Odrex clinic, Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska, who have been accused of improper performance of professional duties by a medical worker. Both remain subject to a personal recognizance obligation, while Rusakov was also suspended from his position, reports UNN.
After the hearing, the accused Rusakov said that he had resigned of his own accord from the position of head of the surgical department at the Odrex clinic. At the same time, the statement does not make clear exactly when he resigned or whether the relevant documents were added to the court case file.
In addition, the hearing took place with court-appointed defense attorneys present: due to the absence of Rusakov’s and Bielotserkovska’s attorneys, the court appointed a separate defense attorney for each of the accused and continued consideration of the issue of preventive measures.
Will the delay in the Odrex case have consequences for the lawyers?16.09.26, 09:01 • 36933 views
This occurred amid the accused doctors’ attorneys’ regular failures to appear and motions to postpone hearings, which have repeatedly impeded consideration of the case in recent months.
Thus, in September, the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa scheduled 13 hearings in the case against the Odrex doctors, but seven of them did not take place or the court was unable to proceed to consideration of the case on its merits. Only six hearings took place in full—less than half.
The presiding judge in the case, Viktor Chaplytskyi, deemed the reasons for the doctors’ attorneys’ regular failures to appear unjustified and sent the relevant information to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar. It is to assess whether the defense attorneys’ actions show signs of a disciplinary offense.
Due to the regular postponements, the court has still been unable to proceed to one of the key stages of the trial—the questioning of the medical expert. The court had planned to hear the expert back in May, but at that time Rusakov’s defense raised the issue of changing the venue.
The medical expert is to analyze the documentation, the findings of the examinations conducted, and compliance with treatment protocols, and explain the medical component of the possible causal link between the doctors’ actions and the patient’s death. The court will provide the final assessment of this evidence and the issue of the accused persons’ guilt.
Reminder
Doctors at the private Odrex clinic, Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska, have been accused under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine—improper performance of professional duties by a medical worker.
According to the investigation, during Adnan Kivan’s treatment, the medical staff made significant errors, as a result of which the patient developed sepsis that, against the background of his oncological disease, led to his death.

Taiwan receives first new F-16s three years behind plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:13:09 UTC
16:13:09 KST

- Taiwan's Air Force took delivery of the first two of 66 F-16V Block 70 fighters at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung on Oct. 2.
- The $8 billion order, approved in 2019, was expected to begin deliveries in 2023 but was delayed by production and software problems.
Taiwan’s Air Force has received the first two of 66 new F-16V Block 70 fighter jets bought from the United States, after the aircraft landed at Chihhang Air Base in the eastern county of Taitung around noon on Oct. 2.
The arrival comes about a month later than expected and roughly three years behind the original schedule. The two jets had been due in Taiwan by late August or early September, but stayed in Hawaii for weeks without explanation, Focus Taiwan reported, after local media said they had turned back shortly after taking off for Guam.
The United States approved the $8 billion sale of 66 F-16 Block 70 jets in 2019, during President Donald Trump’s first term. Deliveries were supposed to start in 2023 and finish by the end of 2026, but production delays, supply chain problems and software integration issues pushed the schedule back. Lockheed Martin unveiled the first newly built F-16 Block 70 for Taiwan at its plant in Greenville, South Carolina, in March 2025.
The new jets will be based at Chihhang, where they will go through ground inspections while pilots and maintainers convert to the aircraft. Taiwan’s government budgeted NT$247.2 billion, about $8 billion, for the purchase between 2020 and 2026, and says the jets will strengthen air defense along the island’s east coast, the side facing the open Pacific, where Chinese aircraft and ships have operated during large-scale drills around Taiwan.
The Block 70 is the newest production version of the F-16, built at Lockheed Martin’s South Carolina line. It carries the AN/APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar, a newer mission computer and updated electronic warfare and communications systems, along with conformal fuel tanks that hug the fuselage to add range without taking up weapons stations. It also has strengthened landing gear to handle heavier takeoff weights and weapons loads.
Taiwan already flies more than 140 older F-16A/B fighters, which have been upgraded to a similar F-16V standard in a program completed in 2023. The 66 new jets will take Taiwan’s F-16 fleet to more than 200 aircraft, giving it the backbone of a force that scrambles almost daily to shadow Chinese military aircraft.
The delivery came about a week after Trump met Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Beijing. Taiwan is still waiting for U.S. approval of a separate arms package worth about $14 billion that Trump paused after Chinese objections, AFP reported.
Taiwanese officials have said more F-16 Block 70s will arrive before the end of the year, but they have not given a number. Remaining deliveries are expected to stretch into 2027 and 2028.

Iran weighing options against US, Israel as nuclear talks stall, Israeli defense official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:13:04 UTC
16:13:04 KST

Iran is weighing how to respond to growing US pressure as nuclear negotiations with Washington remain stalled, creating an increasingly complex regional situation, a senior Israeli defense official said on Friday.
"The Iranians are looking for tools within this campaign. They are asking themselves how they can get out of this situation. It is reasonable to assume that they are also discussing the possibility of influencing the elections in order to understand the other side," the official said.
The senior defense official said there had recently been a large number of unresolved incidents, some of which could potentially develop into attacks on the Israeli home front from a variety of directions, and not necessarily from Iran.
"There were many warnings and many nights when the system was occupied with clarifying the situation and raising and lowering the alert level. There were many nights of heightened readiness. Hezbollah? It definitely factors into Iran's calculations if Iran enters into a confrontation with Israel," the official said.
According to the defense official, the Iranians are constantly assessing the situation in the US and the extent of Washington's readiness to enter into a confrontation with them, and this affects Tehran's own assessment of the situation.
Economic pressure mounts on Iran
The official also stressed that conditions in Iran are deteriorating and that the effect of US sanctions can be clearly seen.
The number of tankers leaving the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz has been rising, and according to IDF data, an average of 30 to 40 tankers are now passing through each day. That figure reflects levels seen before the war. In other words, Iranian influence in the strait is declining.
The official also noted that the Iranian rial had reached a new low in recent days, with nearly 2.5 million rials now equivalent to one US dollar. At the same time, he clarified that Iran had not yet reached hyperinflation.
The official illustrated the economic situation by citing a critical article in an Iranian newspaper identified with the regime that compared the price of eggs in Iran with the average salary, adding that the cost of living in Iran was now "unbearable."
Compounding the economic pressure is what the official described as a US naval blockade of Iran that began this week. In addition to the sanctions, he said, the measure contains elements that are humiliating for Tehran because it prevents even family visits to neighboring countries.
As a result, the Iranians quickly approached neighboring countries and asked them to restore civilian flights. So far, according to the official, only Iraq has agreed, while there are currently no flights with Azerbaijan.
Israel prepares for risk of escalation
Israeli defense officials assess that Tehran is considering how to respond to the situation, what tools remain available to it, and what form its response should take. As evidence, they point to Iranian efforts to target vessels in the Strait of Hormuz that have so far failed.
The defense establishment believes Iran's range of options has narrowed significantly because of the naval blockade. This comes alongside Iranian attempts to carry out attacks abroad that have also failed, according to the assessment.
Israeli defense officials further assess that unless Iran attempts to break the blockade through a deliberate military move or reaches understandings with the US, it will be forced to contend with worsening domestic problems caused by the sanctions.
The IDF is therefore preparing for the possibility that an Iranian initiative could spiral out of control, such as a cruise missile striking a US vessel and causing fatalities, creating a situation in which it would be unclear how Washington would respond.
Israeli defense officials also assess that if the Iranians conclude that they are about to come under attack, or that the regime is losing ground in its confrontation with the US, they could potentially launch attacks against US assets in Jordan or Israel.
A senior official said the Iranians understand very well what the price of such a move would be, and that this is why they have not attacked Israel.

"We can go in a different direction, we can do what we want to do and what's best for the [NRLW] players and the staff."
The women's game is currently managed by the chief executive of the NRL. In contrast, the AFLW has always had its own dedicated leadership, currently headed by Laura Kane.

SINGAPORE, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's electric vehicle (EV) sales are forecast to rise 34.3 percent in 2026 to 34,940 units, lifting EVs' share of total vehicle sales to 54.6 percent, BMI Country Risk and Industry Research said on Thursday.
The Fitch Group unit attributed the growth to government tax incentives, an influx of affordable models produced in the Chinese mainland and the expansion of charging infrastructure.
As of June 2026, EVs accounted for 70 percent of new vehicle registrations, and the BMI expects the trend to continue through 2035, when EVs are projected to make up 44 percent of Singapore's vehicle fleet.
Generous subsidies and rebates, along with measures such as the EV Common Charger Grant, which supports charger installations at private residences, are expected to sustain demand, BMI said. It forecasts EVs will account for 85 percent of total vehicle sales by 2035.
In the first quarter of 2026, EVs accounted for 57.6 percent of new car registrations, or 7,679 vehicles. This was the first time EV sales exceeded those of internal combustion engine and hybrid vehicles. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- China's railway network handled 25.204 million passenger trips on Oct. 1, the first day of the week-long National Day holiday, setting a new single-day record, China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) said Friday.
On Oct. 2, the railway network is expected to handle 20.39 million passenger trips, with 1,462 additional trains scheduled to accommodate the high demand, the company said.
Passenger ticket pre-sales show that Friday's popular departure cities include Beijing, Guangzhou, Shanghai, Chengdu, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou and Nanjing, while popular arrival cities include Beijing, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Hangzhou, Shanghai, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou, Nanjing and Changsha.
Routes such as Xi'an-Chengdu round trips, and Beijing to Shenyang, Zhengzhou and Qingdao are among the busiest.

The China Railway Taiyuan Group has coordinated with local transport departments and scenic spots to add shuttle buses linking Datong South Station with the Yungang Grottoes, a UNESCO World Heritage site featuring over 50,000 Buddhist stone sculptures, and the Hengshan Mountain scenic area in north China's Shanxi Province.
The China Railway Hohhot Group has added 11 multiple-unit trains on the Baotou-Wuhai section of the Baotou-Yinchuan high-speed railway.
The China Railway Wuhan Group, tapping the newly opened Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway, has launched a promotion campaign with local governments in Yichang and Xingshan, offering passengers exclusive discounts at scenic spots, hotels and homestays with their train tickets.
China Railway expects some 284 million passenger trips during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, which extends from Sept. 23 to Oct. 8. ■

TOKYO, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Japan's unemployment rate climbed to 2.5 percent in August from 2.4 percent in July, marking the first deterioration in five months, government data showed Friday.
The number of people with jobs rose by 30,000 from the previous month to a seasonally adjusted 68.34 million, according to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications.
Of those out of work, 810,000 quit their jobs voluntarily, typically in pursuit of better working conditions, up 8.0 percent from July, while 400,000 were let go by their employers, an increase of 5.3 percent.
Meanwhile, the number of people newly looking for work grew 2.2 percent to 460,000, according to the ministry.
Separate data from the Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare showed the job availability ratio in August stood at 1.18, unchanged from the previous month, meaning there were 118 job opportunities for every 100 job seekers.
By industry, job openings fell from a year earlier in eight of the 11 sectors, led by an 11.1 percent drop in accommodation and restaurant services, followed by a 10.2 percent decline in wholesale and retail, the labor ministry said.
Of the three sectors that posted increases, manufacturing rose 3.9 percent, and information and communications gained 3.3 percent. ■

Across China: Horseshoe crab trace fossils reveal ocean life after extinction event
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:12:24 CST
16:12:24 KST

This undated photo provided by Xing Lida, a researcher from China University of Geosciences (Beijing), shows fossilized traces of a large horseshoe crab species. (Xinhua)
BEIJING, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- A new study has identified trace fossils of a large horseshoe crab species dating back more than 240 million years, from the shallow reaches of long-vanished waters in east China.
These findings offer valuable clues to ocean life after the most severe extinction event in Earth's history.
The fossils were preserved in a rock formation in Chaohu City, Anhui, which is now an inland province. Researchers identified nine complex trails and tracks, curved or straight, up to 5 meters long. They found the traces were marked by parallel scratch marks. After comparing them with fish and invertebrate animals, such as insects and spiders, they believed the trace-maker was a horseshoe crab.
Horseshoe crabs are marine arthropods, which are invertebrate animals with an external skeleton and jointed legs. They are named for their horseshoe-shaped bodies but are not true crabs at all. They are actually more closely related to scorpions and spiders. Because their basic structure has changed very little over hundreds of millions of years, horseshoe crabs are often referred to as "living fossils."
In the new study, published in the Journal of Paleontology, researchers said the size of the traces suggested the animal was a true giant, potentially over 70 cm long, making it one of the largest horseshoe crabs ever identified.
Co-author Xing Lida, of China University of Geosciences (Beijing), said previously discovered fossilized horseshoe crabs were mostly small. Records include larger footprints found in France, whose maker was estimated to be about 85 cm long, and records from north China, which indicated a body length of up to 89 cm.
Based on the shape of the traces, the new study inferred that the ancient horseshoe crab lived in a shallow sea and swam or moved near the seafloor. Its appendages or parts of its carapace occasionally brushed the bottom, leaving the distinctive scratches.
Interestingly, modern horseshoe crabs swim upside down, with their belly up. However, the traces imply a back-up swimming posture, indicating that the ancient horseshoe crabs may have behaved differently from living species.
"That's a big surprise and raises new questions about how these animals behaved in the past," said co-author Gabriel E. B. de Barros, at Brazil's Federal University of Sao Carlos. He added that the finding highlights how trace fossils can unlock secrets of animal behavior.
Barros told Xinhua that his main contribution to the international study was comparing the traces with other known traces and determining the likely trace-maker. He has worked on trace fossils from glacial and lake environments since undergraduate studies.
By revealing how extinct horseshoe crabs differed from living ones, the study offers rare evidence of the recovery of shallow marine ecosystems after the Permian-Triassic mass extinction, a global catastrophe that occurred about 250 million years ago, the study noted.
The research team also includes several members from Anhui, home to Chaohu Lake, China's fifth-largest freshwater lake. Before this study, the region had already yielded the Chaohu Fauna, a highly diverse marine community of the Early Triassic period. The presence of large horseshoe crabs adds a new species to this fauna, further enriching the region's biodiversity at that time.
"We believe the future holds many more discoveries in the region," the researchers said. ■

Arab Balad party withdraws its leader from Israel's looming general elections

Said Amori and Rania Abushamala
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Israel’s Arab Balad party decided Thursday evening to withdraw its leader's candidacy from the Oct. 27 general elections after the Supreme Court indicated that a majority of its judges supported his exclusion.
Channel 12 reported that Balad, formally known as the National Democratic Assembly and running as part of the Joint List, agreed that its leader Sami Abu Shehadeh would accept the court’s proposal to withdraw from the parliamentary (Knesset) election.
The decision followed a hearing earlier Thursday during which Supreme Court President Yitzhak Amit told Abu Shehadeh that most judges on the panel favored upholding his disqualification.
The court gave him until Friday to withdraw voluntarily, warning that otherwise it would issue a ruling barring his candidacy, according to Israeli public broadcaster KAN.
Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted on Sept. 23 to disqualify Abu Shehadeh and Joint List lawmaker Ofer Cassif.
The committee also voted to exclude the Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas, from the election.
The case against Abu Shehadeh centers on an article he published on Oct. 8, 2023, a day after a Hamas-led attack on Israeli communities near the Gaza Strip.
Right-wing groups, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party, sought his disqualification, alleging that the article expressed support for the attack. Abu Shehadeh denies the allegations.
Speaking before the court Thursday, Abu Shehadeh said he did not support “armed struggle” and acknowledged that a paragraph in the article had been incorrectly worded. He said his intention was to call for moving the conflict toward a political process.
KAN reported that the judges considered some passages in the article to provoke “displeasure and revulsion.”
Exclusion protested
Adalah, the rights group representing Abu Shehadeh, argued that the request to bar him relied on a single article that contained no explicit call to support armed struggle.
Israel’s attorney general supported disqualifying his candidacy.
Arab lawmakers and supporters held a demonstration outside the Supreme Court in West Jerusalem as hearings on the disqualification decisions began.
Ben-Gvir arrived at the scene and waved an Israeli flag in front of the protesters, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
Under Israeli electoral rules, a decision to disqualify an individual candidate takes effect only after High Court approval. Decisions barring electoral lists can be appealed before the court.
The High Court has previously overturned Central Elections Committee decisions excluding Arab candidates and parties.
Arab citizens make up about 20% of Israel’s population. Voters will elect members of the 120-seat Knesset on Oct. 27.

South Korea unveils new laser combat vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:06:18 UTC
16:06:18 KST

- South Korea publicly showed its Cheongwang Block 2 8x8 laser vehicle and a 100-kW towed laser prototype during Armed Forces Day events on Oct. 1.
- In a live demonstration, the Cheongwang Block 1 shot down two target drones, while two others crashed or were brought down before engagement.
South Korea put its Cheongwang laser weapons on public display for its 78th Armed Forces Day on Oct. 1, showing two new prototypes for the first time, but a live demonstration of the system already in service ran into trouble before the laser burned two target drones out of the sky.
The new hardware included the Cheongwang Block 2, a prototype laser combat vehicle built on an 8×8 wheeled armored chassis, and a prototype 100-kW towed high-energy laser designed to shoot down incoming rockets, artillery shells and mortar rounds. South Korea has not said how far along either program is or when they could enter service.
The demonstration at Gyeryongdae, the military headquarters complex in South Chungcheong province, used the 20-kW Cheongwang Block 1, a fixed-site laser that has been in service since late 2024. Four target drones were prepared. The first crashed on takeoff after a gust of wind damaged the fiber-optic cable used to control it. The second could not complete its flight in poor weather and flew outside the designated safety zone, so the military cut its power and brought it down.
The remaining two drones flew into the laser’s engagement area, and Cheongwang shot both down, setting them on fire as they fell trailing black smoke. Because the other two never reached the laser, the demonstration does not show how well the system would perform against a larger group of drones or in tougher conditions.
Cheongwang works by holding a high-powered fiber laser on a small drone until the heat damages its airframe or key parts and it can no longer fly. The main attraction for militaries is cost. Hanwha Systems, which helped build the system, has put the cost of a single laser shot at about 2,000 won, roughly $1.40, compared with interceptor missiles that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars or more. That figure covers only the electricity for a shot, not the cost of buying and maintaining the system, and a laser still needs enough power and cooling to keep firing.
The Block 1 was developed under South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development, making South Korea one of a small number of countries able to build its own laser weapon. South Korean officials say replacing an imported part, the laser oscillator that generates the beam, with a domestic one raised the system’s local content from 76% to 90% and increased its output from 20 kW to 30 kW. They also said the upgrade cut the time needed to bring down a small rotary-wing drone from two to four seconds to one to two, and for a fixed-wing drone from over 10 seconds to a few seconds. It is not clear whether the laser used in the Oct. 1 demonstration had the new oscillator.
The setbacks were not the first for South Korea’s unmanned systems at public events this year. On Sept. 16, several civilian drones, including a jet-powered one, crashed during an unmanned technology demonstration hosted by the Ministry of National Defense. In August, two medium-sized loitering munitions crashed into the sea during live-fire tests by the Republic of Korea Navy and the Agency for Defense Development aboard the amphibious assault ship ROKS Marado.
President Lee Jae-myung said at the Armed Forces Day ceremony that the government would speed up development of high-energy laser interceptors and artificial intelligence-based command and control systems.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:05:48 UTC
16:05:48 KST

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu called an emergency cabinet meeting on Thursday as student protests over school conditions escalated into what the government described as “urban violence,” with hundreds of schools affected and thousands of teenagers detained.
The demonstrations, initially concentrated in the Paris region last week, have spread nationwide, prompting the government to warn that many schools would move to online teaching to protect students and staff.
Lecornu instructed ministers to cancel their travel plans and attend the crisis meeting. His office said the growing violence was threatening the continuation of public education and putting school employees and students at risk.
“This upsurge in violence makes it virtually impossible to maintain the continuity of public education and is exposing staff and students to danger,” Lecornu's office said.
Education Minister Édouard Geffray is scheduled to meet student representatives on Friday.
Police reported approximately 900 demonstrations, school blockades and related incidents nationwide, with more than 160 high schools forced to close. Around 30 university campuses, including facilities in Paris and Marseille, were also blocked on Thursday.
Nearly 3,000 high-school students aged 15 to 18 have been detained since the protests began, including 1,949 on Thursday alone, according to the Interior Ministry. More than 300 police officers, along with dozens of firefighters, teachers and students, have been injured.
The protesters' complaints include excessive workloads, overcrowded classrooms, a shortage of teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves earlier this year. Riot police have been deployed as demonstrations have become increasingly violent.
Most injuries have resulted from objects thrown during clashes, although some were caused by riot-control projectiles fired by police. The Interior Ministry has launched an internal investigation into allegations that officers used excessive force and acted brutally toward three students.
Fires have been set in rubbish bins outside numerous schools, while more serious attempts to start fires have been reported inside several buildings. Authorities said a school in Nantes, northwestern France, sustained such extensive fire damage that it would remain closed for a month.
In Caen, in northern France, 16-year-old Maelle said she wanted protesters setting rubbish bins alight to express their grievances verbally instead.
“with words” was how she said she wished the protests would be conducted, telling AFP that students were demonstrating “against this government that doesn’t invest in heating, air conditioning, or teachers’ salaries”.
In Strasbourg, northeastern France, tram services were temporarily halted after protesters blocked the tracks with crowd-control barriers. The regional prefect said the suspension was intended to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”.
A 17-year-old student in Strasbourg described deteriorating conditions at school, citing overcrowded classrooms, inadequate toilet facilities, leaking water and insufficient space in the cafeteria.
“There are 35 of us per classroom,” the student said. “There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms. The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources.”
Several rubbish-bin fires were also reported in Toulouse, in southern France, while young people wearing black hoodies destroyed a bus stop in Lille. In Marseille, attempts were made to start fires inside two schools, and a teacher at one of them was splashed with petrol.
Although teachers and several school principals have reported physical threats and occasional attacks, some educators have expressed support for the protesting students.
Juliette Estiville, a Spanish teacher at a Paris high school, said she was disgusted by the police response and had joined the demonstrations to protect students.
“I’m actually here just to provide protection, to form a barrier between the police and the students,” she said. “Today went well, it’s going well, but I think that the teachers who come to the blockades are really there to protect our young people.”
The government has accused the radical-left France Insoumise (LFI) party of encouraging the demonstrations. Several of its lawmakers and mayors, including Bally Bagayoko, the party's mayor of the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, have received cheers at protest gatherings.
LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the party's candidate for the 2027 presidential election, said on Thursday that his party supported nonviolent forms of protest while expressing concern about police conduct toward young demonstrators.
“non-violent methods of struggle” were the approaches backed by LFI, Mélenchon said, adding that his “greatest worry is an unbearable level of police violence against these young people”.

India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement calls protests over voter-list revisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:05:00 UTC
16:05:00 KST

India’s “Cockroach” youth movement has called for fresh protests Friday in Mumbai, the country’s financial hub, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over contentious revisions to voter lists.
The movement, which began as an online campaign and now calls itself the Cockroach Janta Party, forced India’s education minister to resign earlier this year after a series of street protests. Friday’s rally in Mumbai is intended to launch a new wave of demonstrations across the country.
Separately, a coalition of student and civil society groups was scheduled to gather Friday at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in New Delhi, to press the same demand.
The protests have intensified scrutiny of India’s Election Commission, which oversees elections across the country.
Critics and opposition parties accuse the commission of altering voter registrations in ways they say could benefit the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The commission and the government deny any wrongdoing.
The Indian Express reported last month that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders involving voter registration, voter deletions and restorations, appeals and the management of electoral-roll databases.
According to the report, the two commissioners raised concerns about decisions they said were made without their knowledge, including changes involving new-voter registration and access to electoral-roll databases.
The Election Commission disputed the characterization of the disagreements, saying differing views and comments were part of normal deliberations and that its major decisions had the approval of the full commission.
India’s Election Commission consists of the chief election commissioner and two election commissioners of equal rank. Under the 2023 law governing the commission, matters on which the members differ are decided by majority vote.
The voter-list revisions began in the eastern state of Bihar in June 2025 under a process known as Special Intensive Revision, or SIR. The exercise has since expanded to 30 states and federally administered territories, according to The Indian Express.
The newspaper reported that more than 13 crore, or 130 million, names were struck from draft voter rolls during the nationwide rollout.
The revisions have drawn criticism over the documents required to establish voters’ eligibility.
Critics say the requirements could make it difficult for some eligible voters to remain on the rolls, while the Election Commission says the process is intended to identify duplicate and ineligible entries and ensure that eligible voters are included.
The commission has rejected allegations that the revisions are politically motivated. Opposition parties and activists have continued to accuse Kumar of political bias and say the process could exclude legitimate voters and benefit Modi’s party. The BJP and Election Commission have rejected those allegations.
The Cockroach movement emerged earlier this year amid anger among young people over unemployment and examination-paper leaks. Led by Abhijeet Dipke, it gained national attention through protests over alleged irregularities involving examination papers and later expanded its campaign to issues including government accountability and democratic institutions.
The movement’s campaign has since broadened beyond education, with the group calling for greater accountability from government institutions and now making the Election Commission a central focus of its protests.

Breadcrumb
Sudan's jailed former ruler Omar al-Bashir seeks treatment abroad, says lawyer
Sudan's former president Omar al-Bashir is seeking permission to travel abroad for medical treatment, his lawyer told AFP on Friday, saying the jailed ex-ruler requires tests unavailable in war-ravaged Sudan.
Bashir, 82, was recently transferred from a hospital in the northern city of Merowe to Aliaa Specialist Military Hospital in Omdurman, across the Nile from the capital Khartoum, after suffering health complications, his lawyer Mohamed El-Hassan El-Amin said.
El-Amin added that Bashir's condition "requires medical tests and cardiac imaging that are not currently available in Sudanese hospitals".
"There is no specific country being sought for treatment. He could travel to any country able to provide the required care," he told AFP.
In a statement on Wednesday, Bashir's family said his health had deteriorated to the point that treatment abroad had become "urgent", without disclosing details of his condition.
Bashir seized power in a 1989 military coup and ruled Sudan for three decades before being ousted in April 2019 following months of mass protests.
The International Criminal Court has accused him of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity over the Darfur conflict that erupted in 2003 when ethnic minority rebels took up arms, accusing Khartoum of marginalising their region.
Bashir denies the allegations.
He remains wanted by the ICC. However, he has never been handed over and has been in Sudanese custody since his removal from power.
Shortly before war erupted between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in April 2023, authorities moved him from Khartoum's Kober prison to military medical facilities, first in Khartoum and later in Merowe.
His request comes with Sudan's healthcare system devastated by the war, which has damaged or forced the closure of most medical facilities.

Explainer-Why renewed fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray risks a regional war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:03:17 UTC
16:03:17 KST

Explainer-Why renewed fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray risks a regional war
LONDON, Oct 2 - After months of tension, fighting has erupted in northern Ethiopia between federal troops and a rebel alliance headed by Tigrayan forces.
On the surface, the clashes look like the revival of the 2020-2022 civil war that pitted the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) against the federal government and killed hundreds of thousands of people.
This time, however, the Horn of Africa region with Ethiopia at its heart is much more unstable.
TANGLED ALLIANCES AND RIVALRIES
The opposing sides in the fighting have ties to countries embroiled in a string of other interconnected conflicts, rivalries and alliances, all driven by past enmities and competition over influence and territory.
That tangled web stretches from Chad in north-central Africa to the heart of the Middle East. Each intervention across one border risks adjusting calculations across others. Experts fear war could spread far beyond Ethiopia’s frontiers.
Unlike in the 2020-2022 war, Ethiopia and neighbouring Eritrea now find themselves on opposing sides.
Conflict in their shared neighbour, Sudan, has drawn in both countries, alongside other states in Africa and the Gulf.
Down the coast, Somalia's security crises are deepening, threatening to fragment the country further as foreign powers eye its self-governing regions for their coastline.
Against this background, the Iran war and the involvement of Yemen's Houthis just across the Red Sea from Eritrea have increased concerns over trade routes through that waterway.
Underpinning much of the tension is the feud between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, which escalated in Yemen last year but has spilled over into the Horn of Africa.
HOW IMPORTANT IS THE FALLOUT BETWEEN ERITREA AND ETHIOPIA?
In the last war, Eritrean forces supported Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. This time round, Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the rebel alliance, an accusation Eritrea denies. Eritrea severed diplomatic ties with Ethiopia after Addis Ababa ordered the closure of its embassy in Asmara.
Diplomats and analysts say Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki is, for now, providing rebels with access to the coast and the rest of the world through his country. During the last war, Tigrayan forces were cut off on all sides.
At the heart of the shifting alliances are decades of conflict and distrust. Ethiopia and Eritrea fought each other between 1998 and 2000. One core point of contention is Ethiopia’s long-standing quest to restore direct access to the sea, lost when Eritrea gained independence in 1993.
The head of Ethiopia’s military has accused Sudan and Egypt of supporting Eritrean operations in Ethiopia. Both countries have denied any meddling.
Both are also at odds with Ethiopia over its development of a giant hydroelectric dam that they say could threaten their access to water.
WHY IS THE ETHIOPIA FIGHTING LINKED TO WAR IN SUDAN?
Sudan has been divided by a three-year power struggle between its military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) that has created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
Both sides rely heavily on support from external backers, who are pressing for regional influence and pushing their own causes.
The UAE, a major backer of the Ethiopian government, has supported the RSF, according to United Nations experts. The UAE denies the accusations.
Ethiopia has also been accused of backing the RSF, including hosting a secret training camp in the west of the country. Addis Ababa denies it supports the RSF.
For its part, Sudan's military has had backing from a range of actors, including Egypt and Eritrea, while maintaining close ties with Saudi Arabia.
Underscoring how such ties can stoke conflict across borders, several diplomats told Reuters some Tigrayan forces have fought alongside Sudan's army, and that Khartoum hosted meetings that led to the creation of the Ethiopian rebel alliance.
WHY DOES THE UAE-SAUDI RIVALRY MATTER IN AFRICA?
In recent years, the UAE has become an influential player, forging relationships in the Horn of Africa through multi-billion-dollar investments, robust diplomacy and discreet military support.
The UAE has struck deals with Somalia's breakaway region of Somaliland and semi-autonomous Puntland - both of which could help give its landlocked ally Ethiopia access to the Red Sea.
Israel, also an ally of Ethiopia, is the only country to have recognised Somaliland as independent and is training local forces there.
Saudi officials say Emirati activities in Yemen and the Horn threaten their national security and Riyadh has been building its own alliance south of the Red Sea. An Emirati official said the Gulf and the Horn of Africa regions depended on each other and the UAE was providing essential investment and security that African leaders were calling for.
While relationships are not hard and fast, Saudi Arabia is broadly aligned with Sudan’s military, Egypt and Eritrea - all of whom are rivals of Ethiopia. REUTERS

Ukraine's budget revenue lags plan by UAH 49.5 bln in 9M
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:02:52 EEST
16:02:52 KST

The general fund of Ukraine's state budget fell UAH 49.5 billion short of plan in January-September 2026, almost two-thirds of it (UAH 32 billion) in August-September, Budget Committee head Roksolana Pidlasa said in a Facebook post.
"Budget 2026 execution for nine months: the state of budget revenue is deteriorating… The main reason is constant Russian strikes on business," she said.
Revenue from import VAT fell short by UAH 35.7 billion, or 6.8%, VAT on goods produced in Ukraine by UAH 32.9 billion, or 11.4%, domestic excise by UAH 19.1 billion, or 16.5%, and dividends and part of net profit of economic entities by UAH 10.8 billion, or 16%, Pidlasa said.
At the same time, there was overperformance in corporate profit tax of UAH 29 billion, or 12%, and in personal income tax and the military levy of UAH 6.6 billion, or 2.6%, which offsets the shortfall in other taxes, she said.
According to preliminary data, UAH 1.9 trillion was credited to general fund revenue in January-September 2026, excluding international grants, she said.
The biggest sources were import VAT at UAH 491 billion, corporate profit tax at UAH 270 billion, personal income tax and the military levy at UAH 266.3 billion, VAT on goods produced in Ukraine at UAH 255.2 billion, National Bank of Ukraine funds at UAH 146.1 billion, import excise at UAH 134.6 billion, domestic excise at UAH 96.5 billion, dividends and part of net profit of economic entities at UAH 57.1 billion, import duty at UAH 48.4 billion and rent payments at UAH 42.6 billion, Pidlasa said.
About $22 billion in international aid was used to cover general fund spending in January-September, and another UAH 350.6 billion was raised from domestic government bond placements, she said.
The biggest spending categories since the start of 2026 were defense at UAH 2 trillion, or 61.3% of all general fund expenditure, debt repayment (domestic and external) at UAH 427.9 billion, social protection and veteran support (excluding public investment projects) at UAH 342.6 billion, debt servicing (external and domestic) at UAH 275.2 billion, the medical guarantees program and health screening at UAH 144 billion, school teachers' pay (education subvention and top-ups) at UAH 116.7 billion, and basic and additional grants at UAH 48.5 billion, she said.
"Until the second tranche of EU macro-financial assistance ($4.26 billion) is received, the budget situation will remain critical," she said.
The Ukrainian state budget for 2026 was initially adopted with revenue (excluding grants) of UAH 2.90 trillion and expenditure of UAH 4.77 trillion, including UAH 2.61 trillion and UAH 4.38 trillion respectively in the general fund.
In June, parliament raised revenue to UAH 5.20 trillion and expenditure to UAH 6.41 trillion, mainly on the back of a EUR 45 billion EU loan, including UAH 3.38 trillion and UAH 4.50 trillion respectively in the general fund.
Under the International Monetary Fund's Extended Fund Facility program, updated in July, general government revenue is forecast at UAH 6.78 trillion this year, compared with UAH 5.06 trillion last year, and expenditure at UAH 7.94 trillion, compared with UAH 6.63 trillion.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky and representatives of the ruling Servant of the People faction said another increase in defense spending of $27 billion was needed. In September, the government stopped financing capital expenditure because of a funding shortfall.
Total cash expenditure of the general fund reached UAH 2.7 trillion in January-August 2026, compared with UAH 2.23 trillion in January-August 2025, while revenue was almost UAH 2.3 trillion, compared with UAH 1.71 trillion.

Russia is attempting to create a new "shadow fleet" of tankers to circumvent sanctions and preserve the revenues from gas exports that the Kremlin uses to finance its war against Ukraine. The Telegraph reports this, citing a statement by the UK Foreign Office, writes UNN.
Details
It is noted that Russia has built at least two new tankers, approximately 300 meters long, to transport liquefied natural gas (LNG) through the Arctic; both vessels entered service earlier this year.
The UK Foreign Office believes that the Kremlin has requisitioned a number of other vessels to strengthen its secret fleet, which is increasingly becoming subject to seizure by NATO.
The UK government reported Putin's likely attempt to expand the fleet on Thursday and also announced the introduction of new sanctions against Russia.
The Kremlin is attempting to create a dangerous new "shadow fleet" to circumvent sanctions and maintain revenues from gas exports… The new sanctions package includes several vessels acquired to carry out this task, including those that entered service very recently—in July this year
In addition, the United Kingdom imposed sanctions on eight more vessels, including new-generation liquefied natural gas (LNG) tankers—the "Alexey Kosygin" and "Konstantin Posyet," which sail under the Russian flag.
These vessels, with a displacement of 127,555 tons, were built in Russia and entered service earlier this year. Both are capable of breaking through ice up to two meters thick, indicating the possibility of their use as part of Russia's advance into the Arctic and the Far North.
The third vessel, the "Pyotr Stolypin," also joined the fleet this year and was sanctioned along with the "Portovyy," "Chaivo," "Avacha," "Bebek-E" (built in 1979), and "Galle Energy"—a 75-foot personnel transport vessel sailing under the flag of Sri Lanka.
To date, the EU has imposed sanctions on approximately 670 vessels, banning them from entering European ports, while the United Kingdom has taken measures against around 600 tankers used to finance Putin's war machine.
It is noted that the sanctions announced on Thursday also target eight individuals involved in the arbitrary detention, torture, and cruel treatment of Ukrainian civilians, including a current employee of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB).
Sanctions were also imposed on seven more individuals for their role in the indoctrination and militarization of Ukrainian children, including those deported by the Russian authorities.

Unresolved Financial Dispute Cited as Motive in Plovdiv Murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
06:56:14 UTC
15:56:14 KST

Plovdiv Bans Older Cars From City Center Starting October 1
Plovdiv introduces its first low-emission zone today, October 1, 2026, restricting the oldest and most polluting cars from entering the city center during the colder months
Plovdiv police say the evidence gathered so far points to 51-year-old Slavcho Megerov as the perpetrator of the murder of businessman Iliyan Filipov, with prosecutors preparing to request his remand in custody.
Megerov has been formally charged with premeditated murder under the relevant provision of the Penal Code. The Plovdiv Prosecutor's Office announced that the motive was personal and related to unresolved financial matters between the two men.
Senior Commissioner Vasil Kostadinov, Director of the Plovdiv Regional Directorate of the Ministry of Interior, said the suspect had been questioned and the initial procedural actions to document the crime were underway.
“In my opinion, based on my years of experience and work on similar types of crimes, the circumstances provide sufficient grounds to believe that he is the perpetrator of this serious criminal offense,” Kostadinov said.
He added that Megerov appeared in surveillance footage from the crime scene and that investigators had collected substantial evidence implicating him in the killing.
“A vast amount of evidence has been gathered to support our conclusion that he is the actual perpetrator of the crime,” Kostadinov said, adding that the two men had known each other and remained in contact, including one or two weeks before the murder.
The prosecution is expected to request the strictest pre-trial measure, remand in custody, on Saturday or Sunday. Supervising prosecutor Dimitar Molev said the evidence collected was sufficient to support such a request.
The information was presented during an evening briefing attended by representatives of the Prosecutor's Office and the Ministry of Interior.
According to the investigation, Filipov and Megerov had known each other for years, maintained a close relationship and had professional ties before a conflict developed between them. Investigators have not established precisely when their financial disagreements began or the exact nature of their relationship.
The prosecution has not disclosed what Megerov told investigators during questioning, while Molev declined to specify whether Filipov owed money to the accused.
“I cannot say,” the prosecutor said when asked about the possibility that Filipov had been indebted to Megerov.
The authorities have not clarified who owed money to whom, describing the motive only as unresolved financial dealings between the two men.
Kostadinov said investigators were still examining whether Megerov had stalked Filipov before the killing. He also confirmed that witnesses had been identified, although none had seen the actual moment when the shot was fired.
The murder weapon has not been publicly accounted for, and authorities have declined to disclose whether it has been recovered or how many shots were fired. Police have also not provided details about the precise circumstances of the shooting.
According to the Prosecutor's Office, the emergency report about the crime was made to the 112 line by a member of the public.
The suspect, who has lived in Sofia for several years, was apprehended following cooperation between the Ministry of Interior and the State Agency for National Security (SANS). The operation also involved the General Directorate of National Police and the General Directorate for Combating Organized Crime.
Kostadinov said the joint operational and investigative work had helped identify the specific suspect. Police also found traces at the crime scene that were subsequently included in the case evidence.
Authorities did not confirm whether surveillance camera recordings had been used in the investigation, saying only that various operational and procedural methods had been employed to collect information that could serve as evidence.
The police chief said there were reasonable grounds to suspect Megerov of committing the murder, while stressing that investigators had not ruled out any possible theory, including a contract killing.
The 51-year-old Plovdiv native has a criminal history stretching back more than three decades. Although he has since been legally rehabilitated and officially has a clean criminal record, he has previously been convicted of several offenses.
According to Deputy Interior Minister Molev, Megerov's criminal record includes offenses dating from 1993 to 2020, including murder committed while he was a minor, theft and participation in an organized crime group.
Interior Ministry records also link him to vault robberies, a murder in the 1990s and business interests in the construction sector. Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev previously said Megerov had three convictions for robbery, intentional homicide and theft.
His most serious sentence was an 11-year prison term for a killing following a fight at a Plovdiv nightclub in the early 1990s. After his release, he became involved in robberies and thefts and gained a reputation in criminal circles as a skilled safecracker.
In 2013, Megerov and members of his group attempted to rob a public vault in Kardzhali. They subdued security guards and broke into 32 deposit boxes, finding 4,500 euros in one of them while the remaining boxes were empty.
Police arrested Megerov outside the building shortly after the robbery. He subsequently reached a plea agreement with prosecutors and received a seven-year prison sentence.
His criminal activities also included a jewelry store robbery in Plovdiv, during which his group stole nearly 6 kilograms of gold jewelry. Reports indicate that he later spent two years in hiding in Dubai after coming under pressure from police operations in Plovdiv.
After 2021, Megerov began moving into the construction business, becoming a partner in several companies. He also became a business partner of Filipov in one company.
Public records show that Megerov held a 50% stake in a Sofia real estate development project involving a large complex in the Dragalevtsi district, but was removed as a partner in late October last year.
Tihomir Bezlov of the Center for the Study of Democracy said a dispute over the company's interests was one possible explanation for the murder, while cautioning that this remained an initial hypothesis.
“It likely stems from a conflict between them regarding the company, since it has emerged they were partners, though this is a very rough hypothesis,” Bezlov said.
He also noted that Megerov had reportedly been the victim's former classmate and longtime friend, adding that his background included an extensive criminal history.
Former Plovdiv Mayor Zdravko Dimitrov, who was close to Filipov, said he knew of no conflict between the businessman and the suspect.
“We last saw each other at the stadium in Plovdiv during the Bulgaria vs. Luxembourg match. He was in very high spirits. There was no indication things would end this way,” Dimitrov said.
Asked by BNT whether he had ever seen Filipov with Megerov, Dimitrov replied that he did not know the suspect and had first seen him on television the previous day.
BGNES reported that Filipov was killed during the night of September 29-30 in Plovdiv's Hristo Smirnenski district, near Peshtersko Shose. The attack took place in the stairwell of a building constructed by the businessman. Unofficial reports said he had been shot once in the head.
Megerov, who had previously worked for Filipov, was arrested in Sofia and brought to Plovdiv under heavy security on October 1 for questioning.
Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev told Parliament that the evidence collected by the Ministry of Interior left no doubt that the detained man was the actual perpetrator. He added, however, that investigators were still examining whether other people had been involved and what roles they might have played.
Following the murder, a special task force was established with officers from the National Police, the General Directorate for Combating Organized Crime (GDBOP), Border Police, Plovdiv police and SANS.
Demerdzhiev also said Megerov had previously been identified as a person of interest in a 2026 investigation into the theft of a substantial quantity of investment gold in Plovdiv.
The investigation into Filipov's murder remains ongoing, with authorities continuing to examine the financial relationship between the two men and the possible involvement of other individuals.
Twenty-two Bulgarian and foreign nationals were detained for up to 24 hours in a specialized police operation targeting an organized criminal group trafficking illegal migrants from Turkey through Bulgaria to EU countries, the Ministry of Interior’s press
A former employee of Bulgarian businessman Iliyan Filipov, who was shot dead in Plovdiv overnight, has been arrested in Sofia in connection with the killing, according to Bulgarian media reports.

Additional warships

Five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, were arrested in the early hours of Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford base.
British Police arrested a dual UK-Iranian national on Thursday on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a military air base in England that authorities have linked to Tehran.
The 25-year-old man was arrested in central London on Thursday and police have searched two properties in the capital, Counter Terrorism Policing said in a statement.
Five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, were arrested in the early hours of Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran.
The suspects have since been released on bail.
Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swooped on the rural area.
Police later said they had found a quantity of petrol in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.
Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing, said the investigation “is hugely complex and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry.”
“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles, including possible foreign state involvement,” she said.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK sees “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident.
He did not provide details about what the suspects were planning or why the UK thinks Iran was involved.
Iran denies involvement but previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.
RAF Fairford, 160 kilometres west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year’s war with Iran.
Top US officials have criticised the decision to grant the suspects bail, with President Donald Trump saying “I wouldn’t have done that” and Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying a lot of people were “disturbed” by the move.
Trump said on Thursday that “I was surprised they were released on bail."
“I have a lot of respect, however, for Scotland Yard. I think they know what they’re doing. But I was a little bit surprised,” Trump said as he left the White House to fly to Texas.
Burnham said authorities have the investigation under “the strongest grip and the closest control,” and British officials had been “talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done.”
The arrests came at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British security services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on UK soil.
British officials have said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states, including Iran, increased by 50% in the six months to December 2025.
UK officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear.
They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the UK if conflicts in the Middle East continue.

Kyrgyzstan launches its 1st satellite into orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
06:52:19 UTC
15:52:19 KST

Kanyshai Butun
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Kyrgyzstan on Thursday launched its first satellite into orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket that took off from US soil.
According to the Kyrgyz Presidency’s press service, the satellite was placed into orbit from California’s Vandenberg Space Force Base as part of a group of spacecraft launched by the same rocket.
The mission was a joint effort between Kyrgyzstan and the United Arab Emirates, with operations to be managed from a control center in the Kyrgyz city of Bishkek.
Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov attended the launch ceremony during a working visit to the United States.
The launch opens new opportunities for Kyrgyzstan to use space-based data across various sectors, including monitoring agricultural land, glaciers, water bodies, forests, and pastures, as well as tracking changes in natural ecosystems, the statement said.
Satellite data will also be used to detect the illegal extraction of natural resources, unauthorized waste dumps, and other sources of pollution, and to optimize logistics routes.
“Satellite technologies will be particularly significant for monitoring and early detection of natural hazards,” the statement said, adding that the data could help identify signs of droughts, floods, landslides, mudflows and forest fires more quickly, allowing for timely responses and mitigation of potential damage.
In the future, satellite data will be integrated with government digital systems to create spatial maps and analytical models, the statement said. The data will support government decision-making, investment planning, and monitoring of state programs.
“The use of satellite data combined with the capabilities of supercomputing technologies will create a foundation for more accurate and efficient management of Kyrgyzstan's economic and natural resources,” it said.

This winter, Russia is preparing powerful strikes against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in an effort to cause a collapse and a humanitarian crisis in Ukraine. Moscow plans to use up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs. The New York Times reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to the publication, during a meeting in Paris, Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal showed European partners a plan intercepted from Russia that envisages "forcing Ukrainians into submission through the cold."
"Shmyhal described the document as an intercepted Russian plan aimed at causing the collapse of the energy system through systematic attacks. The plan also states that Moscow will target Ukraine’s water supply system with dozens of ballistic missiles and glide bombs, including pumping stations and treatment facilities.
"Russia has never previously carried out large-scale strikes against such facilities. Ukrainian officials have privately expressed concern that the country has limited contingency plans in the event of serious disruptions to the water supply. The ultimate goal is to cut off Ukraine’s major cities from electricity, heating, and water, which could cause a humanitarian crisis. Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa have been identified as the main targets: the plan is to reduce electricity supplies in these cities by 90%, cut heat supplies by up to 90%, and seriously disrupt the operation of the sewage system," the publication adds.

MiG-29s and F-16s to Escort Tsar Samuel’s Remains to Sofia
Bulgaria will receive the remains of Tsar Samuel at a state ceremony in Sofia on October 3, with the Spartan military transport aircraft carrying them to be escorted by MiG-29 and F-16 fighter jets, the Government Information Service said.
More than 1,000 years after his death, the medieval ruler is returning to Bulgaria, whose freedom and independence he devoted his life to, according to the government statement. His remains will be formally handed over to the Bulgarian state on October 3 at the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki, in the presence of Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis.
Once the Spartan enters Bulgarian airspace, two pairs of MiG-29 and F-16 fighters will meet and escort it. The aircraft formation is expected to pass over Knyaz Alexander I Square in Sofia at around 12:30 p.m. The fighters will make another flyover after the transport aircraft lands.
Bulgarian Armed Forces personnel will then take Tsar Samuel's remains from Vasil Levski Airport in Sofia to Knyaz Alexander I Square.
Radev will speak at the state ceremony, titled "Bulgaria Welcomes Tsar Samuel." A 21-gun artillery salute will accompany the Bulgarian national anthem.
About 750 Interior Ministry employees will be deployed to provide security and maintain public order during the ceremony and the reception and interment of the remains in Sofia, Chief Inspector Ivan Georgiev, head of the Mass Events Sector at the Sofia Directorate of the Interior Ministry, told reporters on Thursday.
After the official ceremony, a procession will make its way to the Church of Saint Sophia. Members of the public will be able to pay their respects to Tsar Samuel's remains there, and a trisagion service will be held inside the church.

A dual Russian Australian national accused of attempted foreign interference in Ukraine during the war with Russia faced a court in Brisbane for the first time on Friday.
Vladimir Teslov, 27, spoke briefly via video link during his maiden court appearance, Australian Associated Press reported.
Australian Federal Police arrested him in August and charged him with attempting to engage in intentional foreign interference.
It is the first time the Australian police’s counter foreign interference task force charged a Russian-linked person under foreign interference laws.
Teslov is a Victorian resident, according to the police.
The next hearing in the case is set for Dec. 4, prosecutors said
Police have alleged that Teslov travelled to Russia in 2024, where he “undertook military-style training before returning to Australia” before traveling to Ukraine in 2025, where he joined the Ukrainian Armed Forces to “gain access to information relating to their military personnel, units and locations,” the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported.
Teslov then allegedly “attempted to provide the information to individuals he believed were acting on behalf of Russian intelligence.”
"It is alleged that this conduct created a risk to the safety and security of Ukrainian military personnel," Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said earlier.
Australian prosecutors told the court that their evidence collection and examination of 17 devices is not yet complete.
