====================================================================================================

Ancient Negev wine was a global hit. Can Israeli winemakers - and scientists - bring it back?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
06:03:36 UTC
15:03:36 KST

When wine lovers think of distinctive wine regions, Bordeaux and Champagne in France, Tuscany in Italy or Portugal's Douro Valley usually come to mind. In these places, the vine is more than a crop. It is part of the local identity and cultural landscape, shaped by generations of winegrowers and farmers. History, agriculture and the natural environment come together in a single story.
The terraces clinging to the Douro's slopes, Tuscany's vineyard landscapes and Bordeaux's tiny vineyard plots tell that story: Over generations, the environment shaped the wine, and the wine shaped the environment.
The Negev Desert, in southern Israel, has a story like this, too. This past May, it was recognized as Israel's first desert appellation, a defined winegrowing region. The designation formally recognizes the Negev's distinctive terroir: the interplay of climate, soil, landscape and accumulated human knowledge that gives its wine a character of its own.
But unlike many of the world's celebrated wine regions, the Negev has both a living tradition to celebrate and a forgotten one to rediscover. Alongside today's vineyards and wineries, research is bringing the historic wine route of the Byzantine Negev into ever sharper focus. For some 300 years, from the 4th to the 7th centuries C.E., grape cultivation and winemaking were the economic mainstay of the Negev's settlements. Vineyards, winepresses, wine jars and other archaeological evidence uncovered at Avdat, Shivta, Nitzana and Haluza attest to a thriving industry that exported its wines to markets across the Mediterranean.
Today, the Negev's past and present are coming together in an unusual way. A modern wine industry is seeking to establish an identity for Israeli desert wine, while archaeological, historical and genetic research allows us to reconstruct the region's ancient grape-growing and winemaking heritage. This convergence does more than illuminate history. It opens the way to rethinking heritage, agriculture, regional identity and sustainable development in the Negev.
To understand the depth of this connection, we need to go back some 1,500 years. During the Byzantine period, the Negev was one of the eastern Mediterranean's most important wine-producing regions. Historical sources praise the flavor of its wine, known as "Gaza wine" after the port from which it was shipped. Traces of that industry remain in the landscape: Winepresses, stone terraces and ancient fields still line the streambeds and slopes of the Negev Highlands.
Camel caravans carried the wine in pottery jars from the cities of Avdat, Shivta, Nitzana and Haluza to the ports of Gaza and Ashkelon. From there, it was shipped to markets across the empire: the capital, Constantinople, now Istanbul; Rome and Marseille; and even remote parts of northwestern Europe. Hundreds of thousands of jar fragments discovered at sites throughout the Mediterranean show that wine was far more than an agricultural product. It was the economic engine that sustained settlement in the Negev at its peak.
An interrupted tradition
In contemporary terms, the Byzantine Negev functioned as an appellation – a distinctive wine region – long before the concept acquired its modern meaning. Its desert terroir, encompassing local agricultural knowledge and the relationship between place, crop and product, gave its wines an identity recognized far beyond the region.
Wine was more than an industry. It shaped the entire social and cultural landscape. Growing vines, harvesting grapes and making wine became defining features of life in the Negev, in striking contrast to its harsh, arid surroundings. The Byzantine Negev offers one of the most remarkable examples of ancient human adaptation to extreme conditions.
Its distinctive floodwater collection systems, terraces in the wadis, dovecotes containing abundant grapevine remains, industrial winepresses and trade routes linking production areas to export ports all attest to a sustained effort to adapt Mediterranean agriculture to the desert. Together, they created a unique cultural landscape, shaped by environmental challenges and the knowledge and ingenuity of generations of winegrowers.
But unlike Bordeaux, Tuscany or the Douro, the Negev's wine tradition was interrupted. At the end of the Byzantine period, and increasingly during the early Islamic period in the 7th and 8th centuries C.E., vineyards were abandoned, settlements deserted and agricultural knowledge lost. For more than a thousand years, the fields, winepresses and terraces stood as silent witnesses to a forgotten chapter.
Only in recent decades has archaeological, bioarchaeological, historical and genetic research begun to bring this story back into focus. For us, as researchers studying the Negev's ancient agricultural landscape, one of the most moving moments of our work was realizing that these remains were not merely evidence of what had been. They were also a bridge to what might yet be. Grape seeds some 1,500 years old, uncovered in excavations at Avdat, became the starting point for a journey back to the vineyard and toward the possibility of reviving a tradition that seemed lost forever.
Excavations in the Negev uncovered hundreds of grape seeds, along with the remains of vineyards and wine-production facilities. Sequencing DNA from some of the seeds found at Avdat revealed that the grape varieties grown in the Byzantine Negev were local to the eastern Mediterranean, rather than European. Negev wine was, in every sense, a regional wine. Relatives of those varieties still grow in Lebanon, Crete, the southern coastal plain and the western Negev.
The Byzantine settlers disappeared, the vineyards fell into ruin and the wine route was forgotten, but the vines themselves survived thanks to their exceptional resilience. They continued growing on abandoned land, beside old wells and among the remains of agricultural plots deserted in the 20th century. For the first time, we could establish a living link between the Negev's historic vineyards and vines still growing in the country today.
The significance of this discovery extends far beyond archaeology. A vine is not a potsherd or a coin displayed in a museum. It is living material that can be propagated and planted, allowing us to examine how it copes with today's environmental conditions and assess the character of its grapes and the quality of its wine.
Unlike most archaeological exhibits, a vine is tangible heritage that can still be cultivated. Heritage vineyards allow us to explore how local varieties fare in the Negev's present-day environment while bringing people into direct contact with the history of the place. For the first time in centuries, vines are growing beside ancient terraces and winepresses, in the same agricultural landscape where their ancestral varieties were cultivated more than a thousand years ago. Archaeology thus becomes more than the study of the past. It becomes an exploration of how historical knowledge can once again take root in a living landscape.
Over the past three years, this approach has led to the establishment of several heritage vineyards for research and education, both across the Negev and near the places where the surviving vines were found. These include vineyards at Avdat and Shivta national parks, planted in cooperation with the Israel Nature and Parks Authority and the University of Haifa, as well as at the Ramat Negev Research and Development Center and the Shikmim Field School. They contain local heritage varieties, including Syriki, Be'er and Dabouki, with historical and genetic ties to the vineyards of the Byzantine Negev. These vines have returned to the heart of the landscape where they were once cultivated.
The project has attracted considerable interest beyond the research community, inspiring further initiatives by farmers, winemakers and local communities. In recent years, heritage varieties have been planted in additional vineyards in the Negev Highlands and elsewhere in Israel. Archaeological and genetic findings have become not only tools for understanding the past but also a source of inspiration for agricultural renewal.
An exceptional terroir
The establishment of heritage vineyards is part of a broader trend in Israeli wine. More and more wineries are turning to local heritage varieties and reexamining the relationship between wine, place, identity and belonging. At least 10 Israeli wineries now make wines from heritage varieties or are experimenting with them.
The search for local varieties is driven by more than historical curiosity. For many winemakers, it reflects a desire to produce wine rooted in Israel's history, landscape and culture, beyond the simple fact of being produced here. It is an attempt to establish a distinctive regional identity and ground the country's resurgent wine culture in indigenous grapes, local traditions and history. In the Negev, heritage varieties connect the desert terroir with grapes that developed over generations in the region's environmental conditions.
Beyond their historical and cultural value, these varieties are attracting interest because of their long adaptation to the local climate. This is a pressing concern for a wine industry increasingly forced to contend with extreme environmental changes. As awareness grows of climate change's effects on agriculture, the value of these varieties extends far beyond the history of local wine. The Negev's viticulture shows how human communities developed production systems suited to extreme conditions over generations. In this sense, the Negev's agricultural heritage is more than a memory of the past. It is also an inspiration for the future.
This story matters to more than wine lovers. It raises a broader question about the relationship between heritage and development. Around the world, interest is growing in historic terroirs and agricultural landscapes where local knowledge, farming and tradition have shaped regional identities over generations. The Negev is an exceptional case: It offers an opportunity to bring together advanced scientific research, a well-documented agricultural heritage and an active wine industry seeking to build its future on its past.
Recognition of the Negev as a distinctive wine region is an important step in that direction. The designation's wider significance, however, may lie as much in reconnecting the landscapes of the past with the Negev's future development as in defining a wine region's boundaries. The Douro Valley and Tuscany are more than places where wine is made. They are cultural landscapes shaped over generations. The Negev, too, can cultivate an identity that draws on its deep agricultural heritage to meet the challenges and opportunities of the 21st century.
More than 80 years have passed since Israeli settlers renewed settlement in the Negev with the founding of Kibbutz Revivim, initially conceived as an "outpost for agricultural experimentation." More than 70 years have passed since David Ben-Gurion moved to Sde Boker and declared that "the Negev will yet bloom." Today, we can see a new direction for that vision.
This renewed vision draws on a glorious past, when the Negev's wines captured the attention of the cultural and culinary world of their day. It looks toward a future grounded in that rich wine heritage, with the hope that Negev wines will once again gain renown around the world.
Indeed, most of the world's wine regions now look to the past to establish their prestige. The Negev is in a rarer position: It can use the past to shape its future. The appellation designation is only the beginning of that process. If we can make the knowledge uncovered through excavations, genetics and historical research part of the Negev's living story in the 21st century, its wine route may become more than a tale of past glory. It may also offer a path toward the region's renewal.
The authors, from the University of Haifa's School of Archaeology and Maritime Cultures, study the history of grape cultivation in the Negev and the connections between its historic and modern wine routes.

'A powerful buffer': How solar saved the EU €37.4 billion since the war on Iran began
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
06:02:37 UTC
15:02:37 KST

Europe's solar boom is cushioning households from the crippling costs of gas, as the war on Iran continues to highlight the dangers of fossil fuel reliance.
Europe is cushioning itself from the volatile cost of fossil fuel imports thanks to a surge in solar power.
Gas prices remain sky-high seven months into the war on Iran – mainly due to the effective blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route that usually carries around one-fifth of the world's global liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies.
While POTUS Donald Trump assures the conflict will end "very soon", disruptions to the supply chain have left the EU grappling with yet another energy price crisis.
The benchmark Dutch TTF natural gas price traded at around €31.96 MWh on 27 February, the day before the war broke out. On 30 September, it traded at €72.35MWh, a 126.5 per cent increase.
However, new analysis by SolarPower Europe reveals that harnessing sunlight for power has saved Europe €37.4 billion by lowering demand for gas imports.
Solar is the 'route to long-term energy security'
"Every megawatt-hour generated by solar power reduces our dependence on imported fossil fuels and makes Europe safer," says Walburga Hemetsberger, CEO of SolarPower Europe.
"This news follows solar becoming EU’s largest single source of electricity in June, supplying 25 per cent of the bloc's power. It's a demonstration of the returns on Europe's investment in abundant, homegrown renewable energy resources. We can go further and faster."
Hemetsberger adds that electrification, more renewable generation and non-fossil flexibility solutions such as battery storage can help shield Europe from the risks of future fossil fuel price shocks, becoming the "route to long-term energy security".
How renewables are shielding Europe from rising gas prices
Several European nations have already demonstrated the benefits of revolutionising their energy systems by focusing on green technology prior to the war on Iran.
Since 2019, Spain has doubled its wind and solar capacity, adding more than 40GW to its energy mix. To put that into perspective, a power plant with a capacity of 1 GW could power approximately 876,000 households for one year, if they consume the average of 10,000 kWh of electricity per year.
“Spain’s wind and solar growth has reduced the influence of expensive fossil generators on the electricity price by 75 per cent since 2019,” energy think tank Ember said in a report published last year.
“This decline in the hours where the electricity price was tied to gas power cost was faster than in other gas-reliant countries, such as Italy and Germany.”
In European power markets, the most expensive generator operating to meet demand, which is typically fossil fuels, sets the hourly wholesale electricity price. However, as generation from lower-cost technologies like wind and solar grows, it displaces gas and coal, meaning fossil fuels determine the price less often.
Record wind has also helped the UK break a new renewable record, despite "fantasy" claims that the country needs to drill the North Sea for oil.
On 26 March, British wind energy generation hit a new high of 23,880 megawatts, enough power to cover 23 million homes.
“Wind provided more than half of Britain’s electricity during this record period, and it’s highly significant that earlier in the day low-cost wind and solar squeezed expensive gas off our energy system – with gas falling to its lowest level of generation for nearly two years, providing just 2.3 per cent of our electricity,” says RenewableUK’s Tara Singh.
“That’s what the energy transition looks like in practice, and it shows why we need to continue to build out an ambitious pipeline of new clean energy projects now and in the years ahead.”
Are renewables slipping in the EU?
Despite the boom in solar, the EU is struggling to reduce its reliance on gas.
Recent data from Eurostat found that more than half (54.1 per cent) of electricity generated in the EU came from renewable energy sources during the second quarter (Q2) of 2026. This marks a slight decrease compared to the same period last year (54.3 per cent).
Total EU electricity generation increased by 3.2 per cent year-on-year in Q2, but during that same period gas-fired generation increased by 3.9 per cent while renewable generation only grew by 2.8 per cent.
This is despite solar witnessing significant growth, making up 41.6 per cent of renewable electricity generation – compared to 37 per cent last year.
Jonathan Bruegel, a power sector analyst at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), tells Euronews Earth that the dip highlights the “case for a diversified mix” of hydro, wind and solar power.
“Gas held at 13.3 per cent, even with renewables above 50 per cent,” he adds. “This means that weak hydro and wind generation still bring gas back in, underlining again the need for more solar – which is a more stable intermittent technology than hydro and wind – storage, and flexibility.”

2026-10-02
06:00:13 UTC
15:00:13 KST

Britain’s nursing union has cut its ties with an Israeli drug company over the firm’s links to the country’s military and track record of corporate misconduct.
The Royal College of Nursing (RCN) has axed Teva UK as a commercial partner and as sponsor of a forthcoming event on migraine and headaches at the union’s London headquarters.
Pro-Palestine groups who were pushing the RCN to drop Teva UK claimed the decision was “a major breakthrough for grassroots healthcare organising and the international boycott, divestment and sanctions movement” aimed at isolating Israel worldwide.
The RCN represents more than 500,000 nurses in the UK. Teva UK is the British arm of the global drug giant Teva Pharmaceuticals, which is one of the NHS’s biggest suppliers of medicines.
It acted after coming under pressure from campaign groups Nurses for Palestine and UK Healthcare Petitions to Royal Colleges (UKHPRC) to end its relationship with Teva UK.
Carmel O’Boyle, the chair of the RCN’s ruling council, confirmed the decision in a letter to Nurses for Palestine.
“Going forward [the] RCN is ending its commercial partnership with Teva UK. Teva UK will no longer be a sponsor of the RCNi nursing leadership summit: migraine and headache services event on 30 October 2026. The event will go ahead as planned,” she said.
“We are taking this action because further due diligence showed that there are a number of Teva Pharmaceuticals’ operations, which have been the subject of legal sanction and public scrutiny, which are not in line with RCNi [the union’s publishing and education arm] and RCN values.
“We know how important it is that the RCN only enters commercial relationships with companies that represent the values of the nursing profession.”
Teva said it was “disappointed” at the RCN’s decision and that healthcare had been “politicised”.
Nurses for Palestine welcomed the move. “Teva has no place sponsoring professional bodies dedicated to healing, care and preserving human life,” a spokesperson said.
UKHPRC said: “It is unthinkable that in this day and age healthcare organisations continue to enter into commercial relationships with companies linked to sustaining state systems accused or found by international bodies to involve grave violations of international law, including crimes against humanity, apartheid and genocide.”
Pro-Palestine campaigners are now calling on the Royal College of Pharmacy to drop Teva UK as a sponsor of its annual conference next month and cancel the exhibition stand the firm has booked.
Teva has been ordered to pay about £1bn in fines and other payments by the European Commission and US authorities over the last decade for bribery, price-fixing and abuse of its market position.
In 2024 the European Commission fined Teva €462.6m for blocking rival firms from competing with Copaxone, its treatment for multiple sclerosis, in seven European countries for between four and nine years.
In 2023 it agreed with the US Department of Justice to pay $225m in fines as an alternative to prosecution after it was charged with fixing the price of three drugs.
And in 2016 it struck a deal with the US Securities and Exchange Commission and the US Department of Justice to pay $519m to settle civil and criminal charges involving its bribery of government officials in Russia, Ukraine and Mexico.
A Teva spokesperson said: “As one of the largest suppliers of medicines to the UK we have valued our longstanding partership with the RCN and the opportunity it has provided to support healthcare professionals and the patients they care for.
“We are disappointed by the RCN’s decision to end this relationship and are seeking further dialogue with the organisation. Healthcare is at its best when it remains focused on patients rather than being politicised.”

‘Self-healing’ coach who was banned from working in Australia to speak in UK

A controversial proponent of natural remedies who has been banned from providing any health services in Australia is due to embark on a series of events in the UK and Ireland despite criticism from scientists, health charities and academic bodies.
Barbara O’Neill, who describes herself as a naturopath and nutritionist, lectures internationally on “natural self-healing”.
She has previously claimed that cancer is a fungus that can be treated with bicarbonate soda, that vaccines have caused an epidemic of conditions including autism and cot death, and that pregnant women with Strep B do not have to take antibiotics.
Now experts in the UK have raised concerns in a letter to venues across UK and Ireland where O’Neill, 73, is scheduled to speak.
The letter – which was organised by Dr David Robert Grimes, a science communicator and expert in Biostatistics at Trinity College Dublin – describes O’Neill as “a leading vector of medical misinformation”, adding that she repeatedly made “misguided medical assertions”, gave “unqualified advice” and promoted “abject demonisation of conventional medical treatment.”
The letter notes that O’Neill charges thousands of dollars for retreats and telephone consultations, and raises concerns about the events due to be held at the venues.
“At the event, she will spread dangerous health fictions to a susceptible audience, leeching off an illusion of legitimacy afforded to her by the surrounds of your respectable establishment,” it said.
Among those who have signed the letter are Orla Dolan, the chief executive of Breakthrough Cancer Research; Prof Colin Doherty, head of Trinity College Dublin School of Medicine; Prof David Colquhoun, a fellow of the Royal Society and University College London; and Sander van der Linden, professor of Psychology at the University of Cambridge.
Grimes, who has authored a book on medical misinformation, told the Guardian that O’Neill presented as a kindly grandmother dispensing natural wisdom.
“Medical misinformation kills, and we wrote the letter because we have seen first-hand the profound and tragic harms that health fictions inflict on vulnerable patients … We hope making people aware of this reality mitigates her ability to inflict harm elsewhere,” he said.
According to recent findings by the UK’s Academy of Medical Sciences, 67% of UK adults see health misinformation as a significant or very serious problem, with 89% viewing it as putting lives at risk.
O’Neill is no stranger to controversy. In 2019, the New South Wales Health Care Complaints Commission (HCCC) in Australia concluded an investigation into her professional conduct. Among its findings, the investigation found O’Neill “does not recognise that she is misleading vulnerable people (including mothers and cancer sufferers) by providing very selective information. The misinformation has real potential to have a detrimental effect on the health of individuals because Mrs O’Neill also discourages mainstream treatment for cancer, antibiotics and vaccinations.”
She was permanently barred from providing any health services either voluntarily or in a paid capacity. The HCCC has confirmed its prohibition orders are enforceable across all of Australia.
However, the ruling has not prevented O’Neill and her husband, Michael, from running events in other countries, including the UK, where she has given seminars at the luxury golf resort Trump Turnberry among other venues.
The latest string of engagements includes a five-day retreat at the Cranage Estate in Cheshire in early October.
Titled A Taste of Misty Mountain, the event includes lectures by O’Neill with titles such as What Really Does Cause Disease, The Science of Breath and The Immune System, as well as talks by Michael, including one titled Barbara Under Attack. A ticket for the event, which includes a dinner dance, costs £700.
Another multi-day event featuring Barbara O’Neill, run by the Christian health and wellness group Balm of Gilead, is scheduled for mid-October at the City North hotel and conference centre in Gormanston, Ireland.
O’Neill and her husband are also scheduled to appear at the Founders and Future festival at Glasgow University Union, with the event website noting the pair will be “headlining the main stage”.
In a reply to the letter’s authors, the De Vere Cranage Estate said it wa a hotel and conference venue that hosted a wide range of events on behalf of private clients, organisations and businesses, adding it “would not normally become involved in the content or opinions expressed at privately organised events”.
Cameron MacKenzie, president of Glasgow University Union, told the Guardian the events held in the building by external organisers were in no way affiliated or endorsed by the GUU board of management.
“The organisers of the Founders and Future festival have entered into a booking contract with us, and are free to use the spaces we provide so long as their activities align with our booking terms and conditions, our internal policies and the laws of Scotland and the UK,” he said. “To our knowledge, nothing currently outlined by the organisers seems to violate these terms.”
Michael O’Neill told the Guardian the ban from the HCCC had “serious legal flaws” that were under investigation, and that “there are political moves to place the HCCC organization under investigation for their clear bias against natural wellness practitioners.”
He also stated: “Barbara never received a single complaint of harm from a patient, as the complaints were purely ideology, based on supposition, not facts. The HCCC is largely funded by pharmaceutical money and is a seriously conflicted organisation.”
Prof David Elliman, a consultant at Great Ormond Street hospital and clinical adviser to the UK National Screening Committee and Newborn Blood Spot Screening Programme, said the science did not support Barbara O’Neill’s suggestions.
“If people follow her advice at the expense of evidence-based advice, this will be dangerous and result in the death of some people,” he said. He added that, in principle, he would support a mandatory requirement for people offering health advice for money to state their qualifications to do so.
Prof Liam Smeeth, director of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, said he did not back banning speakers, noting it could be counter-productive and that he was supportive of free speech within the bounds of not inciting direct violence and hatred.
But he said O’Neill’s claims were unscientific and the potential for harm was great. “She’s trying to make a profit out of people’s understandable fears and confusion when it comes to serious health issues,” he said. “And that’s a terrible thing to be making money from.”
A spokesperson for the HCCC said: “The commission permanently prohibited Mrs Barbara O’Neill from providing any health services in 2019, after finding she made dangerous claims not supported by evidence and posed a risk to public safety.
“While the order does not apply overseas, the commission urges people attending events with Mrs O’Neill to be wary of health misinformation and to check any advice she gives with a registered health practitioner.”

Almost half of Fayed abuse accusers are potential trafficking victims, MPs told
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
06:00:13 UTC
15:00:13 KST

Almost half of the women who reported allegations of sexual abuse by Mohamed Al Fayed to the Metropolitan police are potential victims of human trafficking, MPs have been told.
In a briefing for the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) for the survivors of Fayed and Harrods in July, senior Met officers said a review earlier this year found 70 survivors’ accounts bore the hallmarks of trafficking.
The Home Office has confirmed that at least five survivors were victims of international and domestic trafficking.
The Met’s figures suggested the number of confirmed cases could climb much higher, said the Liberal Democrat MP Wendy Chamberlain, a co-chair of the APPG.
“I can’t believe that wouldn’t increase,” said Chamberlain, who also compared the scale of Fayed’s abuse to Jimmy Savile’s.
The Labour MP Dave Robertson, the APPG’s other co-chair, said: “The number of women who were trafficked by Mohammed Fayed and his trafficking ring is certainly much higher.”
Some women were trafficked from Harrods to Fayed’s private offices and residence in Park Lane while others were taken out of the UK and abused overseas, senior police officers running the Met’s investigation, Operation Cornpoppy, told the APPG.
But several survivors told the Guardian that the Home Office had not recognised them as victims of trafficking because they now live abroad.
Amy, who lives in Italy, said she was trafficked from Harrods, where she initially worked on the shop floor, and her home to Fayed’s other properties. She said she was transferred to a PA role in his private residence and office at 60 Park Lane in London, where he allegedly sexually abused her, including groping her breasts and forced kissing.
She said Fayed also took her in his private car and helicopter to his estate in Oxted, Surrey, where she was sexually assaulted in a lagoon-style swimming pool located behind a concealed door.
“I would be removed from my home in Hammersmith and then be changed into clothes like Lacoste polo shirts and Bermuda shorts and boat shoes, which I absolutely hated,” said Amy. “That was robbing me of my actual identity. Whoever saw me leave my bedsit would say that’s not her. That’s a strong component of what trafficking is and was very calculating.”
In a letter sent in June to the then minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Natalie Fleet, Amy raised concerns about the apparent exclusion of survivors living outside the UK from the Home Office assessment of potential trafficking victims, the National Referral Mechanism (NRM).
She received a response from the Home Office in August, which said there was not a requirement that a potential victim be resident in the UK before being referred to the NRM by the police, or another first responder organisation.
But last month Amy was informed by her contact officer at the Met that the Home Office had confirmed it would reject any referrals made for international residents.
KP Law (KPL), which represents Amy and 277 other alleged survivors of Fayed’s abuse, said nearly a quarter of those women now lived overseas.
Lucy Traynor, a senior associate at KPL, criticised the apparently inconsistent advice as to who was eligible to be recognised as a victim of trafficking.
The lawyer said: “We are still seeing individuals whose experiences meet the threshold for trafficking struggling to secure recognition through these systems which are designed to identify and protect victims. Amy’s case is a stark example. Despite the nature of what she experienced, she continues to face barriers to recognition outside the UK. That disconnect between what the Home Office has committed to and what survivors experience in practice is simply not acceptable.”
First responders including police forces and some charities can refer someone to the NRM if they suspect they are a victim of human trafficking.
The Home Oﬃce then makes an initial “reasonable grounds” decision if it believes a crime may have occurred before investigating further and making a final “conclusive grounds” decision. So far it has confirmed that five women allegedly abused by Fayed were trafficking victims.
Eleanor Lyons, the independent anti-slavery commissioner, said the Home Office’s statutory guidance explicitly stated that people needed to be in the UK to be referred to the NRM.
Lyons said this was because the process involved getting access to support including a safe house and counselling, which officials believed would be difficult to provide to people who do not live in the UK.
But she called on the Home Office to reconsider the requirement because many affected people she spoke to just wanted to be recognised as trafficking victims, adding that the situation was causing deep distress for alleged survivors of Fayed’s abuse.
“The government should be doing everything it can to make it easier to identify these women and recognise them as potential victims of modern slavery,” Lyons said. “They’re doing directly the opposite right now, which is causing further harm to the survivors.”
Survivors’ groups say more than 500 women have come forward about abuse that allegedly took place at Harrods, Park Lane, Fulham football club, the Ritz hotel in Paris, and other places owned by Fayed. The Met is investigating 165 victims who have contacted the force directly.
A Met police spokesperson said: “We were previously making referrals to the Home Office for victims living in the UK and abroad, but those relating to victims living abroad were being rejected. As a result, we have paused any further such referrals. Should the Home Office position change, we will restart those submissions. Our support to victims continues, regardless of where they live.”
A Home Office spokesperson paid tribute to “the incredible bravery” of survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse. They added: “We are ensuring modern slavery survivors get the support they need to recover and move on with their lives.”
A Harrods spokesperson said it “supports all survivors in their pursuit of justice and continues to work closely with the Met police on its investigation”.

Winning tip: History, buns and Italianate porticoes in Münster
In an often overlooked corner of Germany, near the Dutch border, Münster is an absolute gem. Covered porticos will convince you you’re in northern Italy, gothic churches will remind you you’re in Mitteleuropa and the buns from Zeit für Brot will insist you’re in heaven. Nature-lovers can take in the Botanical Gardens and relax by the Münstersche Aa river. Those of a historical bent can peek into the room where the Treaty of Westphalia was signed in 1648 and mull the report card of nation states in the nearly 400 years since. But really, it’s a great place just to drop-anchor and lose a few days.
Jeremy
Germany’s highest railway bridge, near Düsseldorf
In the verdant countryside near Düsseldorf, the 129-year-old Müngsten Bridge, the country’s highest railway bridge, rises 107 metres above the River Wupper. The impressive iron and steel structure is billed as Germany’s answer to the Eiffel Tower (yes, really!) and if you’ve got a head for heights, you can don a harness and make the exhilarating climb to the highest point. You’ll be rewarded with incredible views across the valley, especially if you steel yourself (!) for the nerve-racking walk across the narrow beam that spans the top of the bridge. Eat your heart out, Sydney Harbour Bridge.
Bex
A wild North Sea island made for cycling
Sylt is more than a North Sea island to us. My German grandmother met my British army grandfather, and Sylt became my mother’s childhood island. It feels made for cycling, with peaceful paths winding between grassy dunes, sweeping beaches and little villages. Spend the day riding, watching the surfers and eating warm Nutella crepes by the sea, before settling into a traditional hooded Strandkorb (hooded beach chair) to listen to the waves. Bike hire costs €8-€10 per day. It is wild, windswept and magical, somewhere our family history becomes real every time we return.
Fay
Tour the country for a month for €63
Get the Deutschlandticket! An entire month of public transport for €63 – buses, trains, trams, ferries ... The only thing that isn’t included is faster long-distance trains, but you can figure out how to get from A to B using the Deutsche Bahn website, which has a special “Deutschlandticket only” filter; the need to change trains means you’ll end up discovering places you wouldn’t otherwise visit. It’s worth it just for a week, or, if you do want to travel long distances quickly, just for inner-city transport. Use the German public transport app Mopla to buy one at any time. 
Joseph
Cologne’s world-class cocktails bars
Cologne’s famous cathedral dominates the skyline and tops most travel itineraries. But having visited for a day on a previous trip, we returned for a city break with one thing in mind: cocktails. The mixology scene here is world-class. The jewel in the crown is Seiberts (pictured), which often and rightly features in lists of the world’s best bars, but Little Link, Woods and Ona Mor all contend and offer different vibes. While not sat at the bar, you’ll find excellent 20th-century art, street art and a lifesized Milka cow at the chocolate museum.
John
Kite flying in a vast former airfield in Berlin
On a warm autumn afternoon in Berlin, a friend and I rented classic Dutch bikes to explore the city. As the golden hour approached we discovered Tempelhofer Feld. Used as an airfield during a darker era, today it’s a vast recreational green space. Biking on the disused runway was enjoyably bizarre. Berliners and visitors alike were picnicking, kite flying, inline skating, lolling about on bales of hay, skateboarding, tightrope walking, birding … you name it. It is also an important site for rare flora and fauna and grazing animals.
Sarah
An ebike adventure through the Black Forest
Ebikes are the perfect way to explore the beauty and vastness of the Black Forest. Powering up gravel tracks that would be impossible on a push bike was so fun and a real hit with the teenager. Setting off from the astonishingly well preserved town of Gengenbach, we headed to the viewpoint at Moosturm observation tower and the Lothar Monument (pictured), where we were rewarded with a glorious 360-degree view of hills patterned with colour and wisps of cloud. On the way down it seemed churlish not to stop at the Naturfreundehaus Kornebene mountain hut and restaurant for possibly the best sausages of my life. A thoroughly deserved reward: ebiking counts as exercise, right? 
Alex
500 years of architecture in Görlitz
Görlitz, near the Polish border, merited more than just the day trip I had planned from Dresden so I returned later in my holiday to explore its delights. It’s chock-a-block with charming, colourful buildings, making it beloved of German and international film-makers. Strolling through the cobbled streets of the old town is like leafing through a lavish picture book of 500 years of German architecture, from gothic through the renaissance to art nouveau – don’t miss St Peter’s Church. Eat hearty Silesian sausages at beer houses and if you feel like a swim head out by bus to Lake Berzdorf, with views of the mountains from the sandy beach – or even the middle of the lake where I ventured to.
April
Take the family car around a racing circuit in Nürburg
When my son turned 16 we drove to Munich so he could buy his first beer legally. Breaking up the journey we stopped overnight near the Nürburgring racetrack, to take the family estate car around the Nordschleife circuit. You turn up, pay €30-€35, and get in the queue. We were overtaken by everything apart from a coach full of Italian tourists and an ice cream van. 
Tim
A spectacle of water in Kassel
The unexpected highlight of our German road trip was Kassel’s extraordinary Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe, a Unesco world heritage site. On water feature days, park below Wilhelmshöhe Palace (€8.50 per car, including bus travel for up to seven), ride to the Hercules monument, then follow the water downhill on foot. The free spectacle sends 750,000 litres tumbling without pumps through baroque cascades, waterfalls and a Roman-style ruined aqueduct, culminating in a soaring 52 metre fountain. Following the rushing water from one dramatic stage to the next was an adventure, and after the 2.3km descent, your car is waiting at the bottom.

Government extends emergency reservist call-ups through November, lowers cap to 200,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:58:17 UTC
14:58:17 KST

The government approved an extension on Wednesday of the emergency framework allowing the IDF to call up reservists under Order 8 through November 30, while reducing the maximum number of call-ups from 240,000 to 200,000, according to a proposal submitted by the Defense Ministry.
Ministers approved two security-related decisions in a telephone vote. The first extends the authority to call reservists into service under Order 8. The second extends by two months the declaration allowing special arrangements for the detention of unlawful combatants.
A legal opinion prepared by the defense establishment devoted considerable attention to the continuing toll on the reserve system. The decision, it said, raises "extremely significant difficulties regarding equality," since the burden on those who actually serve continues to increase while the state has not fulfilled its obligation to ensure equitable conscription across all sectors of the population.
The opinion also noted that the government has not expanded the range of sanctions or sufficiently enforced conscription requirements against draft evaders. The result, according to the opinion, is a situation in which "with one hand the government increases the burden on reservists, and with the other it does not act to enforce the conscription obligation on draft evaders."
Haredi conscription remains central to reserve burden
The issue of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription also features prominently in the explanation for the continuing need for reservists. According to the IDF's position, expanding the reserve system cannot replace fully utilizing the manpower available through mandatory service, which has a "dramatic impact" on force building.
Call-up orders have been sent to draft-eligible members of the haredi public, and the IDF has stepped up enforcement against draft evaders, but the disparity in the distribution of the burden remains. Despite this, defense officials maintain that the security situation and the IDF's needs do not currently allow the military to end Order 8 reserve call-ups.
In its explanatory notes, the Defense Ministry justified extending the order on the basis of continuing threats, IDF activity in multiple sectors, and operational requirements.
The size of the call-up framework has changed several times over the course of the year. On March 24, amid Operation Roaring Lion and operations against Hezbollah and in other sectors, a framework of up to 400,000 reservists was approved through May 31.
On July 26, a framework of up to 240,000 was approved through September 30. The proposal now approved by ministers will allow up to 200,000 reservist call-ups through November 30, a reduction of 40,000 from the framework expiring on September 30.
The 200,000-call-up framework does not mean that 200,000 reservists may be serving simultaneously. Rather, it is the maximum number of reservist call-ups that may be issued under the order throughout the period.
As a rule, a soldier who is released and subsequently called up again will be counted as an additional call-up, subject to exceptions stipulated in the order. Each call-up will take place only after the available standing forces have been fully utilized and will require individual approval from the head of the IDF Operations Division's Operations Brigade or the official responsible for recruitment and readiness within the brigade.
Nearly three years after October 7, the exceptional use of Order 8 remains necessary, according to the Defense Ministry, because the statutory limitations on reserve service do not allow the IDF to maintain the required force levels for extended periods.
Under the ordinary legal framework, the maximum number of reserve-duty days over a three-year period is 54 days for enlisted personnel, 70 days for commanders, and 84 days for officers. Operational duty may ordinarily be performed once every three years for a period of up to 25 days.
The proposal states that Israel's security needs require maintaining significant troop levels in various sectors for far longer periods, necessitating the continued use of Order 8 call-ups.
The proposal also details steps taken to increase the manpower available to the IDF and ease the burden. Tens of thousands of reservists have been returned from manpower pools to active units, reserve exemptions have been canceled for thousands of soldiers, and the reserve exemption age has been raised to 49 in certain essential professions and units.
In July, a temporary provision stipulated that mandatory service would remain 32 months and would not be shortened to 30 months over the next three years. The defense establishment had originally sought to extend men's mandatory service to 36 months, but the Knesset approved only part of the measure.
According to data attached to the proposal, the total cost of reserve-duty days carried out under Order 8 from January through August stood at NIS 26.7 billion, while the average cost of one day of reserve duty under Order 8 is estimated at approximately NIS 1,000.
The estimated cost of the proposed extension is based on the average volume of reserve-duty days between January and September. If that level continues through October and November, the estimated cost of the additional two months will be approximately NIS 6.6 billion.
Government also extends unlawful combatant detention framework
The second decision submitted for ministers' approval extends the declaration under the Incarceration of Unlawful Combatants Law. The current declaration expires on September 30, and the government sought to extend it through November 30.
The extension means that the special arrangements introduced during the war regarding the detention of unlawful combatants will remain in force. These include the amount of time allowed before issuing a permanent detention order, the possibility of preventing a detainee from meeting with a lawyer, and the timetable for judicial review.
The ceasefire was signed in October 2025 and intensive ground maneuvers in the Gaza Strip were halted, but according to the Defense Ministry, conditions on the ground still justify extending the declaration.
IDF troops remain in enemy territory, friction continues in various sectors, and dozens of people suspected of involvement in terrorism continue to be detained. Thousands of unlawful combatants remain in detention, including detainees for whom permanent detention orders have not yet been issued and others who have been prevented from meeting with a lawyer.
The legal opinion stated that repeatedly extending the declaration "is not a trivial matter." The number of new detainees has fallen, the ceasefire has already entered into effect, and terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip no longer hold hostages.
Defense officials argue, however, that the IDF remains active on several fronts and that some detainees undergo complex investigations during which it is sometimes necessary to prevent them from meeting with a lawyer.
If the declaration expires, existing decisions preventing detainees from meeting with lawyers would expire immediately. In some cases, authorities would be required to issue a permanent detention order and bring the detainee before a court for judicial review before the investigation had been completed and the necessary factual basis had been established.
Against this background, the legal opinion concluded that although another extension presents difficulties, there is no legal impediment to approving it.
The arrangements currently in force are already narrower than those applied during earlier stages of the war. Under the latest amendment to the temporary provision, which entered into effect on July 1, a permanent detention order for an unlawful combatant must be signed within 18 days of detention, or within 10 days in the case of a minor.
The periods before judicial review were shortened by seven days, and the maximum periods during which a detainee may be prevented from meeting with a lawyer were also reduced.
The Defense Ministry stressed that these are maximum periods and that, in practice, efforts are made to shorten them in accordance with the security situation and the number of new detainees.
Both decisions are being made during an election period, when the government is subject to a heightened duty of restraint. The legal opinions determined that the decisions are urgent, security-related, and limited in duration, and are required because the two existing arrangements expire on September 30.
The opinions therefore concluded that there is no legal impediment to approving them during the election period.

3 UAE-owned tankers hit after breaching Hormuz rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:56:19 UTC
14:56:19 KST

In a statement posted on its official account, the PGSA said on Thursday that several tankers have been hit in the strait in recent days, and that the last three of them were owned or chartered by the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
Checks showed that the tankers Al Ruwais, Sinbad and Mersin Prosperity had repeatedly attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz over the past two months.
The authority said the names of all three vessels appear in the latest update of the PGSA non-compliance list. The list covers ships whose status or manner of passage has been found incompatible with the requirements set for safe and authorized transit of the strategic waterway.
This comes as reports said that a supertanker had been hit in the Strait of Hormuz and was burning.
The PGSA has repeatedly warned shipowners and charterers that forcing vessels onto unauthorized routes creates the risk of financial and human losses for the ship, its owner, master and crew, and leads to serious restrictions on any future passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
Charterers found to be pressing ships into illegal transit are themselves liable to be added to the non-compliance list, with passage of all their related vessels restricted.
Vessels placed on the list face limits on future transits, including fines, detention or confiscation.
The authority has also cautioned insurers, P&I clubs and classification societies against servicing non-compliant ships, warning of consequences for continued dealings with them.

What to expect at Caravan Hatta
Experiences offered at Caravan Hatta by Our Habitas are inspired by its location, with activities including sound healing sessions, Arabic coffee rituals and guided practices.

Queensland police seize 558 e-mobility devices in three months

2026-10-02
05:47:58 UTC
14:47:58 KST

Police across Queensland have given out more than 2,400 traffic infringement notices to e-mobility device users in the last three months, seizing 558 non-compliant vehicles.
Of the fines issued, more than 60 per cent were for riders failing to wear a helmet, while 157 users were caught speeding.
What's next?
Queensland Police are urging the community to review new e-mobility laws on their website, including changes that came into effect at the end of August.
Queensland Police are seizing an average of six illegal e-mobility devices every day, as officers crack down on non-compliant e-bikes and e-scooters.
More than 27 infringement notices are also being issued each day.
In the first three months of the statewide Operation Yankee Surety, police seized 558 devices and handed out more than 2,400 traffic infringement notices to riders.
Emergency Response and Coordination Command Acting Assistant Commissioner, Tim Partrige, said the misuse of one of Australia's fastest-growing forms of transportation had "life-threatening consequences".
"Electric power assisted cycles, e-scooter and other e-mobility devices are vehicles, and like any other vehicle, dangerous behaviours like speeding, drink riding or using non-compliant devices can have life-threatening consequences — not only for the rider," Acting Assistant Commissioner Partrige said.
"Non-compliant devices and dangerous riding have no place in our communities, and police will continue to take enforcement action against those disregarding the law."
Since the operation began at the start of July, police conducted targeted enforcement to seize non-compliant devices, ensure age and licensing requirements are adhered to, and deter dangerous behaviour such as speeding, drink riding and riding without a helmet.
Of the 2,400 fines issued, about 1,500 — more than 60 per cent — were for riders failing to wear a helmet, while a further 157 users were caught speeding.
As police conducted 878 roadside breath tests on e-mobility riders over the three months, some 68 drink riders were prosecuted.
"As with any road safety operation, our goal under Operation Yankee Surety is to protect all road and pathway users, including those on e-mobility devices," Acting Assistant Commissioner Partrige said.
Since licensing restrictions for e-bikes and e-scooter came into effect at the end of August, 64 tickets have been issued for non-compliance.
Brisbane, the Sunshine Coast and Capricornia have emerged as the hot spots for illegal e-mobility activity, according to Queensland Police data for the first three months of the campaign.
The Sunshine Coast led the state in terms of non-compliant bikes seized by police, with 146 compared to 88 on the Gold Coast. Brisbane's northside saw the most traffic infringement notices issued.
North Brisbane saw 511 notices given out, while South Brisbane users received 433. Capricornia reported 254 notices issued over the same period, almost twice of neighbouring Mackay Whitsunday (133).
The Queensland capital city recorded the highest number of positive RBTs for e-mobility users with a combined 38.

Where in Europe is data centre hiring growing fastest – and why do these jobs pay more?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:46:03 UTC
14:46:03 KST

Several European countries have seen a significant rise in data centre job postings in recent months. Euronews Business takes a closer look at the reasons behind the growth, including why these roles offer higher pay.
AI is rapidly becoming part of daily life, and demand for data centres is rising too. As of 2025, the US remained the clear global leader in data centres, with more than twice the EU total. At the same time, the European Commission aims to strengthen Europe’s sovereignty and competitiveness in the AI and cloud ecosystem.
Data from global hiring platform Indeed show that data centre job postings are rising in Europe. As of August 2026, they were above pre-pandemic levels across 10 European economies, while postings for other tech roles and overall job postings were lagging behind data centre postings.
So, which countries saw the biggest rise in data centre job postings? How much more do these jobs pay than the same occupations in other sectors? And why is there a pay premium?
The recent rise is most striking in Spain, Italy and Ireland. When data centre job postings on Indeed are indexed at 100 for the average between December 2019 and February 2020, the index exceeded 200 points in all three countries as of August 2026.
This means postings more than doubled compared with pre-pandemic levels. The index stood at 260 in Spain, 237 in Italy and 210 in Ireland.
Aubrey Woessner, an economist at Indeed, and Pawel Adrjan, director of research at Indeed, said that Spain and Italy had more room to grow as both started from a low base.
“They are seeing major new AI-focused build-outs, such as campuses in Aragón and projects around Milan, rather than legacy sites clustered around major population hubs such as Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, and Dublin,” they told Euronews Business.
The rise is also more than 30% in the Netherlands (138), Poland (134) and Switzerland (133).
Belgium recorded the lowest increase at 9%, followed by France at 13%. The rise is 25% in Germany and 24% in the UK.
As of August 2026, tech job postings excluding data centre roles were below pre-pandemic levels in nine of the 10 countries. Spain was the only exception, with the index just one point above its pre-pandemic level.
Data centre job postings significantly outpaced other tech job postings, with the widest gaps in Italy (173 points), Spain (159 points) and Ireland (141 points).
The chart below shows this trend as of August 2026.
Europe’s data centre hiring is spread across more companies
Compared with the US, where just 10 big tech companies account for 71% of data centre postings, data centre hiring in Europe is spread across many companies, according to Indeed.
“Across the ten European countries we analysed, it takes over 500 firms to account for 70% of data centre postings,” Woessner and Adrjan said.
Data centre jobs offer higher pay for the same roles
Advertised salaries for data centre roles are generally higher than for similar jobs in other sectors in the same country.
The pay premium is clear: in 28 of the 29 country-occupation pairs, data centre jobs offer higher salaries. The only exception is very small, at -1% for IT infrastructure, operations and support roles in France.
Data centre employers in Italy offer significantly higher pay than other sectors. For example, management roles in data centres pay 65% more, while installation and maintenance roles offer 50% higher advertised pay.
In the UK, management roles in data centres offer 49% higher pay. In Germany, installation and maintenance roles pay 36% more.
Why do data centre employers pay more for the same job?
Woessner and Adrjan noted that data centres may be a small slice of the overall labour market, but they are competing for the same technicians and infrastructure specialists as other industries going through the digital and green transitions in Europe.
“Postings related to data centre roles ask for more skills, on average, than other postings in the same field,” Woessner and Adrjan said.
“Concrete technical and digital skills – including knowledge of IT systems, software, and cybersecurity – as well as English language requirements are also over-represented in data centre-related roles compared with other roles in the same occupation.”
They noted that higher pay also helps attract workers quickly to keep projects on schedule.
Which jobs dominate data centre hiring?
Woessner and Adrjan explained that the mix of occupations in data centre hiring across Europe points to two trends happening at the same time: continued staffing of existing data storage and cloud facilities, and an emerging boom in new AI-related construction.
Five occupations account for between 50% and 60% of data centre job postings in Europe: IT infrastructure, operations and support; software development; management; installation and maintenance; and project management.
While demand for workers in data centre-related jobs is rising, these roles still make up only a small share of total job postings in each country. In most of the countries analysed, the share is around 1% or less.
Ireland is the exception, where nearly 5% of all job postings on Indeed now mention a data centre.
Is there a skills shortage in data centres?
Indeed economists expect the growth phase to continue for some time, as the EU aims to triple its data centre capacity within five to seven years.
“One concern for employers is that data centres are competing for workers with technical skills that were already in short supply even before the data centre boom,” Woessner and Adrjan said.
As of 2025, Germany (529) and the UK (523) had the highest numbers of data centres in Europe, followed by France (322) and the Netherlands (298). Italy had 168, Spain and Poland each had 144, and Switzerland had 121.
Western Europe dominates the region’s data centre infrastructure, while Northern Europe has a smaller but strategically important presence. Central and Eastern Europe’s infrastructure is more fragmented and less developed.

Lula and Bolsonaro’s mudslinging heats up ahead of weekend vote
The mudslinging between Brazil’s incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his election rival, Flavio Bolsonaro, has heated up ahead of what is expected to be an extremely close vote this weekend. From stating loose rumours as facts, to taking comments completely out of their context, they are both doing everything they can to win a few more votes.
Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his election rival Flavio Bolsonaro are leaving no controversy unturned in their last-ditch efforts to discredit each other and win over voters ahead of Sunday's nail-biter election.
A campaign dominated by scandals and insults has done little to ease the deep political polarisation in Latin America's biggest economy – one of the last major leftist bastions in the region.
The tight race pits Lula, 80, against the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of US President Donald Trump who has backed a wave of victorious right-wing candidates in Latin America.
Trump said Thursday he was watching Brazil's election "very closely".
Opinion polls predict the vote will go to a run-off on October 25, with Lula and Flavio in a dead heat.
Read moreFlavio Bolsonaro probed for corruption as Brazil election tightens
"The race is tied but not at a standstill: the final week will determine where the voters who can still be swayed will go," Felipe Nunes, director of the Quaest polling institute, told AFP.
Many of the nation's 160 million registered voters are disenchanted with their options and were deprived of a debate between the leading candidates when both declined to attend a televised programme on Thursday evening.
Marcelo Vilanova, 32, a fish market manager in the southeastern city of Juiz de Fora, said he was voting for Lula as the "lesser of two evils".
"He did good things for me, for my family," he said, referring to Lula's social welfare programmes. "I have criticisms of him too."
Lucas Sales, 38, a cell phone shop owner in the city, is voting for Flavio Bolsonaro even if "he himself isn't the best option," citing his promise to be tough on crime – a key concern for many Brazilians in this election.
A saintly spat and gynecological gaffe
The race for undecided voters has had both sides on alert for anything they can twist to their advantage.
In recent days, Brazil's beloved patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida, depicted as a Black Madonna, became the focus as rumours erupted that Flavio Bolsonaro planned to strip her of her post if elected.
Flavio issued fierce denials as Lula took to the campaign trail clutching a statue of the saint, declaring that "messing" with her was "unacceptable".
The electoral court ordered Thursday that posts with the "untrue" claims be taken down.
Lula tends to have more support among Catholics while Bolsonaro has the backing of a booming Evangelical population.
Next, Flavio Bolsonaro and his supporters pounced when Lula said that men were "cowards" when it comes to getting their prostates examined, while "women learn to receive a touch from a young age," referring to gynecological exams.
Clips of his comment circulated widely on social media as if it were an allusion to abuse, and Flavio Bolsonaro accused Lula of being "sexist".
"It's really turned into a circus...my vote won't go to any of them," said Gisele Sousa, 45, a clothing shop employee.
In another jab during a podcast Thursday, Lula said he was sure he would win in the first round, over a rival he said was not even qualified "to serve as a building manager".
Lula's political clout
Veteran leftist Lula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, boasting he is fitter than ever despite his advanced age.
The former union leader has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment while massively curbing deforestation in the Amazon rainforest.
Nevertheless, voters complain about a high cost of living and are fed up with violence and crime.
Lula unveiled a flurry of measures in the run-up to the election to win over voters, increasing social welfare payments and banning sports betting that has ensnared many in gambling addiction.
"Only Lula has the political clout and credibility to carry out reforms," Edinho Silva, president of Lula's Workers' Party, said.

African Union urges Ethiopia, Eritrea, Egypt to exercise restraint as regional escalation continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:40:12 UTC
14:40:12 KST

The African Union Commission has called on Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Egypt to exercise maximum restraint and refrain from actions or statements that could worsen tensions and undermine regional peace and stability.
This comes as militiamen allied with Ethiopia's federal government said they were bearing down on the capital of the northern rebel stronghold of Tigray on Friday, as fears grew that fighting could spill into a wider war after Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties.
"The Commission urges the three countries to address their differences through established diplomatic channels and peaceful dialogue," it said in a statement late on Thursday.
On Thursday, Ethiopia ordered the closure of its embassy in Eritrea and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats persona non grata, prompting Asmara to sever all diplomatic ties with its neighbor.
The pro-government Tigray Peace Forces militia said on Facebook it had captured the town of Milazat, about 20 km (12 miles) southeast of Mekelle, the main city in Tigray region.
Video posted on social media and purportedly from Milazat showed TPF fighters in a blue truck chanting: "Mekelle! Mekelle!" Reuters could not immediately verify the video.
The Ethiopian military and allied fighters have made quick advances into Tigray since combat erupted last week with a rebel alliance led by the region's ruling party, the Tigray People's Liberation Front, in the worst escalation of violence since a 2020-2022 civil war.
Spokespeople for Ethiopia's military, its government, and the TPLF did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the reported advance.
It also declared an Egyptian diplomat persona non grata and ordered him to leave the country within 48 hours, and Cairo responded in kind by declaring an Ethiopian embassy counselor in Egypt persona non grata and giving him 48 hours to leave.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea, Egypt, Sudan of supporting opposition alliance
Addis Ababa has accused Eritrea, Sudan, and Egypt of supporting an opposition alliance led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) that has battled troops loyal to Ethiopia's federal government since last week. The three countries deny the accusation.
The clashes mark the biggest escalation of fighting in Ethiopia since the end of a 2020-2022 civil war in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed. Eritrea had fought in support of Ethiopia's federal government in that conflict.
Ethiopia closes embassy in Eritrea
Analysts fear the current conflict could spread beyond Ethiopia's borders in an increasingly fragile region where other powers are competing for influence. Tigray has Ethiopia's longtime foe Eritrea to its north, and Sudan — caught up in a more than three-year-old civil war — to its west.
Ethiopia's government has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting the opposition alliance — an allegation they have all denied.
On Thursday, Ethiopia said it was closing its embassy in Eritrea "in response to Eritrea's direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence" and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave Ethiopia within 48 hours.
Eritrea responded by severing all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia. The two countries fought a border war from 1998-2000 and only restored diplomatic relations in 2018.
Banks, shops shut in Mekelle
Inside Mekelle, banks and shops were closed on Friday in anticipation of possible fighting, two residents, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.
A diplomatic source said senior TPLF leaders had already left Mekelle and the conflict would likely keep going even if federal forces took the city.
In 2020, federal forces captured Mekelle within the first month of the war before the TPLF mounted a counter-offensive that reclaimed the city seven months later.
TPLF chairperson Debretsion Gebremichael acknowledged on Thursday that federal forces had occupied some parts of the region but said his forces would counter-attack "in due course."
"We should ensure that Tigray is their graveyard, not their playground," he said in a statement.
On Thursday, Ethiopia's foreign ministry also expelled an Egyptian diplomat, prompting Cairo to respond in kind by expelling an Ethiopian embassy counselor.
In a statement, the African Union Commission urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise "maximum restraint."
Explosions heard in Ethiopian capital
Ahead of the latest fighting, the TPLF formed an alliance with six other Ethiopian armed groups that say they aim to overthrow Abiy's government.
While the TPLF and allied fighters made some initial gains in Ethiopia's Amhara and Afar regions, that both border Tigray, pro-government forces say those have been largely reversed.
Explosions were heard late Wednesday night in Addis Ababa, in what a source linked to the opposition alliance said were drone attacks targeting the headquarters of the federal forces there and other sites.
Reuters could not independently verify this.
If confirmed, it would be the first known drone attack by anti-government forces on Addis Ababa, which is hundreds of kilometers from the northern front lines.
It would also suggest the TPLF and its allies might have better striking capability than previously thought.
Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopia's federal government against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 war, in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed and millions forced from their homes. Relations have since soured, in part because landlocked Ethiopia insists that sea access is vital to its security and economy.
Eritrea says it fears Ethiopia will try to take its Assab port by force. Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has said Ethiopia intends to secure sea access through peaceful means.

South Korea warns of 'further measures' if Ukraine refuses public apology over POW transfer disclosure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:34:26 UTC
14:34:26 KST

The POWs were captured by Ukrainian forces early last year after being deployed alongside thousands of North Korean troops to support Russia's war against Ukraine.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said on Friday that Seoul would take "further measures" if Ukraine refuses to publicly apologise over what he called its unilateral disclosure of North Korean prisoners of war being sent to South Korea.
Seoul has taken a hard stance on Ukraine disclosing the transfer of two soldiers captured fighting for Russia, warning that their families could be targeted by Pyongyang.
North Korea is known to retaliate against defectors and their families.
Both POWs are identifiable as they had been photographed by South Korean media before their arrival to the South.
The POWs were captured by Ukrainian forces early last year after being deployed alongside thousands of North Korean troops to support Russia's war against Ukraine, in exchange for economic and military assistance to Pyongyang.
Hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed last week the transfer in remarks at the United Nations, Lee expressed his dismay, with Seoul claiming confidentiality was key to protecting the POWs' relatives.
Seoul later demanded an official apology from Ukraine, saying that both sides had reached a "clear understanding" during consultations to keep the transfer confidential.
"If Ukraine continues to refuse to acknowledge the facts and publicly apologise, we will take further measures," the South Korean president said on Friday, accusing Kyiv of making him out to be a "liar."
"This is a matter concerning the dignity of the Republic of Korea and its people and cannot be overlooked," Lee posted on X.
Analysts say that from South Korea's perspective, keeping the transfer of the POWs confidential may have partly been for Ukraine's sake, as making it public could have complicated Kyiv's own prisoner exchanges with Russia.
In domestic South Korean politics, however, Seoul's approach "could prove problematic," Shin Yul, a political science professor at Myongji University, said given the current administration's dovish approach to the nuclear-armed North.
"The government has acted swiftly in this case involving Ukraine, while exercising extreme caution over the North Korean landmine incident (that injured South Korean soldiers). That contrast could leave the public deeply dissatisfied."
Diplomatic misunderstanding
Lee referred on Friday to an interview with Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha published by RBC-Ukraine and other Ukrainian outlets on Thursday.
Sybiha said he would "not like to call it an incident," describing it instead as a "diplomatic misunderstanding."
"South Korea is an important country for us. And I very much hope for momentum, continued cooperation, and concrete results that we are indeed achieving with them," he said.
Seoul's spy agency said that Zelenskyy may have disclosed the transfer of the North Korean soldiers to boost public support in South Korea for Seoul providing arms to Ukraine, a lawmaker said on Wednesday.
South Korea has in recent years emerged as a major arms exporter, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, including through a multibillion-dollar arms deal with Poland.
But it has refrained from supplying Kyiv with lethal weapons, citing its longstanding policy of not arming countries engaged in active conflicts.

Indonesia Needs to Do More to Tackle the Region’s Transboundary Haze Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:33:00 UTC
14:33:00 KST

Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto is the key leader in ASEAN who can and should do better in haze management in the coming years. The current haze situation affecting Southeast Asia is, to a certain extent, a reflection of his leadership and management, given that most of it stems from fires happening in his country.
Forests and peatlands in Indonesia have been burning substantially this year and millions of people in Southeast Asia are suffering as a result. In early September, Kuching had the worst air quality of any large city on earth. Malaysian authorities declared a state of emergency in the Serian district of Sarawak, as the Air Pollutant Index exceeded 500. The Philippines closed schools throughout Metro Manila and more than 12 provinces. The regional haze monitor in ASEAN reached level three, the most severe on the scale.
Indonesia needs to improve its leadership on the haze management issue.
Fire has been used to clear land as it is cheaper than alternative methods. Plantations, companies, and farmers burn the vegetation before the planting season, instead of paying for mechanical clearing. The drained peatlands of Sumatra and Kalimantan also get burnt and this adds fuel to the fire. These fires continue for weeks and release even more toxic particles than an ordinary forest fire. Due to the current El Niño climate cycle, there are drier and longer dry seasons, worsening the situation, as experienced in 1997, 2015, and 2019.
The solutions are relatively straightforward. They are to rewet the drained peatland, enforce a moratorium on new plantation permits in forest and peat areas, punish the recalcitrant companies, and publicize their names so they can be held responsible.
Importantly, there needs to be close tracking of fires and smallholder burning, as well as enhanced local fire-response capacity so as to minimize, control, and extinguish fires before they get out of control. Satellite technology can be used to facilitate the tracking too. These pre-emptive and preventive measures, in addition to effective firefighting capabilities, need to be in place to address this haze situation effectively.
There is precedent for effective action. In 2015, during his first term in office, President Joko Widodo encountered the disastrous 2015 fires, during which 2.6 million hectares were burned and more than a hundred million lives were affected. He created the Peatland Restoration Agency that rewetted more than a million hectares of degraded peat. He also set up a standing haze task force. Furthermore, in 2019, he put a permanent moratorium on new peatlands and primary forest permits.
The results were positive. The fires decreased subsequently. For instance, significant fires in 2023 burned about 1.6 million hectares, a decrease of a million acres compared to 2015. Towards the end of Jokowi’s term in 2024, the Ministry of Environment and Forestry reported a 59.4 percent year-on-year drop in hotspots.
This year, President Prabowo visited fire-hit provinces in Sumatra and Kalimantan. He deployed police and military staff on the ground, and in addition to police investigations, he pledged to revoke the permits of guilty companies. However, these efforts may be inadequate. The cumulative hotspots in late July 2026 exceeded the dreadful 2019 numbers. More needs to be done to anticipate and prevent the wildfire problem.
Other than naming the responsible corporations and holding them accountable, there should be the public prosecution of the indicted corporate leaders, open publication of the concession-ownership data and increased resources for peatland wetting, along with enhanced fire-fighting capabilities.
The ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution, signed in 2002, will only work when the Prabowo administration intentionally and effectively implements the full range of effective, preventive, punitive and responsive measures. Prabowo and his government can implement a combination of measures for the well-being of their citizens and the neighboring countries.
Along with the hundreds of millions in Southeast Asia affected by the haze, we share the hope that the Indonesian administration can be more effective and efficient in managing and reducing the causes of the haze problem, which has plagued Southeast Asia over the past month, so that we can all benefit from cleaner, haze-free air again.
