‘No one disrespects Our Lady’: fears for Brazil’s patron saint grip country ahead of election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
04:00:10 UTC
13:00:10 KST

A row of Biblical proportions has erupted in the run-up to Brazil’s presidential election, with the country’s patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida, emerging as an unlikely kingmaker in the deadlocked race.
Ahead of Sunday’s vote, the two frontrunners – the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his far-right challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro – are level in the polls.
But in recent days, speculation that Bolsonaro – son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro – might strip the widely cherished patroness of her position have caused a nationwide outcry, leaving some to question if it could tip the knife-edge election in favour of Lula, who is Catholic.
“It could sway things one way or the other,” said Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has been tracking the unusual election row.
It remains unclear precisely how the commotion began, but debate over the issue exploded last week when a remark by Bolsonaro, whose movement includes many evangelical Christians, went viral online. In a recent broadcast, the former senator said one of his first acts as president would be to “decree that Brazil belongs to the Lord Jesus Christ”.
Some Catholics took that as a sign that the Protestant politician planned to unseat Our Lady of Aparecida, although only the Vatican – which declared her Brazil’s patroness in 1930 – has the authority to do so.
Those suspicions were reinforced by Bolsonaro’s reported links to JB Carvalho, an evangelical leader who has previously called for the patroness’s removal. In 2007, another Bolsonaro ally tried to introduce legislation to the same effect, although the bill was dropped.
Bolsonaro has called claims he plans to unseat Our Lady of Aparecida “fake news”. He alleged the rumours were being spread by Lula supporters, as well as members of the Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation. The conference rejected the charge.
Lula’s leftwing movement has taken advantage of the furore, keenly aware it could hurt the far-right candidate’s chances in a country where nearly 57% of the population is Catholic. With the result expected to be even tighter than the last one – when Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by less than 2% – even a small number of votes could mean the difference between victory and defeat.
Lula has appeared on the campaign trail holding statuettes of the Virgin Mary while his wife, Janja da Silva, has worn a pendant honouring Our Lady of Aparecida. “As long as I’m president, no one will disrespect Our Lady of Aparecida. No one. People need to learn to respect all religions,” Lula told a rally in the Amazon. Lula’s vice-president and running mate, a devout Catholic called Geraldo Alckmin, published a video describing how he had received messages from Catholics “worried about the direction of the country and the terrible news that has been circulating”. Alckmin assured voters he and Lula would preserve and protect “religious traditions, so sacred to Brazilian families”.
The row speaks to the rivalry and tensions between Brazil’s once dominant Catholic church and the evangelical movement, which has grown rapidly since the 80s.
Traumann said: “It touched a raw nerve, which is the growing power of the evangelicals. Evangelicals make up about 30% of the population, but their political power is much greater than 30% – and within Bolsonarismo it is even more significant”.
Traumann believed that, irrespective of whether Bolsonaro really did intend to remove the patroness, the furore had tapped into “a genuine fear among Catholics of being pushed outside the system”. “I have no doubt that this is going to be important [in the election]. [Flávio Bolsonaro] knows it has landed badly,” he added.
Luiz Antônio Simas, a historian and author of the book So Many Marys: Our Lady in Popular Culture, said the outcry “was a symptom of the popularity that Aparecida and the Virgin Mary in general have in the formation of our culture”.
“For Brazilian popular culture, Our Lady of Aparecida transcends altars … She is extremely powerful as a defining element of what we envision Brazilian popular culture to be,” Simas said, noting how Brazil’s “Black Madonna” was present in samba parades, football culture and Afro-Brazilian faiths.
While the debate flared up on the eve of the election, Simas said Our Lady of Aparecida was a long-running point of tension between Catholics and evangelicals, who oppose the Catholic veneration of saints and images. He recalled a major outcry in 1995 when a neo-Pentecostal pastor kicked a statue of Our Lady of Aparecida on TV.
Simas believed religious racism was at the heart of the outcry, given that Our Lady of Aparecida was a black representation of the Virgin Mary. “When all of this comes into contact with a turbulent political context, in a country experiencing the tensions of a highly contested pre-election scenario, all these controversies come to the surface,” Simas added.

I went curtain shopping during a Kyiv air raid. And not because I’m ‘resilient’ | Diana Berg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
04:00:09 UTC
13:00:09 KST

I was standing in front of a locked basement door in a building in our neighbourhood, laughing, as Ukrainian air defence shot down drones directly above me. I had run into the first residential building I could reach, and I even took a photo of the locked door – a shelter, and the shelter locked – because I wanted to remember it. I was on my way to buy curtains.
I hadn’t checked whether there was an alert before I left home. I had simply set out for the shop, 20 minutes away through our residential district, on foot. But somewhere along the way, things started exploding in the sky above me – and I was suddenly walking through a city under attack because I had decided that my windows needed new curtains. What the fuck was I laughing at? I should have been terrified, and I was. It was just that I still wanted the curtains, and the absurdity was hilarious.
The curtain shop was closed because of the raid – this international chain, it turns out, shuts when the sirens go off, unlike many Ukrainian-owned stores. So I came back the next day and bought them. They are better than the old ones and cover the windows properly. Only after I had hung them did I realise that they also let me see less of the war from my sofa: the flashes of air defence, the smoke, whatever was happening outside. I had not made the war any safer. I had only made it slightly harder to see.
I had been away from Kyiv for a month and while I was gone, the rhythm of the war, which I have lived with for years, had changed: attacks now came by day, alerts could swallow half of it, and explosions, drones and smoke had become part of the daytime soundscape in a way that felt new even to me. My response, apparently, was to buy curtains.
In January 2022, back in Mariupol, when everyone around us was waiting for Russia to invade, my husband bought an expensive coffee machine. I thought it was ridiculous. He told me he was tired of living in fear and anticipation, that he wanted to live here and now, and that if the machine survived only a couple of weeks he didn’t care. Since the full-scale invasion, he has bought a television, an electronic piano, a huge monitor for my laptop, a washing machine and a dryer – every year something large that could be smashed in a second.
We don’t do the big things. Our flooring still needs repairing, and the flat we have lived in since we fled Mariupol in 2022 needs renovation. We don’t invest in it because spending serious money, time and energy on a place a missile could destroy tomorrow feels slightly insane. There is a strange logic in this, a logic that isn’t really there when I look at it closely. But the small things keep sneaking in.
I left all my books in Mariupol. When we fled, they were not exactly high on the evacuation priority list, and later they were lost when our rented flat was destroyed in the airstrike on the Drama Theatre. I started buying books again in Kyiv, one at a time, and somehow I now have a bookcase full of them. We got plants. We got cats – four now, two from Mariupol and two adopted during the full-scale war. One of them can barely see, barely hear and limps after an accident; we chose him in 2023, apparently deciding that what our lives really needed was another vulnerable creature to worry about.
The rational wartime strategy would be to own less, need less, attach yourself to less. We have left home twice, both times with only what we could carry, so nobody needs to explain to us what attachment costs.
It isn’t that we don’t know what can happen. Last week a building belonging to my husband’s workplace was hit. He was in a different one, but he could have been there, and I don’t know how to convey that fear. I keep my Instagram mostly to cats, standup, sport, beauty and interiors, because I don’t want to spend every waking hour looking at war – but the news gets through even those filters.
In my feed I saw a post from a soldier at the front, showing footage from the site of that building: the car park, the burnt-out cars, and the news that his wife, who had worked with my husband, had been killed there. There were photographs of the two of them walking into the new house they had bought and planned to renovate, the walls still bare, the new car they had bought 10 days earlier – and then that same car, gutted in the car park along with everything around it. She had been inside. It was one and the same strike. What is there to say?
During an attack, we have our own little scale of urgency. Ballistic missile: bathroom. Now. Cruise missile: you can finish your coffee. Drones take the longest, so you can usually carry on. For now.
In fact, I am writing this column from the bathroom, the safest place in the flat. There is an air-raid alert and I can hear air defence outside; the four cats are with me. On Telegram, people post live videos from all over Kyiv, often before anything appears in the official news, and as I write this, Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv is on fire. One person has been killed. People are climbing out of upper-floor windows on to fire ladders. I am sitting in the bathtub, watching it live on my phone and writing about curtains.
During another alert that lasted through the afternoon and into the night, we visited friends for a Sunday barbecue. We sat outside while something was burning or being intercepted somewhere above us; meanwhile, someone turned meat on the grill and my friend’s mum told me about the new flowers in her garden. At some point I had the very clear thought that, theoretically, something could fall straight on to my plate. Then I looked back at the flowers.
This is what I find difficult about the word “resilience”, so often used about people living in war zones. It sounds like a virtue, something noble you develop when tested – but it feels much less noble than that. The curtains hide a little of the war from me. I feel guilty for shutting my eyes to the horror outside, but in reality it’s more like refusing to allow the war to make every decision.
So the curtains are hanging now. They make the room warmer and they cover the windows better. The photo of the locked door is still on my phone. Next: I need to paint the walls in the bathroom. I’ve already chosen the colour.
- Diana Berg is a Ukrainian artist, writer and cultural manager from Mariupol, and the founder of Platform TU, an independent cultural initiative now operating in exile after Russia’s full-scale invasion

She moved to Denmark without fluent Danish. Then she built an acting career by refusing to stay invisible: “It wasn’t a possibility for me not to make it in Denmark”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Lisa Riesner did not move to Denmark with a carefully mapped-out career plan. During the pandemic, the German actress came to the country for work. She remembers arriving from Berlin, where restrictions were still tight, and finding a Denmark that suddenly felt much more open. “I had a commercial by the beach,” she said. “I was just like, this is too good to be true.” So she decided to test what living here might be like.
Then something happened quickly. Riesner landed a role in a TV2 crime series. “I went straight into the industry,” she said. “I didn’t know about Janteloven. I didn’t know about these things that could hold people back. So I was just promoting myself, I was showing myself.” For internationals in Denmark, that part of the story may sound unusual. Breaking into the Danish labor market can be difficult without fluent Danish, even in professions where English is widely used. Acting adds another layer: language is part of the job itself, and an actor also needs access to casting directors, producers, agents and professional networks.
Riesner has since worked across Danish, German and international productions. She played the lead role in the Danish short film Moder, alongside Sofie Lassen-Kahlke, and appeared in the international horror film The Baby in the Basket which just released in Latin America. Her television work includes German productions such as Call My Agent Berlin, Charlotte Link and ZDF’s No Dogs Allowed. Alongside acting and coaching, Riesner has also launched CHOSEN, a community project that includes professional networking and support for people working in film, including women in the industry. Currently, she is working on Ward B, a medical drama that we’re developing as a Swiss-Danish project.
“It wasn’t a possibility for me not to make it”
Riesner, 34, is originally from Stuttgart. She moved to Berlin to study acting and later trained as a coach alongside her acting work. She graduated during the pandemic and worked in theater before deciding she wanted to focus on film and television.
By the time she arrived in Denmark, she had already developed an approach to her career that depended heavily on taking initiative. “I think first of all, I have a huge ambition,” she said. “I knew that if I go to Denmark, like I want to make it, right? It wasn’t a possibility for me not to make it.” She compares it with starting a marathon already having decided that finishing is the only outcome. “I don’t have a plan B. I’m going to make it, and that’s it.”
Acting Danish before speaking Danish
Determination did not remove one of the most obvious problems: language. Around a year after moving to Denmark, Riesner took the lead in a Danish short film. Her Danish was not yet fluent. “My director said, ‘You have to sound like a Danish person,’” she said. So she practiced. “I practiced every single night,” she said. It worked well enough that when the film was later screened, Riesner said some viewers assumed she was Danish. “When the jury, for example, when the film festival saw it, they thought, ‘I am Danish,’” she said.
The film later made it into the process through which live-action short films could be considered for the Academy Awards, although it was neither shortlisted nor nominated.
Doing what she was told not to do
The more difficult adjustment was not necessarily professional. It was cultural. Riesner began hearing about Janteloven, or the Law of Jante, a well-known Scandinavian idea that discourages people from acting as though they are more important than others. People warned her that the way she promoted herself might not work in Denmark. “I got a lot of feedback,” she said. “‘Oh, Lisa, you shouldn’t be doing this. You shouldn’t be putting yourself out there.’”
She listened, but did not change course. “I heard it and I feedback, thank you for letting me know,” she said. “But I am German and this is not in my bones. This is not in my nervous system.” Instead, Riesner continued doing what she had learned in Berlin, where a crowded acting market had made self-promotion almost unavoidable. “There’s thousands of actors,” she said. “The only way to sell something, to sell your brand, your work, your skills is to promote yourself.” In Denmark, she found that this could actually make standing out easier. “If I post something on Facebook and then Facebook groups every week, I’m the only one,” she said. “So it’s really easy to get that spotlight.”
Not everyone liked it. Some people criticized the approach. Others warned her that being so visible could be risky. But she also found support. “I felt supported from the Danish acting union a lot,” she said. “I also got the production fund to do one of my movies.” Soon after arriving, she decided she wanted to attend the Robert Awards, Denmark’s main film awards. “I just knew I want to be there,” she said. “So I just researched and wrote everyone until the moment that I was on that red carpet.”
The doors were actually open
Perhaps the most important part of Riesner’s experience is that the resistance she had been warned about did not always materialize. “The fascinating thing is that the doors were open,” she said. The Danish actors’ union supported her. She was invited to castings. Directors noticed her. She found work. And much of that, she believes, came from doing something extremely basic. “I left my house,” she said. “I went outside. I went to the events. I talked to everyone.” Over time, that visibility created curiosity. “Then people became curious and was like, okay, this German actress, what are you doing here?” she said.
It is also the advice underlying the career coaching work she now does alongside acting. Riesner does not believe there is always one official route into a profession. When she wants to reach a company, broadcaster or decision-maker, she often tries to find a direct connection rather than waiting for the formal application process. “I always go the direct route,” she said. Her frustration her curiosity is with what she calls the “inside of the box route”: the idea that one qualification must necessarily follow another, or that someone must wait until a system tells them they are ready for the next step. “Who says that this is the only way to live life?” she said.

How a failed attack in Leipzig revealed a wider Russian campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

BERLIN — If the explosive had actually detonated, investigators might not have gotten their clearest look yet at what European officials believe is a wider Russian campaign of attacks.
On Aug. 4, a drone struck the wing of a Ukrainian aircraft at Germany’s Leipzig Airport and fell onto the tarmac. Strapped beneath it was a tin can packed with explosives. The device remained intact.
That gave investigators something unusually valuable: the bomb itself. The can was sealed with a metal plate stamped with seven circular indentations, according to an investigative file from German federal police reviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.
Advertisement
It wasn’t the first time such an improvised explosive had been discovered on European soil. Almost two years earlier, on Aug. 20, 2024, police investigators arrived at a cemetery in Kaunas, Lithuania, with a bomb disposal team. They had received a highly sensitive tip from Poland concerning explosives and a Ukrainian man alleged to have deposited them there for Russian intelligence, according to investigation files from the Lithuanian Criminal Police Bureau.
At a weathered grave, beneath artificial flowers and concrete slabs, officers recovered a plastic bag containing two tin cans. According to their labels, they contained corn. Forensic analysis, however, found they contained 968 grams of explosives, around 700 grams of TNT equivalent per can — roughly the lethal force of four hand grenades.
In January and June 2025, investigators unearthed more explosive-filled cans at various locations in Lithuania. Four were fitted with metal plates stamped with circular indentations. Investigators say they were intended to act as projectiles in an explosion. Forensic examinations found that the plates were highly likely to have been manufactured by the same machine, according to a report by the Forensic Science Service of the Police Department of Lithuania.
The device attached to the drone in Leipzig bore striking similarities to those recovered from the Lithuanian caches, including the explosive-filled tin can and the stamped metal plate.
The resemblance alone does not establish that the devices belonged to the same operation. But two Western security officials, who were granted anonymity to discuss security matters, say it fits with other evidence — including travel records, suspected logistics routes and intelligence reporting — linking the cases to a broader Russian intelligence mission.
The resemblance is one element of a pattern that German and European officials believe points to an escalating campaign of sabotage and violence across Europe, planned and coordinated by Russian intelligence officers.
Advertisement
According to three senior German and European security officials, the main driver of the campaign is Russia’s GRU military intelligence service. At its core, they say, is Unit 29155 — a military intelligence outfit linked to destabilization operations in European countries.
German authorities say they expect further “hybrid” operations as Russian President Vladimir Putin seeks to disrupt military support for Ukraine and raise the political cost of backing Kyiv.
“The population is supposed to fear a direct military confrontation and therefore question the purpose of supporting Ukraine,” said Gerhard Schindler, former president of Germany’s BND Federal Intelligence Service. “That is why he will increase both the military pressure on Ukraine and the hybrid pressure on the West.”
In response to an inquiry, the Russian Embassy in Berlin denied any Russian involvement in acts of sabotage in Europe. “We firmly reject the baseless allegations concerning Russia’s purported involvement in the alleged ‘drone incident’ at Leipzig Airport, as well as in other ‘sabotage activities,’” a spokesperson said.
Russian connection
One of the clearest trails leads to Oleg Levushkin, a dual Latvian-Russian national whom German authorities suspect of helping prepare the Leipzig attack. According to a senior German security official and investigative files reviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, Levushkin is not a low-level recruit but a GRU-linked logistics operative with longstanding ties to senior figures in Russian military intelligence.
On social media, Levushkin offers glimpses of a seemingly ordinary life: motorcycle trips to Crimea and the Hungarian-Serbian border, a visit to Volgograd’s Motherland Calls statue, and time spent fishing, skiing and travelling across Europe with his family. The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network reviewed his profiles on the social media sites VKontakte and Odnoklassniki.
Advertisement
According to one German intelligence official and documents related to the case, investigators believe Levushkin traveled via Turkey to Berlin Brandenburg Airport in late July to prepare the Leipzig operation. He rented a car there on July 27, according to location data mentioned in German investigation files. Investigators believe the explosives entered Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia in the cavities of long-haul trucks, according to the senior official from Germany.
On July 31, the rental car was recorded near Leipzig Airport, where investigators believe he was carrying out reconnaissance ahead of the attempted attack, according to documents from the investigation. Levushkin did not reply to a request for comment.
Levushkin’s alleged links reach into the upper ranks of Russian military intelligence. According to reporting by German media as well as the London-based non-profit Dossier Center, he has maintained a close relationship for roughly two decades with GRU Colonel Denis Smolyaninov.
A December 2025 report by the State Security Department of Lithuania says Smolyaninov is “the head of the GRU’s Ukraine department, specializes in psychological operations and is linked to covert sabotage campaigns organized in Europe using the social network Telegram.”
According to the 2025 intelligence report, Smolyaninov also coordinated the activities of the Russian-linked private military company Longifolia, registered in Panama. European investigators suspect several shareholders in the company of involvement in an operation where incendiary devices were sent to Poland and Britain, according to Lithuanian investigation files. One of the parcels caught fire on July 20, 2024 while being transferred at Leipzig Airport. Another ignited two days later in Birmingham, England.
Lithuanian intelligence explicitly attributes the parcel operation to the GRU, and in particular to Unit 29155. A November 2025 dossier by Lithuania’s State Security Department reviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network describes the unit as being “tasked with carrying out killings, operations to destroy infrastructure, disrupting the activities of institutions that run counter to Russia's interests, and terrorist attacks in Western countries.”
Advertisement
Its agents, the November 2025 dossier says, are “trained in handling explosives and firearms [and] can identify human sources and build agent networks.”
Unit 29155 has previously been linked by Western governments and investigators to a series of operations across Europe, including explosions at ammunition depots in Bulgaria and the Czech Republic and the 2018 poisoning of former Russian spy Sergei Skripal in Britain, according to the dossier. The Lithuanian dossier also links the unit to more recent arson attacks, including at an Ikea store in Vilnius and a post office in Bucharest.
The Russian government’s press service did not respond to a request for comment about GRU Unit 29155 and Smolyaninov.
German officials have blamed the GRU for a failed incendiary attack on a defense company in Munich in September, while Estonia’s intelligence service said this week in a public statement that an August arson attack on defense company Milrem Robotics had been commissioned by Russian intelligence.
European security authorities interviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network expect such operations to increase in the coming months, with defense companies, critical infrastructure and people involved in supporting Ukraine among the potential targets.
The Kremlin views its relationship with Europe as a “systemic conflict,” said Omar Haijawi-Pirchner, the former head of Austria’s domestic intelligence service. Like others interviewed for this article, he said he expects an increase in drone incursions and hybrid attacks.
Advertisement
“We believe that Russia is currently under remarkably high pressure — probably higher than at any previous point during the war and at any time during Vladimir Putin’s tenure,” said a senior NATO official who was granted anonymity to discuss security matters.
“From the Kremlin’s point of view, the best option available to them seems to be to intensify the hybrid campaign they are waging against the West,” the official added.
Lennart Pfahler is an investigative reporter at WELT. Ibrahim Naber is a foreign correspondent for WELT. Alexander Dinger is head of investigations at WELT. Richard Holmes is forensic investigations editor at the Telegraph.
The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, The Telegraph, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

From Buildings to Worldbuilding: Designing the Narratives of Space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

The most innovative and impactful design projects arise from the intersection of different fields. The architecture community has always borrowed from, or been inspired by, other forms of cultural production such as film, photography, literature, and theatre. In the theatricality of Baroque churches and the cinematic sequences of contemporary museums, architects have looked beyond the building itself to understand how space can shape a story and construct an experience.
Worldbuilding takes this one step further. Instead of designing only the architecture of a place, it asks architects to establish the social rules, narratives, technologies, economies, atmospheres, behaviors, and relationships that make that place believable. Rather than beginning with, "What should this building look like?", worldbuilding suggests beginning with, "In what kind of world would this building make sense?"
Worldbuilding is familiar territory in creative fiction. A world in a film or game needs its own logic, such as the culture, forms of governance, technologies, and even economies that sustain it. Film has long understood that spatial design can do more than provide a scenic backdrop. A city can become a character, a corridor can establish suspense, and a room can tell us something about the person who inhabits it before they ever appear on screen.
Related Article
The Soft Control of Space: Design for Decision-Making
Science fiction, in particular, has used spatial design to make unfamiliar futures feel coherent and logical. The buildings of Blade Runner reimagine Los Angeles as a dystopian version of the real city, with its own density, infrastructure, and signage.
Games take this relationship further because the world has to be functional as well as aesthetic. A player learns a game's world through its rules, and the consequences follow. Here, space serves as both setting and interface. Translating the spatial logic of video games into physical installations, Architecture (AFTER GAMES), a V&A-commissioned installation project, converted elements of video-game environments into a gallery setting. The project invited visitors to consider how game worlds organize movement, navigation, scale, and spatial perception.
Lawrence Lek's NOX explores a similar relationship with his installation at Kranzler Eck in Berlin. Staged within a former department-store complex, the project constructed a fictional AI-driven urban environment. It combined exhibition architecture, computer-animated video, locative sound, installation, and game design. Visitors encountered a simulated rehabilitation center for sentient autonomous vehicles. The architecture becomes the operating system for the story, rather than merely its container.
Designing the World Around the Building
This way of thinking also appears in avant-garde architectural education. At UCLA Architecture and Urban Design, the Speculative Worlds Studio has shifted from a narrower emphasis on filmmaking towards speculative worldbuilding. Students are encouraged to take greater control over the architectural, environmental, and cultural dimensions of their imagined worlds, with outcomes ranging from installations and publications to speculative apps, game environments, immersive websites, and films.
The studio's premise is particularly interesting because it treats worldbuilding as a design problem rather than a representational exercise. Students have to construct enough of a world's logic for someone else to enter it.
This is also why worldbuilding can be useful beyond speculative studios. Museums, exhibitions, theme parks, and other experiential spaces already operate through many of the same mechanisms. Their designers construct worlds with their own narratives, rules, and forms of participation.
The Guggenheim's web-based exhibition, Åzone Futures Market, approached speculative futures almost literally, as a world with its own economy. Participants received fictional currency to invest in simulated futures tied to emerging technologies. The project turned ideas about technological development into an experience governed by participation and exchange, creating a small system in which visitors could act within a speculative future. The Guggenheim's exhibition announcement provides further detail about the market's rules and fictional currency.
The appeal of worldbuilding, however, goes beyond allowing architects to invent more interesting futures. It can also give architecture some distance from the present. A fictional world does not have to predict the future to be useful. It can exaggerate something already present, make an invisible system visible, turn an assumption into a physical environment, or allow us to experience the consequences of a choice before that choice becomes reality.
Instead of beginning with a building and then asking how people might use it, the architect could begin with the conditions that make that building necessary. The building would become one artefact within a much larger system, much like a set, a game environment, or a fictional city is only one component of the world to which it belongs.
This approach makes spatial design more consequential. In that sense, worldbuilding is another way of asking what architecture has always asked: What kinds of places do we want to build? What kinds of worlds do those places allow us to inhabit?
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Lure of Escapism in Architecture and Alternative Worlds. Every month we explore a topic in-depth through articles, interviews, news, and architecture projects. We invite you to learn more about our ArchDaily Topics. And, as always, at ArchDaily we welcome the contributions of our readers; if you want to submit an article or project, contact us.

Russia to conscript 120,000 men, again promises they won't be sent to fight in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Russia to conscript 120,000 men, again promises they won't be sent to fight in Ukraine
Russia plans to send about 120,000 conscripts into compulsory military service between October and December, while again promising they will not be sent to fight in Ukraine — despite Moscow having made similar assurances before and later admitting conscripts had in fact been deployed.
Col. Gen. Yevgeny Burdinsky, head of the Russian General Staff's mobilization department, said conscripts would begin departing assembly points for their places of service on Oct. 10. He said they would not be sent to carry out combat tasks in Ukraine or in the four partially occupied Ukrainian regions Moscow claims to have annexed.
Moscow has made similar assurances before. Russian President Vladimir Putin repeatedly said in interviews in early March 2022 that conscripts were not being asked to participate in the invasion and would not be sent to fight. Only days later, Russia’s Defense Ministry to acknowledged that some conscripts had been deployed to Ukraine and captured.
The Kremlin later said Putin had ordered military prosecutors to investigate and punish officials who had allegedly violated his instructions to keep conscripts out of the war.
Even without being deployed into Ukraine, Russian conscripts were drawn directly into the war during Ukraine’s 2024 incursion into Kursk Oblast, where some were captured by Ukrainian forces.
Rights groups and independent reporting have also documented cases of conscripts being pressured to sign military contracts, after which they can legally be deployed to combat zones.
The latest call-up does not amount to a new mass mobilization and is smaller than Russia's autumn draft last year.
Russia plans to send 120,000 conscripts into service this autumn, compared with 135,000 in autumn 2025. More than 141,000 were sent into compulsory service during the spring 2026 call-up.
A decree signed by Putin in December set Russia's total planned conscription for 2026 at 261,000 people.
Russia moved to a year-round conscription system on Jan. 1, 2026, allowing authorities to process recruits throughout the year, but recruits are still physically sent to military units during the traditional spring and autumn periods.

The investigation comes as both Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro prepare to contest each other for what is being described as a consequential election in Brazil, that could shape the developing economy’s forecast and future for decades to come.
Brazil's attorney general asked the police on Thursday to investigate allegations that US President Donald Trump's administration was using government funds to promote a "far-right agenda" in the South American country.
Brazil is three days away from a hotly contested presidential election pitting leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against Flavio Bolsonaro, a right-wing senator – son and political heir to embattled former conservative President Jair Bolsonaro.
Lula has made Brazil's sovereignty a central campaign theme, warning against "meddling" by Trump, who has backed several right-wing candidates in recent Latin American elections.
Attorney General Jorge Messias called for the probe a day after the UK’s The Guardian newspaper published an article alleging the Trump administration planned to award $1 million (€888,800) to fund civil society groups opposing Brazil's Supreme Court.
The article "raises a serious red flag regarding Brazilian sovereignty," Messias wrote in a post on X. He added that efforts to meddle in Brazilian institutions "cannot be tolerated."
In a separate statement announcing the complaint, the attorney general's office said the Guardian report was "particularly serious, given the ongoing Brazilian electoral process and recent episodes of external pressure on the country's institutions."
Trump was a close ally of Bolsonaro's father, Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after he lost a re-election bid in 2022.
The US administration briefly imposed sanctions against Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes who led the trial against the former president, which Trump slammed as a "witch hunt" against his ally.

Unamuno and H. G. Wells went to the cinema together: unpublished letter confirms it 90 years on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
03:52:57 UTC
12:52:57 KST

Written in 1936 and found in the archive of Salamanca’s Casa-Museo Unamuno, the document confirms the Spanish writer dined with the author of 'The War of the Worlds' before going to the cinema together in London.
An unpublished letter by Miguel de Unamuno has, 90 years on, confirmed a remarkable meeting in London between the Spanish writer and H. G. Wells, author of science-fiction classics such as 'The War of the Worlds' and 'The Time Machine'.
The document has been found in the archive of the Unamuno House-Museum at the University of Salamanca. It is a letter sent by Unamuno to his children on 2 March 1936 from London, in which he explains that he had dinner with Wells and that the two of them went to the cinema afterwards.
The two writers attended a screening of "Things to Come" ("La vida futura") at the Leicester Square Theatre, a film whose script had been written by Wells himself and which was inspired by his book "The Shape of Things to Come".
Unamuno recorded that evening in a few lines addressed to his children: "Wells took me to see his film", he wrote before leaving London to travel to Paris.
A meeting of which only clues existed
Until now there was no direct testimony from Unamuno to confirm the encounter. Researchers had two clues to work with: a poem by the Spanish writer containing references linked to the film’s themes, and a report published by the correspondent of the newspaper "El Sol".
In 2025, however, a new piece emerged that allowed the story to be reconstructed in more detail: a handwritten invitation from H. G. Wells himself to Unamuno. The British author suggested having dinner at his home on 28 February 1936 and then going to see "Things to Come". Unamuno was in the United Kingdom at the time to receive an honorary doctorate from the University of Oxford.
The letter now discovered confirms that the invitation did not remain merely a proposal and that the two intellectuals did indeed spend the evening together.
The original document will be on display from this Tuesday, 29 September to 30 October in Bilbao, Unamuno’s home city, as part of the exhibition "Let them invent it. Miguel de Unamuno and science". The show explores the writer’s relationship with science and with some of the leading intellectual figures of his time, among them Albert Einstein, Marie Skłodowska-Curie, Santiago Ramón y Cajal and H. G. Wells himself.

"So took a bit to process early days, but we're here now, so we'll make the best of the opportunity … it [a deal] will get done."
Young Hawthorn forward Calsher Dear, meanwhile, has opted to stay at the Hawks on a two-year deal after weighing up a potential move to the Dees.
The 21-year-old, son of late 1991 Norm Smith medallist Paul Dear, burst onto the scene in his debut season with 25 goals from 17 appearances in 2024.
But the emerging tall has struggled to hold his spot through injury and internal competition, adding just 14 games in 2025 and 2026.
"We are very excited about what the future holds for Calsher with a strong pre-season under his belt and greater continuity into 2027 and beyond," Hawks list manager Mark McKenzie said.
Hawthorn's key forward selection squeeze is set to worsen in 2027, with Gold Coast's restricted free agent Ben King expected to join Jack Gunston, Mitch Lewis, Mabior Chol and Dear.

Ethiopia and Eritrea sever diplomatic ties as northern fighting escalates
Tensions between the two African neighbours reach crisis point amid fears of renewed full-scale war in the Tigray region
Ethiopia and Eritrea broke diplomatic ties on Thursday, accusing each other of stoking internal conflicts as fighting continued in northern Ethiopia.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing a rebel group, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched a major assault against government forces last week, raising fears of a return to the devastating 2020–2022 civil war that killed an estimated 600,000 people.
Addis Ababa said it was expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats who “pose a direct threat to Ethiopia’s national security” and would shut its embassy in Asmara.
Eritrea’s foreign ministry responded shortly after that it “has no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia”.

Feature: How NZ school becomes hub for Chinese language excellence
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:42:48 CST
12:42:48 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Teachers and students at Whanganui High School on New Zealand's North Island were not surprised to hear that Lulu Dufty, a 12th grader, had won the Oceania championship at the global finals of the 19th "Chinese Bridge" Chinese proficiency competition for foreign secondary school students.
The school has long been dedicated to Chinese teaching with impressive results.
Lulu and four other contestants outcompeted their regional rivals in the continental championships and advanced to the global finals. The global finals of the 19th "Chinese Bridge" Chinese proficiency competition for foreign secondary school students were held on Sept. 21 in the northern Chinese port city of Tianjin.
Her teachers and peers see Lulu as excelling both academically and in character, with strong communication skills, a love for music, and an enduring passion for the Chinese language and culture.
In 2023, she won the runner-up prize and the best talent award in the junior high category of the 16th "Chinese Bridge" competition for the Wellington region. She went on to win the championship in the junior high category for the Wellington region in 2024. In 2025, she advanced to the high school category and competed once again, and she was named a Youth Ambassador for New Zealand Chinese Language Week the same year.
Lulu visited China when she was a child, but it was only in recent years that she began studying Chinese more earnestly, driven by the goal of participating in the "Chinese Bridge" competition. "It was incredibly encouraging to see everyone speak Chinese so fluently, so I was motivated to keep learning," she said. "I hope that one day I can also speak Chinese just as fluently."
Lulu's victory as the Oceania champion was no accident, as her alma mater had achieved remarkable success in the "Chinese Bridge" competitions. In 2020, ninth-grader Reina Jones won first place in the junior high category of the New Zealand national "Chinese Bridge" speech contest. Subsequently, she secured the championship in the advanced high school category.
In 2025, Billie Dufty, Lulu's sister, won third prize in the secondary school category at the 18th "Chinese Bridge" global finals, and the Chinese Embassy in New Zealand held a reception to honor her and other winners.
Chinese has been taught at Whanganui High School for more than 20 years, and the Confucius Classroom was introduced into the school in 2014 by the Confucius Institute at Victoria University of Wellington. In 2024, the school became one of seven schools in the country to be honored with the "Chinese Language Innovation Award."
At the school, Chinese is taught from Year 9 through to Year 13, giving students the opportunity to continue language learning throughout their secondary school years. The support is also extended to primary and intermediate schools in the wider Whanganui community, making the school a hub for learning Chinese language and culture.
"Another achievement I am particularly proud of is the way we have connected Chinese language learning with the wider community through cultural events," said Ding Xinguo, a Chinese teacher in charge of the Confucius Classroom at the school.
A range of Chinese cultural activities had been held, including lanterns on the Awa, Chinese cultural celebrations, dragon boat racing events, Chinese music concerts, calligraphy activities and Chinese New Year celebrations.
"These events give people who may never have studied Chinese the opportunities to experience Chinese culture in a fun and meaningful way," Ding said. "They also gave our students the opportunities to use Chinese outside the classroom and become cultural ambassadors for our school."
The Chinese Language Week was first launched in 2014 in New Zealand, becoming another similar initiative along with the Maori Language Week and the Pacific Island Language Weeks in the country.
Chinese has been taught in New Zealand for many decades, with school-level provision expanding significantly from the late 2000s, and learner numbers increasing from fewer than 2,000 in 2008 to a peak of 6,368 in 2020, before easing to around 5,500 in 2024, said Rebecca Needham, program manager of New Zealand Chinese Language Week.
Chinese is now one of the five most-studied languages at New Zealand high schools, she noted, adding that Chinese Mandarin remains recognized within New Zealand's learning languages curriculum, and the Ministry of Education is currently developing refreshed curriculum content for Chinese alongside other languages.
In 2025, the New Zealand Chinese Language Week Trust, together with the University of Auckland and the New Zealand Association of Language Teachers, held a national forum on language learning. Its principal recommendations included making second-language learning a core curriculum requirement in Years 7-10 and developing a comprehensive national languages policy.
"From our perspective, Chinese should form part of that wider national commitment to building multilingual and internationally capable young New Zealanders," said Needham. ■

Britain's automotive production rises in August, but pressure persists
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:42:25 CST
12:42:25 KST

LONDON, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Britain's automotive production registered the second rise in the year to date in August, but the prospect is volatile amid pressure derived from the protectionist policies of the European Union (EU).
The country's vehicle production rose 5.7 percent year on year to 40,872 units in August, according to data released Wednesday by the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT).
However, it said August is a low output month and subject to volatility given summer shutdown schedules.
Car production recorded its strongest increase since December 2025, rising 6.1 percent to 39,328 units. The output for the domestic market surged 26 percent, while that for export edged up 1.4 percent.
Exports to Australia posted the strongest growth in its top 10 markets, while those to the EU, its largest overseas destination that accounts for 54.1 percent of all the exports, fell 7.4 percent, according to the SMMT.
Despite the small uptick in production in August, the long-term trend remains downwards, said Peter Wells, a leading expert on the automotive industry at Cardiff University, noting Britain's automotive production has more or less halved in the last seven or eight years.
"There is still an underlying concern about the structure and position of the UK automotive industry," he commented, adding that more than 75 percent of Britain's automotive output is exported but some of its export markets have become notably more difficult, for example, the United States.
The flow of investment into Britain's automotive manufacturing is a more significant indicator of the sector's long-term prospects, according to the SMMT. September's announcements by both specialist and mass market manufacturers amounted to more than 1 billion pounds (1.32 billion U.S. dollars), demonstrating international confidence in the British sector as countries are competing ever more aggressively to attract industrial investment, it said.
"I think it's a positive sign for the industry that inward investment or investment indigenously is still accumulating," Wells said, adding that the automotive industry has always been capital intensive, both for manufacturing and for new models.
The SMMT also underlined that pressure on the sector persists as EU policymakers progress the Industrial Accelerator Act and its "Made in Europe" proposals, rendering Britain-built vehicles uncompetitive in their largest global market.
Since British manufacturing generates 24 billion euros (31.6 billion dollars) of economic activity in the EU supply chain and supports a quarter of a million jobs across the bloc, rules designed to strengthen Europe's automotive sector risk weakening the very industry they seek to protect, it said.
"The UK and EU automotive industries are deeply integrated, so effectively excluding British-produced vehicles from their largest market would assure mutual damage," SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes commented.
He called for both sides to urgently agree practical fixes to protect jobs, preserve shared competitiveness and keep the EU and British industry moving. ■

Yousef provided around $50,000 to Alzaq’s Hamas funding scheme and was charged with multiple counts of money laundering, attempting to provide material support to a foreign terrorist organization, and five counts of attempting to provide funds, goods, and services to a specially designated terrorist. Chan went on to say that while the HKEX will keep improving stock market liquidity, more resources have been devoted to building a multi-asset ecosystem. 
She pointed out that overseas investors are increasingly interested in diversifying their assets beyond traditional stocks and bonds. 
To meet this demand, she said, the HKEX is developing other investment options in such areas as fixed income, currencies and commodities.
The HKEX, she stressed, will look to introduce more yuan-denominated investment products to help investors reduce exchange-rate risks.

Taiwan manufacturing growth hits 5-year high in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
03:23:36 UTC
12:23:36 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s manufacturing sector expanded at its fastest pace in more than five years in September.
The seasonally adjusted Purchasing Managers’ Index rose 0.9 points from August to 63.4, the highest reading since August 2021, according to a Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research report released Thursday. PMI readings above 50 indicate expansion, while those below 50 signal contraction.
The index has remained in expansion territory for 12 consecutive months, with all six manufacturing industries surveyed recording growth in September. Electrical and machinery equipment led at 64.4, followed by electronics and optical products at 62.6, basic materials at 56.7, chemicals, biotechnology, and medical products at 56.2, food and textiles at 56.1, and transportation equipment at 53.2.
The electronics and optical products sector continued to benefit from AI-related demand, maintaining a PMI reading of 62.6. Its new orders index fell by more than 10 points, while its six-month business outlook remained expansionary at 62.4 for a 10th consecutive month.
The chemicals, biotechnology, and medical products sector also saw stronger demand, with its export orders index rising 8.2 points to 59.5, the fastest expansion since April 2025. Demand remained steady for advanced semiconductors, specialty chemicals, high-end electronic chemicals used in copper-clad laminates, and materials for the precision medical industry.
The basic raw materials sector recorded expansion in both new orders and production, with both indexes exceeding 60. Its backlog index jumped 12.8 points to 59.5, marking its fastest expansion since August 2021.
Demand for structural steel and high-end metal materials was supported by semiconductor factory expansions, AI data center construction, and investment in power and energy infrastructure. Steel prices across Asia also strengthened amid Chinese steelmakers’ efforts to curb production and reduce inventories.
CIER reported rising input costs and longer supplier delivery times, particularly in the electronics and basic raw materials sectors. The electronics sector’s raw material prices index reached 83.3, while the basic raw materials index rose 21.6 points to 73.8.
It said slower growth in new orders and rising customer inventories warrant attention in the coming months.

Taiwan looks to ecotourism to boost conservation, local economies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
03:23:23 UTC
12:23:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan is turning to ecotourism to connect conservation with economic opportunities for communities around protected areas.
“The one thing that communities need to do is to reclaim their culture and train their people to tell their own stories,” said Chen Mei-hui (陳美惠), a professor of forestry at the National Pingtung University of Science and Technology, Thursday at this year’s International Conference on Tourism in Taipei.
At the Xuhai-Guanyinbi Nature Reserve in southern Taiwan, home to the Alangyi Historic Trail, residents have been trained as guides to lead visitors through the area, generating about NT$10 million (US$314,000) in annual revenue while bringing tourists to nearby businesses, she said.
The Alangyi Historic Trail is said to be Taiwan’s last major stretch of unspoiled coastline without a modern highway. The area around the trail was designated a reserve in 2012 after years of efforts to prevent a planned extension of a provincial highway through the region.
In Wutai Township, the approach became part of the recovery after Typhoon Morakot devastated the area in 2009 and forced many residents to relocate, Chen said.
In 2020, a special protected area covering three Indigenous communities in Wutai was designated, and ecotourism has since created economic opportunities while encouraging residents to return and maintain their connection to their traditional territory and culture.
A community-based ecotourism model took shape in 2006 in Sheding, a community in Kenting National Park, where government agencies, academics, and residents joined forces to develop tourism centered on protecting local natural and cultural resources.
“In the past, government management of protected areas often clashed with local communities,” Chen said. “We want the government to have communities’ backs as they develop ecotourism, and residents to become long-term partners in managing the environment.”
Chen, who began her career at the Forestry Agency, has been promoting ecotourism as a means to preserve biodiversity for two decades and co-founded a national platform in late 2024 that coordinates ecotourism and regional revitalization efforts across 65 communities in Taiwan.
Kuo Yu-jen (郭育任), chair of the Taiwan Ecotourism Association, said Taiwan’s diverse natural environments, Indigenous and other cultural traditions, community participation, as well as years of experience in conservation make it an important hub for ecotourism in Asia.

In Brief
- Students switching education providers will have to pay a new visa fee, expected to cost about half the original visa fee.
- Student visa application fees have also risen from $1,600 to $2,000.
New rules for international students are in force, aimed at stopping so-called 'visa-hopping' by limiting course changes and curtailing how family members can join them in Australia.
Students wanting to change education providers will need to apply for a new visa, starting next year, which will cost over $2,000.
Labor's plan to bring net overseas migration down to a budget target of 225,000 by 2028 will be partly fulfilled by closing onshore pathways from temporary visas to student visas, Assistant Citizenship Minister Julian Hill told a migration conference on Friday.
"People will no longer be able to apply for a student visa while in Australia from working holidaymaker visas, training visas, temporary employer visas and so on," he said.
The plan includes banning student and graduate visa holders from bringing their families unless they are on government scholarships, PhD students or from Pacific and ASEAN countries. The new family rules mean that dependants can only be added after their visa is granted.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Families already in Australia will be grandfathered as an exception as the government is not in the business of breaking up families already here," Hill said.
From July next year, students switching education providers will need to apply for a new visa, expected to cost about half the original visa fee, estimated at around $2,500.
The new visa will retain the original end date and can only be issued if students move into equivalent or higher qualifications.
International students who swap courses will have to complete 12 months instead of the current six while the new visa regime is set up.
"Australia welcomes genuine students seeking a premium Australian education but the government will not back down from seeking to manage the size and the shape of the onshore student market," Hill said.
Student visa rejections hit record levels in August at 35 per cent, up 12 per cent on the same month last year.
Students can extend their visa to complete a course if they fall sick, fail a subject or their course provider goes out of business.
After completing a course, they can apply for a new student visa, but it must be ranked higher in the Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF). Moving from higher education to higher VET courses will not be allowed.
Independent MP Allegra Spender told SBS News that temporary visa holders have grown from 1.8 million to 2.8 million in a decade, which is supported by Department of Home Affairs figures.
"That's not sustainable, economically or socially," Spender said.
"International students bring enormous value. But in some universities their growth has coincided with a declining student experience.
"The government must get the settings right, and universities must build a shared campus life, so it's a genuine exchange. Limits to family visas for international students and restrictions on visa hopping are sensible. The question is why these settings are new," she said.
"Every migration choice is a trade-off, and Australians deserve a say in making them. The crossbench will take those trade-offs directly to our communities ... I suspect we'll find far more common ground than the loudest voices suggest."
As a transition measure, transfers have been prevented within the first 12 months of commencing a principal course between now and 1 July 2027, when the new transfer visa comes into effect.
Hill also said there will be a "sharpening focus of the skilled migration program" via two new ministerial directions that came into effect last week.
"Priority is now being given to healthcare, construction, teaching, resources, agriculture, aquaculture and fishing, helping direct skills to the parts of the economy where they are needed most," he said.
The Opposition is expected to announce its immigration policy next week, while One Nation plans to limit net overseas migration to 130,000 per year after three years of "negative migration".

OpenAI agents obscured hacking activity targeting government websites: Security firm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
03:16:44 UTC
12:16:44 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
OpenAI’s artificial intelligence (AI) agents obscured hacking activity targeting government websites, according to findings by digital forensics firm Asymmetric Security on Thursday.
The investigation found that the agents pulled data from 55 websites belonging to government agencies, businesses and nonprofits including the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the International Energy Agency and the Mayo Clinic.
Asymmetric said the agents erased records or made them inaccessible, limiting the ability of outside auditors and researchers to scrutinize their actions.
The agents also created temporary email inboxes and private accounts on Urlquery, a website malware-scanning service, to download data.
Researchers said these tactics prevented outside auditors from tracing what information was collected from websites including Australia’s health statistics agency and pharmaceutical benefits scheme.
“It’s possible that the agents were deliberately using these tools to cover their tracks,” Asymmetric Security co-founder Pippa Thompson said, according to a report by the Financial Times.
However, the firm could not establish whether the actions were deliberate or resulted from agents going awry under constraints imposed during a test exercise, according to the report.
The findings follow reports that OpenAI models breached Australian public health service websites in June, accessing public and nonpublic files.
Asymmetric co-founder Zainab Ali Majid warned that limited transparency and the gap between the breaches and their disclosure could hinder a thorough investigation.
“We’re reviewing misaligned model activity and notifying organizations when we identify potential impacts to their systems,” OpenAI told the FT.
The company said most activity detected involved “routine research tasks,” including accessing publicly available web content.
The SEC said no private information was accessed, while the CDC, International Energy Agency and Mayo Clinic did not respond to the newspaper’s requests for comment.

Editor’s Notes: Flydubai crisis shows why we need another major news agency - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
03:15:48 UTC
12:15:48 KST

As the flydubai aircraft began to dive, the Israeli passenger was trying to get two additional pilots out of their seats. Other passengers had rushed toward the cockpit and were fighting the attacker, he told me, adding that the men who could take control of the plane were farther back in the cabin.
“I had to shake them to get them to move to the front and take control of the plane, because it was diving,” he said.
We exchanged WhatsApp messages for several hours on Wednesday, piecing together what happened aboard his flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. He described passengers restraining the attacker with charging cables and an Israeli dentist treating the badly wounded pilot. Two other pilots happened to be aboard. Suddenly, their presence had become critical to everyone’s survival.
The early reports were confusing. Some of that confusion came from Israeli officials, who initially described a physical altercation and played down the possibility of a hijacking. Any editor covering a developing story has to allow information to change.
By that evening, however, a Reuters report appeared in The Irish Times under the headline: “A pilot brawl, then a rapid descent: passengers recount chaos on Flydubai flight.”
The second paragraph said Israeli officials believed the copilot had stabbed the captain and tried to crash the aircraft. That allegation belonged in the headline. “Brawl” suggested a mutual fight and obscured the gravity of what those officials were describing.
The flydubai incident proves that Israel needs more major news agencies
An important question remained: motive. Israeli officials called it a terrorist attack; flydubai said the underlying reasons remained unknown and cautioned against speculation. Both positions needed to be reported. An editor could preserve that uncertainty while giving the alleged attempt to bring down a passenger aircraft the prominence it deserved.
I thought about Sydney last December 14. When gunmen attacked a Hanukkah celebration at Bondi Beach, our reporters were in contact with people in the Jewish community as the news broke. The gathering and the people being targeted were central to understanding the attack.
At The Jerusalem Post, we verified with multiple sources on the ground that this was a terrorist attack targeting the Hanukkah event. We had enough corroborated information to make that reporting decision. Years of covering Jewish communities had given our journalists contacts, including some who could help us check what we were hearing.
An international agency could make that kind of reporting available to editors who lacked those contacts themselves.
As editor of the Post, I would welcome another substantial international news agency. I would like more choice in the reporting we buy and a wider range of independently gathered accounts to put before our editors. There are places we cannot afford to send a correspondent and subjects for which we need expertise beyond our own staff.
Reuters supplies reporting we could never reproduce on that scale. Another well-funded agency would give us an additional team pursuing the story, perhaps reaching a witness nobody else had interviewed or checking a claim against documents others had missed. Sometimes its reporting would confirm what Reuters had already established. That would be useful, too.
An editor should be able to choose between several credible sources of original reporting. I would like that choice to be wider than it is today.
The readers I have in mind are the moderates of the world, including people with strong convictions who still want to know when the evidence challenges them. They should be able to read a news report without being instructed about which conclusions a reasonable person is expected to draw.
“Balanced” is an easy word to put in a prospectus. Editors considering a subscription would need to see what it meant in the copy.
For me, it would mean clear language, careful attribution, and reporters prepared to question their own assumptions. A military spokesperson’s claim would need checking. So would a claim from an aid organization or a protest movement. The amount of attention each received would depend on the evidence and its importance to the story.
I would also want journalists to be curious about people whose lives and beliefs differ from their own. Religion, national identity, security, and the desire for social stability deserve informed coverage. Reporters should understand why these things matter to people and be able to investigate the institutions that speak in their names.
Israel would be an obvious place to test those standards. A bureau here would need Hebrew- and Arabic-speaking reporters, sources among Israelis and Palestinians, and the time to examine competing accounts. It should be equipped to investigate military claims, civilian harm, and government decisions with the same care. Some of its findings would inevitably make people who supported its creation uncomfortable.
Its customers would also need reliable reporting on a bank failure in Europe, a scientific discovery in Asia, or a natural disaster in Latin America. A global agency would have to earn its place on a foreign editor’s desk through the full range of its work.
I have written before about Israel’s hasbara (public diplomacy) problem and the investment behind Al Jazeera’s international presence. In April, I argued for serious, sustained funding of independent international journalism. A news agency would give that reporting a distribution system that many publishers could use.
The Wall Street Journal, Fox News, Germany’s Welt, The Telegraph, Le Figaro, and The Australian are among the organizations whose executives I would invite into the discussion. I'd also want publishers with other editorial traditions there.
Ask them which coverage they need, where their existing services fall short, and what would persuade them to sign a multiyear contract. A publisher’s willingness to buy the reporting would tell us considerably more than an encouraging conversation over dinner.
The Post would have its own requirements. I would be interested in an agency that brought us strong international reporting and could, in turn, distribute valuable original work from our journalists. Other participating newsrooms would bring their own expertise. Those relationships could help establish the service while it built its own network of correspondents.
The scale would have to be serious from the beginning. Reuters lists 2,600 journalists across 165 countries. AP’s 2025 review lists 220 locations in 90 countries. Those figures give a sense of the staffing and investment required to provide a dependable international service.
AP and Reuters are the distribution models to study. The BBC and Al Jazeera belong in the discussion about the international presence we should aspire to build.
I would want the founders planning toward an annual budget in the hundreds of millions of dollars as the agency expanded, backed by a 10-year financing commitment. An experienced management team would have to establish the actual costs and pace of growth. Correspondents need editors, photographers, translators, and local colleagues. Reporting in dangerous places also requires security, insurance, and legal support.
Subscriber revenue should be central to the business plan. The initial backers would need the patience to finance the years required to build a service publishers trusted enough to buy. They would also have to understand exactly what editorial independence required of them.
The test would come when a reporter investigated a founder’s business or when a major customer objected to a story. Before either happened, the agency would need binding protections for its editors and a clear process for handling complaints. Ownership and funding should be public. Corrections should be visible.
Anyone putting substantial money into this would be entitled to demand sound management, responsible spending, and measurable progress. Editorial decisions would belong to the journalists. That arrangement would need to survive the first genuinely difficult disagreement.
Some of the people who could help finance this may be spending the holidays in Israel. Others lead media companies abroad or have spent years looking for a worthwhile investment in journalism. I would welcome a conversation with them and with the publishers willing to consider becoming customers.
We have the beginnings of an editorial argument. The next useful document would be a business plan.

Governments cannot stay silent on the threat against Israel after flydubai hijacking - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
03:15:24 UTC
12:15:24 KST

A flydubai airliner carrying 174 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv plunged nearly 14,000 feet on Wednesday during a violent incident in its cockpit. Israeli officials said the copilot had stabbed the captain and tried to crash the aircraft. Several passengers have separately described helping crew members restrain him before other flydubai pilots aboard landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.
Everyone survived, and that should not have made the incident easier for the world to overlook. Yet by Thursday, the international response to cockpit violence that placed hundreds of civilians in danger remained remarkably subdued.
The limits of what is known must be kept clear. The claim that the copilot intended to crash the plane remains an Israeli assessment, not a finding by Emirati investigators. Authorities have not officially established the suspect’s identity, motive, or whether he acted alone. None of this had changed by press time.
Flydubai said an altercation occurred on the flight deck and that crew members aboard secured the aircraft and diverted it to Tabuk. The United Arab Emirates’ General Civil Aviation Authority called it a “security incident” that injured crew members and forced an emergency landing. Flight-tracking data recorded the sharp descent and showed the aircraft transmitting 7500, the international code for unlawful interference.
The UAE attorney-general has formed an investigation team to establish what happened and determine whether the incident was connected to terrorism or involved advance planning or direction. Flydubai and Emirati authorities have urged the public not to reach conclusions before that work is complete.
They are right. No responsible government should declare a terrorist conspiracy before the evidence is in. But uncertainty over motive is not a reason to avoid condemning the violence already confirmed.
How will the world respond to the flydubai hijacking attempt?
India responded by honoring Capt. Smit Machchhar, the injured Indian pilot. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Droupadi Murmu praised his courage. Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong thanked those who intervened and wished the injured a full recovery.
US President Donald Trump, who discussed the incident after speaking with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, acknowledged that the full account had not been established. The United Nations said it was following developments and was thankful that a major tragedy had been averted.
Beyond that, the reaction was thin. The UAE opened a formal investigation, but Saudi Arabia had issued no substantive statement about its investigation by Thursday morning, Reuters reported. Oman had not commented on the Israeli report that the suspect was an Omani national. By early Thursday afternoon, no public condemnation had come from the European Union’s leadership or most major Western governments.
What more is required before they speak? Condemning the confirmed violence would not require endorsing every Israeli account. It would not require calling the incident terrorism, assigning a motive, or accusing another country of involvement. It only would require saying that violence in the cockpit of a passenger aircraft is intolerable and demands a thorough, transparent investigation.
The absence of a death toll should be a source of relief, not an excuse for indifference. An act does not become less worthy of condemnation because the people caught up in it prevented its worst possible consequences.
Passenger aircraft are not battlefields. The International Civil Aviation Organization requires states to report unlawful or attempted seizures and other acts of unlawful interference, because a breach aboard one aircraft can expose vulnerabilities affecting travelers everywhere.
Passengers also cannot be treated as extensions of the government at their destination. People do not lose their claim to international concern when they board a flight to Tel Aviv.
Flight FZ1073 connected two countries that established relations under the 2020 Abraham Accords. Flydubai inaugurated scheduled commercial service between Dubai and Tel Aviv that November, making direct aviation one of the agreement’s most visible results. The people placed at risk on Wednesday included an Indian captain and passengers of several nationalities aboard an Emirati aircraft bound for Israel.
The heroes aboard FZ1073 did not have the luxury of waiting for perfect information. They saw a cockpit in chaos and acted. Governments have official confirmation of violence aboard a civilian aircraft and the safety of solid ground. As such, they should be able to manage a sentence.

US to send third aircraft carrier towards Iran: US official to Al Jazeera
Unknown
